title: Which Two Visits Took the Longest?
blurb: Build a reproducible top list, including what happens when two records have the same value.
openingTitle: The First Two Rows Are Not Necessarily the Longest Visits
opening: Botie is asked to show the two longest recorded inspections. The first two rows currently happen to include a long visit, but the table is a record collection, not a ranked queue.

We need a ranking rule before taking a small portion. We also need to decide what a tie means so the shortlist does not change simply because the database chose a different way to read the same records.

history.title: Storage Independence Also Removed an Accidental Order
blocks: Relational systems separate the logical result from the physical access path. System R explored how a high-level relational interface could work over changing storage choices.

The consequence for a shortlist is practical: order must be requested as part of the query. A scan order that looked stable is not a ranking rule. Our example supplies a tie breaker so the selected visits are reproducible.

reading.experimentTitle: Rank before taking the shortlist
reading.experimentIntro: Order by minutes descending and inspection_id ascending, then take two records.
reading.connectionTitle: Follow the same records into the query
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Return a deterministic top-two report
reading.exampleNote: These maintenance records are invented. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet runs actual SQLite queries.

intuition.title: A tie needs another comparison
intuition.explanation: Each row carries the metric and its stable identity.

scene.caption: A limit of two keeps 101 and 104 under this stated rule.

parts.title: 1. Choose what larger means for this report
paragraphs: The metric is recorded inspection minutes, so descending order puts the longest duration first. A text sort would ask a different question, and dates need a representation that sorts according to their intended timeline.
Our schema stores minutes as numeric values. Unknown durations are excluded from this ranked report because the supervisor asked for recorded durations; they belong in a separate missing-data report.
interpretation: The shortlist is only as meaningful as the metric and population it ranks.

parts.title: 2. Resolve ties with a stable identifier
paragraphs: Two visits can have equal durations. Add inspection_id ascending after minutes descending so the smaller ID comes first within a tie. Each sort term has its own direction.

The final key should uniquely distinguish the rows that could reach the limit boundary. Adding a nonunique description as the final term can still leave an unresolved tie. A stable tie breaker produces reproducibility, not a claim that a smaller ID is more important.
interpretation: The tie rule is a report convention. State it so the reader can interpret the shortlist.

parts.title: 3. Apply ORDER BY before LIMIT
paragraphs: LIMIT asks for a maximum number of result rows. Without a specified order, it does not identify the largest values. ORDER BY supplies that order before the result is limited.

The teaching workshop exposes two components because swapping them makes a visible difference. The SQL planner may implement an efficient top-k algorithm internally; the logical result must still match the requested ordering and limit.
interpretation: The physical algorithm is free to differ from our visible sorting demonstration.

examples.title: Look at the ranked durations before truncating
paragraphs: We exclude unknown durations with a nonnegative comparison, then request a complete ordered report.
interpretation: The zero-minute visit remains a recorded value. It is different from the missing duration.

parts.title: 4. Decide whether the request means two rows or all ties
paragraphs: LIMIT 2 returns at most two rows even when another visit has the same duration as the second. A report asking for every visit tied at the boundary needs a different construction. Later ranking lessons distinguish row numbers from ranks.
This lesson deliberately requests exactly two rows when at least two qualify, using the stated ID tie rule. Do not infer a policy about equal priority from the SQL limit alone.
interpretation: The required result shape must be clear before testing the query.

parts.title: 5. Make NULL ordering and dialect choices explicit
paragraphs: Database defaults differ for the placement of NULL in ordering. SQLite normally places NULL before non-null values in ascending order; PostgreSQL’s default is different. Both support explicit null placement in their documented forms, but our query first excludes unknown durations.
LIMIT is available in SQLite and PostgreSQL. Other systems may use FETCH or TOP. Keep the underlying idea of ordered truncation separate from a particular dialect’s syntax.
interpretation: A query that moves between databases deserves a test with ties and missing values.

parts.title: 6. Do not use a page number as a permanent identity
paragraphs: OFFSET can skip a number of ordered result rows, but newly inserted records can shift later pages. A bookmark based on an actual stable sort key is often a better way to continue a changing stream. We will examine query planning and application access later.
For the workshop, first reverse the source row order. The answer should remain unchanged. Then introduce equal longest durations and check the tie breaker.
interpretation: A repeatable query depends on both its ordering rule and the data snapshot being queried.

quiz.because: The second ordering expression resolves equal first expressions.

title: Was the Visit Instant, or Is Its Duration Missing?
blurb: Keep an unknown measurement distinct from zero, and follow SQL’s true, false and unknown conditions.
openingTitle: The Empty Cell Is Hiding a Different Question
opening: One visit has a recorded duration of zero. Another has no recorded duration at all. Botie cannot treat those as the same fact. Zero tells us what was entered; the missing cell tells us that this field supplies no duration.

The distinction affects filters, averages and whether a record needs follow-up. SQL uses NULL for missing values, and a comparison involving NULL often has an unknown result rather than a simple true or false.

history.title: Database Implementations Had to Agree About Missing Values
blocks: An absent value complicates ordinary comparisons: we cannot determine whether an unknown duration equals ten. SQLite’s NULL documentation describes compatibility tests performed in 2002 to compare how other SQL engines handled these cases.
The resulting behaviours include distinctions between equality predicates, grouping and duplicate removal. We study those operations explicitly instead of treating NULL as a special number.

reading.experimentTitle: Find missing records without discarding real zeros
reading.experimentIntro: Use the missing-value test, then keep visit and asset identities for follow-up.
reading.connectionTitle: Follow the same records into the query
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Find visits whose duration was not recorded
reading.exampleNote: These maintenance records are invented. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet runs actual SQLite queries.

intuition.title: A missing measurement is not a measured zero
intuition.explanation: Evaluate the stated test for each duration.

scene.caption: WHERE keeps true conditions; false and unknown are both excluded.

parts.title: 1. Give absence a meaning in the application
paragraphs: NULL can represent a value that is unknown, unavailable or not applicable. Those reasons are not automatically distinguishable from the marker alone. If the maintenance process needs to distinguish not measured from sensor failed, store a separate status.
The duration of zero is still a stored number. It may be valid or it may need quality review, but replacing it with NULL would change the recorded fact.
interpretation: Missingness needs a domain explanation as well as a database representation.

parts.title: 2. An ordinary comparison cannot establish equality with NULL
paragraphs: A comparison such as minutes = NULL asks whether a value equals an unknown value. It does not become true for a missing cell. Use IS NULL to test whether the marker is present, or IS NOT NULL for its absence.

Most ordinary comparisons involving NULL evaluate to unknown. WHERE retains only true results. Thus minutes <> 10 excludes both known tens and unknown durations, even though an unknown duration has not been shown to equal ten.
interpretation: Negating an unknown comparison does not turn it into a known true statement.

parts.title: 3. Follow unknown through AND and OR
paragraphs: If one condition is false, an AND expression cannot become true regardless of the other condition. If one condition is true, an OR expression is true regardless of the other. Other combinations can remain unknown.

You do not need to memorise every row of a truth table before using the idea. Ask whether the known part is already sufficient to determine the combined condition. Use an explicit missingness clause when missing records should be retained.
interpretation: A condition that keeps known failures may need a separate branch to keep unknown measurements.

examples.title: Keep both unrecorded and zero durations for review
paragraphs: This report intentionally combines two different reasons for attention and leaves their values visible.
interpretation: The two rows remain distinguishable. The query has not replaced one with the other.

parts.title: 4. Do not assume every operation treats NULL like equality
paragraphs: DISTINCT can collapse repeated NULL-containing result rows. GROUP BY collects NULL keys into one group. Those behaviours do not mean that NULL = NULL becomes true in a WHERE predicate.

Keep the operation in view when reasoning about a result. The workshop’s IS NULL filter is a missingness test. Later grouping and aggregation lessons will make their own treatment of missing values explicit.
interpretation: A rule learned for one SQL operation is not automatically the rule for every other operation.

parts.title: 5. Replace a missing value only when the replacement means something
paragraphs: COALESCE can provide the first non-null value from a list of alternatives. A user-facing note may reasonably fall back to awaiting entry. Replacing an unknown duration with zero before calculating an average makes a much stronger claim: it treats the unknown visit as a zero-minute visit.
That may distort both a report and a machine-learning feature. Decide whether the calculation needs known-only observations, an explicit imputation policy, or a missingness indicator.
interpretation: A convenient display fallback and a justified numeric imputation are different decisions.

parts.title: 6. Make exclusions visible in a data pipeline
paragraphs: A dataset filtered with temperature > 75 silently loses rows whose temperature is missing. A model trained on the remaining rows may see a different population if missing readings cluster at particular sites or devices.

Count or inspect missing values alongside the main report. Preserve the original measurement and document any transformation so a later analyst can understand which facts were observed and which were supplied by policy.
interpretation: SQL can express the inclusion rule precisely; it cannot decide whether that rule is appropriate for the analysis.

parts.title: 7. Use the changed case to catch a zero shortcut
paragraphs: The changed workshop includes a zero-minute visit and a missing visit with different identifiers. Select only the missing one. A construction that compares against zero, or replaces NULL with zero and then compares, cannot preserve this distinction.
When the missing field is later filled in, the row should leave the follow-up report automatically.
interpretation: The report is a query over the current state, not a memorised list of problem IDs.

quiz.because: The explicit missingness branch includes otherwise unknown comparisons.

title: What Should Botie Label Each Reading?
blurb: Express a row-level decision with CASE while keeping unknown measurements visible and using fallbacks deliberately.
openingTitle: The Reading Needs a Label, Not Another Spreadsheet Formula
opening: The maintenance dashboard shows temperature readings. The team wants inspect at or above 75, monitor below that point, and unknown when no value was recorded. Botie should apply the same policy wherever the report is read.
SQL can derive that label beside each reading. We will write the conditions in an order that preserves the missing case, then check the exact threshold rather than relying on a few obvious examples.

history.title: A Query Result Can Include a Decision
blocks: A reporting program often needs a decision beside each record: does this reading require attention, or can it remain on the ordinary list? Early relational query work moved record selection and derived results out of hand-written navigation loops. Chamberlin and Boyce’s 1974 SEQUEL proposal expressed questions as operations over tables that could be composed into a larger query.

Conditional expressions extend that style to a value chosen by a rule. Today SQL CASE can attach a label to each returned reading while leaving the observed temperature intact. This is a distinction between calculating a result and changing the stored evidence.

reading.experimentTitle: Keep the measurement beside the derived label
reading.experimentIntro: Use a threshold-label component, then choose the reading identity and result label.
reading.connectionTitle: Follow the same records into the query
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Classify each reading under the stated policy
reading.exampleNote: These maintenance records are invented. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet runs actual SQLite queries.

intuition.title: Check the boundary and the missing case
intuition.explanation: Policy: unknown for NULL, inspect at 75 or more, otherwise monitor.

scene.caption: The chosen policy is invented for SQL practice, not a maintenance safety standard.

parts.title: 1. Write the policy before its syntax
paragraphs: A label must mean something specific. Our threshold is an invented teaching rule, not a diagnosis of equipment health. The known temperature and the missing marker lead to different branches.

Keep the temperature in the source table. A label is a derived interpretation that may change when the maintenance policy changes. Storing only the label would discard the measurement needed to recompute it.
interpretation: For a model pipeline, the policy version may matter as much as the label itself.

parts.title: 2. Take the first condition that is true
paragraphs: A searched CASE expression checks WHEN conditions and returns the value after the first matching THEN. ELSE supplies the fallback when no condition is true. Without ELSE, that fallback is NULL.

Order overlapping conditions from the intended specific case to the broader case. If we later added an emergency threshold above the inspection threshold, putting inspect first could consume readings that should have reached the emergency branch.
interpretation: CASE is a decision sequence. The order of overlapping rules is part of its meaning.

parts.title: 3. Keep the unknown branch explicit
paragraphs: A missing temperature does not satisfy temperature >= 75. If ELSE says monitor, an unrecorded reading could therefore appear to be safe to monitor. Put temperature IS NULL in its own branch.
The alias gives the resulting label a useful column name. Each input reading still produces one result row, so this operation preserves the reading grain.
interpretation: A sensible default for known values can be a misleading default for absent evidence.

examples.title: Make a display fallback without changing the finding
examples.code:
SELECT inspection_id, COALESCE(finding, 'awaiting entry') AS finding_label
FROM inspections WHERE inspection_id <= 103 ORDER BY inspection_id;
paragraphs: COALESCE returns the first non-null argument. It gives the display text for an absent finding while leaving the stored field untouched.
interpretation: The fallback describes the missing entry; it does not invent an inspection result.

parts.title: 4. Use compatible result meanings across branches
paragraphs: CASE returns a single expression value. Keep its branches consistent with the meaning and type the next component expects. A column mixing a number of minutes with a text error message makes later analysis awkward and may behave differently across SQL engines.

Prefer a measured-value column and a separate status column when both are needed. COALESCE is useful for a deliberate fallback, while CASE is useful when the decision depends on a condition beyond simple missingness.
interpretation: A status such as unknown should not be substituted into a numeric measurement column.

parts.title: 5. Test equality at the threshold
paragraphs: A reading of 75 must receive inspect under our at-or-above rule. A strict greater-than condition would mislabel exactly that reading while passing tests with 70 and 80.
Add a changed case at the boundary and another missing value. Those examples distinguish the actual rule from an implementation that merely agrees with the initial handful of rows.
interpretation: Boundary cases reveal decisions that ordinary examples may leave ambiguous.

parts.title: 6. Keep labels separate from actions
paragraphs: The SQL result is a report. Producing the word inspect does not itself schedule a technician or authorise work on a customer’s equipment. An application acting on the label needs its own permission, review and execution rules.
For analysis, also check when the reading became available. A label derived from future observations cannot be used as a feature for an earlier prediction without leakage.
interpretation: A computed label is one input to a decision process, with a definition the next stage must understand.

quiz.prompt: What changes?
quiz.because: The expression derives output without updating the table.

given.data: A stored finding is NULL. COALESCE(finding, awaiting entry) is selected.

quiz.prompt: That automatically authorises a real inspection action.
quiz.because: The query produces data; action permissions are a separate responsibility.

given.data: CASE labels a reading inspect.

title: How Much Inspection Time Did We Actually Record?
blurb: Turn visit rows into a summary without confusing the number of visits with the number of known durations.
openingTitle: Six Visits Do Not Give Us Six Known Durations
opening: The supervisor wants a total and an average inspection duration. Botie has six visit records, but one has no minutes entered. Another records zero. Dividing a known total by every row would silently assign a zero contribution to the unknown visit.

Before writing an aggregate, decide what it is summarising. SQL provides separate operations for counting rows, counting nonmissing values and combining those values. We will keep those quantities visible together.

history.title: A Report Needed Fewer Rows Than the Log
blocks: A list of every inspection is useful when checking individual work. A manager asking how much time the work took needs a different kind of answer. Database reporting therefore needed operations that combine many records into a small result. SEQUEL’s 1974 table-oriented design belongs to this move away from a separate navigation program for each question.

An aggregate describes the reduction we want the database to perform. Counting visits and adding their measured durations are different reductions, especially when some durations are absent. SQL’s documented empty-input and NULL rules preserve that distinction. Our maintenance records make it possible to inspect why the number of visits and the number of measurements need not agree.

reading.experimentTitle: Total the time for loose-component findings
reading.experimentIntro: Filter to the requested finding before summing known durations. An entirely unknown selection must remain unknown.
reading.connectionTitle: Follow the same records into the query
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Report both visit coverage and duration totals
reading.outputLabel: Known minutes for the selected finding
reading.exampleNote: These maintenance records are invented. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet runs actual SQLite queries.

intuition.title: Count the records and known values separately
intuition.explanation: These three visits demonstrate why the denominator matters.

scene.caption: COUNT(*) counts all three rows. COUNT(minutes) counts the two known measurements.

parts.title: 1. Decide what the summary row represents
paragraphs: The source gives us one row for each visit. The supervisor now wants one row describing all those visits together. Calculating a total or an average changes what the output row means: it is a summary, rather than another inspection.

SQL calls a calculation over several input rows an aggregate. Without GROUP BY, this query creates one summary over the whole selected input. Later we will keep separate summaries for different assets.

That is why an inspection ID beside a total needs explanation. Which visit would it refer to? Portable aggregate queries select aggregates or explicit grouping keys rather than an unrelated row’s ID. SQLite permits some bare-column forms, but they can conceal an unintended result.
interpretation: The summary’s grain is the selected collection of visits.

parts.title: 2. Count rows and values for different purposes
paragraphs: COUNT(*) counts input rows. COUNT(minutes) counts rows where minutes is not NULL. A recorded zero is a non-null value and is counted. COUNT(DISTINCT asset_id) instead asks how many different non-null asset IDs occur.
Keeping both visit count and measured-duration count exposes coverage. A total derived from a small measured subset can look authoritative if the missing observations are omitted from the report.
interpretation: The name inside COUNT changes the question being answered.

parts.title: 3. Combine known values while preserving the missingness caveat
paragraphs: SUM and AVG operate on known numeric values in our schema. AVG’s denominator is the number of non-null values, not the number of source rows. MIN and MAX return the extremes of the known values.

These functions describe what is present. They do not estimate the missing duration or correct a biased collection process. If the longest visits are the ones technicians forget to enter, a known-only average can still mislead.
interpretation: Report the population and coverage with the result.

examples.title: Check the range and the number of assets visited
paragraphs: This report combines values from the visit log without pretending it contains all assets in the register.
interpretation: The zero-minute record participates in the range. P4 has no visit and does not appear in this count.

parts.title: 4. Understand an empty selection before adding a fallback
paragraphs: An aggregate query without GROUP BY still returns one row when no source rows qualify. COUNT returns zero; SUM and AVG return NULL when no non-null values exist. An all-null selection has the same missing numeric aggregate, although its row count can be positive.

SQLite also has TOTAL, which returns a floating-point zero for no non-null inputs. It is not a portable substitute with the same meaning as SUM. COALESCE(SUM(...),0) is an explicit policy choice: it may be suitable for no expenditure, but it can conceal unrecorded work.
interpretation: Zero work and no known measurement should be distinguished when the report depends on that difference.

parts.title: 5. Filter the population before calculating
paragraphs: WHERE determines which visits reach the aggregate. Summing durations after finding = loose answers a different question from summing all visits and labelling the total loose afterwards.

The workshop makes this ordering visible. The comparison emits a smaller record list, and the sum component consumes that list. Try the all-missing loose visits case to see why a numeric zero is not an acceptable replacement under the stated rule.
interpretation: The filter defines the report population; the aggregate describes that population.

parts.title: 6. Keep units and precision in the result contract
paragraphs: A duration total and an average both use minutes, while counts use records or assets. Name columns so a downstream reader can distinguish them. Rounding is a display decision; preserve sufficient precision for later calculations.
For money or quantities requiring exact decimal arithmetic, consider the database’s numeric types and units carefully. Our integer minutes avoid that issue for sums, while averages can be fractional.
interpretation: A correct formula with the wrong unit still answers the wrong question.

title: How Much Work Belongs to Each Asset?
blurb: Form a separate group for each asset, then calculate summaries without mixing visits from different equipment.
openingTitle: The Grand Total Hides Where the Work Went
opening: The inspection total tells Botie how much recorded work the team did. It does not tell the supervisor which asset consumed that time. We need to place each visit with the other visits for the same asset before calculating.

GROUP BY defines those collections. The result changes from one row per visit to one row per asset that appears in the selected log. That last qualification will matter when we later include assets with no visits.

history.title: One Summary Was Not Enough for a Comparative Report
blocks: A single total can hide where the work happened. Reporting systems also needed totals for each department, customer or asset. Relational query languages made the operation act on collections of rows; grouping then let the query say which rows should contribute to the same result. SEQUEL’s 1974 proposal is an early documented example of composing table operations for such reporting questions.

The useful idea is a temporary collection defined by shared values. Put P1’s visits together and P2’s visits together, then perform the chosen aggregate within each collection. SQL GROUP BY states that membership rule. It does not require the database to store the inspections in separate files or permanently rearrange them by pump.

parts.title: 1. Choose the grouping key from the requested grain
paragraphs: One row per asset means asset_id is the grouping key. Grouping by finding would answer a different question, even though it uses the same source visits. Multiple grouping columns define a combination, such as one row per asset and finding.
Predict how many groups the visible data should create before running the query. If the output contains more rows than expected, inspect which extra fields were included in GROUP BY.
interpretation: The grouping key describes the new result grain.

parts.title: 2. Calculate inside each collection
paragraphs: Place P1’s visits together and P2’s visits together. Now count or add durations separately inside each collection. A visit for P2 must not contribute to P1’s result.

GROUP BY forms those collections using the selected key values. COUNT(*) counts the visit rows in each group; SUM(minutes) combines that group’s known durations. Changing the grouping key changes which visits are allowed to contribute together.

The select list should describe those group keys and their aggregates. Do not add inspection_id merely because it exists on the source rows. There is no single visit ID for an asset with several visits.
interpretation: A grouped row contains facts about a group, not an arbitrary representative visit.

examples.title: Compare the number of known durations by asset

FROM inspections GROUP BY asset_id ORDER BY asset_id;
paragraphs: The two counts reveal incomplete measurement coverage inside each group.
interpretation: P1 has three visits but only two recorded durations. A grand count would hide where the missing value occurs.

parts.title: 3. Keep all grouping fields in view
paragraphs: If the question becomes one subtotal per asset and finding, include both fields in GROUP BY and in the report. Otherwise two result rows can look identical while actually describing different groups.

NULL grouping values form a group rather than disappearing. This grouping rule differs from an equality predicate involving NULL. A missing finding can therefore appear as its own category in a findings summary.
interpretation: The visible labels should be sufficient to identify which group a result describes.

parts.title: 4. Recognise the missing group
paragraphs: GROUP BY over inspections can only produce groups from visits that survived the input filter. It cannot invent a P4 group when P4 has no inspection row. An asset-register report that must retain P4 needs a different source arrangement, which the left-join lesson will build.
An empty input produces no grouped rows. This differs from the single summary row of an aggregate query without GROUP BY.
interpretation: The table chosen in FROM determines which entities are available to group.

parts.title: 5. Request the output order separately
paragraphs: A grouping implementation may sort keys internally or use another strategy. ORDER BY asset_id explicitly requests the report’s display order. Do not depend on a grouping plan to provide a stable presentation.
The workshop’s changed input interleaves visits for two assets. Group membership depends on key equality, not on adjacent rows or a change in the visible sequence.
interpretation: A group can contain records that were far apart in the source list.

title: Which Assets Keep Returning with the Same Finding?
blurb: Filter individual inspections before grouping, then filter the groups according to the evidence they contain.
openingTitle: One Loose Component Is Different from a Repeated Problem
opening: The supervisor wants assets with at least two loose-component findings. Botie can already find loose visits and count visits by asset. Now he needs to combine those ideas without counting clear findings toward the repeated-problem threshold.

There are two different filters. The first chooses the visit records we mean. The second decides which resulting asset groups have enough qualifying visits. SQL gives that second filter its own clause: HAVING.

history.title: Reports Needed Conditions on Subtotals
blocks: Once reports could calculate a subtotal for each group, they raised another question: which of those groups should be shown? An individual job can tell us its finding, but it cannot by itself tell us whether its pump has several qualifying visits. The compositional approach in the 1974 SEQUEL work allowed one table operation’s result to become the information used by a later operation.

SQL makes the two selection stages explicit. WHERE selects the input rows; HAVING selects groups after their aggregates are available. For recurring maintenance, we first decide which visits qualify, then ask whether each pump’s resulting count meets the report rule. Keeping those stages separate lets the query express the intended population before applying the group threshold.

items: Count qualifying visits in each collection

parts.title: 1. Name the unit at each filter
paragraphs: The first filter asks a question of a visit: was its finding loose? The later filter asks a question of an asset’s group: how many such visits did it have?

Mixing these units creates plausible errors. Counting every visit and then selecting assets with a loose finding can overstate recurrence. The initial report might even match by accident if every visit happens to have the same finding.
interpretation: Write the row population and the group rule as separate sentences.

parts.title: 2. Build the intermediate report before filtering it
paragraphs: Start by showing every asset’s count of loose findings. Inspect that result and only then apply the threshold. This makes it easier to diagnose whether a missing asset was removed by the finding rule or the recurrence rule.
The workshop exposes that intermediate list so you can see counts before the final filter. A numerical result needs its group label beside it.
interpretation: The group filter should receive counts of the intended population.

examples.title: Inspect the counts before the recurrence threshold
paragraphs: This intermediate query keeps every group with at least one loose visit.
interpretation: Only P1 meets the later threshold of two. P2 remains useful evidence while we are checking the counting step.

parts.title: 3. Use HAVING for the aggregate condition
paragraphs: HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 retains groups containing enough input rows. The input has already been restricted by WHERE finding = loose, so those rows are all qualifying findings.

The written SELECT clause appears before FROM, but that writing order is not the logical processing explanation. Think of FROM and WHERE establishing rows, grouping establishing collections, and HAVING choosing among those collections. The optimizer can implement an equivalent plan differently.
interpretation: A group-level count is unavailable as an ordinary row-level WHERE value.

parts.title: 4. Keep the aggregate expression readable across dialects
paragraphs: Some databases permit a result alias in HAVING while others apply different name-resolution rules. Repeating COUNT(*) here is short and portable. Later subquery and CTE lessons offer another way to name intermediate results explicitly.
Do not add a non-grouped finding field to HAVING and hope it represents the whole group. Select the relevant visits with WHERE before aggregating, or express a deliberate conditional aggregate.
interpretation: A bare field from an arbitrary group member does not describe all group members.

parts.title: 5. Distinguish repeated events from duplicate imports
paragraphs: Two inspection rows count as two visits under this schema because they have separate visit identities. If the import accidentally duplicated the same real event under two IDs, SQL cannot discover that business error from COUNT alone.

Use source-event keys and integrity checks in the data pipeline. DISTINCT can answer a deliberately different question, but adding it without understanding the grain may hide a broken import rather than repair it.
interpretation: A correct query still depends on records having the meanings the schema claims.

parts.title: 6. Test an asset with plenty of the wrong evidence
paragraphs: The changed workshop gives one asset several clear visits and only one loose visit. It must remain excluded. Another asset has two loose visits and should appear.
This example trips a construction that groups and counts all visits before checking the finding. Retest the original case after fixing the order so the rule generalises beyond the changed shift.
interpretation: The count’s population is as important as its threshold.

title: Which Site Does Each Inspection Belong To?
topic: Connecting Tables Without Changing the Question
blurb: Connect inspection facts to the asset register by a declared key, then inspect the row pairs the join actually produces.
openingTitle: The Visit Log Has an Asset ID, but the Report Needs a Site
opening: The inspection log records P1 and the minutes spent on it. The asset register records that P1 belongs to the north site. Botie needs both facts in one report, but copying the site into every old inspection would give us another set of values to maintain.
A join can match the shared identifier and put the relevant fields side by side. We will begin with matching pairs, then ask what changes when one side contains more than one possible match.

history.title: Separate Facts Could Be Recombined by Their Values
blocks: The relational model allowed related facts to live in separate relations and be combined through matching values. This reduced the need for applications to navigate a particular chain of stored records.

Our asset-to-visit match uses the asset ID on both sides. This is a teaching example of an equijoin, where the relationship is equality of the chosen keys, rather than a claim that every join uses equality.

reading.experimentTitle: Attach the active asset’s site to each visit
reading.experimentIntro: Filter the register to active assets, match inspection asset IDs to that register, and project the visit report.
reading.connectionTitle: Follow the same records into the query
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Locate visits for active equipment
reading.exampleNote: These maintenance records are invented. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet runs actual SQLite queries.

intuition.title: Write the matching pair out before selecting columns
intuition.explanation: The left record is an inspection; the right record is an asset.

scene.caption: Several visit rows can match the same unique asset row.

parts.title: 1. Identify the shared fact, not the row position
paragraphs: Inspection row 101 refers to P1. The register row for P1 could appear anywhere in its result. Matching by list position would fail as soon as either list were sorted or filtered.

The join condition names the relationship: the inspection’s asset_id equals the register’s asset_id. That condition should follow a documented key relationship, not whichever columns happen to share some values in the initial fixture.
interpretation: A join connects identities or stated relationships, not visually aligned rows.

parts.title: 2. Understand one row per matching pair
paragraphs: An inner join emits matching pairs. An inspection whose asset matches one register row contributes one output row. If an asset has several inspections, its register fields appear beside each inspection.
Repeating the site in the result is expected because the result grain is still one inspection under this many-to-one match. The database has not created additional stored asset rows.
interpretation: A join result can repeat fields without indicating duplicate source records.

parts.title: 3. Use aliases to keep column origins clear
paragraphs: Aliases such as i for inspections and a for assets shorten qualified names. ON i.asset_id = a.asset_id shows which side provides each key. Qualifying repeated column names also avoids ambiguity.
SELECT chooses which fields of the matched pairs to report. Listing them explicitly helps preserve the intended result interface as either source table evolves.
interpretation: Read each alias as a table label, not as another stored object.

examples.title: Attach a site to every inspection
examples.code:
SELECT i.inspection_id, a.site, i.minutes
FROM inspections AS i
JOIN assets AS a ON a.asset_id = i.asset_id
ORDER BY i.inspection_id;
paragraphs: The register’s primary key gives each inspection at most one asset match.
interpretation: The number of visits is preserved because every foreign key finds exactly one register row in this fixture.

parts.title: 4. Filter the relevant relation deliberately
paragraphs: The challenge requests visits for active equipment. Filter on the register’s active field while retaining visits from its matching assets. The inactive P3 record exists, but it does not belong to this requested population.

For an inner join, moving an ordinary row condition between ON and WHERE can be equivalent. That reasoning does not transfer unchanged to outer joins, where unmatched rows are retained. We will make that difference visible next.
interpretation: A missing row in the final report may have failed a filter rather than failed the key match.

parts.title: 5. Inspect the keys before assuming a many-to-one match
paragraphs: The asset table’s unique key establishes at most one register match per inspection. Joining on kind would not: several pumps share that description. A visit could then pair with multiple unrelated pump rows.
Likewise, a join on only one part of a compound key can mix different sites or tenants. Include all columns needed to establish the intended identity.
interpretation: A join condition is a claim about relationships. Constraints provide evidence for that claim.

parts.title: 6. Know what an inner join omits
paragraphs: A row without a matching partner is absent from an inner result. Our enforced foreign key prevents an orphan inspection in the ordinary fixture, but a filtered register can still remove its potential partner. Other data sources may have incomplete mappings.
If the report needs to show unmatched records, an inner join is the wrong operation for that requirement. Use an explicit unmatched-preserving construction and inspect its missing fields.
interpretation: A complete-looking matched report can hide records that never found a partner.

parts.title: 7. Relate the join back to an ML dataset
paragraphs: Attaching site metadata to sensor or inspection rows is a common feature-building step. Verify that the match preserves the intended observation count and that the metadata reflects the time the prediction would be made.

A current site assignment can be inappropriate for an old observation if the asset moved. Historical joins and availability boundaries require additional records and conditions, which later lessons will address.
interpretation: Getting a key match is necessary, but it does not establish that the attached value was available at prediction time.

title: Which Assets Have No Matching Inspection?
topic: Connecting Tables Without Changing the Question
blurb: Keep the whole asset register while attaching whatever qualifying inspection evidence exists.
openingTitle: P4 Disappeared from the Report
opening: Botie joins the asset register to the inspection log, and P4 disappears. That is awkward: the supervisor specifically needs to notice equipment with no recorded visits. A report containing only matches hides the absence they were looking for.

A left join begins from the rows we must retain. When a register entry finds no qualifying visit, SQL keeps the asset and supplies missing values for the visit fields. We will make that placeholder visible before counting anything.

history.title: A Match-Only Query Could Hide Missing Evidence
blocks: Codd’s 1970 relational model made it possible to keep related facts in separate relations and combine them by their values. A matching operation answers which records have a partner. A report often needs to show the missing partnerships too: an asset that has never been inspected must not disappear merely because there is nothing to match.

Outer joins address that reporting need by preserving selected unmatched rows and supplying missing values for the absent side. The left side of a LEFT JOIN says which population remains in the report. Starting from the asset register therefore keeps an uninspected pump visible.

intuition.title: An unmatched asset still contributes a result row
intuition.explanation: The right-side fields are placeholders for absent evidence.

scene.caption: COUNT(*) counts the placeholder row; COUNT(inspection_id) does not.

parts.title: 1. Put the population to preserve on the left
paragraphs: The report must contain every asset, so assets belongs on the left of LEFT JOIN. Reversing the tables preserves visits instead and answers a different question.

A matched asset can still produce several rows when it has several visits. The unmatched asset produces one row with missing right-side fields. Preserving all left records does not mean producing exactly one result row per left record.
interpretation: Retention and multiplicity are separate properties of a join.

parts.title: 2. Inspect the unmatched row before aggregating
paragraphs: Look at the raw left-join output. P4 is present, but its inspection_id is NULL because there was no matched visit. That NULL came from the join operation, not from a stored inspection with a missing primary key.

A non-null key on the right table is useful evidence: if that key is NULL in the outer result, the row has no right partner. Testing a nullable measurement instead would confuse an actual visit with an unknown duration and an absent visit.
interpretation: Use a right-side identity field to distinguish absent records from missing measurements.

examples.title: Keep every asset while exposing visit matches
paragraphs: This raw result lets us see why a later row count needs care.
interpretation: P4 has one placeholder result row and no actual inspection.

parts.title: 3. Place a qualifying-match condition in ON
paragraphs: The new report counts loose-component visits while retaining all assets. Add finding = loose to the join condition, or filter the visit relation before joining. Then an asset with only clear visits has no qualifying partner but remains on the left.

Putting i.finding = loose in WHERE after the left join removes unmatched rows, because their right-side finding is NULL and the comparison is unknown. That would hide precisely the zero-match assets the report needs.
interpretation: ON defines what counts as a match; WHERE filters the result rows after unmatched placeholders have been formed.

parts.title: 4. Count matched keys rather than placeholder rows
paragraphs: After grouping by the asset identity, COUNT(i.inspection_id) counts actual matched visits. COUNT(*) counts every joined result row, including the one retained for an unmatched asset.

COUNT(i.minutes) asks yet another question: how many matched visits have a known duration? An existing visit with NULL minutes should still count as a visit. Choose the expression according to what the report is counting.
interpretation: A non-null record identity is a better count target than a measurement that may be absent.

parts.title: 5. Interpret zero without inventing a measurement
paragraphs: A zero count of matched visits is meaningful evidence about this query’s matching condition. It can mean no visits at all, or visits exist but none have the requested finding. It does not establish that the asset is healthy or that nobody performed unrecorded work.
If we also sum minutes, a NULL sum can arise from no matches or all matched durations being unknown. Keep an actual-visit count and a known-duration count when that distinction matters.
interpretation: The data can establish an absence of recorded evidence under a stated query, not every real-world absence.

parts.title: 6. Use the retained key when labelling the group
paragraphs: Group and display the asset_id from the left register. Grouping by the right inspection asset_id would collect all unmatched assets under a single NULL key. Their identities would disappear even though the join retained them.
This is another reason to qualify column names with aliases: the same spelling can carry different nullability and meaning after an outer join.
interpretation: Keep the identity of the population you promised to preserve.

parts.title: 7. Check an asset with only nonqualifying visits
paragraphs: A good changed case gives one asset several clear visits and another no visits. Both should receive zero loose findings, while remaining separate asset rows.
That case detects a right-side condition placed after the join and a COUNT(*) shortcut. Retest an asset with actual loose visits to ensure the repair has not reduced every count to zero.
interpretation: The output must retain the whole register and count only real qualifying partners.

given.data: A real inspection has a non-null ID but minutes NULL.

practice.title: Count loose findings while keeping every asset
practice.question: Count loose findings while keeping every asset
task: An asset with no loose finding still belongs in the register report. Keep it visible with a zero count.
Return every assets.asset_id and its number of matching inspections with finding loose. Keep zero counts for assets with no qualifying visits. Order by the asset ID.

Restrict loose findings in the join condition. Count the matched inspection key, which is absent on the placeholder row for an unmatched asset.

title: Why Did Joining Readings Double the Inspection Total?
topic: Connecting Tables Without Changing the Question
blurb: Trace a many-to-many multiplication, then summarise each event stream at the intended grain before combining it.
openingTitle: No New Work Happened, but the Total Increased
opening: Botie adds temperature readings to an inspection report so the team can compare work and sensor coverage. The inspection total increases, even though nobody added an inspection. The query runs without an error.

For one asset, several visits can match several readings. The joined rows now describe visit-reading pairs. Adding a visit duration over those pairs counts the same visit repeatedly. We need to decide the final report’s grain before combining the event streams.

history.title: Correct Matching Can Still Change What a Row Means
blocks: The relational model and early query languages made composition possible: the result of one operation could be used by the next. That removed much application-specific record navigation, but it did not remove the need to know what one result row means. SQL joins produce matching combinations, so one parent can appear repeatedly when several children match.

That repetition becomes a problem when a report adds a parent-level quantity after the join. The query may be doing exactly the requested combinations while answering the wrong accounting question. In our repair, each branch first produces one summary per asset. Joining those summaries preserves the intended asset-level meaning before the final total is calculated.

reading.experimentTitle: Make one row per asset on each branch
reading.experimentIntro: Count visits and readings in separate groups, then join the two summaries onto the asset register.

rows.label: Join summaries
items: At most one partner per asset on each branch

scene.caption: Two unique asset-level summaries can be attached without multiplying their counts.

parts.title: 1. Name the grain after every join
paragraphs: Before the join, one inspection row means one visit and one reading row means one observation. After matching both streams only on asset_id, one result row means one visit-reading pair for that asset.

Both keys can be correct and every individual pair can satisfy the join condition. The error appears when we treat that result as though each visit still appears only once. Row counts before and after the join are useful diagnostic evidence.
interpretation: A successful key comparison does not preserve the original grain automatically.

parts.title: 2. Count the combinations for a small asset
paragraphs: Write the pairs by hand for a tiny example. A visit is repeated once for every matching reading, and a reading is repeated once for every matching visit. That gives a concrete explanation for an inflated sum or count.

An asset with only one reading can hide the problem during initial testing. Add a second reading for an asset with multiple visits and watch which metrics change despite no change to the inspection log.
interpretation: The fixture should contain a many-to-many combination, not only one-to-one examples.

parts.title: 3. Do not repair a wrong grain by deleting equal amounts
paragraphs: SUM(DISTINCT minutes) deduplicates numeric values, not visits. If two legitimate visits both lasted ten minutes, their equal amounts collapse into one value even though both visits should count.

COUNT(DISTINCT inspection_id) can correctly count distinct visits in some joined results, but it does not automatically repair other aggregates or justify the whole join. Decide the report’s required grain and build each measure from its own event identity.
interpretation: A repeated amount is not evidence of a duplicated event.

parts.title: 4. Summarise the event streams independently
paragraphs: First group inspections by asset_id and count their rows. Separately group readings by asset_id and count their rows. Each derived table now has at most one row per asset. Join these summaries to the register.

A subquery in FROM creates a named intermediate result for this purpose. Its alias lets the outer query refer to the count. Later lessons study subqueries and common table expressions more broadly; here the nested query has one specific job: establish the correct grain before the match.
interpretation: The outer join combines asset-level facts instead of raw event pairs.

examples.title: Inspect one stream’s asset-level summary
examples.code:
SELECT asset_id, COUNT(*) AS visits
FROM inspections GROUP BY asset_id ORDER BY asset_id;
paragraphs: This is the visit branch that the later combined report will reuse.
interpretation: Each key occurs once in this derived result, so a register row cannot match several visit-summary rows.

parts.title: 5. Preserve assets missing from either stream
paragraphs: Use left joins from the asset register when every asset must appear. An absent summary produces NULL in its count column. In this particular report, COALESCE of that count to zero is justified: there were no source event rows for the asset.
Do not extend that reasoning to an average or sum over unknown measurements without checking its meaning. A missing event-count summary and a summary of unknown durations are different cases.
interpretation: A zero count can be a deliberate result without pretending an unknown measurement was zero.

parts.title: 6. Distinguish record counts from measurement counts
paragraphs: The reading count here includes rows with temperature NULL because the question is how many reading records arrived. COUNT(temperature) would count only records carrying a known temperature. Both can be useful, but they answer different questions.
The query contract names visit records and reading records so the denominator is explicit. A later coverage report could include both reading records and known temperatures.
interpretation: Keep the metric’s event or value population in its name and explanation.

parts.title: 7. Check the repair with changes to only one stream
paragraphs: Add a reading without adding a visit. The reading count should change; the visit count should not. Then add a visit with no corresponding new reading. The visit count should change independently.

These are stronger tests than checking one initial table, because they express an invariant of the report. The workshop uses exactly this kind of changed shift to expose raw-event joins that multiply unrelated measures.
interpretation: Independent source facts should remain independent in the asset-level report.

parts.title: 8. Apply the same check before training a model
paragraphs: A many-to-many join can duplicate training examples, change their effective weights and leak information across splits. An apparently better model may simply have seen repeated or future-related observations.

Check unique observation keys and row counts after feature joins. If time matters, define which event can attach to which observation using a time-aware relationship. Matching by asset alone is rarely enough for a prediction-time feature table.
interpretation: The database returns the pairs you requested. The analyst must ensure those pairs match the learning problem.

quiz.prompt: Which count should change?
quiz.because: Each summary comes from its own event stream.

given.data: A report counts visits and readings separately per asset before joining their summaries. One reading is added, with no new visit.

quiz.prompt: COUNT(*) on that asset’s reading group should include it.

given.data: A reading record exists but temperature is NULL. The requested metric is reading-record count.

practice.title: Combine the two event counts without multiplying them
practice.question: Combine the two event counts without multiplying them
task: Visits and readings are separate histories. Count each independently so joining them cannot multiply one event by another.

Return every asset_id, visit-record count and reading-record count, in that order. Include zero for an asset absent from either stream. Count reading rows even when temperature is NULL. Order by asset_id. Summarise each stream independently or use another query that preserves these meanings.
practice.starter:
-- Write your query here.
SELECT * FROM assets;
practice.solution:
SELECT a.asset_id, COALESCE(v.visits, 0) AS visits, COALESCE(r.readings, 0) AS readings
FROM assets AS a
LEFT JOIN (SELECT asset_id, COUNT(*) AS visits FROM inspections GROUP BY asset_id) AS v ON v.asset_id = a.asset_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT asset_id, COUNT(*) AS readings FROM readings GROUP BY asset_id) AS r ON r.asset_id = a.asset_id
ORDER BY a.asset_id;
hints: A pump with several visits and several readings can create all visit-reading combinations in a direct join. Work out each event count before combining the reports.
Group visits and readings separately by asset_id, then join those one-row-per-asset summaries to assets. Convert absent counts to zero.

title: Which Inspections Took Longer Than the Usual Visit?
openingTitle: The Comparison Value Is Still in the Records
opening: Botie needs the inspections that took longer than the average recorded visit. We could calculate the average, copy it into another query, and remember to repeat both steps when a new visit arrives. That gives us a value that can become stale as soon as the records change.
Instead, let the comparison obtain its value from another query. We will first inspect that small result on its own, then connect it to the inspection rows.
blurb: Use one query’s result inside another without losing track of whether that result is one value, several rows, or a value belonging to the current asset.

history.title: A Query Could Supply Another Query’s Input
blocks: Some questions depend on another answer: show inspections longer than the average, or find assets belonging to sites that meet a separate rule. A program could fetch an intermediate result, store it elsewhere and issue another query. The 1974 SEQUEL work instead treated queries as composable operations, allowing more complex questions to be expressed from simpler ones.

A subquery keeps that dependency inside the SQL statement. An independent subquery supplies a result calculated without an outer row; a correlated subquery uses a value from the row currently being considered. Our inspection-average comparison is a small example. Before using its answer, we still need to know whether the inner query returns one value, several rows or no usable value.

reading.experimentTitle: Connect the recorded mean to the comparison
reading.experimentIntro: Calculate a mean from all known durations and feed it into the row comparison.
reading.connectionTitle: A scalar result becomes a comparison input

reading.exampleNote: The records are invented maintenance examples. The workshop exposes record operations; the SQL worksheet executes a real query in an isolated SQLite database.

intuition.title: Inspect the inner result first
intuition.explanation: The known durations are 20, 40 and 60 minutes. The missing duration remains unknown.

scene.caption: The aggregate produces one row. It does not turn the missing duration into zero.

intuition.title: Use the same value for each outer row
intuition.explanation: The predicate is strictly greater than that recorded mean.

scene.caption: The comparison preserves the individual inspection identity.

parts.title: 1. Run the quantity we need on its own
paragraphs: Begin with AVG(minutes) over the inspection table. AVG ignores NULL values, so this is the average of recorded durations. If every duration is missing, that result is NULL.
The inner query still has a shape: one column and one row when an aggregate without GROUP BY produces this result. Knowing that shape matters before placing it where a single value belongs.
interpretation: A scalar means one value. It does not mean that the database forgot where the value came from.

examples.title: Inspect the average before using it
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE inspections(inspection_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, asset_id TEXT NOT NULL, minutes INTEGER);
INSERT INTO inspections VALUES (1,'P7',20),(2,'P7',40),(3,'P8',60),(4,'P9',NULL);
examples.code: SELECT AVG(minutes) AS mean_minutes FROM inspections;
paragraphs: The setup contains four inspections, one with an unknown duration.
interpretation: The result has one value. The later filter will use that value rather than a typed-in threshold.

parts.title: 2. Put the result beside each inspection
paragraphs: A scalar subquery can appear on the right of the greater-than comparison. The outer query keeps each inspection whose own minutes exceed the supplied mean.

The independent inner query does not refer to the current outer row, so its meaning is the same for every inspection. This is a useful way to read the expression; the optimiser decides the physical execution plan.
interpretation: Describe the dependency rather than claiming that the engine must literally execute the inner query once for every row.

parts.title: 3. Write the nested comparison
paragraphs: Parentheses identify the inner SELECT. Qualify the outer columns with an alias when another occurrence of the same table appears nearby. The final ORDER BY gives the report a reproducible inspection order.
The strict greater-than comparison excludes a visit exactly at the mean. A NULL duration also does not pass it, because that comparison is unknown.
interpretation: Choose the comparison boundary from the question. Greater than and greater than or equal to select different visits.

examples.title: Keep the visits above the recorded mean
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE inspections(inspection_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, asset_id TEXT NOT NULL, minutes INTEGER);
INSERT INTO inspections VALUES (1,'P7',20),(2,'P7',40),(3,'P8',60),(4,'P9',NULL);
examples.code:
SELECT i.inspection_id, i.minutes
FROM inspections AS i
WHERE i.minutes > (SELECT AVG(minutes) FROM inspections)
ORDER BY i.inspection_id;
paragraphs: The average is computed by the query, so another inserted visit changes both the benchmark and the candidates.
interpretation: Inspection 3 exceeds the mean on these records. That is a descriptive comparison, not a diagnosis of why its visit took longer.

parts.title: 4. Correlate the benchmark with the current asset
paragraphs: Suppose pumps have different routine workloads. Comparing each visit with its own asset’s recorded mean asks a different question. The inner WHERE can connect its asset_id to the outer alias.

The same alias must not accidentally refer only to the inner table. Writing inner_visit.asset_id = i.asset_id makes the dependency explicit. Read it as “for this outer inspection, average the visits with this asset ID.”
interpretation: A correlated subquery depends on an outer value. It does not itself guarantee an efficient implementation.

examples.title: Compare each visit with its asset’s own mean
examples.setup:
CREATE TABLE inspections(inspection_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, asset_id TEXT NOT NULL, minutes INTEGER);
INSERT INTO inspections VALUES (1,'P7',20),(2,'P7',40),(3,'P8',60),(4,'P9',NULL);
examples.code:
SELECT i.inspection_id, i.asset_id
FROM inspections AS i
WHERE i.minutes > (
  SELECT AVG(v.minutes) FROM inspections AS v
  WHERE v.asset_id = i.asset_id
)
ORDER BY i.inspection_id;
paragraphs: P7 has two known durations; P8 has only one. A single known visit equals its own asset mean.
interpretation: The selected visit changes because the reference population changed. The query is not interchangeable with the global-average version.

parts.title: 5. Make one-row assumptions explicit
paragraphs: A plain SELECT of minutes can return several rows. SQLite uses the first returned row when such a query is used as a scalar; other engines can reject a multiple-row scalar result. Neither behaviour establishes that the chosen row is the one the task requires.

Use an aggregate when the task asks for an aggregate. Use a unique key for a unique lookup. If the task asks for the latest row, specify its ordering and tie rule before LIMIT 1. A limit added only to suppress a cardinality problem hides the question rather than answering it.
interpretation: The workshop’s one-row reader deliberately rejects multiple rows. It teaches the shape requirement without relying on SQLite’s permissive first-row behaviour.

parts.title: 6. Decide whether the task actually needs a value
paragraphs: Sometimes the question is simply whether an inspection exists. Returning a duration is then unnecessary, and missing durations make the result harder to interpret. The next lesson will use EXISTS for that question.
For an average comparison, keep a test where all values are NULL and another where every known duration is equal. Both should produce no unusually long visits under the strict rule.
interpretation: An empty report can be correct. Check its cause before replacing NULL or loosening the threshold.

title: Which Pumps Still Have No Completed Visit?
openingTitle: A Missing Match Is a Useful Answer
opening: The maintenance desk has an asset list and a visit log. Botie needs the pumps that still lack a completed visit. Joining the tables gives us matching visits, but our question concerns the pumps left without one.
We will ask whether a matching completed row exists for each asset. An incomplete log row with no asset ID should not make every unvisited pump disappear.
blurb: Ask whether a related row exists, keep the outer row’s identity, and avoid treating an unknown key as evidence that every candidate is present.

history.title: Finding Absence Without Manufacturing More Rows

sources.title: PostgreSQL EXISTS and NOT IN semantics

blocks: Relational querying drew on logic as well as table operations. Codd’s 1970 work and the later SEQUEL proposal helped separate a question about stored facts from a program that walks record pointers. One such question is existential: is there any related record satisfying this condition?

SQL EXISTS turns that question into a test on whether the inner query produces a row. It does not ask the outer report to repeat a pump once for each matching inspection. That is useful when a pump can have many visits but the report wants one answer about the pump: some completed inspection exists, or none does. NOT EXISTS expresses the latter case without treating a missing relationship as an ordinary value.

parts.title: 1. Decide what counts as a qualifying match
paragraphs: A visit qualifies only when its asset_id matches the current asset and its status is closed. Put both conditions inside the existence test. An open visit does not satisfy the request simply because it names the same pump.
The output should contain one row per asset. The number of visits associated with a pump must not change that grain.
interpretation: Begin with the relationship and the qualifying condition before choosing the SQL form.

parts.title: 2. Observe EXISTS on a small result
paragraphs: EXISTS returns true when its subquery produces any row. The selected value is usually unimportant, so SELECT 1 communicates that we only need a match. A row containing NULL still exists.
An optimiser may stop once it can determine the result. Do not write functions with side effects inside a subquery and rely on a particular number of evaluations.
interpretation: The question is about row presence, not whether a selected cell is non-NULL.

examples.title: A NULL cell still occupies a row
examples.code: SELECT EXISTS(SELECT NULL), EXISTS(SELECT 1 WHERE 0);
paragraphs: This expression has no maintenance fixture because the row-presence distinction can be demonstrated directly.
interpretation: The first subquery has one row and the second has none. SQLite represents these truth values as 1 and 0.

parts.title: 3. Connect the inner match to the outer asset
paragraphs: The outer alias a identifies the pump currently under consideration. The inner alias v names candidate visit rows. The predicate v.asset_id = a.asset_id ties the two together.
NOT EXISTS keeps an asset when the qualified inner result is empty. Ordering the final asset IDs makes the report stable.
interpretation: A condition using only inner-table columns could accidentally ask the same global question for every asset.

examples.title: Find assets with no closed visit
examples.code:
SELECT a.asset_id
FROM assets AS a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM visits AS v
  WHERE v.asset_id = a.asset_id AND v.status = 'closed'
)
ORDER BY a.asset_id;
paragraphs: The unattributed closed row has a NULL asset_id and cannot satisfy equality with P8 or P9.
interpretation: Both pumps lack a qualifying match. The duplicate P7 visits do not duplicate any outer row.

parts.title: 4. Work through the NOT IN trap
paragraphs: A NOT IN subquery containing NULL can make an otherwise unmatched comparison unknown. The database cannot establish that the named pump differs from an unknown value. WHERE retains true rows, so those unknown results disappear.

Filtering NULL values out of a suitable NOT IN subquery can resolve that particular issue. NOT EXISTS expresses this lesson’s correlated no-match question directly and makes the matching rule easy to inspect.
interpretation: The two forms are not automatically interchangeable when nullable keys are involved.

examples.title: See why the tempting alternative loses rows
paragraphs: The closed-visit list contains P7 and NULL.
interpretation: The empty result is caused by unknown membership comparisons. It does not mean that P8 and P9 were inspected.

parts.title: 5. Keep the anti-join’s conditions in the right place
paragraphs: A left join followed by a missing-right-key check can also express an anti-join. Its match conditions must include the qualifying status, and the field tested for missingness should be guaranteed non-NULL on a real match.
For this schema, visit_id is a primary key. Testing a nullable notes field instead would confuse “a matching visit with no notes” with “no matching visit.” EXISTS avoids needing that sentinel column.
interpretation: Pick the form whose grain and missing-row interpretation you can explain. Check the execution plan when performance becomes material.

parts.title: 6. Test presence, absence and duplicate matches
paragraphs: Add another completed visit for P7: the awaiting list should stay the same. Complete P8’s visit: only P9 remains. Remove every visit: every asset should appear.
These changes test the meaning of the query more directly than requiring a particular spelling. The workshop uses the same existence operation over records, with a separate filter for closed visits.
interpretation: A correct no-match query should still work when there are no matching records at all.

quiz.prompt: Why can P8 NOT IN that result fail to pass WHERE?
options: The comparison with the unknown ID leaves NOT IN unknown
NULL is another spelling of P8
quiz.because: Unknown is not true, so WHERE does not retain it.

given.data: Closed-visit asset IDs are P7 and NULL. P8 is absent from the known IDs.

quiz.prompt: That check always identifies only assets with no visit.
quiz.because: A real matching visit can itself have NULL notes. Use a reliable non-NULL match key or NOT EXISTS.

given.data: An anti-join checks a nullable notes column to distinguish unmatched rows from real visits.

title: Which Pumps Appear on Either List but Are Still Unfinished?
openingTitle: Two Teams Have Reported the Same Pump
opening: Sensor alerts flag P7 and P8. Technician requests flag P8 and P9. Botie needs one candidate list, then needs to remove pumps whose inspection is already complete.
This combines whole result rows. It does not match columns from two records into a wider row as a join does. We will decide when duplicate reports are meaningful before removing them.
blurb: Combine, compare and subtract query results while keeping duplicate policy, column meaning and final ordering explicit.

history.title: Combining Results Needed a Duplicate Policy
blocks: Codd’s relational model used mathematical relations, bringing operations such as union and difference into the description of stored data. Combining query results follows that same family of questions: which assignments appear in either list, which occur in both, and which remain after another list is removed?

SQL also permits repeated result rows, so its combinations must say what to do with repetitions. UNION removes equal result rows, while UNION ALL retains them. The maintenance desk may need both meanings. Two alert events can be worth retaining even when they concern the same pump; a list of pumps assigned to a team may need each pump only once.

parts.title: 1. Align the meanings of the result columns
paragraphs: Each side of a compound SELECT must return the same number of columns. Corresponding positions need compatible meanings and types. Selecting asset_id on one side and site_name on the other may run while producing a meaningless mixed column.
Choose the projected columns first. If you also select source, two rows for the same asset can remain different because their source labels differ.
interpretation: Duplicate elimination compares the complete selected row.

parts.title: 2. Use UNION ALL when repeated events matter
paragraphs: UNION ALL appends every row from the second result to the first. It preserves repeated alerts rather than silently changing their count.

The resulting table still has no guaranteed presentation order without an outer ORDER BY. Input order or the order in which the SELECT clauses were written is not a replacement for a sorting requirement.
interpretation: Preserve event IDs or source information when individual events matter.

examples.title: Retain all five reports
examples.code:
SELECT asset_id FROM alerts
UNION ALL
SELECT asset_id FROM requests
ORDER BY asset_id;
paragraphs: The asset column alone does not identify separate report events, but the repeated rows remain visible.
interpretation: P7 and P8 repeat. UNION ALL has not mistaken those rows for one pump assignment.

parts.title: 3. Use UNION when the result is a set of assignments
paragraphs: UNION removes duplicate complete output rows. With only asset_id projected, it returns one row per reported pump.
If each input is already unique, a pump can still occur in both inputs. Deduplicating each side separately is therefore insufficient for a distinct combined list.
interpretation: The correct place to remove repetition depends on the result you are constructing.

examples.title: Make one assignment candidate per asset
examples.code:
SELECT asset_id FROM alerts
UNION
SELECT asset_id FROM requests
ORDER BY asset_id;
paragraphs: Both source lists contribute candidates, but each ID appears once.
interpretation: The query changes the grain from reports to distinct asset IDs.

parts.title: 4. Ask what both teams found
paragraphs: INTERSECT keeps distinct rows present in both results. In this example it finds the assets supported by both an alert and a technician request.
The operation does not pair every alert with every request. It compares the selected result rows, so duplicate reports do not multiply the intersection.
interpretation: Use a join instead when you need columns from the individual matching reports.

examples.title: Find agreement between the two lists
examples.code:
SELECT asset_id FROM alerts
INTERSECT
SELECT asset_id FROM requests
ORDER BY asset_id;
paragraphs: Only asset IDs are compared.
interpretation: P8 appears on both lists. This tells us about membership, not agreement between the underlying explanations.

parts.title: 5. Remove work that already has a completion record
paragraphs: EXCEPT keeps distinct rows from its left result that are absent from its right result. The order matters: candidates EXCEPT completed asks a different question from completed EXCEPT candidates.

Here we combine the report lists, then subtract completed asset IDs. When several operators appear together, make the intended stages clear. Engine precedence rules differ; a named subquery or CTE is often easier to review than relying on a reader to remember them.
interpretation: The next lesson will give these intermediate result sets useful names.

parts.title: 6. Keep NULL and collation rules in view
paragraphs: SQLite’s compound duplicate comparisons treat NULL values in the same positions as equal for this purpose. That differs from using ordinary equality in a WHERE predicate. Text comparison also follows the chosen collation rules.

Decide whether a NULL asset ID belongs in an assignment report at all. Our exercise excludes NULL IDs explicitly because no pump can be assigned from an unknown identifier. It does not rely on an accidental NULL removal elsewhere.
interpretation: A duplicate policy and a missing-identifier policy are separate decisions.

parts.title: 7. Check the result after each combination
paragraphs: Run each projection, then the combined candidates, then the subtraction. Adding another P7 alert should not create another assignment. Adding P7 to completed should remove it.
The workshop exposes those same intermediate relations. It uses append followed by set difference, whose distinct result supplies the final one-row-per-asset policy.
interpretation: Different valid SQL forms can express this result. The tests check membership and ordering rather than requiring one operator sequence.

title: Can We Read the Query in the Order We Explain the Job?
openingTitle: Filter the Jobs, Then Add Their Minutes
opening: Botie needs pumps whose completed maintenance has consumed more than fifty minutes. Open jobs contain estimates that should not enter this report. A long nested query can make it difficult to see whether those estimates were excluded before the total was calculated.
We can give the qualifying jobs a name, then give the per-pump totals another name. Each stage describes a relation we can inspect.
blurb: Use common table expressions to name meaningful query stages while keeping grain, scope and execution assumptions explicit.

history.title: Names Made Intermediate Relations Easier to Review
blocks: Nested queries let one operation use another’s result, but deeply nested expressions can be awkward to inspect. Common table expressions give those intermediate relations names inside one statement. SQLite added CTE support in its February 2014 release.

This is a language feature for expressing dependencies. Naming closed_jobs does not permanently create a table or promise a particular execution strategy. Its value for our report is that the next stage clearly receives completed work rather than every job in the system.

parts.title: 1. Name a useful intermediate result
paragraphs: WITH closed_jobs AS (...) places a name before the main query. Inside the parentheses is a SELECT describing the relation. Later stages and the final SELECT can refer to that name during this statement.
Start by selecting from closed_jobs directly. If open estimates remain, repair that boundary before adding aggregation.
interpretation: A CTE is scoped to its statement. The next separate statement cannot assume that name still exists.
