title: Pick Up New Changes Without Losing Late Readings
blurb: Repeated full imports become expensive, but a naive timestamp filter misses corrections and deletions. Track source change position, merge versions and commit the checkpoint with the result.
openingTitle: Yesterday’s Reading Arrived After Today’s Import Finished
opening: Botie’s pipeline remembers the latest event time and asks for anything newer on the next run. A delayed sensor message arrives with yesterday’s event time, so it never enters the training source. A later correction has the same problem.
We need to track when the source exposes a change, as well as when its measured event happened. The lesson builds a versioned merge and a checkpoint that can be replayed after a failure.

history.title: Remembering a Change Position Instead of Recopying Everything

sources.title: Mohan and colleagues: ARIES recovery using write-ahead logging (1992)

blocks: Databases needed a record of changes so they could recover meaningful state after a crash. ARIES, published in 1992, is a documented recovery method built around write-ahead logging: record information needed for recovery before the corresponding changed pages become durable. That recovery problem helped make ordered change history a central database mechanism.

Change-data-capture interfaces expose committed changes for other systems to follow instead of repeatedly copying the entire source. PostgreSQL logical decoding is one implementation, with explicit restart and retention responsibilities. Our consumer uses a supplied ingestion sequence and record versions to recognise progress and replay. It demonstrates an application-level consumer rule, not the database’s recovery algorithm or a guarantee supplied by any arbitrary timestamp column.

reading.experimentTitle: Apply the new source changes and keep their checkpoint
reading.experimentIntro: Select changes after the committed cursor, merge each identity by version, then keep resulting state and cursor together.
reading.connectionTitle: A checkpoint must describe the data that was actually committed
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Merge a replayable change batch
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. SQL programs run in an isolated SQLite database; the workshop illustrates the operation with records rather than parsing SQL.

intuition.title: The two orderings answer different questions
intuition.explanation: A late event can be a newly delivered change.

cells: Update R1 to its newer version
Insert R3 even if its event time is old

scene.caption: The cursor follows source delivery order. Per-record version decides whether a payload is newer.

parts.title: 1. Separate event time, arrival order and record version
paragraphs: Event time belongs to the measured phenomenon. Arrival order describes when a change becomes available to the pipeline. Version orders successive states of one identity. A late event can have an old event time and a new arrival sequence.

Our source guarantees unique increasing sequence values and monotonic versions per identity. A production source must document its ordering, transaction and retention behaviour. A poll over updated_at needs careful tie handling and cannot detect hard deletions unless another mechanism records them.
interpretation: Do not turn MAX(event_time) into a reliable ingestion cursor by naming it a watermark.

parts.title: 2. Define exactly what the checkpoint means
paragraphs: The checkpoint is the last source change position whose effects are committed in the sink. Read only later positions for the next batch. If the sink commits data but loses the checkpoint update, a replay can occur. If the checkpoint commits first, a crash can skip data that was never written.

Commit both in one transaction when they share a database. Across systems, use a delivery protocol and idempotent merge that tolerate replay, and reconcile partial outcomes. Exactly-once claims require specifying the entire boundary and its assumptions.
interpretation: The exercise’s checkpoint table and current table share one SQLite transaction.

parts.title: 3. Merge identities by version
paragraphs: A stable primary key identifies the record. A newer version replaces its stored payload; an older version does not. Replaying an equal version with the same payload leaves the result unchanged.

The exercise assumes equal versions always carry equal payloads because conflicting records have already been quarantined. A real pipeline must check that contract. Choosing a random last arrival for equal conflicting versions destroys reproducibility. The workshop rejects that conflict explicitly.
interpretation: Source position and record version solve different ordering problems.

examples.title: Keep a newer value when an old revision arrives
paragraphs: A delayed old payload should not replace the current row.
interpretation: The old version is ignored even though it was delivered now.

parts.title: 4. Represent deletion as a versioned change
paragraphs: If a deleted identity simply disappears from a snapshot, an incremental consumer may never learn what to remove. A deletion event or tombstone tells the sink that this identity was deliberately removed at a particular version.

Retaining that tombstone prevents an older late update from recreating the deleted record. Our current_readings table stores deleted as 0 or 1 and keeps a NULL value for a tombstone. Readers of active data must explicitly filter deleted=0. Tombstone retention needs to cover the source’s replay and late-arrival assumptions.
interpretation: A deletion is data about an identity. It is not equivalent to a missing sensor value.

parts.title: 5. Advance over ignored old versions too
paragraphs: A batch may contain an arrival whose version is older than the current record. Its payload is ignored, but its source position was still processed. Advance the cursor past it once the batch commits. Otherwise the consumer may read the same obsolete change indefinitely.

An empty batch leaves the cursor unchanged. Never move a checkpoint backwards because an old source extract was supplied. The SQL exercise uses the greater of the previous checkpoint and the maximum available change sequence.
interpretation: The resulting cursor describes processed delivery positions, not only rows whose values changed.

parts.title: 6. Bound a batch without skipping changes that share a timestamp
paragraphs: A busy source can keep producing changes while the consumer works. Capture a source-supported upper position for the batch, then read positions after the committed cursor up to that bound. Commit the result before starting the next interval. The source must retain the interval and expose complete changes within it; reading an arbitrary MAX from a changing business table does not establish those properties.

Timestamp polling adds another problem. If two rows share the final timestamp and a row limit splits them, resuming with only updated_at greater than that timestamp skips the remaining row. An ordered timestamp-and-identity cursor can paginate a stable set, but it still cannot detect a later change that reuses an earlier timestamp. Reliable polling needs a source contract, an overlap-and-deduplication policy where suitable, or a change log. Our teaching input uses unique source sequence numbers so that these assumptions are visible.
interpretation: The exercise receives a complete finite extract. A production reader must additionally define how it obtains and retains a complete bounded interval.

parts.title: 7. Plan for backfills and late corrections
paragraphs: A historical backfill may revisit a time range already represented in features. Give it a declared source snapshot and transformation version, and merge by stable identity or rebuild a partition deliberately. Do not mix a backfill cursor into the live stream unless its ordering contract supports that.

Corrections can invalidate previously built aggregates or training examples. Decide whether to recompute affected partitions, keep immutable historical snapshots, or publish a new dataset version. Retain enough lineage to explain which source revisions produced a model’s features.
interpretation: Idempotent row merging does not automatically refresh every derived aggregate downstream.

parts.title: 8. Notice when the source no longer has the required history
paragraphs: Suppose the sink stopped at change position 100, but the source has already discarded everything before 150. Resuming at 150 would silently omit an interval. The consumer needs to detect that its checkpoint is older than the retained history and take a documented recovery path.

A new full snapshot can rebuild the sink, but the snapshot and following change stream need a consistent handoff position. Otherwise changes that occur during the copy can be missed or duplicated. Preserve the old dataset version while rebuilding when it is needed for model reproducibility. Reconcile the rebuilt state before directing readers to it.
interpretation: A successful connection does not prove that the source can still replay the interval the sink needs.

parts.title: 9. Reconcile the incremental result with a complete view
paragraphs: Periodically compare record counts, keys and selected aggregates against a trusted source snapshot. Missing change retention, a broken cursor or a source schema change can produce a plausible but incomplete sink. Monitor lag and checkpoint progress separately from job success messages.
The final challenge replays a batch, introduces an older version after a deletion, and tests an empty source extract. These are ordinary recovery cases to design before the first production outage.
interpretation: The pipeline is ready for the next lesson when its checkpoint and data tell the same story after a restart.

quiz.prompt: Why retain the version-5 tombstone?
options: It prevents the older update from resurrecting R2
It makes the old value a new observation
It removes the need for any cursor

practice.title: Can a change batch survive replay and preserve deletion?
practice.question: Can a change batch survive replay and preserve deletion?
task: A replayed change batch must neither undo newer values nor resurrect a deleted reading. Apply the source changes and advance their checkpoint inside one transaction.

Process changes with seq greater than the single checkpoint.seq. Insert new IDs and replace existing records only with a greater version. Retain deleted records as tombstones, meaning stored deletion markers rather than removing their version history.

Advance the checkpoint to the greatest available processed sequence without moving backwards, then commit. Return id, version, deleted and value ordered by id. The source guarantees unique sequences, nonnegative versions and equal payloads for equal versions.

title: Which Records Does the Technician Need Together?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: A pump screen, a recent-reading lookup and a site report ask different questions of the same records. Start with those requests before choosing how to store the data.
openingTitle: The Pump Screen Keeps Asking for the Same Visits
opening: Botie already has an asset register and a table of inspections. A technician opens P1 and expects its recent visits. Another screen needs the latest temperature for P1. The weekly report needs totals across every pump at a site. Those requests use the same information in different ways.

Before choosing another database, write down exactly what each request knows and what it must return. That gives us something to judge a design against. A convenient record layout for one screen can make another question harder.

history.title: A Shopping Cart Had to Survive a Busy Service
blocks: Amazon’s 2007 Dynamo paper describes services such as shopping carts that needed highly available reads and writes. Its interface retrieved an object by a key. Concentrating on that access pattern let the designers make different tradeoffs from a system intended to answer arbitrary relational queries. Dynamo is a particular distributed design; its choices do not define every database called NoSQL.

Our invented maintenance service is much smaller, but we can ask the same first question: what operation must remain practical? The pump screen supplies an asset ID and wants its visits. Grouping visits under that identity makes the requested association visible. We still have to decide how writes keep the grouping current.

reading.experimentTitle: Keep every visit under its asset
reading.experimentIntro: Build a keyed collection, look up the requested asset, and supply an empty list when it has no visits.
reading.connectionTitle: The request determines the useful grouping
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Retrieve all visits for the requested pump
reading.outputLabel: Visits returned to the pump screen
reading.exampleNote: These maintenance records are invented. The operations model a lookup, not a database benchmark.

intuition.title: One record set, different questions
intuition.explanation: Write the request beside the information it already knows.

records.label: Site report
cells: site north and a date range

scene.caption: A key-only interface needs a key naming the value being requested.

intuition.title: A repeated asset ID is useful information
intuition.explanation: These are visits, so a pump may occur more than once.

parts.title: 1. Describe the read before naming a database
paragraphs: The technician starts with a pump ID and wants that pump’s recent visits, newest first. The weekly report starts with a site and wants totals across many pumps. Write those requests down separately, including how much data each may return and how fresh it must be.

An access pattern is the name for one of these recurring ways of reading or changing data. The distinction matters because a layout that puts one pump’s history together does not automatically put a whole site’s history together.

Ask about writes too. A new inspection arrives while somebody is viewing the history. Does the next refresh need to show it immediately? Can the screen tolerate a short delay? Those are application requirements, and a data model cannot choose them for us.
interpretation: A useful design note names an operation and its constraints. “We need something scalable” leaves the important questions unanswered.

parts.title: 2. Keep the meaning of a record intact
paragraphs: The asset table has one row per asset. The inspection table has one row per visit. If we create a dictionary keyed by asset ID and assign a single visit to each entry, a later visit replaces the earlier one. The code has changed the meaning of the data.

A bucket of visits is different: the asset ID selects a list, and that list retains separate visit identities. This gives the pump screen what it asked for without pretending each pump has only one inspection.
interpretation: Row grain from SQL still matters when the container is a dictionary or a document.

parts.title: 3. Build a lookup while keeping repeated keys
paragraphs: A Python dictionary maps a key to a value. Here each value is a list. Read a visit, find or create its asset’s list, and append the visit. We perform the grouping once in this demonstration, then retrieve a selected list.
Constructing the grouping scans the input. Keeping an equivalent structure in a real service also costs storage and update work. We have made the read simple by doing work elsewhere.
interpretation: This dictionary is an inspectable model of grouping, not an implementation of distributed storage.

examples.title: A repeated pump adds to its list
paragraphs: Use setdefault to create each list only when its key first appears.
interpretation: The first lookup retains both visit identities. The second has no bucket and returns the application’s chosen empty result.

parts.title: 4. Compare the families by the operations they expose
paragraphs: A key-value store starts with a key and returns its associated value. A document database can inspect fields inside a stored record. Wide-column systems organise records around keys and related columns, often with query patterns tied closely to their partitioning. Graph databases make relationships and traversals central to their interfaces. Products vary within each family.

Relational databases can also store JSON and maintain indexes for targeted lookups. A JSON-shaped request alone does not establish that we need a document database. Compare the integrity rules and operational burden of the actual candidates.
interpretation: NoSQL names a broad collection of approaches. It does not promise a particular consistency model, transaction boundary or performance result.

parts.title: 5. Account for the copies a faster read creates
paragraphs: Suppose visits remain in the SQL system of record while a service keeps a pump-history document. Now an inspection write may need to reach both representations. A failed second write can leave them disagreeing. We need a rebuildable projection, a reliable change feed, or another explicit update process.

A screen-specific copy is useful when its freshness contract permits that process. The same copy is a poor authority for a decision that requires the newest committed safety status. Say which store owns each fact and how other representations catch up.
interpretation: Before adding a second representation, write down what happens when only one copy changes.

parts.title: 6. Test the request when the data stops being convenient
paragraphs: The workshop first contains one visit per pump, so assigning a single record might appear sufficient. Then a second visit for the requested pump arrives. Your grouping must retain both. A request for an unseen asset needs an explicit empty response.

Use this failure to challenge a proposed model before measuring speed. Once the answers are correct, investigate the workload with a real database and realistic record sizes. Our in-memory counts cannot predict network latency or server capacity.
interpretation: The next lesson follows the lookup key itself. Two sites can both call their pump P1.

options: How records will be found and combined for that request
Which product has the shortest name
That each pump has only one visit
quiz.because: The result may require an index, maintained summary or scan beyond a single lookup.

given.data: The input is a site ID and a time range; the result is a total across many pumps.

quiz.prompt: That label establishes that every write is immediately visible to every reader.

title: Which P1 Did the Lookup Mean?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: Two sites use the same short asset ID. Build keys that preserve the full identity, and distinguish a missing entry from a stored zero.
openingTitle: North and South Both Have a Pump Called P1
opening: North reports no outstanding inspections for P1. South reports seven. Botie stores each answer under the key P1, and the second write replaces the first. The storage service did exactly what it was asked to do. Our key did not describe the thing we meant.
A key is the complete name used by a lookup. We need to decide which parts make that name unique, how those parts are encoded, and what an absent name means to the caller.

history.title: Small Operations Around Explicit Keys
blocks: Redis began in 2009 under Salvatore Sanfilippo. Its string commands illustrate a small interaction: set a value under a key, then retrieve that key. A server can implement that interface without interpreting the application meaning of a pump name.

That division gives the application responsibility for a naming convention. Our site and asset pair is an invented example. The key must carry enough identity before a key-value service can return the intended record.

reading.experimentTitle: Keep site identity in the lookup
reading.experimentIntro: Encode the requested site and asset before reading the store. Inspect the found flag independently of its value.
reading.connectionTitle: A short asset name is only part of the identity
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Look up a site-specific status

reading.exampleNote: The local mapping uses a JSON-array key convention chosen for the exercise. Redis does not require that convention.

intuition.title: Both writes targeted one name
intuition.explanation: The collision is in the application key.

scene.caption: A layout with one P1 key cannot hold both site-specific answers separately.

intuition.title: A zero count is a useful answer
intuition.explanation: Separate presence from value.

scene.caption: The key exists even though its value is falsey in Python.

parts.title: 1. Choose the scope of the identity
paragraphs: An asset ID can be unique inside a site while repeating elsewhere. The key therefore needs the site and asset. If customers can reuse site names, include the tenant too. A namespace for purpose or format version can keep different representations from colliding.

A well-formed key is still not an access-control decision. The server must verify that the caller may read the identified object. Letting a caller submit another tenant’s key does not establish that permission.
interpretation: Identity describes the requested record. Authorisation decides whether this caller may access it.

parts.title: 2. Preserve boundaries when combining fields
paragraphs: Joining text can erase information. The pairs ["a:b", "c"] and ["a", "b:c"] produce the same colon-joined string. You can escape separators carefully, use length prefixes, or encode a structured sequence.
Our exercise encodes an ordered array of strings as compact JSON. Site always comes before asset. Every writer and reader must use the same encoding; a different spelling is a different key.
interpretation: A key-value lookup performs an exact match.

parts.title: 3. Test membership before interpreting the value
paragraphs: A dictionary can contain a key whose value is zero, False, an empty string or None. Those values describe stored information. A missing key means there is no entry with that name.
Return a found flag separately when callers need to distinguish the states. Then a zero count reaches the screen unchanged, while a miss can trigger a fetch or an unavailable message.
interpretation: bool(value) asks whether a value is truthy. It does not establish presence.

examples.title: A stored zero is still a hit
paragraphs: Check the key before interpreting its count.
interpretation: The first count is known and zero. The second key is absent. A stored None would also need a separate presence check.

parts.title: 4. Try the same operation at a Redis prompt
paragraphs: Redis string values are byte sequences. JSON text is one possible value format. SET replaces the value associated with a key; GET retrieves it. A missing GET has a null reply translated by the client into its own representation.

A real client can also report connection errors and timeouts. Those are different from a successful request reporting that no key exists. The Python worksheet keeps the naming mechanism visible without introducing a server.
interpretation: The namespace in this command is an application choice.

references.title: SET and GET a site-specific count

source.title: SET and GET a site-specific count

references.code:
redis-cli SET 'asset:north:P1:open-count' '0'
redis-cli GET 'asset:north:P1:open-count'
description: These literal identifiers contain no separator characters. Use an unambiguous encoding for arbitrary identifiers.
setup: Install redis-cli and start a disposable local Redis server. These commands do not run in the browser.
interpretation: GET returns the stored string 0; presence does not depend on its numeric value.

parts.title: 5. Consider what another writer can do between requests
paragraphs: Two callers can read one counter, calculate replacements locally and write them back in either order. That read-modify-write sequence can lose an increment. Use the server’s appropriate atomic counter operation or a documented conditional-write protocol.

Also decide whether a replacement preserves expiry. Ordinary Redis SET clears an existing timeout unless an applicable expiry option is supplied. Naming the record correctly does not protect its update sequence or keep an old copy current.
interpretation: The next lesson adds a deadline to the saved value.

title: How Long Should Botie Trust the Saved Reading?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: A cache can answer quickly while showing an old reading. Follow its expiry boundary and the load a cold cache sends back to the source.
openingTitle: The Screen Still Shows Yesterday’s Count
opening: The lookup returns the right pump but still shows eighteen open inspections after the source has changed to twenty-three. We saved the answer to avoid asking the source on every refresh. That saved answer has outlived its usefulness.
A cache is a copy kept for reuse. We need a policy for when it may answer, what happens when it cannot, and how the service behaves if many copies expire together.

history.title: A Helpful Copy Can Become a Dependency

sources.title: AWS Builders’ Library: caching challenges and strategies

blocks: Amazon’s published caching experience describes a recurring operational problem: a service becomes accustomed to the reduced source load of a warm cache, then a cold or unavailable cache exposes the source to many more requests. Caching changes the operating conditions of the service.

Redis makes expiry an explicit property of a key. A timeout gives a copy a limited lifetime; the application still chooses a lifetime appropriate to its data. Our workshop isolates the decision at that boundary. It cannot establish whether a source can absorb refresh traffic.

reading.experimentTitle: Cross the expiry time
reading.experimentIntro: Read the saved value and deadline on separate branches. Compare the clock with the deadline before choosing a copy.
reading.connectionTitle: A correctly named record can still be stale
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Distinguish a usable copy from a refresh
reading.outputLabel: Value returned under the expiry policy
reading.exampleNote: Times are invented seconds on one shared clock. Source values are fixtures, not network responses.

intuition.title: The source changes before the deadline
intuition.explanation: This policy permits the copy until time 120.

scene.caption: TTL limits eligibility; it does not certify that the source stayed unchanged.

intuition.title: A miss needs another route
intuition.explanation: Use existence and time before choosing the saved answer.

scene.caption: A source failure needs a separate application policy.

parts.title: 1. Separate the source from the copy
paragraphs: The source owns the inspection count. The cache stores a previous answer. A hit saves a request; it does not prove the source still agrees.

An approximate activity display might tolerate delay. A current safety state may need a different policy. Decide the acceptable stale interval with the people who depend on the answer. A timeout selected for convenience quietly makes that decision for them.
interpretation: A cache lifetime expresses tolerance for old information.

parts.title: 2. Follow a cache-aside read
paragraphs: In cache-aside, the application asks the cache first. A usable hit returns the copy. A miss asks the source and may store that answer for reuse. A failed source call is a separate outcome.

The application can invalidate a copy when it updates the source, but writes and invalidations can race or fail independently. Expiry limits lingering copies; it does not make separate stores update atomically.
interpretation: Describe the outage behaviour rather than quietly treating an unavailable count as zero.

parts.title: 3. Make the deadline comparison explicit
paragraphs: The fixture has value and expires_at. Both now and expires_at use the same time unit. Our rule uses the saved value only while now is strictly earlier than expiry. At equality, the entry has expired.
Real caches own their clocks and expiry mechanics. Here a shared clock is an explicit assumption, allowing repeatable tests without sleeping or relying on a workstation clock.
interpretation: Test the boundary itself, not only times far from it.

examples.title: Pause on either side of expiry
paragraphs: The contents stay unchanged while their eligibility changes.
interpretation: The exact deadline takes the source branch under this policy.

parts.title: 4. Store the value and lifetime together
paragraphs: A copy needs both its value and a limit on how long it may answer. That permitted lifetime is often called time to live, or TTL. Redis SET can store a value and an EX lifetime in seconds in one command.

Doing both together avoids a gap where SET succeeds but a separate EXPIRE fails, leaving a copy without the intended deadline. Ordinary SET without an applicable expiry option clears an existing timeout, so updating the value also requires an explicit lifetime policy.
Eviction is different: a cache may remove an entry under its memory policy before the nominal deadline. The application must tolerate that miss too.
interpretation: A TTL is not a promise that memory will retain the item until that time.

references.title: Store a count with a lifetime

source.title: Store a count with a lifetime

references.code:
redis-cli SET 'asset:north:P1:open-count' '18' EX 60
redis-cli TTL 'asset:north:P1:open-count'
description: SET supplies the value and expiry together. TTL reports remaining lifetime or a special absence/no-expiry result.
setup: Use redis-cli with a disposable local Redis server. Time passes between commands; this is not a browser exercise.
interpretation: The Python challenge replaces elapsed real time with an explicit clock.

parts.title: 5. Prepare for many misses together
paragraphs: A cold cache can send every request to the source. Popular keys expiring together can also create a burst. Coalescing simultaneous fetches for one key reduces duplicated work; spreading expiry times can reduce synchronised refreshes.

Bound the source request rate and decide what happens when that budget is exhausted. A controlled stale-response policy can suit some displays, but it needs a final deadline and an honest description of the old information being served.
interpretation: Measure source load during misses, not only response speed during hits.

parts.title: 6. Recognise an unexpired but outdated answer
paragraphs: At time 110, our copy is eighteen and the source is twenty-three. The deadline still permits the old answer until 120. That is the allowance we chose.

If the user needs the newest count immediately after a write, a simple TTL is insufficient. Reading the source for that operation or using a version-aware update process changes the design and its costs. A passing deadline test cannot decide whether the allowance is appropriate.
interpretation: Correct code can faithfully implement the wrong freshness policy.

parts.title: 7. Observe the branch without exposing the payload
paragraphs: Track hits, misses and refresh failures separately. Avoid logging private cached values as a substitute for useful metrics. Include tenant and representation version in naming where required, and enforce access at the service boundary.
The challenge returns a route label with its value. That makes a falsey hit and an absent entry distinguishable even when their eventual displayed counts look similar.
interpretation: The workshop evaluates both supplied branches for inspection. It does not issue a source request on every real cache hit.

quiz.because: Coalescing shares work; the source still needs an overall load policy.

quiz.prompt: The application needs a miss path for that request.
quiz.because: Expiry is only one reason a cached entry may be unavailable.

title: Can One Record Describe the Pump and Its Sensor?
blurb: Read a nested maintenance record field by field. Keep missing data separate from null, preserve measurement types, and decide which rules every document must follow.
openingTitle: A Temperature Without Its Unit Is Not Much Use
opening: Botie receives a value of 72 for P1. Is that a temperature? Which unit was used? When was it measured? Those questions belong to the same reading, so keeping their answers together helps us interpret it.

A document stores named fields, and a field can itself contain another document or an array. That gives us a way to keep related details together. It also gives us more ways to create a record that looks reasonable while leaving out something the reader needs.

history.title: Keeping Object Structure in the Stored Record
blocks: MongoDB’s April 2010 manual already describes JSON-style objects and BSON storage. This offered applications a way to retain nested fields instead of flattening every object into one row shape. The historical manual records that design; it is not a claim that MongoDB invented structured records.

For our maintenance screen, a sensor object keeps a reading beside its unit. The remaining question is whether every writer supplies the fields the reader expects. Flexible document shapes make a shared contract more useful, not less necessary.

reading.experimentTitle: Does the sensor actually contain a latest field?
reading.experimentIntro: Read the sensor object, then probe the requested field without turning absence into an observed null.
reading.connectionTitle: Keep the measurement and its meaning together
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Follow a nested field without losing missingness
reading.exampleNote: The fixtures contain ordinary JSON-compatible values. Python dictionaries model their structure; no BSON driver or MongoDB server runs here.

intuition.title: Each part answers a different question
intuition.explanation: This is one invented sensor document.

scene.caption: The nested sensor object keeps context with the reading.

intuition.title: Three records require different interpretations
intuition.explanation: Assume null means the sensor reported no usable measurement.

scene.caption: These meanings are an application contract. The database cannot infer them from the pump itself.

parts.title: 1. Start with the object the screen needs
paragraphs: A pump document might contain asset_id, site and a sensor object. Inside sensor, latest and unit describe one measurement. An array can hold a bounded collection such as the installed sensor channels.

Objects name fields; arrays preserve a sequence of values. If each array member is a reading, put the kind and value inside the same member. Two separate arrays need an additional ordering agreement to say which kind belongs to which value.
interpretation: The structure should keep related facts together without hiding their identities.

parts.title: 2. Agree on types and units before reading values
paragraphs: The JSON number 72 and the JSON string "72" are different types. Converting arbitrary strings to numbers can hide invalid input. A number without a unit can also be misinterpreted even when its type is correct.

Define the writer contract: which fields are required, which numeric range is plausible, how timestamps are represented, and what a missing measurement means. Validate at the appropriate boundary. Database shape checks can support those rules; they cannot establish that a sensor measured the real world correctly.
interpretation: A schema can confirm the presence of unit. Domain validation still needs to check which units are allowed.

parts.title: 3. Read the object one field at a time
paragraphs: Python dictionaries are useful for inspecting this mechanism. A dictionary lookup yields another dictionary at sensor; a second lookup yields latest. Brackets require the field to exist. A presence test allows us to describe an absent field explicitly.

JSON text is a representation sent between systems. json.loads parses it into Python values. MongoDB uses BSON internally, which has types beyond JSON’s basic set, including dates and ObjectIds. Do not assume a JSON round trip preserves every BSON type.
interpretation: The worksheet uses JSON-compatible fixtures so its conversions are visible.

examples.title: Parse a sensor record and follow its fields
paragraphs: The text contains JSON null; Python represents that value as None.
examples.code:
import json
record = json.loads('{"asset_id":"P1","sensor":{"latest":null,"unit":"C"}}')
sensor = record["sensor"]
print("latest" in sensor)
print(sensor["latest"])
print(sensor["unit"])
interpretation: The latest field exists and explicitly contains None. The unit remains a separate string.

parts.title: 4. Keep an omitted field separate from a reported null
paragraphs: Suppose an older writer never supplied latest. A newer writer supplies latest:null when the sensor fails. Both may become None if we call get without testing membership, losing useful evidence about what happened.

Our inspection result contains present and value. A missing field gives present false; a stored null gives present true with value None. For a longer path, an absent or non-object intermediate value means the requested leaf is unavailable. The full original document remains available if we need a richer validation explanation.
interpretation: Zero is a value, null is an explicit marker, and omission means no field was supplied.

parts.title: 5. Use a contract while the document shape evolves
paragraphs: Documents in a collection can have different fields, but the application still needs predictable meanings. A schema version can tell a reader which representation to interpret. A migration may update stored records; a compatibility reader may support both forms during a transition.

MongoDB supports schema validation, including a supported subset of JSON Schema expressed through $jsonSchema. Choose validation level and action deliberately. Requiring a field does not automatically fill it into old documents, and a validator definition alone is not a migration.
interpretation: Test old and new writers together before retiring the older representation.

references.title: A validator for identity and a sensor object

source.title: A validator for identity and a sensor object

references.code: {"$jsonSchema":{"bsonType":"object","required":["asset_id","sensor"],"properties":{"asset_id":{"bsonType":"string"},"sensor":{"bsonType":"object","required":["unit"],"properties":{"unit":{"enum":["C"]},"latest":{"bsonType":["double","int","long","null"]}}}}}}
description: This is a MongoDB validator expression, not a standalone insert command. It requires identity and a sensor object while allowing latest to be absent.
setup: Pass this object as the validator option when creating or modifying a collection in a disposable MongoDB environment. The browser does not install validators.
interpretation: The deliberate optional latest field preserves the missing-versus-null cases. The validator does not prove that a measurement is accurate.

parts.title: 6. Choose where the document should stop growing
paragraphs: A current sensor description is bounded. Every reading ever recorded is not. Embedding an ever-growing history makes each parent larger and complicates retrieval and updates. MongoDB also limits a BSON document to 16 MiB.

Choose a bounded embedded subset or store the history as separately identified records when growth demands it. The next lesson asks which facts belong inside the pump and which should remain references to independently maintained information.
interpretation: A convenient screen shape is a starting point, not a reason to make every related fact part of one document.

Whether a longer field name removes size limits
Whether null should be changed to zero

If a member is absent or an intermediate value is not a dictionary, return {"present": False, "value": None}. Otherwise return {"present": True, "value": a deep copy of the leaf}. Do not mutate the input.
Print the result for sensor.latest in the supplied document. This is a Python structure exercise, not MongoDB query syntax.

title: Should Every Pump Keep a Copy of the Supplier’s Phone Number?
blurb: A copied contact becomes stale when the supplier changes its number. Separate facts owned by a pump from shared current facts and intentional historical snapshots.
openingTitle: One Phone Number Changed, Fifty Pump Records Did Not
opening: Botie opens P1 and finds its supplier phone number inside the pump document. That is convenient until the supplier changes the number. Fifty other pump documents still contain the old contact. Which copy should the technician trust?

Keeping related data together can save a lookup. It also gives us copies to maintain. We need to decide whether a field describes this pump, a shared entity, or the state of that entity at a particular time.

history.title: A Document Boundary Also Became an Update Boundary
blocks: MongoDB’s early manual described embedded objects and references resolved through additional reads. The document model made locality a modelling decision: related information could travel together, while independently maintained objects could keep their own identities.

The maintenance example puts that decision under pressure. A pump’s installed sensor configuration belongs with the pump. A supplier’s current phone number is shared. A purchase-time supplier name may be a historical snapshot that should remain unchanged. Their relationships look similar on a screen but require different update rules.

reading.experimentTitle: Resolve the current supplier through its identity
reading.experimentIntro: Read supplier_id from the pump, look it up in the current supplier directory, and attach the result without changing purchase history.
reading.connectionTitle: The right boundary follows ownership and change
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Attach shared current metadata
reading.exampleNote: The directory is a supplied local map. It models reference resolution without a database server or cross-document transaction.

intuition.title: Three related facts have different owners
intuition.explanation: Decide what each field is intended to mean before choosing a location.

scene.caption: An unchanged historical name is not necessarily a stale-data bug.

intuition.title: Follow the reference before using the contact
intuition.explanation: P1 retains the supplier’s stable ID.

parts.title: 1. Ask which object owns the fact
paragraphs: A pump’s mounting position changes when that pump moves. A supplier’s contact changes for every customer using that supplier. Those facts have different owners even if one screen shows them together.

Embed a fact when its lifecycle and access pattern fit the parent. Use a reference when the related object needs an independent identity or is shared across many parents. These are design questions, not absolute rules that every supplier must live separately.
interpretation: Document ownership helps us locate the write that should change a fact.

parts.title: 2. Distinguish a current copy from a historical snapshot
paragraphs: The purchase order might need the supplier name as it appeared on the day of purchase. Updating that name every time the supplier rebrands would alter the historical record. Store it as a named snapshot with its meaning clear.

By contrast, a field labelled current_supplier_phone promises current information. If duplicated, it needs an update process and a freshness allowance. Field names and timestamps should help readers tell those promises apart.
interpretation: Denormalisation is a choice about repeated data. It is manageable only when we know which copies should change.

parts.title: 3. Resolve a reference by identity
paragraphs: The pump stores supplier_id. A directory maps that ID to the current supplier object. Read the reference, look up the matching object, then assemble the view. Do not match the supplier by list position or by a display name that can change.

A missing reference needs a visible outcome. Our exercise attaches {"missing": True} rather than silently choosing the first available supplier. Real services may reject a write that creates an invalid reference, retain a tombstone, or show an unresolved relationship.
interpretation: The reference itself is not a guarantee that the related record still exists.

examples.title: Reordering the directory does not change the partner
paragraphs: Both pumps can refer to the same supplier without copying its phone.
interpretation: Both results come from S1’s current record. The demonstration does not make a network request or guarantee a consistent snapshot across concurrent changes.

parts.title: 4. Keep growing histories from enlarging the parent forever
paragraphs: A few installed channels form a bounded array. A lifetime of inspection events can grow without a useful limit. Continually embedding those events enlarges the parent and can make reads transfer data the screen never uses.

MongoDB documents have a 16 MiB limit, but staying below that limit is not the whole design test. Consider update frequency, the size of requested subsets and the lifetime of the history. A bounded recent subset plus separately stored full history can be appropriate if its duplication rules are explicit.
interpretation: The largest legal document is not automatically a comfortable working size.

parts.title: 5. Understand the consistency boundary you selected
paragraphs: Suppose one edit changes a pump’s status and its latest-reading note. If both fields are in the same MongoDB document, a single-document write can apply those changes together. Other readers do not see half of that write. That is the atomicity guarantee relevant here.

A change to several separate documents does not acquire that guarantee merely because they share an ID. Where a rule requires those documents to change together, use a supported transaction with its deployment requirements or design a workflow that explicitly handles partial progress.
Embedding can make some related changes fit one document, but it also puts concurrent writes and growth inside that boundary. Weigh those costs against the reads it simplifies.
interpretation: A local dictionary lookup cannot demonstrate database atomicity.

parts.title: 6. Inspect the real reference pattern
paragraphs: A MongoDB reference can be an ordinary field containing another document’s identifier. The database does not automatically enforce a relational foreign-key constraint for that field. Applications need an integrity policy.

The following pair shows the intended representation. Reading the asset and supplier separately is one option; an aggregation $lookup can also combine collections when appropriate. Measure and explain the selected access path in the actual deployment.
interpretation: Keeping a reference does not mean the application must never use a server-side join.

parts.title: 7. Test deletion as well as a phone change

Those cases expose different shortcuts: reusing an embedded current contact, joining by position, and pretending every reference resolves. Keep all three in the tests for the view builder.

title: Did the High Value Belong to the Temperature Sensor?
blurb: An array contains several readings. Keep the sensor kind and its value attached to the same member while filtering documents.
openingTitle: P1 Has a Temperature Reading and a High Number, but They Are Different Readings
opening: P1 contains a temperature reading of 65 and a vibration reading of 95. Botie is looking for temperatures of at least 80. A careless query notices that the document contains the word temperature and also contains a value above 80, then returns P1.
The information we need is present, but the conditions have been applied to different array members. We need to keep each reading intact while deciding whether it satisfies the whole request.

history.title: Queries Followed Fields Inside the Document
blocks: The early MongoDB manual describes reaching into objects through field paths. That let applications ask about nested content rather than fetching every document by ID and inspecting it themselves. Arrays introduced another question: which member must satisfy a combination of conditions?

MongoDB’s $elemMatch expresses that at least one array member must satisfy all of its listed criteria. Our workshop makes the same binding visible by expanding each reading with its parent identity, applying both conditions to that row, and then returning each matching asset once.

reading.experimentTitle: Keep each sensor kind beside its value
reading.experimentIntro: Expand the reading arrays, filter by kind and threshold on the same expanded row, then keep each matching asset once.
reading.connectionTitle: One matching member must satisfy the whole condition

reading.exampleNote: Workshop filters use explicit primitive comparisons. They are not a MongoDB query interpreter and do not implement its full missing-value or array semantics.

items: One row per reading, retaining asset_id

scene.caption: Multiple qualifying readings must not duplicate an asset in this result contract.

parts.title: 1. State whether the result is a document or a reading
paragraphs: The request asks for assets with a qualifying reading. Its output contains each asset once. A different request might ask for every matching reading, in which case several results for one asset are useful.

Decide that result grain first. A database can match a whole document because one nested member qualifies, then return the entire document or a chosen projection. Filtering the parent does not automatically remove its other array members.
interpretation: A matching asset and its matching readings are different result shapes.

parts.title: 2. Follow an ordinary field path
paragraphs: A path such as sensor.latest identifies a nested field when sensor is an object. A path through an array needs additional semantics because there may be several candidate members. In MongoDB, ordinary dotted conditions on array fields can be satisfied by different members unless the query binds them together appropriately.
That distinction explains the P1 error. The document contains a temperature member and a high-value member, but the pair we need does not exist.
interpretation: Keep the member identity until all conditions referring to that member have been tested.

parts.title: 3. Trace one member through both checks
paragraphs: Expand P1’s array into two rows, each still carrying P1. Keep only temperature rows. Its 65 remains, and the 95 vibration row leaves. Now apply the threshold: the remaining P1 row fails. P2’s 85 passes.
This is an explanatory construction. A database can use another execution plan while preserving the requested same-member meaning. We are learning the semantics before discussing its access cost.
interpretation: The order of these two pure filters can change without changing the selected members.

parts.title: 4. Bind the conditions with $elemMatch
paragraphs: MongoDB’s $elemMatch requires at least one member of the specified array to match all the criteria inside it. Put the kind and threshold in the same member condition.

The query object below is supplied to find. Its value is a data structure, not a string to splice together from untrusted fragments. Applications should build allowed fields and operators deliberately rather than accepting an arbitrary query object from a client.
interpretation: A correct predicate still needs tenant and resource scoping in the service that executes it.

references.title: A same-member reading predicate
references.code: {"readings":{"$elemMatch":{"kind":"temperature","value":{"$gte":80}}}}
description: Pass this query object to a MongoDB collection find operation containing the lesson’s readings arrays.
setup: Use a disposable MongoDB collection outside the browser. The workshop explicitly expands rows instead of parsing this JSON.
interpretation: P1 with temperature 65 and vibration 95 does not match; P2 with temperature 85 does.

parts.title: 5. Return the fields the screen needs
paragraphs: Projection chooses which fields appear in the returned documents. If the screen only needs asset identities, avoid transferring complete histories. In MongoDB an inclusion projection ordinarily includes _id unless it is explicitly excluded. Inclusion and exclusion rules have restrictions, so use the documented form.

Projection does not make private records public. Authorise the query separately, then reduce the returned fields. In our expanded workshop, projection leaves asset_id and deduplication removes repeated matches for the same asset.
interpretation: Deduplication changes the output grain after the member checks are complete.

parts.title: 6. Treat missing and null as explicit query choices
paragraphs: In MongoDB, equality to null can match an explicitly null field or a missing field. Use the appropriate existence and type conditions when those states mean different things. That differs from simply carrying over SQL’s equality behaviour for NULL.

Our reading fixture requires a numeric value in every member. The challenge therefore does not pretend to reproduce MongoDB type comparison, collation or null semantics. If your production records allow malformed members, decide whether to reject them at ingestion, exclude them, or report them separately.
interpretation: Make the dataset contract as explicit as the predicate.

parts.title: 7. Write the member test directly in Python
paragraphs: Python any answers whether at least one member passes. The condition inside it reads kind and value from the same reading dictionary. An empty array contains no qualifying member.
The function returns asset IDs in input order. That is our worksheet contract; a real database query needs an explicit sort when presentation order matters.
interpretation: One member supplies both values to the test.

examples.title: Inspect the two conditions for each member
paragraphs: A shared loop variable prevents a high vibration value from being attached to the temperature label.
examples.code:
readings = [{"kind":"temperature","value":65},{"kind":"vibration","value":95}]
for reading in readings:
    qualifies = reading["kind"] == "temperature" and reading["value"] >= 80
    print(reading["kind"], qualifies)
interpretation: Neither member qualifies, even though the separate kind and threshold conditions both appear somewhere in the array.

parts.title: 8. Keep the case that split the evidence
paragraphs: The first workshop fixture has only temperature readings. A shortcut that separately checks the presence of temperature and any high value may pass it. The changed fixture adds a high vibration value beside a low temperature. That is the case that distinguishes the intended predicate.
Also keep an empty array and an asset with several qualifying members. Those test absence and output grain, neither of which the initial fixture establishes.
interpretation: The next lesson changes a document. A correct match must remain part of the write itself when another editor can act concurrently.

practice.title: Which assets have a high reading of the requested kind?
practice.question: Which assets have a high reading of the requested kind?
task: A high vibration reading must not make a separate low temperature look hot. Find a matching kind and value within the same nested reading.

Implement hot_assets(documents, kind, minimum). Each document has a unique text asset_id and a readings list of dictionaries with text kind and finite numeric value. Return asset IDs in document order when at least one reading has the requested kind and value >= minimum. Return each ID once. Empty arrays do not match. Do not mutate inputs.
Print the IDs for temperature with minimum 80 in the fixture.
practice.starter:
def hot_assets(documents, kind, minimum):
    pass
documents = [{"asset_id":"P1","readings":[{"kind":"temperature","value":65},{"kind":"vibration","value":95}]},{"asset_id":"P2","readings":[{"kind":"temperature","value":85}]}]
print(hot_assets(documents, "temperature", 80))
practice.solution:
def hot_assets(documents, kind, minimum):
    result = []
    for document in documents:
        if any(reading["kind"] == kind and reading["value"] >= minimum
               for reading in document["readings"]):
            result.append(document["asset_id"])
    return result
documents = [
    {"asset_id":"P1","readings":[{"kind":"temperature","value":65},{"kind":"vibration","value":95}]},
    {"asset_id":"P2","readings":[{"kind":"temperature","value":85}]}]
print(hot_assets(documents, "temperature", 80))

title: Can Botie Save a Change Without Erasing Somebody Else’s?
blurb: A technician saves an old copy after another editor has changed the pump. Keep unrelated fields intact and bind the write to the version that was actually reviewed.
openingTitle: The Saved Form Was Already Out of Date
opening: Botie reads pump P1 at version four. While the form is open, a technician changes its status and saves version five. Botie now submits the old form with a new note. Replacing the whole document from that old copy can erase the technician’s update.
We need to be precise about what changes and what must still be true when it changes. A small field update limits what is replaced; a version condition protects the assumptions behind the edit.

history.title: Updating an Object Required More Than Replacing Its Copy
blocks: MongoDB’s early interface included field-level update operators as well as document replacement. That distinction let a caller change a specified part of an object without resending every field. It addressed the practical difference between altering a value and replacing an entire stored record.

Current MongoDB documentation describes atomic single-document writes and recommends including an expected current value in a write filter when concurrent updates must be coordinated. Our version check is a teaching example of that condition. The Python function exposes the rule but does not implement concurrent database access.

reading.experimentTitle: Only apply the edit to the reviewed version
reading.experimentIntro: Compare stored and expected versions, prepare the status change and increment, then return the original document if the comparison fails.
reading.connectionTitle: A write must check the state it depends on
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Apply a status change to the expected version

scene.caption: The workshop draws these steps separately; the server must perform their accepted transition as one atomic write.

parts.title: 1. Distinguish replacement from changing a field
paragraphs: A replacement document describes the whole new record. If it was built from an old copy, fields changed by someone else can disappear or revert. A field update describes a narrower change.

MongoDB $set can change a named field. A dotted path can target a field inside an embedded object; replacing the whole embedded object can remove its siblings. Decide which operation the user actually requested before choosing its representation.
interpretation: A short update is easier to review, but its narrow scope alone does not protect every concurrency assumption.

parts.title: 2. Name the assumption behind this edit
paragraphs: Botie’s form was reviewed at version four. The edit is allowed only if the current record still has that version. Store the expected version separately from the proposed new status.

If the versions differ, return a conflict and let the user inspect the newer state. Blindly retrying the same old replacement merely repeats the unsafe assumption. Some independent increments can safely use a different atomic operation, but that is a different contract.
interpretation: A conflict is information about changed state, not proof that the new status is invalid.

parts.title: 3. Put the condition inside the server write
paragraphs: MongoDB update_one accepts a filter and an update. Include identity and expected version in the filter. Set the status and increment the version in the accepted update. If no document matches, do not report success.

Reading the version in one request and writing by ID in another leaves a race between them. The server-side conditional update closes that gap for this single-document transition. Multi-document invariants need an additional design, often a supported transaction.
interpretation: Our graph makes the logic visible; connecting the pieces is not a substitute for a server atomicity guarantee.

parts.title: 4. Inspect a real conditional update
paragraphs: The reference uses a local disposable MongoDB collection and PyMongo. It assumes the pump already has a version field. matched_count reports whether the filter matched a document. A zero count needs investigation: a stale version and a missing record can both fail the filter.
Do not let an untrusted client choose arbitrary update operators. This endpoint accepts one status field and constructs its own filter and update.
interpretation: The worksheet below uses only the Python standard library.

references.title: Condition a status write on its stored version

source.title: Condition a status write on its stored version

references.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient
collection = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017").perceptron_lab_demo.assets
result = collection.update_one(
    {"_id": "P1", "version": 4},
    {"$set": {"status": "inspect"}, "$inc": {"version": 1}},
)
print(result.matched_count)
description: This is real PyMongo syntax for one conditional update, not browser simulation code.
setup: Install PyMongo and run a disposable local MongoDB server with an assets document {_id:"P1",version:4,status:"monitor"}. Use your own development access configuration; no credentials belong in the lesson.
interpretation: A matched write changes status and version together. Repeating the same expected-version request no longer matches.

parts.title: 5. Keep the identity and unrelated fields unchanged
paragraphs: Our function copies the existing document, sets status and increments version only when the expected value matches. Its API does not accept replacements for asset_id or arbitrary fields. Nested notes are deep-copied so a returned object cannot accidentally modify the original fixture.

This helps distinguish the requested transition from unrelated side effects. Validation still needs a domain policy for allowed statuses in a production service. The exercise accepts nonblank text so the concurrency mechanism stays separate from a status taxonomy.
interpretation: The tests should inspect preserved fields as well as the changed field.

examples.title: A field assignment preserves a sibling
paragraphs: This local operation shows the difference between setting one field and replacing a document.
examples.code:
from copy import deepcopy
original = {"asset_id":"P1","status":"monitor","notes":["keep"]}
changed = deepcopy(original)
changed["status"] = "inspect"
print(changed["notes"])
print(original["status"])
interpretation: The new copy retains the notes, while the original remains unchanged. No concurrent write is simulated here.

parts.title: 6. Separate a conflict from an unknown delivery outcome
paragraphs: A confirmed zero-match response tells us the conditional write did not match. A network timeout may leave the client unsure whether the server applied it. Retrying a version-conditioned update can prevent applying that same version transition twice, but the application may still need to read back or use an operation identity to explain the outcome.
Side effects outside the document, such as notifying a technician, need their own retry policy. Incrementing a version does not make a separate message send atomic with the write.
interpretation: Keep the outcome of the stored transition separate from follow-up effects.

parts.title: 7. Replay the edit against a changed version
paragraphs: The first workshop edit expects and finds version four. The changed fixture stores version five but retains the expected version four. A construction that always sets status will fail this case.

Inspect the notes and identity after both attempts. Then try the accepted result again with the old expected version. The unchanged second result demonstrates the intended rejection rule, while the browser remains a single-threaded model.
interpretation: Use a real database concurrency test before claiming that a deployed endpoint enforces this rule under competing writers.

quiz.prompt: Which explanation is justified?
options: The filter did not match; inspect whether the record is missing or its version changed
The server definitely stored the new status
The record definitely belongs to another tenant
quiz.because: A zero match alone does not identify which condition failed.

given.data: A conditional update matches zero documents. The same filter includes both ID and expected version.

quiz.prompt: Single-document atomicity does not settle whether the notification was sent.
quiz.because: The external effect has its own outcome and retry problem.

given.data: A document update succeeds; a separate notification send then times out.

practice.title: Can the old form leave the newer record untouched?
practice.question: Can the old form leave the newer record untouched?
task: An old form must not overwrite a newer document. Apply its status change only when the version it saw is still current.

Implement set_status(document, expected_version, status). document contains version. Require both versions to be nonnegative integers, excluding booleans, and status to be nonblank text; otherwise raise ValueError. Return {"applied": bool, "document": deep_copy}. On a version match set status and increment version by one; on mismatch retain the original contents. Preserve other fields and do not mutate inputs.
Print the resulting version for the supplied matching edit. This models the transition, not a concurrent server.
hints: Validate versions before comparing them; bool is an int subclass in Python.
Copy before changing status, and return an unchanged copy on a conflict.

tests.name: Malformed versions and blank status

build.title: Apply a narrow edit to the reviewed version
build.problem: Botie’s form may be older than the current pump document.
build.challenge: Compare version with expected, set status and increment version on a copied branch, and keep the original document when the comparison fails.
build.why: The condition protects the reviewed state; the narrow update preserves unrelated data.
hints: Build the proposed status-and-version result on one branch.
Use the stored-versus-expected comparison to choose that branch or the original.
build.limitation: The browser runs an explicit model of the mechanism. It does not connect to MongoDB or Redis, simulate their query planners, or establish their concurrency guarantees.

technicalStart: 3. Put the condition inside the server write

checkpoints.after: 3. Put the condition inside the server write
checkpoints.title: Questions on Parts 1 to 3

questions.prompt: What should the status-edit policy do?
options: Leave the record unchanged and report a conflict or unresolved match
questions.because: The current state no longer matches the reviewed version.

given.data: Stored version is 5. The update filter requires asset P1 and version 4.

questions.prompt: That separate read prevents another writer from changing the record between requests.
questions.because: The expected version needs to be part of the write condition.

given.data: A client reads version 4, then sends a separate update filtered only by asset ID.

title: Can We Find North’s Hot Pumps Without Reading Every Document?
blurb: Use a site index to narrow the candidates, then keep the temperature condition. Inspect what an index saves and which work it leaves behind.
openingTitle: The Answer Is Small, but the Search Keeps Reading Everything
opening: The query correctly finds north-site pumps above the threshold. As the register grows, Botie still reads every site’s documents before returning a short answer. Most of that work is spent rejecting records that could never match the requested site.

An index keeps an additional structure arranged for a particular lookup. It can point us toward candidates sooner. We need to understand what it narrows, which conditions still need checking, and how writes keep that structure current.

history.title: Document Queries Still Needed Access Paths
blocks: MongoDB’s early documentation included indexes alongside document queries. Storing a flexible object did not remove the older database problem of finding a small result without scanning every stored record. A secondary structure could organise selected field values for repeated reads.

Our teaching index groups documents by site. It exposes candidate reduction without claiming to reproduce MongoDB’s B-tree implementation or planner. We then examine a real compound index as a server-side way to support the site and temperature conditions together.

reading.experimentTitle: Narrow by site, then check temperature
reading.experimentIntro: Build site buckets, look up the requested site, apply the remaining threshold, and project asset identities.
reading.connectionTitle: An access path supplies candidates, not permission to skip conditions
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Measure candidates and preserve the predicate
reading.outputLabel: Matching asset IDs after candidate filtering
reading.exampleNote: Candidate counts are exact for this local bucket model. They are not MongoDB execution statistics or timing measurements.

intuition.title: The site bucket is smaller than the register
intuition.explanation: The request is north with temperature at least 80.

scene.caption: A site-only index has not evaluated the temperature condition.

intuition.title: Keep the residual check visible
intuition.explanation: The stored index and final query have different jobs.

scene.caption: Dropping the residual filter returns a larger and incorrect result.

parts.title: 1. Distinguish the answer size from the search work
paragraphs: A query returning one document might inspect a million candidates. Count work along the access path as well as returned results. In a real database, distinguish keys examined, documents examined and documents returned.

Our model counts documents in the selected site bucket. Building that bucket still scans the initial input. We do it inside the worksheet to make its contents visible; a real index is maintained across requests rather than rebuilt for every query.
interpretation: A smaller displayed answer does not by itself demonstrate an efficient lookup.

parts.title: 2. Build an entry that points to the relevant records
paragraphs: For each document, read site and append the document to that site’s bucket. Multiple pumps share a site, so one site key must retain a list. Then a lookup can select just that list.

A database index generally stores keys and references to records in a specialised structure. Copying entire documents into Python lists is an explanatory model. Its memory use and complexity should not be presented as measurements of the server implementation.
interpretation: The grouping operation from the first NoSQL workshop now has a narrower role: candidate selection.

parts.title: 3. Apply conditions the index has not decided
paragraphs: The north bucket contains both a temperature of 65 and one of 85. Looking up north proves only the site condition. Filter those candidates against the threshold before returning results.
If the requested site is absent, its candidate list is empty. That should produce no matches rather than falling back to all documents. A “helpful” fallback would change the query’s meaning.
interpretation: Every surviving record still needs to satisfy the complete predicate.

examples.title: Inspect the bucket before the final filter
paragraphs: A lookup can reduce work while leaving a real decision to make.
examples.code:
buckets = {"north":[{"asset_id":"P1","temperature":65},{"asset_id":"P3","temperature":85}]}
candidates = buckets.get("north", [])
print(len(candidates))
print([row["asset_id"] for row in candidates if row["temperature"] >= 80])
interpretation: There are two candidates and one match. The number of candidates alone does not reveal which pump qualifies.

parts.title: 4. Choose compound field order from the request
paragraphs: A MongoDB compound index orders more than one field. An index beginning with site can support its leading site prefix. Adding temperature after site can support a range within a selected site, depending on the query and plan.

A request using only temperature does not generally receive the same efficient leading-prefix lookup from that field order. Sort requirements can also influence the useful order. Compare actual candidate plans with explain instead of treating a mnemonic as a guarantee.
interpretation: The JSON below is an index key specification passed to create_index or createIndex.

references.title: Index site before temperature for this access pattern

source.title: Index site before temperature for this access pattern

references.code: {"site":1,"temperature":1}
description: This compound index key pattern fits equality on site followed by a temperature range. The 1 values specify ascending index order.
setup: Create the index on a disposable MongoDB assets collection outside the browser, then inspect representative find queries with explain("executionStats") in mongosh.
interpretation: Check keys and documents examined as well as returned rows. The local bucket model does not claim to reproduce the selected plan.

parts.title: 5. Budget for writes and storage too
paragraphs: An index must reflect inserts, deletes and changes to indexed fields. More indexes can improve particular reads while adding storage and write work. A useful test workload therefore includes the writes that occur while the maintenance screen is open.

A unique index also enforces a particular uniqueness rule, subject to the product’s supported configuration. An ordinary non-unique index improves an access path without making a field unique. Do not infer an integrity constraint merely because a query is fast.
interpretation: Keep the reason for each index beside the workload it supports.

parts.title: 6. Know when an array creates several index entries
paragraphs: MongoDB can create multikey indexes for array values. One document can contribute several keys. Counting matching index entries is therefore not always the same as counting distinct matching documents. Compound multikey indexes also have restrictions, including constraints on indexing multiple array fields within one document.

Our site example uses a scalar field deliberately. Before applying its intuition to an array, inspect the actual index rules and the execution plan. Keep the same-member predicate from the previous lesson when array fields are involved.
interpretation: An index accelerates a meaning you have already specified. It does not repair an incorrect predicate.

parts.title: 7. Measure the case where nearly everything matches
paragraphs: If almost every document belongs to north, a site bucket barely narrows the work. Another index or a scan may be more appropriate for the workload. Query planners make choices based on supported plans and their estimates; production distributions can change.

Test a busy site, an absent site and a changed threshold. Record actual server statistics and latency under representative load. The browser’s small candidate count is evidence about this construction only.
interpretation: The following lesson uses selected documents as input to a pipeline, where each stage can change the grain again.

quiz.prompt: What does its use establish?
options: An access path was used; meaningful work reduction still needs measurement
Only 1% of documents must have been examined
The query is necessarily the fastest plan
quiz.because: Low selectivity can leave nearly the whole population as candidates.

given.data: An index on site is selected, but 99% of documents have the requested site.

quiz.prompt: Several index entries may refer to the same document.
quiz.because: Multikey entries and distinct document identities have different grains.

given.data: A document has an indexed array with several members.

practice.title: How many candidates did the site lookup actually leave?
practice.question: How many candidates did the site lookup actually leave?
task: A site lookup can narrow the records examined before applying a temperature rule. Report that intermediate candidate count as well as the matches.

Implement indexed_readings(documents, site, minimum). Each document has asset_id, text site and finite numeric temperature. Group by site, take the requested bucket, then retain temperatures >= minimum. Return {"candidates": the bucket length, "matches": deep copies of matching documents in input order}. An absent site has zero candidates and no matches. Do not mutate inputs.
Print the candidate count and matching asset IDs for north at 80. The index is rebuilt here for inspection; this does not benchmark a server.
practice.starter:
def indexed_readings(documents, site, minimum):
    pass
documents = [{"asset_id":"P1","site":"north","temperature":65},{"asset_id":"P2","site":"south","temperature":99},{"asset_id":"P3","site":"north","temperature":85}]
result = indexed_readings(documents, "north", 80)
print(result["candidates"])
print([row["asset_id"] for row in result["matches"]])
hints: Count the selected bucket before the range filter.
The matching list must still apply temperature.

tests.name: Residual predicate
tests.code:
r=indexed_readings([{"asset_id":"A","site":"x","temperature":1},{"asset_id":"B","site":"x","temperature":8}],"x",5)
assert r["candidates"]==2 and [v["asset_id"] for v in r["matches"]]==["B"]

build.title: Retain the threshold after narrowing by site
build.problem: The register has readings from several sites.
build.challenge: Group records under site, look up the requested site, use the supplied empty list if absent, then filter temperature and project asset_id.

cases.name: The index also returns a cool pump

build.why: Looking up site gives candidate documents from that site. Their temperatures still need checking against minimum before asset_id is selected. The bucket is a local illustration of narrowing a search, rather than a measured database index.
hints: Inspect the whole site bucket before deciding which values qualify.
Do not return every bucket member just because the key matched.
build.limitation: The browser runs an explicit model of the mechanism. It does not connect to MongoDB or Redis, simulate their query planners, or establish their concurrency guarantees.

checkpoints.after: 3. Apply conditions the index has not decided
checkpoints.title: Questions on Parts 1 to 3

questions.prompt: What remains after the site lookup?
options: Check both candidate temperatures and retain P3
Return both because the index was used
questions.because: The site lookup did not decide the range condition.

given.data: North’s bucket has P1 at 65 and P3 at 85. The request is temperature >= 80.
