title: A Fast Feature Lookup Still Has to Mean the Right Thing
blurb: A model needs the right entity, feature definition and available measurements in a fixed order. Use a serving document for that contract while keeping historical training evidence separately.
openingTitle: The Model Received a Reading Quickly. Was It the Right Reading?
opening: Botie’s fault model expects temperature followed by vibration. A fast key lookup returns the fields in a different order, using an older feature definition. The storage request succeeded, but the input no longer means what the model was trained to interpret.
The database choice follows the task. We will assemble a serving record only when its identity, definition and freshness match the model request, and retain an explicit fallback when they do not.

history.title: Separating Fast Current Lookups from Reproducible Training History

sources.title: AWS announces SageMaker Feature Store, December 2020

blocks: As models moved from training jobs into live services, teams had to retrieve the same intended features in two different situations: a large historical training calculation and a quick lookup for one current prediction. Separate implementations could drift apart or repeat the same feature preparation. AWS’s December 2020 SageMaker Feature Store announcement described a shared feature repository with online and offline use in response to those needs.

The two storage modes still have different jobs. A current lookup needs the entity’s serving record quickly; training and analysis may need earlier feature history. Our maintenance service already has historical SQL logic, so this lesson concentrates on the current record and its contract. Storing a feature under the right key does not by itself establish its unit, freshness or suitability for the prediction.

reading.experimentTitle: Check the document before handing values to the model
reading.experimentIntro: Match the entity and feature definition, check decision-time availability and age, then assemble the names in the model’s required order.
reading.connectionTitle: A storage success is only the start of an input check
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Assemble a permitted feature vector
reading.exampleNote: Invented maintenance records. These deterministic local models expose a storage decision; they do not run a distributed database or establish its guarantees.

intuition.title: The same values in the wrong positions are different model inputs
intuition.explanation: The model contract names the positions explicitly.

scene.caption: Object field insertion order is not the model’s feature specification.

parts.title: 1. Choose a store from the operation you need
paragraphs: A keyed serving record can be useful when the request already knows the tenant and asset and needs a small fixed set of inputs quickly. A document can keep related feature values and their metadata together. A relational table can also serve keyed reads; measure the existing system before introducing another database.
A fleet-wide historical training join has a different access pattern. Keep the source of truth, derived feature view and serving copy distinct in the design so each has an owner and a rebuild path.
interpretation: The exercise does not rank database brands. It exposes the contract that any chosen serving path must meet.

parts.title: 2. Name the feature definition that produced the values
paragraphs: A feature name can remain the same while its meaning changes. Vibration might move from a raw reading to an average over a different time window. Units, missing-value rules and preprocessing can also change. Record a version or digest for the definition expected by the deployed model.

The feature definition version is separate from the document schema and source record revision. Compatible field shapes do not prove compatible model inputs. Reject or adapt a mismatch under an explicit policy instead of treating every readable dictionary as usable.
interpretation: Our request requires bearing-v2 exactly. The fixture does not implement semantic version negotiation.

parts.title: 3. Keep observation time and availability time visible
paragraphs: Event time tells us when the measurement describes the asset. Availability time tells us when that value became usable by this serving path. An old event can arrive after the decision it is meant to support.

The earlier SQL lesson showed historical point-in-time selection. This lesson checks one retrieved document against a decision time and a maximum measurement age. It cannot reconstruct an overwritten historical value; if the current record fails, the route stays fallback unless another authorised source supplies suitable evidence.
interpretation: A lookup of today’s latest document is not a historical training query.

examples.title: Check a late arrival against an earlier decision
paragraphs: The event existed in the world before the decision, but the serving path received it afterward.
examples.code:
event_time = 100
available_time = 115
decision_time = 110
print(event_time <= decision_time)
print(available_time <= decision_time)
interpretation: The measurement’s event time alone would admit information the service did not yet have.

parts.title: 4. Assemble by the declared names, never by dictionary order
paragraphs: The model supplies an ordered feature-name list. Read each required name from the document in that order. Check for absent, nonnumeric and nonfinite values before constructing the vector. Extra document fields should not silently become model inputs.

A missing value policy belongs to the model’s definition. If training used a particular imputation rule, serving must use the compatible rule. Our exercise has no trained imputer, so it falls back rather than inventing a zero.
interpretation: The vector’s positions are part of its meaning, even when all its entries are valid numbers.

parts.title: 5. Scope the lookup and retain its actual read contract
paragraphs: The authenticated service establishes tenant scope and builds the permitted key. It should use credentials limited to the needed records and operations. A browser should call the application boundary rather than receive broad storage credentials.

The read mode must suit the operation. A stronger table read can reduce one kind of staleness, but it cannot refresh a feature pipeline that has not produced a new document. Check the measurement metadata even when the storage read succeeds.
interpretation: This external reference obtains a document. It deliberately leaves the application’s feature checks as a separate step.

references.title: Read a development serving document by its complete key
description: The prepared table has string partition key pk. Trusted tenant and asset values must come from the authorised application context.
references.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb", region_name="us-east-1").Table("maintenance_features_dev")
response = table.get_item(
    Key={"pk":"tenant:north:asset:P7"},
    ConsistentRead=True,
)
item = response.get("Item")
print(item is not None)
setup: External setup: install boto3 and provision a disposable development table with the stated key and an example feature item.
Use an authorised SDK role with the required read permission. The browser challenge performs no network calls.
interpretation: A found item still needs entity, definition, availability, age and value checks. Key encoding also needs a collision-free production convention.

parts.title: 6. Keep an explicit outcome when the feature contract fails
paragraphs: A missing document, wrong feature version or stale measurement should not silently proceed to prediction. Decide whether the application can use a documented baseline, request a fresh measurement, or ask for human inspection. That decision depends on the task’s consequences.

Our function returns fallback with an empty vector. A production interface should record the reason without leaking another tenant’s data, and should make clear when it is showing a baseline rather than the requested model result.
interpretation: A fallback is an application outcome. It is not evidence that the asset is healthy.

parts.title: 7. Retain enough evidence to reproduce the prediction
paragraphs: A compact serving record often keeps only the latest state. Retain an appropriate prediction log or immutable references that identify the model, feature definition and input data used, subject to privacy and retention requirements. An offline store can support historical reconstruction if its time and revision semantics are understood.

Compare training and serving transformations with shared cases. A correct training query cannot compensate for a serving adapter that changes units or feature order. Monitor missing inputs, age and version mismatches alongside model performance.
interpretation: The record checks test input compatibility, not the accuracy or fairness of the trained model.

parts.title: 8. Change the feature system without losing its reconstruction path
paragraphs: A new feature definition may require a new serving namespace or an explicit versioned rollout. Backfill the required entities, compare representative predictions, and switch the model and feature contract together. Keep the earlier version long enough for the agreed rollback and audit needs.

If another database is added, account for its projection lag, rebuild process and access boundary. A smaller inference lookup can be worth that work, but a second current copy also creates another place whose freshness must be explained.
interpretation: Botie now has a concrete boundary between finding a document and using it as model input.

Return {"route":"predict","vector": values in fields order} only if record matches all three identifiers, has nonnegative integer event_time <= available_time <= as_of, and as_of minus event_time is at most max_age. Every required feature must be a finite number in record.features. Otherwise return {"route":"fallback","vector":[]}. Preserve inputs.

title: Which Equipment Depends on This Supply?
openingTitle: The Pump Record Does Not Contain the Whole Answer
opening: P7 depends on supply S1. Another pump, P8, depends on P7. Botie needs to distinguish the supply P7 needs from the equipment that needs P7. A list of asset names cannot express that difference.

We need to store the connection itself, including what it means and which way it points. A graph makes those connected records explicit. We can then ask a question by following the relationships that matter to it.
blurb: Represent equipment and its directed dependencies as nodes and relationships before choosing how to query the connections.

history.title: Relationships Became Part of the Stored Model

sources.title: Cypher authors on the historical data-model problem

blocks: The Cypher authors describe Neo4j’s early data-model work in a media asset management system around 2000. Its changing structures, relationships and access-control views made variable-length connection queries useful. This is one documented route into modern property graphs, rather than a claim that Neo4j invented graphs. A property graph gives entities nodes and stores typed relationships with properties of their own.

This changes how we express a dependency question. The relationship is a stored fact we can follow from a known starting asset. It does not make every query faster, and relational tables can represent the same facts with keys and joins.

intuition.title: Read the arrows as dependency statements
intuition.explanation: The arrow means the source requires the target. Follow only the direction the question asks for.

scene.caption: P7 directly depends on S1. P8 directly depends on P7. The arrow convention must be stated before interpreting a path.

parts.title: 1. Give each entity a node
paragraphs: P7 is one pump and S1 is one supply. Keep a separate graph record for each of them, because a connection must say which actual piece of equipment it concerns. Each such entity record is called a node.

Two nodes can share the display name Main unit while retaining different identities. A label groups nodes into categories, such as Asset; a property stores a named value, such as an installation date. A property-graph node can have several labels. Our Python records use kind for one teaching category and id for a stable identifier.
A label groups nodes; it is not the node’s identity. A node can have several labels in a property graph. Our Python records use kind for one teaching category and id for a stable identifier.
interpretation: Begin with the things the application must distinguish, rather than turning every cell into a node.

parts.title: 2. Make the relationship a record too
paragraphs: A relationship connects a source node to a target node and has a type such as DEPENDS_ON. Its direction expresses our modelling convention. Properties on that relationship can describe the connection, such as when the dependency became active.
Two relationships may connect the same nodes for different reasons, or represent separate events. Removing them as duplicates without a domain rule can lose information.
interpretation: The source and target describe the relationship, not which object is more important.

parts.title: 3. Ask a one-hop question before following a chain
paragraphs: For “what does P7 depend on directly?”, find outgoing DEPENDS_ON relationships from P7 and read their target nodes. For “what depends on P7?”, match the incoming direction.
Cypher writes node patterns in parentheses and relationship patterns in brackets. The arrow preserves the convention we drew. RETURN chooses the information to display.
interpretation: A direct neighbour is one relationship away. It is different from every node reachable through a longer chain.

references.title: Read P7’s direct dependencies
description: This is an external Cypher query over the setup graph.
references.code:
MATCH (:Asset {id:$asset})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(s:Asset)
RETURN DISTINCT s.id AS dependency
ORDER BY dependency
setup: In a fresh Neo4j test database, run CREATE (p:Asset {id:'P7'}), (s:Asset {id:'S1'}), (q:Asset {id:'P8'}), (p)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(s), (q)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(p).
Supply parameter asset as the string P7. Use a read-only database role for the query.
interpretation: S1 is the result. Reversing the arrow would answer a different question.

parts.title: 4. Represent the same mechanism with ordinary records
paragraphs: The graph dictionary contains a nodes list and an edges list. Each edge names its source and target by ID. We can inspect the relevant edge records without needing a database server.
This program shows the matching edge identities. The challenge takes the next step and returns distinct dependency IDs instead.
interpretation: These loops demonstrate the model; database storage and query planning remain separate topics.

examples.title: Inspect the outgoing edge records
paragraphs: Only the edge whose source is P7 matches.
examples.code:
edges = [{"id": "d1", "source": "P7", "target": "S1", "type": "DEPENDS_ON"}, {"id": "d2", "source": "P8", "target": "P7", "type": "DEPENDS_ON"}]
print([e['id'] for e in edges if e['type']=='DEPENDS_ON' and e['source']=='P7'])
interpretation: The incoming d2 relationship does not describe a resource P7 requires.

parts.title: 5. Choose graphs because the relationships matter
paragraphs: A graph representation is useful when questions repeatedly follow connected entities, especially through changing numbers of hops. A simple tabular report may be clearer and cheaper in a relational database.

The learning task is to preserve identity, direction and relationship meaning. Storage products differ in constraints, transactions and indexing, so a picture of connected circles is not a complete architecture decision.
interpretation: We will keep the maintenance question stable while adding the machinery needed to answer it reliably.

quiz.prompt: Can they always be merged into one edge?
options: Only if the names are short
quiz.because: Relationship type and identity can distinguish facts with the same endpoints.

given.data: Two relationships connect the same pumps but have different types.

quiz.prompt: Choosing a graph model does not prove that every query will run faster.
quiz.because: Query shape, storage and indexing still determine performance.

given.data: Equipment dependencies can also be represented by relational tables and keys.

Use Python’s standard library on the supplied records. This exercise does not execute Cypher or contact a database.

    # Work through the record relationships here.

title: Are These Two Pumps Actually the Same Pump?
openingTitle: Both Plants Called Their Pump P7
opening: Two plants send Botie a record named P7. Both display names say “Main pump.” If we merge on either field, the graph will connect inspections from two different physical machines.
Identity is the rule that tells us when records refer to the same thing. Before importing relationships, we need an identifier whose scope is clear and whose meaning survives a renamed label.
blurb: Separate durable identity from names, qualify external IDs by their source and detect collisions before merging records.

history.title: A Graph Needed Stable References Beyond Display Names

sources.title: RDF identity and shared resource descriptions, W3C 1999

blocks: Sharing descriptions between systems made identity a practical problem for early web metadata. W3C’s 1999 RDF recommendation addressed exchangeable resource descriptions, where common references matter more than a displayed name. Our property-graph import has a related problem at a smaller scale: local pump IDs need enough scope to refer to the intended entity. The mechanisms differ, but neither model can safely equate entities from matching display text alone.

A source-qualified equipment code makes the scope visible. It prevents an import from treating identical local names as global identifiers, while allowing a later display-name change on the same entity.

intuition.title: Keep the plants’ identities separate
intuition.explanation: The same local code belongs to different source systems.

scene.caption: Matching the display name would incorrectly connect these separate maintenance histories.

parts.title: 1. Ask what makes an entity the same over time
paragraphs: A display name can change, be misspelled or be shared. A source system’s local ID may be stable only inside that system. Use a documented application key, and retain the source ID used to resolve imports.
Database internal identifiers are implementation references, not a substitute for a durable cross-system business key. Avoid persisting assumptions about their reuse across deletion or export/import.
interpretation: The question is which physical or logical thing this record refers to.

parts.title: 2. Qualify a local identifier by its namespace
paragraphs: Treat system and external_id as a pair. Concatenating raw text with an unescaped delimiter can collide when either value contains that delimiter. A structured pair or a carefully encoded identifier preserves the boundary.
Our exercise serialises the pair as compact JSON text. That is a teaching key, not an attempt to choose the permanent identifier scheme for every production system.
interpretation: east/P7 and west/P7 remain distinct even when their display names match.

examples.title: Inspect the qualified keys
paragraphs: The same local code is scoped by a different system.
interpretation: The pair remains unambiguous even if a field later contains punctuation.

parts.title: 3. Merge on identity and set mutable properties separately
paragraphs: MERGE matches the pattern supplied. Including a mutable name in the identity pattern can create a new node after a rename. Match the stable key, then update the appropriate properties.

A uniqueness constraint backs the intended key under concurrent writers. MERGE by itself is not a general promise of global uniqueness. Resolve conflicting source records explicitly before applying updates.
interpretation: A repeated import and a changed entity identity are different events.

references.title: Keep a rename out of the identity pattern
description: This writes only in a disposable database after the stated constraint is installed.
references.code:
MERGE (a:Asset {system:$system, external_id:$external_id})
SET a.name=$name
RETURN a.system, a.external_id, a.name
setup: Use a test database. Run CREATE CONSTRAINT asset_source_key IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Asset) REQUIRE (a.system, a.external_id) IS UNIQUE. This enforces uniqueness of complete pairs; it does not require both properties to be present.
Supply system east, external_id P7 and name Renamed pump as parameters.
interpretation: The stable pair locates the entity. The name is updated after matching. Required-key presence is a separate policy.

parts.title: 4. Do not merge two entities just because a similarity model suggests it
paragraphs: Entity resolution may propose that two vendor codes refer to the same equipment. Keep the proposed mapping and its evidence separate from a confirmed identity merge. A mistaken merge can redirect every attached relationship.
Define who approves ambiguous mappings and how a merge can be audited or reversed. Confidence scores are useful evidence, but they do not define identity by themselves.
interpretation: Identity errors propagate through traversals even when the query syntax is correct.

parts.title: 5. Detect duplicate scoped keys before accepting a batch
paragraphs: Two rows with the same qualified key need a replay or conflict policy. A renamed display field may be a valid update, while differing immutable serial numbers may require review. The challenge only reports repeated keys so a later stage can decide.
Do not let dictionary overwrite order silently make that decision. Keep both source records available until the conflict has been interpreted.
interpretation: A collision report identifies work for a policy; it does not prove the duplicate is fraudulent or incorrect.

quiz.prompt: What should happen before merging?
options: Keep whichever row happened to arrive last
Merge because the names sound similar
quiz.because: A key collision needs interpretation before relationships are redirected.

given.data: A batch contains two rows with the same stable key but conflicting serial numbers.

quiz.prompt: Its use alone is not a general guarantee of unique keys under concurrent updates.
quiz.because: The database constraint and application identity policy are separate parts of the design.

given.data: MERGE is used without a supporting uniqueness constraint.

practice.title: Find repeated source-qualified identities
practice.question: Which source-and-ID pairs identify more than one imported record?
task: Two systems can both use P7 for different equipment. Detect repeated identities within the same source rather than treating matching display names as the key.

Implement repeated_identities(records). Encode each [system, external_id] pair with json.dumps(..., separators=(",", ":")), then return sorted distinct keys appearing more than once. Names do not affect the key.
Use Python’s standard library on the supplied records. This exercise does not execute Cypher or contact a database.
practice.starter:
def repeated_identities(records):
    # Work through the record relationships here.
    return None

print(repeated_identities([{"system": "east", "external_id": "P7", "name": "Main pump"}, {"system": "west", "external_id": "P7", "name": "Main pump"}, {"system": "east", "external_id": "P7", "name": "Renamed pump"}]))
hints: The identity has two parts: system and external_id. Preserve their ordered boundaries when encoding it.
Count json.dumps([system, external_id], separators=(",", ":")) results, then return the sorted keys whose count exceeds one.

title: Who Inspected This Pump?
openingTitle: The Technician Is Two Relationships Away
opening: The pump points to an inspection record. That inspection points to the technician who performed it. Botie must keep those connections together: a technician attached to another pump’s inspection is not an answer.

A pattern describes the connected shape we want to find. Its variables remember which node filled each position, so the next relationship continues from the same inspection rather than starting an unrelated search.
blurb: Match a connected pattern and preserve variable bindings across steps instead of accidentally combining unrelated records.

history.title: A Query Could Describe the Connected Shape It Wanted

sources.title: Francis and colleagues, Cypher language paper, 2018

blocks: Cypher developed inside Neo4j as a declarative property-graph language. Its 2018 language paper explains pattern matching as producing rows of variable bindings: each row records which entities satisfy a connected pattern.

That is why the inspection variable matters. Once a row binds it to I1, the technician relationship must extend from I1. The drawing-like syntax makes this connection visible while leaving physical execution to the database.

intuition.title: Follow the same inspection through both links
intuition.explanation: The two pump histories are separate connected patterns.

scene.caption: A search starting at P7 reaches T1 through I1. T2 belongs to the other branch.

parts.title: 1. Make the starting entity specific
paragraphs: Let a stand for the Asset record whose stable ID is P7. We have assigned a particular node to a query variable; that assignment is called a binding. When the query continues from a, it must continue from this same pump.

Our workshop keeps origin as P7 while current changes to the endpoint reached by each relationship. The path list records how that result row was obtained. An index may make the starting lookup cheaper, but the query still has to state which asset it means.
Our workshop binding keeps origin as P7 while current moves to the endpoint reached by each relationship. The path list is evidence of how that row was obtained.
interpretation: A starting ID and a type condition prevent unrelated records from becoming candidates.

parts.title: 2. Extend one binding at a time
paragraphs: The first expansion binds i to an inspection connected to a. The second expansion uses that same i to find t. Several inspections can produce several valid binding rows.

If we instead collect every inspection and every technician independently, a cross-product can pair unrelated records. Reusing a variable expresses a shared entity, just as matching a key constrains a relational join.
interpretation: Keep the connecting inspection ID visible while learning the pattern.

examples.title: Inspect the first-hop inspection IDs
paragraphs: This program stops after the first relationship rather than answering the full technician question.
examples.code:
g = {"nodes": [{"id": "P7", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "P8", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "I1", "kind": "Inspection", "status": "closed"}, {"id": "I2", "kind": "Inspection", "status": "open"}, {"id": "T1", "kind": "Technician"}, {"id": "T2", "kind": "Technician"}], "edges": [{"id": "h1", "source": "P7", "target": "I1", "type": "HAS_INSPECTION"}, {"id": "h2", "source": "P8", "target": "I2", "type": "HAS_INSPECTION"}, {"id": "t1", "source": "I1", "target": "T1", "type": "CARRIED_OUT_BY"}, {"id": "t2", "source": "I2", "target": "T2", "type": "CARRIED_OUT_BY"}]}
print([e['target'] for e in g['edges'] if e['source']=='P7' and e['type']=='HAS_INSPECTION'])
interpretation: The next step must continue from I1, not from every inspection in the graph.

parts.title: 3. Read the Cypher pattern from left to right
paragraphs: MATCH describes the required graph shape. Variables a, i and t name the bound nodes; relationship types describe which links may connect them. RETURN DISTINCT t.id changes the output from one row per matching route to one row per technician.
DISTINCT is appropriate because the question asks which technicians, rather than how many inspections they performed. For an audit of individual visits, retain the inspection identity instead.
interpretation: Projection and duplicate policy determine the report’s grain.

references.title: Find technicians through the bound inspection
description: The parameter supplies the starting asset without rewriting query structure.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset {id:$asset})-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(i:Inspection)
      -[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(t:Technician)
RETURN DISTINCT t.id AS technician
ORDER BY technician
setup: In an empty Neo4j test database, run CREATE (a:Asset {id:'P7'}),(b:Asset {id:'P8'}),(i:Inspection {id:'I1',status:'closed'}),(j:Inspection {id:'I2',status:'open'}),(t:Technician {id:'T1'}),(u:Technician {id:'T2'}),(a)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(i),(b)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(j),(i)-[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(t),(j)-[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(u).
Supply asset as P7 using your driver’s parameter binding.
interpretation: T1 is returned. A second P7 inspection by T1 would still return that technician once.

parts.title: 4. Pass values through parameters
paragraphs: User-controlled asset IDs belong in driver parameters such as $asset. Do not paste them into a Cypher string. Keep query structure under application control and use reviewed templates for supported questions.

Dynamic labels, property keys and relationship-type syntax depend on the database version. If an application lets a user choose a structural option, validate it against a deliberate allowlist or use the documented supported parameter mechanism. String escaping is not a general substitute for that boundary.
interpretation: Parameter binding preserves query structure; it does not authorise the requested asset.

parts.title: 5. Keep access rules on the path, not only the final result
paragraphs: A tenant restriction on the returned technician is insufficient if the match traverses another tenant’s inspection to get there. Restrict the starting node and every relevant intermediate entity and relationship according to the application’s permissions.
Use least-privilege database roles and an application authorisation layer. Hop limits and result limits control work; they do not grant permission to read a node.
interpretation: The Python exercise uses a fully permitted fixture so the matching mechanism remains clear. The retrieval lesson adds an explicit scope before traversal.

parts.title: 6. Know which route repetitions the language permits
paragraphs: A two-hop pattern and a variable-length traversal have different scopes. Cypher has documented rules for reusing relationships in a match, and newer versions provide additional match modes. Do not assume an arbitrary Python loop exactly implements every Cypher mode.
Our workshop refuses to reuse a relationship already present in a binding’s route. It demonstrates this fixed connected pattern, with complete edge identities visible for inspection.
interpretation: The lesson’s mechanism is a small specified subset, not a browser implementation of the query language.

options: By concatenating it into MATCH text
quiz.because: A parameter preserves the query structure while supplying the requested value.

given.data: A user types an asset ID containing quotes.

quiz.prompt: That necessarily enforces the full traversal’s access boundary.
quiz.because: Intermediate records can expose or influence restricted information too.

given.data: Only final returned nodes are tenant-filtered. Intermediate nodes can belong to any tenant.

title: How Many Inspections Were Actually Completed?
openingTitle: A Repeated Link Has Doubled the Report
opening: P7 has one completed inspection. An import has accidentally recorded two relationships to that same inspection. Botie’s first count says two. The query counted matching relationships, while the maintenance team asked for distinct completed inspections.
Before adding numbers, we need to decide what a matched row represents. We can inspect status on the bound inspection, then remove repeated asset/inspection pairs before counting them.
blurb: Filter bound properties and aggregate at the intended grain, distinguishing paths, relationships and distinct inspection identities.

history.title: Graph Matches Still Produce Rows That Need a Grain

sources.title: Francis and colleagues, Cypher language paper, 2018

blocks: Property-graph queries made relationships part of the pattern a person could ask the database to match. The Cypher authors’ 2018 language paper described this declarative approach in terms of rows of variable bindings. A matched relationship can create another row even when its endpoint is an entity already seen through a different relationship.

Reporting over those bindings therefore needed an explicit choice about what to count and which identities to carry forward. Cypher’s aggregate functions and WITH stages provide that control. Our duplicate inspection link keeps the distinction visible: two relationship matches can refer to one inspection. Counting each inspection once requires a stated identity-based duplicate policy, rather than assuming every matched row is a different event.

intuition.title: Two relationship records point to one inspection
intuition.explanation: The duplicate edge IDs are separate records, but the target inspection identity is the same.

scene.caption: The completed-inspection count is one. Counting relationship matches would answer a different question.

intuition.title: Follow the row meaning through the count
intuition.explanation: These are the duplicate-link records drawn above, inspected stage by stage.

records.label: Closed Inspection filter
cells: Two routes still refer to one inspection

records.label: Distinct asset/inspection pairs
cells: Relationship ID is no longer part of the counted grain

scene.caption: Removing duplicates before deciding which fields define the entity can change the answer.

parts.title: 1. Filter the property of the bound inspection
paragraphs: The status belongs to the inspection node. Require the endpoint to have kind Inspection as well as status closed. A mistyped HAS_INSPECTION edge to a technician is a data-quality failure, not completed inspection work.

Inspect the node reached by each binding, then require status closed. An absent status does not pass that equality condition. Decide separately whether missing statuses should trigger a data-quality report.
interpretation: Relationship meaning and node state are different facts.

parts.title: 2. Write down what one matched row represents
paragraphs: After expansion there is a row for each matched asset/relationship/inspection combination. Two edges to I1 therefore produce two rows. If the desired count is distinct inspections, reduce each row to the asset ID and inspection ID before deduplication.
Deduplicating only the inspection ID globally would lose which asset the count belongs to. Some domains legitimately associate the same inspection with several assets.
interpretation: The distinct pair preserves the grouping identity and the counted entity.

examples.title: Collapse repeated asset/inspection pairs
paragraphs: This small program demonstrates the grain change before aggregation.
examples.code:
pairs=[('P7','I1'),('P7','I1'),('P8','I2')]
print(sorted(set(pairs)))
interpretation: The two P7 matches become one pair while P8 keeps its own association.

parts.title: 3. Keep the grouping variable beside the aggregate
paragraphs: In Cypher, non-aggregate returned expressions define grouping keys. Returning a.id with count(DISTINCT i) gives one count per asset. WITH can name that count for a later condition.
If a later relationship match multiplies the rows, an already computed count can also be repeated. Inspect intermediate cardinality before summing a summary again.
interpretation: The group boundary deserves the same attention in Cypher as in SQL.

references.title: Count inspection entities rather than matched links
description: Only assets with at least one completed match appear in this required-pattern query.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(i:Inspection)
WHERE i.status=$status
WITH a, count(DISTINCT i) AS completed
RETURN a.id AS asset, completed
ORDER BY asset
setup: In an empty Neo4j test database, run CREATE (a:Asset {id:'P7'}),(b:Asset {id:'P8'}),(i:Inspection {id:'I1',status:'closed'}),(j:Inspection {id:'I2',status:'open'}),(t:Technician {id:'T1'}),(u:Technician {id:'T2'}),(a)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(i),(b)-[:HAS_INSPECTION]->(j),(i)-[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(t),(j)-[:CARRIED_OUT_BY]->(u).
Bind status to closed.
interpretation: P7 has one completed inspection. P8 is absent because its inspection is open.

parts.title: 4. Do not manufacture zero rows after a required match
paragraphs: If no completed inspection matches an asset, that asset has no binding row in this query. Grouping cannot produce a group for an entity that vanished earlier.

If the report must show zero, preserve the asset population before matching optional inspections. That will be the next lesson’s problem. Replacing a missing number at the end cannot recreate a missing asset row.
interpretation: Absent groups and groups with zero counts are different query results.

parts.title: 5. Filter before aggregation only when the question calls for it
paragraphs: Closed status qualifies individual inspections, so it belongs before the count. A requirement such as at least two completed inspections belongs after that grouped count has been calculated.
Counting all inspections and then asking whether any status is closed mixes two different questions. Keep row-level conditions and group-level conditions on the stages where their inputs exist.
interpretation: Read the count as a statement about a specific population of distinct inspection identities.

quiz.prompt: Where does the minimum-count condition belong?
options: After computing the per-asset distinct count
quiz.because: The condition describes the group result.

given.data: The task asks for assets with at least two distinct completed inspections.

quiz.prompt: Deduplicating only inspection IDs globally can lose per-asset counts.
quiz.because: The asset/inspection pair preserves each group’s relationship to the entity.

given.data: Two assets can share an inspection in a domain that permits that association.

title: Keep the Pumps That Have No Completed Inspection
openingTitle: The Asset Most in Need of Attention Has Disappeared
opening: Botie’s report correctly counts completed inspections, but P8 is missing. P8 only has an open inspection. The maintenance team needs to see that zero, because it is precisely the pump that may need attention.
A required pattern keeps only successful matches. We need to retain each asset even when its qualifying inspection pattern has no match.
blurb: Use optional graph patterns without losing the starting population or mistaking an unmatched placeholder for a real inspection.

history.title: Absence Became a Result Worth Preserving

sources.title: Francis and colleagues, Cypher language paper, 2018

blocks: A graph pattern is useful for finding connected records, but an ordinary match can erase a starting entity that has no matching relationship. A maintenance report then loses exactly the pump whose missing inspection it was supposed to expose. Cypher’s 2018 language paper described optional pattern matching as part of the language’s row-binding semantics, carrying the outer-join idea into property-graph queries.

OPTIONAL MATCH keeps an existing input row and supplies null bindings where the requested pattern has no match. Starting from the asset register therefore lets an uninspected asset remain visible. The missing inspection and the missing asset are different statements. Our report preserves that difference before it counts completed work.

intuition.title: An open inspection does not satisfy the closed-work pattern
intuition.explanation: Both assets remain in the report, but only one has a qualifying target.

scene.caption: Preserving P8 does not relabel I2 as closed. Its qualifying optional match is absent.

parts.title: 1. Begin with the complete asset population
paragraphs: MATCH (a:Asset) establishes every asset that belongs in the report. The next match is allowed to be absent, but the original a remains bound.
In Python, initialise an empty inspection set for every asset before examining edges. That small ordering decision is what keeps a pump with no relationships at all.
interpretation: The output population must exist before optional evidence is attached.

examples.title: Start a count entry for an isolated asset
paragraphs: No inspection edge is required to establish a report row.
examples.code:
nodes=[{'id':'P7','kind':'Asset'},{'id':'P9','kind':'Asset'}]
print({n['id']:set() for n in nodes})
interpretation: Each empty set can later produce a count of zero.

parts.title: 2. Make the qualifying condition part of the optional pattern
paragraphs: The closed-status condition describes which inspection is an acceptable match. In Cypher, a WHERE associated with OPTIONAL MATCH participates in that pattern’s matching conditions.
Moving the condition to a later WITH/WHERE stage can instead remove a row whose optional inspection is NULL. The resulting query may again omit the asset we meant to preserve.
interpretation: The position of the predicate expresses whether it qualifies a match or filters an already preserved result.

parts.title: 3. Count matched identities rather than preserved rows
paragraphs: count(i) ignores NULL bindings, while count(*) counts rows. An asset with no qualifying inspection has an optional placeholder row, so count(*) can produce one even though no inspection exists.
Use count(DISTINCT i) when repeated relationships should not multiply the same inspection. The grouping asset remains in the output with zero.
interpretation: The placeholder preserves the asset. It is not an inspection.

references.title: Keep zero-completion assets
description: The status predicate belongs to the optional pattern.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset)

title: Follow a Dependency Without Following It Forever
openingTitle: The Dependency List Points Back to the Pump
opening: P7 requires S1, S1 requires S2, and a later import says S2 requires P7. Botie’s recursive search keeps returning to the same equipment. Even if the cycle describes a real feedback dependency, our list of affected entities should not repeat forever.

We need to decide what the traversal is collecting and when a node has already been dealt with. For distinct reachable assets, a breadth-first search can remember visited IDs and stop expansion at a stated depth.
blurb: Separate reachability from path enumeration, handle cycles explicitly and interpret bounded traversal results without promising complete discovery.

history.title: Unknown-Length Connections Needed Repeated Expansion

sources.title: Cypher authors on variable-length traversal needs

blocks: The early Neo4j use case described by the Cypher authors included access through variable-length relationships. A fixed sequence of joins or pattern segments cannot express every unknown chain length conveniently. Graph query languages therefore provide bounded or variable-length path matching.

The repeated step does not decide the answer’s grain. A list of reachable nodes, every distinct path and the shortest path are different questions. Our teaching traversal collects nodes once, which gives the visited set a clear purpose.

intuition.title: A cycle returns to an already discovered node
intuition.explanation: P7, S1 and S2 form a directed cycle. S3 lies one step beyond S2.

scene.caption: With maximum depth 2, the report includes S1 and S2, excludes the starting P7, and makes no completeness claim about deeper dependencies.

intuition.title: Watch the frontier meet the cycle
intuition.explanation: Explore P7 with a maximum depth of two. The queue stores a node and its discovered depth.

records.label: If depth were three
cells: S3 at 3; P7 is already visited

scene.caption: The return edge to P7 cannot restart the search. S3 is outside the depth-two answer, rather than proven unreachable.

parts.title: 1. Choose whether the answer contains nodes or routes
paragraphs: Reachability asks whether a node can be reached at all. Path enumeration retains the route, so two different paths to S2 can both be useful results. A global visited set is suitable for our distinct reachability answer, but would suppress alternative routes if we were trying to enumerate them.
State this before writing a recursion. The same graph can legitimately produce different answers under different output contracts.
interpretation: The challenge returns distinct reachable IDs, excluding the starting ID.

parts.title: 2. Keep a queue of nodes still to explore
paragraphs: Breadth-first search begins with the starting node at depth zero. Remove the oldest queued entry, inspect its outgoing dependency edges and add unseen targets at the next depth. Mark a target visited when it is queued so two frontier nodes do not enqueue it repeatedly.
Because each step has equal hop cost, the first discovery gives the minimum number of relationships from the start. Weighted cost is a different question.
interpretation: The queue is work still to do; the visited set records identities already discovered.

examples.title: Expand the first frontier
paragraphs: This program only inspects the first step. The exercise must keep expanding safely.
interpretation: The next frontier comes from outgoing edges of the current frontier, not every edge in the graph.

parts.title: 3. Bound a real path query deliberately
paragraphs: The Cypher range *1..3 requests paths from one through three relationships. DISTINCT on the returned node removes repeated endpoints from different matching paths. The query below also excludes the starting node if a cycle returns to it.

Cypher’s relationship-reuse rules and a global-visited BFS are different mechanisms. For this bounded reachability question their intended endpoint set aligns, but the path rows and search work need not be identical.
interpretation: A hop bound says how far the query may explore; it does not certify the graph has no deeper nodes.

references.title: Ask for dependencies within three hops
description: This uses established variable-length relationship syntax; newer quantified syntax is another documented option.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset {id:$asset})-[:DEPENDS_ON*1..3]->(d:Asset)
WHERE d <> a
RETURN DISTINCT d.id AS dependency ORDER BY dependency
setup: In an empty test database run CREATE (p:Asset {id:'P7'}),(a:Asset {id:'S1'}),(b:Asset {id:'S2'}),(c:Asset {id:'S3'}),(p)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(a),(a)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(b),(b)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(p),(b)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(c).
Bind asset to P7.
interpretation: The result includes S1, S2 and S3. The chosen three-hop cap is part of the report’s scope.

parts.title: 4. Interpret the depth boundary honestly
paragraphs: At depth two, S2 has been discovered but its outgoing edges are not expanded. S3 is therefore absent from the two-hop result. Calling that result “all dependencies” would overstate what was checked.

A depth cap also does not bound the number of nodes tightly in a high-degree graph. Add operational time and result-size limits, and report truncation or failure rather than presenting partial results as a complete answer.
interpretation: The workshop caps the reachable set to protect responsiveness and reports a limit error rather than silently trimming it.

parts.title: 5. Filter allowed relationships before expanding them
paragraphs: An edge type restriction prevents unrelated meanings from entering the traversal. A tenant or access restriction serves a different purpose: it determines which data the caller may use at all. Apply those restrictions before or during expansion, including intermediate nodes.
A shallow traversal can still read forbidden data. Treat depth and output limits as resource controls, never as permission checks.
interpretation: The fixture is fully permitted. Later retrieval applies a scoped graph before either dependency or document expansion.

parts.title: 6. Inspect cycles as domain evidence as well as an algorithm concern
paragraphs: A cycle in a supply dependency may be an impossible import or a real mutually dependent system. A visited set makes our computation terminate, but it does not decide whether the cycle is valid in the domain.

Keep enough edge identity and provenance to investigate it. If the application requires a directed acyclic hierarchy, enforce or audit that separate invariant rather than assuming the traversal repaired the data.
interpretation: Algorithmic termination and domain correctness solve different problems.

title: The Route with Fewer Stops Takes Longer
openingTitle: Two Hops Are Slower Than Three
opening: The maintenance cart can reach B directly from A in nine minutes. Going through C takes four minutes. A search that chooses the fewest relationships selects the direct route, even though the crew asked for the quickest one.

We need to define what “shortest” measures. Hop count treats every edge equally. Travel time assigns a cost to each edge, so the route choice must compare accumulated costs rather than the number of connections.
blurb: Distinguish minimum-hop paths from minimum-cost paths and implement Dijkstra’s nonnegative-cost frontier with explicit unreachable and tie semantics.

history.title: Shortest Routes Needed a Cost-Aware Search

sources.title: Dijkstra, A note on two problems in connexion with graphs, 1959

blocks: Dijkstra’s 1959 paper described a procedure for finding the shortest route between nodes in a weighted graph. The useful step is to separate tentative distances from settled ones: with nonnegative lengths, the least tentative distance cannot later be improved by taking a detour through a more expensive unsettled node.

Dijkstra’s shortest-path method is used to find minimum accumulated cost in graphs with suitable nonnegative weights. Neo4j’s Graph Data Science documentation exposes that method separately from simple hop-count path matching. The algorithm keeps the cheapest unsettled distance visible rather than committing to the first route discovered.

For our cart, that distinction allows a route with an extra stop to win. The Python exercise implements a small nonnegative-weight version so we can inspect why the earlier expensive route is replaced.

intuition.title: Compare route costs rather than counting arrows
intuition.explanation: Each edge label is travel time in minutes.

scene.caption: The cheapest A-to-D route goes through C and B. More relationships can still mean less total time.

intuition.title: Replace a tentative route when a cheaper one appears
intuition.explanation: The pending column shows the heap entries after each expansion, including entries that later become stale.

records.label: D at 5
cells: The stale B 9 entry cannot improve the answer

scene.caption: A tentative cost is replaced only by a cheaper route. With nonnegative edge costs, the cheapest current candidate can be settled.

parts.title: 1. Choose the quantity to minimise
paragraphs: Minimum hops answers how many links must be followed. Minimum travel time answers how much edge cost accumulates. Neither is inherently the correct question; the operational objective decides.
A directed route can be traversable in one direction only. If a corridor is bidirectional, represent both permitted directions or use a graph projection whose orientation is deliberately defined.
interpretation: Our route graph is directed, and every minutes property uses the same unit.

parts.title: 2. Replace first discovery with the best known cost
paragraphs: B is first discovered with cost nine through the direct edge. When C is expanded, the route through C offers a lower cost to B. The algorithm updates B’s best value rather than treating its first discovery as final.

A priority queue makes the lowest current candidate the next one to process. Older queued entries for a node can become stale after an improvement, so the code checks them against the best-known distance.
interpretation: The visited-on-discovery rule from unweighted BFS does not implement this weighted objective.

examples.title: Compare the two routes to B
paragraphs: This isolates the accumulated-cost comparison before implementing a search.
examples.code:
direct=9
via_c=2+2
print({'direct':direct,'via_C':via_c})
interpretation: The longer-in-hops route has the smaller time cost.

parts.title: 3. Use the heap to revisit a tentative choice
paragraphs: A Python heap stores the candidate with the smallest first tuple value at its front. heappush adds a candidate; heappop removes the cheapest one. The second tuple item is the node ID, which also provides a deterministic tie break for these string IDs.

We do not need to find and delete an old heap entry when a better route appears. Update best and push the cheaper candidate. When the old entry eventually comes out, compare its cost with best and skip it if they differ. The program below isolates that mechanism before the challenge adds graph traversal.
interpretation: The heap remembers candidates. The best dictionary records the current best estimate for each node.

examples.title: Replace B’s nine-minute candidate
paragraphs: Suppose A has already produced candidates C at two and B at nine. Expanding C finds a cheaper way to B.
examples.code:
import heapq
best={'B':9,'C':2}
pending=[(2,'C'),(9,'B')]
heapq.heapify(pending)
cost,node=heapq.heappop(pending)
proposed=cost+2  # C to B takes two minutes.
if proposed < best['B']:
    best['B']=proposed
    heapq.heappush(pending,(proposed,'B'))
while pending:
    cost,node=heapq.heappop(pending)
    if cost != best[node]:
        print('skip',node,cost)
        continue
    print('use',node,cost)
interpretation: The old entry remains in the heap but cannot overwrite the improved estimate. This example teaches one relaxation, not the full shortest-path function.

parts.title: 4. Why nonnegative weights matter
paragraphs: Once the cheapest candidate is settled, nonnegative future edges cannot produce a cheaper route by leaving that settled frontier and later subtracting cost. That property supports Dijkstra’s decision rule.

Negative weights require another algorithm and careful treatment of negative cycles. A missing weight is not automatically zero. Validate the graph projection’s weight field and units before running the method.
interpretation: The exercise accepts zero-cost edges but rejects negative or nonfinite costs.

parts.title: 5. Do not mistake Cypher shortestPath for weighted optimisation
paragraphs: A hop-oriented shortestPath pattern does not automatically minimise a minutes property just because the relationship contains it. Weighted algorithms such as GDS Dijkstra use an explicitly projected weight.

For the tiny setup below, the reference query enumerates bounded paths and orders their summed cost. It exposes the objective in ordinary Cypher, but it is not a scalable replacement for a dedicated weighted algorithm.
interpretation: This reference is limited to a tiny acyclic graph with all relevant paths within three hops.

references.title: Inspect accumulated route costs on the tiny graph
description: The small bounded enumeration is for explanation, not a production path planner.
references.code:
MATCH p=(a:Location {id:$start})-[:ROUTE*1..3]->(b:Location {id:$target})
WITH p, reduce(total=0, r IN relationships(p) | total+r.minutes) AS cost
RETURN [n IN nodes(p) | n.id] AS route, cost
ORDER BY cost, route
LIMIT 1
setup: In a fresh test database run CREATE (a:Location {id:'A'}),(b:Location {id:'B'}),(c:Location {id:'C'}),(d:Location {id:'D'}),(a)-[:ROUTE {minutes:9}]->(b),(a)-[:ROUTE {minutes:2}]->(c),(c)-[:ROUTE {minutes:2}]->(b),(b)-[:ROUTE {minutes:1}]->(d),(c)-[:ROUTE {minutes:20}]->(d).
Bind start A and target D. Use GDS Dijkstra with an appropriate projection for larger weighted problems.
interpretation: The route A,C,B,D has cost 5. The LIMIT does not prevent the preceding enumeration from doing substantial work on a different graph.

parts.title: 6. Keep unreachable and zero-cost answers distinct
paragraphs: If the destination cannot be reached, return no distance, represented by None in the exercise. If start equals target, the empty route has cost zero. A reachable route can also legitimately have zero total cost.
Do not replace absence with zero. That would make a disconnected workshop look as though the cart were already there.
interpretation: The challenge returns the minimum cost only, so equally cheap paths do not require a route-selection tie break.

parts.title: 7. A computed route is only as current as its allowed edges
paragraphs: A closed corridor or a restricted area must be removed before routing. Applying permission checks only after choosing the cheapest path can select an unusable route and obscure valid alternatives.

Travel times may change while the cart moves. A graph snapshot provides an estimate under stated conditions, not a guarantee about the physical journey. Validate operational safety separately from minimising cost.
interpretation: The workshop filters ROUTE edges and computes costs from the supplied snapshot.

title: Which Rules Must Every Asset Write Preserve?
openingTitle: The Second P7 Broke the Meaning of Every Match
opening: A query that used to locate one P7 now finds two nodes. Some relationships point to one copy and some to the other. Botie cannot repair that ambiguity by choosing whichever match appears first.

The application needs a durable identity rule enforced at the write boundary. An index can help find an asset, but a constraint is what rejects a forbidden duplicate. Those responsibilities are related without being interchangeable.
blurb: Separate key presence, uniqueness and lookup performance, then audit existing data before installing graph constraints.

history.title: Flexible Records Still Needed Shared Invariants

sources.title: Neo4j constraint creation and backing indexes

blocks: Property graphs let applications evolve node properties without requiring every category to have an identical record shape. As those graphs became application databases, shared write rules remained necessary. The Cypher language paper includes schema-definition capabilities alongside queries and updates; current Neo4j constraints make selected identity and property requirements enforceable.

The purpose here is narrower than making every node identical. All Asset nodes need an unambiguous application identity, while different kinds of equipment can still have different optional properties.

intuition.title: Duplicate node identities split the maintenance history
intuition.explanation: The display shows two different stored nodes with the same forbidden application key.

scene.caption: A uniqueness constraint prevents new duplicate keys. Existing conflicting nodes need review before the constraint can be created.

parts.title: 1. Separate presence from uniqueness
paragraphs: A uniqueness rule prevents repeated known key values. It does not necessarily require every node to carry that key. A node with no application ID can remain difficult to address even when all present IDs are unique.

For this import audit, a valid ID is a nonempty string. Count missing, blank or nonstring IDs separately from duplicate known IDs. Production databases may offer key, existence and type constraints with edition-specific availability.
interpretation: Passing the duplicate check does not establish that every record has a usable identity.

parts.title: 2. Audit the existing records first
paragraphs: Creating a constraint over conflicting data can fail. Inspect the duplicate groups and missing keys, decide which nodes are genuine duplicates, and preserve their attached relationships while repairing them.

Do not delete a duplicate-looking node simply because its ID repeats. Its relationships may contain the only copy of an inspection association. A migration needs a reviewed reconciliation rule and a recovery path.
interpretation: The exercise reports problems without changing the records.

examples.title: Count missing key values separately
paragraphs: These rows have no duplicate valid ID, but one lacks any ID.
examples.code:
nodes=[{'id':'P7'},{'name':'Unregistered pump'}]
print(sum(not isinstance(n.get('id'),str) or not n['id'] for n in nodes))
interpretation: An empty duplicate list would not make this import valid.

parts.title: 3. Install the identity constraint deliberately
paragraphs: The first statement below creates uniqueness for Asset.id. Neo4j backs property uniqueness constraints with an index, so it can also support the identity lookup. This does not turn every other property into a constrained field.

Property existence and type constraints, and node-key constraints, have edition/version requirements. Validate required fields at ingestion and use the database-supported rule set for the deployment; do not advertise a uniqueness-only rule as mandatory-key enforcement.
interpretation: A query plan and a data invariant answer different questions.

description: Run schema changes with an authorised administrative role in a disposable test database.
setup: Use an empty Neo4j test database or first repair duplicate Asset.id values.

This uniqueness constraint does not require id on every Asset. For deployments that support it, CREATE CONSTRAINT asset_id_required IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Asset) REQUIRE a.id IS NOT NULL adds an existence rule; check the edition requirement before running it.
interpretation: The installed constraint rejects duplicate known IDs. Missingness remains a separate obligation.

parts.title: 4. Use indexes for the predicates that actually locate nodes
paragraphs: An index on a label/property combination can help a selective starting lookup. It does not automatically speed every relationship traversal or every expression applied to that property.
Inspect the plan for the actual query and representative parameters. Extra indexes consume storage and add write work, so create them around measured access patterns rather than every possible field.
interpretation: Index presence is not proof that a particular query uses it.

parts.title: 5. Keep application rules alongside database rules
paragraphs: A uniqueness constraint does not verify that an asset belongs to the caller’s tenant or that a proposed dependency is physically sensible. The database may enforce some structural rules while application policy checks the rest.
Document which boundary owns each rule and test writes through every supported path. A bulk loader that bypasses an application check can otherwise reintroduce the same problem.
interpretation: The workshop’s independent duplicate and missing-ID branches are an audit, not an installed database constraint.

task: An import can reuse a valid ID or fail to supply one at all. Report those as separate problems before linking records.

Implement key_issues(nodes). Return [sorted_duplicate_ids, unusable_count]. A usable ID is a nonempty string. Count each repeated usable ID once; missing, blank and nonstring IDs contribute only to unusable_count. Do not mutate inputs.
Use Python’s standard library on the supplied records. This exercise does not execute Cypher or contact a database.
practice.starter:
def key_issues(nodes):
    # Work through the record relationships here.
    return None

print(key_issues([{"id": "P7", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "P7", "kind": "Asset"}, {"kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "P8", "kind": "Asset"}]))
practice.solution:
def key_issues(nodes):
    from collections import Counter
    usable=[n.get('id') for n in nodes if isinstance(n.get('id'),str) and n['id']]
    counts=Counter(usable)
    return [sorted(k for k,n in counts.items() if n>1),len(nodes)-len(usable)]

print(key_issues([{"id": "P7", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "P7", "kind": "Asset"}, {"kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "", "kind": "Asset"}, {"id": "P8", "kind": "Asset"}]))
hints: Keep a frequency table for usable IDs and a separate invalid-record counter. For this exercise usable means a nonempty string; whitespace-only strings are not additionally rejected.
Return a two-element list: sorted repeated usable IDs, then the invalid count. Each repeated ID appears once in the first list.

title: The Graph Changed While the Approval Was Waiting
openingTitle: An Approved Plan Is Now Based on an Old Record
opening: Botie prepared a change for P8 when its revision was three. While a person reviewed that proposal, another technician updated P8 to revision four. Applying the old plan without checking would overwrite a decision made with newer information.

We need to separate preparing a change, approving it and committing it against current state. A snapshot check can reveal an obviously stale request, but only the database transaction can protect the final write from concurrent changes.
blurb: Treat approvals and snapshot checks as preparation, then use authorised, parameterised transactions with explicit conflict and retry behaviour.

history.title: Connected Updates Needed a Transaction Boundary

sources.title: Francis and colleagues, Cypher language paper, 2018

blocks: An application update can span several stored facts. Creating an inspection and connecting it to an asset should not leave an unexplained half-result if execution fails between writes. Transaction-processing work, including Gray’s 1981 account, made the commit-or-rollback unit explicit. Property-graph languages brought updates to nodes and relationships into that same application-database problem; the Cypher authors documented the language in 2018.

Our maintenance approval adds evidence to the transaction’s meaning. A person approved a particular action for a particular observed state, so the database must recheck that state before committing. Neo4j drivers may retry selected transient transaction failures, which means an external effect inside the retried function needs separate handling. A transaction protects its database unit of work, not every action the caller might perform elsewhere.

intuition.title: Approval belongs to a particular proposed change
intuition.explanation: The stored asset has advanced beyond one proposal’s expected revision.

scene.caption: Only P7 passes the snapshot comparison. Passing it still does not commit the change or protect against a later concurrent write.

parts.title: 1. Keep the request separate from the stored entity
paragraphs: A proposal should identify its target, intended change, caller and the state it was based on. The approval should be tied to that proposal rather than a general reusable “yes.”

Our exercise deliberately selects eligible target IDs only. It does not apply status changes, validate arbitrary payloads or claim to perform an atomic update. Those responsibilities belong to the eventual authorised executor.
interpretation: A useful preflight result says which requests need further execution checks.

parts.title: 2. Require explicit approval and the expected snapshot
paragraphs: The proposal carries the revision of the target as it was when reviewed. That recorded view is a snapshot; it is not a reservation preventing later edits. Compare expected_revision with the target’s current snapshot revision, and exclude a missing target.

Only the Boolean value true counts as approval in this example. Text that spells true is a string, which is a different typed value. The distinction keeps an ambiguous response from silently becoming permission to change a record.
A stale request should return to review or be recalculated according to policy. Quietly changing expected_revision to the latest number would remove the protection the field was meant to provide.
interpretation: Approval and freshness are independent conditions.

examples.title: Inspect the revision mismatch
paragraphs: This program reports the two revisions rather than applying a change.
interpretation: The approved request used older state. A new plan may need new approval.

parts.title: 3. The commit must enforce the concurrency rule
paragraphs: Between a browser preflight and a server write, another update can occur. Use a database-supported transaction and locking or conditional-update strategy whose isolation semantics have been checked for the deployed database.

A read in one transaction followed by an unconditional write in another is not optimistic concurrency control. Even a predicate and write in one statement need the engine’s documented concurrent-update semantics; do not assume a snapshot comparison creates a lock.
interpretation: The workshop intentionally stops before commit and cannot establish transaction isolation.

parts.title: 4. Parameterise the approved write and verify its result
paragraphs: The external example demonstrates the simpler unit: update one uniquely identified asset inside an application-managed transaction, then verify exactly one target was returned before committing. It does not implement the revision conflict policy by itself.

Use an authorised driver session, a parameterised reviewed query and explicit rollback when the matched target count violates the contract. Do not execute arbitrary Cypher generated by a user or model as the writer role.
interpretation: Application validation, authorisation and concurrency control remain required around this query.

references.title: A parameterised write inside the executor transaction
description: This query must be run inside the transaction described in setup, not pasted into an unrestricted production console.
references.code:
MATCH (a:Asset {id:$asset})
SET a.status=$status
RETURN a.id AS updated
setup: In a disposable database, create unique Asset.id values and install the uniqueness constraint from the preceding lesson.
Use a Neo4j driver transaction. Bind asset P7 and a validated status. Read the returned rows, require exactly one, and roll back on mismatch before commit.
For revision-sensitive requests, add a tested locking/conditional-update protocol at that same transaction boundary. This snippet does not supply that protocol.
interpretation: The query changes one validated field. The transaction determines whether that change commits.

parts.title: 5. Retries must not repeat outside effects
paragraphs: A driver-managed transaction function may be invoked again after a transient failure. Sending an email, charging a service or issuing a physical maintenance action inside that retried function can repeat the effect even if the database transaction rolled back.

Keep external actions out of automatically retried database callbacks. Where an action must follow a commit, use a durable outbox or another explicit delivery design with idempotency keys and reconciliation. A database rollback cannot undo an email already sent.
interpretation: Exactly-once business effects require more than calling MERGE or retrying a transaction.

parts.title: 6. MERGE and DELETE need their own identity and scope rules
paragraphs: MERGE matches or creates the supplied pattern. Match stable identity separately from mutable fields and back required uniqueness with constraints. A replayed logical request should have a stable idempotency identity if its outcome must be reconciled.

DELETE of a node with relationships and DETACH DELETE have different consequences. Broad deletion patterns can remove connected history. Preview the exact target identities and use least-privilege permissions; the lesson’s preflight does not authorise a deletion.
interpretation: Read the write pattern as a description of everything it may affect.

parts.title: 7. Test stale, missing and ambiguously typed requests
paragraphs: The challenge checks explicit approval, known target and matching integer revision. It retains each eligible target ID once for this report. Real executors still need per-request identity, payload validation and conflict handling when several proposals target the same node.
That limited output makes the lesson’s claim testable: the records qualify for further execution checks under this snapshot. It never says those changes have been safely committed.
interpretation: Keep the displayed result at the same level of authority as the mechanism that produced it.

quiz.prompt: What can happen?
options: The email can be sent more than once
The database always rolls back the email
quiz.because: External effects do not share the database rollback boundary.
