title: A Replayed Import Must Not Create Another Relationship
openingTitle: The Loader Lost Its Response and Tried Again
opening: Botie imports a dependency file, but the connection drops before the loader receives a success response. Retrying every row with CREATE can add another copy of relationships already committed. Some rows also refer to assets that have not been imported.
We need stable identities for imported relationships and an explicit route for records that cannot be applied. An import is a reconciliation process, not simply a loop that draws every edge it sees.
blurb: Stage graph imports by stable identity, distinguish exact replays from conflicts and preserve rejected records instead of silently losing relationships.

history.title: Bulk Data Exchange Had to Survive Partial Progress

sources.title: Francis and colleagues, Cypher language paper, 2018
Mohan and colleagues: ARIES recovery using write-ahead logging (1992)

blocks: An import has two histories to preserve: where the source identities came from and which work has already committed. Database recovery methods such as ARIES used logged information to recognise and reconstruct changes after failure. Application-level imports encounter a related interruption when the database commits a batch but its response never reaches the loader.

Modern graph loaders combine row-oriented input with identity matching and merge operations. Neo4j’s LOAD CSV and MERGE documentation gives concrete interfaces, while transaction batching defines how much work can commit together. Our stable source IDs and saved checkpoint let a retry recognise committed work. They form an application replay policy. MERGE still needs the appropriate constraints when the import must enforce uniqueness.

intuition.title: One new edge is resolvable and another has no endpoint
intuition.explanation: The source batch contains an already known relationship and an unresolved asset reference.

scene.caption: A rejected relationship stays in an import report. Creating a mystery endpoint would invent an asset unless that policy was explicitly chosen.

parts.title: 1. Load or resolve entity identities before connecting them
paragraphs: A relationship requires both endpoints. Import node identities first or resolve them against a known registry. An unmatched endpoint should enter a rejection or deferred-resolution queue with its source row identity.
Silently skipping a MATCH failure can make a loader appear successful while losing relationships. Inventing missing nodes with MERGE can be equally misleading when an ID is misspelled.
interpretation: Choose whether unresolved endpoints are rejected, deferred or explicitly created; do not let query structure choose by accident.

parts.title: 2. Give each imported relationship a replay identity
paragraphs: A stable source relationship ID can identify a logical record across retries. The same ID with the same complete payload is a replay. The same ID with different endpoints, type or properties is a conflict under this lesson’s immutable-import policy.

If the source supports revisions, add a documented version rule rather than treating every changed payload as a harmless repeat. A relationship’s minutes or observation time can matter as much as its endpoints.
interpretation: Identity equality and payload equality are separate checks.

examples.title: Notice a property conflict on a reused ID
paragraphs: The endpoints are identical, but the stored payload is different.
interpretation: A replay check that compares endpoints alone would conceal the changed travel-time fact.

parts.title: 3. Use a parameterised batch to expose the import operation
paragraphs: UNWIND turns a bound list parameter into rows. Matching both endpoint nodes resolves the relationship’s meaning before MERGE uses its stable ID. The example deliberately uses one approved relationship type rather than accepting arbitrary user query structure.

The executor must validate unique IDs and detect changed payload conflicts before this write. It must also compare processed-row counts with the staged batch so unmatched endpoints do not disappear unnoticed.
interpretation: A successful query response does not prove every source row was imported.

references.title: Apply a prevalidated dependency batch
description: Run this only after rejecting unresolved endpoints and reused-ID conflicts.
references.code:
UNWIND $rows AS row
MATCH (a:Asset {id:row.source}), (b:Asset {id:row.target})
MERGE (a)-[r:DEPENDS_ON {import_id:row.id}]->(b)
RETURN row.id AS imported ORDER BY imported
setup: Use a disposable current Neo4j database supporting relationship property uniqueness constraints. Run CREATE CONSTRAINT import_asset_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Asset) REQUIRE a.id IS UNIQUE. Then run CREATE CONSTRAINT dependency_import_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR ()-[r:DEPENDS_ON]-() REQUIRE r.import_id IS UNIQUE. These uniqueness constraints do not require property presence; the importer validates it.
Create the complete stored fixture: CREATE (p:Asset {id:'P7'}),(q:Asset {id:'P8'}),(s:Asset {id:'S1'}),(p)-[:DEPENDS_ON {import_id:'a'}]->(s).

Bind rows to [{id:'a',source:'P7',target:'S1'},{id:'new',source:'P8',target:'S1'}] through the driver. This particular write schema has only immutable endpoint identities and the fixed DEPENDS_ON type; reject additional fields rather than silently ignoring payload properties.

Run in a transaction after source and endpoint validation. The first row matches the stored relationship and the second creates one. Running the same batch again should match both. A reused import ID on different endpoints must fail the uniqueness constraint and enter conflict handling. Reconcile returned IDs against the staged input so an unmatched endpoint is not silently lost.
interpretation: The two import identities are returned on the first and repeated run. Endpoint uniqueness and relationship import-ID uniqueness back this deliberately narrow immutable schema. A richer mutable payload requires its own version/conflict protocol; the workshop demonstrates full-payload classification without committing a database write.

parts.title: 4. Make batch atomicity and checkpoints explicit
paragraphs: A large import may commit in batches to control memory and transaction size. If batch three fails, batches one and two may already be durable. The loader must resume from a checkpoint that corresponds to committed work, not merely rows read from the file.
Record batch IDs, source versions, accepted counts and rejection counts. Keep checkpoints and sink updates consistent through an appropriate transaction or recovery protocol.
interpretation: Batching reduces the rollback unit; it does not make the whole source file one atomic transaction.

parts.title: 5. Validate properties before they become graph facts
paragraphs: CSV text needs explicit type conversion and missing-value rules. A blank date is not an arbitrary default instant, and an invalid cost must not enter a weighted path algorithm. Parameter binding protects query structure but does not validate the values’ domain meaning.
Reject or quarantine malformed records with enough non-sensitive context to repair them. Keep credentials, personal data and restricted payloads out of casual loader logs.
interpretation: Import quality directly changes the answers later traversals can produce.

parts.title: 6. Distinguish the admission list from the import audit
paragraphs: The exercise returns IDs of new resolvable edges only. The workshop exposes a richer classification before selecting ready rows: repeat, conflict, dangling and invalid records remain inspectable in the intermediate output.
Both mechanisms preserve the original graph. They stage work for a real importer rather than pretending a browser result has committed anything.
interpretation: Inspect the classification component when an expected ID does not reach the ready list.

title: Why Did One More Hop Make the Query So Expensive?
openingTitle: A Small Result Can Hide a Large Search
opening: Botie returns three equipment IDs, but the query takes seconds. It began at every asset, followed broad relationship types and only then filtered to P7. The small final answer does not show how many candidates the database inspected.

We need to look at where the search starts and how intermediate rows grow. An index can narrow the start, while selective patterns and early justified predicates can limit expansion. We should measure the plan instead of judging work from the final row count.
blurb: Read query plans, reason about candidate expansion and compare access paths without confusing a toy operation count with measured database performance.

history.title: Declarative Graph Queries Needed Physical Execution Plans
blocks: A declarative pattern describes the answer, leaving the database to choose how to find it. The Cypher authors describe Neo4j’s cost-based planning and physical execution operators. This separation lets equivalent logical queries use different access paths.

For our maintenance graph, locating one asset before expanding relationships can avoid unrelated work. The improvement is a claim to verify in a real plan, because cardinality estimates, indexes and graph degree all affect execution.

intuition.title: An anchored question should not begin from every component
intuition.explanation: Only the outgoing relationships of P7 are candidates for its one-hop question.

scene.caption: The workshop counts candidate checks under two specified algorithms. Those counts are not milliseconds or a prediction of Neo4j’s optimiser.

intuition.title: Count the work that the teaching model actually measures
intuition.explanation: The fixture has two DEPENDS_ON edges: P7 to S1, and P8 to P7. The adjacency lookup already exists.

scene.caption: Both strategies deduplicate starts. The comparison excludes building the lookup and makes no latency claim.

parts.title: 1. Locate the start before explaining the expansion
paragraphs: An equality predicate on a constrained Asset.id can provide a selective starting point. A label narrows the entity category; a property condition narrows the instance. A traversal from a huge unfiltered population asks a different amount of work even if the final WHERE keeps one asset.
The optimiser may reorder compatible operations. Write clear predicates, then inspect the physical plan rather than assuming text order is execution order.
interpretation: The logical query and the physical access path are connected but different descriptions.

parts.title: 2. Count candidate checks in a deliberately small model
paragraphs: A naive one-hop loop scans every edge for each distinct start. An already built adjacency lookup inspects only outgoing edges for those starts. Comparing these counts makes the access-path idea tangible.
Building and maintaining the adjacency lookup costs work and memory too. Our counter excludes that setup and is not an estimate of database latency, cache behaviour or storage I/O.
interpretation: State what the measured quantity includes before interpreting the result.

examples.title: Build one adjacency bucket
paragraphs: This example constructs the lookup rather than the later comparison report.
interpretation: The bucket gives the outgoing edge candidates after the lookup structure has been built.

parts.title: 3. Use EXPLAIN before PROFILE
paragraphs: EXPLAIN shows a planned execution without executing the query. PROFILE executes it and reports actual operator statistics, so profiling a write can perform that write. Begin with read-only queries against representative test data.

Look for starting scans or seeks, expansion operators, estimated versus actual rows and substantial intermediate multiplication. Compare DB hits and timing carefully; warm caches, parameter values and server load can change results.
interpretation: A final LIMIT does not necessarily remove upstream expansion, sorting or aggregation work.

references.title: Inspect an anchored dependency query
description: The same typed pattern is visible beside its plan request.
references.code:
EXPLAIN
MATCH (a:Asset {id:$asset})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(d:Asset)
RETURN DISTINCT d.id AS dependency
setup: In a fresh Neo4j test database, run CREATE (p:Asset {id:'P7'}), (s:Asset {id:'S1'}), (q:Asset {id:'P8'}), (p)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(s), (q)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(p).
Install an Asset.id uniqueness constraint or suitable index, then bind asset P7.
For actual statistics, run the same read-only query with PROFILE in a controlled test environment.
interpretation: Inspect whether the plan locates P7 selectively before expansion. A three-node fixture demonstrates syntax, not a meaningful production benchmark.

parts.title: 4. Watch degree and repeated branches at each hop
paragraphs: One pump may have many outgoing connections. Its degree counts those connections. Following them creates a frontier: the newly reached candidates waiting to be explored. A busy node can therefore make the next step large even after a fast starting lookup.
Several hops can also produce different routes to the same endpoint. DISTINCT removes repeated output rows, but the database may already have processed many earlier matches to discover them.
Constrain relationship types, justified properties and path length according to the actual question. Avoid enumerating all paths when you only need existence, reachability or a shortest-path result.
interpretation: The operation you ask for determines how much route information must be retained.

parts.title: 5. WITH controls scope as well as aggregation
paragraphs: WITH a, count(i) AS n carries only a and n into the next stage. A variable omitted from that projection is no longer available in the ordinary following scope. WITH DISTINCT can deliberately change cardinality before later matches.
Do not drop the identity needed to connect the next branch correctly. An optimisation that accidentally changes grouping or optional-match semantics is a different query, even if it runs faster.
interpretation: Preserve meaning first, then measure the equivalent alternatives.

parts.title: 6. Apply workload limits and monitor production behaviour
paragraphs: Set timeouts, result-size limits and controlled query templates appropriate to the service. A high-degree tenant or newly imported relationship type can change a previously cheap workload. Monitor latency distributions and failure rates, with enough plan context to investigate regressions.
Performance bounds do not replace tenant access checks. They protect capacity while the authorisation boundary determines which records may be touched.
interpretation: The workshop compares one-hop candidate checks so its interpretation stays narrow and testable.

quiz.prompt: What establishes how much work occurred?
options: The execution plan and measured operator statistics

title: Can Two Teams Describe the Same Resource?
openingTitle: Two Files Agree on a Name and Mean Different Things
opening: One supplier calls a pump P7. Another uses P7 for a spare motor. Meanwhile, two teams describe the same supply under different display names. Botie cannot combine these records safely by comparing their text labels.

We need identifiers whose meaning survives the move between datasets, and a shared way to state a relationship. RDF expresses a statement using a subject, a predicate and an object. SPARQL asks which assignments to variables make patterns of those statements match.
blurb: Distinguish resource identifiers from literals, read RDF statements and build SPARQL patterns without confusing RDF with the property-graph model.

history.title: Web Resources Needed Descriptions That Could Travel
blocks: W3C’s 1999 RDF recommendation addressed machine-readable descriptions of Web resources. Shared identifiers and statement structure let descriptions from different applications be combined without agreeing on one table layout. The later RDF 1.1 and SPARQL 1.1 recommendations specify the graph model and its query language.

That helps our two maintenance teams state which resource a claim concerns. Agreement on identifiers and predicates still requires modelling work. Publishing a statement in RDF does not establish that it is correct.

intuition.title: A predicate gives the arrow its meaning
intuition.explanation: The full resource identifiers distinguish entities even when the diagram uses short display names.

scene.caption: Here ex: abbreviates https://perceptronlab.example/. Changing the abbreviation while retaining the same full IRI does not change the resource.

parts.title: 1. Read a statement before choosing a database
paragraphs: Take the statement P7 dependsOn S1. P7 is the thing we are describing, dependsOn names the relationship, and S1 is the thing at the other end. RDF calls those positions subject, predicate and object. The complete statement is a triple.

For records to travel between datasets, those names need a shared scope. RDF can use an internationalized resource identifier, abbreviated IRI, for a resource and for a predicate. Two independently invented properties named dependsOn need not mean the same thing; their full identifiers distinguish them.
A resource IRI is an identifier, not a promise that fetching its URL will return a useful page. Choose and document identifiers that remain stable when a display name changes.
interpretation: The full identifier, rather than the label drawn beside a node, controls matching.

parts.title: 2. An object can be a resource or a literal
paragraphs: A resource object can participate in more statements. A literal is a value, such as a name, a date or a number. A literal whose characters look like an IRI is still a literal. Datatype and language tags carry meaning that a plain string comparison can lose.

Our compact Python fixture uses kind to distinguish IRI objects from literals. It deliberately omits blank nodes and datatype processing. Blank nodes represent resources without a global IRI; their local labels are not durable cross-file business keys.
interpretation: The workshop projects only resource-to-resource statements. It is not a general RDF parser.

examples.title: Keep an identifier separate from its written text
paragraphs: The characters match, but the object categories differ.
examples.code:
objects=[{'kind':'iri','value':'https://perceptronlab.example/S1'},{'kind':'literal','value':'https://perceptronlab.example/S1'}]
print([o['kind'] for o in objects])
interpretation: Selecting a resource relationship must check the kind as well as the characters.

parts.title: 3. Let a variable occupy the unknown position
paragraphs: In SPARQL, ?asset names a variable. A triple pattern with that variable as subject asks which resources have the stated predicate and object. PREFIX only abbreviates IRIs in the query text; SELECT chooses the variables returned.

The braces contain the graph pattern. Several patterns sharing ?asset must agree on the same resource binding. FILTER can constrain a bound value, while OPTIONAL adds bindings when a pattern exists without requiring it for every row.
interpretation: The same variable-binding idea from Cypher appears in a different graph data model.

references.title: Find resources depending on S1
description: Run this against an RDF store or SPARQL engine containing the Turtle fixture below.
references.code:
PREFIX ex: <https://perceptronlab.example/>
SELECT DISTINCT ?asset
WHERE { ?asset ex:dependsOn ex:S1 . }
ORDER BY ?asset
setup: Load this complete Turtle into a disposable dataset: @prefix ex: <https://perceptronlab.example/> . ex:P7 ex:dependsOn ex:S1 . ex:P8 ex:dependsOn ex:S1 . ex:P9 ex:dependsOn "https://perceptronlab.example/S1" . ex:P7 ex:near ex:S2 .
The expected resources are ex:P7 and ex:P8. Bind external values using your chosen RDF client’s supported RDF-term/query-binding mechanism; do not concatenate unchecked query fragments.
interpretation: P9 has a literal object. Its text looks like the resource IRI, but it does not match the resource object ex:S1.

parts.title: 4. Separate graph statements from query-result duplicates
paragraphs: An RDF graph is a set of triples, so repeating an identical triple does not add another graph statement. A query can still produce repeated projected bindings through several matching combinations. DISTINCT applies to the projected query result, not to an imagined duplicate edge identity.

In a property graph, two separately identified relationships can have the same endpoints and type. That difference matters when importing visit events. Do not mechanically convert each event into an identical RDF triple and expect its identity to survive.
interpretation: Model an event as an identified resource when the event itself needs its own properties or evidence.

parts.title: 5. Missing information is not automatically false
paragraphs: If the dataset has no dependsOn statement for P9, we know that this dataset did not produce a match. We have not proved that P9 has no physical dependency. RDF’s open-world interpretation leaves room for information that has not been recorded.

A store can also be configured to derive statements using supplied rules. For example, it might infer a more general equipment type from a more specific one. That inference is an explicit choice; SPARQL does not automatically apply every rule somebody could express. The entailment regime names the configured rules under which statements may be inferred. Check that choice before relying on an inferred match.
interpretation: State whether the report concerns recorded statements, inferred statements or a verified complete inventory.

parts.title: 6. Keep statement evidence when combining sources
paragraphs: A short RDF triple does not by itself say who asserted it or which source document supported it. Named graphs and explicit provenance models can retain source context, but their interpretation must be documented.
Our next lesson keeps claims separate from the sources that support them. That gives Botie somewhere to look when the two teams disagree instead of silently treating the latest import as the truth.
interpretation: Interoperable syntax makes disagreement easier to represent; it does not resolve it.

title: Where Did This Maintenance Claim Come From?
openingTitle: The Graph Contains Two Conflicting Answers
opening: One document says P7 is overdue for inspection. A later log says the inspection is current. If Botie stores one unqualified status on the asset, whichever import runs last can erase the disagreement.

Keep the claims and their supporting records visible. We can then ask who supplied a claim, when it became usable and whether it still applies. Choosing evidence for review is different from declaring one source correct.
blurb: Represent claims and their sources, retain contradictions and apply explicit time boundaries before using graph evidence.

history.title: Derived Results Needed a Traceable History
blocks: W3C’s 2013 PROV recommendations gave applications a shared way to describe the entities and activities involved in producing information, including who was responsible. A chart could be linked to the dataset and transformation that produced it rather than circulating without that history.

Our maintenance claims have the same need on a smaller scale. A recorded source helps us inspect a disagreement or withdraw a superseded claim. Provenance explains how information arrived; it is not a certificate of truth.

intuition.title: Keep each assertion attached to its evidence
intuition.explanation: Two statements concern P7 without being collapsed into one status property.

scene.caption: Both claims can remain visible during review. Their sources and applicability times determine what can be considered at a particular decision time.

parts.title: 1. Make the assertion an identifiable record
paragraphs: A Claim node can contain its statement, subject and stable claim ID. Separate relationships connect it to the asset and source document. This lets several claims concern the same asset without overwriting each other.

Retain enough source detail to locate the supporting passage or inspection event. A document title alone is often insufficient when revisions change its contents. Prefer a stable document/version identifier plus a specific locator.
interpretation: Claim identity keeps disagreement inspectable instead of turning import order into an evidence policy.

parts.title: 2. Distinguish source permission from source reliability
paragraphs: The requested reader may be allowed to use only particular source documents. That access check must happen before evidence is exposed. A separate quality policy decides which sources are acceptable for the task.

Our workshop receives a permitted-source list and retains only those claim records. Inclusion means the claim passes this supplied policy, not that its statement is verified. Real source permissions belong in the server-side access boundary.
interpretation: The browser fixture demonstrates selection over invented data and is not an access-control system.

parts.title: 3. Draw the interval during which a claim applies
paragraphs: For this exercise, observed_at is the hour the claim became available to this decision process. valid_until is the first hour at which we stop treating it as applicable; null means no stated end. All values use one invented integer-hour clock.

At hour eight, a claim with valid_until eight has expired. A claim first available at hour nine cannot justify an hour-six decision. In real systems, keep event time, ingestion time and validity intervals separate when those meanings differ.
interpretation: We require availability at or before the requested time and an end strictly after it, when an end exists.

examples.title: Inspect an exclusive end boundary
paragraphs: The claim was available at hour two and expires at eight.
examples.code:
observed_at=2
valid_until=8
for at in [7,8]:
    print(observed_at <= at and at < valid_until)
interpretation: The exact end hour belongs to the next state, preventing overlapping interpretations at the boundary.

parts.title: 4. Retrieve evidence without hiding a disagreement
paragraphs: Apply the source and time predicates to claim records, then return their identities and source links. If two surviving claims contradict each other, return both for the defined review process. Do not let a dictionary keyed only by asset discard one.
A later stage may resolve conflicts using an approved policy, but that decision should leave an audit trail. A confidence score alone is not proof that an unsupported claim beats a documented one.
interpretation: The query below uses a property-graph claim model inspired by provenance practice; it is not a PROV-O RDF serialisation.

references.title: List current permitted claims about P7
description: All fixture times are integer hours, so the boundaries can be checked by hand.
references.code:
MATCH (c:Claim)-[:ABOUT]->(a:Asset {id:$asset}),
      (c)-[:WAS_DERIVED_FROM]->(d:Document)
WHERE d.id IN $allowed_sources
  AND c.observed_at <= $at
  AND (c.valid_until IS NULL OR $at < c.valid_until)
RETURN c.id, c.statement, d.id
ORDER BY c.id
setup: In an empty test database run CREATE (a:Asset {id:'P7'}),(d:Document {id:'manual-A'}),(e:Document {id:'log-B'}),(c:Claim {id:'C1',statement:'inspection overdue',observed_at:2,valid_until:8}),(f:Claim {id:'C2',statement:'inspection current',observed_at:4}),(c)-[:ABOUT]->(a),(c)-[:WAS_DERIVED_FROM]->(d),(f)-[:ABOUT]->(a),(f)-[:WAS_DERIVED_FROM]->(e).
Bind asset P7, allowed_sources [manual-A, log-B] and at 6 as driver parameters. Enforce access to every matched entity and relationship according to the service policy.
interpretation: Both C1 and C2 survive. The query reports current permitted evidence, including its disagreement.

parts.title: 5. Retain derivation when a model extracts the claim
paragraphs: An extraction model can misread a sentence or associate it with the wrong asset. Record the source span, extraction version and review status so the graph statement can be checked against the original. A citation pointing to an entire unrelated manual is weak evidence.

When a source is withdrawn, investigate derived claims and downstream summaries that used it. Preserve the minimum audit evidence needed under the retention policy rather than copying sensitive source text into every log.
interpretation: Provenance gives a route for correction, provided downstream results retain their dependencies.

parts.title: 6. Keep uncertainty visible to the answerer
paragraphs: A graph can contain stale, contradictory or incomplete evidence. The response may need to say that available records disagree, or request inspection rather than assert a status. That behaviour can be tested using deliberately conflicting fixtures.
The coding task stops at eligible claim IDs. It does not infer truth, apply natural-language contradiction detection or call a language model.
interpretation: A narrow evidence-selection result is useful because its meaning can be inspected and tested.

title: Which Connected Records Can the Assistant Use?
openingTitle: A Relevant Manual Can Still Be the Wrong Evidence
opening: The assistant has found P7, but its own manual does not explain a supply fault. Botie could follow P7’s dependency to S1 and retrieve the supply’s manual too. That connected context might explain what the isolated document misses.

There are limits. One route passes through another tenant’s asset, and one manual was uploaded after the decision we are evaluating. Relevance alone does not make either route acceptable. We need an explicit retrieval policy before handing records to a model.
blurb: Build bounded graph retrieval with access and time boundaries, then preserve evidence and measure whether the added context actually helps.

history.title: Some Questions Needed Connections Across Retrieved Passages
blocks: The 2024 GraphRAG paper studied questions that require a broad view of a document collection. Its method builds an entity graph and community summaries to support query-focused summarisation. It addresses a different failure from simply finding a nearby text passage.

Our maintenance example uses a smaller local retrieval mechanism: start from a known asset and follow approved dependency types to related manuals. It is not a reproduction of that paper’s community-summary pipeline. The common motivation is that useful evidence may be connected across records.

intuition.title: A route has to remain usable all the way through
intuition.explanation: The request belongs to tenant red and is evaluated at hour six.

scene.caption: D2 is future information. D3 is red, but this route crosses blue asset X. Filtering only the final document would miss that boundary violation.

parts.title: 1. Choose the starting entity before collecting neighbours
paragraphs: The request concerns P7. Entity resolution must connect that mention to a stable permitted asset, rather than treating a similar display name as sufficient. Vector search can suggest candidates, but an approximate similarity score does not establish identity or access.

For this lesson the starting ID is already supplied. We also receive the tenant, decision hour and maximum dependency depth. Those inputs define the retrieval question; the model does not get to silently widen them.
interpretation: A known start keeps this exercise focused on connected evidence rather than language-based entity resolution.

parts.title: 2. Apply the scope to intermediate nodes and relationships
paragraphs: Construct the permitted graph before expanding. Keep nodes in the requested tenant and only relationships whose endpoints both remain. This prevents a route through an excluded asset from revealing an otherwise permitted endpoint.

Real policies can also restrict relationship types, individual records or properties within a tenant. The browser receives invented multi-tenant fixtures so we can see the failure. In a deployed system, enforce the policy on the server before forbidden records are exposed to the client or model.
interpretation: A traversal depth limit controls work. It does not grant permission.

parts.title: 3. Keep dependency expansion separate from document lookup
paragraphs: Require the start and every intermediate dependency node to have kind Asset. Starting at P7, follow DEPENDS_ON up to the chosen depth and retain each reached asset once. Include P7 at depth zero so its own manual remains eligible. Then follow HAS_MANUAL from those assets to document records.

This separation prevents a general “follow every edge” search from wandering through technicians, unrelated claims or other relationship types. Inspect the reached asset IDs before inspecting document content.
interpretation: Each stage has a different row meaning: assets reached, document IDs attached, then eligible evidence.

examples.title: Inspect what remains after applying the tenant boundary
paragraphs: Only edges whose two endpoints are in red remain.
interpretation: The cross edge and m3 disappear because X is excluded, even though D3 itself belongs to red.

parts.title: 4. Use only evidence available by the decision time
paragraphs: The supply manual D2 becomes available at hour eight. It cannot support a response evaluated as of hour six. Check availability after resolving document records, and retain version information so a later revision does not leak backward into an old evaluation.

For training features, apply the same point-in-time discipline to graph edges and node properties. A future relationship can leak an outcome even when the final label column is absent. This exercise assumes the graph topology is the authorised snapshot for the decision and varies document availability only.
interpretation: Real historical evaluation needs the graph snapshot and evidence versions that existed at the time.

parts.title: 5. Express the same narrow retrieval policy in a database query
paragraphs: The bounded path begins at the asset, permits zero dependency hops and then matches a manual. all over nodes(p) checks the tenant of every asset along that path. The document has its own tenant and availability predicates.

These query conditions illustrate the policy. A server must derive the permitted tenant from authenticated context and enforce its full access rules. Never accept an arbitrary user-selected tenant as authorisation.
interpretation: The example fixes a two-hop query template and parameterises data values.

references.title: Retrieve manuals through a scoped dependency route
description: This reads a disposable property graph; it does not run in the Python challenge.
references.code:
MATCH p=(a:Asset {id:$asset,tenant:$tenant})-[:DEPENDS_ON*0..2]->(x:Asset)
MATCH (x)-[:HAS_MANUAL]->(d:Document)
WHERE all(n IN nodes(p) WHERE n:Asset AND n.tenant=$tenant)
  AND d.tenant=$tenant AND d.available_at <= $at
RETURN DISTINCT d.id AS document
ORDER BY document
setup: In an empty test database run CREATE (a:Asset {id:'P7',tenant:'red'}),(s:Asset {id:'S1',tenant:'red'}),(x:Asset {id:'X',tenant:'blue'}),(d:Document {id:'D1',tenant:'red',available_at:2}),(e:Document {id:'D2',tenant:'red',available_at:8}),(f:Document {id:'D3',tenant:'red',available_at:1}),(a)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(s),(a)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(x),(a)-[:HAS_MANUAL]->(d),(s)-[:HAS_MANUAL]->(e),(x)-[:HAS_MANUAL]->(f).
Bind asset P7, tenant red and at 6 through the driver. Use server-enforced permissions appropriate to every traversed record.
interpretation: Only D1 is returned. At hour eight, D2 also qualifies. D3 remains unreachable through the permitted graph.

parts.title: 6. Give the model evidence with its limits attached
paragraphs: Return source IDs and relevant passages, rather than an unlabelled bundle of graph text. The answer should cite support for its claims and acknowledge missing or conflicting evidence. Documents can contain hostile instructions; retrieved content remains untrusted data rather than instructions to the application.

Bound expansion, document count and context size using documented policies. If a bound truncates potentially useful evidence, expose that limitation rather than claiming a complete search. A graph makes relationships available; it does not guarantee a factual model response.
interpretation: Graph retrieval and graph neural network training are separate uses of graph data.

parts.title: 7. Evaluate the retrieval decision as well as the generated answer
paragraphs: Use held-out maintenance questions with known supporting records. Check whether required evidence is retrieved, whether forbidden or future evidence is excluded and whether citations support the answer actually given. Include an unresolved question where the correct behaviour is to ask for more information.

Compare this retrieval policy with a simpler document search on the same questions. Measure latency and failure cases alongside answer quality. More connected context can add irrelevant material or repeated claims, so improvement needs evidence.
interpretation: The workshop tests the evidence-selection mechanism. It makes no claim to evaluate a live language model.

title: When a Measurement Is Missing
blurb: An empty thermometer reading does not mean the greenhouse was at zero degrees. We need to distinguish what was measured from what we supplied to keep a calculation working.
openingTitle: What Should We Do With an Empty Cell?
opening: Botie opens the greenhouse report and finds a blank temperature. Perhaps the sensor lost power, or perhaps it stopped reporting when the greenhouse became too hot. Those possibilities have different implications.

The calculation we want to run may still need a number in that cell. We can estimate one from the available readings. But we should keep track of where we made that substitution: we now have a usable input, while the actual temperature remains unknown.

history.title: The Missing Observation Has a Story Too
blocks: Incomplete records posed a problem for statistical inference long before modern neural networks. Ignoring an absent observation can change the group we describe, especially when absence is related to the value we wanted to measure.

Rubin's 1976 paper established conditions under which the missingness process can be ignored for particular forms of inference. It did not say that replacing every blank with an average is universally valid. Our invented greenhouse example uses mean replacement as a transparent baseline so we can inspect exactly what it assumes.

intuition.title: Leave the blank visible
intuition.explanation: A blank is an unknown temperature. Writing zero there would assert something we did not observe.

intuition.title: Use only the recorded training values
intuition.explanation: The two observed training readings give a replacement reference. A later observation must not help choose it.

intuition.title: Keep the new report's measured entries
intuition.explanation: Only the missing entry changes. The recorded temperature stays intact.

parts.title: 1. Separate Missing From Zero
paragraphs: Zero is a possible temperature. Missing means we do not know the temperature. These must remain different values. The workshop uses a blank cell represented internally by null; Python uses a floating-point missing marker called NaN.
First identify which entries were observed. Do not let the missing marker participate in an ordinary average.
parts.calculation:
Training readings: [10, missing, 14]
Observed readings: [10, 14]
interpretation: The set of observed readings may itself be biased. If the hottest sensors stop reporting, its average will not describe the missing temperatures well.

parts.title: 2. Learn the Replacement From Training Data
paragraphs: Suppose one training temperature is blank while the others were measured. We can average the measured temperatures and use that average in the empty position. Supplying a replacement is called imputation; using the mean gives us mean imputation. We estimate the replacement from training data once, then reuse it on later data. The replacement lets the calculation run, but it is still an estimate of the missing measurement.
parts.calculation:
Training reference = (10 + 14) / 2 = 12
New report:    [missing, 18]
Filled report: [12, 18]
interpretation: Including the new report's measured temperature when choosing the reference would change the fitted preprocessing after seeing new data. For evaluation, it would let held-out observations influence the preparation.

parts.title: 3. Keep Track of What Was Replaced
paragraphs: A missingness indicator records which values were supplied. A one in that indicator means the original entry was absent; a zero means it was measured. That information can matter if missingness is related to how the records were collected.
parts.calculation:
New report:          [missing, 18]
Missing indicator:   [1, 0]
Filled temperatures: [12, 18]
interpretation: The indicator preserves a distinction, not a guarantee. It cannot recover the absent reading. Mean replacement also understates variability if we later treat supplied values as independent observations.

parts.title: 4. Choose the Assumption Before the Convenience
paragraphs: A median can resist extreme observed values. A fixed replacement may have domain meaning. More elaborate methods use relationships among features, and some models handle missing entries directly. Each choice still needs evaluation under the intended conditions.

If every training value is missing, there is no observed mean to calculate. Stop and choose a documented fallback or remove that feature for a reason. Silently inventing a zero would hide the failure.
interpretation: Botie's construction must learn from the training readings and fill the new report. It must preserve every value that was actually observed.

parts.title: 5. Fit the Replacement Once, Then Carry It Forward
paragraphs: The training rows provide the reference for missing measurements. Incoming rows receive that reference even when their observed values have a very different average. Otherwise a prediction depends on which other records happened to arrive in the same batch.
Keep a missingness indicator if absence may itself be informative. Decide separately what to do with a training column that has no observed values at all; there is no sample mean to learn from it.

examples.title: An unusually hot batch must not redefine the training mean
paragraphs: Training observations are 10 and 14 degrees. A later batch contains one observation and one blank.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
training = np.array([10., np.nan, 14.])
reference = training[np.isfinite(training)].mean()
incoming = np.array([30., np.nan])
missing = ~np.isfinite(incoming)
print(np.where(missing, reference, incoming).tolist())
print(missing.tolist())
interpretation: The filled value describes our training-based rule. It is not evidence that the second greenhouse was actually at 12 degrees.

parts.title: 6. What If the Hottest Sensors Stop Reporting?
paragraphs: Mean replacement is particularly misleading when missingness depends on the unobserved value. If thermometers fail above a temperature limit, the available readings systematically omit the hottest conditions. Their mean can be too low for the missing group.

Compare reporting rates by device, time and known operating conditions. An indicator may help prediction, but it does not identify the missing temperatures. Investigating the measurement process or obtaining another sensor can be more valuable than choosing a more elaborate filling rule.

quiz.prompt: A missing thermometer reading means the temperature was zero.
quiz.because: Absence is not a physical temperature. Zero would be an invented measurement.

quiz.prompt: Which observations establish our replacement?
quiz.because: The replacement is a fitted preprocessing parameter. It is learned from the observed training values and reused.

quiz.prompt: Keeping a missingness indicator can distinguish supplied values from measured values.
quiz.because: The indicator preserves which entries were absent, although it does not recover their true temperatures.

import numpy as np
training = np.array([10., np.nan, 14.])
report = np.array([np.nan, 18.])
# Learn from training, then fill report.

training = np.array([10., np.nan, 14.])
report = np.array([np.nan, 18.])

np.where can choose the replacement only where the report's missing mask is true.

practice.title: Can you fill a new table without learning from it?
practice.question: Can you fill a new table without learning from it?
task: The imputation workshop used a replacement learned from training data. Now apply that saved reference to any compatible incoming table, and retain a record of which entries were filled so estimated values remain distinguishable from observations.

Write fill_missing(X, reference). X is a two-dimensional float-compatible table whose missing entries are NaN. reference is a finite vector with one saved replacement per column. Return the filled table and a Boolean missingness table. Preserve X.
Reject infinite input values, non-finite references and incompatible shapes with ValueError. Print both demonstration arrays as lists.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def fill_missing(X, reference):
    # Write the procedure here.
    raise NotImplementedError

filled, missing = fill_missing([[30.,np.nan],[np.nan,60.]], [12.,50.])
print(filled.tolist())
print(missing.tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def fill_missing(X, reference):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    reference = np.asarray(reference, dtype=float)
    if X.ndim != 2 or reference.shape != (X.shape[1],):
        raise ValueError('Wrong feature layout')
    if np.isinf(X).any() or not np.isfinite(reference).all():
        raise ValueError('Invalid measurements or reference')
    missing = np.isnan(X)
    return np.where(missing, reference, X), missing

filled, missing = fill_missing([[30.,np.nan],[np.nan,60.]], [12.,50.])
print(filled.tolist())
print(missing.tolist())
hints: Record the NaN positions before replacing anything. An observed zero must remain an observed zero.
Use only the supplied per-column reference. Calculating a fresh mean from the incoming table would change the fitted replacement rule.

title: Categories Without an Invented Ranking
blurb: A roof can be glass, plastic, or mesh. Assigning those names arbitrary numbers can accidentally suggest a ranking. We need a representation that preserves category membership without inventing a numerical relationship.
openingTitle: Is Glass Really Twice as Much Roof as Plastic?
opening: Botie wants to include greenhouse roof material in a temperature model. The materials are glass, plastic, and mesh. A model needs usable inputs, so assigning each name an ID seems like a reasonable start.

The IDs tell us which material a row describes. They don't measure anything about the roof. If we multiply them by one shared coefficient, however, their numerical gaps affect the prediction. We need to tell the model which material is present without making an arbitrary choice of IDs look like a measured difference.

history.title: Giving Each Category Its Own Question

sources.title: Suits: Use of Dummy Variables in Regression Equations (1957)

blocks: A regression equation can use a measured quantity directly, but a category name needs another representation. A zero-or-one indicator asks whether a record belongs to a particular category without assigning that category an invented numerical distance.

Daniel Suits’s 1957 paper examined these indicators, then called dummy variables, and the constraints needed to determine their regression coefficients. One important issue appears when every category has an indicator and the equation also has a constant: some columns repeat information already present in the others.

We will begin with the representation itself. Botie’s roof materials get a fixed set of membership columns and a stated policy for unfamiliar materials. The later fitting method determines whether a reference column or another constraint is needed.

intuition.title: Start with names
intuition.explanation: The roof materials identify categories. Their order here is simply our chosen vocabulary order.

intuition.title: Ask one question per material
intuition.explanation: Each row says whether that roof matches each vocabulary entry.

intuition.title: Reuse the same column meanings
intuition.explanation: Another glass roof must receive the same representation. Changing column order changes what a fitted coefficient means.

intuition.title: An unfamiliar roof still needs a policy
intuition.explanation: A roof made of a material absent from the vocabulary matches none of the known-material columns. An all-zero row can record that result, but it should not silently be interpreted as a known material.

scene.caption: Illustrative roof materials with a fixed vocabulary.

parts.title: 1. Distinguish an ID From a Quantity
paragraphs: A temperature difference has units and a physical interpretation. A material ID does not. Renaming glass from ID one to ID seven should not change the properties of the roof.

Some model families handle categorical IDs specially. A plain numerical coefficient does not: it will multiply the number it receives. We therefore need to consider how the model interprets the representation.
interpretation: Do not conclude that every integer-coded feature is invalid. An ordered category or a categorical-aware algorithm has different assumptions. Our problem concerns unordered names passed to ordinary numerical operations.

parts.title: 2. Make a Column for Each Membership Question
paragraphs: Ask a separate yes-or-no question for each roof material: is it glass, is it plastic, and is it mesh? A glass roof receives one in the glass column and zero in the others. This is one-hot encoding: exactly one membership column is active. The ordered list of materials is the vocabulary. Keeping that order fixed lets each model coefficient retain the same meaning.
parts.calculation:
Column order: glass, plastic, mesh
glass → [1, 0, 0]
mesh  → [0, 0, 1]
interpretation: The zeros do not say that a roof has no properties. They say that it is not a member of those particular categories.

parts.title: 3. Keep the Vocabulary Fixed After Fitting
paragraphs: The model's coefficients attach to column positions. If we fit with glass first and later move mesh into the first position, the arithmetic still runs while the meaning changes. Fit the vocabulary on training data and preserve its order.

An unfamiliar material needs an explicit policy. We can reserve an unknown category, reject the record for review, or use an all-zero representation with care. This workshop uses all zeros and makes that policy visible.
parts.calculation:
Vocabulary: [glass, plastic, mesh]
Unknown foil roof → [0, 0, 0]
interpretation: All zeros cannot identify which unfamiliar material appeared. If one known category is also represented by all zeros after dropping a reference column, unknowns become ambiguous unless handled separately.

parts.title: 4. Decide What the Representation Leaves Out
paragraphs: Separate indicators let a model learn separate contributions. They do not teach it that two materials have similar insulation or cost. If those measured properties matter, we may want additional features that describe them directly.

With an intercept in a linear model, all category columns together create a redundant description. Dropping a reference column is one way to remove that redundancy. We keep all columns here so the membership mechanism is easy to inspect.
interpretation: Botie's workshop constructs the indicator table. Later modelling lessons decide how to fit coefficients to it.

parts.title: 5. Follow a Roof Name into a Prediction
paragraphs: Once the indicators exist, a linear model assigns a separate contribution to each column. The intercept supplies a shared starting prediction. Choosing a reference category removes redundant columns, but changes how the remaining coefficients should be read.
Here we retain every indicator and supply illustrative coefficients so that the routing is visible. We are applying a stated rule, not claiming these materials have measured thermal effects.

examples.title: Apply contributions in the saved vocabulary order
paragraphs: The vocabulary is glass, plastic, mesh. Foil uses the previously declared all-zero policy.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
vocabulary = np.array(['glass', 'plastic', 'mesh'])
materials = np.array(['mesh', 'foil', 'glass'])
X = (materials[:, None] == vocabulary).astype(float)
weights = np.array([2., -1., -3.])
print((20 + X @ weights).tolist())
interpretation: The unfamiliar roof receives only the intercept. That is a fallback policy, not evidence that foil behaves like an average known roof.

parts.title: 6. A Column with One Training Example Has Little Support
paragraphs: A vocabulary can contain many rare names. Giving each its own coefficient asks the model to learn effects from very few observations. Grouping rare categories into an other category or regularising the model can reduce that instability, with different tradeoffs.

Fit any frequency threshold on training data. Keep unknown and missing categories distinct if their meanings differ. If a category is a near-unique identifier, consider whether the prediction task permits remembering that identity at all, especially when evaluating on new greenhouses.

quiz.prompt: Why are arbitrary material IDs risky for a plain numerical coefficient?
options: The IDs may imply meaningful numerical gaps
Numbers cannot represent text in any form
quiz.because: A numerical coefficient uses the size of the ID. Our arbitrary category numbering does not justify that relationship.

quiz.prompt: One-hot column order can change freely after fitting.
quiz.because: Fitted coefficients refer to the original column meanings.

quiz.prompt: What does our all-zero row for foil tell us?
options: Foil was the first training category
Foil did not match the supplied vocabulary
quiz.because: The comparison found no matching known material. It makes no physical claim about foil.

title: When the End Is Beside the Beginning
blurb: The hour after 23 is zero, yet ordinary subtraction puts those hour numbers far apart. A repeating feature needs a representation that keeps its beginning beside its end.
openingTitle: Why Does Midnight Look So Far From Eleven?
opening: Botie records greenhouse temperatures throughout the day. If we encode the hour as a number from zero to 23, late evening and early morning sit at opposite ends of the number line. On a clock they are neighbours.

A clock gives us a useful picture here. The hour moves around the face and returns to its starting position each day. We can put our hour values on a circle too, then use two coordinates to describe each position. Hours on either side of midnight will stay close together.

history.title: Representing a Repeating Cycle as a Position

sources.title: Fisher: Statistical Analysis of Circular Data (1993)

blocks: Measurements of direction posed an awkward problem for ordinary straight-line statistics: values near opposite ends of a written scale can be neighbours on the circle. Clock time has the same difficulty at midnight.

Nicholas Fisher’s 1993 Statistical Analysis of Circular Data developed methods for observations such as orientations and bearings, where that circular relationship matters. It documents a statistical setting for treating a cycle as a position around a circle. In our model inputs, sine and cosine coordinates preserve that same adjacency. We will use the pair together so a single coordinate cannot confuse distinct parts of the day.

intuition.title: The written hour wraps around
intuition.explanation: The order continues through midnight. Zero belongs immediately after 23 on the next day.

intuition.title: Use two coordinates on a clock face
intuition.explanation: Quarter turns give easily recognised positions. The coordinate order here is cosine, then sine.

scene.caption: Invented clock positions on a unit circle. One full day returns to the starting point.

intuition.title: The cycle closes
intuition.explanation: The position at hour 24 is the same as the position at hour zero. Here eleven at night and one in the morning sit beside midnight. The date must be stored separately if it matters.

scene.caption: Invented clock positions on a unit circle. One full day returns to the starting point.

parts.title: 1. Decide What Repeats
paragraphs: An hour of day repeats every 24 hours. Elapsed time since an experiment began does not. We should use a circular representation only for the repeating feature, while keeping nonrepeating information elsewhere.
For this lesson, the input is an hour measured from midnight and the period is 24 hours. Fractions such as half past six can be represented too.
interpretation: The period is a modelling assumption. A weekly pattern needs a different period, and calendar months do not all contain the same number of days.

parts.title: 2. Turn the Fraction of a Cycle Into an Angle
paragraphs: First ask how far the hour has travelled around the clock. Divide it by the full 24-hour period to get a fraction of one turn. Mathematics often measures angles in radians, where one complete turn has size two pi. Multiplying our fraction by that full-turn angle gives the position we will pass to sine and cosine.
parts.calculation:
Hour 6:  fraction = 6 / 24 = 1/4
         angle = (1/4) × 2π = π/2
Hour 12: fraction = 12 / 24 = 1/2
         angle = (1/2) × 2π = π
interpretation: Radians are a way to measure an angle. The important fact here is that a full period brings us back to the same position.

parts.title: 3. Use Both Coordinates
paragraphs: Cosine gives the horizontal coordinate of our point on a unit circle. Sine gives its vertical coordinate. We need both because a single coordinate is shared by different positions.
interpretation: Sine alone would give zero at both midnight and noon. The cosine coordinate distinguishes them. Near midnight, both coordinates change smoothly across the written day boundary.

parts.title: 4. The Representation Is Not the Whole Prediction Rule
paragraphs: Two coordinates tell a model where we are in the cycle. They do not guarantee that the daily temperature follows a simple sinusoid. Weather, heating controls, and the season can still matter.

A linear combination of this single sine-cosine pair describes one smooth daily oscillation. More complicated recurring shapes may need additional harmonics, splines, or a flexible model. Choose that complexity through appropriate evaluation.
interpretation: The workshop builds the pair for one hour. The Python practice builds it for several times and then changes the period to a week.

parts.title: 5. A Circle Fixes the Boundary, Not Every Daily Pattern
paragraphs: Putting hours on a circle makes late night and early morning neighbours. A linear model using one sine and one cosine can then describe one smooth rise and fall per cycle. It cannot independently place several sharp peaks wherever we choose.

If demand rises at two watering times, additional harmonics or another representation may help. Each additional harmonic introduces a faster repeating pattern. Choose that flexibility with validation rather than assuming a circular representation solves every time-related prediction problem.

parts.title: 6. Represent a Pattern That Repeats Twice a Day
paragraphs: The first harmonic completes one turn over a day. The second completes two. They are separate features, so a model can combine broad daily variation with a repeated morning-and-evening pattern.
Hour-of-day does not identify the date, season or timezone. Preserve those when they matter, and handle irregular or repeated clock times before treating array positions as equal time intervals.

examples.title: Compare one daily cycle with two
paragraphs: The table samples four six-hour positions. Cosine is enough here to show the different frequencies.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
hour = np.array([0., 6., 12., 18.])
angle = 2 * np.pi * hour / 24
print(np.round(np.cos(angle), 3).tolist())
print(np.round(np.cos(2 * angle), 3).tolist())
interpretation: The second feature gives midnight and noon the same value. A model still needs data to learn whether that repetition is relevant.

quiz.prompt: Hour 24 and hour zero share the same cyclical position.
quiz.because: They are separated by one full period. A separate date feature would be needed to distinguish the days.

quiz.prompt: Why do we keep both sine and cosine?
options: To distinguish positions that share one coordinate
To create an arbitrary category ID
quiz.because: For example, sine alone gives zero at both midnight and noon.

quiz.prompt: Encoding the hour on a circle proves temperature follows a single smooth daily wave.
quiz.because: The representation preserves periodic position. It does not establish the complete relationship between hour and temperature.

practice.title: Where do the quarter-day readings sit on the circle?
practice.question: Where do the quarter-day readings sit on the circle?
task: For hours 0, 6, 12, and 18, create rows containing cosine first and sine second.
Print the nested list rounded to four decimal places.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
hours = np.array([0.,6.,12.,18.])
# Convert to angles, then make two-coordinate rows.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
hours = np.array([0.,6.,12.,18.])
angles = hours / 24 * (2*np.pi)
print(np.round(np.column_stack((np.cos(angles),np.sin(angles))),4).tolist())
hints: One full day maps to two pi radians.
np.column_stack keeps the two coordinate columns in the stated order.

practice.title: Can the same construction describe the week?
practice.question: Can the same construction describe the week?

Print cosine-sine rows rounded to four decimals.

import numpy as np
days = np.array([0.,1.,6.])
# Use the weekly period.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
days = np.array([0.,1.,6.])
angles = days / 7 * (2*np.pi)
print(np.round(np.column_stack((np.cos(angles),np.sin(angles))),4).tolist())
hints: Only the period changes: use seven rather than 24.
Day six and day zero are neighbours around the weekly cycle.

build.problem: Botie's hour feature should preserve that the day repeats. We will return the position around a circle, with cosine first and sine second.
build.challenge: Divide the hour by the period, multiply by a full turn of 2π radians, then collect cosine and sine in that order. The Full turn source supplies 2π.
build.why: Dividing identifies the fraction of a cycle. Sine and cosine locate that fraction on a circle, so a full turn returns to the start.
build.limitation: This encodes a fixed-period feature. It does not fit a temperature curve or handle calendar irregularities.

title: What Does One Row Represent?
blurb: Two identical-looking rows might be a duplicated import or two genuine observations. We need to establish a record's identity before cleaning a dataset or trusting its counts.
openingTitle: Did We Observe It Twice, or Import It Twice?
opening: Botie joins two greenhouse log files and finds the same event ID twice. If both entries describe the same measurement, counting both gives that event extra influence. If two different events happen to have the same temperature, removing one would discard real information.

Before deleting either row, we need to know how an event was identified and recorded. Its time and units help us interpret the measurement. The collection rule tells us whether two matching rows could legitimately describe separate events.

history.title: Why a Dataset Needs Its Own Instructions

sources.title: Gebru and colleagues: Datasheets for Datasets

blocks: A dataset can outlive the people who remember how it was collected. When collection details disappear, later users may mistake a convenient table for a complete description of a population.

Gebru and colleagues introduced datasheets for datasets in 2018, with a later journal publication, to document matters such as motivation, composition, collection, and recommended uses. Our duplicate-log exercise handles one small part of that broader problem: recording what an observation means before deciding how to clean it.

intuition.title: Two exports can overlap
intuition.explanation: The same event identifier appears in both files. It names one event even though the import contains two rows.

intuition.title: Count the distinct event identities
intuition.explanation: There are three distinct IDs. We have not yet decided which conflicting version to keep if repeated IDs disagree.

intuition.title: Count the excess copies
intuition.explanation: One imported row exceeds the distinct event count. This is a duplication audit, not an automatic cleaning decision.

parts.title: 1. Define the Unit of Observation
paragraphs: A row might represent one greenhouse, one thermometer reading, or one daily summary. These are different units of observation. If we combine them without checking, the row count stops having a clear meaning.
For this example, one row represents one sensor event, and each event is assigned a stable ID. Repeated IDs therefore deserve inspection. Repeated temperature values alone do not.
interpretation: A primary key is a field, or combination of fields, intended to identify one record. It is useful only when the collection process actually respects that meaning.

parts.title: 2. Audit Repeated Identities
paragraphs: Count all imported rows, then count distinct event IDs. Their difference reports excess copies. An ID appearing three times contributes two excess copies, not three.
parts.calculation:
Imported IDs: [101, 102, 102, 103]
Total rows = 4
Distinct event IDs = 3
Excess copies = 4 - 3 = 1
interpretation: This count tells us how much duplication to investigate. It does not tell us whether two versions contain identical measurements or which one is authoritative.

parts.title: 3. Check Values Against Their Meaning
paragraphs: After identity, check units, timestamp conventions, required fields, and plausible ranges. A measurement in Fahrenheit can look like an unusually warm Celsius reading while remaining a perfectly valid number.

Keep a reason for every exclusion or correction. A surprising value may be a faulty sensor, but it may also be the event we are trying to detect. Deleting surprises because they complicate the model can remove the signal.
interpretation: Quality checks should separate impossible records, inconsistent records, and unusual but possible observations. They do not all deserve the same response.

parts.title: 4. Preserve the Evidence Behind a Cleaned Table
paragraphs: Retain the original records and document the transformation into the modelling table. If duplicate IDs disagree, resolve the conflict using the source system's rules rather than whichever row happens to arrive first.

The workshop only measures excess copies. A real cleaning workflow also needs a conflict policy and an audit trail. Later validation must keep copies or related observations together so they cannot appear on both sides of an evaluation split.
interpretation: In the coding exercise, distinct-ID counting is enough because the requested result is an audit count, not a cleaned temperature estimate.

parts.title: 5. Two Equal Temperatures Are Not Necessarily One Event
paragraphs: An event identifier says which observation a row claims to describe. Equal temperatures on different events can be perfectly legitimate. Conversely, two rows with one identifier but different temperatures are a conflict, not harmless duplication.

Before dropping anything, group by the identity rule and distinguish exact repeated reports from conflicting reports. A later timestamp may indicate a correction, but only if the data producer defines it that way. Otherwise send the disagreement for review and retain its source.

parts.title: 6. Count Identities Before Choosing Which Report to Keep
paragraphs: Botie can produce a small audit table before cleaning. It should show which identities repeat and how many rows each supplied. This does not yet select a correct value; it tells us which records need the resolution policy.
Retain the raw input and record which rule selected or rejected each row. If an implausible measurement later proves valid, we can revisit the decision without recreating a deleted observation.

examples.title: Find repeated greenhouse events
paragraphs: The third row repeats the first event identifier; equal values under different identifiers would not count as a duplicate event.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
event_id = np.array(['north-1', 'south-1', 'north-1', 'north-2'])
identities, counts = np.unique(event_id, return_counts=True)
print(identities[counts > 1].tolist())
print(counts[counts > 1].tolist())
interpretation: The next step is to compare the two source records and apply the declared resolution rule. Counting duplicates alone cannot decide which measurement is true.

quiz.prompt: Which repetition identifies a potential duplicate event in our example?
options: Two events at the same temperature
Two rows with the same event ID
Two readings from the same greenhouse on different days
quiz.because: The stable event ID is defined to identify a single observation.

quiz.prompt: An event ID appearing three times contributes two excess copies.
quiz.because: One copy represents the distinct event; the other two exceed that count.

quiz.prompt: A duplicate count tells us which conflicting temperature is correct.
quiz.because: Counting identities does not resolve disagreements between versions.

Print the number of distinct event IDs, then the number of excess copies.

# Count identities, then excess copies.
practice.solution:

event_ids = np.array([101,102,102,103])

print(distinct)

practice.title: What if one event was imported three times?
practice.question: What if one event was imported three times?
task: Print the distinct count and excess-copy count for the new import.
Count copies beyond the first, not the number of IDs that repeat.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
event_ids = np.array([8,8,8,9,10,10])
# Audit the import.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

An ID occurring three times contributes two excess copies.

build.title: Audit repeated greenhouse events
build.problem: Botie combined sensor exports that may overlap. Each stable ID names one event, so extra copies should be counted before analysis.
build.challenge: Return the number of imported rows beyond the number of distinct event IDs.
build.why: The two branches count all records and distinct identities. Subtracting them measures extra copies rather than genuine repeated values.
build.limitation: This audit assumes IDs identify events reliably. It does not decide which conflicting record should be kept.

title: What Could We Know at Prediction Time?
topic: Keep Future Answers Out of Training
blurb: A model can appear remarkably accurate when a feature contains information that arrives after the decision. We need to reconstruct what was actually available when each prediction would have been made.
openingTitle: Can We Predict a Repair Using the Completed Repair Report?
opening: Botie wants to predict at noon whether a greenhouse sensor will need repair later that day. The data export includes a morning reading, a noon reading, and a completed repair report entered that evening.
The evening report could make the prediction look easy. It may even state the answer. But it was not available at noon, so using it would test a different task from the one we intended to solve.

history.title: When a Successful Evaluation Used Unavailable Information

sources.title: Kaufman and colleagues: Leakage in Data Mining (2012)
Scikit-learn: Common pitfalls and data leakage

blocks: When we combine records from several systems, a later event can slip into the inputs for an earlier prediction. Preprocessing can also use information from data we intended to hold out. The resulting score then reflects information the model would not have had when it needed to make the real decision.

Kaufman and colleagues examined leakage as information about a target that is not legitimately available to the prediction process. Our invented repair records make the timing issue explicit. Other forms include fitting preprocessing on test data or placing copies of an observation on both sides of a split.

intuition.title: Fix the decision time
intuition.explanation: The task is to make the decision at noon. That time determines the boundary of available evidence.

intuition.title: Check when each field became available
intuition.explanation: Use availability time, not merely the date written inside a later report.

intuition.title: Keep only the evidence available then
intuition.explanation: The boundary includes the noon reading under this exercise's convention. The evening report is excluded.

parts.title: 1. Define the Decision Before Selecting Features
paragraphs: State what is predicted, for whom, and at what time. Without that definition, we cannot judge whether a feature was available legitimately.
Our task is a noon prediction of later repair need. A completed evening report fails the timing requirement even if it is stored in the same row as the morning measurements.
interpretation: A column's name is not enough. Investigate how the value was created, updated, and joined into the table.

parts.title: 2. Compare Availability With the Cutoff
paragraphs: Each field has an availability time. Keep it only when that time is at or before the prediction cutoff. The workshop uses whole hours to make this boundary visible.
parts.calculation:
Prediction cutoff: 12
Availability times: [9, 12, 18]
Available by cutoff: [1, 1, 0]
interpretation: The timestamp of the underlying event can differ from the time the system learned about it. A report describing a morning event but uploaded in the evening still cannot be used at noon.

parts.title: 3. Keep Fitting Inside the Evaluation Boundary
paragraphs: Leakage does not require an obviously future-looking column. A mean, vocabulary, selected feature, or imputation reference learned using held-out observations has also crossed the evaluation boundary.

Split first according to the intended prediction setting. Fit preprocessing and the model on training data. Apply those fitted choices to validation or test data without relearning from the held-out group.
interpretation: Pipelines help with the order of fitting operations. They cannot determine whether a raw field was available at the intended decision time. That requires knowledge of the data collection process.

parts.title: 4. Test the Procedure You Can Actually Run
paragraphs: A realistic evaluation replays the information constraints of deployment. Time order, delayed labels, related entities, and record updates may all matter. A random row split is not automatically wrong, but it answers the wrong question when it ignores the dependency we care about.
The workshop returns the eligible measurements in their original order. It does not decide whether those features are useful or ethically appropriate; it checks the stated timing boundary.
interpretation: Removing leakage may lower the score. That is a better measurement of the intended task, not a reason to put the unavailable information back.

parts.title: 5. A Record Has an Event Time and an Availability Time
paragraphs: A repair may concern a noon failure but only be entered that evening. If Botie predicts at noon, the repair report is unavailable even when a retrospective export assigns it the failure's date. An event timestamp alone does not establish that a feature was usable.

For each input, record how it is obtained and when it becomes available. Reconstruct training rows from that point of view. A lag must account for reporting delay, not merely move a value to an earlier-looking column.

parts.title: 6. Ask Whether Changing Tomorrow Changes Today’s Input
paragraphs: A useful test is to alter future observations while leaving the available history fixed. A correctly constructed historical feature should stay unchanged. This does not prove the whole pipeline is clean, but it catches a direct violation of the information boundary.

Apply the same reasoning to preprocessing, category vocabularies and feature selection. If future rows influence a fitted reference, the leak can remain even when the final model sees only historical rows.

examples.title: Perturb the unavailable suffix
paragraphs: The prediction is made at index three using the two preceding readings.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
def trailing_mean(y, origin):
    return float(y[origin-2:origin].mean())
y = np.array([10., 12., 14., 16., 18.])
changed = y.copy()
changed[3:] = 999
print(trailing_mean(y, 3))
print(trailing_mean(changed, 3))
interpretation: A centred rolling window would fail this check because it would include an unavailable reading.

quiz.prompt: A report entered at 18:00 was available for a 12:00 prediction just because it describes a morning event.
quiz.because: Availability depends on when the prediction system could access it, not only when the described event happened.

quiz.prompt: Where should a replacement mean be learned during evaluation?
options: From the full dataset before splitting
quiz.because: Preprocessing parameters are fitted choices and must respect the same boundary as the model.

quiz.prompt: A pipeline can determine whether a raw field was uploaded after the decision.
quiz.because: A pipeline controls fitting steps. The feature's real availability still needs to be established from its provenance.

options: Yes: a mean cannot leak a target
Yes: its slice starts in the past
