topic: Find the Mistakes Behind the Score
title: Which Alerts Deserve an Inspection?
blurb: A fault detector can look accurate while missing almost every fault. Follow the alerts and the faults separately, then choose a threshold the inspection team can actually use.
openingTitle: What If Almost Every Pump Is Healthy?
opening: Most pumps on Botie’s route work normally. A detector that always says healthy could get a very high accuracy simply because faults are rare. It would also give the inspection team no help finding them.

We need to ask what fraction of actual faults we find and what fraction of our alerts lead to a real fault. Those questions use different denominators. Let’s keep the individual pumps visible while we calculate both.

history.title: Finding Relevant Items in a Much Larger Collection

sources.title: NIST: TREC’s shared retrieval evaluations, begun in 1992

blocks: Search researchers needed to compare systems that returned different sets of documents. A system could retrieve plenty of relevant material by returning far too much, or produce a short clean list while omitting most relevant material.

NIST began TREC in 1992 to support shared, large-scale retrieval evaluations. Participants received common documents and questions, then returned ranked results for relevance assessment. Precision and recall address the two different counts in that setting: how much of the returned material is relevant, and how much of the relevant material was found.
Our fault detector has the same counting problem. Its returned set is the inspection queue, so we will keep the queue size and the missed faults visible beside the percentages.

reading.experimentTitle: Lower the threshold and follow the alerts
reading.experimentIntro: Connect score selection to the actual fault labels before calculating either ratio.
reading.connectionTitle: Two denominators, two questions
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Count what the inspection team receives
reading.exampleNote: Invented fault scores and binary labels. Scores are supplied; their calibration has not been established.

intuition.title: A score orders the inspection queue
intuition.explanation: A larger score puts a pump nearer the front. The actual label remains separate from the score.

scene.caption: Predict an alert when the score is at least the chosen threshold.

intuition.title: A lower threshold finds another fault and a false alert
intuition.explanation: The positive class is fault. Both thresholds use the same four pumps.

scene.caption: The team gains coverage of actual faults at the cost of another unnecessary visit.

parts.title: 1. Name the positive event before counting
paragraphs: Here a positive means a fault requiring inspection. A true positive is an alerted pump with that fault. A false positive is an alerted healthy pump. A false negative is a fault the detector did not flag.

The definition matters. If a record’s label means “inspection booked” instead of “fault confirmed”, we are evaluating a different prediction. Confirm how labels were collected and which failures might never receive a label.
parts.calculation:
At threshold 0.70:
TP = 2; FP = 1; FN = 0
interpretation: A confusion matrix begins with a clear target and a credible observation process.

parts.title: 2. Ask about the alerts and the missed faults
paragraphs: Precision asks how many issued alerts were genuine. Recall asks how many actual faults were found. Counting all healthy pumps in the denominator would answer neither question.

We use null for an undefined ratio in the workshop and None in Python. With no alerts, there is no observed precision. With no actual positive labels, there is no observed recall. Libraries sometimes substitute zero or another convention; declare that choice when comparing results.
parts.calculation:
Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 2 / 3
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 2 / 2 = 1
interpretation: A score without its denominator can be misleading, especially in a small evaluation set.

parts.title: 3. Move through the thresholds together
paragraphs: Sort distinct score values from high to low. At each value, include every observation whose score reaches it. Tied scores enter together; their row order must not create an imaginary operating point.

Recall cannot decrease as we include more observations. Precision can rise or fall depending on which labels enter next. A precision-recall curve displays these operating points so we can inspect the tradeoff.
interpretation: Choose a threshold on development data. Report the frozen rule on an independent assessment instead of picking the best point after seeing final labels.

parts.title: 4. A curve summary still leaves a decision to make
paragraphs: Average precision, AP, weights precision by each increase in recall as the threshold falls. It summarises ranking across operating points. Trapezoidal area joins neighbouring points with straight lines and is a different summary. Name the calculation you report.

ROC curves compare true-positive rate with false-positive rate among actual negatives. They can be useful, but a small false-positive rate may still create many alerts when negatives greatly outnumber positives. Precision makes that workload visible.
parts.calculation:
For this ranked example:
Recall increments: [0.5, 0, 0.5, 0]
AP = 0.5 × 1 + 0 × 0.5 + 0.5 × (2/3) + 0 × 0.5
   ≈ 0.8333
interpretation: AP does not choose a usable threshold, price a missed fault or establish calibration.

parts.title: 5. Check whether the queue fits the team
paragraphs: A threshold that finds every labelled fault may send more pumps than the team can inspect. Record alerts per day beside precision and recall. A capacity rule might take the highest scores within a shift; tied scores then need a declared operational policy.

Precision changes with prevalence, the proportion of actual faults. If healthy pumps become much more common while sensitivity and false-positive rate stay the same, the alert queue becomes less precise. A benchmark with balanced classes can misrepresent a rare-event deployment.
parts.calculation:
If sensitivity = 0.8, false-positive rate = 0.1, prevalence = 0.01:
Expected precision = (0.8 × 0.01) / ((0.8 × 0.01) + (0.1 × 0.99))
                   ≈ 0.0748
interpretation: This calculation assumes those rates transfer to the new population. Measure whether they do.

parts.title: 6. Build the mask before the report
paragraphs: A NumPy comparison produces a Boolean array with one position per pump. Combining that mask with labels identifies true positives. Sum only after the masks express the intended set.
interpretation: The challenge adds shape checks and explicit undefined-ratio handling.

examples.title: Count selected faults
paragraphs: Inspect one threshold using a different set of pumps.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
scores = np.array([.6, .4, .9])
y = np.array([0, 1, 1])
alert = scores >= .5
print(alert.tolist())
print(int(np.sum(alert & (y == 1))))
interpretation: The middle pump is a missed fault. The first is a false alert; selecting it does not make it positive.

quiz.prompt: High AP alone establishes that this threshold is operationally useful.
quiz.because: AP is a ranking summary. The deployed queue still needs capacity and cost checks.

given.data: A detector has high AP but issues more alerts than the team can inspect at its deployed threshold.

quiz.prompt: Under this lesson’s convention, what is the report?
quiz.because: There are no alerts to assess precision, while both actual faults were missed.

given.data: A threshold issues no alerts on ten pumps, two of which have confirmed faults.

    raise NotImplementedError

print(alert_report([.95,.8,.7,.1], [1,0,1,0], .7))
hints: Create the inclusive alert mask, then count selected positive labels.
Use all alerts for precision and all actual positives for recall.

checkpoints.after: 3. Move through the thresholds together

questions.because: Recall measures how many actual faults were found, so both found and missed faults belong in its denominator.

given.data: TP = 2; FP = 3; FN = 2. Positive means an actual fault.

questions.because: A threshold cannot distinguish equal scores. Selecting one by row order would be a different policy.

topic: Find the Mistakes Behind the Score
title: Better for Which Cases?
blurb: Most readings come from the day shift. A model can improve its overall score while getting worse at night. Keep group sizes beside group errors before calling that a repair.
openingTitle: The Day Shift Is Drowning Out the Night Shift
opening: Botie’s revised temperature model improves on most readings. The night team disagrees: their predictions are worse. Both observations can be true if the evaluation contains far more daytime readings.
Let’s keep the same error calculation and change how we group its results. We want to see who benefits from the revision and where we still need evidence.

history.title: A Model Report Needs to Say Who Was Measured

sources.title: Mitchell and colleagues: Model Cards for Model Reporting, 2019

blocks: A single reported score can hide differences across populations and operating conditions. Model Cards proposed structured documentation of intended uses, evaluation conditions and disaggregated performance. That documented reporting proposal helps us ask where a model’s evidence actually applies.
We will use shifts in an invented greenhouse. The calculation is small enough to inspect, while the reporting question also applies to devices, locations and carefully defined population groups.

reading.experimentTitle: Keep the night readings visible
reading.experimentIntro: Calculate one absolute error per reading, then aggregate within the supplied shift names.
reading.connectionTitle: The denominator determines whose errors dominate
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Report every observed shift
reading.exampleNote: Invented readings. One mutually exclusive shift label per observation is used here; real evaluation slices can overlap.

intuition.title: A smaller overall error can conceal a regression
intuition.explanation: The same four readings are used for both versions.

scene.caption: The candidate improves three daytime readings but doubles the night error.

intuition.title: Keep the sample size beside the metric
intuition.explanation: The aggregate weights each reading equally, so daytime receives most of the weight.

scene.caption: One night reading is a warning worth investigating, not a precise estimate of all nights.

parts.title: 1. Keep the comparison on the same observations
paragraphs: Retain an ID, an observed outcome and both predictions for every evaluation case. Attach the shift from the original record. Compute absolute error before aggregating.

If the candidate’s report excludes a failed night prediction, its lower average may come from removing a difficult case. Count missing outputs separately and require the declared evaluation set to remain accounted for.
interpretation: The workshop assumes complete aligned predictions. In a production report, missing results need their own explicit status.

parts.title: 2. Choose slices for a reason
paragraphs: A slice is a subset defined by a condition, such as night readings or a particular sensor model. Start with conditions that matter to the task and are available in the evaluation data. Record the definitions before comparing candidates.

Exploring additional slices can reveal a problem you did not anticipate. Mark that as a discovery to confirm on new evidence. Searching hundreds of tiny slices and presenting only the worst or best result can create misleading certainty.
parts.calculation:
Night slice: shift == "night"
Day slice: shift == "day"
interpretation: For people-related groups, the labels, collection process and reporting choices need particular care. An error comparison alone does not establish a complete fairness claim.

parts.title: 3. Distinguish equal readings from equal groups
paragraphs: Suppose the day shift contributes many more readings than the night shift. Averaging all absolute errors gives the day shift more influence simply because it supplied more rows. That is overall mean absolute error, or MAE. We can instead calculate each shift's MAE and average the shift results equally; this is a macro average. The two reports answer different questions about whose errors should receive equal weight.

For disjoint groups covering the dataset, weighting each group MAE by its count recovers the overall MAE. Overlapping slices cannot simply be added this way because some observations would be counted more than once.
parts.calculation:
Candidate group MAEs: day = 1, night = 4
Observation-weighted MAE = (3 × 1 + 1 × 4) / 4 = 1.75
Equal-group MAE = (1 + 4) / 2 = 2.5
interpretation: Name the averaging rule. Changing the weights is a decision about which population or cost the report represents.

parts.title: 4. Small slices need visible uncertainty
paragraphs: A group with one observation can produce a dramatic number without telling us how stable it is. Report the count and, where appropriate, an uncertainty interval based on the actual independent sampling units. Repeated readings from one greenhouse do not become independent buildings because they occupy separate rows.
Do not silently suppress a small slice’s failure. Mark the evidence as limited and decide what additional observations would help distinguish a persistent problem from one unusual case.
interpretation: No observations means no measured performance. Display “not evaluated” rather than a perfect score.

parts.title: 5. Use a mask to preserve group membership
paragraphs: The groups array names the shift at each position. Comparing it with one group name creates a Boolean mask. Apply that mask to the error array, then reduce the selected values.
A Python dictionary preserves first-seen key order. We use that to keep reports predictable without hard-coding that only day and night can occur.
interpretation: The reusable challenge must handle a new group name as well as a new number of readings.

examples.title: Inspect the night slice directly
paragraphs: The example extracts a group before calculating its mean.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
errors = np.array([1., 2., 5.])
groups = np.array(["day", "night", "night"])
selected = errors[groups == "night"]
print(selected.tolist())
print(float(selected.mean()))
interpretation: The daytime error never enters the night denominator.

parts.title: 6. Turn a group regression into a testable repair
paragraphs: Inspect the night cases. Perhaps the heater behaves differently after sunset, or the sensor measures a different part of the room. A plausible missing feature gives us something specific to test.

Keep day performance in the comparison while developing the repair. Declare acceptable group regressions and minimum evidence before the final assessment. A tiny apparent gain should not automatically excuse a large error where the system is most needed.
interpretation: The later model iteration project combines this report with paired gains and runtime requirements.

quiz.prompt: Its measured error should be reported as zero.
quiz.because: There is no observed error estimate for an empty slice.

given.data: A night slice has no observations in the assessment.

quiz.prompt: Why not reconstruct the overall error by adding both slice totals?
options: Slice metrics cannot ever be useful
quiz.because: Overlapping slices answer useful local questions but cannot be treated as a partition.

given.data: Slice A contains rows 1 and 2; slice B contains rows 2 and 3.

practice.question: Can the report keep a newly arriving shift?
task: A small night shift can be poorly predicted while a large day shift makes the overall score look good. Keep each temperature error beside its shift name before taking group means.

Implement slice_errors(observed, predicted, groups). Return a list of (group, count, MAE) tuples in first-seen group order. Accept aligned, nonempty finite 1D numeric arrays and one nonempty string group per observation.
Raise ValueError for invalid inputs. Do not alter inputs or hard-code the group names. Print the supplied example.

import numpy as np
def slice_errors(observed, predicted, groups):
    raise NotImplementedError

print(slice_errors([10,10,10,10], [9,9,9,5], ["day","day","day","night"]))

Use a mask for each distinct group, keeping first-seen order.

build.problem: The night team needs to see its mistakes even when daytime dominates the data.

build.why: The earlier residual calculation survives. Grouping changes which errors are averaged together.
build.limitation: Counts and means alone do not quantify uncertainty, establish fairness or explain the cause of a group difference.

options: Overall MAE improved while the night observation worsened

title: Did the Revision Help on the Same Cases?
blurb: A lower score on an easier dataset tells us little about a revision. Match the cases, inspect their gains and regressions, then resample the paired observations to explore uncertainty.
openingTitle: Did We Improve the Model or Give It Easier Days?
opening: Botie tests the old temperature model during a cold week and the candidate during a mild one. The candidate has a lower error. We still do not know how much of that difference belongs to the revision.

Run both models on the same held-out observations. Then each day supplies a comparison: how much error did the change remove, or add? That pairing also matters when we ask how uncertain the average improvement is.

history.title: Preserving the Comparison When We Resample

sources.title: Cawley and Talbot: selection bias in performance evaluation, 2010

blocks: Comparing learning procedures requires separating a method change from variation in the evaluation data. Cawley and Talbot examined how selection itself can overfit an estimated performance criterion. A favourable comparison becomes harder to interpret when it was selected from many attempts.

Here we begin with a simpler fixed comparison. Both frozen models see the same cases. We keep each pair together when resampling so the uncertainty calculation still describes their difference on shared observations.

reading.experimentTitle: Keep each gain attached to its case
reading.experimentIntro: Subtract candidate loss from baseline loss before summarising. Positive gains mean lower candidate loss.
reading.connectionTitle: The unit of comparison must survive resampling
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Resample the paired gains
reading.exampleNote: Invented per-case losses for frozen models. The workshop counts improvements; the Python exercise explores resampling uncertainty.

intuition.title: The candidate helps some days and hurts another
intuition.explanation: Each row is one shared observation.

scene.caption: Gain is baseline loss minus candidate loss. The mean alone would hide day B.

intuition.title: Resample whole comparisons
intuition.explanation: Each draw selects case positions with replacement. Use the same positions for both models.

scene.caption: These are two illustrative draws, not enough to estimate an interval.

parts.title: 1. Pair by identity before subtracting
paragraphs: An evaluation service may return predictions in a different order. Join them by case ID, check for duplicate or missing IDs, then calculate both losses against the same observed outcome. Equal array lengths cannot establish that correspondence.
The workshop begins after that join. Every position represents the same case in both input arrays. Its output keeps improved, regressed and unchanged counts beside mean gain.
parts.calculation:
Gains = baseline losses - candidate losses
[4, 1, 3] - [2, 2, 2] = [2, -1, 1]
Mean gain = (2 - 1 + 1) / 3 ≈ 0.6667
interpretation: A positive mean is evidence about this evaluation sample. Inspect the negative entries before deciding the revision is acceptable.

parts.title: 2. Choose a difference that matters to the task
paragraphs: A measured improvement can be too small to matter operationally. Declare a useful effect size in the metric’s units before inspecting the candidate. If a slower model saves a negligible temperature error, the trade may be unattractive.
Also retain group performance. A meaningful average gain does not excuse every local regression, and a nonzero estimate does not by itself establish that the gain will persist.
parts.calculation:
Example development requirement:
MAE improvement at least 0.5 °C
No declared shift increases MAE by more than 0.2 °C
interpretation: These are invented requirements for an example. A real application must justify its own limits.

parts.title: 3. Resample pairs rather than separate score lists
paragraphs: The bootstrap treats the observed independent cases as an empirical population. Draw the same number of positions with replacement and average the selected paired gains. Repeat many times to inspect how the estimate changes under that resampling model.

Drawing baseline and candidate positions independently breaks the shared-case relationship. Easy and difficult cases can then be compared against unrelated observations, changing the uncertainty calculation.
parts.calculation:
gain = baseline_loss - candidate_loss
indices = rng.integers(0, n, size=(repeats, n))
bootstrap_means = gain[indices].mean(axis=1)
interpretation: The practice function receives explicit indices so its tests are reproducible. A complete analysis would generate many draws with a recorded seed.

parts.title: 4. Read an interval without turning it into certainty
paragraphs: A percentile bootstrap interval takes lower and upper quantiles of the resampled means. For example, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles form a conventional approximate 95% interval under suitable sampling conditions. It is not a statement that a fixed unknown gain has a 95% probability of lying in that realised interval.
Few cases, heavy tails or a badly represented population can make the interval unreliable. A narrow interval around a biased sample still describes the wrong population precisely.
parts.calculation: lower, upper = np.quantile(bootstrap_means, [0.025, 0.975])
interpretation: Compare the interval with the practical improvement requirement, not only with zero. Do not estimate a serious interval from the two teaching draws above.

parts.title: 5. The independent unit may be a greenhouse
paragraphs: If one greenhouse contributes hundreds of related readings, resampling individual rows can understate uncertainty. Resample whole greenhouses when the claim concerns new greenhouses, preserving both models’ predictions within each selected group. For dependent time series, use an appropriate temporal design rather than assuming row independence.

This exercise conditions on already fitted models. To assess a learning procedure that will be retrained, the design must also account for fitting and selection variation. Repeating seeds on the same held-out cases does not create new independent cases.
interpretation: Choose the sampling unit from the claim you want to make, then choose the resampling method.

parts.title: 6. Inspect the indexing on a small draw
paragraphs: NumPy can use a two-dimensional integer array to select several draws from a one-dimensional gain array. Each resulting row is one bootstrap sample. Reducing along axis 1 computes one mean per draw.
interpretation: Keep the operation inspectable before scaling up the number of draws.

examples.title: Repeated positions really are repeated observations
paragraphs: This shows indexing only; the challenge adds loss pairing and validation.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
gain = np.array([2., -1., 1.])
positions = np.array([[0, 0, 2], [1, 1, 2]])
print(gain[positions].tolist())
interpretation: The repeated positions retain whole comparisons. They do not refit either model.

parts.title: 7. Record the attempts that led here
paragraphs: Save the baseline version, candidate version, case IDs, metric definition and selection history. If this was the best of many candidates on the same data, a fixed-pair interval does not erase that selection.
Use development comparisons to decide what to try. Reserve independent evidence for the chosen procedure or candidate, with a plan for when that evidence has been used up by further decisions.
interpretation: The next lesson separates choosing a model from estimating how well the whole choosing procedure works.

quiz.prompt: Row-wise resampling automatically estimates uncertainty for new greenhouses correctly.
quiz.because: Related readings are not independent greenhouses. Preserve groups when the target claim is about new groups.

given.data: Both models have predictions for the same greenhouses, with many related readings per greenhouse.

quiz.prompt: How should those positions be used?
quiz.because: Shared positions preserve the paired comparison and each case’s difficulty.

given.data: A bootstrap draw selects case positions [0,0,2].

practice.title: Can the bootstrap keep the same days together?
practice.question: Can the bootstrap keep the same days together?
task: Resampling a comparison must keep both models on the same days. A positive baseline-minus-candidate gain means the candidate made a smaller loss on that particular case.

Implement paired_bootstrap(baseline, candidate, draws). Loss arrays must be aligned, nonempty, finite and nonnegative. draws is a nonempty 2D integer array with n columns, where n is the number of cases. Every index must be in range.
Return a NumPy array containing one mean baseline-minus-candidate gain per draw. Raise ValueError for invalid input. Print the supplied means rounded to four decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
def paired_bootstrap(baseline, candidate, draws):
    raise NotImplementedError

print(paired_bootstrap([4,1,3], [2,2,2], [[0,0,2],[1,1,2],[0,1,2]]).round(4).tolist())
hints: Calculate the paired gain array once.
Index that array with draws and average across each row.

tests.name: Reject invalid draws

build.problem: Botie needs to compare frozen revisions on shared cases.
build.challenge: Subtract candidate losses from baseline losses, then return meanGain and counts improved, regressed and tied. Every position must refer to the same case in both lists.
build.why: Pairing removes a difference in case difficulty from the direct comparison. It does not remove sampling or selection uncertainty.
build.limitation: This workshop summarises supplied losses. Use the Python exercise and an appropriate sampling design to investigate uncertainty.

title: Who Checks the Model-Choosing Process?
blurb: Trying enough settings can produce an attractive validation score by chance. Put the search inside a separate assessment so the result includes the cost of choosing.
openingTitle: The Winning Score Has Been Chosen for Looking Good
opening: Botie tries several feature sets and regularisation strengths. One has the lowest validation error, so we keep it. That is a reasonable development decision. Reporting that same winning score as an independent assessment is another matter.
The validation results helped choose the winner. Some of its advantage may belong to the particular observations we happened to use. We need fresh observations outside that choosing process.

history.title: The Search Can Overfit Too

sources.title: Cawley and Talbot: On Over-fitting in Model Selection, 2010

blocks: Model fitting was already understood as a source of overfitting, but the criterion used to choose a fitted model also varies with the sample. Cawley and Talbot examined how optimising that noisy criterion can bias the reported result.
Nested cross-validation separates the search from an outer assessment. The outside observations ask whether the entire inner choosing procedure produces useful predictions on data it did not use.

reading.experimentTitle: Keep the outer answers out of the choice
reading.experimentIntro: Select each fold’s candidate using its inner validation losses. Only then read that candidate’s outer loss.
reading.connectionTitle: Evaluate the search procedure
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Audit which results selected the winner
reading.exampleNote: These are invented recorded fold losses. The workshop audits selection and aggregation; it does not run cross-validation training.

intuition.title: One outer fold has a boundary around the search
intuition.explanation: All inner training and validation happen inside the outer training portion.

rows.label: Assessment
items: Refit chosen settings on outer training

scene.caption: Repeat with other outer test portions. Preprocessing must stay inside each fitted pipeline.

intuition.title: The tempting outer winner is ineligible to choose itself
intuition.explanation: Rows represent outer folds and columns represent candidate procedures A and B.

scene.caption: The selected outer losses are 4 and 5, even though another outer cell looks better in each row.

parts.title: 1. State whether we are evaluating a model or a procedure
paragraphs: There are two things we might want to assess. We could test one already fitted model, keeping all its choices fixed. Or we could test the whole way we choose a model: try settings, select a candidate, and fit it. Nested cross-validation addresses that second question. It gives the selection process its own training and validation records, then checks the selected result on an outer held-out portion. Different outer portions can legitimately lead the procedure to choose different settings.

Neither description makes the other unnecessary. A development team may use nested evaluation to compare procedures, then train its final chosen pipeline and assess it on a separately reserved dataset.
interpretation: Write down the object being evaluated before selecting a split design.

parts.title: 2. Create an outer boundary first
paragraphs: Set aside one outer test portion. The rest is the outer training portion, containing every record available to the inner search. The inner search divides that portion again to fit candidate pipelines and score them.

The outer test labels cannot select features, thresholds, stopping epochs or hyperparameters. Treat all those choices as part of the procedure. A manual feature decision informed by outer errors is still selection.
parts.calculation:
Outer training → inner training + inner validation
Outer test → assessment only
interpretation: For new patients or machines, split at that group boundary. For forecasting, preserve the available history at each origin. Nesting does not fix an inappropriate split.

parts.title: 3. Choose inside, refit, then look outside
paragraphs: Average each candidate’s inner validation losses using a declared aggregation rule. Select the candidate with the lowest loss. Refit its complete pipeline on the outer training portion, then predict the outer test portion once.

Repeat across outer folds. Report the outer assessment results, not the average of the best inner scores. Declare whether folds receive equal weight or predictions are pooled; those differ when fold sizes differ.
parts.calculation:
Inner choices: [A, B]
Selected outer losses: [4, 5]
Equal-fold mean = (4 + 5) / 2 = 4.5
interpretation: Our teaching tables assume equal-size outer folds. The practice function explicitly reports an equal-fold mean.

parts.title: 4. Fit transformations inside the same boundary
paragraphs: Imputers, scalers, feature selectors and learned encoders must be fitted on the current training partition. Even an unsupervised scaler can leak distribution information if it sees the outer test data before evaluation.

In scikit-learn, a Pipeline inside GridSearchCV keeps fitted preprocessing with the estimator. Cross-validating that search object creates the outer assessment. Supplying a transformed full dataset before the search defeats that boundary.
parts.calculation:
outer training
  → fit inner pipeline on each inner training split
  → score each inner validation split
  → select settings
  → refit entire pipeline on outer training
  → transform and predict outer test
interpretation: For grouped searches, ensure both levels actually receive and respect group information. API convenience does not establish a correct information boundary.

references.title: Run the complete nested search with scikit-learn
description: The workshop audits recorded losses. This reference actually fits a scaled ridge-regression pipeline inside an inner search and evaluates that whole search in outer folds. The synthetic observations are independent by construction; this split is not a template for grouped records or time series.
references.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
X = rng.normal(size=(60, 2))
y = 10 + 2 * X[:, 0] + 4 * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(size=60)

pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("ridge", Ridge()),
])
inner = KFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=11)
outer = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=19)
search = GridSearchCV(
    pipeline, {"ridge__alpha": [0.1, 1.0, 10.0]},
    scoring="neg_mean_squared_error", cv=inner, refit=True,
)
outer_mse = -cross_val_score(
    search, X, y, cv=outer, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
)
print("Outer MSEs:", outer_mse)
print("Equal-fold mean MSE:", outer_mse.mean())

# After settling the procedure, fit it on all development observations.
# This fitted object's best_score_ is an inner selection score.
search.fit(X, y)
print("Final development settings:", search.best_params_)
setup: Run in a Python environment with NumPy and scikit-learn installed. This reference is separate from the NumPy-only browser challenge.
Record package versions when saving results. The code creates a synthetic dataset and does not contact a provider or download records.
interpretation: GridSearchCV refits the selected complete pipeline on each outer training portion. Its scaler therefore never fits on that fold’s outer test inputs.

Scikit-learn scorers maximise scores. neg_mean_squared_error is negated again here to report ordinary nonnegative MSE. The final search.fit uses all development data; its best_score_ must not replace the outer assessment.
These runs do not supply a fresh final test set. Changing the procedure after inspecting outer scores requires new assessment evidence.

parts.title: 5. Do not promote the best outer fold to the final model
paragraphs: The outer folds are assessment runs, not contestants. Picking the fold with the best score creates another selection. After settling the procedure, run its search on the full development dataset and refit the selected pipeline there.

If you change the search space after inspecting outer results, those results have informed development. Reserve new evidence for the resulting procedure. Report the number and nature of those decisions.
interpretation: Fold scores share overlapping training data. Their standard deviation is descriptive and is not automatically a valid standard error from independent experiments.

parts.title: 6. Audit selection with explicit array axes
paragraphs: In the tables below, axis 0 is outer fold and axis 1 is candidate. argmin along axis 1 gives one choice per fold. Advanced indexing then picks one outer score from each corresponding row.
interpretation: The challenge combines the two operations and checks that malformed tables cannot silently broadcast.

examples.title: Read a candidate from each fold
paragraphs: These choices are supplied so we can inspect the row-and-column indexing separately.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
outer = np.array([[8., 3.], [4., 7.]])
choices = np.array([1, 0])
print(outer[np.arange(2), choices].tolist())
interpretation: Each row contributes exactly one selected score. Flattening the table would lose the fold boundary.

parts.title: 7. Pay for the question you need answered
paragraphs: Nested evaluation repeats fitting many times, so it can be expensive. A sufficiently large independent test set with a disciplined development process may answer the immediate question more simply. If data are limited and model selection is substantial, nesting helps expose that selection to independent outer cases.
Record the candidate space, splits, seeds and software versions. A repeated experiment should reproduce the protocol, not merely a rounded final average.
interpretation: Use nesting where it answers the evaluation question. More folds cannot manufacture missing populations or future conditions.

quiz.prompt: What should the final fitting step normally do?
options: Keep the best-scoring outer fold’s fitted object
Run the settled search procedure on all development data and refit there
quiz.because: Outer runs assess the procedure. They are not finalists from which to cherry-pick a model.

given.data: Different outer folds select different hyperparameters.

Choose each row’s candidate from inner only, breaking ties by first position. Return (choice positions as a list, selected outer losses as a list, equal-fold mean). Raise ValueError for invalid tables. These are recorded losses, not a training implementation.

topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
title: Is the Model Wrong, or Is the Record Wrong?
blurb: A suspicious label deserves a closer look. Use out-of-fold disagreements to organise review while preserving original records and the boundary around the final assessment.
openingTitle: The Fault Label Describes the Wrong Inspection
opening: Botie repeatedly predicts a fault for a pump labelled healthy. We inspect the record and discover that its label came from an earlier visit. Changing model settings would not fix that timestamp.
Other disagreements will be genuine model mistakes. We need a review process that can tell those cases apart without treating the model’s own opinion as the answer.

history.title: Looking for Problems in the Labels

sources.title: Northcutt, Jiang and Chuang: Confident Learning

blocks: Datasets are often treated as a fixed answer key even though their labels may contain mistakes. Confident Learning developed methods for estimating label uncertainty and identifying likely label issues using predicted probabilities under stated assumptions.

Our review queue is a simpler teaching rule, not an implementation of Confident Learning. It flags strong disagreements for investigation. The original observation and an independent review remain the evidence for any correction.

reading.experimentTitle: Request review without rewriting the answer
reading.experimentIntro: Keep eligible development records before applying the disagreement threshold.
reading.connectionTitle: A suspicion needs evidence
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Build a label review queue
reading.exampleNote: Invented records with supplied out-of-fold positive scores. The browser does not infer true labels or run a label-noise estimation method.

intuition.title: The same disagreement can have different causes
intuition.explanation: The score concerns the probability of a fault; the label records the reviewed outcome.

records.label: A
cells: Does the label belong to this visit?

records.label: B
cells: Did the model confuse harmless vibration with a fault?

scene.caption: A high score does not decide which record is wrong.

intuition.title: Keep an audit trail for a correction
intuition.explanation: A reviewer needs the original evidence and a defined target.

rows.label: Revision
items: Refit and evaluate under the declared split

scene.caption: Never silently replace a label with the model prediction.

parts.title: 1. Check the target and the join first
paragraphs: A record may join a sensor reading to the wrong pump, an inspection to the wrong day, or a label to an event that was unavailable when prediction was supposed to happen. Inspect identifiers and timestamps before diagnosing model capacity.

Write the target in operational terms. “Fault present at inspection” differs from “maintenance performed within a month”. A team’s maintenance decisions may depend on the existing model, so those labels can reflect the policy as well as the condition.
interpretation: An accurate calculation on misjoined records still answers the wrong question.

parts.title: 2. Look for duplicates across the split
paragraphs: Exact duplicates can place the same example in training and assessment. Near duplicates, repeated patients and multiple views of one event can do the same less obviously. Group related observations before splitting when they share the information the model could memorise.

Deduplication itself needs a definition. Two pumps with equal temperature readings are not automatically duplicate events. Preserve event identity and domain context instead of dropping equal numeric rows indiscriminately.
interpretation: A data audit can change the split plan, not only the label values.

parts.title: 3. Use predictions made without fitting that record
paragraphs: If Botie asks a model about a record it trained on, agreement may come from remembering that record. For a more useful check, set one group of development records aside, fit on the others, and predict the group that was excluded. Repeat until every group has been excluded once. These are out-of-fold predictions: each record receives a prediction from a fit that did not use it. A confident disagreement can then enter a review queue, without becoming proof that the recorded label is wrong.

Respect group and time boundaries inside those folds. Keep label review on the development side; do not feed final test answers back into training while retaining the old test score as independent evidence.
parts.calculation:
For a recorded label 0: disagreement score = p(fault)
For a recorded label 1: disagreement score = 1 - p(fault)
interpretation: An overconfident model can produce strong but mistaken flags. The queue is a prioritisation aid.

parts.title: 4. Make the review rule explicit
paragraphs: Our teaching rule flags eligible records when disagreement confidence reaches a threshold above one half. Threshold inclusion is deliberate: a score equal to the threshold enters the queue.

Review records in a stable order and keep unique IDs. A real queue might combine disagreement with group coverage or expected correction value. Sample some unflagged cases too; otherwise you may never see errors the model confidently agrees with.
parts.calculation:
Record A: label 0, score 0.95, threshold 0.90 → review
Record B: label 1, score 0.95, threshold 0.90 → no disagreement flag
interpretation: The rule does not estimate how many labels are wrong, and unflagged does not mean verified.

parts.title: 5. Keep correction provenance and unresolved cases
paragraphs: A reviewer should see the evidence needed for the target, with a written annotation policy. Record the previous label, new label if any, reason and data version. Where feasible, independent or blinded review reduces the chance of simply agreeing with the model.
Some cases remain ambiguous. Keep that status rather than manufacturing certainty. Agreement rates between reviewers, adjudication rules and sampling design help explain what the revised labels mean.
interpretation: If a final evaluation label really is wrong, correct it transparently and report the changed assessment version. Do not silently tune on it and continue calling it untouched.

parts.title: 6. Filter records without mutating them
paragraphs: The review function returns IDs only. It should not rewrite labels, reorder source records or substitute predictions. That separation makes an accidental automatic relabelling harder to hide.
interpretation: The challenge adds eligibility, threshold and duplicate checks around this inspection.

examples.title: Read the evidence behind one flag
paragraphs: This example computes a disagreement score without changing its record.
examples.code:
record = {"id": "P4", "label": 1, "p": 0.08}
disagreement = 1 - record["p"]
print(round(disagreement, 2))
print(record["label"])
interpretation: The label remains 1. A score of 0.92 requests review; it is not a replacement label.

parts.title: 7. Test the dataset revision as a change
paragraphs: After corrections, refit the same procedure first so the comparison can isolate the data revision. Record any additional feature or algorithm change separately. Keep prior difficult cases in regression tests and assess on evidence outside the correction process.

Report how many records were reviewed, corrected, retained and unresolved. A model may improve because labels became more consistent, because the task definition changed, or because difficult cases were removed. Those explanations have different implications.
interpretation: A cleaner development dataset is useful. It still needs an assessment that represents the intended use.

quiz.prompt: What should the audit retain?
options: An unresolved status with the original evidence
quiz.because: Unresolved evidence belongs in the report. Forced labels and silent deletion hide uncertainty.

given.data: A reviewer cannot determine whether the inspection label applies to the current visit.

practice.title: Can Botie request review without editing the labels?
practice.question: Can Botie request review without editing the labels?
task: A confident model-label disagreement is a reason to request review, not permission to overwrite the label. Out-of-fold probabilities are predictions made for a row by a model that did not train on that row.

Implement review_queue(records, threshold). Each record has a unique nonempty string id, split (development or test), binary label, and finite p in [0,1]. Scores are supplied out-of-fold probabilities for the positive class.

Return development IDs whose disagreement score is at least threshold, preserving record order. Require 0.5 < threshold <= 1 and raise ValueError for invalid inputs. Empty input returns []. Do not alter records.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
def review_queue(records, threshold):
    raise NotImplementedError

print(review_queue([{'id':'A','split':'development','label':0,'p':.95},
                    {'id':'B','split':'test','label':0,'p':.99}], .9))
hints: Filter by declared split; confidence does not change eligibility.
For label 1, disagreement uses one minus p. Preserve the label itself.

topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
title: When Should the Model Ask for Help?
blurb: Sending uncertain cases to a person changes both the error rate and the workload. Measure what the model handles and what it leaves for the review team.
openingTitle: The Review Desk Has Only So Much Time
opening: Botie classifies pump inspections, but a person can review cases it is unsure about. That seems helpful until almost every inspection lands on the desk. We have reduced the model’s workload by giving it to someone else.
We need to measure two things together: how much work the model accepts and how often it is wrong on that accepted work. Then we can check whether the remaining queue is manageable.

history.title: Allowing a Classifier to Decline a Decision

sources.title: Geifman and El-Yaniv: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks, 2017

blocks: Selective classification studies predictions with a reject option: the system can decline some cases and trade coverage for lower error on accepted cases. Geifman and El-Yaniv developed a method for deep networks with risk control under their stated procedure.

Our threshold exercise measures empirical coverage and error on supplied cases. It does not implement that paper’s guarantee. The useful intuition is that refusing a case changes the population whose errors we report.

reading.experimentTitle: Watch both sides of the handoff
reading.experimentIntro: Threshold the supplied confidence, then count accepted errors and cases sent for review.
reading.connectionTitle: The rejected cases still exist
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Measure what the model accepts
reading.exampleNote: Invented confidence scores and observed error flags. Confidence is a supplied selection score, not a verified probability of correctness.

intuition.title: Acceptance changes the denominator
intuition.explanation: An error flag of 1 means the frozen model’s predicted class was wrong.

scene.caption: The review queue contains C even though the recorded prediction happened to be correct.

intuition.title: A confident mistake can survive a stricter rule
intuition.explanation: Now A is the error. Raising the threshold keeps that wrong prediction.

scene.caption: Confidence thresholding does not guarantee that the accepted error rate decreases on every sample.

parts.title: 1. Separate the prediction from the decision to use it
paragraphs: The classifier produces a predicted label. A selector decides whether the application should accept that label or request review. These are distinct decisions. For a binary probability, confidence might be the larger class probability, but a different selection score can be trained or calibrated.

Our inputs already contain confidence and an observed error flag for each frozen prediction. A low positive-class probability is not necessarily low confidence: it may express confidence in the negative class.
parts.calculation:
Binary p(fault) = 0.05
Predicted class = healthy
Maximum class probability = max(0.05, 0.95) = 0.95
interpretation: Do not reuse a positive-class alert threshold as a confidence threshold without changing its meaning.

parts.title: 2. Measure coverage and the errors left inside it
paragraphs: Start with all incoming cases and count how many the model accepts without referral. That fraction is coverage. Now restrict attention to accepted cases and ask what fraction of their predictions were wrong. This is selective risk when an error costs one and a correct answer costs zero, a convention called zero-one loss. Referred cases leave that error denominator, but they still belong in the report of work sent to people.
If nothing is accepted, selective risk is undefined. Reporting zero would make a system that refuses every task look flawless.
parts.calculation:
At threshold 0.75:
Accepted = 2 of 3
Coverage = 2 / 3
Accepted errors = 1
Selective risk = 1 / 2
interpretation: A lower accepted error rate can accompany a much larger review queue.

parts.title: 3. Test the confident mistakes
paragraphs: Raising the threshold changes which cases remain. It often removes difficult examples when the selection score is useful, but overconfident mistakes can stay. Examine them directly and report the coverage-risk tradeoff across development thresholds.

Calibration of probabilities and ranking of correctness are related questions with different answers. A system can order cases usefully while overstating their probabilities, or be well calibrated in broad bins while still failing in an important subgroup.
interpretation: Freeze a chosen selector before assessing it on new cases. Repeatedly tuning against the final assessment reuses its evidence.

parts.title: 4. Treat review as part of the system
paragraphs: Count arrivals and service capacity over time, not only a daily total. Cases can arrive in a burst while the reviewer is unavailable. Decide what happens when the queue is full and how urgent cases are prioritised.

Human review is not automatically correct. Measure reviewer agreement, turnaround time and downstream outcomes. If the model’s label is shown to reviewers, consider whether it anchors their decisions.
parts.calculation:
100 cases arrive in a shift
Coverage = 0.70
Review arrivals = 100 × (1 - 0.70) = 30
Review capacity = 20
Unserved cases in this simplified shift = 10
interpretation: This count ignores arrival timing and existing backlog. A deployment plan needs those details too.

parts.title: 5. Check who is being referred
paragraphs: Compare acceptance rates and accepted errors across relevant groups. A model could look better overall because it sends nearly every case from an underrepresented group to a slower manual route.

Report outcomes for all incoming cases where they can be obtained, including rejected ones. Labels collected only for accepted cases create a selective observation problem: the missing outcomes can hide failures in the selection policy.
interpretation: A useful selector needs an evaluation of the complete service, not only its easiest accepted cases.

parts.title: 6. Use the mask on the errors, not on the denominator twice
paragraphs: The acceptance mask selects the observed error flags. Averaging those flags gives accepted risk. Averaging the mask gives coverage because its zeros and ones refer to every incoming case.
interpretation: The challenge must handle the empty accepted set explicitly.

examples.title: Inspect accepted cases
paragraphs: This example demonstrates the mask on a different three-case batch.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
confidence = np.array([.9,.4,.8])
errors = np.array([0,1,1])
accepted = confidence >= .8
print(errors[accepted].tolist())
print(int((~accepted).sum()))
interpretation: The rejected error remains part of the workload to resolve. It is excluded only from the accepted-error metric.

options: The accepted model subset improved, but review capacity is unresolved
quiz.because: The deferred work remains part of the task and must be assessed.

topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
title: Should This Change the Prediction?
blurb: The same measurement can arrive in different units or a different batch. State the behaviour that should survive those changes, then test the actual prediction pipeline.
openingTitle: The Sensor Started Reporting Fahrenheit
opening: A greenhouse sensor update changes its output from Celsius to Fahrenheit. The physical temperature has not changed. If our prediction service feeds the new number into the old feature position, Botie sees a much hotter greenhouse.

A random test split may never contain that deployment change. We need tests built around a relationship we understand: after the correct unit conversion, the same physical input should produce the same result from a deterministic frozen pipeline.

history.title: Testing Behaviour That a Single Score Misses

sources.title: Ribeiro and colleagues: Beyond Accuracy, CheckList, 2020

blocks: A held-out average can miss a specific behaviour that users rely on. CheckList applied behavioural testing ideas to language models, including tests of capabilities and expected responses to input changes.

We use that testing perspective for a temperature service. Our unit and batching checks are examples of declared relationships between inputs and outputs, not a claim to implement the CheckList software or certify robustness.

reading.experimentTitle: Test a declared relationship
reading.experimentIntro: Compare each transformed run with its expected output and a stated absolute tolerance.
reading.connectionTitle: Choose the transformation before declaring invariance
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Report each behavioural check
reading.exampleNote: The workshop uses recorded expected and observed outputs. The worked Python program runs a real unit conversion; no trained model is called in the workshop.

intuition.title: Equivalent measurements should remain equivalent
intuition.explanation: The adapter converts the incoming value into the feature unit expected by the frozen pipeline.

scene.caption: The adapter needs the unit label. Guessing from the magnitude is not a reliable contract.

intuition.title: Some changes should matter
intuition.explanation: Define the expected relationship before constructing a test.

records.label: Reorder batch rows
cells: Same outputs after restoring row order

scene.caption: Changing a feature value is not automatically an invariance test.

parts.title: 1. Name the behaviour we rely on
paragraphs: An invariance test changes representation while preserving something the task should treat as equivalent. A unit conversion is one example. A metamorphic test describes a relationship between multiple runs even when we do not know an exact answer for every input.

Begin with the intended use. Flipping a photo may preserve its object label but change the meaning of left and right. Removing “not” from a sentence should often change its meaning. A convenient transformation is not automatically a valid test.
interpretation: Write the expected relation and the conditions under which it holds.

parts.title: 2. Keep the adapter inside the tested pipeline
paragraphs: A model receives numbers in a particular schema. Test from the input boundary through the adapter to prediction. A unit test of the coefficient multiplication alone will not catch a wrong conversion before it.
Keep named feature order as part of the contract. If temperature and heater setting swap columns, a matrix still has the right shape while representing the wrong input.
parts.calculation:
Fahrenheit to Celsius:
C = (F - 32) × 5 / 9
For F = 68:
C = (68 - 32) × 5 / 9 = 20
interpretation: Reject unknown units rather than silently assuming the training unit.

parts.title: 3. Use a tolerance that fits the output
paragraphs: Floating-point calculations can differ slightly across implementations. For a deterministic numerical pipeline, compare differences with a justified absolute or relative tolerance. State the units and avoid a tolerance so broad that a real bug passes.
Our workshop uses an absolute tolerance. Equality at the limit passes. NumPy isclose also supports relative tolerance; if you use it, understand how both terms combine.
parts.calculation:
pass = abs(observed - expected) <= absolute_tolerance
Expected: 20; observed: 20.25; tolerance: 0.25 → pass
interpretation: A stochastic generator needs repeated-distribution or task-level checks, not an assumption that every run produces identical text or pixels.

parts.title: 4. Test batches without mixing up identities
paragraphs: For a row-independent deterministic predictor, predicting records individually should agree with predicting them as a batch. Permuting rows should permute outputs in the same way. Restore IDs before comparing.

Some models legitimately use context across records, such as sequence models. Their batching and ordering contracts need different tests. State that dependency instead of treating every order effect as a bug.
interpretation: A test can reveal a contract mismatch even when the model’s ordinary benchmark remains unchanged.

parts.title: 5. Try plausible corruptions and measure degradation
paragraphs: Sensor noise, missing fields and delayed measurements deserve separate tests. These can change the available information, so identical outputs may be the wrong requirement. Check degradation against a task-specific allowance or require a clear rejection of unsupported inputs.
Record corruption severity and why it is plausible. Test important slices too. Passing a few perturbations does not establish resistance to arbitrary adversarial inputs or unseen distribution shifts.
interpretation: Use failures to create specific regression tests. Keep a fresh assessment to check whether the resulting repair generalises.

parts.title: 6. Run the conversion before comparing results
paragraphs: The program below uses an explicit unit argument. It tests an equivalent measurement through the adapter instead of comparing two unrelated raw numbers.
interpretation: The challenge builds a reusable report for many recorded checks, including one failure.

examples.title: Convert the same physical temperature
paragraphs: This is an executable adapter example, not a fitted model.
interpretation: The conversion establishes equal physical inputs. A model test would now send both through the same frozen prediction pipeline.

parts.title: 7. Keep the failed input with the repair
paragraphs: When a test fails, preserve the smallest meaningful example, the expected relationship and the pipeline version. Repair the adapter or model behaviour that violated the contract. Rerun earlier tests as well as the new one.
A passing count is useful only alongside what was tested. Document excluded conditions and keep observing production inputs for new ones.
interpretation: The final project combines behaviour checks with errors and operational requirements before a limited trial.

quiz.prompt: Which claim is supported?
options: The pipeline passed those specified conversion checks
The model is robust to every input change
Future data cannot cause a failure
quiz.because: A finite set supports the tested behaviours under its assumptions, not a universal guarantee.

given.data: Three unit-conversion tests pass.

Raise ValueError for invalid input. These arrays represent matched runs of declared behavioural tests. Print the supplied example.

print(behaviour_report([10,20,30], [10,20.25,33], .25))

topic: Build and Check a Model Revision
title: Repair the Night-Shift Model Without Breaking the Day Shift
blurb: Diagnose a missing condition, fit a revised predictor and compare it with the baseline. Botie then checks whether the overall gain survives group and runtime requirements on a fresh shift.
openingTitle: The Same Heater Setting Produces Different Nights
opening: We have enough evidence to try a specific repair. Botie’s temperature baseline uses the heater setting, but its night readings are consistently underpredicted. The night indicator is available before prediction, so we can test whether adding it helps.

Keep the original model as a reference. We will fit both versions using the same training records, compare their predictions on development data, and write down what the candidate must satisfy before a limited trial. The next shift will challenge those requirements.

history.title: A Fitted Equation Needs an Evaluation Record

sources.title: Mitchell and colleagues: Model Cards for Model Reporting

blocks: A revised model can improve its overall score while becoming worse for the people or conditions it is supposed to help. A saved parameter file does not tell its next user where the evidence supports its use.

Mitchell and colleagues’ Model Cards proposal, published at FAT* in 2019 after a 2018 preprint, called for structured accounts of intended use and evaluation, including performance under different conditions. That reporting problem is part of our repair project. We will fit a specific change to the greenhouse model, test the old and new procedures on shared cases, and retain the day/night results that explain the decision.

reading.experimentTitle: Give the revision a fair trial decision
reading.experimentIntro: Compute both error arrays from shared observations, inspect group changes, then enforce the declared policy.
reading.connectionTitle: A repair needs a record of what changed
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Fit both versions without reading the answers early
reading.exampleNote: Workshop predictions and runtime are supplied measurements for an invented comparison. The Python challenge actually fits both least-squares models on training data.

intuition.title: The missing condition is visible in matched settings
intuition.explanation: The heater setting alone cannot distinguish these day and night records.

scene.caption: The night indicator is known at prediction time. These four exact values are a teaching construction, not a field dataset.

intuition.title: Carry a specific hypothesis into the comparison
intuition.explanation: Each boundary answers a different question.

rows.label: Development
items: Fit both versions on training only

rows.label: Assessment
items: Check fresh cases before a limited trial

scene.caption: A failed assessment that prompts another repair becomes development evidence for that repair.

intuition.title: A better average can still fail a requirement
intuition.explanation: Both candidates are compared with baseline absolute errors of 2 on each of four readings.

scene.caption: The second candidate has the same average improvement but breaks the night requirement.

parts.title: 1. Write the hypothesis before changing the code
paragraphs: Our hypothesis is that a missing night condition contributes to the residual pattern. The candidate adds a night indicator and keeps the rest of the fitting procedure unchanged. Save the dataset version, split IDs and baseline first.

An indicator can capture an association without identifying its physical cause. It may stand in for ventilation or other scheduled changes. If that schedule changes, the association may fail. The diagnosis gives us a useful experiment, not a causal proof.
interpretation: Confirm the new feature is available at prediction time and uses the same definition in training and serving.

parts.title: 2. Represent both models with visible columns
paragraphs: The baseline has a constant column and heater setting. The candidate adds the night column. Each row is an observation; each coefficient multiplies its matching column.

NumPy column_stack combines the one-dimensional columns into those matrices. The leading ones let the fitted coefficient represent an intercept. The candidate design must have independent columns to identify all three coefficients in this exercise.
parts.calculation:
Baseline row:  [1, heater]
Candidate row: [1, heater, night]
Prediction = design row @ coefficients
interpretation: Keep column names and order with the saved model. A two-column input matrix should not silently accept a swapped schema.

parts.title: 3. Fit on training records, then freeze the coefficients
paragraphs: linalg.lstsq returns a least-squares solution. We use its first returned item, the coefficient vector, and multiply a separate evaluation design matrix by those coefficients. Evaluation outcomes enter only after the predictions exist.
The model is fitted by squared error while this task reports MAE. That is deliberate: the fitting objective and the operational report need not be identical, but their difference should be stated.
parts.calculation:
For the exact training table:
Baseline coefficients: [12, 2]
Candidate coefficients: [10, 2, 4]
New rows: [[2, 0], [2, 1]]
Baseline predictions: [16, 16]
Candidate predictions: [14, 18]
interpretation: The exact candidate fit was designed for teaching. Real data include noise and may not support this simple relation.

parts.title: 4. Use a small fitting program before the full comparison
paragraphs: The example below fits one intercept-and-slope model. Inspect the design matrix and prediction before building both versions in the challenge.

The reusable challenge returns predictions as well as scores. That allows a test to change evaluation labels and verify that the predictions do not move. If they do, the fitting step has leaked evaluation information.
interpretation: Rank checks here produce a clear teaching failure instead of silently fitting an unidentified candidate.

examples.title: Fit one frozen rule
paragraphs: This example uses one input feature and a different dataset. The challenge adds a candidate feature and evaluation checks.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([0., 1., 2.])
y = np.array([3., 5., 7.])
design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
weights = np.linalg.lstsq(design, y, rcond=None)[0]
print(weights.round(4).tolist())
print(round(float(np.array([1.,3.]) @ weights),4))
interpretation: The new input uses the fitted coefficients. No outcome for that new input was needed to produce its prediction.

parts.title: 5. Compare the repair where it was meant to help
paragraphs: Calculate both absolute-error arrays on the same development observations. Report mean gain and group changes. A night repair that damages daytime performance deserves another look even if it meets an overall target.

Keep a ledger of attempts: hypothesis, changed feature or setting, observations used, outcome and next decision. Use paired uncertainty analysis at the appropriate independent unit when the data support it. Do not select one lucky seed and omit the other runs.
parts.calculation:
Group increase = candidate group MAE - baseline group MAE
Worst group increase = maximum over declared groups
Overall improvement = baseline MAE - candidate MAE
interpretation: A negative worst-group increase means every observed group improved. Small or absent groups still limit the evidence.

parts.title: 6. Declare the policy before the fresh shift
paragraphs: For the workshop, require at least the specified overall gain, no group increase above its allowance, and runtime no greater than its limit. Preserve every failure reason. A faster candidate does not compensate for a failed error requirement unless the policy explicitly allows that trade.

Real runtime assessment needs a defined hardware and workload distribution, often including tail latency. A single supplied runtime in this fixture only teaches how an independent requirement enters a decision.
parts.calculation:
Teaching policy:
minimum MAE gain: 0.5
maximum group MAE increase: 0.25
maximum recorded runtime: 10 ms
interpretation: Passing this small gate means eligible for a limited trial under these rules. It does not establish safety or justify automatic broad deployment.

parts.title: 7. Let a fresh shift challenge the repair
paragraphs: The investigation keeps the overall improvement but moves the candidate’s errors into the night group. Predict which requirement will reject it before running the construction. Then test the slow candidate, where errors improve but the runtime limit fails.

Retain both failures as regression cases. If either changes the model or policy, obtain new independent assessment data for the resulting candidate. Repeatedly repairing against one “fresh” set eventually makes it another development set.
interpretation: The learner’s actual comparison graph must explain which requirement failed; a memorised decision cannot handle the changed cases.

parts.title: 8. Keep the evidence with the model that enters a trial
paragraphs: Save the feature schema, fitted parameters, data version, evaluation IDs and metric definitions. Record the trial limits and how to revert to the baseline. Monitor delayed outcomes as well as input changes, since a running service can look healthy while predictions degrade.

For language-model and agent revisions, the same discipline applies but task outcomes and stochastic runs need their own evaluators. The agent iteration section continues that problem with tool contracts, traces and reviewed cases.
interpretation: A revision is easier to improve when we can reconstruct what changed and why we thought it would help.

quiz.prompt: What should Botie report?
options: Hold because of a group regression
quiz.because: The group requirement fails even though the average and runtime pass.

given.data: Policy: gain >= 0.5, group increase <= 0.25, runtime <= 10 ms. Candidate: gain 1, worst group increase 2, runtime 5 ms.

quiz.prompt: That shift now provides development evidence for the next candidate.
quiz.because: Its outcomes have influenced the next decision, so they no longer form an untouched assessment of that decision.

given.data: A new shift changes the next feature choice.

practice.title: Can the repair learn the night effect without seeing the evaluation answers?
practice.question: Can the repair learn the night effect without seeing the evaluation answers?
task: Implement compare_revision(train_x, train_y, test_x, test_y). Input matrices have two columns in order: heater setting, night indicator. Outcome arrays have one value per row. Require nonempty finite arrays with those shapes and a full-rank candidate training design [1, heater, night]; otherwise raise ValueError.

Fit a baseline [1, heater] and candidate [1, heater, night] by NumPy least squares using training data only. Return (baseline predictions, candidate predictions, baseline MAE, candidate MAE). Predictions must be NumPy arrays in test-row order.
Print predictions rounded to four decimals and the two rounded MAEs. The exact fixture is for learning the procedure, not claiming a deployed model has zero error.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
def compare_revision(train_x, train_y, test_x, test_y):
    raise NotImplementedError

train_x = [[0,0],[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]]
train_y = [10,12,14,16]
old, new, old_mae, new_mae = compare_revision(train_x,train_y,[[2,0],[2,1]],[14,18])
print(old.round(4).tolist())
print(new.round(4).tolist())
print(round(old_mae,4), round(new_mae,4))
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
def compare_revision(train_x, train_y, test_x, test_y):
    x, y = np.asarray(train_x,dtype=float), np.asarray(train_y,dtype=float)
    z, truth = np.asarray(test_x,dtype=float), np.asarray(test_y,dtype=float)
    if x.ndim != 2 or z.ndim != 2 or x.shape[1] != 2 or z.shape[1] != 2 or not len(x) or not len(z):
        raise ValueError("Use nonempty matrices with heater and night columns")
    if y.shape != (len(x),) or truth.shape != (len(z),):
        raise ValueError("One outcome per row")
    if not all(np.isfinite(a).all() for a in (x,y,z,truth)):
        raise ValueError("Use finite values")
    old_train = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x[:,0]])
    new_train = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
    if np.linalg.matrix_rank(new_train) < 3:
        raise ValueError("Training data must identify all candidate coefficients")
    old_w = np.linalg.lstsq(old_train,y,rcond=None)[0]
    new_w = np.linalg.lstsq(new_train,y,rcond=None)[0]
    old_pred = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(z)),z[:,0]]) @ old_w
    new_pred = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(z)),z]) @ new_w
    return old_pred, new_pred, float(np.abs(truth-old_pred).mean()), float(np.abs(truth-new_pred).mean())

train_x = [[0,0],[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]]
train_y = [10,12,14,16]
old, new, old_mae, new_mae = compare_revision(train_x,train_y,[[2,0],[2,1]],[14,18])
print(old.round(4).tolist())
print(new.round(4).tolist())
print(round(old_mae,4), round(new_mae,4))
hints: Build training and evaluation design matrices separately, with the same column order.
Fit coefficients with training outcomes only. Use test outcomes only after matrix multiplication produces predictions.
