title: What Would This Prediction Actually Change?
blurb: A model can flag a pump that may fail, but someone still has to decide what to do. Begin with that decision and work backwards to the information it needs.
openingTitle: Botie Has an Alarm. Who Is Going to Answer It?
opening: Suppose we want to help a maintenance team find pumps that need inspection. We could start by choosing a model. But imagine that it sends the team hundreds of warnings each morning. They can inspect only a few pumps, so most of those predictions never lead to anything.

Before building that model, let's work out what the team can actually do. Who receives a warning? How much time do they have? What happens if a faulty pump is missed? Those answers give our design something to aim for.

history.title: A Requirement Has to Describe Something People Need

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: development since 1995

blocks: A maintenance team asks for fewer unexpected breakdowns. A model builder reports a better prediction score. Those statements can both be true while the inspection service remains unusable, perhaps because it asks for more inspections than the team can perform. We need to connect the prediction to the decision it changes.

Large engineering projects had to make this connection between a broad need and independently built components. NASA first published its Systems Engineering Handbook in 1995 to collect methods suited to its projects, then revised it as experience exposed further problems. Its design process begins with stakeholder expectations and develops technical requirements that can be checked. A stakeholder is somebody whose use of, or responsibility for, the system affects what it must accomplish.

For Botie's inspection service, that means identifying the action before choosing the model. We can then test a proposed inspection policy against the team's capacity. Whether the predictions are useful still needs evidence from representative pumps; design reasoning cannot supply missing measurements.

reading.experimentTitle: How much inspection work does this policy create?
reading.experimentIntro: Change the inspection decisions or the time each inspection takes. Botie totals the work the team would receive.
reading.connectionTitle: From a prediction to an appointment
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Allocate the inspection time
reading.exampleNote: These are invented maintenance records, with one row per pump.

intuition.title: Follow one warning
intuition.explanation: A warning needs a recipient and an action before it can help a pump.

scene.caption: The model is one part of the decision procedure.

intuition.title: Count the work that reaches the team
intuition.explanation: These decisions schedule two inspections. Their durations differ, so counting warnings alone would miss the time requirement.

scene.caption: 1 means schedule an inspection; 0 means defer.

parts.title: 1. Name the action someone can take
paragraphs: “Predict failures” leaves several questions unanswered. A failure next year and a failure before tomorrow’s shift require different responses. For this service, the decision is whether to schedule an inspection during the next shift. A technician receives the assignment and records what they find.

A software example follows the same reasoning. If we predict that a support message is urgent, who will move it ahead in the queue? The prediction needs an agreed action and enough time for that action to help.
interpretation: Write the action in ordinary language before choosing the model output. If nobody can act on the answer, revisit the problem.

parts.title: 2. Separate the outcome from the signal
paragraphs: The outcome we care about is avoidable pump downtime. The model sees measurements such as vibration and temperature. An inspection finding is another observation, while a risk score is an estimate produced from observations. These are different things.

We might label a training row by whether a fault was found within a day. That label is convenient, but only inspected pumps get findings. A model trained on those records may learn the old inspection policy as well as the faults. Ask how each label becomes observable.
interpretation: A proxy is a measurable substitute for something we care about. State what it misses. More warnings is a poor substitute for less downtime.

parts.title: 3. Turn “manageable” into a limit
paragraphs: The maintenance team has 60 inspection minutes available in this small example. Each proposed assignment consumes part of that time. Represent a decision with 1 for inspect and 0 for defer. Multiplying a decision by its duration gives the minutes assigned to that pump.
The inputs are aligned lists: the first decision and first duration both belong to pump A. A dot product multiplies matching entries and adds the contributions.
parts.calculation:
Decisions = [1, 0, 1]
Durations in minutes = [20, 40, 30]
Assigned minutes = 1 × 20 + 0 × 40 + 1 × 30 = 50
Remaining minutes = 60 − 50 = 10
interpretation: The policy fits the time budget. We have not yet shown that it chooses the pumps that most need help.

examples.title: Count a different pair of appointments
paragraphs: NumPy stores the decisions and durations in one-dimensional arrays. Their positions must describe the same pumps.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
decisions = np.array([1, 1, 0])
minutes = np.array([15, 25, 35])
print(int(decisions @ minutes))
interpretation: The scalar result is total scheduled time. The zero prevents the third duration from contributing.

parts.title: 4. Keep facts separate from assumptions
paragraphs: A shift length may be a contractual limit. Inspection duration is usually an estimate with variation. The chance that an inspection prevents a breakdown is a further assumption that needs evidence. Writing all of these as bare numbers makes them look equally certain.

Keep a small design record: what each quantity means, its units, where it came from, and what range seems plausible. For an unknown duration, a timed trial tells us more than another decimal place in the estimate.
interpretation: We will deliberately vary these assumptions in later workshops. The design should make it clear which measurement could change our decision.

parts.title: 5. Give the model an information boundary
paragraphs: A prediction made before a shift can use earlier sensor readings. It cannot use the technician’s later findings. Define a prediction time and an outcome window before assembling training rows.

Also decide what happens when readings are missing. A missing temperature should not silently become a normal temperature. The design may defer to a technician, use a documented fallback, or decline to make a prediction.
interpretation: The next lessons develop this boundary into a testable data contract.

parts.title: 6. Write a requirement we can check
paragraphs: “The service should be useful” gives us no acceptance test. “The scheduled inspections must fit the available minutes” gives us an immediate calculation. Predictive usefulness needs a separate requirement, such as a limit on missed faults in a representative evaluation, with its sample size reported.

A requirement also needs an owner. Someone must decide whether a miss is tolerable and what evidence would justify changing that limit. An engineer should not quietly bury those choices inside a default threshold.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop handles the scheduling calculation. Our Python challenge also reports remaining capacity, including a negative result when the proposed schedule is too long.

title: Do We Need a Learned Model Yet?
blurb: A fixed rule already catches some faults. Work out what a learned model would have to improve before paying for its extra work.
openingTitle: The Temperature Rule Already Catches Some Problems
opening: Botie can send an inspection request whenever a pump gets unusually hot. It is a simple rule, and it will miss some faults. Before replacing it with a trained model, we should find out where it helps and where it fails.
A model might catch more faults while creating extra inspections. We need a comparison that accounts for both effects, using the same pumps and the same opportunity to act.

history.title: Learning Needs Something to Improve On

sources.title: Martin Zinkevich: Rules of Machine Learning

blocks: A request to improve inspections does not tell us that a learned model is the next useful component. We might lack reliable fault labels, or a simple temperature rule might already handle the decision adequately. Without a working comparison, a model's score tells us little about what it improved.

Drawing on production work at Google, Martin Zinkevich collected Rules of Machine Learning to describe the engineering problems around a model. Its early guidance recommends establishing metrics and starting without machine learning when suitable data are unavailable. An existing rule can make the service usable while exposing which outcomes need to be recorded. Later, that experience gives a learned method something concrete to improve on.

That is the role of our temperature rule. We will count missed faults beside the inspections it requests, using declared illustrative costs. The question is whether another design makes a useful improvement under the same conditions. A more complicated implementation has to earn its place through that comparison.

reading.experimentTitle: Which policy loses less on the same pumps?
reading.experimentIntro: Change the fault labels, decisions, or costs. Compare each policy under the same assumptions.
reading.connectionTitle: Give a more complicated design a reason to exist
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Compare inspection policies fairly
reading.outputLabel: Policy loss in illustrative cost units
reading.exampleNote: This cost model is an invented comparison, not a measured financial return.

intuition.title: Keep the pumps fixed
intuition.explanation: A fair comparison gives both policies the same cases. Fault labels are known here because this is a retrospective exercise.

scene.caption: The model catches an extra fault but still sends one healthy pump for inspection.

intuition.title: Name what each outcome costs
intuition.explanation: An inspection costs time whether or not a fault is found. A missed fault adds a separate loss.

scene.caption: We assume an inspection catches the fault in this teaching example.

parts.title: 1. Start with a rule we can explain
paragraphs: A baseline is a reference procedure whose results we will compare with the proposed model. It can be as simple as a fixed rule, provided it addresses the same decision. It might inspect pumps above a fixed temperature or show the most frequently requested help article. It gives us an answer to compare against and often exposes missing infrastructure early.
Run that rule through the complete path from input to action. Discovering that warnings reach nobody is useful before spending a week tuning a model.
interpretation: Keep the baseline available throughout development. A candidate should earn its extra maintenance burden.

parts.title: 2. Put both policies on the same evidence
paragraphs: Use pumps from the same evaluation period, with fault outcomes obtained in a comparable way. Preserve a separate development set for choosing thresholds. Otherwise, repeatedly adjusting the model to beat the evaluation pumps turns them into training information.

The fault labels below are supplied for every pump. Real inspection data may lack that coverage. A fair trial might need some independently sampled inspections to learn about pumps the old policy ignored.
interpretation: Missing outcomes weaken the comparison. They cannot be repaired simply by giving uninspected pumps a healthy label.

parts.title: 3. Charge for the action and the miss
paragraphs: Let a decision of 1 mean inspect. Subtracting it from 1 identifies a deferred pump. Multiplying that result by the fault label identifies a missed fault. An inspection has a fixed cost in this example, even when the pump is healthy.
We assume inspection prevents the whole stated miss loss. If inspection sometimes fails to help, the outcome model needs another term.
parts.calculation:
Labels = [1, 0, 1, 0]
Rule decisions = [1, 1, 0, 0]
Misses = labels × (1 − decisions) = [0, 0, 1, 0]
Rule loss = 3 × 2 inspections + 20 × 1 miss = 26
Model decisions = [1, 0, 1, 1]
Model loss = 3 × 3 inspections + 20 × 0 misses = 9
interpretation: On these pumps and these costs, the model has lower decision loss. That statement still depends on the evidence and assumptions.

examples.title: Find the misses before costing them
paragraphs: Boolean comparisons can show which faulty pumps a policy defers. These arrays align one position per pump.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
fault = np.array([1, 0, 1])
inspect = np.array([0, 1, 1])
missed = (fault == 1) & (inspect == 0)
print(missed.tolist())
interpretation: The middle pump incurs an inspection, but it is not a missed fault.

parts.title: 4. Count the work needed to keep it running
paragraphs: Training a model once is only part of its cost. Someone must maintain input definitions, investigate failed requests, collect later labels, and check new versions. The heat rule also needs maintenance, so compare the additional burden fairly.

Use the same time horizon. A monthly operating estimate cannot be added directly to a loss measured over four pumps. First estimate how many comparable decisions occur in a month and how uncertain that extrapolation is.
interpretation: A small measured improvement may disappear under a plausible operating cost. That is a reason to gather better evidence, not automatically a reason to abandon ML.

parts.title: 5. Some requirements stay outside the cost score
paragraphs: If a requirement says the team can perform only a certain number of inspections, a low cost score does not grant extra capacity. Check the hard limit separately. The same applies to a service that must respond before a machine’s next cycle.
A weighted score allows one quantity to compensate for another. Use it only where that trade is actually acceptable. We will make this distinction explicit when comparing several designs.
interpretation: Inspect-all can be a useful reference policy, even if it is infeasible. It reveals how much of the apparent improvement comes from doing more work.

parts.title: 6. Choose the next experiment from the disagreement
paragraphs: Find the pumps where the baseline and candidate disagree. Are those cases genuinely different, or does the candidate rely on a sensor that is often unavailable? Examine which conditions create misses, then decide what additional observations would clarify them.

Report results by relevant operating condition as well as overall. A rule that works for one pump family may fail on another. Improvement on this tiny table is an arithmetic fact, not evidence of generalisation.
interpretation: Botie will calculate the loss for several policies. Python will package that calculation so we can compare new aligned records without rewriting it.

quiz.prompt: What does this estimate suggest?
options: The proposed model does not yet justify its extra cost
The model must be deployed because its prediction score improved
quiz.because: Compare the additional benefit and burden on the same horizon.

given.data: A model saves an estimated 50 units each month but adds 80 units of monthly upkeep. Other consequences are assumed equal.

quiz.prompt: It meets the capacity requirement.
quiz.because: A soft cost score cannot override a hard limit.

given.data: A policy has the lowest cost score but requires more inspections than the team can perform.

practice.title: Can the same calculation judge a new inspection policy?
practice.question: Can the same calculation judge a new inspection policy?
task: A candidate that finds more faults may also send the team on more inspections. Compare both consequences on the same labelled pumps before calling it an improvement. Write policy_loss(labels, decisions, inspection_cost, miss_cost). Return total loss as a float. Labels and decisions must be aligned one-dimensional arrays containing only 0 and 1. Both scalar costs must be finite and nonnegative; invalid inputs raise ValueError. Empty arrays have zero loss.
For labels [1,0,1,0,1], compare decisions [1,1,0,0,0] and [1,0,1,0,0], with inspection cost 4 and miss cost 15. Print the two losses as a list.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def policy_loss(labels, decisions, inspection_cost, miss_cost):
    pass

y = [1,0,1,0,1]
print([policy_loss(y, d, 4, 15) for d in [[1,1,0,0,0], [1,0,1,0,0]]])
hints: Count all inspections, including healthy pumps.
A miss needs both a fault and a decision to defer.

tests.name: Invalid label

build.title: Cost the inspection policy
build.problem: Botie needs a comparison that charges for inspections and missed faults on the same pump records.
build.challenge: Construct the per-pump loss, then add it. A miss occurs when a fault label is 1 and the inspection decision is 0.
build.why: The two terms represent different consequences. Adding them makes the cost assumptions visible.
build.limitation: Fault labels are supplied for all pumps. This omits uncertain inspection effectiveness, upkeep, and limited capacity.
hints: Keep inspection cost and missed-fault cost on separate branches until each is calculated.
Subtract each decision from 1. Multiplying that result by the fault labels marks only faulty pumps we deferred.
Multiply each branch by its cost, add the contributions, and total the list. An inspection still costs something when the pump is healthy.

checkpoints.after: 3. Charge for the action and the miss
checkpoints.title: Questions on Parts 1 to 3

questions.prompt: Which cost belongs to this pump?
questions.because: The policy takes no inspection action, but it misses a fault.

given.data: A faulty pump is deferred. Inspection cost is 3 units and a missed fault costs 20 units. An inspection is assumed to prevent the miss loss.

questions.prompt: The difference in loss can reflect the populations as well as the policies.
questions.because: Use comparable evidence before attributing the difference to the model.

given.data: A temperature rule and a learned model are tested on different pump populations.

title: What Can the System Know at Decision Time?
blurb: A reading can describe an earlier event and still arrive too late. Design a data contract that respects both clocks.
openingTitle: The Reading Existed. Botie Still Had Not Received It.
opening: At minute 10, Botie must decide whether to inspect a pump. One sensor recorded a vibration spike at minute 8, but its network connection delayed the message until minute 12. A historical table now contains that spike. The running system could not have used it at minute 10.

This distinction also affects software. A support article may have been written yesterday but added to a search index only this afternoon. We need to design around the information the service could actually retrieve.

history.title: A Model Inherits Its Data Dependencies

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Production ML systems often depend on data produced by other systems. Sculley and colleagues described how these dependencies and changes in the surrounding system create maintenance problems that model code alone does not reveal. A field can retain its name while its meaning or availability changes.

Our two-clock example makes one such dependency explicit. Event time describes the measurement; availability time describes when our service could use it. These invented timestamps are a teaching contract, not a guarantee that every database preserves the history needed to reconstruct them.

reading.experimentTitle: Which readings were available for this decision?
reading.experimentIntro: Move the decision time or delay a record. Both clocks must be at or before the decision.
reading.connectionTitle: Reconstruct the information Botie actually had
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Enforce the time boundary
reading.outputLabel: Eligibility mask, one entry per record
reading.exampleNote: Times are minutes on the same clock. Values equal to the cutoff are eligible in this example.

intuition.title: Read both timestamps
intuition.explanation: Compare each record with the decision at minute 10. An earlier event does not undo a later arrival.

scene.caption: The availability time belongs to this service, not just the sensor.

intuition.title: Preserve the boundary through the pipeline
intuition.explanation: A retrieved record still needs its meaning checked before a model consumes it.

rows.label: Select
items: Use records available by the decision time

rows.label: Predict
items: Save the input contract and model version

scene.caption: An input contract describes what each field means and when it is usable.

parts.title: 1. An event and its arrival are different facts
paragraphs: A sensor samples the world at one time and delivers the record at another. Clocks, buffering, and network interruptions can separate them. For an offline training table, the delay is easy to overlook because all the records are now present.

A decision-time reconstruction needs the timestamp when the consuming system could actually access the record. If a later repair changes a historical value, preserve the earlier version too. The final corrected table may describe a different information state.
interpretation: Document which clock each timestamp uses and how clock disagreement is handled. A precise-looking timestamp is not proof of a synchronised clock.

parts.title: 2. Describe an input with more than its name
paragraphs: A field called temperature could mean Celsius, Fahrenheit, or a moving average calculated over a window. A feature contract should state units, shape, missing-value behaviour, and the aggregation window. It should also say which entity the record describes.
For text retrieval, include when a document version entered the index and what permissions the requester had. The existence of a document somewhere does not mean this request could retrieve it.
interpretation: These are interface requirements. A fitted model cannot reliably repair a changed meaning that the pipeline does not identify.

parts.title: 3. Build the eligibility check from two comparisons
paragraphs: Start with two yes-or-no questions for each record. Did its event happen by the cutoff? Was the record available by the cutoff? Both must hold. We use inclusive comparisons, so a record available exactly at the decision time is accepted.

In the workshop, a Threshold gate reports 1 when its first input reaches its second. Connect the cutoff to the Score input and the record timestamps to Cutoff. This tests whether the decision time has reached each timestamp. Multiplying the two binary masks implements “both”.
parts.calculation:
Event times = [8, 8, 11]
Availability times = [9, 12, 11]
Decision time = 10
Event-time mask = [1, 1, 0]
Availability mask = [1, 0, 0]
Eligible = [1, 1, 0] × [1, 0, 0] = [1, 0, 0]
interpretation: The labels on the wires matter. Reversing a comparison would admit future information.

examples.title: A boolean mask keeps record identities aligned
paragraphs: Comparison produces a boolean array of the same shape. Selection uses its True positions.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
arrival = np.array([4, 9, 6])
reading = np.array([20., 99., 24.])
known = arrival <= 6
print(known.tolist())
print(reading[known].tolist())
interpretation: This program demonstrates only the arrival check. The challenge also enforces event time and a valid timestamp order.

parts.title: 4. Eligibility does not mean freshness
paragraphs: A reading from last week can pass both comparisons. That does not make it a useful description of a pump now. Add a maximum permitted age when the task requires recent evidence, and say which timestamp the age uses.
Do not confuse a freshly delivered old reading with a fresh measurement. A freshness check usually needs event time. A separate transport monitor can detect long delivery delays.
interpretation: The workshop deliberately checks eligibility alone. A complete pump service would also choose a freshness rule and a response when no acceptable reading remains.

parts.title: 5. Labels have an availability time too
paragraphs: A fault may happen after the prediction and be confirmed several days later. The outcome window tells us what we want to predict. Label availability tells us when we can train or evaluate using the confirmed result.

For a retrospective training simulation, include only labels that would have been known at that training date. A final dataset with every later confirmation can overstate how quickly the system could have adapted.
interpretation: Keep the prediction identity so a later outcome can be joined to the correct earlier decision. An outcome must never be inserted into its own input features.

parts.title: 6. Make missing information an explicit branch
paragraphs: If no eligible reading exists, the pipeline needs a response. It might request a manual check or keep using a previous reading within a defined age limit. Filling a missing value with zero quietly assigns a numerical meaning to absence.
Record the branch taken so later evaluation includes the cases where the model could not run. Reporting accuracy only on successfully served cases hides coverage failures.
interpretation: Our reusable Python function returns an eligibility mask. The caller can then decide how to select records or handle an all-False result without pretending the evidence existed.

parts.title: 7. Test the boundary itself
paragraphs: Include records just before the cutoff, exactly at it, and just after it. Include a record with an early event and a late arrival. Those cases exercise the design rule more directly than a large random table.

This lesson assumes arrival cannot precede the event on our shared clock. A violation raises an error. Real systems with uncertain clocks may need an explicit tolerance or interval model instead of silently accepting impossible ordering.
interpretation: A contract is useful when another component can test it. The challenge’s invalid-input behaviour is part of that contract.

quiz.prompt: What does the two-clock check establish?
options: It was available, but may be too old for the task
It must be a correct measurement
quiz.because: Eligibility does not establish freshness or measurement quality.

given.data: A record has event time 2, arrival time 3, and decision time 100. No maximum age is specified.

quiz.prompt: The record passes both comparisons.
quiz.because: Equality is explicitly allowed here.

given.data: Event time and arrival time both equal the decision time. The contract uses inclusive comparisons.

practice.title: Which records could a prediction have used?
practice.question: Which records could a prediction have used?
task: A historical reading is useful only if the service had received it before the prediction. A timestamp saying when it happened cannot answer that second question. Write eligible(events, arrivals, cutoff). Return a NumPy boolean array. Inputs are aligned one-dimensional arrays of finite timestamps, cutoff is finite, and each arrival must be at or after its event. Invalid inputs raise ValueError. Empty arrays return an empty mask.
For events [2,5,8,9], arrivals [3,7,8,12], and cutoff 8, print the mask as a list.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def eligible(events, arrivals, cutoff):
    pass

print(eligible([2,5,8,9], [3,7,8,12], 8).tolist())
hints: Use two elementwise comparisons joined with & and parentheses.
Check arrival order separately from eligibility.

tests.name: Invalid ordering

build.title: Keep future records out of the inspection decision
build.problem: Botie needs to reconstruct which pump readings existed in the service at a chosen time.
build.challenge: Use two threshold comparisons and combine their masks. Output 1 only when both event and availability timestamps are at or before the decision time.
build.why: The comparisons preserve each record’s position, so multiplying joins the two conditions for that same record.
build.limitation: This assumes a common clock and trustworthy timestamp history. Freshness, permissions, and measurement quality need additional checks.
hints: An early event can still arrive late. Check both timestamps against the decision time.
Threshold gate checks whether its first input is at least its second. Put decision time first and the timestamps second.
Multiply the two masks. A record needs both flags to be 1.

title: Where Does the Prediction Pipeline Run Out of Room?
blurb: A fast model can sit inside a slow service. Follow requests through preparation, inference, and storage to find the stage that limits the whole path.
openingTitle: Why Is the Queue Growing When the Model Is Fast?
opening: Botie’s image service can classify many pictures each second. Yet users are waiting. The model is only one step: each picture must first be decoded, resized, and later written to a result store. Any of those steps can hold up the rest.
We need a small model of the service before buying more hardware. How much work can each stage finish? How quickly does new work arrive? Start with quantities we can compare in the same units.

history.title: Put Numbers Against the Boxes in a Design

sources.title: Google: Non-Abstract Large System Design, SRE Workbook, 2018
Google SRE Workbook: resource estimates in a concrete design

blocks: An architecture diagram can connect image decoding to inference without saying whether either stage can keep up with the cameras. Adding more inference workers will accomplish little if decoding is where the requests are accumulating.

Google's 2018 SRE Workbook described Non-Abstract Large System Design as a response to this gap between a diagram and a running system. The approach drew on experience designing production services. It required turning a workload into approximate resource needs, then revising the proposal when those numbers exposed an impractical assumption. The estimates gave teams something to question before discovering a constraint during deployment.

Our image service follows that reasoning on a small pipeline. We will calculate each stage's ideal capacity and find which stage limits the complete path. Those estimates tell us where to measure next. Contention and scheduling overhead still need a real benchmark.

reading.experimentTitle: What capacity does each stage contribute?
reading.experimentIntro: Change worker counts and per-worker rates. The smallest stage capacity limits this ideal pipeline.
reading.connectionTitle: A request has to pass through every stage
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Locate the limiting stage
reading.outputLabel: Ideal pipeline capacity, requests per second
reading.exampleNote: The model assumes independently pipelined stages and equally shareable work.

intuition.title: Trace one image
intuition.explanation: The stages can work on different images at the same time, but each image still visits them in order.

scene.caption: Concurrent stages improve throughput; they do not remove stages from an individual request.

intuition.title: Compare capacities on one scale
intuition.explanation: Multiply worker count by rate per worker before comparing the stages.

scene.caption: Storage is the limiting stage under these assumptions.

parts.title: 1. Distinguish elapsed time from completed work
paragraphs: Latency is how long one request takes from arrival to response. Throughput is how many requests finish per unit time. A pipeline can finish many requests per second while each request spends a noticeable time travelling through it.

Imagine several images at different stages. Preparation can work on the next image while inference processes the current one. That overlap explains why adding all stage durations answers a different question from finding the smallest stage capacity.
interpretation: Keep both quantities in the design. A throughput requirement alone does not protect a user from a long wait.

parts.title: 2. Turn a worker measurement into a stage estimate
paragraphs: Measure a worker using representative images and the intended model. If one worker completes six requests each second, two independent workers would ideally complete twelve. The word independent matters: workers sharing a saturated disk may not provide twice the rate.
Our arrays use one entry per stage. Multiplying aligned worker counts and rates gives a capacity for each stage, all in requests per second.
parts.calculation:
Workers = [2, 1, 2]
Per-worker rates = [6, 20, 5] requests/s
Stage capacities = [2 × 6, 1 × 20, 2 × 5] = [12, 20, 10] requests/s
interpretation: This is an estimate to test. Treat measured per-worker rates as specific to a workload and resource allocation.

examples.title: Name the stage beside its capacity
paragraphs: Keep names in a separate aligned array so a minimum remains interpretable.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(["prepare", "infer", "store"])
capacity = np.array([8., 15., 11.])
i = int(np.argmin(capacity))
print(names[i])
print(float(capacity[i]))
interpretation: argmin returns a position. Indexing uses that position to recover the stage name.

parts.title: 3. Find the narrowest stage
paragraphs: Every request must pass through storage, so a storage stage that completes ten requests per second prevents the whole pipeline from sustaining more than that rate. Increasing inference capacity alone does not change this bound.

The minimum rule assumes each request visits each stage once and stages can overlap. If two stages share one worker, or some requests visit an expensive stage repeatedly, describe that shared work explicitly before taking a minimum.
parts.calculation:
Ideal pipeline capacity = min(12, 20, 10) = 10 requests/s
Incoming rate = 8 requests/s
Capacity minus demand = 10 − 8 = 2 requests/s
interpretation: Positive spare capacity is useful, but it does not prove that bursts or slow images will meet a latency target.

parts.title: 4. Check units before changing the architecture
paragraphs: A rate reported per minute must be converted before comparing it with requests per second. A batch rate is not a request rate until batch size is known. A camera producing frames and a model producing crops may not even use the same unit of work.

For example, one frame can contain several candidate objects. The detection stage’s frame rate and the classifier’s crop rate need a conversion based on crops per frame. An average may hide unusually crowded frames.
interpretation: Write the unit on the wire. The arithmetic is easy to inspect once each rate refers to the same work.

parts.title: 5. Speed up the part that changes the answer
paragraphs: If storage is limiting, first investigate that stage. More storage workers, a different write pattern, or fewer unnecessary writes may help. Once it improves, preparation may become the new limit.
The same reasoning applies to physical inspection. A model can flag pumps faster than a technician can inspect them. Increasing prediction throughput will not create inspection capacity.
interpretation: Recalculate after each proposed change. The identity of the limiting stage is a property of the whole current design.

parts.title: 6. Leave room for variation and failures
paragraphs: Operating exactly at an estimated capacity leaves no room for bursts, slow requests, or a worker going away. Choose a target using workload measurements and a service requirement. There is no universal percentage that makes every design safe.
Measure both normal and degraded conditions. If a model server loses one worker, check whether the remaining capacity can keep up and how the service handles the accumulated queue.
interpretation: Botie’s next workshop follows that queue over time. Here, Python reports all stage capacities as well as the minimum so we can see why a design is limited.

quiz.prompt: What additional interpretation is needed before comparing with a request rate?
options: Convert batches into requests using batch size
quiz.because: The unit of work must match.

given.data: A worker processes 5 batches/s, each containing 8 independent requests.

quiz.prompt: The estimate alone guarantees the latency target.
quiz.because: Queueing and request variation still need testing.

given.data: A pipeline has estimated capacity above average demand. No burst or latency measurements were taken.

practice.title: Which stage should Botie investigate first?
practice.question: Which stage should Botie investigate first?

Return (stage_capacities, bottleneck_index), where stage_capacities is a NumPy array and ties choose the first index. Inputs are nonempty aligned one-dimensional arrays; worker counts are positive integers and rates are finite and positive. Raise ValueError otherwise.
Use workers [3,2,1] and rates [4,9,15]. Print the capacities as a list, then the index.

Worker entries count parallel workers at each stage, and rates are items per worker per common time interval. Keep stage order in the capacity array; return the zero-based bottleneck index separately.

def capacity(workers, rates):
    pass

stages, index = capacity([3,2,1], [4,9,15])
print(stages.tolist())
print(index)

argmin gives the first minimum position. Keep the capacities too.

title: What Happens When Requests Arrive Together?
blurb: Average demand can fit while a burst still leaves people waiting. Follow unfinished requests from one interval to the next.
openingTitle: The Service Was Quiet, Then Everyone Uploaded a Picture
opening: Botie’s image service looks comfortably fast when we average requests over a minute. Then a class uploads its pictures together. The service must either keep those requests somewhere, reject some, or make the class wait.

A queue is the unfinished work we carry forward. We can understand its behaviour without beginning with a probability distribution. Let’s follow a short sequence of arrivals and give the server a fixed amount of work it can complete each interval.

history.title: Waiting Work Can Become Another Source of Failure

sources.title: Little: A Proof for the Queuing Formula, 1961

blocks: A service can have enough capacity for an average day and still struggle when requests arrive together. Requests that cannot run immediately wait. That waiting work occupies resources and can remain after the arrival burst has ended.

Queueing research gave engineers ways to relate workload to waiting. In 1961, John Little proved a relationship between the average arrival rate, time spent in a system and number of items present, under stated assumptions. Counting requests in flight therefore tells us something about the time users are spending there. A burst that is still building a queue needs its own time-by-time account; a steady average cannot describe every interval.
Google's later account of cascading failures showed how production queues interact with timeouts and retries. A delayed request can provoke more work, which delays the remaining requests further.

Botie's first queue excludes those retries so we can inspect the accumulation itself. We will follow arrivals and completed work through separate intervals rather than replacing the changing workload with one daily average.

reading.experimentTitle: Will the queue drain after the burst?
reading.experimentIntro: Change arrivals or completion capacity. Each interval starts with the unfinished work left by the preceding one.
reading.connectionTitle: Work cannot disappear between intervals
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Simulate the unfinished requests
reading.outputLabel: Backlog at the end of each interval
reading.exampleNote: Arrivals enter at the start of an interval, then service occurs. The initial queue is empty.

intuition.title: Carry the unfinished work forward
intuition.explanation: Unused service capacity cannot be saved for a future burst.

scene.caption: The quiet first interval does not let the second interval complete more than four requests.

intuition.title: One interval of the queue
intuition.explanation: Start with what was already waiting, then admit new work before using this interval’s service capacity.

rows.label: Keep nonnegative
items: An empty queue has zero backlog

scene.caption: Repeat using the previous result as state.

parts.title: 1. Choose what one time step means
paragraphs: Our interval could be a second or a minute, but arrivals and service capacity must use that same interval. Arrivals are counts of requests, not a rate to add directly to a count. Here, requests arrive at the start and the server works afterward.
Changing that ordering changes results near a boundary. A finer simulation might use individual arrival and completion times. The coarse model is useful because we can inspect every step.
interpretation: We start with an empty queue. If a service already has unfinished work, that initial state must be supplied.

parts.title: 2. Account for the work that remains
paragraphs: Add the previous backlog to new arrivals. The server completes at most its capacity, so subtract that capacity and clamp a negative remainder to zero. A negative queue would mean saving unused processing slots, which the server cannot do.
parts.calculation:
backlog[t] = max(0, backlog[t−1] + arrivals[t] − capacity[t])
Initial backlog = 0
Interval 1: max(0, 0 + 2 − 4) = 0
Interval 2: max(0, 0 + 7 − 4) = 3
Interval 3: max(0, 3 + 1 − 4) = 0
interpretation: The burst creates a queue that drains in the next interval. This is a recurrence: the next answer depends on the previous answer.

parts.title: 3. Store state explicitly in Python
paragraphs: A NumPy array can hold the arrivals, but each backlog depends on the preceding one. A short loop makes that dependence clear. An elementwise subtraction would incorrectly pretend each interval starts empty.
The workshop’s Queue over time component performs this recurrence and exposes the entire backlog sequence. Its inputs are aligned arrivals and capacities, so we can model a temporary worker loss too.
interpretation: A component can contain a repeated operation once we have explained and inspected that operation.

examples.title: Follow two intervals by hand in code
paragraphs: The variable waiting carries state. Each appended result records the end of an interval.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
arrivals = np.array([5, 0])
waiting = 0
trace = []
for incoming in arrivals:
    waiting = max(0, waiting + int(incoming) - 2)
    trace.append(waiting)
print(trace)
interpretation: The second interval starts with three waiting requests, even though no new request arrives.

parts.title: 4. A stable average does not remove a burst
paragraphs: When long-run arrivals exceed sustainable service, a queue generally cannot stay bounded without dropping work. A lower average gives it a chance to drain, but a large burst can still violate a waiting-time requirement. Equality leaves no spare capacity to recover from variation.
Our sequence is finite. Seeing its queue end at zero does not prove that a future traffic pattern will behave similarly. Keep the workload assumptions beside the result.
interpretation: Measure the maximum backlog and the time to drain, not only the final queue length.

parts.title: 5. Queue length is not an individual latency measurement
paragraphs: A backlog counts requests waiting or unfinished at a boundary. Latency measures time for a particular request. To calculate individual latency, we would need service order, arrival times within the interval, and request durations.

For a first-in-first-out queue with similar jobs, more work ahead usually implies a longer wait. That intuition is useful, but dividing a coarse queue count by a rate is only an estimate under stated assumptions.
interpretation: We will report backlog directly. Calling it measured p95 latency would claim evidence this simulator does not produce.

parts.title: 6. Decide what happens at a queue limit
paragraphs: Real queues need resource limits. When full, a service may reject new work with a retry policy, defer nonurgent jobs, or run a cheaper fallback. Unlimited retries can send even more requests into an already overloaded service.

For a camera inspection system, an old frame may become useless before it reaches inference. The appropriate response could be dropping stale frames while recording the coverage gap. A support request may instead need durable storage.
interpretation: Queue policy depends on the task. Our later failure lesson will make the response explicit rather than pretending every request eventually receives a useful prediction.

parts.title: 7. Compare designs using the same arrival trace
paragraphs: Replay the same burst against alternative capacities. Also include a worker outage and a quiet recovery period. These tests help separate a capacity change from a workload change.
The Python function will reject negative or fractional request counts. If jobs have unequal work sizes, replace counts with a meaningful workload measure or simulate jobs individually.
interpretation: Botie’s construction asks for the maximum unfinished work. You will need the Queue over time component and an operation that inspects its sequence.

quiz.prompt: Which statement is supported?
options: Every request met its latency target
The service can handle all future traffic
quiz.because: The final state says nothing by itself about each request’s delay.

given.data: A trace has a large backlog halfway through and zero backlog at the end.

quiz.prompt: Those retries can increase overload.
quiz.because: They add work when the service already lacks capacity.

given.data: A waiting request triggers repeated immediate retries against the same overloaded service.

practice.title: Can you replay a burst and a worker outage?
practice.question: Can you replay a burst and a worker outage?
task: An average arrival rate hides a busy interval and a worker outage. Replay the waiting work through both instead of letting spare capacity from a quiet interval erase a later queue. Write backlog(arrivals, capacities). Return a NumPy array of end-of-interval backlogs, starting from zero, with arrivals before service. Both inputs must be aligned one-dimensional arrays of finite nonnegative integers; invalid inputs raise ValueError. Empty inputs return an empty array.
Use arrivals [3,8,2,0] and capacities [4,4,0,6]. Print the backlog list, then its maximum.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def backlog(arrivals, capacities):
    pass

trace = backlog([3,8,2,0], [4,4,0,6])
print(trace.tolist())
print(int(trace.max()))
hints: Carry waiting into the next iteration.
An interval with zero capacity still receives its arrivals.

tests.name: Reject fractional work

build.title: Find the worst queue during the upload burst
build.problem: Botie needs room for unfinished image requests, including work carried from earlier intervals.
build.challenge: Connect arrivals and service capacities to Queue over time, then find the largest backlog in the returned trace.

sources.capacity: Requests that can finish per interval

build.why: The queue component preserves unfinished work between intervals. Largest value finds the worst boundary backlog rather than only the final state.
build.limitation: This counts fixed-size requests in discrete intervals. It does not measure individual latency or implement queue limits and retries.
hints: The queue must remember unfinished requests from the preceding interval. Queue over time performs that recurrence.
Connect arrivals and service capacities to their named ports. The output is a backlog for every interval; find its Largest value.

title: Will the Model Fit on the Device?
blurb: A model file can fit while its running process runs out of memory. Account for parameters, temporary values, and the rest of the runtime.
openingTitle: The File Fits. Why Does Inference Run Out of Memory?
opening: Botie copies a model onto an inspection device. The file is smaller than the available memory, but the process fails when it receives a batch of images. Running a model needs room for more than its saved parameters.

Let’s put names on the pieces of memory before adding them. We will separate what stays fixed from what grows with the batch, then work out how many images the device can handle under a stated estimate.

history.title: Small Devices Made the Whole Inference Engine Matter
blocks: MCUNet examined neural-network inference on microcontrollers with tight memory and compute limits. Its design combined choices about the network with an inference engine suited to those limits. A useful model had to fit the way the device actually executed it.

Our budget is much simpler. We count parameter storage, an estimated peak activation cost per example, and fixed runtime memory. We are not reproducing MCUNet’s engine or claiming that this linear estimate describes every network.

reading.experimentTitle: Where does the remaining memory go?
reading.experimentIntro: Change parameter count, storage precision, batch size, or runtime estimates. A negative remainder means the proposed allocation exceeds the budget.
reading.connectionTitle: Budget for a running model
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Find the batch that fits
reading.exampleNote: Small invented byte counts keep the arithmetic readable. All quantities use bytes, not a mixture of MB and MiB.

intuition.title: Give each allocation a place
intuition.explanation: Some memory is shared by the batch; some grows as we process more examples.

scene.caption: Peak live memory matters more than the sum of every tensor ever created.

intuition.title: Compare two batch sizes
intuition.explanation: For this toy device, parameter storage uses 40 bytes, runtime uses 12, and activations use 8 per example. The limit is 100 bytes.

scene.caption: Batch six exactly fills the estimate and leaves no allowance for errors in it.

parts.title: 1. Count bytes for the saved parameters
paragraphs: A parameter is a stored value such as a weight or bias. With a fixed-width representation, multiply the number of parameters by bytes per parameter. Eight-bit values use one byte each; 32-bit values use four. Quantised formats may also store scales and other metadata.
A file can be compressed or contain additional information, so its size need not equal the in-memory parameter allocation. Ask what the runtime loads and in which format.
parts.calculation: 10 parameters × 4 bytes/parameter = 40 bytes
interpretation: This toy count is deliberately small. The same dimensional calculation applies to a larger model.

parts.title: 2. Make room for intermediate results
paragraphs: A layer creates outputs that later layers consume. Those intermediate values are called activations. Some can be released or reused; others must remain live for a skip connection or another operation. The peak depends on which values coexist.

We will use an estimated peak activation cost per example and assume it scales with batch size. Real kernels may allocate workspaces or choose different algorithms for a larger batch, so validate that assumption by measuring peak memory.
interpretation: Summing all layer outputs without considering their lifetimes can overestimate memory. Ignoring them can underestimate it.

parts.title: 3. Keep runtime memory in the budget
paragraphs: The process also needs input and output buffers, library workspaces, and runtime state. For this exercise they are a fixed allocation. That is an accounting assumption, not a claim that runtime overhead is always fixed.
Training adds other allocations, often including gradients and optimiser state. A serving estimate that omits them cannot be reused as a training-memory guarantee.
parts.calculation:
Estimated bytes = parameter_count × bytes_per_parameter
                  + batch_size × activation_bytes_per_example
                  + runtime_bytes
For batch 2: 10 × 4 + 2 × 8 + 12 = 68 bytes
Headroom = 100 − 68 = 32 bytes
interpretation: The workshop returns headroom. A negative answer is useful feedback that the proposed design does not fit this budget.

examples.title: Separate fixed memory from batch memory
paragraphs: A vector of candidate batches lets us inspect several totals without changing the fixed allocation.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
batches = np.array([1, 2, 3])
fixed_bytes = 24
activation_bytes = 6
print((fixed_bytes + batches * activation_bytes).tolist())
interpretation: Each entry is a candidate total. These are separate proposed runs, not allocations to add together.

parts.title: 4. Solve for the maximum batch under this model
paragraphs: Subtract fixed allocations from the limit. Divide the remainder by activation bytes per example, then round down because a batch contains a whole number of examples. If the fixed allocations already exceed the limit, even batch zero fails the budget.
Our function returns zero when no positive batch fits. That is a design failure to investigate, not permission to serve an empty batch as a successful request.
parts.calculation:
Available for activations = 100 − 40 − 12 = 48 bytes
Maximum batch = floor(48 / 8) = 6
interpretation: Rounding up would exceed the limit. Exact equality fits the arithmetic but leaves no reserve for an inaccurate estimate.

parts.title: 5. Changing precision changes more than storage
paragraphs: Fewer bits can reduce parameter storage and sometimes computation. The model’s numerical behaviour may also change, and some hardware needs particular formats to gain speed. Measure prediction quality and runtime after conversion.
Shrinking parameters may have little effect when activations dominate peak memory. Inspect the allocations before deciding which optimisation is worth trying.
interpretation: A smaller file is evidence about storage. It is not by itself evidence about latency or task accuracy.

parts.title: 6. Measure the intended workload
paragraphs: Use the real input sizes, batch pattern, runtime version, and device. Variable-length text or larger images can change activation requirements. A warm process may retain allocations, and peak allocation metrics may differ from total device memory use.
Record what the measurement includes and repeat it under representative conditions. Keep a reserve chosen from that evidence rather than relying on the exact boundary of an optimistic estimate.
interpretation: Botie lets you change one allocation at a time. The Python challenge calculates the maximum batch, then tests that it obeys the limit under the stated linear model.

quiz.prompt: How should a maximum whole batch be obtained?
quiz.because: The next whole example might exceed the limit.

given.data: There are 47 bytes left for activations, at 8 bytes per example.

quiz.prompt: Its accuracy and latency still need measurement.
quiz.because: Storage reduction does not establish either result.

given.data: A model is converted to a smaller parameter format. No quality or speed tests have run.

practice.title: What is the largest batch this estimate permits?
practice.question: What is the largest batch this estimate permits?
task: The model’s fixed allocations are already using part of the device. How many whole examples can share the remaining memory without exceeding the estimate? Write max_batch(limit, fixed, per_example). Inputs are finite scalars; limit and fixed are nonnegative and per_example is positive. Raise ValueError for invalid inputs. Return an integer, using zero when even one example cannot fit.
For a 250-byte limit, 73 fixed bytes, and 24 bytes per example, print the maximum batch and its estimated total as a list.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def max_batch(limit, fixed, per_example):
    pass

b = max_batch(250, 73, 24)
print([b, 73 + b*24])
hints: Subtract fixed bytes before dividing.
Use floor, then prevent a negative batch count.

tests.name: Reject zero activation cost

build.title: Budget the inspection device memory
build.problem: Botie must leave room for the model, its intermediate values, and the runtime.
build.challenge: Calculate total bytes from the supplied allocations, then subtract that total from the memory limit. Keep negative headroom visible.
build.why: Each multiplication converts a count into bytes. Adding compatible allocations gives a total we can compare with the limit.
build.limitation: The model assumes linear activation scaling and fixed runtime overhead. Actual peak memory and quantised-model quality need measurement.
hints: Give parameters and activations separate branches. Each needs a count multiplied by bytes per item.
Add parameter bytes, batch activation bytes, and fixed runtime bytes. All three allocations use the same unit.
Subtract the total from the memory limit. Keep a negative answer when the batch is too large.

title: Should the Prediction Happen Here or on a Server?
blurb: Sending an image away adds work before inference can begin. Compare communication and computation, then examine what happens when the connection disappears.
openingTitle: A Faster Server Still Has to Receive the Image
opening: A camera watches parts moving through an inspection station. Botie can run a small model beside the camera or send each picture to a larger server. The server computes faster, but the picture has to get there and the result has to return before the part moves on.
There is no useful answer in “the cloud is faster” by itself. Let’s describe the path in units of time, then look at the assumptions a local-versus-remote comparison leaves out.

history.title: Communication Belongs in the Design

sources.title: Satyanarayanan: The Emergence of Edge Computing (2017)

blocks: Satyanarayanan’s discussion of edge computing describes the role of computation close to data sources when latency and bandwidth make distant processing difficult. The location of computation changes how much information has to travel and how long a response takes.

Our inspection example compares a local estimate with a simplified remote path. It does not claim that local computation always wins. A larger remote model may be more useful, and many systems divide work between the device and a server.

reading.experimentTitle: Does faster inference make up for the upload?
reading.experimentIntro: Change image size, effective bandwidth, network overhead, or compute time. The result is remote time minus local time.
reading.connectionTitle: Count the journey before choosing where to compute
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Compare two inference paths
reading.exampleNote: The estimates exclude queueing and assume negligible response payload, with return delay included in fixed overhead.

intuition.title: Follow the remote route
intuition.explanation: The server cannot classify an image it has not received.

rows.label: Upload
items: Image bytes / effective bytes per second

scene.caption: For this simplified path, the times are sequential and can be added.

intuition.title: Compare a local and a remote proposal
intuition.explanation: Both proposals must be evaluated on the same inspection task. The times here are invented.

scene.caption: A faster remote model still waits for communication.

parts.title: 1. Separate the data size from the link rate
paragraphs: Image size is an amount of data. Bandwidth is an amount per unit time. Dividing bytes by bytes per second gives seconds. Network links are often advertised in bits per second, so convert units before using that number.
Use an effective rate measured for the workload, including the practical effects that reduce payload throughput. A maximum link specification may be a poor estimate of an upload during a busy shift.
parts.calculation: Upload time = 600,000 bytes / 3,000,000 bytes per second = 0.20 s
interpretation: Compression changes the payload size. If it also changes image details, evaluate whether the inspection model loses useful evidence.

parts.title: 2. Add the time between sending and acting
paragraphs: Remote response time includes upload, network overhead, server computation, and any response payload or queueing. Our first estimate treats the response payload as negligible and includes its travel delay in a fixed overhead term.

For local inference, preparation and actuation also take time. In this toy comparison, shared preparation and actuation are excluded from both alternatives, so we compare the part of the path that differs.
parts.calculation:
Remote estimate = 0.20 + 0.04 + 0.03 = 0.27 s
Local estimate = 0.12 s
Remote minus local = 0.27 − 0.12 = 0.15 s
interpretation: A positive difference means the remote path is slower under these estimates. It says nothing yet about which model is more accurate.

parts.title: 3. Find the network conditions that change the choice
paragraphs: A smaller payload or a faster effective link can make the remote path competitive. A slower connection can reverse that result. Sweep several rates instead of treating one measurement as permanent.
NumPy can calculate a time for each candidate rate. Keep the array positions aligned so each result belongs to the intended link condition.
interpretation: The comparison becomes more useful when we see where its conclusion changes.

examples.title: Inspect two network conditions
paragraphs: This separate example uses a 200-byte teaching payload and a fixed overhead of 0.1 seconds.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rates = np.array([1000., 2000.])
seconds = 200 / rates + 0.1
print(np.round(seconds, 2).tolist())
interpretation: Doubling bandwidth reduces the upload term. The fixed overhead remains.

parts.title: 4. Check whether the two predictions solve the same task
paragraphs: A tiny local model and a large remote model may have different errors. Compare them on representative inspection images, including difficult lighting and uncommon faults. If the remote model improves quality, decide whether that improvement is usable within the response deadline.
A hybrid might run locally for routine cases and send selected cases for review. That selection rule needs its own evaluation; a confidence score does not automatically identify all difficult cases.
interpretation: Compare whole decisions under requirements. A latency-only winner may still be unsuitable.

parts.title: 5. Treat a missing connection as a real condition
paragraphs: A disconnected camera cannot receive a remote answer by waiting for an upload estimate. Decide whether the machine can pause, use a local fallback, or record the part for later inspection. The appropriate choice depends on the consequences of proceeding.
Buffering helps only if a later answer is still useful and storage is sufficient. A stale decision about a part that has already passed the station may have no operational value.
interpretation: Do not encode a network outage as zero latency. It is an unavailable path requiring another action.

parts.title: 6. Consider energy and data exposure separately
paragraphs: Sending data can consume energy, as can local computation. The balance depends on the hardware, radio, workload, and duty cycle. Measure it when battery life is a requirement rather than assuming one location is always cheaper.

Moving images off a device also changes where data are stored and who can access them. Determine whether the task needs raw images, cropped regions, or a smaller representation, and document retention and access requirements.
interpretation: The workshop compares response-time estimates. A deployment decision also needs evidence about accuracy, resource use, and the permitted data path.

quiz.prompt: What must the design specify?
options: A timely local response, pause, or other explicit failure action
An assumption that buffering always solves the problem
quiz.because: A late answer may no longer support the action.

given.data: A camera cannot connect to the server, and each result is needed before a moving part leaves the station.

quiz.prompt: The latency comparison establishes equal usefulness.
quiz.because: Task quality requires separate evidence.

given.data: Two candidate models have equal response time. Their errors were never compared.

practice.title: How does the preferred path change with the connection?
practice.question: How does the preferred path change with the connection?
task: A fast remote model still has to receive the image. Work out how different upload connections change the total wait. Write remote_seconds(payload_bytes, rates, overhead, compute). Return a NumPy array, one time per effective upload rate. Rates must be a one-dimensional array of finite positive values. The other inputs are finite nonnegative scalars. Raise ValueError otherwise.

Use payload 900 bytes, rates [3000,6000], overhead 0.05 seconds, and compute 0.02 seconds. Print remote times rounded to two decimals, then a boolean list showing which are no slower than local inference at 0.25 seconds.
The upload rates are bytes per second, matching payload_bytes. Return seconds, retain full precision for the local-versus-remote comparison, and round only the displayed times.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def remote_seconds(payload_bytes, rates, overhead, compute):
    pass

times = remote_seconds(900, [3000,6000], .05, .02)
print(np.round(times, 2).tolist())
print((times <= .25).tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def remote_seconds(payload_bytes, rates, overhead, compute):
    r = np.asarray(rates, dtype=float)
    fixed = np.asarray([payload_bytes, overhead, compute], dtype=float)
    if r.ndim != 1 or not np.isfinite(r).all() or (r <= 0).any() or not np.isfinite(fixed).all() or (fixed < 0).any():
        raise ValueError("Invalid payload, rate, or duration")
    return payload_bytes/r + overhead + compute

times = remote_seconds(900, [3000,6000], .05, .02)
print(np.round(times, 2).tolist())
print((times <= .25).tolist())
hints: Divide the scalar payload by the rate array.
Keep full precision for the comparison; round only the printed times.

build.problem: Botie needs a prediction before an inspected part moves on. The server is faster at inference but requires communication.
build.challenge: Divide payload bytes by effective bandwidth, add network overhead and remote computation, then subtract local computation time.
build.why: The sign tells us which estimated path is faster. Changing the payload or link can reverse that comparison.
build.limitation: Shared preparation is excluded equally. Server queueing, response payload, outages, energy, and prediction quality need further evidence.
hints: The upload term converts bytes into seconds. Which input is bytes per second?
Divide payload by effective bandwidth, then add network overhead and remote compute time.
Subtract local time last. A positive answer means this remote estimate takes longer.

title: Which Designs Are Actually Acceptable?
blurb: A design can be fast, accurate, or inexpensive without meeting the job’s requirements. Remove infeasible options before comparing the choices that remain.
openingTitle: The Fastest Model Misses Too Many Faults
opening: Botie has several candidate models for the inspection camera. One responds quickly but misses more faults. Another catches more faults but cannot respond before the part leaves the station. Which should we use?

We first need to separate requirements from preferences. A response deadline is a limit the design must meet. Among designs that meet it, we might prefer a lower operating cost. Mixing those two decisions into one score can hide an unacceptable compromise.

history.title: A Trade Study Needs Criteria Before a Winner

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: how the guidance developed

blocks: An accurate model can be too slow for the decision, while the fastest model may miss too many faults. Combining those results into one attractive score before checking the limits can hide a design the maintenance team could never use.

NASA's systems-engineering guidance collected lessons from building systems whose components had competing demands. Across revisions following its 1995 first edition, the handbook developed decision-analysis guidance for comparing alternatives with explicit criteria and assumptions. The contribution we use here is a recorded trade study: state what must hold, compare alternatives against it, and leave the reasons for the choice inspectable.

Begin with the hard limits on Botie's table of model results. Among acceptable designs, a dominated choice is one another candidate matches or improves on every stated objective, with an improvement on at least one. Removing those choices narrows the decision without pretending that accuracy and latency are interchangeable. A person still has to judge the remaining trade-offs.

reading.experimentTitle: Which candidates survive both limits?
reading.experimentIntro: Change the latency or miss limits and inspect which candidate rows remain eligible.
reading.connectionTitle: Make the unacceptable choices visible first
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Find feasible and undominated options
reading.exampleNote: Miss counts come from the same invented set of 100 faulty parts. Latency values represent the same stated benchmark statistic.

intuition.title: Keep each candidate on one row
intuition.explanation: The limits are at most 100 ms latency and at most 4 misses on the shared evaluation.

scene.caption: An excellent result in one column cannot compensate for breaking a hard limit.

intuition.title: Look for an unnecessary compromise
intuition.explanation: Among these feasible options, B is no worse than E on either quantity and better on both.

scene.caption: B and D trade speed against misses. E is dominated on these reported quantities.

parts.title: 1. Write the requirement before looking at the leaderboard
paragraphs: Suppose the part leaves the camera station after a fixed time. That gives a response deadline. The team also chooses an acceptable miss limit for the evaluation. These requirements should be justified from the task, not adjusted merely so a favourite model passes.

Specify the metric itself. Mean latency and a high latency percentile answer different questions. A miss count needs an evaluation size and population. Without those definitions, a threshold can appear precise while comparing unlike evidence.
interpretation: Our table uses the same benchmark statistic and the same 100 faulty parts for every candidate. That makes this small comparison interpretable.

parts.title: 2. Turn each requirement into a mask
paragraphs: For each candidate, compare latency with its maximum and misses with their maximum. A boolean mask records the candidates that pass one requirement. Combining the masks with AND keeps candidates that pass both.
In the workshop, use the limits as the first inputs of Threshold gates. Each gate returns 1 when its limit is at least the measured value. Multiply the resulting masks to require both conditions.
parts.calculation:
Latency = [60, 90, 120, 80] ms
Misses = [5, 3, 1, 4]
Latency at most 100: [1, 1, 0, 1]
Misses at most 4: [0, 1, 1, 1]
Feasible: [0, 1, 0, 1]
interpretation: B and D remain. Returning a mask keeps their positions aligned with the candidate names.

examples.title: Select rows without losing their names
paragraphs: A boolean mask can index the same positions in a name array and a measurement table.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(["small", "medium", "large"])
latency = np.array([40., 70., 130.])
print(names[latency <= 80].tolist())
interpretation: This demonstrates a single limit. The challenge needs every limit to hold for each row.

parts.title: 3. What if no candidate passes?
paragraphs: The feasible set contains the candidates that meet every stated requirement. If that set is empty, none of the tested designs is acceptable under those requirements. That is useful information. We may need to improve the implementation, collect better training data, change the operating process, or negotiate a requirement with the person responsible for it.
Do not quietly return the least bad candidate as if it passed. If a limit is a preference rather than an absolute requirement, label it that way and show the consequence of relaxing it.
interpretation: A design review should be able to say “none of these yet”. That is more useful than a ranking that hides a failed requirement.

parts.title: 4. Remove choices that lose on every reported objective
paragraphs: Among feasible candidates, say B dominates E if B is no worse on every objective and strictly better on at least one. Here, smaller latency and fewer misses are both preferred. A dominated candidate offers no improvement on either reported quantity.

Candidates that are not dominated form a Pareto set. B and D both remain because one is faster while the other misses fewer faults. This identifies the trade; it does not decide how much a miss is worth.
parts.calculation:
B = [90 ms, 3 misses]
E = [95 ms, 4 misses]
B is no worse in both columns and better in at least one
D = [80 ms, 4 misses]
D is faster than B; B misses fewer than D
Neither B nor D dominates the other
interpretation: Equal rows do not strictly dominate each other. A duplicate may still differ in an unreported property such as maintainability.

parts.title: 5. Do not add incompatible units without a reason
paragraphs: Adding milliseconds to a miss count does not produce a naturally meaningful measure. A weighted score needs a stated preference model, including scales and the meaning of each weight. Changing units can change an unjustified score’s ranking.

An explicit consequence model, such as the inspection costs from the earlier lesson, gives a more interpretable comparison when the costs are defensible. Some consequences should remain hard limits instead.
interpretation: A Pareto comparison can remove clearly inferior choices without inventing a conversion between units.

parts.title: 6. Remember that the table contains estimates
paragraphs: Latency varies, and a sample miss count does not reveal the exact future failure rate. Two close candidates may exchange places on another representative sample. Report uncertainty and relevant subgroups before treating small differences as settled.
Also check whether an omitted property changes the choice. Memory, a disconnected camera, or a requirement to explain decisions can make an apparently dominated model worth keeping.
interpretation: Dominance is relative to the objectives and evidence we supplied. Python will calculate it exactly for a table, while we remain responsible for choosing the right table.

parts.title: 7. Make the selection reproducible
paragraphs: Save the candidate versions, benchmark procedure, requirements, and reasons for the choice. If the deadline changes, someone should be able to repeat the comparison rather than infer your preferences from a final model filename.

Start with feasibility, then examine the remaining compromises. Botie’s workshop builds the first step. The second Python challenge implements dominance on a small matrix so the comparison stays inspectable.
interpretation: The functions deliberately keep all candidate positions. They return masks instead of silently renaming or reordering the designs.

quiz.prompt: Which candidate is dominated by B?
quiz.because: B is no worse than E in both columns. D is faster than B, so neither dominates the other.

practice.title: Which candidates meet every limit?
practice.question: Which candidates meet every limit?
task: A quick candidate can miss too many faults, and an accurate one can miss the deadline. Keep the requirements separate so one success cannot hide the other failure. Write feasible(values, limits). values is a nonempty finite two-dimensional NumPy-compatible table, with one candidate per row. limits is a finite one-dimensional array with one maximum per column. Return a boolean mask, requiring every value in a row to be at most its limit. Raise ValueError for a malformed table or mismatched limits.
Use rows [[45,6],[70,3],[85,2],[55,4]] with limits [80,4]. Print the mask.

import numpy as np

def feasible(values, limits):

print(feasible([[45,6],[70,3],[85,2],[55,4]], [80,4]).tolist())

practice.title: Can you identify the trade-offs without adding unlike units?
practice.question: Can you identify the trade-offs without adding unlike units?
task: Two candidates may trade speed against missed faults without either being worse on every measurement. Keep those trade-offs visible instead of adding unlike units into an arbitrary score. Write pareto(values) for a finite, nonempty two-dimensional table. Every column is minimised. Return a boolean array marking rows that no other row dominates. A row dominates another only if it is no worse in every column and strictly better in at least one. Invalid inputs raise ValueError.
Use [[5,5],[4,6],[6,6],[5,5],[7,3]]. Print the mask. Keep equal rows.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def pareto(values):
    pass

print(pareto([[5,5],[4,6],[6,6],[5,5],[7,3]]).tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def pareto(values):
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    if v.ndim != 2 or not v.size or not np.isfinite(v).all():
        raise ValueError("Use a finite nonempty table")
    keep = np.ones(len(v), dtype=bool)
    for i, row in enumerate(v):
        dominates = (v <= row).all(axis=1) & (v < row).any(axis=1)
        keep[i] = not dominates.any()
    return keep

print(pareto([[5,5],[4,6],[6,6],[5,5],[7,3]]).tolist())
hints: Compare every row with the candidate being examined.
Combine no-worse-in-all with strictly-better-in-any. The candidate cannot dominate itself.
