title: Which Records Should Botie Bring into the Conversation?

appliedIn.title: deciding which data may leave the service

blurb: The manual collection is larger than one request can hold. Select permitted evidence, leave room for the reply, and keep each excerpt attached to its source.
openingTitle: The Relevant Page Is Buried in a Room Full of Manuals
opening: A technician asks about a seal on P-2. Botie has maintenance manuals for several sites, years of service tickets, and a limited amount of text it can send in one model request. Copying everything would include irrelevant records and perhaps records this technician is not allowed to read.
We need to choose what enters the conversation. This means finding useful material, respecting permissions, and preserving enough of its identity to check the eventual answer.

history.title: A Model Could Read Retrieved Material at Answer Time

sources.title: Lewis and colleagues: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (2020)

blocks: A model’s stored parameters are inconvenient for information that changes or needs a source check. Lewis and colleagues’ 2020 retrieval-augmented generation work combined a passage-retrieval component with a model that generates text. Retrieval found material to supply at answer time; generation could use that material alongside what the model had learned during training.

Our maintenance assistant needs that separation because a manual can change without retraining every model that may consult it. This workshop begins after candidate passages have been ranked. It decides which the current request may read and which fit the available input budget. The small list procedure is not the paper’s trained retrieval model; it exposes the permission and capacity decisions around retrieved context.

reading.experimentTitle: Which source IDs survive the request budget?
reading.experimentIntro: Filter candidate passages by asset permission before taking the ordered prefix that fits. Try a passage that consumes the remaining room exactly.
reading.connectionTitle: Context is selected evidence with a boundary
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Pack permitted excerpts without losing their IDs
reading.exampleNote: The supplied token counts are invented whole counts. This workshop does not tokenize text or call a retriever.

intuition.title: Keep source identity beside each passage
intuition.explanation: These candidates are already ordered by a separate retriever. The first one is not permitted for the current caller.

scene.caption: A high retrieval rank does not grant access.

intuition.title: Allocate the window before adding excerpts
intuition.explanation: The model input and possible answer share a finite allowance in this teaching budget.

records.label: Reserved input
cells: Instructions, question, tool descriptions and message overhead

scene.caption: Actual providers expose model-specific limits and accounting rules. Use their tokenizer and reported usage when implementing the real budget.

parts.title: 1. Separate retrieving a candidate from selecting context
paragraphs: Suppose the question asks when to inspect a seal. A search might first find passages containing “seal” and “inspection”. This is lexical search: matching words in the question with words in the collection. Another search could represent each passage as a numerical vector and compare it with a vector for the question. Those vectors are embeddings. A further model can then score the shortlisted passages against the question; that extra ordering step is reranking. Each stage can miss useful evidence for a different reason. None automatically knows every application permission or guarantees that a passage answers the question.

Our inputs begin after ranking. We receive records containing an ID, an asset, text and a supplied token cost. Selection decides which permitted records reach the model. Keeping those stages distinct lets us ask whether a failure came from missing candidates or from discarding useful candidates later.
interpretation: A relevant-looking passage about a different pump can be dangerous if the asset identity is lost during selection.

parts.title: 2. Filter by permission before constructing the request
paragraphs: The authenticated caller’s scope determines which records are eligible. Apply access restrictions during retrieval where supported, and enforce them before selected content reaches the model or any externally visible log. A prompt saying “do not reveal restricted manuals” is too late if the service already sent the restricted text.

In this example, a record is eligible when its asset occurs in an authoritative allowed list. A real document system may require organisation, role, document version and operation-specific checks. Asset membership is our deliberately small permission model.
interpretation: The workshop lets you inspect the candidate records locally. Its fixtures contain no private documents; they illustrate where an application would enforce the boundary.

parts.title: 3. Reserve space for the parts we cannot discard
paragraphs: A model request contains more than excerpts. Instructions, the question, tool schemas and conversation messages all consume context. The reply may need an allowance as well, depending on the model’s limit semantics. Start by measuring or reserving those parts, then decide how much remains for evidence.

Our invented accounting uses one total window and explicit input and output reserves. Costs are supplied whole-token counts; word count is not token count. Message wrappers and formatting can add overhead, so a production implementation should count the final serialised request with the correct model tokenizer and leave margin where needed.
parts.calculation:
Total allowance = 20 tokens
Reserved non-evidence input = 8 tokens
Reserved output = 4 tokens
Evidence allowance = 20 − 8 − 4 = 8 tokens
interpretation: If reserves exceed the total, reject the configuration or deliberately shorten something. Do not silently call the remaining budget zero and claim the request fits.

parts.title: 4. Choose a packing rule and admit what it leaves out
paragraphs: After filtering, our rule keeps complete records in ranked order until the next record would exceed the available budget. It stops at that point. This preserves a prefix of the ranking and avoids chopping a sentence in half.

It can waste room. If the first permitted passage is too large, a shorter passage later in the list will not be selected. Skipping oversized passages, compressing them, or changing chunk sizes are different policies with their own tradeoffs. State which policy you use so a test can distinguish an intended choice from a bug.
parts.calculation:
Permitted passage costs = [6, 5]
Evidence allowance = 8
Take the first passage: used = 6
The next total would be 6 + 5 = 11
11 exceeds 8, so stop
interpretation: The result contains one source. We have made a budget decision, not shown that the remaining source is sufficient to answer the question.

examples.title: Keep an ordered prefix of simple costs
paragraphs: This small program demonstrates the budget rule without permissions or document records. Notice that it stops instead of skipping to the last item.
examples.code:
costs = [3, 8, 2]
budget = 7
used = 0
selected = []
for position, cost in enumerate(costs):
    if used + cost > budget:
        break
    selected.append(position)
    used += cost
print(selected)
print(used)
interpretation: The final cost of 2 would fit on its own, but this chosen prefix policy never reaches it.

parts.title: 5. Carry the citation through every transformation
paragraphs: A passage should retain its source ID, document version and useful location such as a page or section. If it is split, keep the chunk-to-document mapping. If it is summarised, retain the underlying evidence and make the summary’s status clear. Otherwise an answer can name a document without giving anyone a way to check the relevant text.

A citation ID proves only that the answer points somewhere. Check whether the cited material supports the claim, refers to the right asset, and was available to the user. An outdated manual can be perfectly cited and still inappropriate for the current machine.
interpretation: The workshop outputs IDs from the selected records. Read the corresponding text in the input records to inspect what the model would actually receive.

parts.title: 6. Treat retrieved instructions as document content
paragraphs: A service ticket may contain an instruction directed at the assistant. A manual page might even include a quoted conversation. Keep that text labelled as evidence, as we did in the prompt lesson. It must not change the application’s tool permissions or approval state.

Retrieval makes prompt injection a practical data-flow problem: content from outside the application enters the model’s input. Restrict available tools and validate their calls regardless of how convincing the generated explanation sounds. If a task only needs an answer from manuals, do not grant it a general-purpose write tool.
interpretation: Encoding the document cleanly helps inspection, but it does not establish that a model will respect the data boundary.

parts.title: 7. Decide what the conversation should remember
paragraphs: Conversation history can consume the same room as evidence. An old summary may omit a qualification or carry forward an earlier mistake. Keep durable facts separate from provisional model statements, and preserve source links for facts that need verification.

A short-lived conversation state is different from a long-term user memory. Decide which values should persist, who may see them, how corrections replace stale values, and when they expire. Loading every past message is a memory policy, even if it was chosen accidentally.
interpretation: For this maintenance task, the asset ID and current question matter. An unrelated ticket from last week should not displace the manual excerpt needed now.

parts.title: 8. Measure missing evidence before changing the prompt
paragraphs: When an answer fails, inspect the selected records. Was a relevant passage retrieved? Was it authorised? Did it fit? Did the selected text actually contain the needed fact? A prompt change cannot recover evidence that the request never contained.

Evaluate retrieval coverage on labelled questions separately from answer support. Include a case where no permitted document answers the question. The correct system behaviour may be to explain the gap or request more information, rather than invent a plausible maintenance interval.
interpretation: A later observability lesson will record these stages. Here the selected IDs make the budgeting consequence visible without a live model.

quiz.prompt: What still needs checking?
options: Whether this evidence applies to the requested machine version
Whether a citation ID exists anywhere
Whether the output contains more words
quiz.because: Accurately quoting an inapplicable source does not answer the question.

given.data: The selected document cites an older machine version. The answer repeats its interval accurately, but the question asks about the new version.

quiz.prompt: Under that stated policy, no passage is selected.
quiz.because: The rule stops at the first overflow. A skip-and-continue policy would behave differently.

given.data: The prefix policy is given a first permitted passage larger than the evidence allowance, followed by a tiny passage.

practice.title: Which permitted manuals fit this request?
practice.question: Which permitted manuals fit this request?
task: The model’s input must leave room for instructions and a reply. Choose permitted evidence within that allowance, without letting a restricted passage consume the useful space. Write select_sources(chunks, allowed, window, reserved, output). Each chunk must be a dict with nonempty string id and asset, and nonnegative integer tokens excluding bool. allowed is a list of nonempty asset strings. The three budget values are nonnegative integers excluding bool; reserves must fit inside window. Invalid inputs raise ValueError, including a malformed chunk outside the allowed scope.

Filter by allowed asset, preserving order. Keep a prefix of complete permitted chunks until the first overflow, then return their IDs as a list. Do not mutate inputs. For costs 4,7,2 on assets P-9,P-2,P-2, with allowed=[P-2], window=24, reserved=10 and output=4, print the IDs.
practice.starter:
def select_sources(chunks, allowed, window, reserved, output):
    pass

chunks = [{"id":"X", "asset":"P-9", "tokens":4}, {"id":"A", "asset":"P-2", "tokens":7}, {"id":"B", "asset":"P-2", "tokens":2}]
print(select_sources(chunks, ["P-2"], 24, 10, 4))
hints: Validate all input records before the selection loop.
A forbidden record consumes no evidence budget.
Use break for an overflowing permitted record, and continue for an unpermitted record.

tests.name: Exact boundary and no mutation
tests.code:
rows=[{"id":"a","asset":"P","tokens":3},{"id":"b","asset":"P","tokens":4}]
copy=[dict(r) for r in rows]
assert select_sources(rows,["P"],10,2,1) == ["a","b"]
assert rows == copy

tests.name: Reject overspent reserves
Validate a forbidden malformed record

build.challenge: Subtract reserved input and output from the total window. Filter chunks by allowed asset, then keep a prefix within the remaining token budget. Stop at the first permitted chunk that would overflow. Return the selected id fields in order.

cases.name: The first permitted chunk is too large

build.limitation: Costs are supplied, ranking is already done, and the prefix rule is deliberately simple. No selected-ID list proves relevance or factual support.

title: What Should Botie Do After a Tool Replies?

appliedIn.title: choosing between a workflow and an agent
sharing a budget across concurrent work

blurb: One search may reveal that a second search is needed. Follow the observations through an agent loop, then give that loop explicit ways to finish or ask for help.
openingTitle: The Manual Search Returns the Wrong Version
opening: Botie searches for an inspection interval and finds a manual for an older pump. The excerpt is readable and the source is real, but it does not settle the technician’s question. A useful next step might be another search using the exact model number.

This is where selecting a next action can help. The model receives the search result and proposes what to do next. We still need a program that validates the proposal, records what happened, and stops when further attempts are no longer justified.

history.title: An Observation Could Change the Next Action
blocks: A language model answering from its initial input cannot inspect a tool result that has not arrived yet. ReAct explored sequences that interleave reasoning and actions, letting observations affect the next step. This supplied a concrete way to combine language-based task handling with information gathered during execution.

Our controller is smaller than a full agent implementation. It consumes supplied proposals and results so we can inspect termination behaviour. The workshop does not run a language model or reveal its private reasoning. It shows the operational decisions an application must make around whatever model supplies the proposals.

reading.experimentTitle: When should the next operation be allowed?
reading.experimentIntro: Try a successful final answer, a request for another tool at the limit, and a permanent tool failure. Build the decision from comparisons and branches.
reading.connectionTitle: Let observations affect the route without losing control
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Replay a bounded sequence of tool proposals
reading.exampleNote: All actions and observations are scripted offline fixtures. No model or external tool is called.

intuition.title: Follow a question through observable events
intuition.explanation: The next proposal can depend on what the previous search actually returned.

records.label: Search result
cells: Only model A manual was found
Try a corrected search or report missing evidence

records.label: Second result
cells: Model B interval with source M2B

scene.caption: An event log needs proposals and results. It does not need a private reasoning transcript to show the sequence.

intuition.title: Stop for different reasons
intuition.explanation: The same construction must distinguish an answer from a request to keep searching.

scene.caption: Here the limit counts tool attempts. Other budgets, including model requests and elapsed time, require separate counters.

parts.title: 1. Name the state that must survive between calls
paragraphs: The next model request needs the task and the observations gathered so far. The application also needs control state: which tools are allowed, how many attempts have been made, and whether an earlier operation failed. These serve different purposes.

Store tool-call IDs with their results so parallel or delayed responses can be matched to the right proposal. Keep error results distinct from successful results. A timeout is evidence that a response was not received in time; it does not necessarily prove that a side effect never happened.
interpretation: The previous lesson’s context selection decides what the model sees. The controller’s budgets and permissions remain authoritative even if older messages are summarised.

parts.title: 2. Separate proposing, executing and observing
paragraphs: At each turn, the model may propose a tool call or a final response. The application validates the proposal. If it is a tool call, the server checks the tool name and arguments, checks permission, then executes and records its result. A later model request receives that observation.

This cycle is what makes a tool-using agent different from simply displaying model text. The software decides what actually executes. A proposal containing a function name must never be evaluated as arbitrary code. Look up the name in a bounded registry of approved implementations.
interpretation: An unknown tool name should produce a controlled failure or repair opportunity. It should not become a shell command.

parts.title: 3. Give the loop an explicit termination decision
paragraphs: Our controller accepts a validated action of finish or tool. A finish action can return a checked final response, including an honest statement that evidence was unavailable. A tool action may continue only while the tool-attempt count is below its limit and the last status is ok. Otherwise control passes to a handoff response.

The workshop uses comparisons and Choose from a check to make this decision visible. It has no feedback wire: the real loop lives in the host program, which calls the controller again after the next observation. The Python exercise replays that host loop using a supplied list of events.
parts.calculation:
If action is finish: return answer
Otherwise, if used < limit and status is ok: return continue
Otherwise: return handoff
interpretation: This order permits a final response after the last allowed tool attempt. It does not permit another tool just because the model says it is almost done.

parts.title: 4. Count attempts at the boundary you intend to limit
paragraphs: A tool-attempt budget counts calls that were attempted, including calls that failed. Counting only successes allows an unreliable tool to be retried indefinitely. Increment the attempt counter when the call is issued, and persist it if execution can resume after a restart.

A tool limit does not bound every expense. One tool may take a long time, and the model may consume tokens between tool calls. A deployed system normally needs additional limits on elapsed time, model requests and token or monetary usage. Name each counter and decide what happens at its boundary.
interpretation: This workshop’s used and limit refer only to tool attempts. We will not describe it as a complete cost limiter.

examples.title: Failures still consume a tool attempt
paragraphs: This program demonstrates counting observations from attempted tools. It does not decide whether to retry them.
examples.code:
observations = ["ok", "timeout", "ok"]
attempts = 0
for status in observations:
    attempts += 1
    print(attempts, status)
interpretation: The timeout is the second attempt. Its cost and uncertain outcome do not disappear because it failed to return useful information.

parts.title: 5. Classify errors before offering a retry
paragraphs: A temporary connection failure may justify a retry with a limit and delay. A permanent permission denial will not become authorised because the model repeats it. A schema error may need corrected arguments. Keep these categories distinguishable in the tool result.

Our workshop controller treats permanent_error as a stop for further tools. It can still return an already prepared and checked final response explaining the limitation. The Python replay uses a more immediate policy: it hands off as soon as that error arrives, before accepting another proposal. These are deliberately different application choices; neither may execute another tool after the denial.

If a production service retries a side effect after an uncertain outcome, it must reuse the original idempotency identity and follow the tool contract. Otherwise an apparently helpful retry can duplicate an inspection.
interpretation: Neither example implements timed retries. Repeated calls that return no new information can also justify a stop, but a progress detector needs a defined comparison of inputs and outcomes.

parts.title: 6. A final response is still a candidate answer
paragraphs: When the model requests finish, validate its response schema and evidence before showing it as a successful answer. It may correctly report that the available manuals are insufficient. That is different from claiming the maintenance question was resolved.

Record why execution ended: answered, missing evidence, denied action, exhausted budget or a service failure. A single completed flag loses those distinctions. Evaluations should distinguish successfully answering a question from merely reaching a terminal state.
interpretation: In the workshop, answer means return the supplied final-response branch. The fixture does not include its text or verify factual correctness.

parts.title: 7. Preserve a useful handoff
paragraphs: If the loop cannot continue, tell the technician what remains unresolved and which relevant sources were checked. Where appropriate, suggest the missing asset number or manual version that would let work resume. Avoid claiming that an unconfirmed tool action succeeded.

A human review path needs the actual proposed action and its evidence. A generic “approve agent” button provides too little information. When review changes a request, revalidate its payload and permissions before execution, just as in the tool-contract lesson.
interpretation: The handoff is part of the task’s designed behaviour. It should be understandable even when the underlying service error was technical.

parts.title: 8. Replay the controller before paying for live runs
paragraphs: Scripted events let us test control logic cheaply and consistently. Include a normal path, a failure and a boundary where no further tool may run. The fixtures can prove that the counter and branching rules behave as specified on those inputs.

They cannot establish that a model selects useful tools, understands observations, or writes supported answers. Those require representative model runs and evaluation. Keeping these tests separate makes a failure easier to locate: deterministic control code, model behaviour, or the external service.
interpretation: The following exercise returns both the terminal reason and attempted-tool count. Change a replay to predict where the host loop stops before running it.

quiz.prompt: What should this lesson’s controller do?
options: treat denial as an empty successful result
quiz.because: Remaining budget cannot repair a permanent denial.

given.data: A tool returns permanent_error because the caller is denied access. The model proposes the same tool again; one of three attempts has been used.

quiz.prompt: That result alone establishes that a live model will choose useful searches.
quiz.because: Replay tests check deterministic behaviour on supplied decisions, not the quality of decisions generated by a model.

given.data: A scripted replay passes every control-flow test without calling a language model.

practice.title: How many tool attempts does this replay actually make?
practice.question: How many tool attempts does this replay actually make?
task: A controller should stop asking for tools without throwing away an answer it already has. Replay the supplied decisions and count the attempts actually permitted. Write replay(events, limit). limit is a nonnegative integer excluding bool. events is a list of dicts. Each event has exactly action="finish", or exactly action="tool" and status="ok" or "permanent_error". Validate the complete list first; malformed inputs raise ValueError.

Start with zero attempts. A finish event returns ("answer", attempts). A tool event at the limit returns ("handoff", attempts) without executing it. Otherwise count the tool attempt; a permanent_error returns handoff immediately. If the events end without finish, return handoff. Ignore later events after returning, but still validate them before replay.
For events tool/ok, tool/ok, finish with limit 2, print the result. Then print the same events with limit 1. This replay calls no external tools.

def replay(events, limit):

events = [{"action":"tool", "status":"ok"}, {"action":"tool", "status":"ok"}, {"action":"finish"}]
print(replay(events, 2))
print(replay(events, 1))

Check for finish before checking whether another tool would exceed the limit.
Increment attempts for a permitted tool before inspecting its result status.

title: Does Botie Need to Choose the Next Step?
topic: Choosing How Much Autonomy to Give
blurb: A request to find a maintenance record and an investigation of an unfamiliar fault ask different things of the program. Compare what fixed steps can do before giving a model more decisions.
openingTitle: We Have Built a Tool Loop. Do We Need It for This Job?
opening: A technician asks for the inspection date of pump P7. We already know the steps: check access, look up P7, and display the date. Giving Botie freedom to invent a plan adds decisions to a job whose route we can write down ourselves.

Now consider a request to explain why several pumps began vibrating after a maintenance visit. The useful follow-up depends on what the records reveal. We need a way to decide where a model’s choice of next step actually helps. We will compare candidate controllers on the same invented maintenance requests, including their mistakes.

history.title: Separating a Predetermined Route from a Model’s Choice

sources.title: Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system

blocks: Once language models could call tools, developers could give them control over a sequence of operations. That raised a practical question: which decisions should remain in ordinary application code? Anthropic’s December 2024 engineering article distinguished predefined workflows from systems in which a model chooses its next operations. It described patterns used in applications, rather than claiming to have invented workflows or software agents.

Think about the maintenance desk. Retrieving a known record already has a route. Investigating a poorly described fault may require looking at a result before deciding what to inspect next. Our examples use invented measurements to make that design choice visible. They are not benchmark results for any provider or framework.

reading.experimentTitle: Which controller meets the maintenance desk’s requirements?
reading.experimentIntro: Keep the task checks beside each controller’s time and cost. Connect the comparison before choosing the amount of autonomy.
reading.connectionTitle: Use evidence to decide who chooses the next operation
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Select a controller from its trial records
reading.exampleNote: The trials are invented. This workshop compares records; it does not run a model or establish production reliability.

intuition.title: The same request can travel through different controllers
intuition.explanation: The route belongs to application code in a workflow. A model chooses the next operation in our agent candidate.

records.label: When was P7 inspected?
cells: Missing or inaccessible record has a defined error path

records.label: Explain the new vibration
cells: The next useful record depends on the evidence returned

scene.caption: A workflow can contain a model call. Using a model does not automatically give it control of the route.

intuition.title: Compare success before preferring fewer moving parts
intuition.explanation: Each candidate receives the same three fictional requests. Here the workflow already satisfies the task checks.

scene.caption: This tiny fixture demonstrates the comparison. A maximum over three observations is not a production latency percentile.

parts.title: 1. Write down what a completed maintenance request means
paragraphs: Start with the result the technician needs. For a record lookup, success means returning the correct authorised record or accurately reporting that it is unavailable. For an investigation, success may mean identifying relevant evidence and explaining what remains uncertain. A fluent response that omits the missing evidence does not complete that job.

Choose the acceptance checks before trying architectures. Keep cases where a record is missing, where access is denied, and where two assets have similar names. If only the happy path appears in the test set, the most fragile controller can look convincing.
interpretation: The checks describe the job. The controller is one proposal for doing it.

parts.title: 2. Try the route we can already specify
paragraphs: A direct database lookup is a useful baseline for a date request. A baseline is a working comparison that tells us what extra machinery improves. It may be ordinary code, a search interface, or one model call with supplied evidence.

A fixed workflow can validate a request, retrieve a manual, ask a model for a supported summary, then check its output. Branches for absent evidence and failed validation remain explicit. We can test each branch without asking a model to discover the order again. The wording step may still be uncertain, so fixed orchestration does not make the whole system deterministic.
interpretation: Give the baseline a fair implementation. An intentionally weak prompt would make a larger architecture appear more useful than it is.

parts.title: 3. Find the decision that depends on a previous result
paragraphs: Suppose the first maintenance record points to a replacement coupling. Botie might need the coupling specification next. A different record might point to a changed sensor. We can allow a model to choose among a limited set of read operations based on that evidence.

This creates a new responsibility: checking whether each proposed action is permitted and whether the investigation has enough evidence to stop. Tool feedback tells the loop what happened. A missing record can trigger a supported answer about uncertainty rather than another speculative query. Keep the earlier output and permission checks when adding this freedom.
interpretation: Choose an agent because the task benefits from adaptive decisions. The presence of several tools alone does not establish that benefit.

parts.title: 4. A second agent adds a handoff we must explain
paragraphs: Separate specialists can examine genuinely independent records in parallel. Before adding them, identify what each receives, what it must return, and who combines conflicting findings. A handoff should preserve the request identity and source IDs. The coordinator needs a way to recognise partial or failed work.

Sending the same full conversation to several agents repeats input work and introduces several proposals to reconcile. Parallel work can reduce elapsed time while increasing total compute. A copied mistake may appear in every answer, so agreement is not independent evidence. Begin with one controller and measure whether delegation improves the task enough to justify its coordination and operating costs.
interpretation: For the maintenance desk, two independent manual searches may be useful. Two agents that both create the same work order introduce a different problem.

parts.title: 5. Keep trial results aligned with their measurements
paragraphs: The workshop stores each controller as a dictionary. passed is a list of boolean outcomes in the agreed case order. latency_ms and cost_units have one entry for each of those same cases. rank records our declared preference for less autonomy: rules first, then workflow, then agent. A rank is a design policy, not a measure of intelligence.

We summarise how many checks passed, the slowest observed request, and total cost over the fixture. Comparing different case sets would confound architecture with task difficulty. Real evaluations should retain case IDs and versions, repeat stochastic runs, and report uncertain estimates. Our short list assumes that alignment has already been checked.
interpretation: Latency and cost answer different questions. A parallel controller may have a smaller wall-clock maximum and a larger total bill.

examples.title: Read one controller’s aligned trial rows
paragraphs: zip pairs the values by position. Check equal lengths first so a missing measurement cannot disappear silently.
examples.code:
passed = [True, False, True]
latency_ms = [420, 510, 470]
cost_units = [2, 3, 2]
assert len(passed) == len(latency_ms) == len(cost_units)
for case, (ok, elapsed, cost) in enumerate(zip(passed, latency_ms, cost_units), start=1):
    print(case, ok, elapsed, cost)
print("passes:", sum(passed))
interpretation: The failed case remains in the measurements. Removing it would hide both the failure and the resources it consumed.

parts.title: 6. Apply requirements before choosing simplicity
paragraphs: Filter the summaries against the acceptance requirements. Our fixture requires every supplied task check to pass and bounds observed latency and total cost. Among candidates that meet those requirements, choose the lowest autonomy rank. If ranks tie, choose lower total cost, then the alphabetically earlier name so the result is repeatable.

This is an explicit teaching policy. A real service may prioritise tail latency, audit requirements, operating effort or a risk threshold differently. State that policy before looking at the candidate scores. If no candidate passes, return a review outcome. Quietly selecting the least bad failure would erase the meaning of the requirements.
parts.calculation:
eligible = task_passes >= required_passes
           and worst_latency <= latency_limit
           and total_cost <= cost_limit
interpretation: Passing this fixture is permission to investigate a candidate further. It is not a guarantee about future requests.

parts.title: 7. Let a new kind of fault challenge the chosen route
paragraphs: The changed workshop case gives the fixed workflow a request it cannot resolve. Its score now fails the task requirement, while the agent candidate meets the same requirements. Keep the selection policy unchanged and inspect which evidence changed the decision.

A single adaptive example should not make every request autonomous. Routing well-defined requests through the simpler path and reserving an agent for measured difficult cases can be useful. The router needs its own evaluation, including false escalations and difficult requests it incorrectly keeps on the simple path.
interpretation: The useful outcome is a design tied to task evidence, with a clear fallback when the evidence is insufficient.

parts.title: 8. Keep the operating boundary when the controller changes
paragraphs: A workflow and an agent can use the same scoped read tool, output validator and human approval boundary. Changing who chooses the next step does not change who is authorised to read a customer’s records or create an inspection.

Version the controller along with prompts, tools, model settings and evaluation data. Re-run the comparison after a meaningful change. Watch the real request mix: a controller chosen for mostly date lookups may need reconsideration when most users begin asking open investigations. Frameworks in the next lessons can organise these components, but their abstractions should leave the decision boundaries visible.
interpretation: We can now ask a more useful framework question: does it make the controller we chose easier to implement, test and inspect?

quiz.prompt: Which controller does this declared policy select?
quiz.because: The rank is compared first among eligible candidates. Cost breaks a tie at the same rank.

given.data: Workflow and agent both pass all required cases. Workflow rank is 1 and total cost is 8. Agent rank is 2 and total cost is 6. Both satisfy the time and cost limits. Policy prefers lower rank before cost.

quiz.prompt: Returning review requirements preserves the fact that no candidate was accepted.
quiz.because: The selection function should not turn a failed requirement into a successful deployment decision.

given.data: No candidate meets the minimum task requirement in the supplied trial records.

practice.title: Which controller earns a trial at the maintenance desk?
practice.question: Which controller earns a trial at the maintenance desk?
task: The desk needs a controller that completes its required jobs within its operating limits. Give extra autonomy a trial only when the measured task calls for it. Write choose_controller(candidates, policy). Each candidate has unique nonblank name, nonnegative integer rank, nonempty boolean passed list, and equally long lists latency_ms and cost_units containing nonnegative integers. Every candidate uses the same case count and order. policy contains nonnegative integer min_passes, max_latency_ms and max_cost_units. Reject malformed input with ValueError; booleans are not valid integer measurements.

Keep candidates meeting all three requirements. Return the name with the smallest tuple (rank, total cost, name), or "review requirements" if none qualify. Do not mutate inputs. Print the result for the two supplied trial records.
practice.solution:
def choose_controller(candidates, policy):
    def whole(value):
        return type(value) is int and value >= 0
    if not isinstance(policy, dict) or any(not whole(policy.get(k)) for k in
            ("min_passes", "max_latency_ms", "max_cost_units")):
        raise ValueError("Invalid acceptance requirements")
    if not isinstance(candidates, list):
        raise ValueError("Candidates must be a list")
    eligible, names = [], set()
    case_count = None
    for row in candidates:
        if not isinstance(row, dict):
            raise ValueError("Each candidate needs named fields")
        name, rank = row.get("name"), row.get("rank")
        passed, times, costs = (row.get(k) for k in ("passed", "latency_ms", "cost_units"))
        if not isinstance(name, str) or not name.strip() or name in names or not whole(rank):
            raise ValueError("Invalid candidate identity")
        names.add(name)
        if not isinstance(passed, list) or not passed or any(type(v) is not bool for v in passed):
            raise ValueError("Provide boolean task results")
        if case_count is not None and len(passed) != case_count:
            raise ValueError("Use the same cases for every controller")
        case_count = len(passed)
        if any(not isinstance(values, list) or len(values) != case_count or
               any(not whole(v) for v in values) for values in (times, costs)):
            raise ValueError("Align nonnegative latency and cost measurements")
        total_cost = sum(costs)
        if (sum(passed) >= policy["min_passes"] and
                max(times) <= policy["max_latency_ms"] and
                total_cost <= policy["max_cost_units"]):
            eligible.append((rank, total_cost, name))
    return min(eligible)[2] if eligible else "review requirements"

trials = [
    {"name":"workflow", "rank":1, "passed":[True, False], "latency_ms":[300, 500], "cost_units":[2, 2]},
    {"name":"agent", "rank":2, "passed":[True, True], "latency_ms":[900, 1200], "cost_units":[4, 5]},
]
policy = {"min_passes":2, "max_latency_ms":1500, "max_cost_units":12}
print(choose_controller(trials, policy))
hints: Check list alignment before aggregating measurements.
Keep the acceptance filter separate from the ordering policy. min on a list of tuples follows the declared priority.

title: Give Botie a Typed Job with Pydantic AI

appliedIn.title: checking the meaning and destination of an answer

blurb: Botie can read a manual, but the application still needs a usable answer and real citation IDs. Give the agent its dependencies and check what comes back.
openingTitle: The Answer Sounds Fine. Where Did That Citation Come From?
opening: A technician asks Botie what to inspect when a pump vibrates. The response includes a sensible sentence and a manual reference. Unfortunately, that reference was never in the material we gave him. How should the program notice before displaying it?

We have already built a tool loop and an output contract. Now we can give those responsibilities to a framework while keeping our own checks. Pydantic AI connects Python functions, typed results and the data belonging to a particular request.

history.title: Making a Model Response Fit an Ordinary Python Application
blocks: A useful model response still has to fit into an ordinary Python application. The next function may need a particular record, and a tool may need this request’s permitted manual data. Pydantic AI is a Python framework that organises model calls and tools around those requirements. It lets the application declare expected output fields and provide dependencies such as the records a tool may read.

The Pydantic team’s September 4, 2025 v1 announcement emphasised those software-engineering concerns and a stable interface after months of development. The output can be checked before other code consumes it, while dependency injection gives the tool its application-supplied resources. That term means passing in what the tool needs, rather than making it discover a global source itself. Our citation check still has to establish that the named manual supports the answer; accepted Python structure cannot do that alone.

reading.experimentIntro: Wire the field check before the citation check. Then change the proposed answer or the excerpts available to this run.

parts.title: 1. Give the program a result it can inspect
paragraphs: Suppose the interface has an answer panel and a source panel. An arbitrary paragraph forces the interface to guess where one ends and the other begins. A record with answer and citations fields gives each panel something named to read.

We use a Pydantic BaseModel to declare those fields. Constraints can require a nonempty list and reject unexpected keys. A declared type is a contract about representation. It does not establish that the answer is useful or true.
interpretation: Keep the distinction visible when testing. A correctly shaped invented citation passes a type check and fails an evidence check.

parts.title: 2. Pass the manual as a dependency
paragraphs: The excerpts belong to this request. Passing them into the run makes that relationship visible and lets a test substitute a small fixture. In Pydantic AI, deps_type describes the dependency type, while deps supplies the actual instance when the agent runs.

RunContext gives a tool access to those application-provided dependencies. The model chooses tool arguments; it does not construct the authenticated user or database connection. A dependency might hold a scoped database client instead of our small dictionary. Enforce access inside that client or tool.
interpretation: Do not paste a service credential into the prompt to make it available. Server code can use a credential without returning it as tool output.

parts.title: 3. Expose a small read operation
paragraphs: The read_manual tool returns the excerpts allowed for the request. Its Python signature tells the framework what inputs exist, and its docstring describes the operation to the model. Our tool has no model-chosen arguments, which prevents the model from supplying another customer’s identity.

The returned dictionary still becomes information the model can use. If an excerpt contains text that tells Botie to ignore instructions, treat it as manual content. A tool result does not acquire authority over the application because it arrived through a Python function.
interpretation: The tool’s job is reading evidence. Creating an inspection job will require a separate permission boundary later.

parts.title: 4. Connect Agent, dependencies and output_type
paragraphs: Agent holds the model configuration and the permitted tool definitions. run_sync executes a run from an ordinary synchronous script; use await agent.run in an asynchronous server. The returned result has an output value matching the declared type when the run succeeds.

This recipe sends an invented excerpt to your chosen provider. Its output validator checks citation membership after the structural check. ModelRetry asks for a corrected response within the framework’s retry limits. Exhausted retries and provider failures still need an application error path.
interpretation: Follow the names through the code: Manuals is request data, Answer is the result contract, and read_manual is an operation. They have different jobs.

description: This is a server-side reference recipe, separate from the offline Python challenge below.
setup: Create a Python environment and install pydantic-ai and pydantic. Resolve compatible versions, then record them in your project lockfile.

Set PERCEPTRON_LAB_AGENT_MODEL to a provider-qualified model available to you. Configure that provider’s credential in the server environment, for example OPENAI_API_KEY for an OpenAI-backed model. Never enter credentials into the browser worksheet.
Running this script makes a provider request and can incur charges. The generated wording varies; no output transcript is promised here.

parts.title: 5. A citation ID is only the start of evidence checking
paragraphs: An answer can cite manual-7 correctly while saying the opposite of its text. Membership asks whether we have that source. Entailment asks whether the source supports the claim. Those are different questions, so keep different tests for them.

A useful fixture can contain two excerpts with different pump types. Then a response that cites the available but wrong pump manual should fail the task evaluation even though it passes our membership validator. Preserve the original excerpt and its version so a reviewer can understand the disagreement.
interpretation: The workshop output says accept for content review. That wording names exactly what passed.

parts.title: 6. Test the boundary before spending a model call
paragraphs: Start with deterministic unit tests of the tool and validators. Give the citation check an absent ID, an empty list, and an extra field. A live model is unnecessary for those cases.

Then run provider-backed evaluation separately to investigate whether the model reads the right excerpt and handles missing evidence. Repeating those runs tells us something different from repeatedly checking a Python dictionary. Mocking the provider helps test control flow, but it cannot establish answer quality.
interpretation: Our offline exercise implements the two boundary checks directly so you can see what the framework is organising.

examples.title: Test membership with a set

examples.code:
available = {"manual-2", "manual-7"}
candidate_ids = ["manual-7", "manual-9"]
missing = [key for key in candidate_ids if key not in available]
print(missing)
interpretation: The missing ID needs repair. The available ID still needs a content-support check.

parts.title: 7. Let a failed answer remain failed
paragraphs: If validation cannot produce a usable result, return a clear unsuccessful state to the application. Do not replace the answer with an empty success object, and do not keep retrying indefinitely. Record the failure category without logging credentials or unnecessary manual content.

A technician can supply another excerpt or ask for review. That is a useful next step even when the agent has no supported answer. Later evaluation lessons will distinguish those justified refusals from failures to answer questions the manual could resolve.
interpretation: A framework reduces repeated plumbing. The acceptance policy still belongs to the application.

practice.title: Which candidate answers need repair?
practice.question: Which candidate answers need repair?
task: The application cannot review an answer’s evidence if the answer fields are unreadable or its citation IDs were never supplied. Build those checks before accepting the proposal for content review. Write answer_route(candidate, available). candidate is a dictionary whose only keys must be answer and citations. answer must be a nonblank string. citations must be a nonempty list of strings, all present in available, a list of strings. Return "accept for content review" or "repair answer". Malformed candidate values take the repair route; malformed available raises ValueError. Do not mutate the inputs.
Print the route for {"answer":"Inspect the coupling.","citations":["manual-2","manual-8"]} with available ["manual-2","manual-4"].
practice.solution:
def answer_route(candidate, available):
    if not isinstance(available, list) or any(not isinstance(x, str) for x in available):
        raise ValueError("Available IDs must be a list of strings")
    if not isinstance(candidate, dict) or set(candidate) != {"answer", "citations"}:
        return "repair answer"
    text, ids = candidate["answer"], candidate["citations"]
    valid = isinstance(text, str) and bool(text.strip())
    valid = valid and isinstance(ids, list) and bool(ids)
    valid = valid and all(isinstance(x, str) and x in available for x in ids)
    return "accept for content review" if valid else "repair answer"

print(answer_route({"answer":"Inspect the coupling.","citations":["manual-2","manual-8"]}, ["manual-2","manual-4"]))

title: Put Limits Around a LangChain Agent
blurb: Botie keeps looking for a manual that does not exist. Use an agent runtime with explicit tool access and limits, then inspect the messages that explain its decisions.
openingTitle: How Many Times Should Botie Ask the Same Question?
opening: The manual reader works for pump P7. A technician then asks about P8, whose manual has not been uploaded. Botie tries another lookup, receives the same missing result, and tries again. The loop needs a stopping rule that does not depend on the model deciding it has done enough.

LangChain provides an agent runtime that coordinates messages and tools. We will keep the task small, give it a read-only tool, and put a call limit around execution. The workshop lets you build the permission and budget decision yourself.

history.title: When Every Application Was Rebuilding the Same Loop

sources.title: LangChain team: first Python release on October 24, 2022

blocks: Developers connecting models to documents and external programs kept rebuilding similar pieces of code. LangChain’s first Python package was released on October 24, 2022 to make those pieces easier to combine. A framework supplied reusable components and ways to connect them, while the application still defined the job those components should perform.

The project changed as agent applications became more common. Its October 2025 v1 release focused the high-level interface on the repeated model/tool loop, using LangGraph underneath. Middleware provides named places where application code can intervene during that loop. For the maintenance desk, that is where a bounded unsuccessful search needs an enforced limit. Asking the model to stop and preventing another tool execution are different mechanisms.

reading.experimentTitle: May this requested lookup run?
reading.experimentIntro: Combine the application’s permitted tool list with the remaining call budget. The output names the reason a request stops.
reading.connectionTitle: A runtime needs checks at the execution boundary
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Enforce a tool-call policy
reading.exampleNote: This is a deterministic execution policy, not a simulation of a model deciding which tool to request.

intuition.title: Separate the request from permission to execute it
intuition.explanation: The model proposes read_manual. The server knows which tools are permitted and how many have executed.

scene.caption: A model-proposed tool call does not grant itself permission.

intuition.title: The same request can reach a different route
intuition.explanation: Assume read_manual is allowed and the execution limit is two calls.

scene.caption: This lesson checks permission before budget so a denied tool never becomes a permitted one.

parts.title: 1. Know what create_agent is coordinating
paragraphs: A message describes what the technician asked. The model may return answer text or structured requests to call tools. The runtime executes permitted tools and adds their results to the conversation so the model can continue.

create_agent constructs this repeated model-and-tool process. Its interface is useful when that loop fits the task. If every step is predetermined, a small ordinary function may be clearer. Reaching for an agent is a design choice, not a requirement for using a language model.
interpretation: We are using the same maintenance question as before so the runtime change does not hide a change in the task.

parts.title: 2. Keep messages paired with their tool results
paragraphs: A model response can contain a tool-call ID as well as a tool name and arguments. The result must refer to the matching call. That pairing lets the next model request distinguish one lookup from another, including when several tools were requested together.

Do not reduce the whole conversation to the last sentence while debugging. Inspect which arguments were requested and which result came back. An empty lookup and a network failure need different handling even if both prevented a useful answer.
interpretation: LangChain returns agent state containing messages. The final message alone can hide the reason a run became expensive.

examples.title: Find the result belonging to a lookup
paragraphs: These ordinary Python dictionaries represent an invented trace, not LangChain message objects. The list retains arrival order; the call ID establishes which request a result belongs to.
examples.code:
requested = {"id": "call-7", "name": "read_manual", "args": {"asset": "P7"}}
results = [
    {"call_id": "call-8", "found": False},
    {"call_id": "call-7", "found": True},
]
matched = next(item for item in results if item["call_id"] == requested["id"])
print(requested["args"]["asset"])
print(matched["found"])
interpretation: Nested dictionary access reads the requested asset. The matching result can appear later in the list, so using the first result would attach the wrong outcome to this lookup.

parts.title: 3. Make the tool small enough to describe precisely
paragraphs: The @tool decorator uses a Python function as a tool definition. Type annotations describe the arguments, while the docstring tells the model what the operation does. Our example accepts an asset ID and returns either an excerpt or an explicit missing result.

For a real service, scope the lookup to the authenticated technician’s permitted equipment before reading data. The model-supplied asset string is a request, not evidence that the user owns that asset. A service layer can enforce that check regardless of which framework invokes it.
interpretation: The example’s one-entry dictionary is deliberately invented. It demonstrates lookup semantics without giving the agent access to real maintenance records.

parts.title: 4. Use middleware where the operation happens
paragraphs: Middleware is code that runs at defined points around the agent loop. Hooks can inspect model requests or wrap tool execution. This gives the application a place to enforce limits and record what happened without burying every check in prompt text.

A limit on model calls and a limit on tool calls measure different things. One model response may request several tools. Choose the quantity that bounds the work you care about, and make the stopping behaviour visible to the caller.
interpretation: The workshop checks an individual tool request against a count of executed calls. It is a small policy exercise, not a reproduction of every framework middleware counter.

parts.title: 5. Build the bounded reader
paragraphs: This server recipe uses create_agent with the read_manual tool and separate model and tool limits. The selected error behaviour raises when a limit is exceeded. In a web service, catch that failure at the application boundary and return an unsuccessful result the interface can explain.
The tool only reads from a fixture. There is no create_job tool to call. Keep that narrow surface while learning how the messages and limits behave, then add capabilities with their own tests.
interpretation: Provider responses vary. Compare the actual call sequence and final evidence with the task requirements instead of copying a displayed answer.

references.title: A reader with separate model and tool limits
description: This reference is for your own Python service environment. The browser exercise uses no external provider.
setup: Install a compatible LangChain 1.x release and your model integration, such as langchain-openai for an OpenAI-backed model. Record resolved versions in a lockfile.
Set PERCEPTRON_LAB_AGENT_MODEL to a provider-qualified identifier your integration accepts, and configure its credential on the server. Provider requests may incur charges.
Run the script as a local Python program with invented data. Add application exception handling before exposing it as a service.
interpretation: The two middleware limits bound different operations. This example uses per-run limits; a limit across a thread additionally needs persistent thread state.

parts.title: 6. A retry needs a reason and a budget
paragraphs: A temporary connection failure may justify another attempt. An asset absent from the catalogue generally needs different evidence, not immediate repetition of the same lookup. Classify these outcomes before choosing retries.

When an operation changes external state, a timeout can mean the effect happened but the reply was lost. Retrying create_job blindly can create a duplicate. Keep write operations separate from our read example and give them an idempotency key that the receiving service enforces.
interpretation: A bounded retry can still repeat a mistake. Investigate whether another attempt can supply information the previous attempt lacked.

parts.title: 7. Keep policy checks outside model-written arguments
paragraphs: Our offline gate receives the allowed tool names and used-call count from trusted application state. It checks permission first, then whether another execution fits. These inputs must not come from the model’s claim that it has permission or from its own reported count.

For concurrent requests, reserving budget needs an atomic operation in shared state. A pair of workers can both read one remaining slot unless the runtime coordinates them. The worksheet is sequential so that you can inspect the underlying comparison before adding concurrency.
parts.calculation:
Allowed = ["read_manual"]
Used calls = 2
Limit = 2
Requested = "read_manual"
Next route = "budget exhausted"
interpretation: The limit is reached when used calls equals the limit. There is no spare call at equality.

parts.title: 8. Decide whether a framework is helping this particular job
paragraphs: Keep a small set of maintenance fixtures while trying implementations. Does each version preserve citation IDs, reject disallowed operations and stop when evidence is missing? Can you inspect a failure without reading framework internals?

Pydantic AI and LangChain both support more than the features introduced here. Compare the behaviour your service needs and the code your team can maintain. Moving to a larger abstraction does not remove the need for the contracts we have already built.
interpretation: The next lesson takes explicit control of state transitions when a single model-tool loop no longer describes the work clearly.

title: Resume Botie’s Work with LangGraph

appliedIn.title: recovering from a reply that never arrived

blurb: The technician returns after a pause. Preserve the right request’s evidence, merge updates deliberately, and resume a review without repeating an external action.
openingTitle: The Technician Comes Back. Does Botie Remember the Right Job?
opening: Botie has found a manual excerpt and prepared a proposed inspection. The technician needs to ask a colleague before continuing. Closing the page should not turn that request into an unrelated conversation or repeat work that already happened.

We need an explicit record of where the request stopped and what information it had. Think of the work as named steps: find the manual, prepare a proposal, then wait for review. A step is a node, and a route says which step may follow it. LangGraph expresses those connections in code and carries the request’s data, called state, between them. We will decide what to preserve before adding pause and resume.

history.title: A Useful Workflow Sometimes Needs to Go Around Again
blocks: A fixed sequence of language-model calls can work until an early step returns insufficient evidence. The application then needs a route back to retrieval, or a pause for a person. LangGraph’s January 2024 introduction described cycles and explicit state machines as a way to control those paths.

For Botie, the state contains the evidence gathered for one maintenance request. A node returns an update, and the application decides how that update changes what was already stored. The workshop builds that merge operation on small invented records before the reference code introduces a paused graph.

reading.experimentTitle: What evidence should survive this update?
reading.experimentIntro: Choose the request checkpoint, then merge incoming excerpts by ID. Observe what happens when a lookup returns an excerpt already seen.
reading.connectionTitle: A saved request needs explicit update rules
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Merge evidence without duplicating a replay
reading.exampleNote: The workshop demonstrates a reducer on checkpoint fixtures. It does not run the LangGraph scheduler.

intuition.title: A checkpoint belongs to one request
intuition.explanation: Two technicians can discuss the same pump without sharing the same unfinished task.

scene.caption: Only the selected request should change.

intuition.title: Choose a merge rule instead of hoping a list does the right thing
intuition.explanation: Our policy keeps the position of an existing ID and replaces its text. New IDs go at the end.

scene.caption: Blind concatenation would keep duplicate IDs and conflicting versions.

parts.title: 1. Give the unfinished request a state
paragraphs: State is the data the workflow needs as it moves between operations. For our request, it includes collected evidence and whether review has happened. A thread ID identifies the request whose saved state we want to continue.

Keep this ID separate from the asset ID. A pump can have several maintenance requests. Also keep it separate from user identity: the application must check that the signed-in user may access the selected thread. Knowing or guessing an ID does not grant access.
interpretation: Write down which fields belong to the request before choosing how to save them. Otherwise unrelated concerns accumulate in one unstructured transcript.

parts.title: 2. Make nodes return updates
paragraphs: A node is a function that performs one step and returns changes to state. A retrieval node can return new evidence. A review node can return a decision. Edges describe which node runs next; a conditional edge chooses a route from the current result.

This can describe deterministic work as well as model calls. Our reference uses an invented manual lookup so that the behaviour of the graph is easier to isolate. Adding a model inside a node does not change the need to define that node’s inputs and outputs.
interpretation: Use a fixed route when the sequence is known. Add a conditional route or cycle only when the task actually needs one.

parts.title: 3. Decide what an update means for each field
paragraphs: If a node returns a new approved value, replacing the previous boolean is sensible. Evidence is different: replacing the whole list may lose earlier excerpts, while appending everything may duplicate a repeated lookup.

A reducer is the function that combines a previous field value with an incoming update. Our evidence reducer uses each excerpt’s ID. New IDs are appended, and existing IDs receive their updated text in place. This is an application policy, not LangGraph’s automatic rule for every list.
parts.calculation:
Before = [{"id":"manual-7","text":"old wording"}]
Update = [{"id":"manual-7","text":"revised wording"}]
After = [{"id":"manual-7","text":"revised wording"}]
interpretation: The same update applied twice leaves one excerpt. That makes this particular merge idempotent: repeating it has the same result as applying it once.

examples.title: Replace one identified excerpt
paragraphs: A dictionary uses the excerpt ID as its key. Assigning that existing key replaces its value without adding another entry. dict creates a new outer dictionary for this small mapping of strings.
examples.code:
saved = {"M2": "Old coupling wording.", "M5": "Inspect the filter."}
updated = dict(saved)
updated["M2"] = "Revised coupling wording."
print(list(updated))
print(updated["M2"])
print(saved["M2"])
examples.output:
['M2', 'M5']
Revised coupling wording.
Old coupling wording.
interpretation: The ID stays in its original position and the saved mapping stays unchanged. The later challenge generalises this operation to lists of evidence records.

parts.title: 4. Messages and evidence need different reducers
paragraphs: LangGraph has an add_messages reducer for message histories. It can append messages and handle updates using message IDs. Our evidence records are ordinary dictionaries, so the example supplies a different reducer for them.

Do not reuse the word id without deciding what it identifies. A tool-call ID, message ID and document ID name different objects. If two document revisions need to remain separately citable, use versioned document identifiers instead of overwriting one ID’s text.
interpretation: The workshop’s replace-by-ID policy is chosen for this fixture. An audit trail should retain the prior version somewhere separate when the application needs it.

parts.title: 5. Save a checkpoint that can actually survive the pause
paragraphs: A checkpointer stores graph state for a thread so a later invocation can continue it. InMemorySaver is convenient for learning, but its contents disappear when that Python process ends. A production service needs an appropriate persistent backend and an access policy for the saved data.

A store is a different persistence mechanism for application data shared across threads. Keep a technician’s preference separate from the unfinished state of a particular inspection request. Retention and deletion rules apply to both.
interpretation: An in-memory demonstration of resume is not a demonstration of crash recovery across process restarts.

parts.title: 6. Pause at review and resume the same thread
paragraphs: interrupt exposes a value to the caller and pauses execution. When the application later invokes the same graph and thread with Command(resume=...), that value becomes the result of the interrupt call. The code in the interrupted node begins again on resume.

The reference pauses after collecting an invented excerpt. The automatic True near the end stands in for the service’s authenticated review handler. It is useful for observing control flow, but it is not an approval system.
interpretation: Use the same thread configuration for resume. Creating a new thread would describe a new request rather than continuing the paused one.

references.title: A small graph that pauses with its evidence
description: This local reference uses no language model and requires no provider key. It demonstrates graph APIs outside the browser worksheet.
setup: Create a Python environment and install a compatible LangGraph 1.x release. Record resolved versions in a lockfile.
Run as a local script. InMemorySaver persists only while this process remains alive.
The sample uses a fixed review value to demonstrate resume. A deployed handler must authenticate the reviewer and bind the decision to the exact proposed action.
interpretation: The reducer controls evidence updates. The checkpointer controls saved thread state. Neither gives permission to execute an external action.

parts.title: 7. Keep replay away from unprotected side effects
paragraphs: Imagine creating a work order before the review node pauses. Resuming the node could run that statement again. Now the technician has two orders even though there was one request. Place the effect after the decision, and still design the operation to tolerate retries and process failures.

An idempotency key lets the work-order service recognise the same intended action. The receiving service must store and enforce that key, ideally atomically with creation. A local set of completed IDs does not protect against a crash between creating the order and recording its ID.
interpretation: Checkpointing the graph and making external effects idempotent solve related but different problems. Neither creates a universal exactly-once guarantee.

parts.title: 8. Concurrent updates need a deliberate conflict policy
paragraphs: Two retrieval branches may find different text under the same document ID. Our simple last-update-wins reducer assumes an ordered update stream. If the order is not meaningful, the answer can depend on which result reaches it last.

Use immutable versioned IDs, reject conflicting updates, or define an ordering from trusted revision information. Choose a rule that matches the source system. Adding a reducer removes an implementation ambiguity only when its policy is appropriate for the data.
interpretation: The workshop is sequential. Its fixtures make the update order explicit rather than claiming to settle concurrent document conflicts.

parts.title: 9. Follow the saved evidence through a changed request
paragraphs: Select another thread in the workshop and run the same construction. It should load that thread’s excerpts before applying its update. Then replay an existing excerpt and check that one ID remains.

If the old machine simply concatenated lists, the repeated-lookup fixture exposes the mistake. If it hard-coded one thread’s evidence, the other-request fixture exposes that instead. These are different failure modes, so keep both checks after making a repair.
interpretation: The Python challenge asks you to write the merge operation without mutating either input. Saved state is easier to reason about when an update does not quietly rewrite the fixture used by another test.

quiz.prompt: Which behaviour must the application account for?
options: Code before the interrupt runs again when the node resumes
The Python instruction pointer is restored without rerunning code
Every external write is automatically deduplicated
quiz.because: Keep effects carefully placed and make the external operation retry-safe.

given.data: A node writes a work order before calling interrupt. The reviewer later resumes it.

quiz.prompt: This is still necessary even when thread IDs are difficult to guess.
quiz.because: An identifier selects state; it does not establish authority to read it.

given.data: An application checks access to a saved thread before loading it.

practice.title: Can a repeated lookup update evidence without duplicating it?
practice.question: Can a repeated lookup update evidence without duplicating it?
task: A repeated lookup can bring a revised manual excerpt. Keep the newest text without adding another copy or moving the excerpt out of its original position. Write merge_evidence(old, incoming). Both inputs must be lists of dictionaries with a nonempty string id and a string text. Ignore extra record fields. Invalid inputs raise ValueError. Return new dictionaries in a new list. Keep the position where each ID first appeared, replace its text with the last value seen, and never mutate either input.
Print the merge of [{"id":"M2","text":"initial"}] and [{"id":"M2","text":"revised"},{"id":"M5","text":"appendix"}].
hints: Python dictionaries preserve insertion order. Replacing a value does not move its key.
Copy each retained record so changing a result cannot rewrite an input.

once = merge_evidence([], update)
assert merge_evidence(once, update) == once

tests.name: No shared mutable record
tests.code:
old = [{"id":"A","text":"original"}]
result = merge_evidence(old, [])
result[0]["text"] = "changed"
assert old[0]["text"] == "original"

tests.name: Reject missing identity
