title: Ask Before Botie Creates the Inspection Job
blurb: A technician approves one inspection, then the proposal changes. Bind the decision to what was reviewed and check it again where the job is created.
openingTitle: The Technician Said Yes. Yes to Which Job?
opening: Botie proposes inspecting pump P7. The technician approves, then a follow-up message changes the asset to P9. If the program remembers only approved = True, it may apply the old decision to a job nobody reviewed.

We need a record of the particular proposal the person saw. Then the execution service can compare that record with what it is about to do. A pause in the interface is useful only if the permission survives that comparison.

history.title: Permission Has to Belong to an Operation

sources.title: Saltzer and Schroeder: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems

blocks: Long before language-model agents, shared computer systems needed to control who could read or change an object. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 account describes protection mechanisms and distinguishes authentication from authorisation. Their discussion also includes requirements for human judgement before granting access.

An inspection assistant adds generated proposals to that old problem. It still needs a trusted component that grants access to a particular operation. Our approval record is a teaching design for binding a decision to a proposal. It is not a claim that a language model, a checkbox or a checkpoint supplies that authority automatically.

reading.experimentTitle: Does this approval still cover the proposed job?
reading.experimentIntro: Compare the action fields, check the expiry and require the reviewer’s current permission. Change one field to see which check stops execution.
reading.connectionTitle: Carry a decision with the action it actually approved
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Check an action-bound approval
reading.exampleNote: All records are invented trusted fixtures. The workshop does not authenticate a reviewer or create an inspection job.

intuition.title: A yes needs something specific to refer to
intuition.explanation: The proposal identifies the maintenance request as well as the asset and operation. Its revision changes when the reviewed details change.

scene.caption: The old approval cannot authorise the changed proposal.

intuition.title: Keep the decision at the execution boundary
intuition.explanation: The backend retrieves the authoritative review record and evaluates it against the action it will submit.

rows.label: Compare
items: Same request, asset, operation and revision

rows.label: Check reviewer
items: Reviewer still has the required permission

rows.label: Execute or review
items: All checks pass, or request a new decision

scene.caption: A model-provided statement that a person approved is not the authoritative record.

parts.title: 1. Separate preparing a job from submitting it
paragraphs: Reading a manual and drafting a proposed inspection can happen before anyone grants permission to create a work order. Keep the proposal as data that a technician can inspect. The final write should be a distinct operation with a clear permission check.

Our proposal names requestId, asset, operation and revision. A real proposal would also include every consequential argument, such as timing, assignee and affected site. If a field can change what the action does, it belongs in the reviewed snapshot.
interpretation: A description such as perform maintenance is too vague to bind to a later write. Show the concrete action the receiving system will get.

parts.title: 2. Record what the person actually reviewed
paragraphs: The approval record includes the proposal’s identity and revision, the decision, and an expiry. The service also records the authenticated reviewer and evaluates their authority. These records come from the review service, not from text generated by Botie.

If the reviewer edits a proposal, the application needs a new approved snapshot for those edited values. Do not approve the old object and quietly mutate it afterwards. Store immutable versions or compare a canonical digest of the complete approved payload.
interpretation: A digest can identify a payload, but it is not a signature and it does not authenticate who approved it. The trusted server record is still required.

examples.title: Show the reviewer which fields changed
paragraphs: The tuple names the fields in a fixed display order. Both dictionaries supply every named field. The list comprehension retains the names whose values differ.
interpretation: The operation label stayed inspect, but its target and revision changed. This diagnostic helps explain why the complete approval gate must request another review.

parts.title: 3. Recheck the decision immediately before the effect
paragraphs: Our toy gate requires matching action fields, an unexpired approval and a reviewer who is currently permitted. It treats a missing or mismatched condition as a request for review. The current time comes from the server; the model cannot extend expiry by supplying its own clock.

A production write should bind this check to the exact action being committed. Otherwise another request could change the proposal between checking it and creating the job. Use an immutable action version and a transaction or equivalent concurrency control in the service that owns the effect.
parts.calculation:
Approved asset = P7
Current asset = P9
Action match = false
Unexpired = true
Reviewer permitted = true
Route = request review
interpretation: Remaining time and an authorised reviewer do not repair a mismatch in the action itself.

parts.title: 4. Make expiry and revocation visible
paragraphs: An approval can become inappropriate while a workflow waits. The pump may have been serviced already, the reviewer’s role may change, or the proposed time may pass. Decide which facts must be checked again at execution.

In this lesson, expiry is exclusive: an approval is expired at its expiry timestamp. A revoked reviewer permission also blocks the action even if the recorded decision remains yes. Keep a reason code so the interface can tell a technician whether to refresh the proposal or request another review.
interpretation: Do not ask for the same decision again after a successful execution simply because the response was lost. That is an idempotency problem, which needs a stable operation identity.

parts.title: 5. A resumed graph still needs an authenticated caller
paragraphs: Command(resume=...) delivers a value to a paused LangGraph node. The application decides who is allowed to provide that value and which pending action it refers to. A publicly reachable resume endpoint with no access check would let another person supply the decision.

Keep the reviewer identity and permissions outside model-controlled state. Check ownership of the thread and the pending review record, then pass a validated result into the workflow. Never accept a generated sentence saying that a technician approved as a substitute for that record.
interpretation: The paused graph coordinates the conversation. The service that changes the work-order system remains responsible for authorisation.

parts.title: 6. Make one approved action survive a retry safely
paragraphs: After approval, the job-creation request can still time out. Use a stable idempotency key derived from the intended action identity, and have the receiving service enforce it. Reusing a key for changed arguments should be rejected rather than silently treated as the earlier job.

Test both halves: an approved unchanged action creates one job across retries, and an altered action cannot reuse the earlier approval. Also check rejected decisions and expired records. These cases often reveal more than a successful approval click.
interpretation: The worksheet implements the decision gate only. A complete service also needs trusted storage, authenticated review, concurrency control and an idempotent effect.

quiz.prompt: What can the write service conclude?
options: It has no authoritative approval for the effect
The quoted sentence is enough to authorise the job
quiz.because: Generated text is not a trusted review record.

given.data: A model message says "The technician approved". No authenticated review record exists.

quiz.prompt: Blindly submitting another job without an idempotency policy can create a duplicate.
quiz.because: The lost reply leaves uncertainty about the effect, not proof that nothing happened.

given.data: A job-creation request timed out after the server accepted it.

practice.title: Is this still the action the technician approved?
practice.question: Is this still the action the technician approved?
task: A technician approved one proposal. If the asset, operation or revision changes, the application must notice that it is being asked to use the old decision for different work. Write approval_route(proposal, approval, now, permitted). Require matching nonempty string values for requestId, asset, operation and revision. Require approval["approved"] is True, permitted is True, and nonnegative whole-number now and approval["expires"] with now < expires. Booleans are not timestamps. Return "authorised for this action" only when all conditions hold, otherwise "request review", including malformed records. Do not mutate inputs.

Use proposal {requestId:R21, asset:P4, operation:inspect, revision:2}. Approval has the same fields except revision:1, with approved True and expires 90. At now 70 and permitted True, print the route.
hints: Compare every consequential field instead of only the request ID.
Use exact booleans for approval and permission. A string saying true should not grant authority.

Expiry boundary and revoked reviewer
Changed operation and malformed decision
Missing records fail closed

assert approval_route({}, {}, 0, True) == "request review"
assert approval_route(None, {}, 0, True) == "request review"

title: Connect Botie to Tools with MCP

appliedIn.title: restricting what a tool may send outside

blurb: Several assistants need the same maintenance tools. Share an interface while keeping server identity, permissions and returned content visible.
openingTitle: Why Write the Manual Connector Again for Every Assistant?
opening: The maintenance team now uses Botie in a web app and in an internal support tool. Both need the same manual lookup, but each integration describes and calls it differently. Maintaining two copies makes it easy for their behaviour to drift.

A shared protocol can describe what a server offers and how a client requests it. Model Context Protocol, or MCP, provides that interface. We will follow a manual lookup across the connection, then see why discovering a tool does not automatically make it safe or permitted to call.

history.title: A Common Interface for Data Kept in Different Systems
blocks: Assistants could generate text but often lacked a consistent connection to the systems holding a user’s documents and tools. Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024 to standardise those integrations. A service can describe its capabilities through one protocol instead of requiring a separate custom interface for every assistant.

Our invented maintenance service uses that idea to expose manual content. Sharing a protocol does not settle whether a server is trustworthy, which technician may read a record, or whether a proposed action needs approval. Those decisions remain in the host application and the service that owns the data.

reading.experimentTitle: Which server would receive this lookup?
reading.experimentIntro: Keep the server identity attached to the tool name, check the host allowlist, then resolve the registered handler.
reading.connectionTitle: Shared interfaces still need explicit trust boundaries
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Resolve a permitted MCP endpoint
reading.exampleNote: The workshop uses a local registry of labels. It does not open MCP connections or execute remote tools.

intuition.title: Follow one lookup across the boundary
intuition.explanation: The host manages the model and user interface. Its client connection carries the request to the configured manual server.

rows.label: Host application
items: Chooses permitted capabilities for this request

rows.label: MCP client connection
items: Names the server and sends read_manual arguments

rows.label: Manual server
items: Validates access and reads the excerpt

rows.label: Host again
items: Checks the result and provides it as evidence

scene.caption: The model is not the network connection, and the server need not run a model.

intuition.title: Two tools can have the same local name
intuition.explanation: The configured server is part of the identity. The host allowlist includes only maintenance/read_manual.

scene.caption: Dropping the server name would make these different capabilities look interchangeable.

parts.title: 1. Distinguish the host, client and server
paragraphs: The host is the application coordinating the user, model and available connections. An MCP client maintains a connection to a server. The server exposes capabilities such as reading maintenance records. A host can connect to several servers, each with a distinct scope and trust relationship.

That separation lets us put the manual integration beside the system that owns the manuals. The host can decide how much returned text enters a model request without moving all data ownership into the assistant.
interpretation: MCP is an interface between programs. It is not itself an agent loop, a language model or a guarantee that an answer is correct.

parts.title: 2. Choose whether something is a tool, resource or prompt
paragraphs: A tool exposes an operation with named arguments, such as read_manual(asset). Tools can read or write; the word tool does not imply that every invocation changes state. A resource exposes content at an identifier such as manual://P7. A prompt supplies a reusable message template a user can choose.

These roles suggest different interfaces: a tool call, a document the application can include, or a prompt menu. They do not override permission checks. A read operation can reveal private data, and a prompt template can contain instructions the host should inspect before trusting.
interpretation: The same manual service can offer several of these capabilities because they answer different application needs.

parts.title: 3. Discover a capability before calling it
paragraphs: The client establishes the connection and negotiates the protocol features supported by the server. Listing tools returns descriptions and input schemas. The host can select permitted definitions to make available to a model, then send a requested name and arguments to the correct server.

A schema describes the argument shape. It does not prove that an asset belongs to the technician or that a URL is safe to fetch. The receiving service still validates both data and access. If a server paginates discovery results, the client must follow its cursor rather than assuming one page contains everything.
interpretation: Keep discovery, selection and execution distinct in the trace. A tool can be listed successfully while a particular call is correctly denied.

parts.title: 4. Expose the invented manual service in Python
paragraphs: The reference defines a tool, a fixed resource and a prompt. It then uses an in-process client to discover and call the tool without a model. That is enough to test the service interface before adding an agent that chooses calls.

The example follows the current official Python SDK 2.x API. Older tutorials often use FastMCP from mcp.server.fastmcp; do not mix imports from different major versions. Pin your resolved environment once the example works.
interpretation: The result describes the fixture’s lookup. No model decides what to request in this program.

references.title: A manual server and a local protocol test
description: This is a standalone service reference using the official MCP Python SDK. Its test stays inside one Python process.
setup: Use Python 3.11 or later in a separate environment. Install mcp>=2,<3 and anyio, then record resolved versions in a lockfile.
No provider API key is needed for this program. The Client receives the server object for an in-process test.
The fixture has no authentication because it contains only invented public text and is not exposed on a network. Add real access control before connecting private data or deploying a network server.
interpretation: The SDK builds the tool schema from the signature. The application still needs to handle tool failures and decide what content to trust.

parts.title: 5. Read the result before treating it as evidence
paragraphs: A completed transport request can carry a tool failure. Inspect the result’s error status before reading structured data as a success. Also distinguish an application outcome such as found = False from a failure to contact the service at all.

The returned content may include text and other content blocks. Preserve provenance when adding it to context: which server returned it, from which record, and at what revision? Text that says to change the assistant’s rules is still returned content, not new authority over the host.
interpretation: The typed client API uses its documented Python field names. A raw protocol JSON payload may spell fields differently, so do not interchange the two representations by guesswork.

parts.title: 6. Keep the configured server identity with the tool
paragraphs: Suppose the maintenance service and a community-notes service both expose read_manual. If the host indexes tools only by their local name, one can accidentally replace the other. Use an unambiguous mapping from the model-visible tool to its configured connection and local name.

The workshop writes that mapping as server/tool for readability. This slash convention is our local teaching registry, not an MCP naming requirement. The allowlist uses the same qualified identity, so permitting maintenance/read_manual does not also permit community/read_manual.
interpretation: If a permitted tool disappears, report it as unavailable. Quietly falling back to a similarly named tool would change the source and possibly its authority.

examples.title: Preserve the connection when indexing a discovered tool
paragraphs: The list holds two discovery records. Each dictionary has a server field and a local tool name. Constructing both labels before using a set keeps the two identities distinct.
examples.code:
discovered = [
    {"server": "maintenance", "tool": "read_manual"},
    {"server": "archive", "tool": "read_manual"},
]
qualified = [item["server"] + "/" + item["tool"] for item in discovered]
print(qualified)
print(len(set(qualified)))
interpretation: Two distinct qualified names remain. A set containing only the local tool name would collapse these records and lose their connection identity.

parts.title: 7. A local server still runs real code
paragraphs: A server launched over standard input and output is a local program with the permissions of its process. Connecting it does not automatically confine its filesystem or network access. Review the program, its configuration and the permissions it receives.

A remote service brings another trust boundary. Imagine the maintenance server accepting a token intended for the payroll service just because the token has a valid signature. The signature tells us who issued it; we still have to check who may use it and where. An HTTP MCP server using the protocol’s authorisation scheme must validate that a token was issued for that server. It must not pass the incoming token through to a downstream API.

Keep credentials in the host or service environment. Grant the scopes needed for this job, and check object access inside the receiving service. Tool descriptions and annotations are claims from the server, not independent proof of its behaviour.
interpretation: Start with a narrow read-only integration and invented fixtures. Add a write tool only after the approval and idempotency rules from the preceding lesson are enforced by the effect-owning service.

parts.title: 8. Test the connection without confusing it with task quality
paragraphs: A protocol test can establish that a tool is discoverable, accepts the expected arguments and returns the expected fixture. The workshop adds a host routing check, including a same-name tool on a different server. Those are useful integration tests.

A separate agent evaluation must ask whether Botie chose the right capability and used its output correctly. Keep both layers. When a technician receives an unsupported answer, we want to distinguish a misrouted lookup from an incorrect interpretation of a correctly retrieved excerpt.
interpretation: The next work is observing a complete run so we can see where a failure began, rather than judging only the final sentence.

quiz.prompt: What must the host preserve when routing?
options: The configured server identity as well as the tool name
quiz.because: Names from different servers can collide; they represent different endpoints.

given.data: maintenance/read_manual and community/read_manual have the same local name. Only the maintenance endpoint is allowed.

quiz.prompt: That test alone proves the agent will select the right tool for every technician question.
quiz.because: The test checks the interface, not the model’s selection or use of the result.

given.data: A protocol fixture returns the right manual excerpt when called directly.

practice.title: Can a same-name tool on another server sneak into the route?
practice.question: Can a same-name tool on another server sneak into the route?
task: Two servers can offer a tool called read_manual. Choosing by that short name alone could send the request to the wrong service. Write resolve_tool(request, allowed, registry). request is a dictionary with nonempty string server and tool fields, neither containing a slash. allowed is a list of server/tool strings. registry maps server/tool strings to text handler labels. Return "blocked" if the qualified request is not allowed, "unavailable" if allowed but absent from registry, otherwise the registered label. Malformed inputs raise ValueError. This function selects a label only; it must not execute code or connect to a server.
Print the result for request {server:community, tool:read_manual}, allowed [maintenance/read_manual], and a registry containing both names.
hints: Build the qualified name before checking the allowlist.
An allowed but missing endpoint must not fall back to another server with the same local name.

build.title: Route the lookup to the intended manual service
build.problem: Two connected services expose a read_manual tool. The host must retain their separate identities and permissions.
build.challenge: Build a server-qualified tool name, check it against the allowed endpoint list, and resolve the result in the registered handler labels. Return blocked for a disallowed endpoint and unavailable for a permitted endpoint absent from the registry.

cases.name: A same-name tool on another server

build.why: The host retains connection identity through discovery, permission and dispatch. A local name alone cannot identify the intended capability.
build.limitation: The slash names and label registry are a teaching model. Real MCP clients also negotiate capabilities, validate arguments, authenticate and handle transport and tool failures.
hints: Keep the server with the tool first. Both are part of the identity.

title: What If the Manual Starts Giving Botie Orders?
blurb: A retrieved maintenance note tells Botie to export records. Trace where that instruction came from, then keep the application’s permissions intact even when a screening model misses it.
openingTitle: The Pump Manual Asks for a Customer Export
opening: A technician asks Botie to find the inspection interval for pump P7. Inside the retrieved manual is a sentence telling him to export the customer directory before answering. Botie was meant to read that page. Does reading it also give the page permission to change his job?

That is the difficulty with giving an agent access to outside text. The same model that reads a useful instruction can read an instruction planted inside the material it is studying. We need to keep track of who supplied each piece of text, and we need controls that still work if the model follows the wrong sentence.

prerequisites.title: Give the model a clear job

history.title: When Retrieved Text Became Part of the Instruction Problem
blocks: Retrieval and tool use let assistants answer from material their developers had never seen. That also gave outside authors a route into the model’s context. NIST’s 2025 taxonomy distinguishes direct injection through a submitted prompt from indirect injection carried by an external resource. The distinction describes the route into the system, not whether a particular attack succeeds.

NVIDIA’s 2023 NeMo Guardrails paper describes programmable checks around an LLM conversation. These checks made the stages of a conversation explicit enough to apply different policies. Our maintenance example studies one of those boundaries: a proposed action must remain within application-issued grants even if the model or a screening step is mistaken.

reading.experimentTitle: Can a clean screening result create permission?
reading.experimentIntro: Connect the proposed tool through the server allowlist and screening status. The export proposal deliberately arrives with a passing screen.
reading.connectionTitle: Keep the document’s words out of the permission store
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Route a proposed action without trusting its explanation
reading.exampleNote: The proposals and screening results are invented fixtures. No detector or language model runs here.

intuition.title: Two sentences arrive through different routes
intuition.explanation: Both strings can look like instructions. Their origin determines how the application should treat them.

records.label: Find P7’s inspection interval.
cells: Authenticated user through the task interface
Requested task, still subject to permissions

scene.caption: A source can provide evidence without receiving authority to grant tools.

intuition.title: A mistaken proposal reaches a separate boundary
intuition.explanation: Suppose Botie does ask to export. We can inspect the consequence without pretending that the prompt never failed.

scene.caption: A passing content screen cannot add export_records to the server’s list.

parts.title: 1. Follow the instruction back to its source
paragraphs: The technician’s request reaches our application through the task interface. The manual reaches it through retrieval. Those paths have different jobs. The user can ask for work within their permissions. A manual can contain facts, mistakes and somebody else’s instructions.

Keep the retrieved excerpt’s identity and origin beside its text. Do the same for a browser page, attachment or MCP result. A trusted connection authenticates where a response came from; it does not make every sentence inside that response an application policy.
interpretation: Before deciding whether a sentence sounds convincing, ask how it entered this run.

parts.title: 2. Recognise direct and indirect injection
paragraphs: A direct injection arrives in the submitted prompt, such as a request to ignore the application’s access rules. An indirect injection arrives through another item the agent reads, such as our altered manual. A saved conversation or memory can carry an earlier planted instruction into a later run as well.

A request to change the topic is not automatically an attack. Classification depends on the task and policy. The useful question is whether lower-trust content is trying to redirect behaviour across a boundary it does not control. The attacker may want a misleading answer, an unauthorised tool call, or disclosure through a seemingly ordinary link.
interpretation: Record the attempted effect as well as the entry point. Blocking an export and detecting the suspicious sentence are separate observations.

parts.title: 3. Make the distinction readable without assuming it is enforced
paragraphs: Use the API’s intended message roles and keep retrieved excerpts in a clearly labelled data section. Quote them when appropriate. Those choices help the model and make traces easier to inspect.

They do not create an isolation boundary inside the model. A document can contain words resembling a new system message, and a model can still respond to them. Removing a few known phrases also leaves paraphrases and unfamiliar attacks. Put credentials outside the context, restrict the tools exposed to the task, and check proposed actions in code before execution.
interpretation: Do not report a prompt template as injection-proof because one malicious example was ignored.

parts.title: 4. Keep grants in application-owned data
paragraphs: A grant says which operation this request may attempt. Our fixture gives a manual-reading task only read_manual. The proposal has a tool field and may include a reason. The application compares the tool name with its own grants. It never extracts permission from the reason.

The workshop’s grants are editable so we can investigate the rule. In a deployed service the authenticated session and policy store supply them. A model-controlled argument named grants, role or tenant must not replace that state. Passing this first comparison leads to argument and resource checks, which we will build in the next lesson.
interpretation: A tool allowlist limits capabilities. It does not by itself authorise a particular customer record.

examples.title: Separate a proposal from the permission list
paragraphs: The record can contain a confident explanation without changing what the set of grants contains.
interpretation: The dictionary stores a proposal; the independently supplied set answers the membership question. Neither result measures whether the sentence was detected as an injection.

parts.title: 5. Treat screening as a measurement that can fail
paragraphs: A guardrail model may classify an input or action as acceptable, suspicious or outside policy. That measurement can miss an attack and can flag legitimate work. A timeout adds another state: we did not obtain a result.

For this lesson’s policy, a disallowed tool is denied immediately. A permitted tool continues only when the required screen passes. A flagged or unavailable screen holds the proposal for review. That review still cannot override a missing tool grant; an authorised administrator would have to change policy through a separate process. Other applications may allow a low-risk read during an outage, but that exception needs an explicit policy and tests.
interpretation: Fail closed means the protected operation does not proceed without its required evidence. It need not mean that the interface stops explaining what happened.

parts.title: 6. Place NeMo rails where their evidence exists
paragraphs: NeMo Guardrails names input, retrieval, dialog, execution and output rails. That placement matters. A user-input check has not inspected a manual fetched later, and an output check may run after a tool has already changed a record. Use retrieval checks for fetched material and execution checks around tool activity when those boundaries need inspection.

The package coordinates checks and their actions. The model, prompts and policies you choose determine what a content check can notice. Keep the service’s actual authorisation beside the tool handler even when an execution rail performs an additional semantic assessment. Consult the documented rail types and supported integrations for the version you deploy.
interpretation: A guardrail product is a place to implement controls, not a measurement that your own configuration is adequate.

parts.title: 7. Test the missed attack as well as the detected one
paragraphs: A useful test deliberately supplies a passing screen for a forbidden export proposal. The permission boundary should still deny it. Then test an ordinary read with a flagged screen: it should hold for review under our policy, allowing us to observe a false positive separately.

Provider-backed evaluations can vary the malicious document and preserve the original legitimate task. Count successful unauthorised effects, blocked legitimate tasks and detector availability separately. Repeat stochastic cases under a stated attempt budget. Save a safe fixture when a failure is discovered, with secrets and unrelated customer content removed.
interpretation: The offline workshop tests the routing rule. It cannot establish the accuracy of an injection detector or the resistance of a live model.

parts.title: 8. Keep the technician informed when the route stops
paragraphs: Botie can explain that the proposed export is outside the current task and continue with an authorised way to answer the inspection question. If the requested answer cannot be obtained safely, leave it unresolved and describe what information or review is missing.

Avoid copying an entire suspicious document into an alert. A run ID, document reference, attempted tool and decision category often give an investigator a useful starting point. Protect access to the underlying record separately. Later tracing lessons will connect these decisions to the run that produced them.
interpretation: A refused operation is useful evidence about the boundary. It is not evidence that every other part of the run was correct.

quiz.prompt: Which route follows the stated policy?
options: Execute the export because the classifier passed
quiz.because: The classifier cannot create application permission.

given.data: Server grants are ["read_manual"]. The proposal requests export_records. A classifier returns {"status":"pass"}.

quiz.prompt: Holding the proposal for review follows this policy.
quiz.because: An unavailable check has supplied no passing result.

given.data: read_manual is granted, but its required screen timed out. Policy requires a passing screen before continuing.

practice.title: Which proposed operations remain outside the job?
practice.question: Which proposed operations remain outside the job?
task: A model can propose a forbidden operation after reading a malicious manual, even when a content screen reports no problem. The application’s grant list still decides what is permitted. Implement action_route(proposal, grants, screen). The proposal must be a dictionary with a nonblank string tool. grants must be a list of nonblank strings supplied by the application. Return "deny tool" for a malformed proposal or grants, or an unlisted tool. Extra proposal fields are untrusted commentary and do not grant permission.

For a granted tool, return "continue to argument checks" only when screen is a dictionary with status exactly "pass". Every other screening value returns "hold for review". Do not mutate inputs. Print the number of denied proposals in the supplied list.
practice.starter:
def action_route(proposal, grants, screen):
    pass

proposals = [{"tool": "read_manual"}, {"tool": "export_records"}, {"tool": "create_job"}]
routes = [action_route(item, ["read_manual"], {"status": "pass"}) for item in proposals]
print(routes.count("deny tool"))
practice.solution:
def action_route(proposal, grants, screen):
    if not isinstance(grants, list) or any(not isinstance(x, str) or not x.strip() for x in grants):
        return "deny tool"
    name = proposal.get("tool") if isinstance(proposal, dict) else None
    if not isinstance(name, str) or not name.strip() or name not in grants:
        return "deny tool"
    status = screen.get("status") if isinstance(screen, dict) else None
    return "continue to argument checks" if status == "pass" else "hold for review"

proposals = [{"tool": "read_manual"}, {"tool": "export_records"}, {"tool": "create_job"}]
routes = [action_route(item, ["read_manual"], {"status": "pass"}) for item in proposals]
print(routes.count("deny tool"))
hints: Read permission from the supplied grant list, never from another field in the proposal.
Check the tool grant before handling the screening result. A timeout cannot turn a denied operation into a reviewable grant.

tests.name: Malformed and exact-name cases
tests.code:

assert action_route({"tool":"read_manual"}, "read_manual", {"status":"pass"}) == "deny tool"
assert action_route({"tool":"read"}, ["read_manual"], {"status":"pass"}) == "deny tool"

title: Whose Pump Is Botie Allowed to Inspect?
blurb: The tool name is allowed, but its arguments point at another customer’s asset. Build the service-side checks that connect the caller, operation and stored record.
openingTitle: A Valid Pump ID Belongs to the Wrong Customer
opening: Botie now asks for an allowed tool: read_manual. The request contains a real asset ID, and the service can find a record for it. There is still a problem. The record belongs to a different customer.

We cannot settle that by asking Botie whether the caller seems trustworthy. The service needs the identity established by login and the permissions attached to that identity. Then it must compare those permissions with the particular object being requested.

history.title: Permission Had to Follow the Object Being Accessed
blocks: Shared computers had to keep one user’s programs from freely using another user’s files. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 paper describes design principles including least privilege, fail-safe defaults and complete mediation. The recurring problem is deciding whether a particular operation on a particular object is allowed.

An agent introduces a new way to propose that operation, but the service still has the same responsibility. In our invented workshop, the model proposes an asset operation while application-owned records establish the caller’s tenant and grants.

reading.experimentTitle: Does this caller have this permission on this asset?
reading.experimentIntro: Build separate tenant, asset and operation comparisons. Then change the stored asset’s tenant without changing its visible ID.
reading.connectionTitle: An allowed tool still needs an authorised object
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Authorise an asset operation from server records
reading.exampleNote: The identity and policy records are invented server-side fixtures. This browser does not authenticate a real user.

intuition.title: A familiar ID is not enough
intuition.explanation: The same short asset name may occur in two organisations. Keep its owner beside it.

records.label: North tenant; P7 grant; read grant
North tenant; P7 grant; read grant

scene.caption: The second object fails this tenant-scoped policy even though its short ID matches.

intuition.title: The handler checks the object it actually loaded
intuition.explanation: Resolve the model-supplied ID inside the authorised tenant, then enforce the operation policy before returning data or making a change.

scene.caption: Use application-owned identity fields. Model arguments are requests, not authenticated claims.

parts.title: 1. Separate identity from permission
paragraphs: Authentication establishes which account is making the request, under the assumptions of the login system. Authorisation decides what that account may do. A signed-in technician may read manuals for assigned assets and still be unable to create jobs or access another site.

The service should derive the principal from the verified session or token, not from a field Botie supplies. Here principal means the application’s representation of that caller. Our small dictionary stores a tenant and two grant lists. Here a tenant identifies the customer organisation whose records the account belongs to. A grant names an operation or object that account may access. A real application may query a policy service or database instead.
interpretation: A model-generated role such as administrator has no effect on the authenticated principal.

parts.title: 2. Check the object before returning its contents
paragraphs: Our service stores P7 under tenant north. A caller from north still needs a grant for P7. Checking the tenant alone would grant access to every asset in that organisation. Checking only the short ID would confuse two tenants that both use P7.

In the workshop, Match the tenant and Check this asset grant are separate components so their results remain visible. In a database, a scoped query can require both tenant and object ID before it returns the row. Keep a clear policy for objects shared across tenants rather than quietly removing the tenant condition.
interpretation: The example’s policy denies cross-tenant access. Sharing would require an explicit additional rule.

parts.title: 3. Deny requests that have no matching rule
paragraphs: The operation list contains read. A request to export, delete or schedule has no matching grant and is denied. That is a default-deny policy: absence of permission does not become permission. Missing or malformed principal fields must also fail the check.

Use exact identifiers from a controlled operation vocabulary. Substring matches are dangerous here: read is contained in some longer names without meaning the same operation. An unchecked wildcard can expand a narrow role into authority over future capabilities.
interpretation: This is a deterministic decision over server records. A second language model is unnecessary.

examples.title: Look up the owner before considering an operation
paragraphs: A dictionary can use a tuple as a compound key. Include the tenant in the lookup instead of searching by the short ID alone.
examples.code:
records = {("north", "P7"): "North pump manual", ("south", "P7"): "South pump manual"}
caller_tenant = "north"
requested_id = "P7"
print(records.get((caller_tenant, requested_id)))
print(records.get((caller_tenant, "P8")))
interpretation: The absent row remains absent. This lookup illustrates tenant scoping; operation and assignment checks still belong beside it.

parts.title: 4. Enforce the check where the action happens
paragraphs: Hiding an export button or removing a tool from a model prompt helps guide normal use. Neither prevents a caller from reaching an exposed service route another way. The service that reads or changes the asset must enforce the policy for each request.

For writes, keep the authorisation decision and the relevant state change together closely enough that an intervening ownership or permission change cannot silently invalidate the check. A database transaction, version comparison or policy revision check may be needed. The right mechanism depends on where those records live.
interpretation: This is the reason to test the handler directly, without a model or the website interface in the path.

parts.title: 5. Give the tool less authority than the whole service
paragraphs: A maintenance assistant that only reads manuals should use a scoped read capability. It should not receive a general database administrator credential or an unrestricted command runner. Credentials belong in the service environment and should stay out of model-visible arguments and results.

The application must account for both the user’s authority and the service’s own authority. A powerful service account does not mean every user who can ask Botie a question may exercise all of its permissions. Check the caller before using that service account on their behalf.
interpretation: Least privilege makes a mistaken request less consequential, while per-request authorisation decides whether that request may proceed.

parts.title: 6. Bind approval to what will actually be executed
paragraphs: An approved inspection for P7 does not authorise an inspection for P8. Preserve the action identity, arguments and revision that the reviewer saw, then compare them again at execution time. Recheck the reviewer’s current authority and the caller’s current access when your policy requires it.

Approval and authorisation answer different questions. A permitted caller may still need a human decision for a consequential write. A human saying yes does not give the application permission to cross a tenant boundary. Keep both checks in the execution path.
interpretation: The earlier approval workshop supplied an exact-action match. This lesson adds the object-access boundary around that action.

parts.title: 7. Make access failures observable without revealing the record
paragraphs: A denied caller should not receive the protected manual inside an error message. Depending on the application, even revealing whether an asset exists may disclose information. A consistent external response can hide that distinction while a protected audit record retains the internal reason.

Test a permitted read, another tenant’s matching ID, an unassigned object in the same tenant, and a forbidden operation. Add a case where permissions change before execution. These cases catch different mistakes; one successful read says little about the deny paths.
interpretation: The construction is correct only if it preserves the permitted case while closing the gaps exposed by the changed records.

title: How Much of the Maintenance Record Does Botie Need?
blurb: A manual lookup needs an asset and a symptom, but the original record also contains private contact details. Build the smaller payload and control where it can go.
openingTitle: The Lookup Works Without the Technician’s Phone Number
opening: Botie needs the pump model and reported symptom to find the right inspection notes. Our application has those fields, but they live in a larger maintenance record alongside a technician’s contact details and a building access code. Passing the whole record to the model would be convenient. What would the extra fields help it do?

If they do not help with this job, we can leave them out before making a request. That is easier to reason about than sending everything and hoping the model never repeats the wrong part. We also need to control the destination, because a small payload can still be sent to the wrong service.

history.title: Managing Data Meant Following It Beyond the Database
blocks: Keeping a database private does not settle what happens when an application copies its contents to another system. NIST’s January 2020 Privacy Framework organised privacy risk around data processing and the organisations involved in it. That gives us a useful question for an agent: which information leaves each boundary, for what purpose, and under whose controls?

Tools such as Presidio address a narrower part of that problem by identifying and transforming sensitive entities in text and other data. Its documentation explicitly warns that automated detection cannot find every sensitive item. Our workshop begins earlier, with a new record containing only the fields this lookup needs.

reading.experimentTitle: What actually leaves the maintenance record?
reading.experimentIntro: Project the necessary fields, inspect their application-owned release labels, and check the configured destination before releasing the payload.
reading.connectionTitle: A useful context is smaller than the source database row
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Prepare only the approved lookup payload
reading.exampleNote: All records are invented. The construction produces a local value; it sends nothing to a service.

intuition.title: Give each field a reason to travel
intuition.explanation: The manual lookup has a narrow purpose. Classify and select its inputs before serialization.

scene.caption: These values are invented. In a deployed service, field policy belongs to the application.

intuition.title: A destination is another independent decision
intuition.explanation: The selected fields must be approved for release and sent only to a configured service.

rows.label: Release
items: The checked payload or an empty withheld result

scene.caption: This model does not inspect free text for hidden secrets or implement a network firewall.

parts.title: 1. Choose inputs from the job backwards
paragraphs: Start with the lookup we want to perform. It needs an asset identifier and a controlled symptom code. A controlled code is a value from a vocabulary the application defines, such as VIBRATION. It is not an unrestricted note field.

Now create a new payload containing those fields. This operation is often called projection: select named columns or fields from a larger record. Keeping the source record intact is useful because another authorised operation may need its contact field later. It does not follow that this model request needs it now.
interpretation: Ask what each field helps this particular request accomplish.

parts.title: 2. Separate the right to read from the right to send
paragraphs: The technician may be permitted to view a contact number inside the maintenance system. That does not automatically permit sending it to an external model provider or logging platform. Destination, purpose and retention matter independently of the original read permission.

For the exercise we use a deliberately simple release label: approved. Every selected field needs that exact label. An unknown label or missing classification withholds the payload. Real classifications may depend on the tenant, destination, jurisdiction or contractual arrangement, and the application must resolve that policy before release.
interpretation: Our label is trusted metadata for this teaching example. A model-generated approved field would have no authority.

parts.title: 3. Inspect the smaller record before encoding it
paragraphs: A dictionary comprehension can select fields into a new dictionary. We iterate over the fields chosen by the application, rather than copying every key and trying to remember what to remove afterwards.

Do not silently ignore a requested field that does not exist. The resulting payload might still look valid while missing the information needed for the task. The workshop stops on that configuration error. A field added to the source record, however, stays excluded unless the application deliberately selects it.
interpretation: An allowlist of needed fields survives an unrelated source-schema addition more predictably than a list of known secret fields.

examples.title: A new internal field stays out of a summary payload
paragraphs: The source contains an internal note, but this summary only needs two named fields. The comprehension creates a separate dictionary.
interpretation: The payload has the selected keys. The original record still retains the internal note for authorised uses.

parts.title: 4. Constrain the destination before any network request
paragraphs: Our workshop chooses a service ID such as manual-index from an application allowlist. Server configuration resolves that ID to a known connection. Letting the model supply an arbitrary URL would introduce more decisions: scheme, hostname, port, resolved address and redirect behaviour.

A request to a permitted-looking hostname can redirect elsewhere, and DNS resolution can produce an address the service must not reach. Server-side request forgery is the problem of making a server request a destination it should not access. Use a narrow egress policy and a network client that enforces it. Revalidate redirects or disable them, and block inappropriate internal and metadata endpoints.
interpretation: An exact service-ID comparison is only one part of controlling egress. The workshop intentionally does not claim to validate URLs.

parts.title: 5. Treat a sandbox as a set of enforced limits
paragraphs: If Botie can run code, ask what that process can read, write and contact. Giving it a separate working directory is useful but does not establish isolation from the host, environment variables or network. A sandbox needs an actual enforcement mechanism and a defined threat model.

Restrict filesystem mounts, avoid inherited credentials, run without unnecessary privileges, and place limits on execution time, memory and output. Network access should follow the task’s egress policy. Review the isolation technology’s documented guarantees and patch it. A container can help package these controls, but its default settings are not a complete policy.
interpretation: The coding worksheet here is for learning. It is not a template for executing arbitrary model-written code inside your production service.

parts.title: 6. Use PII detection where the source really is free text
paragraphs: Sometimes a technician’s note is needed, and personal information can appear inside a sentence rather than a dedicated field. Presidio separates identification from transformation: recognizers locate possible sensitive entities, then an anonymisation step can replace, mask or otherwise transform the detected spans.

Evaluate recognizers on the languages and formats your application sees. A missed entity remains in the text; an incorrect detection can remove useful maintenance information. NeMo also exposes integrations for detecting or masking sensitive information at different points in a conversation. Choose where the check runs by following the actual data flow, including retrieved material and final answers.
interpretation: Redaction after a provider request cannot undo data already sent to that provider. Minimise and inspect before the relevant boundary.

parts.title: 7. Check logs, traces and saved conversations too
paragraphs: The model request is only one copy. Debug traces may store prompts, responses and tool results. Checkpoint storage can preserve the same fields for later runs. An error report may include an entire failed payload.

Define what each store needs, who can read it and when it should be deleted. Prefer identifiers and decision categories when full content is unnecessary. Apply redaction before export to a telemetry service. If you need protected sample traces for investigations, make that a controlled collection with its own access and retention policy rather than the default for every run.
interpretation: A redacted user interface tells us nothing about whether a raw request was copied into an observability tool.

parts.title: 8. Make the unknown case visibly withhold
paragraphs: The changed workshop case adds contact to the selected fields but leaves its release label restricted. The destination is still approved. Only the field-classification branch should explain why the result is withheld.

Then try an approved payload with an unapproved destination. This exposes a construction that checks only the fields. An empty result here is intentional: the output does not carry the disallowed payload along with a warning that a downstream component might ignore. A production audit record can separately retain a protected reason code.
interpretation: Do not let a convenient fallback resend the full original record after the minimised request fails.

parts.title: 9. Keep the teaching boundary honest
paragraphs: This construction checks field names and trusted classifications. It does not inspect the meaning of values. If a free-text symptom contains a password, labelling its field approved will not remove that password. If an asset identifier is itself sensitive, it also needs an appropriate policy.

Use realistic test fixtures for those cases in the actual application. The controlled symptom codes here let us study selection and routing without pretending to have built a complete privacy classifier. Keep that assumption in the test description when comparing implementations.
interpretation: A passing release test means this stated policy passed for these records. It is not a general privacy guarantee.

title: Can We Safely Use the Answer Botie Returned?
blurb: A response can be valid JSON and still name the wrong pump or contain unwanted markup. Check its structure, its relationship to the request, and the context that will consume it.
openingTitle: A Valid Answer for the Wrong Pump
opening: Botie returns a neat record with an asset, a citation and an inspection note. Every field is a string. The interface can read it. Then the technician notices that the answer concerns P8, while the request was about P7.

There is another boundary after generating an answer. We have to decide whether the record means what this request requires and how the next program will use its contents. A string that belongs in a text panel should not quietly become executable markup or a command.

history.title: A Correct String Can Become an Instruction to Another Program

sources.title: CERT: Malicious HTML Tags Embedded in Client Web Requests, advisory CA-2000-02

blocks: When web applications began building pages from submitted and stored text, the browser could mistake some of that text for instructions. CERT’s 2000 advisory on malicious HTML in generated web responses documented this problem. The author of the text and the web page did not have to be the same person; copying untrusted content into a page could give it the page’s apparent authority.

A language model supplies another source of text to the same consuming browser. The application must choose whether that content is displayed as text or interpreted as markup, and encode it for the chosen context. Structured validation answers a different question about field names and values. Botie’s response therefore needs both a usable record and a safe route into the display, while the correctness of the maintenance advice still needs its own evidence.

reading.experimentTitle: Which boundary rejects this draft?
reading.experimentIntro: Check the fields, then compare the requested asset and citation map. Encode accepted draft text for an HTML text node.

parts.title: 1. Begin with the contract the next component needs
paragraphs: The draft panel expects exactly asset, citation and text. Require those fields to contain nonblank strings and reject unexpected fields. This prevents a hidden execute flag from being accepted merely because the visible note looks ordinary.

Schema validation deals with representation. It can describe types, required properties and some value constraints. Provider-supported structured generation can help produce that representation, but the application should still validate what it receives. A truncated response, changed configuration or different producer can reach the same boundary.
interpretation: A valid structure makes the next check possible; it does not make the content correct.

parts.title: 2. Compare identifiers with this request’s evidence
paragraphs: The asset field must equal the requested asset. The citation must appear in the evidence supplied to this run and refer to that asset. These are semantic constraints because they concern relationships between the record and its surrounding data.

Our workshop stores a citation-to-asset map to make the comparison visible. It is deliberately incomplete as an evidence check. A citation can refer to the correct pump while the sentence contradicts its manual. Content support needs examination of the actual excerpt, possibly with domain rules, a reviewer or a separately evaluated model judge.
interpretation: Avoid a success label that claims more than was checked. We call the surviving record a draft for review.

parts.title: 3. Use strict types deliberately
paragraphs: Validation libraries may convert values into the declared type. Coercion is useful in some interfaces, but a boundary may need to reject a value supplied in the wrong representation. Pydantic provides strict validation controls for that choice.

The local recipe declares strict string fields, rejects extra keys and checks for whitespace-only values. It validates a Python dictionary with model_validate. Other input modes and types have their own rules, so test the actual entry point used by the application. A type annotation alone does not run a check over arbitrary incoming data.
interpretation: Keep this structural recipe separate from the request-specific evidence checks.

references.title: Declare the draft shape with Pydantic
description: Run this structural check in your own Python environment. The later asset and citation comparisons still belong in application code.
setup: Install a compatible Pydantic 2.x release in a local virtual environment and record the resolved version in your lockfile.
This example validates invented local data. It needs no model provider or credential.
interpretation: Strict fields and forbidden extra keys establish the record contract. This program has not checked permissions, citation support or how the text will be rendered.

parts.title: 4. Render text according to where it will appear
paragraphs: An HTML parser gives angle brackets a meaning beyond ordinary text. If the draft contains Inspect, a text panel should show those characters as text unless the product intentionally supports that markup. Use a text-content API or the framework’s normal escaped interpolation.

The offline example uses Python’s html.escape to demonstrate encoding before insertion into an HTML text node. Encoding is specific to the destination context. It does not make a string safe as JavaScript, a shell command, SQL or an arbitrary URL. Do not pass this encoded string to another interpreter and assume the same protection applies.
interpretation: If the frontend already escapes text, pass it raw text and let that boundary encode once. Double encoding would show the escape sequences themselves.

examples.title: Keep markup characters visible as text
paragraphs: This standard-library program encodes a short draft for an HTML text context. It does not execute or render HTML.
examples.code:
from html import escape

note = "Inspect <coupling> & mounting."
encoded = escape(note, quote=True)
print(encoded)
print(note)
interpretation: The source string stays unchanged. The encoded version is suitable for the stated HTML text context only.

parts.title: 5. Treat links, rich text and executable requests separately
paragraphs: If the interface allows Markdown, decide which features it needs. A remote image can cause a network request when rendered, and a link can point to an unwanted scheme or destination. Disable raw HTML when it is unnecessary, restrict URL schemes and destinations as appropriate, and use a maintained sanitizer for the rich content the product intentionally supports.

If the result is meant to query a database, use parameterized queries and application-owned query structure. If it proposes a tool call, return to the authorisation and argument checks before execution. Never use an LLM’s output as an unrestricted command just because it passed a text-quality filter.
interpretation: Every consumer introduces its own interpretation rules. Name the actual consumer when choosing the protection.

parts.title: 6. Choose what a failed validator does
paragraphs: Guardrails AI validators define criteria and report a pass or failure. Configured failure actions determine what happens next. A retry may request a different answer; a failure can also stop processing or trigger another application path. Inspect the outcome and use only a result that passed the required checks.

Automatic repair is appropriate only when changing the value preserves the intended task and policy. Silently replacing an invalid asset with the requested asset could attach a note about P8 to P7. For this lesson, inconsistent fields return repair draft with empty display text. A bounded retry can ask for a new candidate, which must pass every check again.
interpretation: A repaired string is a new candidate, not an exemption from validation.

parts.title: 7. Hold streamed content until its required checks finish
paragraphs: Streaming makes an interface feel responsive, but a final output check cannot take back text already shown or a tool already executed. Decide which parts can be displayed before full validation. A typing indicator or progress state can be useful while a protected result is withheld.

If validation operates on chunks, test content that spans a chunk boundary and check the final assembled message as needed. Structured output may be incomplete until the stream finishes. Keep cancellation, truncated output and validator errors distinct from successful completion.
interpretation: The workshop uses complete records so its validation order is visible. A streaming application needs additional tests for that order.

parts.title: 8. Test misleading success cases
paragraphs: Keep a correctly shaped draft for the wrong asset in the suite. Add a citation from the right evidence collection but for another asset. Then supply markup characters in an otherwise matching draft and verify that the output remains text.

A correct implementation should preserve ordinary drafts while repairing invalid relationships. Separately test whether the note is supported by the excerpt and whether a technician finds it useful. This separation gives a failure a location: representation, request relationship, display handling or advice quality.
interpretation: A single overall guardrail score would hide which of those responsibilities failed.

title: Did Botie Create the Inspection, or Did the Reply Get Lost?
topic: Keeping an Agent Run Under Control
blurb: A request times out after Botie submits an inspection. Work out what the service may already have done before sending another request.
openingTitle: One Approved Inspection Has Become Two Jobs
opening: The technician approves an inspection of P7. Botie submits the request, but the connection closes before the reply arrives. He tries again. The service now shows two inspection jobs for the same request.

From Botie’s side, the first attempt failed to produce a reply. From the service’s side, it may have succeeded. We need to keep those facts separate. This lesson builds a recovery decision that can reuse a recorded result, wait for a pending operation, or stop when another attempt would be unsafe.

history.title: A Lost Reply Was a Problem Before Models Called Tools

sources.title: Amazon Builders’ Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
Amazon Builders’ Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

blocks: Distributed services have long faced the problem of a request whose effect succeeds while its reply is lost. Amazon’s Builders’ Library describes how client request identifiers let a service recognise repeated intent; its idempotent API article was announced in January 2021. An agent calling a work-order service inherits this same communication problem.

The practical idea is to give the intended inspection a stable identity. A repeated delivery of that operation can then recover its earlier result within the receiving service’s documented contract. Our receipt ledger is a teaching model. It does not implement a distributed transaction or promise that every request eventually succeeds.

reading.experimentTitle: What should happen after the missing reply?
reading.experimentIntro: Keep the receipt lookup, retry safety and run deadline visible on separate branches. Then combine them into one recovery action.
reading.connectionTitle: Recover an operation without inventing another one
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Decide the next recovery action
reading.exampleNote: No work-order service is called. Receipt records and clocks are supplied fixtures.

intuition.title: A timeout describes the caller’s observation
intuition.explanation: The effect and the reply happen at different points. A broken connection can separate them.

rows.label: Work-order service
items: Create WO-41 and store the operation receipt

rows.label: Botie
items: Sees a timeout; cannot infer that no work occurred

scene.caption: The service receipt answers a question that the missing reply cannot.

intuition.title: Look at what the receiver knows
intuition.explanation: Use the same operation key and compare the complete action payload.

records.label: Completed, same payload
cells: The intended effect has a recorded result

records.label: Pending, same payload
cells: Query status within a bounded policy

records.label: Same key, different payload

records.label: No receipt

scene.caption: An absent receipt is usable evidence only within the service’s consistency and idempotency contract.

parts.title: 1. Classify the failure before choosing another attempt
paragraphs: A permission denial or invalid asset identifier will not improve because the same request is sent again. Route those permanent failures to repair or review. A temporary overload or interrupted connection may justify a retry, but the tool’s contract must establish whether repeating the operation is safe.

Keep unknown outcomes distinct from known rejections. For a write, a timeout can mean the service completed the effect without delivering a reply. For a read, another request usually avoids duplicate business effects, though it still consumes resources and can return changed data. Our fixture labels outcomes success, transient, permanent or unknown; real adapters map their documented error codes into those categories.
interpretation: The model does not get to reinterpret a permission denial as an invitation to try different arguments until something works.

parts.title: 2. Give the intended operation an identity
paragraphs: Create an operation key when the application accepts the approved intent. Persist it before sending the write. Reuse it when delivering that same operation again. A genuinely new inspection needs a new key, even if its asset and other fields match an earlier inspection.

The receiver binds the key to the caller’s scope and the relevant payload. The same key with a different pump or schedule must be a conflict. Avoid relying on the model to invent or remember this identity. It belongs to application state alongside the approved action revision.
interpretation: A key in a request header is only useful if the receiving service enforces the contract.

parts.title: 3. Recover the receiver’s answer before scheduling more work
paragraphs: A completed receipt can return the earlier work-order ID. A pending receipt tells us the operation is already under way. A status query or a bounded wait is appropriate; launching a second operation is not.

This requires an authoritative ledger. A stale cache or an unavailable status endpoint cannot prove that the operation never happened. When the receiving service offers neither an idempotency contract nor a reliable reconciliation path, retain the ambiguous outcome for review. Do not turn it into an automatic new write. The workshop’s absent receipt assumes a trustworthy snapshot within the stated service contract.
interpretation: Approval answers whether we may perform the action. A receipt answers what happened when we tried. Neither replaces the other.

parts.title: 4. What the idempotency boundary has to store
paragraphs: The service needs a unique operation identity, a fingerprint or canonical representation of its payload, a processing state, and a stored result. Concurrent deliveries of the same operation must compete at an atomic boundary so both cannot decide they are the first.

The exact transaction depends on where the effect happens. A database write and its receipt may share a transaction. An external email or another service cannot automatically join that transaction; outbox delivery and downstream idempotency may be needed. Receipt retention also matters. Once a receiver forgets a key, a late replay may be treated as new work. Read the actual API contract and keep retries inside its scope and retention window.
interpretation: Our Python dictionary lookup demonstrates the decision only. It is not a concurrency-safe store.

examples.title: Recover a known operation result
paragraphs: A dictionary indexed by operation key makes a completed receipt easy to find. This example performs no write.
interpretation: The result belongs to the earlier operation. The full challenge will also reject a reused key whose payload changed.

parts.title: 5. Give every attempt a timeout and the whole run a deadline
paragraphs: A per-attempt timeout bounds how long the caller waits for one operation. A run deadline bounds the whole recovery process, including delays and repeated attempts. Starting a fresh timeout after each failure can otherwise keep the run alive far longer than intended.

Count attempts that have actually started, including the first. Before scheduling another, check the remaining attempt allowance and whether its delay plus timeout fits the remaining deadline. Use a monotonic clock for elapsed-time accounting in a real process. Pass the remaining deadline to downstream calls where supported. Timing out locally does not roll back an effect already accepted elsewhere.
interpretation: The supplied fixture clock is an integer millisecond counter so every branch can be tested without sleeping.

parts.title: 6. Spread retries without letting them continue forever
paragraphs: Repeated immediate requests can worsen an overloaded service. Exponential backoff increases the upper delay after successive attempts, and a cap prevents unbounded waiting. Jitter chooses a delay within a range so many clients do not all retry at the same instant.

Our full-jitter demonstration supplies a fraction between zero and one rather than drawing randomness during a test. We multiply that fraction by the capped upper delay and round down to whole milliseconds. In production, draw the random value per attempt and honour the service’s documented Retry-After guidance. Keep a separate total deadline; a capped delay alone allows infinitely many retries.
parts.calculation:
upper_delay = min(cap_ms, base_ms * 2 ** max(attempts_started - 1, 0))
delay_ms = floor(upper_delay * jitter_fraction)
next_attempt_fits = now_ms + delay_ms + timeout_ms <= deadline_ms
interpretation: Equality is allowed in our scheduling fixture. Actual transport scheduling and cancellation are not precise guarantees that a remote operation finishes at that instant.

parts.title: 7. Choose one place to own automatic recovery
paragraphs: A provider SDK may already retry a request. A framework may retry a model response that fails validation. A tool adapter may retry its service call. If each surrounding layer also repeats the whole operation, the actual number of requests can grow much faster than the visible loop count.

Inspect the layers and give each failure one deliberate recovery owner. Count transport attempts separately from model turns and tool proposals. Record the operation key, attempt number, error category and final outcome without leaking sensitive request bodies. A validation retry asks for corrected content; a transport retry resends delivery. They have different purposes and may consume different budgets.
interpretation: An agent’s friendly message that it is trying again should correspond to a recorded recovery decision in the application.

parts.title: 8. Let a cancellation leave an honest outcome
paragraphs: If the user cancels after submission, stop scheduling new work and request cancellation of any supported in-flight operation. The receiver may already have committed the effect. Preserve its operation identity and reconcile the final state before reporting that nothing happened.

For a workflow with several external effects, recovery may involve a compensating action such as cancelling a created appointment. That compensation is a separate authorised operation with its own possible failure. It does not erase the fact that the original effect occurred. Make partial outcomes visible to the person responsible for the request.
interpretation: The next lesson will keep budget reservations for unresolved work rather than pretending a cancelled caller immediately receives its resources back.

parts.title: 9. Trip the retry loop with a completed write
paragraphs: Begin with the missing-reply case whose service supports a stable key. The recovery rule can permit another delivery within the deadline. Then load the completed receipt. The same construction should return its stored work-order ID immediately.

Change the payload under that key and check that the result becomes a conflict. Finally, remove the idempotency guarantee and leave the result unknown. Time remaining is no longer enough to justify another write. These cases test different reasons for stopping, so a single retry-until-success loop cannot satisfy them.
interpretation: The result of this lesson is a recovery decision. Executing that decision still requires the live service contract and current authorisation checks.

practice.title: Which recovery action can Botie safely take next?
practice.question: Which recovery action can Botie safely take next?
task: A timeout does not tell us whether a write happened. Look for the receiving service’s record of the operation before deciding whether another attempt is safe. Write next_action(command, receipts, outcome, schedule, state), returning a dictionary with route, delay_ms and result. Match a receipt by command.key and compare the complete payload. A conflict returns "reject changed payload". A matching completed receipt returns "return stored result" and its result; pending returns "query operation status". Otherwise success returns "done", permanent returns "repair request", and a write without receiver-enforced idempotency returns "reconcile outcome".

For other transient or unknown outcomes, calculate capped full-jitter delay as shown in Part 6. Permit "retry same operation key" only when attempts is below max_attempts, now_ms is before deadline_ms, and delay plus timeout fits. Otherwise return "stop at run limit". Non-retry routes have delay_ms 0; result is None except for stored completion. Inputs use the displayed dictionary fields. Each completed receipt must include result, which may explicitly be None. Compare nested payload values with JSON type semantics: True is different from 1, while numeric 1 and 1.0 match. Reject missing or malformed fields, duplicate receipt keys, negative integer counters, zero timeout, and jitter outside [0,1] with ValueError. Do not mutate inputs. This exercise makes no network calls.
Print the recovery dictionary for the supplied request after an unknown outcome.
hints: Match the operation key and complete payload before looking at retry timing. A completed matching receipt supplies the earlier result; a changed payload is a conflict.
An uncertain write needs a receiver-enforced rule that repeats one intent under one key. Extra time alone cannot make an unsafe duplicate acceptable.
For work that may be retried, keep the jittered delay and per-attempt timeout inside the remaining deadline. Delay is not additional execution time that can be ignored.
