title: Can Two of Botie’s Calls Spend the Same Remaining Budget?
topic: Keeping an Agent Run Under Control
blurb: Two proposed lookups each appear affordable until they start together. Reserve shared resources before dispatch and keep the whole run within its operating limits.
openingTitle: Both Calls Saw Enough Budget, and Together They Spent Too Much
opening: Botie wants to summarise a manual and compare it with the repair history. The application checks both proposals against the same remaining allowance. Each fits on its own, so both begin. Their combined work exceeds the allowance.

Checking the balance was only part of the job. We also needed to reserve the resources when admitting each call. We will build that decision, then see what changes when the user cancels, a dependency starts failing, or the next request cannot finish before the deadline.

history.title: An Agent Run Inherits the Resource Problems of a Service

sources.title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Circuit Breaker pattern
Pydantic AI: Usage limits and cancellation
Dijkstra: Cooperating sequential processes, semaphore and bounded-resource mechanisms

blocks: Two concurrent programs can each read that the last resource is available before either records that it has taken it. Dijkstra’s account of cooperating sequential processes developed semaphore operations for coordinating access to shared resources. The important step is treating the check and acquisition as one coordinated operation, so the resource is not promised twice.

An agent run inherits that problem when several calls share its remaining allowance. A model can propose work, but the application must reserve the capacity before starting it. Circuit breakers address a separate failure pattern by temporarily stopping calls to an unhealthy dependency. Our reservation ledger keeps completed spending and still-running work visible, so a limit is enforced by the program rather than left as a request in a prompt.

reading.experimentTitle: Reserve work before allowing parallel calls
reading.experimentIntro: Subtract settled usage and in-flight reservations first. Check cancellation and circuit state on a separate branch, then admit calls in the declared queue order.
reading.connectionTitle: A proposed call still needs an execution slot
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Reserve a batch of proposed calls
reading.exampleNote: All amounts are invented. Cost units are integer accounting units, not provider prices.

intuition.title: The allowance has three different states
intuition.explanation: The application must count work that started but has not yet reported final usage.

records.label: Limit
cells: Maximum reserved or settled work for this run

records.label: Settled usage
cells: Usage already reported by completed work

records.label: Still reserved

scene.caption: A reservation represents a bound used by the admission policy. Real usage is reconciled when the operation ends.

intuition.title: Reserve before the next proposal reads the balance
intuition.explanation: Both proposed calls need a reservation of 300 tokens. Queue order is deliberate in this fixture.

scene.caption: A real shared ledger needs an atomic check-and-reserve operation. Two workers cannot safely check separate stale copies.

parts.title: 1. Name the work that each limit counts
paragraphs: A model request is one interaction with a provider, but an agent framework may count a model turn differently from transport attempts. A tool proposal is a request to use a capability; a tool execution is the actual work performed by its handler. Decide whether your operational counters count attempts, successes or both.

A tokenizer splits the text into pieces the model processes; those pieces are tokens. Count the pieces sent in and the pieces generated separately. Money depends on prices and provider accounting, so equal token totals can have different costs. Elapsed time measures what the user waits for. These quantities cannot substitute for one another. The workshop carries separate tokens, cost_units, model_requests and tool_calls fields, with a wall-clock deadline checked separately.
interpretation: Document counter semantics at the boundary that enforces them. A limit whose name is ambiguous will be hard to test.

parts.title: 2. Keep one request small enough to send
paragraphs: A run can stay below its total allowance while one request exceeds the model’s context window or your application’s input-size limit. Measure the request after assembling its instructions, evidence and conversation state. Reserve room for the response according to the provider’s actual context rules.

The workshop supplies input_tokens and checks it against max_input_tokens. Its token reservation includes that input plus a chosen output allowance. This is a teaching contract, so a reservation smaller than the input is rejected as malformed. Real systems need a tokenizer or provider counting interface appropriate to the model, including any special messages and tool definitions.
interpretation: A cumulative token cap and a per-request context cap protect different boundaries.

parts.title: 3. Count work still in flight
paragraphs: Settled usage records operations whose accounting has arrived. A reservation records work already admitted whose final usage is not known. Subtract both when deciding what remains.

If an operation finishes below its reserved bound, move actual usage to the settled ledger and release only the unused remainder. If accounting is missing, keep an unresolved entry and reconcile it. Treating missing usage as zero creates fictional capacity. Where provider behaviour can exceed an estimate, choose conservative limits and enforce output caps where supported. Application reservations are only as reliable as their bounds and the accounting contract.
parts.calculation: available = limit - settled_usage - in_flight_reservations
interpretation: Never subtract a reservation from one run and charge its result to an unrelated run. Keep the request and operation identities with both entries.

parts.title: 4. The second proposal must see the first reservation
paragraphs: Our two calls each request 300 tokens. The shared remainder is 500. Checking them independently against that initial value admits too much work. Checking the first, reserving it, then checking the second produces a different outcome.

We use queue order as a transparent admission policy. Other schedulers may prioritise urgent work or maximise useful work under a budget, but they still need a shared atomic reservation step. In a multi-worker service this commonly belongs in a transaction or another concurrency-safe store. Our single-process dictionary calculation only demonstrates the policy.
interpretation: A reservation is an execution decision made by the application. The model’s belief that a call is affordable does not reserve anything.

parts.title: 5. Represent each proposed call as an inspectable record
paragraphs: Each proposal has an id, input_tokens, timeout_ms and a reserve dictionary. The reserve dictionary names the same four resources as the run limits. A list preserves the queue order. A dictionary stores the remaining amount for each named resource, so tokens cannot accidentally be compared with tool calls.

The admission function validates every proposal, including one it will later refuse. It returns accepted IDs, rejected IDs with reasons, and the remaining budget. It does not perform network work or mutate the input ledger. That separation makes a test able to inspect the decision before any actual expense or effect occurs.
interpretation: The caller must commit the returned reservations atomically before dispatching accepted calls.

examples.title: Subtract a reservation on a copy of the ledger
paragraphs: A dictionary copy keeps the supplied starting allowance intact while we inspect one proposed reservation.
interpretation: The copied result shows the proposal’s effect. The original record remains available for a transaction or a failed-decision comparison.

parts.title: 6. Carry the run deadline into every branch
paragraphs: Parallel calls spend resources at the same time. Their elapsed durations do not simply add, but each must respect the run’s remaining deadline. The fixture admits a call only if its full timeout fits before deadline_ms. It uses a shared now_ms snapshot because it is making one batch decision.

A live dispatcher must recheck remaining time immediately before each launch. Waiting in a queue consumes the same deadline. Downstream operations need the remaining budget rather than a new full timeout at every hop. Reserve time for combining results and returning a response, especially if the calls are only an intermediate stage.
interpretation: The timeout is a bound on local waiting, not proof that a remote effect will be undone when the clock expires.

parts.title: 7. Cancellation stops new work before it frees old work
paragraphs: When the user cancels, stop admitting proposals and signal cancellation to supported in-flight operations. Keep each in-flight reservation until the operation’s final usage or an authoritative cancellation outcome is known. A closed local stream may still leave provider work running or an external write committed.

The workshop’s cancelled flag blocks the batch and leaves its supplied reservations in place. It does not simulate a remote cancellation protocol. A production UI should distinguish requested cancellation, confirmed cancellation, and an unresolved effect. Partial output also needs a clear status so it is not mistaken for a completed answer.
interpretation: Returning early to the user and stopping all downstream work are separate events.

parts.title: 8. Stop feeding a failing dependency
paragraphs: A circuit breaker watches failures associated with a dependency. In its closed state, calls can proceed subject to other limits. When the configured failure policy opens the circuit, new calls fail promptly rather than repeatedly spending the request budget on the same unavailable service.

After a recovery interval, a half-open state can allow a limited probe. A successful probe can support closing the circuit; another failure can reopen it. Our fixture receives the current state and an application-granted probe slot. It admits at most one proposal while half-open. It does not compute failure windows or recovery transitions, which need service-specific policy and tests.
interpretation: An open circuit should describe the dependency that is failing. It should not silently turn every unrelated tool off.

parts.title: 9. Read the library’s limit contract before relying on its name
paragraphs: Pydantic AI documents usage limits for requests, tool calls, tokens and cost. Its current tool_calls_limit counts successful tool invocations. Its request_limit counts model responses acted on by the agent loop, rather than every provider transport attempt. Provider retries and some continuation or fallback requests can therefore make transport activity differ from the turn count.

The enforcement moment matters too. Output-token and cost checks can occur after a response, and cancelled-stream usage may be incomplete. These controls do not all provide a pre-dispatch spending guarantee. Read the installed version’s documentation and test the cases your application relies on. Add application reservations or provider-side limits where the requirement calls for them. Keep unknown prices or usage visible as unknown.
interpretation: The workshop’s queue policy is our own teaching design. It does not claim to reproduce a particular framework’s scheduling policy.

parts.title: 10. Use limits at more than one scope
paragraphs: A per-run allowance protects one request. It does not stop thousands of permitted requests from exhausting a shared provider quota. A service may also need per-user rate limits, organisation spend controls, concurrency limits, and a bounded queue. Decide which boundary owns each limit.

A queue is a promise of future work. Bound it and provide a clear overload response instead of accepting an unlimited backlog. Reserve capacity for essential recovery and status work where appropriate. Otherwise an exhausted task budget might prevent the very reconciliation needed to discover whether a write completed.
interpretation: Fallbacks need permissions and accounting too. Switching providers or launching a helper agent should not reset the original run’s allowance.

parts.title: 11. Test contention, cancellation and recovery as different cases
paragraphs: The first fixture exposes two proposals competing for one remaining allowance. The next gives the second call enough room by changing the existing reservation; the same construction should then admit both. A cancelled run must admit neither, regardless of its apparent budget.

The half-open fixture tests a different rule: only one probe can run even when resources are plentiful. Additional cases isolate the context cap and the deadline. Keep refusal reasons visible so a learner can explain which boundary acted. When a real service refuses work, those same reasons help distinguish expected limits from faulty accounting.
interpretation: The next observability lessons will follow these decisions through traces and outcomes instead of reducing every stopped run to one generic error.

quiz.prompt: What does this lesson’s admission policy allow?
options: Both because the resource budget is sufficient
Unlimited calls until a failure occurs
quiz.because: The probe allowance is an independent concurrency decision. The second proposal must wait for the probe policy’s next decision.

practice.title: Which proposed calls can share the remaining allowance?
practice.question: Which proposed calls can share the remaining allowance?
task: Two queued calls can each look affordable while promising to spend the same remaining tokens. Reserve the first call’s resources before deciding on the next one. Write reserve_calls(proposals, limits, used, reserved, control, clock). Subtract used and reserved from limits for tokens, cost_units, model_requests and tool_calls. Each is a nonnegative integer and booleans are invalid. An overdrawn ledger raises ValueError. Process proposals in list order without mutating inputs.

Each proposal has a unique nonblank id, nonnegative input_tokens, positive timeout_ms, and a reserve dictionary with those four resource fields. Reserved tokens must cover input_tokens. Validate all input records. control contains boolean cancelled, circuit (closed, open or half-open), and boolean probe_granted. clock contains nonnegative integer now_ms, deadline_ms and max_input_tokens.

Refusal precedence is cancelled; circuit unavailable for open or ungranted half-open; probe slot used after one accepted half-open call; request too large; deadline; resource budget. An accepted call reserves every resource before the next call is checked. Return {"accepted": IDs, "rejected": [{"id": ID, "reason": reason}], "remaining": resource dictionary}. Reject malformed input with ValueError. Print the supplied example’s result.
hints: Calls already in flight occupy budget even before their final usage arrives. Subtract both settled usage and outstanding reservations into a new resource dictionary.
Validate every proposal before dispatch decisions, then process proposals in their supplied order. An accepted reservation reduces the remainder used by the following proposal.
Keep the declared refusal order. Cancellation and dependency health can stop work even when the resource ledger has room; a half-open circuit permits only its granted probe.
A call also needs a permitted input size and enough time for its timeout. Those checks do not follow automatically from a positive token balance.

tests.name: Two calls cannot spend the same remainder
Cancellation and circuit refusal
tests.code:
for update, reason in [({"cancelled":True},"cancelled"),({"circuit":"open"},"circuit unavailable")]:
    answer = reserve_calls(proposals,limits,used,reserved,{**control,**update},clock)
    assert answer["accepted"] == []
    assert all(row["reason"] == reason for row in answer["rejected"])

tests.name: Half-open allows one probe despite spare capacity
No mutation and invalid ledger rejection

title: Which Examples Should We Put in the Prompt?
blurb: Botie keeps making an inspection sound mandatory. Show what a supported answer looks like, then check that the examples teach the distinction we intended.
openingTitle: Our Example Accidentally Teaches “Always Inspect”
opening: We give Botie an example: a noisy pump, a manual excerpt, and an answer recommending inspection. The next technician asks what a warning light means. Botie recommends an inspection again. Perhaps it copied the most obvious pattern in the example.

An example shows more than the desired format. It also shows which evidence led to which decision. We need cases that make the distinction visible, including a question the supplied evidence cannot answer. Then we need questions that were never used to choose those examples.

history.title: Showing a Task Inside the Input
blocks: The 2020 GPT-3 paper studied tasks presented through instructions and a small number of demonstrations in the model’s input. In that setting, adapting to the task did not require gradient updates during inference. This made the contents of the prompt part of how the task was specified.

For our maintenance desk, that means we can show a supported answer and a request for clarification side by side. It does not guarantee that a model will infer the intended rule. We still have to test what it does with unfamiliar questions.

reading.experimentTitle: Choose examples without peeking at the exam
reading.experimentIntro: Select relevant development examples, then fit them into the reserved prompt space.
reading.connectionTitle: Selection comes before packing
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Turn demonstrations into message pairs
reading.outputLabel: Selected example IDs and remaining allowance
reading.exampleNote: These are invented, recorded examples. The browser runs your construction without calling a language model. Passing them checks the surrounding program, not the quality of a live model.

intuition.title: Give the decision a reason
intuition.explanation: These are abbreviated teaching examples, not complete maintenance advice.

records.label: Meaning of a warning; manual explains it
Whether inspection is due; revision missing
cells: Do not fill an evidence gap

records.label: Request to book; no approval
cells: An answer is not authority to act

scene.caption: The differences matter more than repeated phrasing.

intuition.title: Keep a question out of the selection pool

scene.caption: Even when C fits more easily, using it as a demonstration would compromise this test’s independence.

parts.title: 1. Write the rule before choosing a demonstration
paragraphs: Our rule is to answer from the supplied approved evidence and ask for missing information when that evidence is insufficient. Start there. Then choose examples in which the evidence changes what a good answer can say.

If every example ends in inspection, the prompt leaves an important boundary unexplained. Include a supported explanation that needs no proposed action. Avoid real customer details; synthetic examples can teach the structure without exposing private records.
interpretation: Examples illustrate the written instruction. They do not grant access or override the tool’s permission checks.

parts.title: 2. Keep input and response together
paragraphs: A demonstration has an input and a reviewed response. The input should include the evidence available at that moment. The response should show only claims that evidence supports. A polished answer without its source passage teaches a less useful relationship.

Use the message format your provider supports. A common representation alternates user and assistant messages after the system instructions. Keep the current user request last and label retrieved material as data.
interpretation: Do not mix an example answer into the current user’s request as though the user supplied it.

examples.title: Inspect the structure before adding more examples
paragraphs: Each dictionary is one message. The role tells the API how that message participates in the conversation.
examples.code:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "Use the supplied manual. Ask if evidence is missing."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "P7: which revision applies? Evidence: none."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Which revision is listed on P7?"},
]
print([message["role"] for message in messages])
interpretation: The example response belongs to an assistant turn. The programming challenge will append a separate current request.

parts.title: 3. Reserve space before selecting examples
paragraphs: The request also needs instructions, tool definitions, retrieved material and room for the output. Decide how much of the context allowance examples may use. Measure costs with the provider’s tokenizer or usage tools, including message overhead where applicable.

Our workshop supplies recorded costs for complete examples. It selects the requested kind from the development split, then scans in order and accepts each example that fits. This first-fit rule is easy to inspect. It does not find the most informative combination.
parts.calculation:
Example allowance: 80 tokens
A costs 40 → select A; 40 remain
B costs 55 → skip B; 40 remain
interpretation: The recorded costs are teaching fixtures, not token counts calculated by the browser. A production request needs a full context check after assembly.

parts.title: 4. An example can be correct and still be a poor choice
paragraphs: Two nearly identical supported answers may use the space that would have shown a missing-evidence case. An example may also depend on information absent from its input, or contain an obsolete policy. Review content as well as length.

For a small task, begin with a few deliberately contrasting demonstrations. Compare their order and selection on development cases. If dynamic retrieval chooses demonstrations, test that selector too: a relevance score does not enforce privacy or keep held-out questions out of the pool.
interpretation: Longer prompts are not automatically better. The evaluation must justify the added examples and their cost.

parts.title: 5. Leave the test answers outside the prompt
paragraphs: Keep development cases separate from the held-out set used to assess the chosen prompt. Near duplicates can leak the answer just as easily as exact copies. Split by the unit that matters, such as asset family or customer conversation, when related records would otherwise cross the boundary.

Once you inspect held-out failures and use them to change the prompt, those examples have become development evidence for the next revision. Retain them as regression tests and collect fresh cases for another independent assessment.
interpretation: Record the example IDs, their order and the prompt version with the run. A changed demonstration is a changed experiment.

parts.title: 6. Test the distinction the example was meant to teach
paragraphs: Try a new warning with sufficient evidence, then remove the decisive passage. The expected behaviour should change. Also try a different asset whose manual uses different wording. This checks whether the candidate learned a useful task pattern rather than simply repeating our sample answer.
A test double can verify message assembly. Only runs against the intended model can provide evidence about its responses, and those responses may vary across repetitions.
interpretation: The next lessons will keep this distinction between testing our program and evaluating the model visible.

practice.title: Can we assemble the examples without confusing them with the current question?
practice.question: Can we assemble the examples without confusing them with the current question?
task: A demonstration has a question and an answer, while the current request has no answer yet. Keep those conversation turns in order so the request does not become another answered example. Implement messages_for(instruction, examples, question). Each example dictionary contains input and output strings. Return a system message, a user/assistant pair for each example in order, and the current user question last. Leave the supplied list unchanged.

Use the supplied instruction, one demonstration and final question. Print only the roles in message order as the starter does. Constructing messages here neither selects a provider nor measures how a model would answer them.
practice.starter:
def messages_for(instruction, examples, question):
    pass
practice.solution:
def messages_for(instruction, examples, question):
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": instruction}]
    for item in examples:
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": item["input"]})
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": item["output"]})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": question})
    return messages

print([m["role"] for m in messages_for("Use evidence.", [{"input":"P7?", "output":"Need revision."}], "P8?")])
hints: Start a new list for the messages.
Append both turns for an example before moving to the next one.

assert [m["content"] for m in messages_for("S", items, "Q3")] == ["S","Q1","A1","Q2","A2","Q3"]
assert len(items) == 2

title: Why Did Botie Take So Long?
blurb: An answer arrives late, but the text cannot tell us where the time went. Follow one maintenance request through retrieval, tool calls and the final response.
openingTitle: The Answer Is Right. The Technician Is Still Waiting.
opening: A technician asks Botie which inspection procedure applies to pump 7. He finds the manual and gives a useful answer, but it takes much longer than yesterday. Was the manual search slow? Did a tool fail and retry? Did Botie keep asking the model for something he already had?

The final answer has thrown away most of that story. We need a record of the operations that produced it, with their relationships and timings still attached. Then we can change the part that actually caused the delay.

history.title: Following a Request Across Machines
blocks: A slow response was already difficult to explain when a request crossed several services. Each machine could have a local log without showing which work belonged to the same user request. Google’s 2010 Dapper paper described connecting that work through a trace. Individual spans record particular operations and their timing; relationships between spans show how those operations belong together.

OpenTelemetry supplies shared conventions for recording and carrying that relationship across service boundaries. Botie’s manual lookup and model call can then be examined as parts of the request that caused them. The contribution is the connection between those records, not another total-duration number. Our invented timings let us inspect that connection without treating them as measurements of a deployed assistant.

reading.experimentTitle: Which span measures the technician’s wait?
reading.experimentIntro: Select one request, find its root span, and measure its elapsed time. Compare that result with the child intervals when two tools overlap.
reading.connectionTitle: Keep the cause attached to the operation
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Measure one request
reading.exampleNote: Invented spans use a shared clock. Short trace names stand in for real trace identifiers.

intuition.title: Start with the whole request
intuition.explanation: The request begins before retrieval and ends after the answer has been assembled. Its interval contains the work the technician is waiting for.

scene.caption: The two lookups overlap. The answer call waits until both have finished.

intuition.title: Two kinds of duration answer different questions
intuition.explanation: Child time can count the same wall-clock interval twice when work runs in parallel. The root interval gives the elapsed request duration.

records.label: Child durations
cells: Sum of the selected operation durations

scene.caption: These invented spans also leave time outside the child operations. Do not silently call every uninstrumented interval model time.

parts.title: 1. Write down an operation while it happens
paragraphs: A span is a record for one operation. Give it a useful name, a start time and an end time. A manual lookup might also record which document version it searched and whether the service returned an error.
A log line tells us that something happened at a moment. A span gives the operation a duration. Both can be useful, provided we can connect them to the same request.
interpretation: Begin with boundaries you can act on: the request, a retrieval call, a model call and any tool whose failures matter.

parts.title: 2. Give related work an identity
paragraphs: A trace groups the spans belonging to one request. Each span has its own ID, and a child records the ID of the operation that started it. The request span has no parent in our complete fixture.

Two technicians can call the same tool at the same time. A tool name and timestamp alone cannot reliably tell us which request produced which call. The trace and parent IDs preserve that relationship.
interpretation: A parent describes causal context. It does not imply that siblings ran one after another.

parts.title: 3. Keep concurrent work on the same clock
paragraphs: Botie can request the manual and equipment details concurrently. On our table, both operations are active for part of the same interval. Adding their durations counts that shared time twice.

For the technician’s elapsed wait, measure the root request. To investigate its slow path, examine when dependencies actually finished and what the next operation was waiting for. Adding every descendant also double counts nested spans.
parts.calculation:
Request duration = end − start
Request duration = 900 − 0 = 900 milliseconds
interpretation: A sum of span durations is not automatically CPU time, either. An operation can spend much of its duration waiting on a network.

parts.title: 4. A retry needs its own visible attempt
paragraphs: Suppose manual search times out and succeeds on the second attempt. Recording only the successful call hides the first delay and its failure. Keep an enclosing operation and separate attempts, or otherwise record attempt numbers and errors clearly.
Marking an HTTP call successful only says it returned normally under that call’s definition. A model response can still cite the wrong manual. Later lessons will attach quality judgements separately.
interpretation: The trace should let us distinguish a slow successful call from a quick failure followed by a second call.

parts.title: 5. Carry the context across the tool boundary
paragraphs: When Botie calls another service, that service needs the current trace context if its work is to appear in the same trace. Instrumentation can inject that context into a request and extract it at the receiver. OpenTelemetry commonly uses the W3C traceparent header for this.

If propagation is lost, the receiver may create a new root. The work still happened, but the picture becomes disconnected. For queued or fan-in work, span links can express relationships that do not fit one parent.
interpretation: Do not infer that missing spans mean no work occurred. First check instrumentation, propagation and sampling.

parts.title: 6. Read a recorded span with Python
paragraphs: A dictionary keeps a timestamp beside its meaning. A list contains several span records. Selecting a trace should happen before choosing the root; otherwise another technician’s request can supply the duration by accident.
interpretation: This small program inspects recorded data. It does not install a tracer or send telemetry.

examples.title: Find the operation with no parent
paragraphs: The two records describe one request and a lookup inside it. None marks the root’s absent parent.
examples.code:
spans = [
    {"id": "request", "parent": None, "start": 10, "end": 210},
    {"id": "manual", "parent": "request", "start": 20, "end": 170},
]
roots = [s for s in spans if s["parent"] is None]
print(roots[0]["id"])
print(roots[0]["end"] - roots[0]["start"])
interpretation: The child describes part of the interval. The challenge adds selection between traces and rejects ambiguous root data.

parts.title: 7. Instrument the same boundaries in OpenTelemetry
paragraphs: A tracer creates spans. An SDK provider collects them, and an exporter sends them somewhere we can inspect. Start with the console exporter so we can see a small record without configuring a hosted dashboard.

The nested context manager below establishes the parent relationship for a local lookup. A real remote client also needs propagation. Use instrumentation suited to that client instead of assuming a Python with block follows an HTTP request into another process.
interpretation: This example records a real local function execution. Its tiny in-memory manual is still a fixture, and it performs no model inference.

references.title: Record a local lookup with the OpenTelemetry SDK
description: Run as a separate Python script. The SDK prints spans with generated identifiers and measured timestamps, so there is no fixed output to copy.
references.code:
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor, ConsoleSpanExporter

provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(ConsoleSpanExporter()))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
tracer = trace.get_tracer("perceptronlab.maintenance")

with tracer.start_as_current_span("maintenance-request"):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("manual-lookup") as lookup:
        manual = {"P7": "Request inspection before restart."}.get("P7")
        lookup.set_attribute("manual.found", manual is not None)

provider.shutdown()
setup: Install opentelemetry-api and opentelemetry-sdk in your own Python environment.
Run once in a new process; applications normally configure their provider once at startup.
interpretation: Inspect the child’s parent ID and the common trace ID. Console export is a first check, not a production storage policy.

parts.title: 8. Count tokens where they were consumed
paragraphs: Record usage on the model generation that consumed it. Input tokens and output tokens can have different prices, and caching or other provider categories may change the bill. Keep the model identifier and the pricing assumptions with a cost estimate.

A parent summary may already include its children’s usage. Summing that summary with those same children charges the work twice. A retry that reached the provider may add usage even if the application later discarded its answer.
parts.calculation:
Illustrative input cost = (1200 / 1000000) × 2 = 0.0024 currency units
Illustrative output cost = (300 / 1000000) × 8 = 0.0024 currency units
Estimated generation cost = 0.0024 + 0.0024 = 0.0048 currency units
interpretation: These rates are invented to show the calculation. Use the actual provider’s pricing categories and usage records for accounting.

parts.title: 9. Keep useful evidence without copying private records
paragraphs: A technician’s request can contain names, internal equipment locations or secrets pasted by mistake. Logging every prompt verbatim creates another copy of that information. Decide which fields are necessary before exporting them.

For our maintenance flow, a document version and a controlled error code may answer the debugging question without retaining the full manual. Redact before export, restrict access, and set retention deliberately. Do not put credentials or personal information in tracing baggage that may travel to other services.

Record boundary decisions where the application makes them: the policy revision, the resource identity and an access-controlled reason code for an allowed or denied action. Link the decision to its action ID so a later investigator can distinguish a blocked attempt from a write that actually happened. Do not copy secrets or hidden model reasoning to explain that decision.
interpretation: A redacted trace should still preserve operation identities and relationships. Redaction that removes every useful distinction makes diagnosis harder.

parts.title: 10. Use traces beside rates and distributions
paragraphs: One trace explains one recorded execution. Metrics can tell us whether slow requests are becoming common, while logs can retain details of a particular error. Correlating them lets us move from a rising error rate to an example of the failing path.

Sampling reduces the stored trace volume. A sampled set can miss rare failures, and selecting only slow traces biases latency summaries. Record the sampling policy and compute service-wide metrics from appropriate observations.
interpretation: A missing failure in the viewer is weak evidence if the relevant request was never retained.

parts.title: 11. Repair the part the trace points to
paragraphs: If retrieval dominates the elapsed time, changing the answer prompt may barely change the wait. If repeated model calls dominate, inspect the loop’s stopping rule and what each call receives. If the root has a large unexplained gap, instrument that gap before guessing.

Compare the repaired request with fresh requests under similar conditions. Keep quality checks beside timing so an answer that arrives quickly but ignores the manual does not look like a successful repair.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop measures the root of a chosen trace. The changed case introduces overlap, and the fresh case mixes in another request to test whether the construction still follows the right technician.

quiz.prompt: Which fields let us attach a lookup to the correct request?
options: Its trace ID and parent relationship
The order in which log lines reached storage
quiz.because: Transport and storage can reorder events. The identifiers retain the intended relationship.

given.data: Two requests call manual-lookup concurrently. Their trace IDs differ, and each lookup records its parent span ID.

quiz.prompt: This record fully explains the request’s latency.
quiz.because: The failed attempt and any retry wait are missing from the explanation.

given.data: A retry succeeds after the first attempt times out. Only the successful attempt is stored.

practice.title: How long did the selected technician wait?
practice.question: How long did the selected technician wait?
task: A technician waits for the whole request, not for the sum of every nested operation. Find the selected request’s outer span before measuring its elapsed time. Write request_duration(spans, trace_id). Each span has trace, parent, start and end. Return the selected trace’s root duration in milliseconds.

Require exactly one selected span with parent=None. Raise ValueError for missing or multiple roots, nonnumeric or nonfinite root times, Boolean times, or an end before its start. This function measures the root; it does not validate every child relationship.
Use the supplied two-trace fixture and print the duration for A.
practice.starter:
def request_duration(spans, trace_id):
    pass

spans = [
    {"trace": "A", "parent": None, "start": 20, "end": 470},
    {"trace": "A", "parent": "root", "start": 30, "end": 310},
    {"trace": "A", "parent": "root", "start": 50, "end": 330},
    {"trace": "B", "parent": None, "start": 0, "end": 900},
]
print(request_duration(spans, "A"))
practice.solution:
import math

def request_duration(spans, trace_id):
    selected = [s for s in spans if s["trace"] == trace_id]
    roots = [s for s in selected if s["parent"] is None]
    if len(roots) != 1:
        raise ValueError("Expected exactly one request span")
    root = roots[0]
    start, end = root["start"], root["end"]
    if (isinstance(start, bool) or isinstance(end, bool)
            or not isinstance(start, (int, float))
            or not isinstance(end, (int, float))
            or not math.isfinite(start) or not math.isfinite(end)
            or end < start):
        raise ValueError("Invalid root timing")
    return end - start

spans = [
    {"trace": "A", "parent": None, "start": 20, "end": 470},
    {"trace": "A", "parent": "root", "start": 30, "end": 310},
    {"trace": "A", "parent": "root", "start": 50, "end": 330},
    {"trace": "B", "parent": None, "start": 0, "end": 900},
]
print(request_duration(spans, "A"))
hints: Select trace A before looking for its root.
A root has parent=None. Subtract its start from its end; do not add child durations.

tests.name: No root
Ambiguous root
Invalid timing

build.problem: Botie needs the elapsed request time while lookup calls may overlap and other technicians are active.
build.challenge: Keep records matching the requested trace, find its one request span, measure that span and return its single duration. All times use milliseconds on the same clock.

cases.name: Another technician is in the same export

build.why: The elapsed request interval follows one trace’s root, independently of overlapping children or unrelated traces.
build.limitation: These invented complete traces have a single root and a shared clock. Real exports can be sampled, incomplete or affected by clock skew.

Find the request span before measuring durations. Return the first entry of that one-span duration list.

questions.prompt: Which measurement describes elapsed request time?
questions.because: The request boundary measures the whole wait. The child intervals overlap and omit some surrounding work.

given.data: A request spans 0–900 ms. Its children span 50–350, 100–500 and 500–850 ms.

questions.prompt: The shared parent alone does not establish a sequential execution order.
questions.because: Parentage records context, while timing and dependencies determine execution order.

given.data: Two child spans have the same parent and overlap in time.

title: Can We Find the Run Behind This Score?
blurb: A dashboard says answers improved. Connect scores to their requests and prompt versions so we can see which answers were actually checked.
openingTitle: Which Version Gave That Answer?
opening: Botie’s new prompt seems better at answering maintenance questions. The average quality score has gone up. Before we celebrate, which requests received scores? Were both prompt versions tested on comparable questions? Did a tool-level score get mistaken for a judgement of the final answer?

Langfuse gives us somewhere to connect execution records, prompt versions and evaluations. We will work through the records first, then see how the SDK records those relationships. A useful dashboard depends on those relationships being correct.

history.title: The Answer and Its Test Used to Live Apart

sources.title: Langfuse project history: tracing, prompt management and experiments

blocks: After a language-model application ships, its developers need to connect a poor answer with the work that produced it. Ordinary request analytics often missed model-specific questions about quality, cost and changing prompts. Langfuse’s July 19, 2023 launch described open-source product analytics for LLM applications built around those needs.

The project first concentrated on tracing and later added prompt management and dataset experiments. That development connects two records that otherwise drift apart: the actual execution and the judgement of its answer. In the maintenance example, a run identifier lets us return from a suspicious score to the retrieved manual and model output that were judged. Langfuse organises that evidence; the evaluator still has to justify what the score means.

reading.experimentTitle: Are the improved scores covering the whole version?
reading.experimentIntro: Attach one rubric version’s scores by trace ID, select the prompt version, and report the available-score mean beside its coverage.
reading.connectionTitle: Make every judgement traceable to its run
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Summarise scored runs honestly
reading.outputLabel: [Mean available score, fraction of runs scored]
reading.exampleNote: The records are invented exports. No data is sent to Langfuse by this workshop.

intuition.title: A score needs an address
intuition.explanation: The score rows arrived in a different order from the request rows. Joining by row position would attach a good answer’s score to the wrong request.

scene.caption: Missing means we do not have this judgement. It is different from a score of zero.

intuition.title: Keep the denominator visible
intuition.explanation: Only two of the three requests have the selected judgement. Report both what those judgements say and how much of the version they cover.

records.label: Coverage
cells: About two thirds received this judgement

scene.caption: A high score with low coverage can hide failures that never reached the evaluator.

parts.title: 1. Choose the boundary of one trace
paragraphs: Use one trace for a maintenance request whose outcome we want to inspect. Its observations describe operations within that request, such as retrieving a manual and producing an answer. A session can group several requests from the same conversation.
Keep these meanings stable. If one deployment records a whole conversation as one trace and another records each turn separately, a trace-level latency comparison mixes different units of work.
interpretation: The trace boundary should answer a question someone actually asks about the service.

parts.title: 2. Give observations the right jobs
paragraphs: A general span can enclose application work. A generation describes a model interaction and can carry the model identifier, input, output and usage. A retrieval operation should keep the retrieved document identities attached to that operation.

The resulting tree lets us inspect the evidence available before an answer. It cannot reveal private model reasoning, and it should not be presented as a complete explanation of why the model chose particular words.
interpretation: Instrument actual operations. A recorded answer fixture should not be labelled as a live model call.

parts.title: 3. Send a small real execution to Langfuse
paragraphs: Start with a harmless local lookup and a surrounding request observation. The context manager keeps the active parent while the child runs. When the script ends, flush queued telemetry so a short-lived process does not exit before export.

Configure credentials and the destination in your own environment. The browser workshop has neither, so its records stay local. A successful export checks the instrumentation path, not the correctness of a maintenance assistant.
interpretation: This example deliberately records a span for a dictionary lookup. It does not claim to run a model.

references.title: Trace a lookup before adding model instrumentation
description: The lookup below actually runs locally. Its timing is measured by the SDK and its records are sent to your configured Langfuse project.
references.code:
from langfuse import get_client

client = get_client()
manuals = {"P7": {"revision": "r4", "procedure": "inspection-required"}}
with client.start_as_current_observation(as_type="span", name="maintenance-request") as request:
    with client.start_as_current_observation(as_type="span", name="manual-lookup") as lookup:
        result = manuals.get("P7")
        lookup.update(output={"found": result is not None, "revision": result["revision"]})
    request.update(output={"lookup_complete": result is not None})
client.flush()
setup: Install langfuse in a separate Python environment.
Set LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY, LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY and LANGFUSE_BASE_URL for your project. Keep credentials out of browser code and source control.
Use an appropriate test project and inspect its data retention before sending real requests.
interpretation: Open the request and inspect the manual-lookup child. These fixture values describe a local dictionary, not a production retrieval result.

parts.title: 4. Record the prompt that was actually used
paragraphs: A label such as production can point to a different prompt tomorrow. A version identifies a particular saved revision. Record the resolved version with the run so we can distinguish changes to instructions from changes in questions.

The compiled text also depends on its variables. Keep the manual revision, the retrieval configuration and the model configuration identifiable. A prompt version alone cannot reproduce an answer whose evidence changed.
interpretation: Resolved versions describe what ran. A movable label describes how the application chose it.

parts.title: 5. Connect a managed prompt to its generation
paragraphs: Passing a managed prompt object to a Langfuse generation links the observation to that prompt. The helper below accepts a real text-generation callable from your application; the lesson does not replace it with a canned model answer.

Create a text prompt named maintenance-answer with a question variable before using the helper. Decide separately whether retaining its compiled input is appropriate for the data your service handles.
interpretation: This records the input and output of the supplied callable. Its result and cost depend on the provider and implementation you supply.

references.title: Wrap your application’s text generator
description: Supply generate as a callable that receives the compiled prompt and returns the real model’s text response. This helper does not invoke itself.
references.code:
from langfuse import get_client

def traced_answer(question, generate, model_name):
    client = get_client()
    prompt = client.get_prompt("maintenance-answer")
    compiled = prompt.compile(question=question)
    with client.start_as_current_observation(
        as_type="generation", name="maintenance-answer",
        model=model_name, prompt=prompt, input=compiled,
    ) as generation:
        answer = generate(compiled)
        generation.update(output=answer)
        return answer
setup: Configure the Langfuse SDK as in the preceding example.
Create the named text prompt and provide your application’s authenticated generator and matching model name.
Call client.flush() during orderly shutdown of a short-lived script. Add actual provider usage if your integration does not already record it.
interpretation: Keep the provider call inside the observation so the recorded duration covers it. Do not report invented token counts.

parts.title: 6. A score needs a meaning as well as a number
paragraphs: An outcome score might describe the whole request. A retrieval score might describe whether a particular result contains the answer. Attach each score at the level it evaluates, using the trace ID and, for an observation-level judgement, its observation ID.

Name the criterion and identify the evaluator or rubric version. A rubric is the written scoring rule, including what earns each score. For example, citation support asks whether the cited passage actually supports the answer. A score named quality is hard to compare if another evaluator is judging writing style instead. A human judgement and a model judgement can disagree without either being a transmission error.
interpretation: The numeric scale is part of the contract. Our workshop uses zero to one; other evaluations can use categories or different ranges.

parts.title: 7. Join by identity before averaging
paragraphs: The scoring worker may finish requests in a different order. It may also score yesterday’s request while today’s run is still waiting. Use trace IDs to connect scores to runs, then filter the desired prompt version.

For this workshop, select one rubric revision first. Each run has at most one resulting score. Duplicate scores for that selection are an error that requires a policy, not an invitation to keep whichever arrived last.
interpretation: An identity join protects the meaning of a row when execution order changes.

examples.title: A score of zero is present
paragraphs: A dictionary indexed by trace ID can distinguish a missing judgement from a low judgement.
interpretation: Using a truthiness check would incorrectly treat the zero score as absent. Compare against None or check key membership.

parts.title: 8. Show coverage beside the available-score mean
paragraphs: If the evaluator fails on malformed answers, discarding those rows can make a broken prompt look excellent. Keep the run in the denominator for coverage even when its score is absent. Report evaluation errors separately so someone can fix them.

Our mean uses only present scores and is explicitly labelled that way. If none are present, its value is missing rather than zero. Deciding that an evaluation failure should fail a release is a separate policy we will define later.
parts.calculation:
Available-score mean = sum of present scores / number of present scores
Evaluation coverage = number of scored runs / number of selected runs
interpretation: Neither replacing every missing score with zero nor silently dropping it answers all questions. Preserve its missing state first.

parts.title: 9. Keep experiments attached to their cases
paragraphs: A dataset item describes one task and its expected behaviour. An experiment runs a candidate on items and connects its outputs to the corresponding cases. The experiment identity should include the application and prompt revisions being compared.

A production conversation is useful evidence, but copying it into an evaluation dataset requires review. Remove sensitive fields, preserve the information boundary and record why the case matters. Do not expose a hidden expected answer to the agent under test.
interpretation: The next lesson builds these cases so an experiment can measure more than a few favourable conversations.

parts.title: 10. Use the viewer to ask a specific question
paragraphs: When a score falls, open the underlying run. Did retrieval return the right manual revision? Did the answer omit a required warning? Did the evaluator judge against evidence that the agent never received?
Then compare like cases across versions. A chart filtered to prompt 3 is useful, but a higher score on an easier set of requests does not establish that prompt 3 improved the same task.
interpretation: Observability helps us find evidence. Evaluation design determines what comparison that evidence supports.

parts.title: 11. Plan for the tracing service being unavailable
paragraphs: A telemetry timeout should have a defined effect on the application. Decide whether export is buffered, retried, sampled or allowed to fail without blocking the maintenance response. Monitor dropped observations so an empty dashboard cannot quietly appear healthy.

Separate optional diagnostic export from the durable evidence required to authorise a write. If the application requires an approval record before dispatch, losing that record should prevent the write under that policy. A temporarily unavailable dashboard does not need to stop an otherwise permitted read-only manual lookup.

Treat exporting input and output as a data flow with access controls. The presence of a tracing SDK does not make every field appropriate to collect. Keep organisation boundaries in the tracing project’s access policy too, and test that a dashboard user cannot inspect another organisation’s requests merely by knowing a trace ID.
interpretation: Keep a stable set of non-sensitive identifiers even when you reduce payload detail.

parts.title: 12. Choose an inspection tool that fits the environment
paragraphs: Langfuse combines tracing with prompt and evaluation records. Phoenix also provides trace inspection and evaluations, using OpenTelemetry and OpenInference conventions for model-related data. Existing teams may already have an OpenTelemetry collector and a tracing backend.

Compare how the tools preserve your required IDs, where the data is stored, and how evaluators attach their results. Installing several exporters does not by itself produce better evidence, and can duplicate records if instrumentation overlaps.
interpretation: The portable skill is following a judgement back to the exact execution. The named tools provide different places to do that.

quiz.prompt: What must accompany the mean when discussing prompt 3?
options: Its evaluation coverage and reasons for missing scores
Only the mean, because two scores are sufficient
A claim that every unscored request failed
quiz.because: Missing judgement is not known failure or success. Coverage makes the evidence gap visible.

given.data: Prompt 3 has scores [1,1] on two of twenty requests. Prompt 2 has scores on all twenty comparable requests.

quiz.prompt: These scores can legitimately disagree.
quiz.because: The passage can be relevant while the final answer misuses it, or an answer can draw on a different passage.

given.data: A trace-level score checks the final answer; an observation-level score checks one retrieved passage.

practice.title: Which requests were actually evaluated?
practice.question: Which requests were actually evaluated?
task: Scores can arrive later and in a different order from their requests. Match the evidence by trace identity, retaining requests whose review has not arrived. Write score_report(runs, scores, version, rubric). Run records have traceId and promptVersion. Score records have traceId, rubric and value. Select the requested rubric and join by traceId, then report the requested prompt version.

Return (mean_available, coverage), using None for the mean if no selected runs have scores. Coverage includes every selected run. Reject an empty version selection, duplicate run IDs, duplicate IDs within the selected rubric, or selected-rubric score values outside [0,1], including nonfinite values and Booleans.

title: What Would Count as Doing the Job?
blurb: A plausible answer can still come from an unacceptable sequence of actions. Build maintenance cases that check the answer, permitted tools and failure behaviour.
openingTitle: The Answer Sounds Fine. It Also Created a Job Nobody Approved.
opening: A technician asks whether a manual requires an inspection. Botie correctly answers yes, but he also creates a job in the maintenance system. The wording is accurate. The behaviour is wrong because the technician asked for information, and job creation required approval.

How would a test catch that? We need to describe what the case permits, what it should produce and what it must leave untouched. A list of questions with attractive reference answers is not enough to evaluate an agent that can take actions.

history.title: Testing an Interaction Instead of One Answer

sources.title: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (2022)

blocks: Benchmarks built around isolated answers leave out much of an agent’s work. AgentBench evaluated language models acting through interactive environments, making sequences of decisions part of the task. HELM separately emphasised evaluating models across scenarios and multiple metrics rather than reducing capability to one favourable number.

Our maintenance tests borrow that question about behaviour: what did the system do in the environment it was given? The small cases here are invented regression fixtures, not a reproduction of either benchmark and not evidence about a particular model’s capability.

reading.experimentTitle: Which cases met both the task and the permission contract?
reading.experimentIntro: For each recorded case, check its expected outcome and the allowed tool list. Combine the per-case flags before averaging.
reading.connectionTitle: Turn failures into cases we can replay
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Evaluate a recorded trajectory
reading.outputLabel: Fraction of cases passing both checks
reading.exampleNote: The fixture’s outcome labels and tool names are deterministic. Semantic answer quality needs a separate evaluator.

intuition.title: Keep the permission beside the task
intuition.explanation: The allowed list is specific to each case. A job proposal is different from creating a job in the maintenance system.

scene.caption: The second case can use correct words and still violate its action contract.

intuition.title: Check the two branches before combining them
intuition.explanation: One branch checks the result label. The other checks whether each recorded call was permitted in that case.

scene.caption: The multiplication represents a logical AND for these binary flags. It is a teaching evaluator, not a language-understanding model.

parts.title: 1. Start with a failure someone would care about
paragraphs: “The assistant should be good” does not tell us what to test. “It must not create an inspection job before approval” does. So does “When the manual is absent, it should say the procedure is unknown rather than invent one.”

Choose cases from the work the service is expected to handle and from failures observed during development. Preserve why each case exists, so someone updating the dataset does not delete an awkward example merely because it lowers the score.
interpretation: A dataset is a collection of task contracts and evidence, not a scrapbook of impressive answers.

parts.title: 2. Separate input, environment and expectation
paragraphs: The input is the technician’s request. The environment includes the manual revision, equipment details, available tools and approval state. The expected behaviour records what would satisfy this case.

Expected information belongs to the evaluator. The assistant should see only what it would have at the decision point. If we slip the correct action into its context under a field called expected, we have changed the task.
interpretation: Store related fields together for evaluation, then deliberately construct the narrower input passed to the agent.

parts.title: 3. Allow several valid answers when the task allows them
paragraphs: Two technicians may phrase the same justified advice differently. Exact string matching can reject a good answer because a sentence changed. Define required claims, evidence and unacceptable omissions instead.

Some fields really are exact. A document ID, a structured outcome label or the absence of an unapproved write can have a deterministic check. Use those checks where the contract is precise, and reserve semantic review for the part that requires interpretation.
interpretation: Our workshop compares outcome labels exactly. It does not pretend that a matching label proves the accompanying prose is accurate.

parts.title: 4. Evaluate the route as well as the final response
paragraphs: Keep the executed tool calls and their arguments in the run record. Check whether the calls were authorised, whether the selected equipment matched the request, and whether an operation happened more often than allowed.

A list of permitted tool names is a useful first check. It cannot establish correct arguments, correct order or idempotence. A create_job call for the wrong pump is still wrong even when create_job was allowed.
interpretation: The small evaluator we build covers names and outcomes. A real maintenance test also inspects side effects in a sandbox or controlled fake service.

parts.title: 5. Make the test environment repeatable
paragraphs: A manual search that changes its results between candidate runs makes the comparison harder to interpret. Use a versioned retrieval snapshot or a controlled tool fixture when isolating a prompt change. When evaluating the live integration itself, record that it is a different kind of test.
A fake tool should enforce the same important input contract and return realistic failures. Returning success for every call removes the part of the problem we need the agent to handle.
interpretation: Use fixtures to isolate behaviour, then retain separate integration checks for permissions, network errors and actual service compatibility.

parts.title: 6. Keep failed and unfinished runs in view
paragraphs: A timeout, exhausted step budget or invalid structured response is a result of the test, even if no final answer exists. Store its failure category and the work completed before it stopped.

If a chart computes answer quality only for completed runs, show completion coverage beside it. Decide which failure categories automatically fail a task rather than letting an aggregation silently omit them.
interpretation: The unit being tested is the assigned task. A missing answer does not remove that task from the workload.

parts.title: 7. Build the deterministic check from named fields
paragraphs: A Python dictionary keeps each case’s expected outcome beside its observed outcome. Tool lists remain lists because a run may call several tools, including the same one more than once. A set is useful for membership checks against the allowed names.
The complete program below checks permissions on one case. The challenge adds outcome checking across a list of cases and validates the supplied record structure.
interpretation: An empty call list passes this narrow permission check. It may still fail the task because no useful work was done.

examples.title: Inspect an unapproved write
paragraphs: This question permits searching and proposing. Creating the job is outside that permission list.
examples.code:
case = {
    "allowed": ["search_manual", "propose_job"],
    "calls": ["search_manual", "create_job"],
}
allowed = set(case["allowed"])
violations = [name for name in case["calls"] if name not in allowed]
print(violations)
interpretation: The result identifies the call that needs investigation. A production check would also inspect the tool arguments and resulting state.

parts.title: 8. Look at slices before trusting the aggregate
paragraphs: Separate cases with missing manuals, ambiguous equipment IDs and approval requirements. These groups are slices of the evaluation dataset. A change can improve ordinary lookups while making the small approval slice worse.

Report the number of cases in each slice. A perfect rate on one unusual case is weak evidence, and repeating that same case with slightly different wording does not necessarily add an independent situation.
parts.calculation:
Illustrative ordinary cases: 18 passing / 18 tested = 1.0
Illustrative approval cases: 0 passing / 2 tested = 0.0
Combined rate: 18 / 20 = 0.9
interpretation: The combined rate hides a complete failure on the approval cases. Whether that blocks a release depends on the explicit contract, not on averaging it away.

parts.title: 9. Keep a set you do not tune against
paragraphs: Use development cases while changing prompts and tools. Keep a separate held-out set for checking the selected candidate. Split related conversations and documents together where needed so near copies do not appear on both sides.

Once a held-out failure becomes a debugging example, that case is no longer untouched evidence for the next change. Retain it as a regression case and refresh the independent evaluation process deliberately.
interpretation: A private test set can still leak through repeated manual inspection. The information boundary applies to people tuning the system as well as to its prompt.

parts.title: 10. Repeat runs without pretending they are new tasks
paragraphs: A model can choose different actions on repeated attempts. Run a case more than once when that variability matters, retaining the repetition number and configuration. Report both the case-level pattern and the individual failures.

Ten executions of one question help estimate variability on that question. They do not provide the same coverage as ten different maintenance situations. Compare candidates on the same case set and use a consistent repetition plan.
interpretation: Seeds and fixed settings can help reproducibility where supported, but they do not promise identical behaviour across every provider or infrastructure change.

parts.title: 11. Run the evaluator through Langfuse
paragraphs: The SDK can execute a task over local dataset items and attach evaluator results. This example deliberately uses recorded outputs so we can verify the evaluation plumbing before spending money on model calls.

The task reads only the case ID. The evaluator receives the expected outcome separately. Replacing the lookup with an agent runner later should preserve that separation and should include the recorded trajectory in the returned result.
interpretation: The experiment reports on these fixtures. It is not a benchmark of a live model.

references.title: Publish a small recorded-output experiment
description: The expected output is used by the evaluator, while the task retrieves a stored result for the input case.
references.code:
from langfuse import Evaluation, get_client

recorded_outputs = {"missing-manual": {"outcome": "abstain", "calls": ["search_manual"]}}
data = [{"input": {"case_id": "missing-manual"},
         "expected_output": {"outcome": "abstain", "allowed": ["search_manual"]}}]

def task(*, item, **kwargs):
    return recorded_outputs[item["input"]["case_id"]]

def evaluate_contract(*, output, expected_output, **kwargs):
    outcome_ok = output["outcome"] == expected_output["outcome"]
    tools_ok = all(name in expected_output["allowed"] for name in output["calls"])
    return Evaluation(name="task-contract-v1", value=float(outcome_ok and tools_ok))

client = get_client()
result = client.run_experiment(
    name="maintenance-recorded-fixtures", data=data,
    task=task, evaluators=[evaluate_contract],
    metadata={"application_revision": "fixture-1", "dataset_revision": "fixture-1"},
)
print(result.format())
client.flush()
setup: Install and configure langfuse for a test project as in the preceding lesson.
This experiment exports the supplied synthetic data. No model-provider credential is needed for this recorded-output task.
Pin the SDK version used by your own project and consult its matching reference when upgrading.
interpretation: The experiment’s results link outputs to cases. A hosted dataset can provide shared versioned items; keep its revision identifiable when comparing runs.

parts.title: 12. Check the checks with deliberate counterexamples
paragraphs: Give the evaluator an accurate outcome accompanied by an unapproved call. Then give it permitted calls with the wrong outcome. Both should fail. Also include a valid abstention with no write operation so the evaluator does not mistake restraint for failure.
These are tests of the evaluator itself. If it cannot reject a known bad record, a green dashboard is not useful evidence about the agent.
interpretation: Botie’s changed workshop case keeps the answer label correct while introducing an unauthorised action. The repair must preserve the outcome check and add the missing permission check.

parts.title: 13. Record what this dataset still cannot establish
paragraphs: A small regression suite can show that known cases still work. It does not enumerate every possible instruction, manual revision or sequence of tool failures. Extend coverage from real problems and planned stress cases, while protecting sensitive production data.

Some properties need tests outside the language-model loop. Access control should be enforced by the service, and a duplicate write should be prevented by a transaction or idempotency rule rather than merely discouraged by a prompt.

The tool-name check in this lesson is deliberately incomplete: search_manual can be permitted while its requested organisation or equipment record is forbidden. Add executor-level tests for those arguments and inspect the resulting state. Include useful allowed cases near each forbidden boundary so a repair that refuses everything cannot appear successful.
interpretation: The evaluator checks evidence of behaviour. The application still needs boundaries that remain effective when the model chooses badly.

Return a list of booleans in case order. A case passes only if outcome equals expected and every calls entry is in allowed.

Require a list of dictionaries. Each expected and outcome must be a nonempty string; allowed and calls must be lists of strings. Raise ValueError otherwise. An empty cases list returns []. This evaluator intentionally does not check tool arguments or free-text correctness.
Print results for the supplied two cases, then print their passing fraction.

topic: Testing the Program Around the Model
title: What Can We Test Without Calling a Model?
blurb: An agent framework can run our tools, but a test model and a real model answer different questions. Build contract checks before spending time on live evaluations.
openingTitle: The Model Changes Its Wording, but Our Bug Is in the Code
opening: We rename a tool argument and accidentally pass the wrong asset to the manual service. Running the real model ten times will not make that wiring clearer. We need a test that supplies a known call and checks exactly what our program does with it.
Then we need a different kind of test: will the intended model choose the correct tool on an unfamiliar request? Both matter. Keeping them separate makes a failed test much easier to investigate.

history.title: A Test Double Gives Us Control Over One Boundary
blocks: Software tests often need to observe a caller’s reaction without depending on a slow or unpredictable service. Test doubles replace that dependency with controlled behaviour. Martin Fowler’s 2007 account distinguished several forms, including stubs that supply prepared answers and mocks that can check expected interactions. This was a testing technique before the dependency was a language model.

Pydantic AI’s TestModel and FunctionModel, and LangChain’s mock-model tests, apply the same idea to agent code. Supply a known response and check what the application does next. That lets us reproduce a malformed proposal or a tool error cheaply. It deliberately leaves the real model out, so it cannot establish how often a provider will produce a useful answer; integration tests and task evaluations answer that later question.

parts.title: 1. Draw the boundary you are replacing
paragraphs: Our program sends messages and tool definitions to a model, receives a proposed call, validates it, and invokes a service. For a wiring test, we can supply a predetermined model response, such as a call naming P7, and check where our code sends it. That substitute is a test double. A separate fake service can record the requested asset and return an invented manual without contacting the maintenance system.

Replacing the model alone does not make tool effects harmless: framework test models may still call real tool functions. Inject isolated dependencies and block unexpected network requests in the test environment.
interpretation: Choose a known fixture at each external boundary. Never let a local test accidentally create a production work order.

parts.title: 2. Assert the argument that matters
paragraphs: For this exercise, each case expects exactly one manual-read call. We compare its tool name and asset. In a real test, also inspect identity, authorisation decisions and the returned observation. A correct-looking final answer cannot establish these facts.
If several valid routes can solve the task, do not require one exact sequence unless that sequence is itself a requirement. Strict trajectory equality can fail useful alternatives.
interpretation: Our single-call contract is intentionally narrow. A full trajectory requires call IDs, ordering constraints and effect checks.

examples.title: Compare named fields, not sentences
paragraphs: This test inspects one recorded call. It does not ask a model to grade its own wording.
interpretation: Choosing the right tool did not prevent it from receiving the wrong asset.

parts.title: 3. Run a Pydantic AI test with the network disabled
paragraphs: TestModel is a procedural stand-in, not a small language model. The following smoke test has no tools and returns a supplied string. It establishes that the application can run an agent and read its output through the framework API.

For a tool test, override the model on your existing agent and supply fake dependencies. TestModel normally exercises tools with generated arguments; FunctionModel gives finer control when a particular sequence matters. Read the recorded calls rather than assuming a final string proves the calls were correct.
interpretation: The recipe runs in your own Python environment. The browser challenge below tests a plain-Python report over recorded calls.

references.title: A provider-free Pydantic AI smoke test
description: No provider credentials are needed for this example. No external tools are registered.
references.code:
from pydantic_ai import Agent, models
from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel

models.ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS = False
agent = Agent(TestModel(custom_output_text="Manual lookup needs an asset."))
result = agent.run_sync("Which manual applies?")
assert result.output == "Manual lookup needs an asset."
print(result.output)
setup: Create a separate virtual environment and install pydantic-ai using python -m pip install pydantic-ai.
Record the installed version in your project lockfile. This recipe was checked against the documentation on 19 October 2026.
interpretation: A passing assertion checks this framework boundary. It says nothing about the choice a production model would make.
Keep ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS disabled for this test suite and replace any real service dependencies before adding tools.

parts.title: 4. Keep the same separation in LangChain and LangGraph
paragraphs: Use a mock chat model when testing application reactions to a known response. If the agent uses LangGraph persistence, use an isolated checkpointer and a distinct thread for each test unless the test deliberately exercises resumption. Otherwise an earlier run can supply state that hides a missing step.

A small provider integration suite can then exercise tool schema compatibility and message formatting. A task evaluation tests the assembled system on representative requests. Record provider errors separately from scored answers.
interpretation: The earlier framework lessons show the actual agent and graph APIs. These testing boundaries apply whichever framework owns the loop.

parts.title: 5. A missing result is not a passing test
paragraphs: Expected cases form the denominator. Match observed calls by ID and mark absent results as missing. Reject duplicate IDs because there is no unambiguous call to compare under this one-call-per-case contract.
The same rule applies when workers finish out of order. Joining two lists by their positions can compare P7’s expected call to P8’s actual call and create misleading failures.
interpretation: An empty batch reports zero passes, zero failures and zero missing results. It provides no acceptance evidence.

parts.title: 6. Add the broken case before repairing the wiring
paragraphs: Keep the wrong-asset call as a failing regression fixture. Change the application mapping, rerun that fixture, then try another asset and a missing result. This tests the repair against the rule rather than only the particular name P7.
Finally run the intended model on new task cases. A deterministic test can establish that a valid call is handled properly; it cannot establish how often the model proposes one.
interpretation: Keep unit, integration and task-evaluation results separately named in CI so a reader knows what passed.
