title: The Right Numbers in the Wrong Columns
blurb: An API changes its field order. Keep the trained model attached to what each feature means.
openingTitle: Why Did the Same Pump Get a Different Score?
opening: Botie receives the same temperature and vibration readings as yesterday. The model has not changed, yet its score has. Someone changed the order of the fields in the response. Both entries are numbers, so the matrix multiplication happily carries on.
We need a boundary between the outside record and the model. That boundary names the measurements, checks their meaning, and arranges them in the order the model was trained to use.

history.title: A Model Can Depend on More Than Its Code

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: A model project can look like a small program wrapped around a learning algorithm. In practice, the learned coefficients also depend on the records that supplied their inputs. Sculley and colleagues’ 2015 technical debt paper examined how those surrounding dependencies make ML systems difficult to maintain. An upstream change can alter the meaning of a prediction even when the model’s source code stays untouched.

Feature order is one particularly small dependency we can inspect. A coefficient learned for temperature must keep receiving temperature when another program sends the record. A schema describes the named fields; an adapter arranges accepted fields into the representation the model expects. This agreement is a software contract. Keeping names attached to values gives us a way to check it before a matrix calculation conceals the mix-up.

parts.title: 1. A list keeps order; a record keeps names
paragraphs: A Python list stores values in a sequence. A dictionary lets us address a value by a key. Neither structure tells us the unit automatically. A temperature field still needs a stated unit and a policy for missing measurements.
Our adapter receives column names and aligned values. The saved model supplies its required names. Looking up each required name gives us the positions to gather.
interpretation: Reject repeated names. If temperature appears twice, choosing the first one conceals an ambiguous input.

parts.title: 2. Arrange the features before multiplying
paragraphs: The incoming record puts vibration first. The model expects temperature first. We gather by name, then perform the weighted sum. The adapter belongs before scaling as well, because the saved scaling values also belong to specific features.
parts.calculation:
incoming names = [vibration, temperature]
incoming values = [3, 20]
model order = [temperature, vibration]
arranged values = [20, 3]
score = 20 × 2 + 3 × 10 = 70
interpretation: Multiplying the original sequence would produce 206. Both answers are finite, so a numerical check alone cannot find the mistake.

examples.title: Read by name
paragraphs: A dictionary can make the intended order explicit.
examples.code:
row = {"vibration": 3, "temperature": 20}
print([row[name] for name in ["temperature", "vibration"]])
interpretation: The dictionary order is irrelevant because the requested names determine the output order.

parts.title: 3. Give the boundary a useful failure
paragraphs: A missing required field should identify the field. An unexpected optional field can be ignored if the contract says so. Reject unequal name and value lengths before pairing them; zip otherwise truncates silently.
Version a unit change or implement an explicit conversion. Accepting the same name with a different meaning creates the original bug again.
interpretation: The challenge checks structural correctness. A production adapter also validates types, finite values, ranges and units before serving a prediction.

parts.title: 4. Test a change that should preserve the score
paragraphs: Reorder the incoming names and values together. The arranged model vector should stay unchanged. Then remove a required field and expect an error. These tests describe observable behaviour and survive a rewrite of the adapter.
Store the required feature order with the fitted artifact. Keeping it in a second handwritten list gives the next change two places to drift.
interpretation: A passing contract test does not establish predictive accuracy. It establishes that the model received the intended representation.

parts.title: 5. Version the boundary with the artifact
paragraphs: Suppose the temperature name remains unchanged while its unit changes. A name-based gather will pass every shape test and still send the wrong quantity to the model. Store feature units and accepted schema version with the artifact, and make the adapter either convert a documented version or reject it.

A migration test should send the same physical reading through both supported representations and compare the resulting model vector. Keep that test separate from predictive evaluation so a unit bug cannot hide behind a favourable score.
interpretation: The feature contract is part of the model procedure. Review it whenever preprocessing or the producer changes.

title: A Fitted Object Should Remember Its Training
blurb: Separate fitting from prediction so a new request cannot quietly redefine the model’s reference.
openingTitle: Why Does One Visitor Change Another Visitor’s Result?
opening: Botie centres sensor readings before predicting. A helper computes the mean of whatever batch it receives. That seemed convenient during training. In the service, the same pump now gets a different centred value depending on which other requests arrive beside it.
We need the fitted reference to belong to the trained object. Prediction reads that reference. It does not relearn it from the current visitors.

history.title: Fit Once, Apply the Same Preparation

sources.title: Buitinck and colleagues: scikit-learn API design, 2013

blocks: Machine-learning libraries needed different algorithms to work together without every caller learning a new interface. The scikit-learn team’s 2013 API-design paper described a common arrangement: fit learns from a dataset, while prediction and transformation methods use the resulting state. That consistency lets a preprocessing object and a predictor participate in the same application.

For a centring procedure, the learned state includes the training mean. Later requests should use that stored reference. Relearning a mean from each request would give the same measurement a different meaning whenever its neighbours change. Separate fit and transform methods make the intended distinction visible, and a changed-batch test checks that the implementation actually respects it.

parts.title: 1. Give the reference an owner
paragraphs: Make one Python object responsible for the mean learned by one transformer. An object created from a class is an instance, and a named value stored on it is an attribute. Here the mean is that attribute. Creating a second instance gives another model its own mean. A mutable global variable would let unrelated models overwrite each other.
Fit calculates the reference from training values. Transform checks that fitting happened and subtracts the stored reference from each incoming value.
interpretation: Keep learned state separate from configuration. A setting says what fitting should do; an attribute records what fitting learned.

parts.title: 2. Follow a batch through the object
paragraphs: The training mean stays fixed while requests change. A NumPy array holds the numerical batch; the object owns the scalar reference.
parts.calculation:
training mean = (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 4
transform([7]) = [7 - 4] = [3]
transform([7, 100]) = [3, 96]
interpretation: A request-local mean would centre the lone value to zero and change it again beside 100.

examples.title: A request should not mutate its input
paragraphs: Subtraction creates a new array, leaving the stored readings available for another check.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
raw = np.array([7., 100.])
centred = raw - 4
print(raw.tolist())
print(centred.tolist())
interpretation: The object in the challenge owns the reference. The request still owns its original array.

parts.title: 3. Make invalid states hard to overlook
paragraphs: Before fitting, there is no learned centre. Raise a clear error instead of using an arbitrary zero. Reject empty or nonfinite training arrays. A deployment can load a previously fitted reference, but loading must check its schema and version.
Return a new transformed array. Changing the caller’s array in place makes later tests depend on call order.
interpretation: Re-fitting is an explicit operation. Serving code should use an immutable snapshot or coordinate replacement so concurrent requests see a consistent version.

parts.title: 4. Test the object across calls
paragraphs: Compare a reading transformed alone with its result inside a batch. Check that the stored mean remains unchanged. Use a second instance to detect accidental shared state.
When a model is saved, save its fitted preprocessing too. Reconstructing a mean from today’s data creates a new model procedure even if the weights are unchanged.
interpretation: These are software invariants. The best centre for the population remains an empirical modelling question.

Fit accepts a nonempty finite one-dimensional array, stores mean_, and returns self. Transform requires fitting and returns a new NumPy array using the saved mean. Reject nonfinite or non-vector inputs.

Store mean_ on each instance, so two independently fitted objects keep separate references. Raise ValueError for transform before fitting. Fit on [2,4,6], transform [7,100], and print the new array as a list.

title: Keep the Useful Candidates Without Losing Their IDs
blurb: Use indices and a bounded heap to select retrieval candidates while preserving ties and identities.
openingTitle: Botie Can Read Five Passages. We Found Fifty Thousand.
opening: A retrieval system assigns scores to passages. Passing every passage to an agent would consume its context and bury the useful evidence. We need a shortlist, and we still need to know which document produced each score.

Sorting is a useful first implementation. When the candidate collection is large, we need not sort every candidate to retain a small shortlist. Keep the current shortlist with its weakest member easy to find. A new candidate replaces that member only if it ranks better. A heap is a data structure that supports this repeated comparison efficiently. Both implementations must agree on what happens at a tie.

history.title: Keeping the Current Best Candidate Close
blocks: Selecting the next best item was an algorithm problem long before a retrieval system had thousands of passages to rank. J. W. J. Williams’ 1964 Heapsort algorithm described a heap: an array organised so an extreme item stays at its root. In his formulation the least item is immediately available, and insertion or extraction repairs the ordering without sorting the entire collection again.

That idea also helps a bounded shortlist. Keep only the best k candidates, with the weakest retained candidate easiest to inspect. A better arrival can replace it. Our workshop uses sorting to show which positions win; the Python challenge builds the bounded heap. Both must preserve passage IDs and the declared tie rule. Efficient selection does not decide whether the retrieval scores identify useful evidence.

parts.title: 1. Keep a candidate together
paragraphs: Store a candidate as an identity plus a score and original position. An identity names the evidence; position resolves equal scores. Sorting only the score list throws away the mapping back to text.
The workshop first returns ranked positions. Gather uses those positions to select IDs from the original list.
interpretation: Keep later permission filters attached to the same records. A highly ranked passage may still be inaccessible to this user.

parts.title: 2. Define the shortlist before choosing a structure
paragraphs: Select descending scores, retaining original order at equal scores. Clamp the requested length naturally to the number of available candidates. A request for zero results returns an empty list.
parts.calculation:
scores = [0.8, 0.9, 0.9]
ranked positions = [1, 2, 0]
first two IDs = [manual-B, manual-C]
interpretation: The workshop ranking tool uses sorting for inspectability. The coding challenge uses a heap to express the same selection rule.

examples.title: An index keeps the evidence attached
paragraphs: Pair an original position with each score before ordering.
examples.code:
scores = [.8,.9,.9]
ranked = sorted(enumerate(scores), key=lambda pair: -pair[1])
print(ranked)
interpretation: Each tuple contains a position and its score. Python’s stable sort retains input order for the tie.

parts.title: 3. Why keep the weakest retained item at the root?
paragraphs: Once the shortlist is full, a new candidate matters only if it outranks the weakest retained one. Comparing with that root avoids sorting every retained candidate on every arrival. Store score and negative original position in the heap so a later equal score is the weaker tie.
For n candidates and shortlist k, a bounded heap uses O(k) auxiliary storage and O(n log k) selection work for k greater than one. Sorting the final k items adds O(k log k).
interpretation: For small lists, a full sort may be simpler and faster in practice. Measure with realistic workloads instead of treating asymptotic notation as a timing result.

parts.title: 4. Test the uninteresting-looking ties
paragraphs: Distinct random scores miss identity and tie bugs. Include equal scores, negative scores, an empty list, and a shortlist longer than the input.
Ranking quality is a separate evaluation: an efficient shortlist can still contain irrelevant passages. Inspect relevance and answer support after testing selection correctness.

title: Which Jobs Can Start Before the Model Is Ready?
blurb: Represent a training workflow as dependencies, detect cycles, and separate readiness from completion.
openingTitle: The Evaluation Job Read Yesterday’s Features
opening: Botie starts data preparation and evaluation together. Evaluation finishes first because it found a file from yesterday. Every process returned successfully, but the result does not describe the model we intended to assess.

A workflow needs explicit dependencies: evaluation must wait for the preparation work it uses. It also needs run-specific artifacts, meaning the files or saved results produced by this particular run. A job becoming runnable means its prerequisites are satisfied. It does not mean the job has succeeded.

history.title: Dependencies Outlive a Single Script

sources.title: Kahn: Topological sorting of large networks, 1962

blocks: A job cannot use an input that another job has not produced yet. Large project networks made that ordering problem important well before ML pipelines. A. B. Kahn’s 1962 paper presented a method for topological sorting: arrange network activities so prerequisites come before the activities that depend on them. A cycle means that no ordering can satisfy all those dependencies.

Workflow systems such as Airflow apply dependency graphs to executable tasks. A directed edge says which task must precede another; an acyclic graph has no route that leads back to itself. For Botie, preparing training data must finish before the job that fits the model. The readiness matrix below isolates that ordering question. A real workflow also needs to identify the actual dataset version and record task failures.

parts.title: 1. Describe the jobs before launching them
paragraphs: Use a dictionary from job ID to a set of prerequisite IDs. Sets avoid counting the same dependency twice. Keep run status separate from this static structure.
A job with no prerequisites can start immediately. A job whose dependencies are all complete can start next, unless it is already running or complete.
interpretation: A production scheduler needs an atomic claim so two workers do not both start the same ready job.

parts.title: 2. Count satisfied dependencies
paragraphs: The dependency matrix has one row per waiting job and one column per possible prerequisite. Multiplying by the completion flags counts completed prerequisites in each row. Compare that with the row’s total requirement.
parts.calculation:
dependencies = [[1,0], [1,1]]
completed = [1,0]
satisfied = [1,1]
required = [1,2]
ready = [1,0]
interpretation: The workshop only receives waiting jobs. Otherwise readiness would also need to exclude jobs already claimed or completed.

examples.title: Which prerequisites are still missing?
paragraphs: A set difference names the unmet dependencies of one job.
interpretation: The set contains job IDs. A nonempty result means this job is still waiting.

parts.title: 3. A cycle cannot be solved by waiting longer
paragraphs: If fitting requires evaluation and evaluation requires fitting, neither can start. A topological ordering repeatedly removes jobs whose dependencies have been resolved. If unresolved jobs remain with no candidate, report a cycle.
Unknown dependency IDs are a different error. Validate references before sorting so a misspelled job is not reported as a mysterious deadlock.
interpretation: Feedback between training rounds belongs in explicitly bounded iterations or separate runs, not a hidden cycle in one run’s DAG.

parts.title: 4. Successful execution needs the intended artifact
paragraphs: Mark a prerequisite complete only after its output is committed and identified. A filename alone can point at stale data. Use run-specific identities and pass them to downstream jobs.
Retries should reuse the same logical input and avoid publishing partial output. This extends the fitted-object rule: state has an owner and a lifecycle.
interpretation: An order checker verifies graph structure. Integration tests must still inspect which model and dataset each job actually read.

parts.title: 5. A retry needs a commit boundary
paragraphs: A preparation job may write half its output before failing. Marking it complete because a path exists lets evaluation consume that partial file. Write to a temporary artifact identity, validate the result, then publish a complete manifest as the commit boundary.

A retry of the same logical job should either find the verified complete artifact or produce a new complete attempt. An orchestrator’s successful task status and an artifact’s publication should agree; test the interruption between them.
interpretation: This connects task dependencies to the later lineage lesson. Scheduling order alone does not establish output integrity.

Reject unknown dependencies or cycles with ValueError.

Assume job names and prerequisite names are strings. Print the order for the supplied prepare, fit and evaluate graph. An empty graph returns an empty list; this creates an ordering and does not execute or claim jobs.

title: Did the Caller Leave It Out, or Send No Reading?
blurb: Give absent measurements, explicit nulls and real zeroes different meanings before a request reaches the model.
openingTitle: The Default Replaced a Real Zero
opening: Botie receives a temperature reading of zero. The helper checks whether the value is true or false in Python, sees that zero counts as false, and substitutes yesterday’s default. Nothing crashes. The model now receives a temperature the sensor never sent.

Before arranging values into the model’s feature order, we need to decide which values the service accepts. A field can be absent, present with no measurement, or present with a number. Those are different situations. Let’s keep them separate long enough to choose a sensible policy.

prerequisites.title: Feature order at a model boundary

history.title: A Named Field Still Needs an Agreement

sources.title: JSON Schema: object properties and required fields
JSON Schema: null is a value
Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: An API, or application programming interface, lets one program ask another to do something. Here a sensor client sends readings to a prediction service. The two programs need an agreement about what those messages mean. Does leaving out temperature ask the service to use a default? Does sending null mean that no reading was available? Without that agreement, a harmless-looking replacement can change the model’s input.

A schema records rules that a program can check, including which field names must be present and which values they may contain. JSON Schema treats presence and null as separate questions. That distinction addresses a practical problem in exchanging records: a sender can produce a readable message that the receiver misunderstands. Sculley and colleagues’ 2015 paper describes how such upstream dependencies become a maintenance problem in ML systems. We will make this small part of the agreement explicit before applying the model’s saved transformations.

parts.title: 1. Look for the key before looking at its value
paragraphs: A Python dictionary connects a name, such as temperature, to a value. First ask whether that name is in the dictionary. Then, if it is, inspect what was supplied. A present None says something different from an omitted name; JSON decoding represents a supplied null as Python None.

The expression record.get(name) returns None in both of those situations. One option is to test name in record first. Another is to give get a unique object to return when the key is absent. That object is called a sentinel: it marks absence without being confused with a real supplied value.
interpretation: The field-order adapter from the earlier lesson still matters. We are now checking whether each named measurement is usable before arranging it.

parts.title: 2. Choose the missing-value policy deliberately
paragraphs: Our contract makes temperature optional and gives absence a documented default. Explicit null is rejected because this particular model path needs a measurement. Zero remains a measurement.

A default is part of model behaviour. If a service uses a training-derived replacement, save it with the fitted model. Recomputing a replacement from each request would reintroduce the mutable fitted-state problem.
parts.calculation:
default temperature = 5
request {}                         → use 5
request {temperature:0}            → use 0
request {temperature:null}         → reject
request {temperature:"0"}          → reject
interpretation: These are policy decisions, not estimates that the sensor is working correctly.

parts.title: 3. A number-shaped string is still another type
paragraphs: Converting every incoming value with float can accept text that a caller sent accidentally. It also hides which producer changed. Decide whether conversion belongs in a separately named compatibility adapter or whether the public boundary rejects it.

Python bool is a subclass of int. A numerical type check that accepts all int instances therefore also accepts True. Our small validator excludes booleans explicitly and rejects infinite or not-a-number values.
interpretation: JSON does not define nonfinite numerical literals. The Python procedure checks them too because internal callers can bypass JSON decoding.

examples.title: Inspect before replacing
paragraphs: This small program distinguishes presence and shows why a zero must survive. It does not implement the later reusable validator.
interpretation: Presence distinguishes the first two rows. The third row contains a valid number even though bool(0) is false.

parts.title: 4. Keep validation separate from preprocessing
paragraphs: First decide whether the record is acceptable. That is validation. For an accepted record, put the measurements into the model’s feature order and apply its saved transformations. Those steps prepare the input for prediction. Keeping them separate lets us say which part failed.

If temperature contains text that this service rejects, return an input error identifying that field. Passing the text onward and waiting for NumPy to fail would make the caller diagnose a later calculation instead. Keep sensitive raw readings out of general-purpose logs.
interpretation: The workshop keeps rejected entries visible as null beside a reject decision. Those entries are diagnostic output and must not be treated as model inputs.

parts.title: 5. Required and nullable answer different questions
paragraphs: A required property must be present. A nullable property permits the explicit null value. It is possible to require a property while allowing null, or make a property optional while rejecting null when it is supplied.

A complete service schema also specifies extra fields, collection sizes and accepted ranges. In JSON Schema, properties alone does not require a field, and additional fields are allowed unless the schema constrains them. These defaults deserve a deliberate review.
interpretation: These rules let a caller distinguish an omitted optional input from an invalid supplied measurement.

parts.title: 6. Do not let two producers invent two defaults
paragraphs: The Python client library and the server can each supply a default. If they choose different values, two callers can get different predictions while sending messages that both look valid. Decide whether omission asks the server to choose, and keep that decision with the model release.

Track rejected fields so a change becomes visible. A sudden rise in nulls could come from a failed sensor or a change in the code that writes messages. The validation result tells us where to investigate; it does not identify the cause by itself.
interpretation: Preserve the original request identity when reporting failure so the caller can correct that request rather than create an unrelated prediction.

practice.question: How can Botie replace an omitted reading without replacing a real zero?
task: Botie needs one reusable boundary check. Write read_optional_number(record, name, default). record is a dictionary and name is a nonempty string. The default must be a finite int or float, excluding bool. If name is absent, return the default. If present, keep a finite int or float, excluding bool; reject None with ValueError, another type with TypeError and a nonfinite number with ValueError.
Raise TypeError for an invalid record or field name, and ValueError for an invalid default. Do not mutate the dictionary or convert strings. Print the two values requested in the starter, in order.

    pass

print([read_optional_number({"temperature":0}, "temperature", 7),

title: Yesterday’s Client Still Sends the Old Request
blurb: Introduce a new request shape without guessing what an older client meant or silently changing its results.
openingTitle: A Rename Broke an Agent That Had Not Changed
opening: Botie’s tool searches maintenance manuals. It used to accept a text field and a limit on the number of results. A server update renames them query and count. Yesterday’s agent still sends the old names, so its searches fail even though neither the agent nor the manuals changed. Updating the server did not update every program that calls it.

We need an explicit way to recognise the message we received and translate supported older messages into one internal form. The question is which old behaviour we are promising to preserve, and for how long.

history.title: Two Programs Rarely Upgrade at the Same Instant

sources.title: JSON Schema: object properties and required fields
JSON Schema: dialect and vocabulary declaration
Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: A client is the program making the request; the server is the program handling it. They are often installed or updated separately. That creates the compatibility problem: how can we improve the server while existing clients still depend on yesterday’s messages? A request schema describes the accepted fields and values, but it cannot make all those programs upgrade together.

The ML technical debt paper published in 2015 discusses dependencies and consumers that can be difficult to track. An agent calling a retrieval tool is another such consumer. We will keep two explicitly supported message versions and write a small translator for each. These translators are adapters. They let the rest of the search code receive one agreed record while older callers finish migrating.

parts.title: 1. Separate the message version from the model version
paragraphs: A request version tells the server which names and rules the caller is using. A model version identifies the trained model being used to answer it. Changing the model does not necessarily require changing the message, and renaming a message field does not necessarily require retraining the model. Give those changes separate identifiers.

JSON Schema has its own versions too, called dialects. A dialect identifies the rules used to interpret the schema document. It is separate from our decision to call the old search message version 1 and the new one version 2.
interpretation: Give each identifier one job. Recording all of them is more useful than calling an entire deployment version 2.

parts.title: 2. Translate at the edge, then use one internal form
paragraphs: Read the declared version before choosing field names. For version 1, copy text into query and limit into count. Version 2 already has those names. In both cases, remove surrounding query whitespace, require remaining text, and apply the same count rules.

The result is one common internal record. Documentation may call this the canonical form; here that simply means the search code can always read query and count. It no longer needs to know which public message produced them.
interpretation: Both public messages now describe the same query and requested result count. Retrieval can consume that common form.

examples.title: Adapt a known historical fixture
paragraphs: A one-off fixture makes the rename visible. The challenge extends it into validation and version dispatch.
interpretation: Only the boundary knows these legacy names. This short demonstration assumes a valid version 1 fixture.

parts.title: 3. A new optional field can still break a reader
paragraphs: Compatibility has a direction. Can the new server read an old request? Can an old client read a new response? A strict reader that rejects unknown fields may reject an added optional field. A reader that ignores them might continue normally.
Changing a default is also observable. An omitted count can suddenly return a different number of passages even though every key still validates. Test behaviour as well as schema acceptance.
interpretation: Check the actual reader before promising compatibility. A version label alone cannot tell us whether that reader accepts a new field.

parts.title: 4. Do not guess a version from a convenient key
paragraphs: A message containing both text and query is ambiguous unless a declared version and its schema resolve it. Our contract rejects keys outside that version’s allowed set. An unsupported version returns an explicit error rather than falling through to the latest parser.
This strictness is a design choice for a small public request. Other systems allow extensions deliberately. Whichever policy you choose, test it in the direction your callers depend on.
interpretation: The workshop keeps both adapter branches visible. Version selection chooses a branch; it does not merge their outputs.

parts.title: 5. Plan a migration that existing callers can actually make
paragraphs: Publish the new shape, identify consumers and keep the agreed legacy adapter while they migrate. Record use by contract version without logging private queries. State a retirement date through the normal support channel and make unsupported-version errors actionable.
A rollback needs to understand requests already accepted by the new release. Returning to a server that recognises only version 1 can strand a client upgraded to version 2.
interpretation: A rollback plan therefore needs to name the client contracts it will still accept.

parts.title: 6. Save examples from both sides of the boundary
paragraphs: Keep representative request and response fixtures for supported versions. Verify that each accepted request becomes the intended canonical record and that ambiguous or unsupported forms fail. Add a previously broken client request as a regression test.

When responses evolve, define which extra fields clients may ignore and which values have changed meaning. Schema compatibility cannot establish that a new score still means the old thing; that is the next lesson’s problem.
interpretation: Fixtures from each supported client let us review a server change before coordinating every caller’s deployment.

parts.title: 7. Review success and error responses together
paragraphs: A client depends on the error contract too. Renaming a validation code or changing whether an unsupported version is retried can break recovery even if successful responses stay identical. Keep error types stable, and include the supported versions in safe public documentation.
Treat an invalid count as an input error. Quietly clamping it changes the operation the caller requested and can hide a bug in an agent’s tool arguments.
interpretation: The diagnostic workshop returns an error object. A real HTTP service also chooses a documented status and content type.

title: The Number Was Valid, but It Meant Something Else
blurb: Keep units and score direction attached to numerical values before reusing fitted preprocessing or ranking evidence.
openingTitle: Botie’s Temperature Suddenly Looks Dangerous
opening: The sensor response passes its schema checks. It has the expected field, and the value is a finite number. Botie’s model nevertheless reports a much larger score than yesterday. The device started reporting Fahrenheit while the fitted preprocessing still expects Celsius.

The number’s type cannot tell us its unit. We need the meaning of the number to cross the boundary with it, and we need to convert it before using the model’s saved reference. Retrieval scores have a similar trap: a smaller distance can be better, while a larger similarity can be better.

history.title: An Interface Can Carry the Right Type in the Wrong Unit

sources.title: NASA: Mars Climate Orbiter mishap investigation, PhaseI
Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Programs have exchanged numerical measurements much longer than they have served learned models. A number can be well formed while using the wrong unit. NASA’s 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation identified a ground-software file that supplied impulse data in English units where the receiving calculations expected metric units. The software interface specified a convention, but the integration failed to enforce it.

Our temperature service has the same kind of disagreement on a smaller scale. The fitted model saved a Celsius reference, and the new sensor supplies Fahrenheit. We need a semantic contract: an agreement about what the values mean, including their units. Checking field names and numerical types comes first, but the model also needs the measurement expressed in the representation it learned.

parts.title: 1. Attach a unit before comparing a value
paragraphs: Temperature in Celsius and temperature in Fahrenheit describe the same kind of quantity using different scales. The number needs its unit before another program can interpret it. A field called value leaves that information out; a documented unit field or a name such as temperature_c can make it explicit.

Guessing from the range is unreliable. Ordinary operating temperatures can produce plausible-looking numbers in either scale, so a range check may accept the value while the model interprets it incorrectly.
interpretation: A version adapter can make a documented conversion. It should not silently reinterpret an unknown unit.

parts.title: 2. Convert before applying fitted state
paragraphs: The model’s reference temperature was learned in Celsius. Convert the request into that representation first, then subtract the saved centre and apply the coefficient. Reversing those operations changes what the centre means.
Temperature conversion needs an offset as well as a scale. Converting a temperature difference uses the scale without the absolute-temperature offset.
parts.calculation:
incoming temperature = 68 F
Celsius = (68 - 32) × (5 / 9) = 20 C
saved centre = 4 C
centred reading = 20 - 4 = 16
coefficient = 2
illustrative score = 16 × 2 = 32
interpretation: Both requests now reach the same Celsius input and produce the same illustrative score.

examples.title: A complete conversion for an unseen measurement
paragraphs: This program converts an absolute temperature and centres it. The challenge adds accepted-unit and numerical-input checks.
examples.code:
fahrenheit = 50
celsius = (fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9
training_centre = 4
print(celsius)
print(celsius - training_centre)
interpretation: Both resulting quantities are expressed relative to the Celsius representation used during fitting.

parts.title: 3. A valid shape can conceal a different score definition
paragraphs: A retrieval tool may return a number beside each passage. That number needs an explanation too. A Euclidean distance describes how far two representations are apart, so the smaller distance comes first. Cosine similarity measures how closely their vector directions align, so the larger similarity comes first. A descending sort cannot be correct for both meanings.

Record the metric and its ranking direction with the index version. A similarity is not automatically a probability of relevance. A probability would need a defined event and evidence that its claimed likelihood agrees with observed outcomes; a finite similarity score supplies neither by itself.
parts.calculation:
IDs = [A,B,C]
reported distances = [0.7,0.2,0.2]
order for smaller-is-better = [B,C,A]
first two IDs = [B,C]
interpretation: The equal-distance tie keeps the declared incoming order. The score stays attached to its passage ID.

parts.title: 4. Name the normalisation a score assumes
paragraphs: Dot products, cosine similarities and squared distances are related only under stated assumptions. Cosine similarity divides by vector lengths. A zero vector needs an explicit policy because that division is undefined. Squaring a distance preserves its ordering, but changes its numerical scale and threshold meaning.
Do not transplant a threshold merely because two metrics return the same-shaped array. Keep the preprocessing, metric and threshold as one reviewed configuration.
interpretation: This lesson’s ranking challenge takes an explicit ordering direction. It does not infer the metric or calibrate its threshold.

parts.title: 5. Validate a batch’s interpretation, not only its length
paragraphs: An array shape tells us how many entries exist, not which axis means examples, features or time. A batch of two examples with three features has a different contract from three examples with two features. A transpose can create a valid matrix that answers a different question.
Document feature names, axis meanings, units and numerical dtype beside the model input. Validate these before relying on broadcasting or a matrix multiplication.
interpretation: The model’s first coefficient must receive the same named quantity, in the same unit and axis position, that it received during fitting.

parts.title: 6. Test equivalent representations at the boundary
paragraphs: Use two independently specified fixtures that describe the same physical input. Their canonical values and model predictions should agree within a justified numerical tolerance. Include a temperature where an offset matters; testing only a special point can hide a broken conversion.

For score adapters, use a case where the best score is the smallest, a negative-score case where larger is still better, and a tie. These fixtures expose meaning rather than checking only whether the function returned a list.
interpretation: Equivalent representations must really describe the same situation. Arbitrary perturbations are not automatically prediction invariances.

parts.title: 7. Make an unsupported meaning visible
paragraphs: If a caller sends Kelvin to a C/F-only interface, reject it with an actionable error. Adding Kelvin support later requires an explicit conversion and tests; it does not require guessing today. Similarly, a retrieval response that omits its metric should not inherit an unrelated threshold by accident.
Track contract versions and model versions with incident reports so a discrepancy can be reproduced. Avoid logging complete private prompts merely to record which representation was in use.
interpretation: When a device changes its calibration, review that assumption alongside the unit contract.

practice.question: How do we give the saved Celsius model the same temperature when a sensor sends Fahrenheit?
task: Write to_celsius(value, unit). Accept a finite int or float, excluding bool. unit must be exactly "C" or "F". Return a float in Celsius. Raise ValueError for an unsupported unit or invalid numerical value; do not infer units or change the caller’s record.
Print the converted value and its centred illustrative score using the saved Celsius centre and coefficient in the starter. The tests also use negative temperatures and an unsupported unit.
practice.starter:
import math

def to_celsius(value, unit):
    pass

c = to_celsius(77,"F")
print(c)
print((c-4)*2)
practice.solution:
import math

def to_celsius(value, unit):
    if type(value) not in (int,float) or not math.isfinite(value) or unit not in ("C","F"):
        raise ValueError("Unsupported temperature")
    return float(value) if unit=="C" else (value-32)*5/9

c = to_celsius(77,"F")
print(c)
print((c-4)*2)
hints: Validate the declared unit instead of guessing from the number.
An absolute Fahrenheit temperature needs both the offset and scale before Celsius centring.

practice.question: Does this score mean nearer or more similar, and which evidence IDs follow from that choice?
task: Write rank_ids(ids, scores, k, higher_is_better). The ID and finite-score lists have equal lengths and IDs are distinct strings. k is a nonnegative integer and higher_is_better is a Boolean. Return up to k IDs in the stated score direction, preserving input order at ties.
Assume these input contracts already passed validation. Print the shortlist for the supplied distances. Do not sort the IDs independently from their scores.
practice.solution:
def rank_ids(ids, scores, k, higher_is_better):
    order=sorted(range(len(ids)),key=lambda i: -scores[i] if higher_is_better else scores[i])
    return [ids[i] for i in order[:k]]

hints: Decide which score direction represents the best result. Sort positions in that direction, then use those positions to retrieve the matching passage IDs.
Python’s stable sort retains original order when score keys tie.

title: Should Botie Repeat the Request, or Find Out What Happened?
blurb: Give callers stable failure types, bounded retry rules and a separate path for operations whose outcome is unknown.
openingTitle: The Tool Timed Out After Creating the Job
opening: Botie asks a service to start a training job. The connection drops before the answer arrives. A second request might recover from a temporary network problem. It might also start a second expensive training job, because the first request may already have succeeded.

An error message needs to tell the caller what it can safely do next. We must distinguish an invalid request from a temporary refusal, and distinguish both from an operation whose outcome we have not yet established. A timeout describes what the caller observed, not necessarily what the service did.

history.title: A Lost Answer Leaves the Caller Unsure What Happened

sources.title: RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs (2023)

blocks: When one program calls another over a network, performing an action and receiving its answer are separate events. A training service can create a job just before the connection fails. The caller needs a way to describe that uncertainty, because repeating the command may create another job. A sentence written for a person is difficult for a program to use reliably: its wording can change without the failure changing.

HTTP, the request-and-response protocol used by web services, supplies status and method rules. RFC 9457, published in 2023 as a replacement for RFC 7807, adds a standard format for more specific problem details. A stable problem type lets the client recognise the category while the explanatory wording improves. We will use short outcome codes to decide what can happen next, and keep a lost answer separate from a confirmed failure.

parts.title: 1. Give a caller a stable failure identity
paragraphs: Suppose an invalid result count produces a response with a documented type. The caller can recognise that type and correct its arguments. The title and detail explain the occurrence to a person; changing those sentences should not force every client to rewrite its parser. An HTTP status still describes the broader response category.
Leave secrets and internal stack traces out of public details. Keep a safe operation identifier so the caller can later ask whether that particular training job was created.
interpretation: The browser examples use short application codes. A real RFC 9457 response uses its documented media type and a type URI.

parts.title: 2. Classify before choosing an action
paragraphs: Sending the same invalid argument again will not repair it. A service that temporarily lacks capacity may be able to accept it later. A failed sign-in may require a new login. Those cases need different next steps, even though none returned the answer Botie wanted.

Our policy calls the temporary outcomes rate_limited and unavailable. The usual technical word for temporary is transient. We keep outcome_unknown separate: it means the caller still needs to find out whether the operation happened. An unrecognised code stops until the service’s documented handling is known.
parts.calculation:
outcomes = [rate_limited, invalid_request, outcome_unknown, ok]
safe to repeat = [1,1,0,1]
attempts remaining = 2
next actions = [retry, stop, reconcile, done]
interpretation: The same repeat flag does not make an invalid request valid. An unknown outcome needs investigation before another creation attempt.

examples.title: A small machine-readable failure
paragraphs: This fixture separates a stable type from wording a user may read. It does not contact a service or perform a retry.
examples.code:
problem = {"type":"https://example.invalid/problems/invalid-count",
           "title":"Invalid result count", "status":400,
           "detail":"count must be an integer from1 to20"}
print(problem["type"].rsplit("/",1)[-1])
print(problem["status"])
interpretation: A client can recognise the documented type while the explanatory sentence changes. The example.invalid URI is an invented documentation identifier.

parts.title: 3. Repeating safely is an operation property
paragraphs: An idempotent operation has the same intended effect when repeated as when performed once. That does not mean it produces identical logs or uses no extra compute. Prediction may be repeatable while a tool that creates a purchase, sends a message or starts a job needs stronger handling.

An idempotency key can identify one logical operation if the service documents and enforces its scope, lifetime and behaviour for changed arguments. Adding an arbitrary key to a request does not create those guarantees.
interpretation: The workshop’s safe-to-repeat flags are supplied policy facts. They must not be trusted merely because a model put true in its tool arguments.

parts.title: 4. A lost response leaves two possible histories
paragraphs: After a lost create-job answer, there are still two possible histories: the job exists, or it does not. Keep the original operation ID and ask the service for its recorded result. This lookup is what reconcile means here. Finding the existing job avoids creating it again. A definite failure or confirmed absence may permit a retry under that service’s rules.
If the service cannot resolve the uncertainty, report it. Calling the request successful would invent an answer, and creating a fresh operation could duplicate the work.
interpretation: The browser simulation recommends reconcile. It does not implement an operation ledger, durable delivery or a network recovery protocol.

parts.title: 5. Bound waiting as well as the number of attempts
paragraphs: Even a safely repeatable request can cause trouble if every waiting client sends it again immediately. A backoff policy increases or otherwise spaces the waits between attempts. Small random differences in those waits, called jitter, can stop clients from all returning at the same instant. Respect the server’s documented Retry-After instruction as well.

The user still needs an answer within an overall deadline, so also bound the attempts and total wait. Retry-After can contain a date or a number of seconds. Interpret the documented form before deciding whether another wait fits.
parts.calculation:
server minimum wait = 3 seconds
local backoff = 1 second
chosen wait = max(3,1) = 3 seconds
remaining wait budget = 2 seconds
result = stop waiting; no retry fits this budget
interpretation: The exercise receives already parsed seconds. A production caller must also leave time for the next operation itself.

parts.title: 6. Review retries across the whole call chain
paragraphs: A browser, gateway, SDK and worker can each retry. Their combined number of attempts may greatly exceed the one loop you inspected. Assign ownership of recovery and preserve the logical operation identity across layers.
Record attempt counts, stable error categories and final outcomes. Separate a successful retry from an unresolved operation so observability does not turn uncertainty into a success rate.
interpretation: A temporary-failure label is evidence about this attempt. It does not establish that repeating a side effect is safe.

parts.title: 7. Keep failure behaviour compatible too
paragraphs: An older agent may know how to handle a documented invalid-count problem but not a newly invented replacement code. Keep supported error types stable or version their changed meaning. Test recovery branches alongside successful requests.

Use synthetic failures in local tests: an invalid request must stop, a bounded repeatable refusal may retry, and an uncertain side effect must reconcile. These tests should not send real messages or start training jobs.
interpretation: The challenges calculate decisions only. No code here creates a network operation, waits in real time or grants permission to repeat an actual side effect.

practice.question: Is there enough time to honour both the server’s minimum wait and the remaining budget?
task: Write allowed_wait(retry_after, backoff, wait_budget). All inputs are finite nonnegative numerical seconds, excluding bool. Return the larger of retry_after and backoff as a float if it is at most wait_budget; otherwise return None. Raise ValueError for invalid inputs.
The wait budget has already reserved time for the next request. Retry-After has already been parsed into seconds. Print both decisions in the starter; do not sleep or contact a service.
practice.starter:
import math

def allowed_wait(retry_after, backoff, wait_budget):
    pass

print(allowed_wait(3,1,2))
print(allowed_wait(1,2.5,5))
practice.solution:
import math

def allowed_wait(retry_after, backoff, wait_budget):
    values=(retry_after,backoff,wait_budget)
    if any(type(v) not in (int,float) or not math.isfinite(v) or v<0 for v in values):
        raise ValueError("Invalid wait budget")
    delay=max(retry_after,backoff)
    return float(delay) if delay<=wait_budget else None

print(allowed_wait(3,1,2))
print(allowed_wait(1,2.5,5))
hints: The server’s minimum and your own backoff are both lower bounds on a permissible wait.
A delay that exceeds the remaining wait budget has no permitted schedule in this policy.

title: One Correct Prediction Did Not Test the Interface
blurb: Turn expected relationships between requests into tests, then retain the small example that exposed a broken contract.
openingTitle: The Test Passed Until Another Pump Joined the Batch
opening: Botie tests a centring function on a batch whose mean happens to equal the saved training mean. It returns the expected values. The same pump moves into a busier batch, and its centred value changes because the helper recalculates the mean from current requests.

We could save this one bad batch as a test. We should. But we can also ask a more useful question: if the fitted transformation processes examples independently, should adding another example change the first result? That relationship gives us a way to look for a whole class of mistakes.

history.title: Write What Must Hold Across Many Inputs

sources.title: NumPy: allclose tolerance and broadcasting rules

blocks: A hand-calculated example can tell us what one prediction should be. It cannot list every future request. Some promises are easier to describe as relationships: if the same named measurements arrive in another order, the result should stay the same. Property-based testing starts from such a promise and tries many inputs that could contradict it.

Claessen and Hughes first published QuickCheck in 2000. The tool generated inputs for developer-written properties and helped reduce failures to smaller examples. Hypothesis brings this approach to Python. The useful result is a counterexample: a concrete input that breaks the stated promise. For our model interface, we will begin with the saved-centre mistake, then test whether changing feature order exposes another mistake. Each relationship must follow from the model’s actual behaviour.

parts.title: 1. Begin with a claim the interface actually makes
paragraphs: Our centring function promises to subtract the saved training centre from each example independently. Adding a neighbour to the batch should therefore leave the first example’s result alone. A statement like that, intended to hold across accepted inputs, is called a property.

Check the promise before turning it into a test. A model that deliberately ranks an example against its neighbours should depend on the batch. Training-mode batch normalisation also uses batch statistics. The same independence test would be wrong for those operations.
interpretation: A test that encodes the wrong promise can reject correct implementations.

parts.title: 2. Keep one calculated reference beside the relationship
paragraphs: The original batch happens to have the saved training mean. A helper that wrongly relearns the mean can therefore pass it. Move the same first reading into a different batch to separate the two implementations.
parts.calculation:
saved centre = 4
first batch = [2,6]
correct first result = 2 - 4 = -2

changed batch = [2,100]
correct first result = 2 - 4 = -2
wrong request mean = (2 + 100) / 2 = 51
wrong first result = 2 - 51 = -49
interpretation: The unchanged first reading becomes a diagnostic probe of which reference the code used.

examples.title: Observe the batch-independence relationship
paragraphs: This program uses a fixed fitted reference. It demonstrates the relation before the later challenge tests permutations of a named-feature interface.
examples.code:
centre = 4
def transform(values):
    return [value-centre for value in values]

print(transform([2,6])[0])
print(transform([2,100])[0])
interpretation: The neighbour changes, but the first example’s transformation keeps its meaning.

parts.title: 3. Change representation while preserving the underlying request
paragraphs: Keep every feature name attached to its value, then rearrange the pairs. A predictor that reads by name should receive the same observation and produce the same result. Rearranging values without their names would describe another observation.

This is a metamorphic test: change an input in a specified way and check the relationship we expect between the two results. Equality is the relationship here. Other tests may expect a known change in the result instead.
interpretation: The feature names must be distinct, and the prediction must be deterministic for the comparison to mean what we intend.

parts.title: 4. A property can pass for a useless implementation
paragraphs: A predictor that always returns zero is invariant to every feature permutation. It is still wrong for most requests. Combine relationship checks with independently calculated fixtures and other requirements.
Round-trip tests have a similar limitation: an encoder and decoder can share the same mistaken convention. A second source of expected meaning is useful when both sides could be wrong together.
interpretation: Passing a finite collection of tests is evidence about those inputs and assumptions. It is not a proof that the whole model or interface is correct.

parts.title: 5. Choose comparisons appropriate to numerical output
paragraphs: Floating-point evaluation can change slightly when arithmetic is rearranged. Define a tolerance from the calculation and its consequences, rather than choosing a loose value merely to make tests pass. Check shapes before comparing arrays so broadcasting cannot conceal a missing axis.

A common array check uses an absolute tolerance plus a relative term. Near zero, the absolute term matters. Decide explicitly how nonfinite values should be treated; do not let two NaNs count as a successful measurement comparison by accident.
parts.calculation:
scalar absolute-error rule:
|actual - expected| ≤ absolute tolerance

common relative-plus-absolute rule:
|actual - expected| ≤ absolute tolerance + relative tolerance × |expected|
interpretation: The workshop uses the first rule for one finite scalar. The exercise’s contract also uses a finite scalar prediction.

parts.title: 6. Generate cases that could contradict the claim
paragraphs: A property-based testing tool needs instructions for generating accepted inputs. Those instructions are called a strategy. For example, it could generate short lists of named finite measurements and then rearrange their pairs. Invalid-message tests ask a different question and need their own expected errors.

Our challenge keeps the list small and tries every permutation of its positions. That covers those particular reorderings completely. It still leaves other measurement values to be tested, and the number of reorderings grows too quickly to use this approach on a large feature list.
interpretation: Factorial growth makes full permutation enumeration unsuitable for a large feature schema. Keep this exercise’s feature lists small.

parts.title: 7. Keep the counterexample after fixing the code
paragraphs: When a generated case fails, save the smallest useful input and the expected behaviour as an incident regression. That test should fail on the old implementation and pass on the repair. Preserve the incident’s contract and relevant model/configuration versions.
A smaller case helps diagnosis, but do not remove the condition that made the failure real. An extreme neighbour may be exactly what distinguishes fitted-state reuse from request-local fitting.
interpretation: Record the seed or reproducible generated fixture when randomness participates. Avoid making a flaky retry the way a failing test disappears.

parts.title: 8. Test that the test can detect the known mistake
paragraphs: Run the property against a deliberately simple broken implementation in local test code: a positional feature reader, or a request-local mean. If the property never fails, inspect whether the generator changes anything relevant.
Keep that testing double separate from production code. It is a check of the test’s sensitivity to this known defect, not evidence that all other defects are covered.
interpretation: The challenge includes both a correct name-aware predictor and a broken positional predictor. Neither calls a live model service.

practice.title: Find feature permutations that break the prediction contract
practice.question: Which alternative message order exposes a predictor that attached meaning to position instead of a name?
task: Write permutation_failures(predict, names, values, atol). names contains distinct feature names, values contains aligned finite numbers, and atol is a finite nonnegative absolute tolerance. predict is a deterministic, nonmutating function accepting name and value lists and returning a finite scalar. Compare its baseline prediction with every permutation of aligned name/value pairs.

Return a list of the failing name orders, in itertools.permutations order; include a permutation only when its absolute prediction difference exceeds atol. Keep this exercise’s feature lists small. Print the failure list for the supplied positional predictor. A constant predictor can pass this property, so independent expected-value fixtures remain necessary. Then print how many of the four-feature first-value predictor’s name orders fail the same property.
hints: Rearrange a list of positions, then use that one arrangement for both feature names and values. Otherwise the test would change the observation itself.
Compare every changed prediction with the baseline using the declared tolerance.
Preserve enumeration order in the failure report so the counterexample is reproducible.

options: More copies of the same invariance claim

title: One Training Dataset, Several Unequal Files
blurb: Merge sufficient statistics instead of averaging the averages of unequal partitions.
openingTitle: Why Did Splitting the File Change the Mean?
opening: Botie’s training records no longer fit comfortably in one read. We process each file separately and average the file means. That sounds reasonable until one file has a hundred readings and another has two. The tiny file now has as much influence as the large one.
We need a summary that can be combined without forgetting how many observations it represents. For a mean, the sum and count are enough.

history.title: Move Summaries Instead of Every Row
blocks: Suppose a training dataset is spread across more files than one worker can process quickly. We can give each worker a portion, but then we need a way to combine its answer. Sending every original row back to one machine can recreate the bottleneck we were trying to remove.

Dean and Ghemawat's 2004 MapReduce paper described a programming model that separated work on individual records from combining results with the same key. The system handled distributing that work and retrying failed tasks. It gave programmers a way to describe the calculation without writing a separate scheduling system for every job.

For our mean, each worker can send a sum and a count. Those quantities still tell us how much data its answer represents, even when file sizes differ. A local mean alone has discarded that information. We will follow these small summaries through the same kind of merge, using ordinary Python before needing a distributed service.

parts.title: 1. A partition boundary is not a sampling weight
paragraphs: A partition is a storage or processing division. Its size may follow a date, a machine, or an upload batch. It need not represent an equally important population.
Keep a pair of numbers for each partition: the sum of accepted values and their count. Missing values must follow the same inclusion policy in both numbers.
interpretation: Selecting one feature column avoids reading irrelevant fields, but does not change the meaning of the observations.

parts.title: 2. Merge the quantities that add
paragraphs: Sums add across disjoint partitions. Counts do too. Divide only after those two merges.
parts.calculation:
total sum = 30 + 90 = 120
total count = 3 + 1 = 4
combined mean = 120 / 4 = 30
interpretation: An empty partition contributes zero to both totals. An entirely empty dataset has no mean; return an explicit missing result.

examples.title: Keep the count with the subtotal
paragraphs: One tuple describes each file without pretending it represents an equal-sized sample.
examples.code:
parts = [[10,10,10],[90]]
print([(sum(p),len(p)) for p in parts])
interpretation: The first tuple summarises three observations; the second summarises one.

parts.title: 3. A retry can count the same file twice
paragraphs: A merge assumes each observation contributes once. Retrying a successful task and appending its summary again violates that assumption. Store summaries by partition identity and input version, replacing the result for that logical partition.
Use immutable input snapshots during a training run. If a partition changes halfway through processing, even a correct reducer can combine incompatible versions.
interpretation: This is where data engineering meets the workflow graph: completion must refer to one identified input.

parts.title: 4. Precision and other summaries
paragraphs: Floating-point sums can differ slightly with merge order. Use suitable precision and numerical tolerances. Variance needs more information than a sum and count; quantiles generally cannot be recovered by averaging partition quantiles.
Choose a mergeable summary for the statistic you actually need, and compare it against an unpartitioned calculation on a small fixture.
interpretation: The workshop uses supplied sums and counts. The Python challenge constructs them from records so we can test changing partition boundaries.

parts.title: 5. A sum can lose small contributions
paragraphs: Floating-point arithmetic has finite precision. Adding many small values to a much larger total can lose information, and a different partitioning can change the reduction order. Pairwise or compensated summation can reduce the error.
Use a high-precision reference on a small difficult fixture and compare with a justified tolerance. Do not fix a mismatch by rounding every intermediate value, which may introduce still more error.
interpretation: The merge identity is exact over real arithmetic. Its floating-point implementation needs numerical testing as well as correct weights.

practice.title: Merge training batches without reweighting them
practice.question: Can the training mean stay unchanged when we repartition the same readings?
task: Three ordinary readings in one partition and one high reading in another should not give the two partitions equal influence. Write merged_mean(partitions) for lists of finite numerical readings. Return None if all partitions are empty. Otherwise return the mean over all readings.
Print the pooled mean for [[10,10,10],[90]]. Preserve the individual observation count when combining partitions, including partitions with no observations.
practice.solution:
def merged_mean(partitions):
    total = sum(sum(part) for part in partitions)
    count = sum(len(part) for part in partitions)
    return total / count if count else None

print(merged_mean([[10,10,10],[90]]))
hints: Keep counts until the final division.

tests.name: Empty partitions
tests.code: assert merged_mean([[],[3],[]]) == 3 and merged_mean([[],[]]) is None

build.why: The denominator preserves the number of contributing readings.
build.limitation: Counts are nonnegative and the workshop has at least one observation. Python handles the all-empty case.

title: Rebuild What the Model Could Have Known
blurb: Choose the latest eligible feature using both event time and availability time.
openingTitle: Today’s Database Knows Tomorrow’s Answer
opening: We want to train Botie using yesterday’s decisions. Today’s feature table contains corrections that arrived after those decisions. Joining each decision to the latest record would give the training model information its deployed counterpart never had.
We need to reconstruct the information boundary for each decision. First decide which records existed, then choose the latest event among those records.

history.title: Historical Retrieval Needs a Time Boundary

sources.title: Gojek and Google Cloud introduce Feast, January 2019

blocks: A corrected reading can tell us more about yesterday while still being something we did not know yesterday. Database researchers had to represent that distinction long before it became a training-data problem. In their 1986 paper, Snodgrass and Ahn separated when a fact applied in the world from when it was recorded in a database. Keeping both lets us ask what was believed at an earlier time, even after a correction.

Machine-learning teams face a related difficulty when rebuilding inputs for old predictions. Feast, announced by Gojek and Google Cloud in 2019, provided a shared feature store for training and serving. Its historical retrieval selects feature values against each training row's timestamp rather than attaching today's value to every old example.

Our lesson keeps an additional availability timestamp explicitly. A measurement may describe an earlier event but arrive after the prediction. We must check both boundaries to reconstruct what the service could have used. That extra rule is part of this example's contract; a feature store's point-in-time label alone does not promise it.

parts.title: 1. Keep the observation and its arrival separate
paragraphs: Event time describes when the feature refers to. Availability time describes when the serving system could use that version. A late correction can have an early event time and a late availability time.

For multiple assets, first group records by asset identity, then make the selection within each group. This grouping is the partition used by the query. Otherwise the newest reading may belong to a different pump.
interpretation: Retain historical versions. A table that overwrites every correction cannot reconstruct earlier knowledge merely by adding a query filter.

parts.title: 2. Filter first, then select the latest event
paragraphs: Both timestamps must be at or before the decision. Of the surviving rows, choose the greatest event time. Our coding contract breaks event-time ties by latest eligible availability, then by input order.
parts.calculation:
decision = 10
events = [8,9,6]
availability = [9,12,7]
eligible mask = [1,0,1]
eligible values = [20,18]
selected latest event value = 20
interpretation: The workshop exposes the eligibility stage. The Python challenge completes selection and handles the no-record case.

examples.title: Retain the late record in the history
paragraphs: The row is retained in raw history even when it is unavailable to a particular decision.
examples.code:
record = {"event":9, "available":12, "value":30}
print(record["available"] <= 10)
interpretation: Rejecting it for this decision does not mean deleting a correction that later decisions may use.

parts.title: 3. Freshness asks a different question
paragraphs: A record may have been available but be too old for the task. A maximum age compares the decision time with event time. Define that duration in the feature contract.
Availability histories depend on trustworthy timestamps. Clock uncertainty or ingestion bugs need investigation; a precise comparison over incorrect clocks is still incorrect.
interpretation: A missing eligible feature should trigger a declared fallback rather than pulling a later record into the past.

parts.title: 4. Replay the online procedure
paragraphs: Use the same entity keys, units and freshness limits in training and serving. Replay a small decision log against recorded historical inputs and compare chosen feature identities.
Keep the selected version ID in the audit trail. Matching a numerical value alone can hide a join to the wrong record.
interpretation: This reconstructs data eligibility. It does not prove labels, measurement quality or evaluation splits are correct.

practice.title: Select the last feature the service actually knew
practice.question: Which feature value was most recent among the records available at prediction time?
task: A later correction may describe an earlier event without having been available to the prediction. Choose the newest version the service actually knew at its cutoff. Write asof(rows, cutoff), where each row is (event, available, value) for one entity. Return the value with greatest (event, available, input position) among rows with both times <= cutoff, or None if none qualify.

All timestamps use a common clock and unit. The last input position wins an exact event-and-availability tie. Print the selected scalar for the starter’s unsorted records, or return None if no record qualifies.
practice.solution:
def asof(rows, cutoff):
    candidates = [(event, available, i, value) for i,(event,available,value) in enumerate(rows) if event <= cutoff and available <= cutoff]
    return max(candidates, key=lambda row: row[:3])[3] if candidates else None

print(asof([(8,9,20),(9,12,30),(6,7,18)], 10))
hints: Eligibility comes before max.
Include the declared tie fields in the comparison key.

build.problem: Botie needs the records that existed at a historical decision.
build.challenge: Build both timestamp masks, combine them, and filter values in original order.
build.why: Filtering preserves eligible versions for later latest-event selection.
build.limitation: One entity with valid timestamps is supplied; this stage returns eligible rows, not the final selected feature.

title: Stop a Broken Sensor Batch Before It Reaches Training
blurb: Separate row validation from batch acceptance and preserve rejected evidence for investigation.
openingTitle: The New Firmware Sends Plausible-Looking Numbers
opening: A sensor upgrade starts reporting values outside its documented range. Dropping those rows lets training continue, but it also removes nearly the entire night shift. The cleaned file looks tidy while the training population has changed.
We need two decisions: which rows meet the contract, and whether enough of this batch remains to use it. Keep the rejected rows so the producer can be repaired.

history.title: Checking Data Before Fitting

sources.title: Breck and colleagues: Data Validation for Machine Learning, SysML 2019

blocks: A training program can finish successfully after a producer changes the meaning of a column. There need not be a syntax error or a crash. The model simply learns from the wrong observations, and its predictions may later feed more bad examples into training.

Breck and colleagues described this production problem in their 2019 paper on data validation at Google. Their system, part of TensorFlow Extended, compared incoming data with a schema and examined differences between datasets. A schema records expectations such as which fields exist and which values are allowed. Checking those expectations gives a pipeline a chance to identify a bad input before fitting another model.

We will make the decision visible on one sensor batch. First inspect readings against an allowed interval, then decide whether the rejected fraction requires stopping the batch. The example is small enough to check by hand, but the responsibility is the same: a completed calculation does not establish that its input was suitable.

parts.title: 1. A contract describes meaning
paragraphs: A field type answers whether a value is numeric. A range says which numerical values are valid under a specific measurement contract. A unit says what those values measure. None replaces the others.
Do not infer the contract from every incoming batch. A producer error would then redefine its own acceptance rule.
interpretation: The exercise assumes finite numerical readings; parsing and missing-value policies belong before this range check.

parts.title: 2. Keep both branches visible
paragraphs: Compare each value with the lower and upper bounds. Combine the comparisons into a mask. Use that mask for accepted records, and its complement for rejected records.
parts.calculation:
readings = [20,-3,120]
accepted mask = [1,0,0]
accepted = [20]
rejected = 2
rejection fraction = 2 / 3
interpretation: The workshop returns accepted values and a rejection count together so cleaning cannot hide its effect.

examples.title: A mask preserves the rejected positions
paragraphs: NumPy comparisons return one boolean for each original reading.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([20,-3,120])
keep = (x >= 0) & (x <= 100)
print(keep.tolist())
print(np.flatnonzero(~keep).tolist())
interpretation: The rejected indices can be used to retain identities and reasons in a separate report.

parts.title: 3. Decide whether the batch is usable
paragraphs: A batch with one faulty reading may still meet a declared tolerance. A batch missing nearly every night observation may need to be held. Our Python policy holds a batch when its rejection fraction exceeds the supplied limit, and holds empty batches explicitly.
Inspect rejection rates by producer and relevant group. A small overall fraction can conceal a complete failure in a small population.
interpretation: Passing a structural contract does not prove a dataset is unbiased, representative or correctly labelled.

parts.title: 4. Repair upstream and replay deliberately
paragraphs: Preserve the raw input version and reasons for rejection. When the producer is fixed, reprocess into a new version and compare accepted counts and model behaviour.
Quarantine must itself have retention and access controls. It is an investigation path, not an indefinite dumping ground for sensitive records.
interpretation: A pipeline should make failure visible to its operator rather than silently training on whatever survived.

practice.title: Report and decide on the batch
practice.question: Does this batch contain too many rejected readings to release?
task: Dropping invalid readings should not hide how much of the incoming batch failed its contract. Write inspect(values, low, high, limit). Assume finite numbers, low <= high, and 0 <= limit <= 1. Return (accepted, rejected_count, release). Release requires a nonempty input and rejected fraction <= limit.

The bounds are inclusive, and limit is the permitted rejected fraction. Return the accepted list in input order, rejected count and release flag in that order. Print the starter’s report; an empty batch must not receive a release flag of True.
practice.solution:
def inspect(values, low, high, limit):
    accepted = [v for v in values if low <= v <= high]
    rejected = len(values) - len(accepted)
    release = bool(values) and rejected / len(values) <= limit
    return accepted, rejected, release

print(inspect([20,-3,120], 0,100,.1))
hints: Compute the rejected count before deciding the batch status.

build.challenge: Build an inclusive range mask. Return accepted readings and the number rejected as a pair.
build.why: The original batch size remains visible after filtering.
build.limitation: This checks finite numeric ranges. Release thresholds and producer diagnosis are developed in the Python challenge.
