title: The Reading Happened Before the Window Closed
blurb: Assign event-time windows and make late-data policy explicit before updating an online feature.
openingTitle: A Late Packet Changes Yesterday’s Hour
opening: Botie’s agent uses a recent sensor average. Most packets arrive quickly, but a disconnected device sends its backlog later. Grouping by arrival time makes an old event look like a current condition.
Window membership should follow the time the event describes. Deciding when a window is complete is another problem, because we cannot wait forever for missing packets.

history.title: Streaming Systems Cannot Wait for an End of File

sources.title: Akidau and colleagues: The Dataflow Model, VLDB 2015

blocks: A file eventually ends. A stream of sensor readings may keep arriving, with yesterday's disconnected sensor sending a reading after today's records. Waiting for every possible late record would prevent us from publishing an answer at all.

The 2015 Dataflow Model paper addressed this tension between timely results and out-of-order data. It separated the time an event happened from the time a system processed it. Windows grouped events into intervals; watermarks estimated how far event time had progressed. Triggers made the decision about when to emit a result explicit. These ideas became part of Apache Beam's processing model.

A watermark is an estimate, so a late reading still needs a policy. We will inspect membership in one event-time window and watch what a delayed record changes. The local exercise exposes that decision; it does not implement Beam's distributed state or recovery.

parts.title: 1. A half-open interval avoids double counting
paragraphs: Choose a start that is included and an end that is excluded. An event exactly on a shared boundary belongs to the next window, so adjacent windows do not count it twice.
Keep event time with the raw record even when ingestion adds a separate arrival timestamp.
interpretation: Window width should follow the feature’s meaning and the response time the application needs.

parts.title: 2. Build membership without using arrival order
paragraphs: Compare each event time against the start and end. Use the resulting mask on the aligned readings.
parts.calculation:
events = [10,19,20]
window = [10,20)
keep = [1,1,0]
values = [4,8,100]
window mean = (4 + 8) / 2 = 6
interpretation: The record at event 19 still belongs here when it arrives at 25. Whether to revise an emitted result depends on the lateness policy.

examples.title: The shared boundary appears only once
paragraphs: Compare one event with two neighbouring intervals.
examples.code:
event = 20
print(10 <= event < 20)
print(20 <= event < 30)
interpretation: The same timestamp belongs to the later window because the earlier upper endpoint is excluded.

parts.title: 3. An emitted feature may have versions
paragraphs: A service can emit a provisional result, then revise it when permitted late data arrive. Preserve the revision and its availability time. A training replay must use the version available at its decision, not the final corrected average.
Alternatively, a policy may drop overly late events from online state while retaining them for investigation. Make that exclusion measurable.
interpretation: The historical retrieval lesson applies again: a correction’s event window and availability are different facts.

parts.title: 4. Recovery must preserve contributions
paragraphs: If a stream restarts from an earlier offset, records may replay. Deduplicate by a stable event identity where the delivery semantics require it. A window mean needs a sum and count with consistent update semantics.
The coding exercise processes a finite fixture and returns None for an empty window. A running system also needs bounded state retention and checkpoint recovery.
interpretation: Tests should include boundary events and out-of-order arrivals, not only an already sorted stream.

practice.title: Summarise the intended event window
practice.question: Which readings belong to this event-time window before we average them?
task: An event on the boundary between adjacent windows should belong to one window, even when records arrive out of order. Write window_mean(events, values, start, end), with aligned finite inputs and start < end. Use start <= event < end. Return None for no matching events. Input order is arbitrary.

Events, start and end share a time unit. The start is included and the end excluded. Print the scalar mean for the supplied records; values remain attached to their event times rather than their arrival positions.
practice.solution:
def window_mean(events, values, start, end):
    kept = [v for t,v in zip(events, values) if start <= t < end]
    return sum(kept)/len(kept) if kept else None

print(window_mean([20,10,19],[100,4,8],10,20))
hints: Write both comparisons before gathering values.

build.why: The upper comparison is strict so adjacent windows remain disjoint.
build.limitation: Arrival handling, watermarks and persistent streaming state are explained but not simulated by this finite membership circuit.

title: Which Inputs Produced This Model?
blurb: Bind reusable artifacts to input versions and code versions so a changed dataset invalidates the right work.
openingTitle: The Cache Returned a Perfectly Good Model for the Wrong Data
opening: Botie caches prepared features to avoid repeating expensive work. The cache key is a filename. Someone replaces the file’s contents, and the next run reuses yesterday’s features. The workflow graph is correct, but the identity of its inputs is not.
A reusable artifact needs a description of the exact inputs and transformation that produced it. That description also gives us a way to investigate a bad model later.

history.title: Track a Run’s Inputs and Outputs
blocks: A model file can outlive the job that created it. When a prediction changes later, the filename alone tells us very little. Which source records were read? Did preparation code change, or did somebody replace a file in place? Answering those questions becomes harder when each pipeline tool records its work differently.

OpenLineage brought projects including Airflow and dbt into a common effort to describe these relationships. Its September 2021 initial release included a shared specification and integrations. The model distinguished a job, which describes work to do, from a run, which is one execution, and identified the datasets involved. That lets information from separate tools describe a connected processing history.

We will start with a much smaller record: the exact dependencies of one prepared feature file. This record is a manifest. Comparing its input and code identities lets us explain why a previous result can be reused, or why replacing an input requires doing the calculation again.

parts.title: 1. Separate location from identity
paragraphs: A path tells us where to look. A content digest is an identifier computed from the file’s bytes. Changing those bytes changes the digest except in the rare case of a hash collision. A trusted digest or an immutable version lets us check which input we found. Keep human-readable metadata beside it so an investigator can understand the dependency.
A manifest lists the input versions, code version, configuration and schema that define the transformation.
interpretation: Do not include credentials or raw personal data in a public manifest. An identifier may itself be sensitive.

parts.title: 2. Every required dependency must match
paragraphs: For our small example, compare input version and code version separately. Both must match before using the cached result. A full key includes all behaviour-changing configuration as well.
parts.calculation:
input matches = 0
code matches = 1
cache reusable = 0 AND 1 = 0
interpretation: Equal versions are meaningful only if the version identifiers are immutable and trustworthy.

examples.title: Serialise the meaning rather than insertion order
paragraphs: The manifest is a dictionary of declared dependencies.
interpretation: The challenge hashes these deterministic bytes. It does not infer dependencies that were omitted from the manifest.

parts.title: 3. Canonicalise before hashing
paragraphs: Two dictionaries can contain the same manifest entries in different insertion orders. Serialising with sorted keys gives a deterministic representation for our JSON-compatible manifest. Hash its UTF-8 bytes.
A digest detects a difference in bytes. It does not prove who published those bytes or whether they are safe to load.
interpretation: For a production format, specify canonicalisation, numeric representations and versioning explicitly rather than assuming every serializer agrees.

parts.title: 4. Use lineage when the model fails
paragraphs: Follow the served model to its training run, prepared dataset and raw input versions. This can distinguish a new training bug from a changed producer. Record failed runs too, without labelling their partial artifacts as complete.
If a source dataset is withdrawn, lineage helps locate affected artifacts. Deleting a manifest alone does not remove data from every copy or a trained model.
interpretation: The workshop checks two dependencies; the Python manifest exercise extends the identity to arbitrary nested configuration.

practice.title: Name the artifact by its dependencies
practice.question: Can equivalent dependency manifests produce the same artifact key?
task: Two manifests can describe the same dependencies while their dictionary keys appear in different orders. Their artifact identity should agree. Write artifact_key(manifest) using deterministic JSON with sorted keys and compact separators, then SHA-256 of UTF-8 bytes. Manifests contain JSON-compatible finite values. Do not mutate the manifest. Print whether differently ordered equal manifests match.

Return the hexadecimal digest string. A digest records these serialised dependencies; it is not a signature proving who supplied them. The demonstration prints whether the two equal manifests produce equal keys.
practice.starter:
import json, hashlib

def artifact_key(manifest):

title: Writing the Steps Is Different from Running Them
blurb: A cleaning rule works on one file. What do Spark and Databricks add when a team needs to run that rule across many files, and when does the calculation actually happen?
openingTitle: Why Did the Original Table Still Contain That Broken Reading?
opening: Suppose our pump readings have grown from one file we can inspect to years of files arriving from several sites. We still need to remove the readings our sensor contract calls invalid. Now we also need somewhere for the team to run that calculation and see which data it used. Databricks is a managed cloud platform for this shared data and machine-learning work. In these lessons, Spark is the computation engine we use inside that environment.

We will begin with a small puzzle from that larger job. Botie asks for the temperatures above a declared minimum, then looks at the original table. The broken reading is still there. Did the filter fail? Before running a bigger job, we need to understand what names the source records, what describes a proposed result and what actually asks Spark to calculate it.

history.title: Why a Table Calculation Became a Platform Problem

sources.title: Zaharia and colleagues: reusable distributed data, NSDI 2012

blocks: Training can revisit the same observations many times. On a large collection of machines, repeatedly writing intermediate results out and reading them back adds work that does not improve the model. Spark began as a Berkeley research project in 2009 and was released as open source in 2010. The researchers’ 2012 paper explained how keeping reusable data in distributed memory could help repeated calculations, while recording the operations made lost portions of the data recoverable.

Spark supplies the engine: it can divide work between processes and combine their results. Running that engine for a team creates another job. Someone has to provide compute, connect the approved data and make executions inspectable. Spark’s creators founded Databricks in 2013 to build a company around this kind of shared data work. Databricks is the managed platform; Apache Spark is a separate open-source project that can also run elsewhere.

Our first calculation uses Spark’s table interface. The Spark SQL work published in 2015 described how named columns and declared operations give a query engine information it can use to plan execution. A request for a filtered table describes a result; it need not calculate every row immediately. That is the distinction Botie will build on the workshop floor.

parts.title: 1. Why would one cleaning rule need several computers?
paragraphs: One file of pump readings is easy to inspect with a Python program. Years of readings from many sites are a different workload. The files may exceed one machine’s memory, or the team may need an answer sooner than one process can produce it. We can divide work into portions and give several processes the same declared operation.

Apache Spark is an engine for organising and executing that kind of calculation. A portion of the records is called a partition. For a filter, separate partitions can apply the same condition independently; a later grouped total may have to combine their contributions. Spark can also run locally for small work, so its name does not by itself mean that several machines are involved.

A driver coordinates the application. Executor processes carry out tasks on the available compute. Describing operations through Spark’s table interface lets the engine choose how to carry them out while preserving the requested result.
interpretation: Adding workers changes where the calculation runs. We still have to explain which records the calculation should return.

parts.title: 2. Who keeps that shared work running?
paragraphs: A working filter leaves the team with practical questions. Where will the scheduled job run? How will a colleague inspect the code and the records from a failed attempt? Providing a shared environment is work of its own.

Databricks is a managed cloud platform for this work. Its workspace gives a team a place to develop and run data and machine-learning jobs while the service manages supported compute and connects the work to configured storage and access controls. In these lessons we use Spark there for the table calculations. Apache Spark also exists independently as an open-source project.

Choosing the platform does not choose a cleaning rule for us. We still decide what an invalid sensor value means and what a model may learn from it. Later lessons will follow the other responsibilities that appear once the calculation is shared: keeping a table version, recording a training attempt and checking the job’s permission to read an input.
interpretation: The local workshops let us inspect those decisions on a handful of records. The optional code references show where the same ideas meet a real Databricks workspace.

parts.title: 3. Begin with the records, not a cluster diagram
paragraphs: A Python list can hold several dictionaries. Each dictionary keeps one pump identifier beside its temperature and status. That way, selecting or rejecting a reading keeps the fields describing that observation together. A column is one named field read across those records.

Spark’s DataFrame is a table-shaped object with named columns and declared data types. We can ask for a new DataFrame by describing which rows and columns we want. The original object continues to describe the source. Later, when we request rows, Spark’s driver process coordinates the calculation and executor processes carry out its tasks.
interpretation: Follow the named records first. The small program below reads their pump identifiers while leaving each complete dictionary available to inspect.

examples.title: A list of complete sensor records
paragraphs: Read the field from each dictionary without changing the dictionaries.
examples.code:
records = [{"pump": "P7", "temperature": 12}, {"pump": "P2", "temperature": -3}]
print([row["pump"] for row in records])
interpretation: The identifiers stay aligned with their readings because each dictionary remains a complete record.

parts.title: 4. Give the proposed result its own name
paragraphs: Give the source a name, raw, and the requested result another name, clean. A transformation is an operation that describes a new result from an earlier one. A filter keeps the rows that satisfy a condition. A projection keeps the named columns we request.

For our sensor example the condition is temperature at least zero. We are checking that particular field. A different column describing a temperature change could legitimately be negative, so the rule needs both a field name and its meaning.
parts.calculation:
raw temperatures = [12, -3]
keep temperature >= 0
clean temperatures = [12]
raw temperatures remain [12, -3]
interpretation: After the transformation, raw still names the source and clean names the requested subset. We can inspect either one deliberately.

parts.title: 5. Ask when the rows are actually needed
paragraphs: Spark transformations are generally lazy: they construct a plan rather than immediately materialising every intermediate table. An action such as count, show or collect asks the engine for a result. Analysis and some metadata work can still happen before the action, so lazy does not mean absolutely nothing happens.

The browser model makes this distinction concrete. Plan a numerical filter and Plan the output columns return instructions. Execute the plan receives those instructions and a batch. Reading the plan alone is different from inspecting its output.
interpretation: When timing execution, include the action and state which reading and transformations it requested.

parts.title: 6. Read a Spark plan before collecting a result
paragraphs: The optional snippet builds a small DataFrame with an explicit schema: a declaration of column names and data types. The where expression returns another DataFrame. explain displays its plan; show requests displayed rows. Ordering here makes the small demonstration repeatable.

collect transfers the complete result to the driver process. That is useful for a genuinely small result, but defeats the purpose of distributed storage if the full training table cannot fit there. Keep large transformations on the workers and inspect bounded results.
interpretation: A real physical plan may fuse operations or change their order while preserving their meaning. Our instruction list keeps the teaching order instead.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

raw = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("P7", 12.0), ("P2", -3.0)],
    "pump string, temperature double",
)
clean = raw.where(F.col("temperature") >= 0).select("pump", "temperature")
clean.explain("formatted")
clean.orderBy("pump").show()

parts.title: 7. Reuse the procedure, not an accidentally captured answer
paragraphs: The next file may contain different pumps or more readings. A reusable cleaning procedure accepts the current records and applies the same declared rule. It should not return a result copied from the first demonstration.

In the workshop, the same plan runs against every supplied case. In Python, write a function whose arguments carry the records, threshold and requested columns. Keep their roles separate. A fresh list of result dictionaries also prevents a later edit of the result from changing the source records.
interpretation: Where should matching pump contributions meet when they begin on several workers?

practice.title: Build the cleaning result without mutating its source
practice.question: Which readings survive the new minimum, and how do we keep their fields together?
task: Write clean_rows(records, field, minimum, columns). records is a list of dictionaries containing every requested field. The checked value is a finite number or None; None fails the filter. minimum is a finite number and columns is a list of distinct field names. Return new dictionaries for accepted rows, preserving input row order and the requested column order. Do not mutate records.

This is a new batch with a minimum of five degrees. Print the retained pump and temperature fields, then the sum of the retained temperatures. The sum is a check of which rows survived, not a feature to feed to the model. This function executes locally and models filter and projection semantics.
practice.starter:
def clean_rows(records, field, minimum, columns):
    pass

records = [{"pump":"P8","temperature":17.5,"status":"ok"}, {"pump":"P9","temperature":None,"status":"missing"}, {"pump":"P4","temperature":-8,"status":"placeholder"}, {"pump":"P6","temperature":31.5,"status":"ok"}, {"pump":"P1","temperature":4,"status":"below minimum"}]
cleaned = clean_rows(records, "temperature", 5, ["pump","temperature"])
print(cleaned)
print(sum(row["temperature"] for row in cleaned))
practice.solution:
def clean_rows(records, field, minimum, columns):
    return [{name: row[name] for name in columns}
            for row in records if row[field] is not None and row[field] >= minimum]

records = [{"pump":"P8","temperature":17.5,"status":"ok"}, {"pump":"P9","temperature":None,"status":"missing"}, {"pump":"P4","temperature":-8,"status":"placeholder"}, {"pump":"P6","temperature":31.5,"status":"ok"}, {"pump":"P1","temperature":4,"status":"below minimum"}]
cleaned = clean_rows(records, "temperature", 5, ["pump","temperature"])
print(cleaned)
print(sum(row["temperature"] for row in cleaned))
hints: Decide whether each complete record passes before copying its requested fields. What should happen when the checked value is None?

title: One Busy Pump Can Keep Every Worker Waiting
blurb: Most workers have finished, but one pump’s records keep the job running. Follow where matching records must meet before deciding how to share that work.
openingTitle: We Added Workers. Why Did the Job Barely Move?
opening: Botie can filter each file independently. Now he wants a count for each pump across all files. Most pumps have a few readings, but P7 supplies nearly everything. Several workers finish while the worker responsible for P7 keeps running.

The problem is how the records meet. Adding workers does not divide a group that is still assigned to one worker. We need to see the routing rule before deciding whether more machines, a different join plan or a partial aggregation would help.

history.title: Why Matching Records Can Leave One Worker Waiting
blocks: Counting records for one pump across many files requires combining contributions that began in different places. The same issue appears when two tables need to match rows by an identifier. A distributed system must arrange for the matching contributions to meet somewhere; this movement between partitions is called a shuffle.

Spark SQL’s 2015 paper described planning table calculations as operations the engine can optimise and execute across a cluster. The plan still has to respect the grouping we requested. If one pump owns most of the work, sending all of that group to one task can leave the other workers waiting. More machines help only when the work can actually be divided between them.

We will split one pump’s work into temporary partial groups while preserving its original identifier. A count can later add those partial counts. Spark may already perform local aggregation or choose an adaptive plan, so the workshop exposes a routing decision we can reason about rather than predicting a real cluster’s task counts.

parts.title: 1. Ask which records must meet
paragraphs: A filter can decide whether a reading passes by looking at that reading alone. Counting all readings from P7 is different: P7 may occur in files handled by several workers. Those workers have to combine their contributions before they can give us P7’s total.

The grouping value, P7 here, is called the key. A partition is one portion of the work. A shuffle moves records or partial summaries between partitions so that the contributions for a key can be combined. The movement can take longer than the final addition.
interpretation: In Spark’s physical plan, an exchange marks a place where that movement is required.

parts.title: 2. Averages hide the last unfinished partition
paragraphs: Suppose one worker receives most records. The other workers cannot complete that unsplit group merely by becoming idle. This uneven work distribution is skew. Counts are a first clue; row sizes and the cost of processing each row can also differ.

Look at the slowest tasks and shuffle statistics rather than only the average task time. A long tail can come from a large key, a large record, a spill to disk or another resource problem. Our workshop supplies equal-cost records so routing is the only variable.
interpretation: Follow one hot pump through the routing rule before deciding whether more partitions would change its destination.

examples.title: Count the original keys before changing their routes
paragraphs: A dictionary maps each original pump identifier to its accumulated count. The routing marker does not belong in this logical count.
interpretation: Keep this original-key result as a correctness reference when later experimenting with worker routes.

parts.title: 3. Make partial groups only when they can be recombined
paragraphs: For a count, split a hot pump into temporary subgroups, count each subgroup, then add counts by the original pump. Adding a small subgroup marker is often called salting. Keep the original key because the marker is an execution detail, not a new pump.

This reasoning relies on a mergeable calculation. Summing counts is valid; averaging subgroup averages without their counts is not. Joins need their own correct treatment of both sides. Arbitrarily salting one join input can lose matches.
parts.calculation:
A subgroup counts = [2, 2]
A final count = 2 + 2 = 4
B final count = 1
interpretation: Inspect the existing partial aggregates before adding an extra salting stage.

parts.title: 4. Inspect a grouped calculation in Spark
paragraphs: The reference groups by pump and requests counts. Explain shows the engine’s chosen plan; the bounded display then requests the result. A larger workload can use adaptive execution, but the exact plan depends on Spark and Databricks versions and the available statistics.
Keep a small unpartitioned reference result while changing execution strategy. Performance work has failed if it produces a faster answer for a different grouping rule.
interpretation: On a real workload, compare the slow-task distribution before and after a justified plan change.

raw = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("A", 0), ("A", 1), ("A", 2), ("A", 3), ("B", 4)],
    "pump string, reading_id long",
)
counts = raw.groupBy("pump").count()
counts.explain("formatted")
counts.orderBy("pump").show()

This teaching input is tiny. Inspect a larger approved dataset’s task metrics separately before drawing performance conclusions.
interpretation: The correct count per original pump is the invariant. Exchanges and partial aggregates are implementation choices around it.

parts.title: 5. Use the declared hash only to understand the workshop
paragraphs: The workshop adds routingKey to each dictionary. It cycles the hot key through the requested number of salt groups, then routes by a stated character-code hash. Count each resulting worker list, including empty lists.

That hash makes our expected answers inspectable. Spark uses different hashing and can change its physical partitioning. The resulting worker counts are therefore outputs of this small routing model, not predictions of a real Databricks task layout.
interpretation: The Python challenge returns group counts under the original pump key as well as worker loads. Both matter: better balance and unchanged meaning.

parts.title: 6. Test a different frequency pattern
paragraphs: Yesterday P7 produced most of the readings. Today another pump may be busiest. A routing choice should follow the records that actually arrived, so inspect the new key frequencies before reusing yesterday’s hot-key setting. Creating extra groups also adds work that our count-only model leaves out.

Check two results together: how much work reaches the busiest worker, and whether the final counts still describe the original pumps. An evenly divided list is useful only if every observation still contributes to the right total.
interpretation: Next we will hold the calculation steady and change which version of the readings it receives.

practice.title: Balance partial groups without inventing new pumps
practice.question: Can we spread C’s work across workers while still counting it as one pump?
task: Write routing_report(records, hot, salts, workers). records is a list of dictionaries with a text pump field. salts and workers are positive integers. For hot, cycle consecutive occurrences through salts beginning at zero; all other pumps use salt zero. Form pump + "#" + str(salt), sum its character code points, and take the remainder by workers. Return (loads, counts): loads has one record count per worker, and counts maps each original pump to its total count. Do not mutate input records.

Use the new sequence in the workspace, with C as the hot pump, three salt groups and four workers. Print its load list and original-pump counts. The character-code hash is an explicitly defined teaching rule rather than Spark’s production partitioner.
practice.solution:
def routing_report(records, hot, salts, workers):
    loads, counts, seen_hot = [0]*workers, {}, 0
    for row in records:
        key = row["pump"]
        salt = seen_hot % salts if key == hot else 0
        if key == hot:
            seen_hot += 1
        routing = key + "#" + str(salt)
        loads[sum(map(ord, routing)) % workers] += 1
        counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0) + 1
    return loads, counts

print(routing_report([{"pump":p} for p in ["C","C","D","C","C","E","C","D","C","C"]], "C", 3, 4))
hints: There are two identities to keep: the original pump for its final count, and the temporary routing label for choosing a worker.
Cycle the salt only when the record belongs to the hot pump. Then apply the stated character-code rule to the complete routing label.

title: Which Version of the Table Did the Model Read?
blurb: The code stayed the same, but a corrected input changed the result. Give the run a particular table version so we can tell a new model from a new dataset.
openingTitle: The Same Training Script Now Reports a Different Mean
opening: Botie saves the cleaning code and runs training again. The code has not changed, but a corrected sensor file has. The rerun reads today’s table while yesterday’s model read an older one. Comparing their scores no longer isolates the code change.
A table name tells us where to look. It does not, by itself, identify which committed contents we used. We need a version that a run can name and read consistently.

history.title: How Could Readers Agree While Files Were Changing?

sources.title: Delta batch reads and time travel

blocks: A training job may read a collection of files while another job is replacing part of that collection. Seeing only half of an update can produce a dataset that no writer intended to publish. The problem is deciding which files belong together as one complete table state.

Delta Lake puts a transaction log alongside the data files. A successful commit records which files form the next table version. A reader can use one committed version even while later work creates another. Databricks released Delta Lake as an open-source project on April 24, 2019; the 2020 research paper explained the design for reliable analytical tables over object storage.

Spark performs the table calculation. Delta Lake supplies the versioned table storage that this read relies on. On the floor we keep full local snapshots so you can see exactly which records a version selects. The real format uses its log and retained files to reconstruct that state.

parts.title: 1. Separate a table address from its contents
paragraphs: The name lab.training.sensor_features tells us which table to open. The name alone does not freeze what is inside it. Suppose someone corrects a reading tomorrow. The address can stay the same while the records behind it change.

A version identifies one committed state of that particular table. Keep the table identity beside its version when recording a model’s inputs. In our Python example, history is a list of dictionaries, each holding a version and its complete rows. Those outer versions belong to table states; they are different from the per-pump changes we will meet later.
interpretation: The useful record is specific: this model read this table at this version.

examples.title: Inspect the nesting of a retained snapshot
paragraphs: The outer list holds table versions. Inside one matching dictionary, rows holds the complete sensor records.
examples.code:
history = [{"version":0,"rows":[{"pump":"A","temperature":10}]}, {"version":1,"rows":[{"pump":"A","temperature":30}]}]
matching = [entry for entry in history if entry["version"] == 0]
print(matching[0]["rows"])
interpretation: The challenge must additionally reject absent or duplicated version identities and handle an empty committed snapshot.

parts.title: 2. Read one committed state for this calculation
paragraphs: Select the requested version before extracting the temperature column. A Delta commit records one complete table update as a published version; the mere presence of some new data files does not make them the current table. All readings in the calculation then come from that supplied snapshot. The correction in a later commit does not replace a value inside an already selected older snapshot.

A committed snapshot is the boundary we rely on here. It is not permission to combine unrelated versions of several tables and call the result a single transaction. Record the required version of every independently managed input.
parts.calculation:
version 0 temperatures = [10, 20]
mean = (10 + 20) / 2 = 15
version 1 temperatures = [30, 20]
mean = (30 + 20) / 2 = 25
interpretation: The changed mean follows the corrected input. A comparison meant to isolate a code change must keep that input fixed.

paragraphs: The reference asks Delta for a specific retained version. Another writer can commit a newer table state without turning this read into a request for latest. Save the chosen version with the model’s training metadata.

A current table read is useful when we intentionally want current data. A reproducibility claim needs a declared input identity. Avoid querying latest in one part of a workflow and assuming another query still means that same state.
interpretation: Check that the requested table version is retained before promising a future rerun.

parts.title: 4. A retained version is not an indefinite backup
paragraphs: Older snapshots need both sufficient log history and the data files they reference. Retention and cleanup can make an old version unreadable. A version number written in a report does not recreate deleted files.

Plan retention around reproducibility and recovery requirements. Export or otherwise preserve approved training inputs when that requirement exceeds ordinary table retention. Privacy and deletion requirements can also constrain what may be kept; do not copy personal data indefinitely merely to make a model reproducible.
interpretation: Our Python function raises ValueError when the requested version is absent. Returning the latest version would silently answer a different question.

parts.title: 5. Time travel and historical features answer different questions
paragraphs: Delta time travel asks which committed state of a table to read. A historical feature lookup asks which feature value belongs to a particular prediction time inside that table. One table snapshot can contain feature rows for many prediction times.
We will use both ideas later. Pinning a snapshot does not automatically remove future features from a join, and filtering feature timestamps does not make an overwritten table version recoverable.
interpretation: The next ingestion lesson will make a retry safe without appending the same discovered file again.

practice.title: Read the version the run actually names
practice.question: What temperature mean did this run see at its requested table version?
task: Write snapshot_mean(history, version, field). history is a list of dictionaries with an integer version and a rows list; each requested row field is a finite number. Exactly one history entry must match version. Return its numerical mean, or None when that snapshot has no rows. Raise ValueError if the requested version is absent or duplicated. Do not fall back to the newest version or mutate history.
Print the temperature mean of version zero in this new three-reading snapshot. The histories are complete local snapshots for teaching rather than a transaction-log implementation.
practice.starter:
def snapshot_mean(history, version, field):
    pass

history = [{"version":0,"rows":[{"temperature":12},{"temperature":35},{"temperature":55}]}, {"version":1,"rows":[{"temperature":30},{"temperature":20}]}]
print(snapshot_mean(history, 0, "temperature"))
practice.solution:
def snapshot_mean(history, version, field):
    matches = [entry for entry in history if entry["version"] == version]
    if len(matches) != 1:
        raise ValueError("Expected one retained version")
    values = [row[field] for row in matches[0]["rows"]]
    return sum(values)/len(values) if values else None

history = [{"version":0,"rows":[{"temperature":12},{"temperature":35},{"temperature":55}]}, {"version":1,"rows":[{"temperature":30},{"temperature":20}]}]
print(snapshot_mean(history, 0, "temperature"))
hints: Find the requested version before extracting temperatures. How many history entries should identify that one snapshot?
An existing snapshot with no rows returns None. An absent or duplicated version means we cannot identify the requested input and must raise ValueError.

title: A Retried File Should Not Become New Training Data
blurb: A file finished, but its acknowledgement disappeared. Keep enough committed progress for the retry to recognise work that already reached the dataset.
openingTitle: The Job Recovered. Why Did the Dataset Grow Again?
opening: Botie’s loader finishes a sensor file and the connection fails before the interface sees its success. The scheduler retries the job. Appending the same file again makes the training dataset larger, even though no new observations arrived.

We need a durable answer to which files have already contributed. We also need that answer to agree with the output: recording progress before the rows are safely written can lose data instead of duplicating it.

history.title: Why Finding a File Was Not the Same as Finishing It
blocks: As cloud storage filled with incoming files, repeatedly listing every directory became an expensive way to discover the next input. Teams also had to remember which discoveries had actually reached their output after failures and retries.

Databricks announced Auto Loader in public preview in February 2020 to handle incremental discovery and loading of files from cloud storage. It is a file source used with Spark streaming, with checkpointed progress so a restarted query can continue. A checkpoint is the durable recovery record for that query; it has to work with the destination’s commit behaviour.

That distinction is what we will build. A discovery says there is a file to consider. A completed-file record says its effect belongs in the committed output. Keeping the output rows and progress together prevents a lost acknowledgement from becoming a second copy of the observations.

parts.title: 1. Identify the unit that was processed
paragraphs: Imagine a short list of files waiting to be loaded. Each file has an identity and a list of sensor records. The checkpoint keeps the identities whose rows have already reached the committed output. That is the information a restarted job needs before deciding what remains to do.

Our Python representation mirrors those pieces: a list of file dictionaries, a rows list inside each file, and a checkpoint list. A set is useful for asking whether an identity is already present, while the returned list preserves a deliberate order.
In this example, one identity always refers to the same contents. If a producer overwrites a path with new data, we need a version or a different replacement policy before the same rule is safe.
interpretation: Two different files can still contain the same business event. Detecting that requires an event identity as well as file progress.

examples.title: Ask whether a file identity has completed
paragraphs: A set supports membership checks without attaching a numerical meaning to an identifier.
interpretation: This checks only committed identities. The full ingestion procedure also has to suppress repeated new discoveries and return progress with the output.

parts.title: 2. Do not confuse discovered with committed
paragraphs: A notification tells us that a file may be available. It does not prove the file has contributed to the output. Select discoveries absent from committed progress, and suppress identical repeated discoveries in the current batch.

If one batch presents different contents under the same immutable file identity, stop rather than arbitrarily taking the first. The conflict is evidence that the identity contract is broken. The checkpoint alone cannot compare a new file with historical contents that were never retained in this model.
interpretation: The accepted-file preview lets us review what the next commit will include.

parts.title: 3. Keep the output and the progress consistent
paragraphs: There are two ways to leave a misleading recovery record. We could write the rows and fail before recording that their file completed. A retry would append them again. Or we could record completion before the rows are safely stored. A retry would skip a file whose output is missing.

Our commit component returns both changes as one new state, leaving the earlier state untouched. That is the relationship we want from an atomic update: the rows and their progress agree about what completed.

A real destination, often called the sink, needs a durable transaction or an operation identity that makes the same write have one effect when repeated. That repeat-safe property is called idempotency. Returning two Python fields together helps us inspect the rule; real storage must enforce it through failures.
parts.calculation:
earlier checkpoint = [f0]
new accepted file identities = [f1]
next checkpoint = [f0, f1]
retry with this checkpoint: accepted file identities = []
interpretation: On a successful replay, the committed dataset should be the same even when the scheduler has attempted the job more than once.

parts.title: 4. Let Auto Loader keep its progress on an approved sink
paragraphs: The reference uses a fixed schema and a persistent checkpoint path, then writes to a Delta table. availableNow asks the query to process the available input and finish; awaitTermination waits for that query. Keep the checkpoint associated with this logical query.

Choose source, checkpoint and output locations deliberately. Deleting a checkpoint is a state change with replay consequences. It is not a harmless way to clear an error. Changing the target or reusing a checkpoint for another query requires a reviewed recovery plan.
interpretation: Lakeflow can manage checkpointing for its own pipelines. This standalone reference makes the path visible because checkpoint identity is what we are learning.

references.title: Read immutable JSON files incrementally
references.code:
source_path = "/Volumes/lab/training/landing/sensors"
checkpoint_path = "/Volumes/lab/training/checkpoints/sensor_ingest"
query = (spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")
         .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
         .schema("pump STRING, temperature DOUBLE")
         .load(source_path)
         .writeStream
         .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_path)
         .trigger(availableNow=True)
         .toTable("lab.training.raw_readings"))
query.awaitTermination()

setup: Use your own Databricks workspace with both existing Unity Catalog volumes: lab.training.landing holds the approved source JSON files, and lab.training.checkpoints holds this query’s checkpoint directory. Use Unity Catalog-compatible compute. The job needs USE CATALOG on lab and USE SCHEMA on lab.training, READ VOLUME on lab.training.landing, and READ VOLUME plus WRITE VOLUME on lab.training.checkpoints. Creating the target requires CREATE TABLE on lab.training; appending to an existing target requires MODIFY on lab.training.raw_readings. This reference writes data and consumes compute.
Use a dedicated persistent checkpoint for this query. Do not copy the example paths over an existing production query.

parts.title: 5. Keep unrelated side effects outside the claimed guarantee
paragraphs: Sending an email, charging a customer or calling a tool during a streaming batch is another effect. The table transaction cannot automatically make an arbitrary remote API call exactly once. Give such effects their own durable operation identities and recovery procedure.

Even a valid file checkpoint does not decide how to handle late events, corrected records or schema drift. Those require their own declared contracts. We are adding one reliable boundary to the pipeline, not declaring every later operation safe.
interpretation: The next lesson gives corrected entity records an explicit source sequence so arrival order cannot choose the current truth.

parts.title: 6. Try both a replay and a genuinely new file
paragraphs: A useful test runs the accepted result back through the same discoveries. Nothing should be appended. Another test supplies a new file identity and checks that its rows do arrive. Include an empty file: it can still be a completed input even though it contributes no rows.
Keep old input structures unchanged in these tests. Otherwise a successful assertion can depend on the function having quietly altered the checkpoint or removed rows from the discovery fixture.
interpretation: Try an empty file as well as a replay, and check the checkpoint alongside the output rows.

practice.title: Commit file progress with the accepted records
practice.question: If this file turns up twice, which readings should reach training?
task: Write ingest_files(previous, discoveries). previous is {"rows": [...], "checkpoint": [file IDs]}; discoveries is a list of {"file": text, "rows": [record dictionaries]}. Identities refer to immutable contents. Ignore already committed files and repeated identical discoveries. Conflicting contents for the same file identity within this discovery batch raise ValueError. Return a new state; preserve previous row order and append new files in first-discovery order. Advance progress even for an empty file. Do not mutate inputs.

Use json.dumps with sort_keys=True when comparing record contents, so dictionary key order does not invent a conflict. In this new batch f7 is already committed, f8 appears twice and f9 is empty. Print the returned state, then the sum of its retained temperatures to check whether any reading was counted twice.
practice.starter:
def ingest_files(previous, discoveries):
    pass

title: The Last Message to Arrive May Be an Older Reading
blurb: A newly arrived file can contain an old correction. Keep each pump’s source version, including its deletion, so delivery order cannot choose the current reading.
openingTitle: Why Did a Deleted Pump Reappear?
opening: Botie’s loader no longer repeats completed files. A new file contains a correction for P7, followed by a delayed older update. Later a deletion arrives. If we simply keep the last message in each file, delivery order chooses the current record. If we forget the deletion entirely, an old message can recreate it.
The source needs to tell us which change is newer for that pump. We will keep that sequence beside the entity and carry deletion evidence forward until it is safe to discard.

history.title: Keeping a Copy Current When the Source Keeps Changing
blocks: Once a source table can correct or delete a reading, copying it once is no longer enough. A downstream training table needs to learn which records changed and what happened to them. Change data capture, usually shortened to CDC, is the process of communicating those inserts, updates and deletions.

The Delta Lake work described in the 2020 paper addressed dependable table updates over analytical files. Delta’s MERGE operation can match incoming rows to stored rows and apply declared insert or update rules. That gives us somewhere to express a correction, but we must still decide which source change is authoritative when messages arrive out of order.

Here the source gives each pump’s changes an increasing sequence. A later arrival can therefore be recognised as an older change. We also keep the version of a deletion behind the consumer’s view, so an old update cannot make a deleted pump reappear.

parts.title: 1. Give an entity and a change separate identifiers
paragraphs: The pump field says which entity changed. The seq field says where that change sits in this pump’s source history. Think of the distinction as which pump and which revision of its record. Revisions for unrelated pumps do not need one shared numbering system.

Each change also carries deleted and value. deleted is a boolean. A deletion can have value=None and still be an important record: it tells us that this pump became absent at a particular source sequence.
interpretation: File identity tells us whether an input file completed. The pump and sequence tell us which state its records describe.

parts.title: 2. Choose one unambiguous source change per key
paragraphs: A batch can contain several versions of the same pump. Select its highest source sequence before merging. An exact duplicate at that sequence is harmless; different contents at the same sequence are ambiguous and should stop the update.

Do not use whichever row happens to appear last after a distributed operation. An ordering must be declared. A tie-breaker that arbitrarily prefers one contradictory record hides the broken upstream contract.
interpretation: This preprocessing also prevents an ambiguous collection of source rows from matching the same target row in a MERGE.

parts.title: 3. Compare the incoming change with the stored version
paragraphs: A newer source sequence can replace the stored state. An older one must leave it alone. An identical repeated current change is a no-op. Conflicting contents at the same sequence require investigation rather than an unconditional overwrite.
An absent entity can accept its first known change, including a deletion marker. Otherwise an earlier update arriving later would look like a new entity and resurrect it.
parts.calculation:
stored P7 sequence = 9, deleted = true
incoming P7 sequence = 8, deleted = false
8 < 9
keep stored deletion at sequence 9
interpretation: The current state follows source-version order across different deliveries.

examples.title: Compare the source sequence before replacing state
paragraphs: A deleted record still has an entity identity and source sequence. Reading those fields does not require a numerical value to be present.
interpretation: The arriving active value is older. The fuller challenge handles batches, independent entities and contradictory ties.

parts.title: 4. Keep deletion evidence behind the visible view
paragraphs: The stored state retains tombstones: records saying that an entity was deleted at a known sequence. A consumer view filters deleted rows out. That makes the current visible table empty for the entity without forgetting why an older update must be ignored.

Retention is a policy decision. Tombstones cannot be removed safely while older updates can still arrive under this contract. This is also not a claim that personal data has been erased from logs, snapshots or model weights. Logical visibility and deletion obligations need separate treatment.
interpretation: The workshop output shows active rows. Inspect the merge component’s intermediate output to see retained deletion state.

parts.title: 5. Express the version rule in Delta MERGE
paragraphs: The reference assumes latest_changes already has one unambiguous source row per pump. It stores deleted as a column, so an unmatched deletion can also be retained. A separate view or filter supplies visible nondeleted records.

The source DataFrame must use the same declared columns and compatible types as the target. Reject contradictory equal-sequence rows before this step. The conditional update keeps older and identical-sequence source rows from overwriting stored state; it is not an upstream conflict detector.
interpretation: Production CDC can have richer ordering and retention semantics. Inspect the source’s guarantees before replacing its ordering with an ingestion timestamp.

references.title: Merge only a newer entity version
references.code:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

# latest_changes has pump, seq, deleted, value.
# It has one unambiguous row per pump, checked before this step.
target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "lab.training.pump_state")
(target.alias("t")
 .merge(latest_changes.alias("s"), "t.pump = s.pump")
 .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="s.seq > t.seq")
 .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
 .execute())
visible = spark.table("lab.training.pump_state").where("deleted = false")
description: This optional reference runs in your own Databricks environment. The browser exercise below uses ordinary Python and does not contact Databricks.
setup: Use your own Delta table and a validated source DataFrame with pump STRING, seq BIGINT, deleted BOOLEAN and value DOUBLE. The target retains tombstones.
This reference modifies the target. Use an isolated approved table, preserve its earlier version, and validate source uniqueness and equal-sequence consistency before execution.
interpretation: A physical delete would remove the sequence guard for an unmatched later insert. This example deliberately keeps tombstones in the state table.

parts.title: 6. Test sequences across more than one delivery
paragraphs: A first batch can delete a pump; a second can contain an older update. Testing only that each batch works independently misses the resurrection. Feed the first returned state into the second call and check the retained deletion.

Also test a genuinely newer update after deletion. Our declared source contract permits that to create a new visible state. If the business requires permanent deletion instead, its identity and retention rules must forbid that transition explicitly.
interpretation: The same version logic will matter when a historical feature table is corrected. We must decide which changes a past prediction was allowed to know.

practice.title: Keep a late update from resurrecting a deleted entity
practice.question: Which pump values are still current after this mixed delivery?
task: Write apply_changes(state, events). Both arguments are lists of dictionaries containing pump (text), seq (nonnegative integer), deleted (boolean), and value (number or None). state has at most one record per pump. Return new current state sorted by pump, including tombstones. Keep the largest sequence per pump. Ignore older updates; identical duplicates are harmless. Conflicting records at the same pump and sequence, either within events or against state, raise ValueError. Do not mutate arguments.

This delivery also includes two active pumps that were absent from the reading’s example. Print only active rows from the returned state, then the sum of their values. Retain the P7 tombstone inside the returned state even though it is excluded from this display. Every active value in this supplied delivery is numerical.
practice.starter:
def apply_changes(state, events):
    pass

state = [{"pump":"P7","seq":8,"deleted":False,"value":22}]
events = [{"pump":"P7","seq":9,"deleted":True,"value":None},{"pump":"P7","seq":5,"deleted":False,"value":17},{"pump":"Z8","seq":2,"deleted":False,"value":49},{"pump":"Z9","seq":1,"deleted":False,"value":6}]
updated = apply_changes(state, events)
active = [row for row in updated if not row["deleted"]]
print(active)
print(sum(row["value"] for row in active))
hints: Keep the latest known sequence beside each pump even when the latest change is a deletion. The visible active rows are a view of that stored state.
Check every (pump, seq) pair for contradictory contents before choosing the largest sequence. Otherwise a newer row could hide an older contradictory tie in the same batch.

blurb: The dashboard found an invalid reading, yet training still received it. Decide what a failed check should change in the published dataset.
openingTitle: The Dashboard Counted Bad Readings, but Training Still Used Them
opening: Botie’s pipeline reports that one temperature is invalid. The next model still trains on it. The check ran; it simply did not have the effect the team assumed. Did we intend to record a warning, exclude the row or prevent this dataset update?

We need to separate the condition that marks a row as invalid from the policy applied when that condition fails. A visible failure count is evidence. Whether the output may be published is another decision.

history.title: A Pipeline Needed More Than a Working Query
blocks: A query can produce the right table once and still leave a team with a difficult daily job. Its input tables must be ready, failed attempts must be recoverable, and a bad reading needs a declared consequence. Those responsibilities used to be scattered around the transformation code.

Databricks announced Delta Live Tables in May 2021 to let authors declare datasets, their dependencies and quality expectations together. The pipeline system could inspect those definitions and manage their updates. The current interface used here is Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines. Delta Lake remains the versioned storage underneath; a pipeline is the process that builds and refreshes datasets.

An expectation is a named condition that a row should satisfy. It still needs a policy: keep and report the failing row, exclude it, or stop this update. We will keep the condition and its consequence visible as separate components, then inspect the actual rows training receives.

parts.title: 1. State what a passing row means
paragraphs: Suppose our sensor contract requires a temperature to be present and at least zero. We can test that rule on every row, but a boolean by itself tells the next part of the pipeline very little. Keep it attached to the reading that produced it.

Lakeflow calls a named quality condition an expectation. Its name identifies the check in reports; its condition supplies the rule to evaluate. Our local component returns each complete row beside a passed flag. It leaves the publication decision to the next component.
interpretation: The lower bound belongs to this invented sensor contract. Other temperature measurements can legitimately be negative.

examples.title: Keep each condition result beside its record ID
paragraphs: The boolean marks the condition only. It does not decide which rows should be published.
examples.code:
records = [{"id":"r1","temperature":10},{"id":"r2","temperature":None}]
checks = [(row["id"], row["temperature"] is not None and row["temperature"] >= 0) for row in records]
print(checks)
interpretation: Warn, drop and fail consume this evidence differently. The later challenge implements those consequences.

parts.title: 2. Choose what the failed condition should do
paragraphs: A warn policy retains the candidate records while recording the condition. A drop policy excludes failing rows from that output. A fail policy stops this dataset update when its condition fails. These policies answer different operational questions.

Dropping a rare fault case can bias the dataset. Stopping every update for an optional descriptive field can unnecessarily block useful work. Choose a policy from the meaning and consequences of the field, and preserve the evidence needed to inspect failures.
interpretation: Choose the failure consequence from what downstream training is allowed to use.

parts.title: 3. A failed update is not a new successful snapshot
paragraphs: In our atomic candidate-publication model, fail preserves the earlier published rows when any candidate row fails. The result also identifies that this attempt failed. Do not relabel the older dataset as newly validated output.

This is a boundary around one teaching dataset. Real pipelines can contain independent flows and datasets; failing one update is not a general promise that every separate effect in the pipeline has been rolled back. Platform metrics for a failed update can also differ from the counts we calculate locally here.
parts.calculation:
candidate readings = [10, -1, 20]
passing rows = 2
failing rows = 1
policy = fail
published rows remain the earlier snapshot
interpretation: Here the counts describe the candidate, while the returned rows identify which snapshot remains available.

parts.title: 4. Attach an expectation to a Lakeflow dataset
paragraphs: A materialized view stores the result of a query, which the pipeline can refresh from its declared sources. The reference describes one and attaches an expectation that fails its update. It belongs in a Lakeflow pipeline source file with a configured catalog and schema. The function returns a DataFrame; the pipeline manages its evaluation.

Use the current pyspark.pipelines interface in a supported Databricks runtime. Expectations shown here are Databricks extensions, not a claim that every open-source Spark installation supplies the same decorators. Keep arbitrary side effects out of dataset definitions.
interpretation: Use expect to retain rows and record checks, or expect_or_drop to remove invalid records from that output, when those policies are appropriate. They are different from expect_or_fail.

references.title: Fail an invalid candidate dataset in Lakeflow
description: This optional reference runs in your own Databricks environment. The browser exercise below uses ordinary Python and does not contact Databricks.
setup: Add this source to an optional Databricks Lakeflow pipeline configured with an approved target catalog/schema and an existing raw source table. Running the pipeline materialises data and can incur charges.
Use a runtime providing the documented pyspark.pipelines and Databricks expectation APIs. This is not an ordinary standalone Pyodide script.
interpretation: A failed expectation blocks this dataset update. Test the actual pipeline’s dependency and failure behavior separately from the local policy simulation.

parts.title: 5. Quarantine is an output you must design
paragraphs: Dropping a row from one result does not automatically create a quarantine dataset. If the team needs to inspect rejected readings, preserve them in an approved raw or rejected-record path with their failure reason and input identity. That path still needs access and retention rules.
Keep the source immutable while fixing the transformation or producer. A corrected input should produce a new explainable result, rather than silently rewriting the evidence behind an old model.
interpretation: The earlier quarantine lesson supplies the row-level reasoning. Here we make sure a platform policy does what that reasoning requires.

parts.title: 6. Test the output, not only the check name
paragraphs: Give the same candidate batch to warn, drop and fail policies. Compare rows as well as counts and status. Then use a batch where every row passes and check that fail does not prevent an acceptable update.

A fresh missing value tests another branch of the predicate. Keep these tests separate from a real pipeline dry run or integration test: our Python function can establish the local policy logic without establishing cluster permissions or storage atomicity.
interpretation: The next lesson connects a model’s measured score to the dataset and split on which that score was obtained.

practice.title: Make the publication policy match the intended consequence
practice.question: What should remain available when the new temperatures fail the check?
task: Write publish_candidate(records, minimum, policy, previous). records and previous are lists of dictionaries with temperature values that are finite numbers or None. policy is "warn", "drop" or "fail"; other values raise ValueError. A row passes when temperature is not None and is at least minimum. Return {"status", "rows", "passed", "failed"}. fail plus any invalid row returns status "failed" and a copy of previous; otherwise status is "published" and rows contains all candidates for warn/fail or only passing candidates for drop. Do not mutate inputs.

Try this new candidate batch containing temperatures 17, -2, 21, a missing value and 38. The earlier published temperature is 7. Print the result under the fail policy. The passing and failing counts describe the new candidate batch even when earlier rows remain published.
hints: Evaluate and count the candidate rows before deciding which dataset will be published.
Under fail, keep a copy of the earlier published rows when any candidate fails. The counts must still describe the attempted candidate, not those earlier rows.

title: A Better Score on Which Dataset?
topic: Connecting model evidence to an artifact
blurb: A lower error is tempting. First find out which observations produced that score and which saved model belongs to it.
openingTitle: The Winning Run Used a Different Validation Table
opening: Botie lists several training runs and chooses the smallest error. The new run looks excellent until we notice that it used a different validation table. Both tables happen to be at version four. Another score was measured on the final test set. Sorting those numbers together does not tell us which model improved on the same evidence.
We need a run record that connects the model to its inputs and assessment. Then we can decide which records belong in this particular comparison before choosing an artifact.

history.title: Which Experiment Produced This Model?
blocks: After several training attempts, a folder of model files and a list of scores are hard to interpret. Which settings changed? Which input version did each model see? Can a colleague repeat the run that produced the good result? A useful record has to keep the model file attached to the procedure and evidence that produced it.

Databricks introduced MLflow as an open-source project on June 5, 2018. Its announcement described the difficulty of tracking experiments and reproducing them across different machine-learning tools. MLflow Tracking groups a training attempt’s settings and results under a run ID. Code can log those details through its programming interface, and a person can compare the runs on a screen. It also keeps output files, such as the trained model, with the run that produced them.

A managed MLflow service is available in Databricks, and the open-source software can also be used elsewhere. In this lesson we use the tracking idea: keep a complete record for each attempt, then compare only attempts measured against the same validation evidence. Recording a score makes it inspectable; choosing a fair comparison is still our responsibility.

parts.title: 1. Make the run record readable before sorting it
paragraphs: Think of a run as the record of one execution of our experiment. It keeps what we tried beside what happened. The run ID names that execution. The saved model file is an artifact, meaning an output we keep, and its URI is the address another program can use to request it.

The input needs an address too: record the training table identity beside its version, and do the same for validation. Another table can have its own unrelated version four. The split says which assessment rows were used inside the selected validation snapshot. A dictionary keeps those meanings attached to the score and model.
interpretation: Throughout this example the metric is validation mean absolute error in the same temperature unit, and a smaller value is better.

parts.title: 2. Choose a comparison before choosing a winner
paragraphs: Declare the validation table identity, its version and the split used for this selection. Exclude records with different assessment evidence and records marked as final test results. Only then rank the remaining candidates by validation MAE.

Candidates may deliberately use different training tables, training versions or parameter settings. That can be the experiment we want to run. Hold the assessment evidence fixed while recording those training differences so we can investigate what changed.
interpretation: Repeatedly selecting on the validation set can still overfit that selection process. The final untouched assessment remains separate.

examples.title: A table-local version needs its table identity
paragraphs: Both rows have version four and the same split. Keep the row from the declared assessment table.
examples.code:
runs = [{"runId":"a","validationTable":"lab.validation.easy_readings","validationVersion":4,"split":"S"}, {"runId":"b","validationTable":"lab.validation.sensor_readings","validationVersion":4,"split":"S"}]
print([row["runId"] for row in runs if row["validationTable"] == "lab.validation.sensor_readings" and row["validationVersion"] == 4 and row["split"] == "S"])
interpretation: The full selector also checks assessment role, ranks the eligible errors and preserves both input table identities in the manifest.

parts.title: 3. A dataset digest does not replace a retained input
paragraphs: An MLflow dataset record can describe where rows came from and include a compact digest, a summary used to recognise that dataset. The record is useful for inspection, but it does not contain all the source files. Keep the named Delta table and version, with a retention plan that allows the needed read.

Training may transform those rows before the model sees them. Record the transformation code and settings as well as any preprocessing learned from training data. Otherwise two runs could name the same raw table while training on different representations.
interpretation: This is why the earlier lineage work matters: we want to follow a model back through the actual operations that produced its input.

parts.title: 4. Log the input that the run actually read
paragraphs: The reference constructs dataset records from explicitly versioned training and validation Delta reads. It selects the named validation split before logging that input. The supplied fitted model and measured validation MAE must come from that exact declared procedure.

The input example omits the label and must match the model’s actual input representation. Use the returned model_uri rather than inventing an artifact path from a displayed metric. Keep the runtime and dependency versions with the project.
interpretation: The tracking run now names both tables, their versions and the assessment split beside the model artifact.

references.title: Attach both dataset identities and the artifact to one MLflow run
references.code:
import mlflow
import mlflow.sklearn

training_table, training_version = "lab.training.sensor_features", 4
validation_table, validation_version = "lab.validation.sensor_readings", 8
validation_split = "S"
training = spark.read.option("versionAsOf", training_version).table(training_table)
validation = spark.read.option("versionAsOf", validation_version).table(validation_table)
validation = validation.filter(validation["split_id"] == validation_split)
training_dataset = mlflow.data.from_spark(
    training, table_name=training_table, version=str(training_version), targets="target",
)
validation_dataset = mlflow.data.from_spark(
    validation, table_name=validation_table, version=str(validation_version), targets="target",
)
with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_input(training_dataset, context="training")
    mlflow.log_input(validation_dataset, context="validation")
    mlflow.log_param("training_table", training_table)
    mlflow.log_param("training_table_version", training_version)
    mlflow.log_param("validation_table", validation_table)
    mlflow.log_param("validation_table_version", validation_version)
    mlflow.log_param("validation_split", validation_split)
    mlflow.log_metric("validation_mae", float(validation_mae))
    model_info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(
        fitted_model, name="model", input_example=input_example,
    )
    print(run.info.run_id, model_info.model_uri)
description: This optional reference runs in your own Databricks environment. The browser exercise below uses ordinary Python and does not contact Databricks.
setup: Use an optional Databricks MLflow environment supporting the documented MLflow 3 name parameter, with both retained Delta tables and permission to read them. Each has target; the validation table also has split_id. Replace the example identities and retained versions with the inputs your procedure actually used.

Before running, supply fitted_model, input_example and validation_mae from training on the declared training read and evaluating on the declared validation read after its split filter. This reference logs those results; it does not train or evaluate a model.
Logging writes experiment metadata and a model artifact. Use an approved tracking location; never log service credentials or unnecessary personal example records.
interpretation: The dataset records and explicit parameters preserve table identity as well as version. The split and role identify which assessment a metric describes.

parts.title: 5. Return the artifact identity with the decision
paragraphs: Once a comparable run is selected, return a manifest containing its run ID and model URI together with both training and validation table identities, their versions and the split. Keeping version numbers without their table identities would leave the next consumer guessing which histories to read.

A real release also needs input/output contracts, runtime dependencies and approval evidence appropriate to the application. Loading an artifact must follow the model-file security boundary from the other course area.
interpretation: The manifest should let another piece of software identify the artifact and its declared evidence.

parts.title: 6. Handle missing comparisons and exact ties deliberately
paragraphs: If no run used the required validation table, version and split, the result is no eligible comparison. Raise a clear error instead of choosing the smallest number from another dataset. In our challenge, exact metric ties use run ID order only to make the output deterministic.
That tie-breaker is not evidence of statistical superiority. Small observed differences may need paired analysis and uncertainty estimates before a practical conclusion can be defended.
interpretation: Keep that complete chosen record on the wire all the way to the manifest.

parts.title: 7. Try a tempting but invalid winner
paragraphs: A useful fresh case gives a run on another validation table an extremely good number while leaving its version and split unchanged. If it still wins, part of the evidence identity was lost. Other cases change the version or split.
Keep final-test rows out of this selection altogether. Looking at a test score to choose a candidate spends the independence that test set was meant to provide.
interpretation: Can the job identity read the table named in this manifest?

practice.title: Choose a comparable run and retain its manifest
practice.question: Which saved model actually improved on the same validation records?
task: Write choose_run(runs, validation_version, split, validation_table). Each run dictionary contains role, validationTable, validationVersion, split, mae, runId, modelUri, trainingTable and trainingVersion. Table identities are nonempty fully qualified names. Keep role="validation" only when its validation table identity, version and split exactly match the request. Different training tables remain eligible. Eligible MAE values must be finite and nonnegative; raise ValueError for an invalid eligible value or an empty eligible set. Choose minimum (mae, runId). Return a new dictionary containing runId, modelUri, trainingTable, trainingVersion, validationTable, validationVersion and split, in that order. Do not mutate runs.

In this new comparison E has a tempting score on another validation table with the same version and split. Print the selected manifest for lab.validation.sensor_readings version 4, split S. Then print its MAE reduction relative to run A with two decimal places. Model URIs are illustrative identifiers that the function must not load.

practice.solution:
import math

def choose_run(runs, validation_version, split, validation_table):
    eligible=[r for r in runs if r["role"] == "validation" and r["validationTable"] == validation_table and r["validationVersion"] == validation_version and r["split"] == split]
    if not eligible or any(not math.isfinite(r["mae"]) or r["mae"] < 0 for r in eligible):
        raise ValueError("No valid comparable selection")
    selected=min(eligible,key=lambda r:(r["mae"],r["runId"]))
    return {k:selected[k] for k in ["runId","modelUri","trainingTable","trainingVersion","validationTable","validationVersion","split"]}

runs = [
 {"runId":"A","modelUri":"models:/A","trainingTable":"lab.training.raw_features","trainingVersion":3,"validationTable":"lab.validation.sensor_readings","validationVersion":4,"split":"S","role":"validation","mae":2.0},
 {"runId":"B","modelUri":"models:/B","trainingTable":"lab.training.raw_features","trainingVersion":4,"validationTable":"lab.validation.sensor_readings","validationVersion":5,"split":"S","role":"validation","mae":0.5},
 {"runId":"C","modelUri":"models:/C","trainingTable":"lab.training.calibrated_features","trainingVersion":8,"validationTable":"lab.validation.sensor_readings","validationVersion":4,"split":"S","role":"validation","mae":1.4},
 {"runId":"D","modelUri":"models:/D","trainingTable":"lab.training.raw_features","trainingVersion":7,"validationTable":"lab.validation.sensor_readings","validationVersion":4,"split":"S","role":"validation","mae":1.8},
 {"runId":"E","modelUri":"models:/E","trainingTable":"lab.training.raw_features","trainingVersion":7,"validationTable":"lab.validation.easy_readings","validationVersion":4,"split":"S","role":"validation","mae":0.01}]
chosen = choose_run(runs,4,"S","lab.validation.sensor_readings")
print(chosen)
selected_error = next(row["mae"] for row in runs if row["runId"] == chosen["runId"])
print(f'{runs[0]["mae"] - selected_error:.2f}')
