title: SELECT Is Not the Whole Permission to Read a Table
blurb: The table is there, and a colleague can read it. Why does the scheduled training job still fail to access the same records?
openingTitle: The Model Job Can See the Table Name but Cannot Read Its Rows
opening: Botie’s experiment manifest names the right table. The scheduled job fails when it tries to read it, even though someone granted SELECT. The person who explored the data in a notebook and the service running training may also have different permissions.

A table belongs inside a schema and catalog. Reading it needs the relevant access at those boundaries, under the identity actually executing the job. Granting broad administrator access would conceal which permission was missing.

history.title: A Shared Table Needed a Shared Access Decision

sources.title: Unity Catalog history and open-source announcement, June 2024

blocks: As teams used the same data from different workspaces and tools, finding a table and deciding who could read it became connected problems. Separate catalogs and access settings could disagree. A job that found a useful training table still needed an enforceable answer about whether its actual identity was allowed to use it.

Databricks introduced Unity Catalog in 2021 as a shared governance system. The managed service now covers data and AI objects. Databricks announced an open-source Unity Catalog project in June 2024. The managed Databricks service and the open-source project are related products with different operational scope; the SQL reference here uses the managed service’s documented privileges.

A catalog records what objects are called and where they belong. Access rules attach privileges to those objects and to principals, the users, groups or service identities receiving permission. We will follow one training job through those relationships, so a successful read in somebody else’s notebook cannot stand in for the job’s own permission check.

parts.title: 1. Resolve the full name before asking who may read it
paragraphs: Start by locating the object the job wants. In lab.training.features, lab names the catalog, training names a schema inside it, and features names the table. These names let the service distinguish this features table from a table with the same short name in another team’s schema.

Our teaching check asks for permission to use the catalog and schema, then permission to read the table. Keep each privilege beside the object it refers to. A free-floating SELECT label would not tell us which table the job may read.
interpretation: A complete name makes the scope of the next permission question explicit.

examples.title: A privilege is paired with its object
paragraphs: Tuples can keep privilege and object together in a set. Matching SELECT does not make the enclosing requirements disappear.
interpretation: This component omits principal identity. The challenge adds that boundary instead of assuming every shown grant belongs to the caller.

parts.title: 2. Check the principal that actually runs the job
paragraphs: A principal is the identity receiving privileges, such as a user, group or service principal. A scheduled training job can run as a different principal from the notebook author. Inspect that execution context before editing grants.

The workshop receives verified principal and group identities as application-provided data. It does not let an agent authenticate itself by writing a group name. Real group membership must come from the identity system and be enforced at the data service.
interpretation: For a read under this explicit model, SELECT must be accompanied by USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA at the enclosing objects.

paragraphs: The SQL reference grants the explicit read permissions to an example training group. An authorised owner or administrator must choose and apply actual grants. Do not run it on a production catalog merely to make an exercise pass.

Real Unity Catalog can inherit some privileges from ancestor objects, and owners or administrators can have other authority. The browser model checks direct explicit grants only. Use the platform’s actual effective permission evidence when diagnosing a real job.
interpretation: Permission to use a namespace is different from permission to read every table in it. Keep the selected table grant narrow when that matches the job’s scope.

parts.title: 4. Preserve the missing requirements in a refusal
paragraphs: A useful refusal can say which declared boundary is missing without returning the protected rows. Our result is {allow, missing}; missing contains privilege/object pairs. Requiring every listed result prevents one successful SELECT check from masking a failed enclosing requirement.

Passing this educational check does not authorise a real data request. The server and platform must still enforce current permission when data is accessed, including revocations after an earlier run was approved.

parts.title: 5. Test a different identity and a different schema
paragraphs: First provide SELECT but omit USE SCHEMA. Then keep all grant records unchanged and replace the principal with an unrelated job. Finally move the same short table name to another schema. Each case tests whether identity and object scope remain attached to the privilege.

The next lesson assumes the feature rows were obtained through a permitted read. It will ask which of those rows were available at the time of each prediction, another boundary permission alone cannot establish.
interpretation: The next decision is which historically available rows belong to each prediction.

practice.question: Why does night-job still lack permission to read this table?
task: Write read_access(table, grants, principals). table is catalog.schema.table, with each name matching [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*; otherwise raise ValueError. grants is a list of dictionaries containing principal, object and privilege. principals is a trusted list of the actual identity and its established groups. Require direct matching grants for USE CATALOG on catalog, USE SCHEMA on catalog.schema, and SELECT on the full table. Return {"allow": boolean, "missing": [requirement strings]} in catalog/schema/table order. Do not infer inheritance or mutate inputs.

The new job reads operations.sensors.daily_features. One shown grant belongs to an analyst rather than the job. Print the job’s decision, then the number of the three required permissions it actually holds. This is an explicit-grant teaching check rather than a real authentication or Unity Catalog enforcement service.

def read_access(table, grants, principals):
    pass

grants = [{"principal":"night-job","object":"operations","privilege":"USE CATALOG"},{"principal":"night-job","object":"operations.sensors.daily_features","privilege":"SELECT"},{"principal":"analyst","object":"operations.sensors","privilege":"USE SCHEMA"}]

print(decision)
print(3 - len(decision["missing"]))
practice.solution:
import re

def read_access(table, grants, principals):
    pieces=table.split(".")
    if len(pieces)!=3 or any(re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*",p) is None for p in pieces):
        raise ValueError("Use a complete simple table name")
    requirements=[("USE CATALOG",pieces[0]),("USE SCHEMA",".".join(pieces[:2])),("SELECT",table)]
    missing=[privilege+" "+obj for privilege,obj in requirements
             if not any(g["principal"] in principals and g["object"]==obj and g["privilege"]==privilege for g in grants)]
    return {"allow":not missing,"missing":missing}

grants = [{"principal":"night-job","object":"operations","privilege":"USE CATALOG"},{"principal":"night-job","object":"operations.sensors.daily_features","privilege":"SELECT"},{"principal":"analyst","object":"operations.sensors","privilege":"USE SCHEMA"}]
decision = read_access("operations.sensors.daily_features", grants, ["night-job"])
print(decision)
print(3 - len(decision["missing"]))

title: Give Each Prediction the Features It Could Actually Have Seen
blurb: The current temperature is useful for a prediction now. An old prediction needs the value that was available then, including a deliberate rule for missing or stale readings.
openingTitle: The Training Table Knows the Answer Before Botie Could Have Known It
opening: Botie can read the approved table. He now joins the latest temperature to every old inspection. Unfortunately, a temperature correction published after an inspection becomes an input to that inspection’s prediction. The training example has learned something from its own future.

We need a feature value belonging to that pump and available by that prediction time. We will also decide how old a feature may be. A missing value must remain visible rather than being quietly replaced by the newest reading.

history.title: Reusing a Feature Without Rewriting Its Past

sources.title: Uber Engineering: Michelangelo and its shared feature store, September 2017

blocks: A feature is an input a model reads. Temperature is one simple feature in our example. When several models need the same input, rebuilding it separately can give training and live prediction different definitions. A feature store keeps reusable feature data and metadata so those consumers can request a shared input.

Uber’s September 2017 account of its Michelangelo platform described a shared feature store for training and prediction. It is an influential published example of the need to reuse inputs consistently, rather than a claim that one company invented every part of feature storage. Databricks’ feature engineering interfaces address related work through reusable tables and model-linked lookups.

Reusing a definition still leaves a time question. A prediction made before a correction was published could not have read that correction. Databricks documents point-in-time feature lookup for matching each prediction to its earlier eligible feature rows. Delta time travel chooses a table snapshot; this lookup chooses a row for each prediction within that retained history.

parts.title: 1. Write down the two kinds of rows
paragraphs: Keep the two kinds of records visible. A feature-history row names a pump, the minute its value was published and the value. A prediction row names a pump and the minute when a decision needed to be made. These timestamps describe different events.

For a prediction about P7, begin with P7’s feature history. Then ask which values had been published by the decision minute. A recent reading from another pump cannot fill this input just because its timestamp is convenient.

Both Python inputs are lists of dictionaries. The same pump can occur in several prediction dictionaries because it needs decisions at different times. Our invented shift uses integer minutes from one start time; real timestamp fields need consistent types and a clear time-zone convention.
interpretation: Keep one result per prediction in its original order, including predictions with no usable feature.

parts.title: 2. Use availability, not a backdated event label
paragraphs: An event timestamp says when something happened. A publication timestamp says when this particular computed feature became usable. A correction can refer to an old event while arriving after the prediction.

The workshop compares publishedAt with the prediction’s at field. Published history must not be backdated or overwritten in a way that invents earlier availability. An as-of API cannot recover the true arrival history if the table falsely labels a later correction as previously known.
interpretation: Read the timestamp definition as an input contract: when did this computed value become usable?

parts.title: 3. Select candidates before choosing the newest one
paragraphs: First match the pump. Then keep features published no later than the prediction. Finally apply the declared maximum age. The workshop treats both timestamp boundaries as inclusive. Only after those checks do we choose the greatest remaining publication time.

If no candidate remains, return null for that prediction’s feature. A legitimate missing value is different from zero, and neither is permission to read a future row. If the latest available row explicitly contains null, keep that null instead of quietly searching backward for a nicer value.
parts.calculation:
prediction minute = 6
feature publication minutes = [3, 8]
maximum age = 5 minutes
3 <= 6 and 6 - 3 <= 5: eligible
8 > 6: unavailable
selected value = 10
interpretation: A fresh sensor value can still be wrong; the earlier range and quality checks remain part of the pipeline.

examples.title: Find a prediction’s available same-pump candidates
paragraphs: Start with entity and availability. This small component has not yet applied the age limit or chosen the newest row.
examples.code:
history = [{"pump":"P7","publishedAt":3,"value":10},{"pump":"P7","publishedAt":8,"value":99},{"pump":"P2","publishedAt":4,"value":20}]
candidates = [row for row in history if row["pump"] == "P7" and row["publishedAt"] <= 6]
print([(row["publishedAt"], row["value"]) for row in candidates])
interpretation: The complete lookup additionally applies freshness, preserves every prediction row and handles absent or explicitly missing latest values.

parts.title: 4. Keep snapshot identity separate from lookup time
paragraphs: A Delta snapshot identifies which committed contents of a table we read. A point-in-time lookup selects suitable feature rows inside those contents for each prediction timestamp. Both may be needed for an honest training reconstruction.

Record a feature-table snapshot and the lookup contract. If later backfills rewrite old feature rows, an unpinned latest-table read may change an old training set even though its prediction timestamps stay unchanged. Retained snapshots or immutable publication history prevent that change from being hidden.
interpretation: A feature key identifies the entity. The timestamp key must be explicitly designated for time-series lookup; merely adding a timestamp to an ordinary equality key does not create as-of semantics.

parts.title: 5. Declare the time-series keys in the real feature interface
paragraphs: The optional reference registers a time-series feature table and builds a training set from prediction rows. FeatureLookup names the entity and prediction-timestamp columns. Its lookback window provides a training-time age bound.

The feature history is assumed to use actual publication availability as its timestamp. Registering a column cannot prove that semantic claim. Check the selected runtime’s table constraints and API support, and do not use preview pipeline primary-key features unless you deliberately choose a preview environment.
interpretation: Databricks distinguishes this historical join from online latest-value lookup. Do not assume a training lookback setting automatically enforces the same age policy in every online serving path.

references.title: Build a training set from published feature history
references.code:
from datetime import timedelta
from databricks.feature_engineering import FeatureEngineeringClient, FeatureLookup

fe = FeatureEngineeringClient()
fe.create_table(
    name="lab.training.published_temperatures",
    primary_keys=["pump", "published_at"],
    timeseries_columns="published_at",
    df=published_features,
)
lookup = FeatureLookup(
    table_name="lab.training.published_temperatures",
    feature_names=["temperature"], lookup_key="pump",
    timestamp_lookup_key="prediction_at",
    lookback_window=timedelta(minutes=5),
)
training_set = fe.create_training_set(
    df=predictions, feature_lookups=[lookup], label="target",
    exclude_columns=["pump", "prediction_at"],
)
training_rows = training_set.load_df()
description: This optional reference runs in your own Databricks environment. The browser exercise below uses ordinary Python and does not contact Databricks.
setup: Use your own Unity Catalog-enabled Databricks workspace with a compatible databricks-feature-engineering client. Current Unity Catalog examples use timeseries_columns; timestamp_keys belongs to the legacy Workspace Feature Store interface.

Provide published_features with pump STRING, published_at TIMESTAMP and temperature DOUBLE, unique per entity/timestamp, and predictions with pump STRING, prediction_at TIMESTAMP and target. Use a consistent timestamp convention.
The reference creates a table; use a new approved name and inspect uniqueness, permission and retention requirements before running it. No workspace or credential is required for the local exercise.
interpretation: The timestamp key activates historical lookup. It cannot make a backdated correction truthful or prove that an online serving policy uses the same age bound.

parts.title: 6. Make training and serving agree about missing and stale values
paragraphs: Training can return a missing feature for an early prediction. Serving needs an explicit policy for that same condition: use a declared fallback, request another measurement or decline the prediction. Filling missing values differently in the two paths creates a new model procedure.

Publish and test the transformation version as well as feature values. A shared table name is insufficient if training calculates a five-minute window while serving uses an hour, or if one side clips readings and the other retains them.
interpretation: Pass missing results to a declared fallback policy after this lookup.

parts.title: 7. Test the future, the boundary and the absent entity
paragraphs: Move only the prediction time across a publication boundary and predict when the selected value changes. Then shorten the maximum age so the previously eligible row becomes stale. Add another pump with a recent feature and make sure it never fills a missing value for the requested pump.

Conflicting values at the same entity and publication time are another data-contract failure. Stop rather than letting a distributed row order choose one. A fresh result should preserve which prediction is missing and why it could not use the later record.
interpretation: When a new correction arrives, inspect its publication timestamp before letting it change a historical training row.

practice.title: Reconstruct the feature available for each prediction
practice.question: Which reading could each prediction have used at the time?
task: Write historical_features(history, predictions, maximum_age). history contains dictionaries with pump (text), publishedAt (integer shift minute) and value (number or None). predictions contains pump and at in the same unit. Return one {"pump", "at", "temperature"} dictionary per prediction in original order. Match the pump, require publishedAt <= at and at - publishedAt <= maximum_age, then use the greatest eligible publishedAt. Return None when absent; preserve an explicit latest None. Conflicting values for one pump/publication timestamp raise ValueError. maximum_age is nonnegative. Do not mutate arguments.

The new history contains different feature values and three prediction rows. Print all three lookup results in their original order, then the sum of the numerical temperatures that were available. Keep None for the absent pump; it contributes nothing to that diagnostic sum. This is a local reconstruction under an immutable-publication contract.
practice.starter:
def historical_features(history, predictions, maximum_age):
    pass

history = [{"pump":"P7","publishedAt":3,"value":14},{"pump":"P7","publishedAt":8,"value":61}]
results = historical_features(history,[{"pump":"P7","at":6},{"pump":"P7","at":9},{"pump":"P2","at":9}],5)
print(results)
print(sum(row["temperature"] for row in results if row["temperature"] is not None))
practice.solution:
def historical_features(history, predictions, maximum_age):
    versions={}
    for row in history:
        identity=(row["pump"],row["publishedAt"])
        if identity in versions and versions[identity] != row["value"]:
            raise ValueError("Conflicting feature version")
        versions[identity]=row["value"]
    result=[]
    for prediction in predictions:
        pump, at=prediction["pump"],prediction["at"]
        candidates=[r for r in history if r["pump"]==pump and r["publishedAt"]<=at and at-r["publishedAt"]<=maximum_age]
        latest=max(candidates,key=lambda r:r["publishedAt"]) if candidates else None
        result.append({"pump":pump,"at":at,"temperature":latest["value"] if latest else None})
    return result

history = [{"pump":"P7","publishedAt":3,"value":14},{"pump":"P7","publishedAt":8,"value":61}]
results = historical_features(history,[{"pump":"P7","at":6},{"pump":"P7","at":9},{"pump":"P2","at":9}],5)
print(results)
print(sum(row["temperature"] for row in results if row["temperature"] is not None))

title: Faster Batches Can Still Make a User Wait
blurb: Compare throughput with request latency before choosing an inference batch policy.
openingTitle: The GPU Got Faster. The First User Did Not.
opening: Botie’s image model processes several images together more efficiently than one at a time. We wait for a larger batch and throughput improves. The first request, however, spends that waiting time in a queue.
We need to measure the experience of each request, not divide the batch runtime and call that the user’s latency.

history.title: Batching Trades Waiting for Shared Computation
blocks: Training software often processes several examples together because a processor can share work across them. An online service receives requests one at a time, and the first person in a group must wait while the others arrive. The batch that makes good use of the hardware can still give that person a slow answer.

The Clipper system, presented in 2017, treated prediction serving as a separate problem from training. Its adaptive batching adjusted how many queued requests a model processed together while respecting a latency objective. The useful change was to make batch size depend on the model's observed performance rather than assuming a larger batch was always better. Current servers such as Triton also expose controls for queue delay and batching.

Our first example follows requests already assigned to one batch. We will distinguish time waiting in the queue from time spent computing. A later scheduler has to make its decision using both, because sharing computation cannot recover time a request has already spent waiting.

parts.title: 1. A batch shares computation, not arrival time
paragraphs: Two independent image requests can often be calculated together because neither needs to remember the other’s earlier work. Such requests are stateless. A continuing conversation is stateful: its saved history must remain attached to that conversation. Combining those sequences needs additional scheduling rules as well as compatible input shapes.
Track arrival, dispatch and completion separately. Queue delay occurs before dispatch; execution time occurs after it.
interpretation: Padding incompatible lengths can consume memory and computation. A larger batch is not automatically a better batch.

parts.title: 2. Calculate latency from the common completion
paragraphs: For the fixture, execution takes eight milliseconds and dispatch happens at six. Each arrival has a different wait.
parts.calculation:
completion = dispatch + execution = 6 + 8 = 14
arrivals = [0,4,6]
latencies = [14,10,8] ms
batch throughput = 3 / 0.008 = 375 requests/second
interpretation: That throughput describes execution of this batch. It does not include idle time, queueing or transport overhead.

examples.title: Separate queue delay from execution
paragraphs: A list retains one waiting time for each request.
examples.code:
arrivals = [0,4,6]
dispatch = 6
print([dispatch-t for t in arrivals])
interpretation: All requests still have to execute after these waits. The earliest request has waited longest.

parts.title: 3. Set a delay limit before chasing utilisation
paragraphs: At low traffic, waiting for a full batch may take too long. A maximum delay lets a partial batch leave. Under heavy traffic, queues can grow even when batches dispatch immediately.
Compare latency distributions at realistic arrival rates. Include slow shapes and cold starts; one average runtime is insufficient.
interpretation: A service objective should state whether it measures model execution or the full user-visible request.

parts.title: 4. Keep the measurement honest
paragraphs: Use monotonic clocks for elapsed durations within a process. Cross-machine timestamps need a clock model. Include cancellations and failures in the report rather than counting only successful fast requests.
The coding challenge checks impossible dispatch times so a negative wait cannot quietly improve the result.
interpretation: The workshop is a timing model of one batch, not a measured GPU benchmark.

title: A Tool Call Cannot Spend the Whole Deadline Again
blurb: Propagate remaining time through an agent’s tool calls and preserve an explicit response margin.
openingTitle: Every Tool Timed Out Correctly. The Answer Was Still Late.
opening: Botie has a deadline for answering a technician. Retrieval uses most of it, then a second tool receives the original timeout again. Each service obeys its local setting, but the overall run exceeds the technician’s budget.
The next call needs the time remaining in this run. We should also reserve enough time to assemble and return the answer.

history.title: A Deadline Follows the Request

sources.title: gRPC and Deadlines, Google SRE guidance, February 2018

blocks: A service can call another service, which calls a third. If each starts a fresh timeout, the complete request may take much longer than its caller agreed to wait. Work can also continue consuming resources after the caller has given up.

In a 2018 gRPC article, Google site reliability engineer Gráinne Sheerin explained why clients should set deadlines deliberately. gRPC is a framework for calling procedures in another process across a network. Its deadline support lets the caller put a time boundary on that work, and implementations can propagate the remaining allowance to downstream calls. The allowance shrinks as work happens; another service does not receive a fresh budget simply because it started later.

An agent making several tool calls has the same dependency. We will calculate what remains before starting the next call. Cancelling a request still requires cooperation from the work it started, especially if an external action may already have happened.

parts.title: 1. A timeout is local; a deadline names the endpoint
paragraphs: A timeout says how long a particular operation may wait. A deadline says when the overall result stops being useful. Before each downstream operation, compute what remains.
Across machines, propagate a supported relative timeout or protocol deadline rather than comparing unsynchronised wall clocks yourself.
interpretation: Reserve time for serialisation and returning the response. That reserve should come from measurements, not wishful thinking.

parts.title: 2. Stop when no allowance remains
paragraphs: Subtract elapsed time and the response reserve from the total budget, then clamp at zero.
parts.calculation:
remaining = max(0, 1000 - 700 - 100) = 200 ms
after 950 ms elapsed:
remaining = max(0, 1000 - 950 - 100) = 0 ms
interpretation: A zero allowance means do not start another ordinary tool call. It does not mean an instantaneous call will somehow complete.

examples.title: The reserve is already spoken for
paragraphs: A raw remainder can be negative, which is a reason to stop allocating new work.
examples.code:
budget, elapsed, reserve = 1000, 950, 100
print(budget-elapsed-reserve)
interpretation: The negative value is not a valid network timeout. The caller must clamp the allowance and choose its terminal response.

parts.title: 3. Cancellation does not undo an action
paragraphs: A timeout may occur after a service committed an external effect. Retrying a write requires an idempotency or reconciliation design. Cancelling a local task cannot recall an email already sent.
Propagate cancellation to work you control, release resources, and record uncertain outcomes explicitly.
interpretation: The agent retry and side-effect lessons cover effect recovery. Here we restrict the amount of time new work can consume.

parts.title: 4. Observe where the budget went
paragraphs: Record elapsed stages and cancellation reasons alongside a run identifier. Distinguish waiting for a worker from execution and network delay. Avoid putting private prompts into every timing log.
Test a run that has already exceeded its deadline and one exactly on the reserve boundary.
interpretation: A remaining-time calculator is one component. Enforcing it requires the caller and every relevant downstream service to cooperate.

practice.title: Pass only the time that remains
practice.question: How much of this run’s time budget may the next tool use?
task: Each tool cannot begin again with the whole run’s original timeout. Keep enough of the remaining time to send the response. Write remaining(total, elapsed, reserve). Inputs must be nonnegative finite numbers; reject invalid values with ValueError. Return the nonnegative allowance.
All three durations use the same unit; the demonstration uses milliseconds. Print the remaining allowance for its supplied values. When elapsed work and the reserve exhaust the budget, return zero.
practice.starter:
import math

def remaining(total, elapsed, reserve):
    pass

print(remaining(1000,700,100))
hints: Keep the response reserve outside the tool allowance.

title: The Model Fits Until the Conversations Grow
blurb: Account for transformer key/value cache growth separately from model weights.
openingTitle: We Loaded the Model. Why Did the Next Conversation Run Out of Memory?
opening: Botie’s language model loads successfully onto the accelerator. Several long conversations later, the service runs out of memory. The parameter count did not change. The stored attention keys and values did.

In attention, each earlier token has a key used for comparisons and a value containing information a later position can gather. Saving those arrays avoids calculating them again for every new token. This is the key/value cache, often shortened to KV cache; the arrays are also called tensors. Its memory grows with the tokens retained for active sequences, so the weights alone cannot tell us how many conversations fit.

history.title: Reusing Attention State Consumes Memory
blocks: A language model generates a response one token at a time. Earlier tokens still matter to later ones. Saving the intermediate arrays called attention keys and values avoids calculating them again at every generation step, but the saved state grows as conversations grow. Fitting the model's weights in memory does not establish that all those conversations will fit too.

Kwon and colleagues studied this serving problem in their 2023 PagedAttention paper. Requests had different, changing cache sizes, so reserving large contiguous regions could leave memory unused inside or between allocations. Their design borrowed paging ideas from operating systems: manage attention state in smaller blocks and keep a record of which blocks hold each sequence. The vLLM serving system used that arrangement to support more useful work within its memory budget.

Before comparing ways to reserve memory, we need to count the values a conversation actually requires. This lesson calculates the storage for those arrays first. A real server also has bookkeeping overhead and temporary arrays, so its measured memory will exceed this deliberately isolated quantity.

parts.title: 1. Weights and conversation state have different lifetimes
paragraphs: The model weights are shared across requests for one loaded version. Cached keys and values belong to token positions in active sequences. Generated tokens extend that state.
Use the number of key/value heads, which can differ from query heads in grouped-query attention. Count both key and value tensors.
interpretation: Some servers share prefixes or use sliding windows. Those change the effective retained tokens and must be reflected in a more detailed estimate.

parts.title: 2. Multiply the dimensions, then count active tokens
paragraphs: For uncompressed dense cache entries with no sharing, multiply the storage per token by the sum of retained sequence lengths.
parts.calculation:
bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per scalar
example = 2 × 2 × 1 × 4 × 2 = 32
lengths = [3,5]
KV bytes = 32 × (3 + 5) = 256
interpretation: The first factor of two counts keys and values. It is unrelated to the numerical precision.

examples.title: Inspect one token’s dimensions
paragraphs: Keys and values share the same dimensions in this simplified cache model.
examples.code:
layers, kv_heads, width, scalar_bytes = 2,1,4,2
print(2*layers*kv_heads*width*scalar_bytes)
interpretation: This scalar is bytes per retained token. It still needs the total retained token count to describe the active workload.

parts.title: 3. Admission needs room for future tokens
paragraphs: A request can fit at admission and grow beyond the limit during generation. Bound generation length or reserve capacity for the configured maximum. Decide what happens when the bound is reached.
Physical allocation can round up to blocks. Fragmentation and temporary attention buffers make measured memory larger than the simple logical estimate.
interpretation: Do not advertise the logical estimate as an exact GPU capacity. Compare against measured peaks under realistic concurrent lengths.

parts.title: 4. Tie memory policy to user-visible behaviour
paragraphs: A server may queue, reject or shorten requests under pressure. Each choice changes latency or output completeness. Record these outcomes rather than counting only successful requests.
Use this estimate with the earlier deadline model: admitting every request can leave all of them waiting too long.
interpretation: The coding function deliberately exposes each dimension so a head-count or precision change is testable.

parts.title: 5. A request scheduler must leave headroom
paragraphs: A server may allocate cache in blocks and reserve space before every token is generated. Logical tensor bytes are therefore a lower-level accounting quantity, not a direct promise about admission capacity.

Measure peak allocated memory while varying concurrent lengths, batch size and output limits. Leave headroom for temporary buffers and exceptional paths. If a request must be rejected or queued, make that behaviour visible to the caller and the latency report.
interpretation: Memory policy and deadline policy must be evaluated together. A queue that avoids an allocation failure can still miss every response deadline.

Print the dense byte estimate for the starter’s settings; runtime allocation overhead and cache sharing are excluded.

title: A Cached Agent Answer Belongs to a Particular Context
blurb: Separate response reuse from semantic similarity by preserving tenant, evidence and model identity.
openingTitle: The Same Question Came from a Different Team
opening: Two technicians ask Botie the same question. Their teams can read different manuals. A cache keyed only by the question returns the first team’s answer to the second. Faster inference has created a data boundary failure.
A response belongs to the context that produced it. We need a reuse key that includes the relevant authority and evidence versions, then permission checks at the point of use.

history.title: A Cache Entry Needs a Reuse Contract
blocks: Reusing an earlier response can save a network request and the work behind it. Web caches also exposed the uncomfortable question: when is the earlier answer still an answer to this request? A page can change, and the same address can produce different responses for different callers.

The 1999 HTTP/1.1 specification documented rules for caching, including freshness and matching the request to the stored response. Later specifications refined those rules; RFC 9111 brought the caching specification forward in 2022. A cache key identifies a possible match, while reuse rules decide whether that match may actually be served. An address by itself cannot settle both questions.

An agent response has further dependencies, such as retrieved evidence and model configuration. We will identify those dependencies before deciding whether an old answer is reusable. This is an application-level contract. HTTP headers alone cannot decide whether the current user may see a previously generated answer.

parts.title: 1. List the dependencies of the answer
paragraphs: The question text is only one input. Relevant context can include the customer organisation, its current permissions, the evidence snapshot, model version, prompt version and generation settings. The organisation is often called the tenant. Keeping it in the context prevents identical questions from making two customers’ answers interchangeable. A conversation-dependent answer also depends on the relevant history.
Do not put secrets into the key itself or assume a hashed key makes sensitive metadata public-safe.
interpretation: A semantic similarity score is not evidence that two requests have the same authorisation or evidence.

parts.title: 2. Compare complete context, not one convenient field
paragraphs: In the workshop, each context record contains the fields required by a declared simplified contract. Compare those records and the question separately, then require both matches.
parts.calculation:
same question = true
same context = false
reuse = true AND false = false
interpretation: Production reuse also needs expiry and a fresh permission decision. A revoked permission must not remain valid because the cached context is old.

examples.title: Do not concatenate ambiguous fields
paragraphs: A structured encoding retains the boundary between question and tenant.
examples.code:
import json
print(json.dumps(["ab","c"],separators=(",", ":")))
print(json.dumps(["a","bc"],separators=(",", ":")))
interpretation: Plain concatenation would turn both inputs into abc. The structured representation keeps them distinct.

parts.title: 3. Version changes should invalidate the result
paragraphs: A corrected manual changes the evidence. A revised prompt changes the procedure. A model replacement can change outputs. Keeping these identities in the key makes invalidation explicit.
For nondeterministic generation, reuse intentionally returns an earlier sample. Decide whether that behaviour is acceptable for the application.
interpretation: Caching an embedding, a retrieved candidate set and a final answer are different choices with different dependencies.

parts.title: 4. Test across boundaries
paragraphs: Use the same wording across tenants, change only the evidence version, and then change only the model version. Each should produce a different key under this contract. Equivalent records with different key order should match.
Keep a bounded cache and remove expired entries. Correct identity does not itself limit storage growth.
interpretation: The challenge hashes a declared tuple of fields. It performs no retrieval and is not an authorisation service.

practice.title: Build a context-specific response key
practice.question: Does changing the tenant prevent reuse of the old response key?
task: The wording of a question can stay the same while the caller’s team or evidence changes. That must produce a different response-cache identity. Write response_key(question, tenant, evidence, model, prompt), hashing a JSON list of those exact strings using SHA-256. Preserve boundaries between fields. Print whether changing only tenant changes the key.

Return a hexadecimal digest of the serialised five-field list in the stated order. The demonstration prints whether changing tenant alone changes that key. Current permissions and expiry remain separate reuse conditions.
practice.starter:
import json, hashlib

def response_key(question, tenant, evidence, model, prompt):
    pass

print(response_key("why?","A","e1","m1","p1") != response_key("why?","B","e1","m1","p1"))
hints: Serialise a list instead of concatenating strings without boundaries.

title: The Answer Starts Late, Then Arrives in Bursts
blurb: Botie’s answer can start late or pause halfway through. Follow those two waits separately before deciding what to change in the service.
openingTitle: Botie Has Read the Manual. Why Is the Screen Still Empty?
opening: A technician asks Botie a short question, but the request also contains several pages from an equipment manual. The answer eventually appears quickly. Before that, the screen sits empty. Another request starts promptly, then produces words slowly.

Where is each request spending its time? The empty screen comes before the first visible piece of the answer. The later pauses occur while that answer is being continued. We will keep both in view, because improving one can leave the other unchanged.

prerequisites.title: Shared batches and individual waiting times

history.title: Why Generating an Answer Changed the Serving Problem

sources.title: vLLM: serving metrics and their definitions

blocks: Once a model has learned its parameters, using it to produce an output is called inference. A service has to arrange that work for the people sending requests. Putting several requests through a model together can use the hardware more efficiently. That arrangement is a batch. Generating text complicates it: the model produces a token, uses that growing text as context, and returns to produce another. One answer may finish while its neighbour still has a page to write.

In 2022, the Orca research serving system addressed batches that stayed fixed for an entire response. Its iteration-level scheduling reconsidered the participating requests after each generation step. That gave finished requests a way out and waiting requests a way in. We will return to that decision later. First, we need to see where a reader waits. The invented timestamps below explain timing measurements used by serving systems such as vLLM; they are not measurements of either implementation.

parts.title: 1. Reading the supplied text is work too
paragraphs: Before continuing a prompt, the model processes the supplied tokens and calculates information that its attention layers will use again. Here that prompt includes the manual as well as the technician’s question. This initial processing is called prefill. Many input positions can be processed together, depending on the model and runtime, but the attached pages still require work before an answer can begin.

The request may also wait in a queue before the model starts. Converting text to tokens takes time, as can sending the response across the network and displaying it in the browser. Decide where the clock starts and stops before treating the whole empty-screen interval as model computation.
interpretation: A server timestamp and a browser timestamp do not automatically share a clock. The teaching trace deliberately uses one clock.

parts.title: 2. Starting an answer and continuing it are different waits
paragraphs: Start a clock when the request reaches the boundary we have chosen. Stop it when the first token is emitted. That elapsed interval is time to first token. Afterward, the model continues the answer using the text accumulated so far. This continuation is called decoding. The timestamps let us distinguish starting the answer from keeping it moving.
The first token can be sampled from the prompt-processing result. Do not assume every runtime has an additional, separately timed “first decode” stage after prefill.
parts.calculation:
arrival = 0 ms
first visible token = 140 ms
time to first token = 140 - 0 = 140 ms
interpretation: The technician waited this long before seeing any of the answer. Faster later tokens do not erase that initial wait.

parts.title: 3. Keep the pauses instead of hiding them in an average
paragraphs: Subtract neighbouring emission timestamps to obtain the gaps between tokens. A single-token response has no such gap. Here one pause is longer than the other, which a mean alone would conceal.
parts.calculation:
emission times = [140, 170, 230] ms
between-token gaps = [170 - 140, 230 - 170]
                   = [30, 60] ms
mean gap = (30 + 60) / 2 = 45 ms
arrival-to-last-token time = 230 ms
interpretation: The number of between-token intervals is one smaller than the number of emitted tokens. Streaming chunks can contain several tokens, so chunk timestamps require a different interpretation.

parts.title: 4. More tokens per second can coexist with slower answers
paragraphs: Batching can keep an accelerator busier and increase the total tokens completed across requests. Each individual request can still wait longer between its own turns. System throughput measures completed work across a time window; it is not the reciprocal of every user’s latency.

Compare workloads with similar prompt and output lengths. Report distributions and offered load, including rejected or cancelled requests, rather than presenting one fast completed example as capacity.
interpretation: A token rate from one response and an aggregate service token rate answer different questions.

parts.title: 5. Decide what an experiment would distinguish
paragraphs: Suppose the queue wait grows while the model’s measured processing times stay similar. That points us toward the arriving workload and the decision about when to admit requests. If attaching a longer manual instead increases prompt-processing time, we have a different question: could some repeated prompt work be reused? Long prompt processing can also delay answers already being generated, which gives us a reason to examine the scheduling policy.

We would need timestamps around the relevant stages to test these explanations on a real service. Repeat the measurement with realistic request arrivals and keep network delays visible. Some optimisations propose several continuation tokens before checking which can be accepted, a method called speculative decoding. Such methods change the relationship between model operations and emitted tokens, so the measured boundaries still matter.
interpretation: The timestamps give us a specific question to investigate with stage instrumentation.

practice.title: Read a generated response as a timing trace
practice.question: Where did this response make the reader wait?
task: Why did this answer feel slow? Write response_timing(arrival, token_times). Use finite timestamps in milliseconds from one clock. Require at least one token, nondecreasing emission times, and no token before arrival; otherwise raise ValueError.

Return (first_wait, gaps), where first_wait is a float and gaps is a NumPy array of adjacent emission differences. Do not divide the total duration by token count. Print the first wait and the gap array as a list on separate lines.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def response_timing(arrival, token_times):
    pass

first, gaps = response_timing(5, [85, 110, 150, 175])
print(first)
print(gaps.tolist())
hints: Mark the request’s arrival and its first emitted token. The interval between them is the reader’s initial wait.
Adjacent differences preserve pauses. One token produces an empty gap vector.

title: The Same Manual Can Be Read Once, Until Its Prefix Changes
blurb: Several questions begin with the same manual. Work out which earlier attention calculations can be reused when the question or model configuration changes.
openingTitle: Why Read the Same Instructions for Every Question?
opening: Botie answers several questions about the same manual. Each request begins with the same instructions and document, followed by a different question. Reprocessing that unchanged beginning can repeat substantial work.

Could the next request use the calculations already made for that beginning? Sometimes. We need to know exactly which tokens stayed the same and whether the saved arrays were produced by the configuration now answering the question. A matching document name alone does not tell us either.

history.title: The Same Beginning Was Being Calculated Again
blocks: An attention layer calculates arrays called keys and values for the tokens it has processed. Later tokens use those arrays when attending to the earlier context. Keeping them avoids recalculating the entire earlier sequence for every generated token. This saved working information is the key/value cache, usually shortened to KV cache. Its memory grows as requests retain more tokens.

The 2023 PagedAttention work addressed how to manage that growing memory without requiring one large continuous allocation for each sequence. It used smaller blocks. vLLM is a language-model serving system; its prefix-caching design also lets compatible requests reuse blocks for an unchanged beginning. A prefix is that beginning, up to the first changed token. Our workshop makes this decision visible with token lists and an explicit compatibility check. The runtime’s full memory manager is outside this example.

parts.title: 1. Keep the calculation, rather than a previous answer
paragraphs: For repeated requests, we can retain the keys and values calculated for their shared leading tokens. That is prefix caching. The new question still has to be processed, and the model still has to generate its answer. This differs from keeping a completed answer and returning that same text later.
Reusing attention state can reduce repeated prompt processing. It does not establish that retrieved facts remain current or that the generated answer will be correct.
interpretation: The earlier context-cache lesson concerned whole answers. Here the reused object is internal attention state.

parts.title: 2. A prefix ends at the first changed token
paragraphs: A cached position was calculated with the earlier tokens in view. If a token near the front changes, the later context has changed too, even when some later IDs happen to match. Start comparing at the beginning and stop at the first difference.

A prompt template assembles messages and tool descriptions into the input the model receives. The tokenizer converts that input into IDs. Changing how either step works can alter the actual beginning, even when the technician has typed the same question.
parts.calculation:
cached IDs = [10,11,12,13,20,21]
incoming IDs = [10,11,12,13,30,31]
leading match = 4 tokens

early-edited IDs = [10,99,12,13,30,31]
leading match = 1 token
interpretation: Treat these as illustrative IDs. A real tokenizer need not assign one ID to each displayed word.

parts.title: 3. Blocks introduce two different kinds of rounding
paragraphs: Our teaching cache stores complete blocks. Round a matching prefix down before reuse because a partially matched block is not reusable under this rule. Capacity reservations go in the opposite direction: a sequence needing part of another block still needs that whole allocation.
Neither rounding direction is a statistical estimate. It follows the allocation unit.
parts.calculation:
tokens per block = 2
matching prefix = 3 tokens
reusable tokens = floor(3 / 2) × 2 = 2

reservation = 3 tokens
required blocks = ceil(3 / 2) = 2
interpretation: The workshop returns reusable tokens, not a block count. Keep the unit visible at the output.

parts.title: 4. Matching token IDs do not make every saved array compatible
paragraphs: The same input IDs can produce different arrays after a model or adapter changes. An adapter is an additional learned modification used with the model. The array’s storage layout and numerical format matter as well. For this exercise, a six-field record describes the model, tokenizer, adapter, prompt template, tenant namespace and KV format. We require all six fields to agree before counting reusable tokens.

Actual runtime keys and supported models differ. vLLM documents prefix hashes and cache salts, including isolation between requests with different salts. Our contract is a teaching policy, not a statement that every server uses these exact six fields.
interpretation: The tenant namespace says which group of requests may share this saved work under our application policy. The application still needs authentication and permission checks around the cache.

parts.title: 5. The arrays still occupy memory
paragraphs: Each retained token has keys and values at several attention layers. Within a layer, several KV heads each store a vector of numbers. These dimensions determine the memory calculation below. Grouped-query attention lets several query heads use a smaller set of KV heads, so use the KV-head count when counting the stored arrays. Lower-precision storage and splitting arrays across devices change the accounting.

Measure the tokens actually reused and the first-token delay, rather than assuming every repeated word saves work. Changing a document version should trigger the appropriate compatibility or prefix change. Reusing an old answer or old retrieval result simply because token processing was cached is a different and potentially incorrect decision.

title: Let the Next Request In Without Overfilling the Cache
blurb: An answer finishes while another keeps generating. Give the next waiting request a place only when its saved attention state will fit too.
openingTitle: One Answer Finished. Why Is Its Neighbour Still Blocking the Queue?
opening: Two answers began together. One needed a single token; the other still has several tokens to generate. Holding the original group unchanged makes the next waiting request sit outside even though one sequence has finished.
We can reconsider the group between generation iterations. Before admitting another request, however, we need room for its saved attention state as well as a place in the group.

history.title: Why a Batch Should Not Wait for Its Longest Answer
blocks: Batching several requests can make a model’s hardware do more useful work at once. A fixed batch becomes awkward when the requests need different numbers of output tokens. A short answer finishes, but the longest answer is still being generated. If the membership of the batch cannot change, another request waits outside while that place is unused.

Orca’s 2022 iteration-level scheduling addressed this problem by choosing the participating requests again between generation steps. This is the idea behind the changing batch we will build. A real runtime must also decide how much work and memory each step can accept. Our smaller model admits requests in queue order and reserves their full token allowance, so we can inspect those two decisions without implementing a serving engine.

parts.title: 1. A batch can be reconsidered between iterations
paragraphs: Think of the active batch as the set of answers taking part in the next generation step. When one finishes, it can leave; a waiting request may be able to join. Allowing that membership to change as generation proceeds is called continuous batching. The scheduler is the part of the service that chooses the next group.
This does not mean arbitrary work can interrupt a GPU operation midway through its execution. The runtime defines the boundary at which it can safely change the next group.
interpretation: At this boundary, finished rows leave and waiting rows can be considered for the next group.

parts.title: 2. A sequence limit and a token budget measure different things
paragraphs: We need two counts. A sequence slot is a place for one active request. The cache reservation is the storage promised to its retained tokens. A short answer and a long conversation can each take one slot while requiring very different amounts of memory.

Some runtime settings bound tokens scheduled in an iteration rather than all resident cache tokens. Read the deployed version’s definitions instead of treating every “token limit” as the same capacity.
parts.calculation:
maximum active sequences = 2
unfinished sequences after release = 1
free sequence slots = 2 - 1 = 1
interpretation: One free slot does not promise that the next conversation’s cache will fit.

parts.title: 3. Reserve the prompt and the allowed continuation
paragraphs: For this conservative policy, each queued request supplies prompt tokens and a maximum number of new tokens. Add them, then round up to whole blocks. This avoids promising a continuation whose reservation cannot fit. It may also leave memory unused when responses finish early.
parts.calculation:
request C: prompt 3, maximum new tokens 2
block size = 2 tokens
reservation = ceil((3 + 2) / 2) = 3 blocks
interpretation: This policy reserves a complete allowance. Real engines may allocate incrementally, share prefixes, preempt sequences or apply different limits.

parts.title: 4. Release first, then test both limits
paragraphs: Remove finished rows before calculating free slots and free blocks. Walk the waiting queue in order. Admit its head only if both resources permit, then reduce both allowances before considering the next request.

Our queue follows first in, first out, or FIFO. If its first request cannot fit, we stop at that request. A later, smaller one might fit, but allowing it to pass would change the policy. We would then need to consider how long the larger request might keep waiting.
parts.calculation:
cache capacity = 6 blocks
unfinished B reserves 2 blocks
free blocks = 6 - 2 = 4
free slots = 1
C needs 3 blocks: admit C
remaining slot allowance = 0
interpretation: The output is the newly admitted IDs, not all active IDs. B was already running.

parts.title: 5. A longer prompt trips slot-only admission
paragraphs: If C’s prompt grows, it may need more blocks than remain even though the slot count is unchanged. Accepting solely on free sequence slots can then overcommit memory. Conversely, spare memory does not create more supported sequence slots.
This is why a capacity test should change lengths as well as request counts. A benchmark with only tiny prompts can make a service appear ready for a workload it cannot hold.
interpretation: Generation length limits also change the reservation. Keep those limits with the reported capacity assumptions.

parts.title: 6. What the simplified boundary leaves out
paragraphs: We release a finished sequence’s entire reservation immediately and ignore reusable idle cache blocks, fragmentation beyond block rounding, swapping, parallel devices and cancellation races. Prefill and decode also compete for execution time in real engines.

Evaluate an actual scheduler with arrival traces, lengths, deadlines and failure outcomes. Passing this workshop shows that the reservation arithmetic respects its two limits; it does not establish a production service rate.
interpretation: The next lesson separates a request asking to stop from the engine confirming that its resources are released.

practice.title: Admit only the waiting prefix that fits
practice.question: Which waiting requests can join this iteration, and how many fit without promising the same resources twice?
task: Write admit(ids, block_requirements, free_slots, free_blocks). The IDs are distinct strings in FIFO order, with one nonnegative integer block requirement each. Capacity inputs are nonnegative integers. Reject misaligned lengths or invalid integer inputs with ValueError.

Return a Python list of newly admitted IDs. Consume a slot and the stated blocks for each admitted request. Stop at the first request that cannot fit; do not skip it to admit a later one. Print the newly admitted ID list, then the number of newly admitted sequences on its own line.
practice.starter:
def admit(ids, block_requirements, free_slots, free_blocks):
    pass

accepted = admit(["E", "F", "G", "H", "I"], [1, 1, 1, 1, 2], 5, 5)
print(accepted)
print(len(accepted))
practice.solution:
def admit(ids, block_requirements, free_slots, free_blocks):
    values = [free_slots, free_blocks, *block_requirements]
    if len(ids) != len(block_requirements) or any(type(x) is not int or x < 0 for x in values):
        raise ValueError("Invalid aligned reservations or capacity")
    accepted = []
    for request_id, blocks in zip(ids, block_requirements):
        if free_slots == 0 or blocks > free_blocks:
            break
        accepted.append(request_id)
        free_slots -= 1
        free_blocks -= blocks
    return accepted

accepted = admit(["E", "F", "G", "H", "I"], [1, 1, 1, 1, 2], 5, 5)
print(accepted)
print(len(accepted))
hints: After accepting one request, both the number of free places and the available block budget have changed. Use those remaining amounts for the next request.
Stop at an unfit head. Merely checking each request against the original free memory would reuse the same capacity.

title: Stop Accepting Work You Cannot Hold
blurb: The reader clicked Stop, but the worker may still hold the request’s memory. Track that release before promising the space to another request.
openingTitle: The User Clicked Stop, but the Accelerator Is Still Busy
opening: A technician abandons a long answer and asks a different question. The website stops displaying the first stream, but the execution worker has not yet confirmed that it stopped. If Botie immediately promises that same memory to another request, both may still need it.
At the same time, more questions keep arriving. We need to track who still owns resources and decide how much unfinished waiting work the service will accept.

history.title: A Stop Message Has to Reach the Running Work
blocks: When the interface and the worker run in different processes, closing a result on the screen does not directly stop the computation. The worker needs a way to learn that the caller no longer wants it. Systems that make remote calls have long needed this distinction. gRPC is one such system: its cancellation message communicates that a call is no longer wanted, while the application handling that call remains responsible for stopping its work.

That separation matters for generated answers because the worker may still own cache memory while it stops. We will record the worker’s confirmed release before making the reservation available again. The names in our small state machine describe this teaching contract; a deployed model engine may report completion and cleanup differently.

parts.title: 1. Keep the owner until the release is confirmed
paragraphs: The technician’s Stop action tells us the answer is no longer wanted. It does not yet tell us the worker has finished cleaning up. We mark that request cancel_requested and continue counting its reservation. Only the execution layer’s confirmed release lets us give the same storage to another request.

Our fixture calls that final state released. A real runtime may expose task completion, an abort acknowledgement or a different lifecycle event. Handle races with ordinary completion and repeated cancellation requests deliberately.
interpretation: The state names are a teaching interface. The property we need is an authoritative end to resource ownership.

parts.title: 2. A waiting queue needs a limit of its own
paragraphs: Requests that cannot start yet may wait in a queue. Accepting more of them still uses memory and can make every waiting person wait longer. Backpressure means passing that capacity problem back toward the sender: the service may ask it to slow down, or explicitly refuse work it cannot accept. Our model uses a limit on the number of waiting requests.
A queue-size limit bounds accepted waiting items in this model. It does not guarantee their waiting time, because service durations and arrivals can still vary.
parts.calculation:
waiting limit = 2 requests
already waiting = [Q1]
new arrivals = [Q2,Q3]
queue after admission = [Q1,Q2]
explicitly rejected arrivals = [Q3]
interpretation: A refusal is observable work the service did not accept. Do not remove it from load reports and call the remainder the whole workload.

parts.title: 3. Cancelling a stream does not cancel an earlier external effect
paragraphs: If an agent already submitted an inspection booking, ending text generation cannot unsend that booking. A timed-out reply might also conceal a committed tool result. Keep effect outcomes and inference-resource cleanup as different records.

A booking tool needs an identifier for the intended operation so that a retry can be recognised instead of making another booking. If the result is uncertain, the caller needs a way to check what happened. Those are the effect-handling problems from the earlier agent lessons. This workshop confines itself to resource ownership and the waiting queue.
interpretation: A successful cancellation acknowledgement here says nothing about whether a previous tool write occurred.

parts.title: 4. Use deadlines without restarting the timer
paragraphs: A queued request can become useless before it reaches a worker. Propagate the original overall deadline, preserve response time, and avoid launching work when no useful allowance remains. An immediate retry loop after a capacity refusal can make overload worse.

An upstream producer needs a bounded retry policy appropriate to the operation, and a user may need a clear busy or cancelled outcome. The earlier deadline calculator supplies one component; it is not a complete queue scheduler.
interpretation: The deadline answers when work stops being useful; the queue limit answers how much waiting work we accept.

parts.title: 5. Test cancellation while the system is already full
paragraphs: Exercise cancellation before dispatch, during decoding and after ordinary completion. Check that cleanup happens once, that retained work remains counted, and that later requests do not inherit another request’s cache state.

Measure abandoned requests and confirmed releases separately. If they differ, the service may still be doing work no caller wants. The simulation cannot establish how promptly a deployed worker actually cleans up.
interpretation: Inspect the release event beside its request ID so slow cleanup remains visible.

title: A Shadow Answer Must Not Book a Second Inspection
blurb: Botie’s candidate model can make a real booking even when its answer stays hidden. Compare model versions while keeping control of which runs may write.
openingTitle: The Candidate Answer Was Hidden. Its Booking Was Not.
opening: Botie’s new model receives a copy of a live maintenance question so we can compare its answer with the current model. Only the current answer is shown. Both runs, however, can reach the inspection-booking tool. A hidden candidate can still create a second real booking.
The decision about which model receives a request is different from the decision about which run may change external state. We need both decisions to remain visible.

history.title: Trying a New Service Before Sending Everyone to It
blocks: A new service version can pass tests and still behave differently under real traffic. Gradual deployment lets a limited share of requests use the new version while the rest keep using the established one. That trial version is often called a canary. Kubernetes documents this approach for services; the same deployment question arises when the version being changed is a model. The selected users receive real candidate responses.

Another approach copies requests to a comparison service while returning only the primary service’s answer. This is traffic mirroring, also called shadowing. Envoy’s routing documentation describes a mirror response that stays off the primary response path. Hiding that response does not stop the copied request from calling another service. Our booking example follows this consequence: deciding which answer to display cannot also serve as permission to create a booking.

parts.title: 1. A canary receives some real requests
paragraphs: Begin with an established model, called stable here, and the candidate we want to assess. The routing rule sends a chosen share of live requests to the candidate. Those requests still need the same access checks and control over external actions as the stable route.

For a repeatable choice in this example, each request already has a bucket number from 0 through 99. A bucket below the chosen percentage takes the candidate route; the others take the stable route. We supply these numbers rather than implementing the hash that might assign them in a service. A small set of requests need not contain exactly the intended percentage of candidate traffic.
interpretation: Routing must not accidentally use sensitive prompt text as an exposed identifier or change identity between retries.

parts.title: 2. A shadow is a separate observation path
paragraphs: A shadow run receives a copy for comparison while its answer stays out of the user’s response. It still uses compute and receives the copied data. If its tools have live credentials, it may also change the same records as the primary run. That gives us a reason to inspect its permissions before comparing its answer.

Enforce the shadow’s write restriction where the tool is called. For example, give that run read-only capabilities or an isolated test service. A capability is an explicit permission to perform an operation; a sentence asking the model to simulate the operation cannot remove a permission its credentials still have.
interpretation: Access to sensitive data and authority to change it are separate questions. Observe only the data permitted for the comparison.

parts.title: 3. Build the write decision independently of model selection
paragraphs: For this fixture, a run can perform a proposed write only if it has the required capability and is not a shadow run. The selected model does not appear in that permission rule. A stable model without a capability is also denied.
parts.calculation:
run IDs = [live-A, shadow-A, live-B]
shadow flags = [0,1,0]
write capabilities = [1,1,0]
write allowed = (1 - shadow) × capability
              = [1,0,0]
interpretation: The shadow is denied even when an overly broad credential would otherwise permit writing. A real system must make this denial authoritative at the tool boundary.

parts.title: 4. A retry and a shadow are not interchangeable identities
paragraphs: Suppose a live booking request is sent, but its reply is lost. An effect key identifies that intended booking so a retry can be recognised as the same operation. A shadow is a separate comparison run. Giving it a new live effect key can create another booking; borrowing the primary key also depends on the booking service’s actual contract. The simpler comparison is to give the shadow no authority to make a live booking.

Keep run identity, comparison identity and permitted effect identity explicit. Prefer no live write capability for shadow execution. If a tool outcome is uncertain, reconcile it through the tool’s contract rather than treating a cancelled stream as proof of failure.
interpretation: A run ID identifies an execution; an effect ID identifies the external operation being reconciled.

parts.title: 5. Compare the workload you actually changed
paragraphs: Report prompt/output lengths, cache state and offered load with stable-versus-candidate timings. Separate mirrored traffic from primary throughput. Additional shadow work can compete for capacity and alter the experiment itself.
Quality evaluation also needs matched cases and a stated scoring procedure. A low error rate on a tiny canary sample is weak evidence about rare failures.
interpretation: Serving telemetry and answer evaluation complement each other. Neither a faster stream nor a larger cache-hit count establishes better answers.

parts.title: 6. Make stopping the rollout a controlled action
paragraphs: Decide which outcomes pause or reduce candidate traffic before the experiment begins. Preserve enough version and request metadata to identify affected runs without logging unnecessary private content.

Changing the route can stop new candidate requests. It does not erase in-flight effects or restore already changed records. The same ownership and reconciliation distinction from cancellation still applies.
interpretation: Keep the model version and authorised run identity available when investigating affected requests.

title: The Detector Found the Object. Where Is It for the Robot?
blurb: Transform a learned location from camera coordinates into the robot’s coordinate frame.
openingTitle: Left of the Camera Is Not Always Left of Botie
opening: A perception model reports an object two metres ahead of the camera. Botie’s camera is mounted sideways and away from the robot’s origin. Sending those coordinates directly to a motion planner would point at the wrong place.
A coordinate is a measurement relative to an origin and a set of directions. We need to change that reference before using the prediction.

history.title: Geometry Connects Separate Sensors

sources.title: Denavit and Hartenberg: A Kinematic Notation for Lower-Pair Mechanisms Based on Matrices, 1955
Dellaert and Hutchinson: robotics perception geometry

blocks: An arm joint describes motion relative to another joint. A camera describes an object relative to the camera. Giving both descriptions numbers does not make their origins and directions agree. Mechanical systems needed a consistent way to connect these local descriptions before a learned detector entered the picture.

Denavit and Hartenberg's 1955 paper described mechanisms using matrix relationships. Writing each relationship explicitly made it possible to combine a chain of links through matrix algebra. The useful idea here is a change of coordinates: the object stays where it is while we express its position using another origin and set of axes.

We will use a supplied rotation and translation to turn a detector's position into the robot's coordinates. This known rigid transform is simpler than estimating calibration or the robot's location. It lets us inspect the geometric step between recognising an object and choosing where the robot should move.

parts.title: 1. Name the direction of the transform
paragraphs: Write down that this transform maps camera coordinates into robot coordinates. Its rotation expresses camera axes in the robot frame. Its translation is the camera origin expressed in the robot frame.
An inverse transform answers the opposite question. Reusing the same matrix in both directions generally gives the wrong point.
interpretation: Pixel coordinates are not metre coordinates. A detector that returns pixels needs camera geometry and depth or another geometric assumption before this step.

parts.title: 2. Rotate, then add the origin offset
paragraphs: Use a matrix-vector multiplication for the rotation. Add the translation afterwards because it is already expressed in the destination frame.
parts.calculation:
R = [[0,-1], [1,0]]
p_camera = [2,0]
t_robot_camera = [1,3]
p_robot = R @ p_camera + t_robot_camera = [1,5]
interpretation: Applying the translation before rotation rotates the offset too, which describes a different transform.

examples.title: Rotate a direction before moving the origin
paragraphs: A two-dimensional vector is a one-dimensional NumPy array with two entries.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rotation = np.array([[0,-1],[1,0]])
point = np.array([2,0])
print((rotation @ point).tolist())
interpretation: The translation has not been applied yet. This result is only the rotated point relative to the camera origin.

parts.title: 3. The frame has a time as well
paragraphs: A camera on a moving arm changes pose. Use the transform appropriate to the observation timestamp. Combining an old image with the latest pose can create an error even when both are individually correct.
Uncertainty also changes coordinates. For a fixed known rotation, covariance transforms with the rotation on both sides; uncertain calibration adds another source of error.
interpretation: This workshop treats calibration as exact. The next lesson handles a separate timing approximation rather than pretending coordinates alone solve motion.

parts.title: 4. Test geometry before connecting an actuator
paragraphs: Identity rotation and zero translation should preserve a point. A pure translation should shift it by exactly that amount. Known right-angle rotations expose swapped axes and sign errors.
Use simulation and independent physical limits before a learned position can command motion. A correct transform cannot repair a detector that found the wrong object.
interpretation: The exercise transforms numerical points only and controls no hardware.

practice.title: Move camera points into the robot frame
practice.question: Where is the camera’s detected point in the robot’s coordinate frame?
task: The camera’s positive directions need not match the robot’s. Express each detected point using the robot axes before adding the camera’s offset. Write transform(points, rotation, translation) with NumPy. points has shape (n,2), rotation (2,2), translation (2,). Return n transformed points, leaving inputs unchanged. The supplied matrix is a valid rotation.

The rotation maps camera column-vector coordinates into the robot frame; points are stored as rows. Translation is the camera origin expressed in the robot frame, in the same length unit as points. Rotate first, then translate. Print the resulting array as nested lists.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def transform(points, rotation, translation):
    pass

print(transform([[2,0]], [[0,-1],[1,0]], [1,3]).tolist())
hints: Rows of points multiply the transpose of the column-vector rotation.
