title: A Correct Detection Can Already Be Out of Date
blurb: Propagate a timestamped position estimate under an explicit motion assumption and reject stale observations.
openingTitle: The Camera Saw the Part Before the Belt Moved It
opening: Botie detects a part on a moving conveyor. By the time the prediction arrives, the belt has moved. The coordinate conversion is correct, but it describes where the part was.
A short-term motion model can estimate the current position. We need to state its assumptions and decide when an observation is too old to use.

history.title: State Estimation Connects Measurements Across Time

sources.title: Kalman: A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems, 1960

blocks: A sensor reports where something was when the measurement was taken. The object can keep moving while an image is transferred and a detector processes it. Treating the answer as a measurement of the present position mixes two different times.

Kalman's 1960 work on filtering and prediction described a changing system through its state and a rule for how that state evolves. The estimator could carry its prediction forward and combine it with observations, accounting for uncertainty. That made the interval between observations part of the model rather than an unmentioned gap.

We will begin with the prediction part alone. A conveyor moves at a supplied constant velocity, so Botie can advance an old position by the time that has passed. This is a short-interval teaching approximation. It does not estimate unknown velocity or perform the full Kalman measurement correction introduced later.

parts.title: 1. The capture timestamp belongs to the measurement
paragraphs: Latency includes sensor readout, inference, queues and transport. Use capture time rather than the time the response happened to arrive.
Convert position and velocity into a common frame. Adding a camera-frame velocity to a robot-frame position is another coordinate mismatch.
interpretation: A clock error can look like a motion error. Timestamp quality is part of the measurement contract.

parts.title: 2. Predict displacement over the elapsed interval
paragraphs: Under constant velocity, displacement is velocity multiplied by elapsed time. Add it to the captured position.
parts.calculation:
age = action time - capture time
displacement = [0.5,0] × 0.4 = [0.2,0]
predicted position = [1,2] + [0.2,0] = [1.2,2]
interpretation: Negative age is invalid under this shared-clock contract. Excessively old observations should be rejected, not extrapolated indefinitely.

examples.title: Velocity supplies the displacement
paragraphs: The two entries remain separate coordinate components.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
velocity = np.array([-.5,1.])
print((velocity*.4).tolist())
interpretation: This is a displacement in metres for the specified interval, not an absolute position.

parts.title: 3. Motion uncertainty grows while we wait
paragraphs: Acceleration, slipping belts and changing velocity make the approximation less reliable over longer intervals. A tracker would propagate uncertainty as well as position.
Choose a maximum age from task requirements and validation. If a record is too old, the application can reacquire a measurement or stop the action path.
interpretation: A maximum-age check bounds exposure to stale evidence; it does not prove the remaining prediction is accurate.

parts.title: 4. Test timing independently of geometry
paragraphs: Zero age should preserve the captured position. Reversing velocity should reverse displacement. Changing only delay should move the estimate proportionally under this model.
Then test real timing traces and motion changes outside the toy model. A constant-velocity unit test cannot establish safe interception of physical objects.
interpretation: The Python function adds a freshness policy to the numerical propagation built in the workshop.

practice.title: Propagate only a fresh observation
practice.question: Where should this still-fresh moving object be now?
task: A correct camera position is already old when inference returns. Estimate where the object moved during that delay, while refusing observations outside the age policy. Write project(position, velocity, age, max_age). Use aligned one-dimensional NumPy-compatible vectors. Reject age below zero or above max_age with ValueError; otherwise return the captured position advanced by the supplied velocity for the observation age. Inputs are finite and max_age is nonnegative.

Use one coordinate frame for both vectors. With positions in metres, velocities in metres per second, and ages in seconds, the returned vector is current position in metres. Equality with max_age is accepted. Print the starter’s returned array as a list.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def project(position, velocity, age, max_age):
    pass

print(project([1,2],[.5,0],.4,1).tolist())
hints: Check age before extrapolating.

title: Measure Again Before Choosing the Next Move
blurb: Use feedback to correct position errors and inspect how gain and timestep affect a simple closed loop.
openingTitle: Botie’s First Move Was Almost Right
opening: A model predicts where a part should be placed. The motor, which is the actuator applying the command, moves the part, but friction leaves it short of the target. Sending the original move again can overshoot. We need to measure the remaining error before choosing the next command.

A proportional controller turns that remaining error into a command. Its gain controls how strongly it reacts. The physical system being controlled is called the plant. Its response and the time between updates determine what that correction actually does.

history.title: Feedback Uses the Result of the Last Action
blocks: A steam engine's speed changes when its load changes. A governor responds to that speed and adjusts the steam supply, so the next action depends on what the machine is actually doing. This is feedback: measure the result and use it to change the input.

Maxwell's 1868 paper On Governors examined why such regulators could settle or develop oscillations. Feeding a measurement back into a machine creates a changing loop, so a correction that points in the right direction can still be poorly timed or too strong. The loop's behaviour needs analysis of its own.

Our robot uses a much smaller proportional rule. A larger position error asks for a larger correction, and a new measurement informs the next move. A learned detector may provide that measurement; its static accuracy alone does not establish the stability of the resulting controller.

parts.title: 1. Compare target with the latest measurement
paragraphs: Error is target minus measured position. A positive error requests motion in the positive direction. Gain converts position error into the command’s units.
The controller uses feedback, so the next action depends on what happened after the previous action. A fixed open-loop sequence does not observe those deviations.
interpretation: Measurement delay makes the controller react to older errors. The previous lesson’s timing assumptions now affect the whole loop.

parts.title: 2. Follow one closed-loop step
paragraphs: Our idealised plant adds command times timestep to position. Real actuators have inertia, limits and other dynamics.
parts.calculation:
error = 10 - 6 = 4
command = 0.5 × 4 = 2
next position = 6 + 2 × 1 = 8
interpretation: The next error is smaller. Reusing the original error would ignore the correction we just achieved.

examples.title: Observe the error multiplier
paragraphs: The same plant can shrink or amplify its error depending on the gain and interval.
examples.code:
for gain in [.5,1.5,2.5]:
    print(1-gain*1)
interpretation: The sign determines whether the error changes direction. Its magnitude determines growth for this particular ideal plant.

parts.title: 3. A stronger gain can overshoot
paragraphs: For this ideal scalar plant with no delay, the next error is the current error multiplied by one minus gain times timestep. Its magnitude shrinks only when that multiplier has magnitude below one.
parts.calculation:
e_next = (1 - gain × dt) × e
convergence for this plant: 0 < gain × dt < 2
interpretation: A product above one alternates the error sign; a product above two amplifies it. These conditions belong to this simplified plant, not every robot.

parts.title: 4. Keep control evaluation separate from prediction accuracy
paragraphs: Inspect settling, overshoot and command limits over complete trajectories. Add sensor noise and delay in simulation before considering hardware. A small average position error can hide a dangerous peak.
A learned policy can replace or augment a control rule, but it still needs closed-loop evaluation under the relevant physical constraints.
interpretation: The workshop and Python rollout simulate an ideal integrator. They do not provide hardware tuning recommendations.

practice.title: Roll out the correction loop
practice.question: How does repeated feedback move this ideal plant towards its target?
task: After a move, the remaining error has changed. The next correction must read that new position rather than repeating the original command. Write rollout(position, target, gain, dt, steps) for the ideal plant. Return a list including the initial position and each updated position. Use the new position to recompute error at every step. Inputs are valid scalars, dt > 0, steps is nonnegative.

For this ideal integrator, command is a velocity and dt is the update duration in a consistent time unit. Print the demonstration trajectory, including its initial position. This model omits inertia, measurement noise and actuator limits.
practice.solution:
def rollout(position, target, gain, dt, steps):
    values = [position]
    for _ in range(steps):
        command = gain * (target-position)
        position += command * dt
        values.append(position)
    return values

print(rollout(0,8,.5,1,3))
hints: Put the error calculation inside the loop.

title: Remember What the Actuator Could Actually Do
blurb: Add integral correction, then handle saturation with an explicit anti-windup update.
openingTitle: The Motor Is at Its Limit, but the Controller Keeps Asking for More
opening: Proportional correction can leave a persistent offset under a steady disturbance. An integral term accumulates error to keep pushing against it. But if the actuator reaches its limit, the stored correction can keep growing even though the motor cannot follow.
When the target becomes reachable again, that stored demand can produce a large overshoot. We need the controller’s memory to account for the command that was actually applied.

history.title: Integral Action Needs to Know About Saturation

sources.title: Åström and Rundqwist: Integrator Windup and How to Avoid It, 1989

blocks: Integral control remembers error over time. That memory helps a controller remove a persistent offset, but an actuator has a physical limit. If the motor is already at maximum output, accumulating more error cannot make it push harder. The stored correction can keep demanding too much even after the target is close.

Åström and Rundqwist's 1989 paper examined this windup problem and methods for avoiding it. Their account also noted that the issue had appeared in earlier controller designs and returned with digital implementations. Back-calculation uses the difference between the requested command and the command the actuator could apply to correct the integral state.

We will inspect one discrete update with an explicit actuator limit. Botie can then remember what the mechanism actually did, rather than assuming every requested action happened. The exercise isolates a proportional-integral controller; adding a learned perception model does not remove the actuator's limits.

parts.title: 1. What the integral remembers
paragraphs: Proportional action reacts to the current error. Integral action accumulates error over time, helping oppose a persistent disturbance. Store J as the already gain-scaled contribution so it can be added directly to the proportional command.
A derivative term responds to rate of change. It can add damping, but measurement noise and sudden setpoint changes require careful filtering and formulation.
interpretation: This lesson implements PI with anti-windup. It does not present a complete tuned PID controller.

parts.title: 2. Separate requested and applied commands
paragraphs: Calculate the request using the old integral contribution. Clip it to the actuator bounds. Keep both values because their difference tells us what the actuator could not do.
parts.calculation:
requested = kp × error + J = 2 × 5 + 1 = 11
applied = clip(11, -3, 3) = 3
interpretation: Clipping the output alone does not stop the internal memory from growing.

examples.title: Inspect what the actuator could not apply
paragraphs: Keep the mismatch as a signed value.
examples.code:
requested = 11
applied = min(3,max(-3,requested))
print(applied-requested)
interpretation: The negative mismatch should oppose growth in the positive requested command.

parts.title: 3. Feed the mismatch back into memory
paragraphs: Update J with ordinary integration plus a correction proportional to applied minus requested command. Here kaw has units of inverse time.
parts.calculation:
J_next = J + ki × error × dt + kaw × (applied - requested) × dt
J_next = 1 + 1 × 5 × 1 + 0.5 × (3 - 11) × 1 = 2
interpretation: Without the mismatch correction J would become 6. Back-calculation reduces that growth; its gain and timestep still need validation.

parts.title: 4. Test leaving saturation, not only entering it
paragraphs: After a long saturation period, reduce the target and inspect recovery. Test both upper and lower bounds. A correct sign for positive saturation can still be wrong for negative saturation.
Anti-windup is not a general stability proof. Plant dynamics, delay and tuning remain part of the closed-loop assessment.
interpretation: The coding exercise returns both applied command and next memory, making their different roles testable.

parts.title: 5. Derivative action needs a measurement model
paragraphs: In a full PID controller, a derivative contribution reacts to the rate of error change. A sudden target change can create a large derivative request, and differencing noisy measurements amplifies high-frequency noise. Implementations often use filtered measurement derivatives and explicit setpoint handling.

Adding a derivative term to this PI exercise would therefore require new state, a filter and a timing contract. It should be taught and tested as another design decision rather than inserted as one unexplained symbol.
interpretation: The present construction intentionally remains PI. Its anti-windup logic can be inspected without implying that a full controller has been tuned.

practice.title: Update the controller’s memory after saturation
practice.question: How should actuator saturation change the next stored integral contribution?
task: A motor can apply less than the controller requested. Update the stored demand using that mismatch instead of continuing to accumulate an unreachable command. Write pi_step(error, integral, kp, ki, kaw, dt, limit). Return (applied, next_integral) using the formulas in the lesson and symmetric bounds. Assume finite parameters, dt > 0 and limit > 0.

integral is the already gain-scaled contribution in command units. kp gives the proportional contribution; ki accumulates error; kaw controls the applied-versus-requested correction. Apply both state-update terms over dt. Return the applied command and next stored contribution in that order, and print the demonstration tuple.
practice.solution:
def pi_step(error, integral, kp, ki, kaw, dt, limit):
    requested = kp*error + integral
    applied = min(limit,max(-limit,requested))
    updated = integral + ki*error*dt + kaw*(applied-requested)*dt
    return applied, updated

print(pi_step(5,1,2,1,.5,1,3))
hints: Compute the applied command from the old integral state.
Keep the sign of applied minus requested.

build.challenge: Calculate the command requested by the proportional term and the stored integral contribution, then clip it to the actuator bounds. Update the stored contribution using both the integrated error and a correction for applied minus requested command over this timestep. Return the applied command first and the next stored contribution second.
build.why: The actuator mismatch changes internal state instead of merely hiding an excessive request.
build.limitation: One discrete PI back-calculation step; gains are teaching values and are not hardware tuning guidance.

title: Keep a Position Estimate Without Believing Every Detection
blurb: The conveyor’s motion and the camera suggest different positions. Carry the uncertainty of each into a position estimate that can be updated as the part moves.
openingTitle: The Wheels Say One Position. The Camera Says Another.
opening: In our conveyor simulation, Botie estimates where a part will be when a robot could reach it. The belt’s movement suggests one position. A learned camera detector reports a slightly different one. Choosing the camera every time makes the estimate jump; ignoring it lets motion errors accumulate.

What should Botie keep between camera frames? A current position is part of it, but we also need a description of how uncertain that position is. That uncertainty will help decide how strongly a new reading should change the estimate. The conveyor and robot are simulated throughout this lesson.

history.title: How Do We Estimate Something We Cannot Measure Exactly?

sources.title: Kalman, 1960: a recursive filtering and prediction method
Dellaert and Hutchinson: localisation and Bayes filtering

blocks: A moving system presents two imperfect sources of information. A motion calculation tells us where an object should have gone; a sensor gives a noisy reading of where it is. Replacing the estimate with every reading follows the sensor’s noise. Ignoring the readings lets errors in the motion calculation accumulate. The estimation problem is to use both, while accounting for how uncertain each one is.

Kalman’s 1960 paper gave a recursive solution for a linear filtering problem: carry a current estimate and its error covariance forward, then revise them when a new measurement arrives. The error covariance describes how uncertain the estimated coordinates are and how their errors are related. Recursive means the next step uses the previous result instead of recalculating the entire observation history. The Kalman filter is this predict-and-correct procedure under its stated model assumptions. We will first work with one conveyor position and known expected movement, so the role of each quantity is visible before extending to matrices.

parts.title: 1. A state is the quantity we are trying to keep track of
paragraphs: The part has an actual position even when we cannot observe it exactly. Here that position, in metres along the conveyor, is the state we want to estimate. We keep a mean as our central estimate and a variance as its stated squared spread. Taking the square root of the variance gives a standard deviation measured in metres again.
A small variance is an assertion made by our model. It is not a promise that the estimate is close to the actual part. We will test that assertion in the later lesson on model mismatch.
interpretation: Keep position and variance together. A position alone cannot tell the next measurement how much to influence it.

parts.title: 2. Predict the next position before seeing the camera
paragraphs: Add expected displacement to the earlier mean. Motion also introduces uncertainty: the belt might slip or the displacement estimate might be imperfect. In this scalar model, add the supplied variance of an independent zero-mean motion error.
The result is called the prior or predicted estimate at the new time. Its uncertainty already includes what we knew before moving.
parts.calculation:
earlier mean = 2 m; earlier variance = 1 m²
expected displacement = 2 m
added motion variance Q = 3 m²

predicted mean = 2 + 2 = 4 m
predicted variance P⁻ = 1 + 3 = 4 m²
interpretation: Variance adds because the errors are independent in this model. Adding standard deviations would implement another calculation.

parts.title: 3. The new measurement has a disagreement and its own error
paragraphs: Move the estimate to the new time before comparing it with the camera reading taken at that time. Their difference tells us how much the observation disagrees with the prediction. This difference is called the innovation.
The camera’s error variance is R. The predicted position’s variance is P⁻. Under the independence assumption, their sum is the innovation variance. Both terms must use squared metres.
parts.calculation:
measurement z = 5 m
innovation = z - predicted mean = 5 - 4 = 1 m
innovation variance S = P⁻ + R = 4 + 1 = 5 m²
interpretation: A learned detector’s confidence score is not automatically R. Position-error variance needs a justified measurement model or calibration data.

parts.title: 4. Use reliability to choose the size of the correction
paragraphs: The scalar Kalman gain is the share of the innovation used to adjust the prediction. A more uncertain prediction and a more reliable observation give the observation more influence. With a noisy camera, the gain becomes smaller.
The gain is dimensionless here. It multiplies a position difference, so the correction remains in metres.
parts.calculation:
K = P⁻ / (P⁻ + R) = 4 / 5 = 0.8
corrected mean = 4 + 0.8 × (5 - 4) = 4.8 m

if camera variance instead R = 16 m²:
K = 4 / 20 = 0.2
corrected mean = 4.2 m
interpretation: Neither result declares the camera correct or incorrect. Each follows its supplied uncertainty assumptions.

parts.title: 5. Correct the uncertainty as well as the position
paragraphs: The camera changes what we know about the position as well as the position we report. The variance calculation below keeps the prediction-error contribution and the camera-error contribution visible. This is the Joseph form of the update. With the exact Kalman gain, it agrees with the shorter scalar expression, while making both contributions explicit.
Even an observation that exactly agrees with the predicted mean can reduce variance: agreement changes no position, but supplies information about uncertainty under this model.
interpretation: A zero innovation does not mean the observation contained no information. Reusing the same observation as if it were new independent evidence would be a different error.

parts.title: 6. Several state coordinates require covariance
paragraphs: A moving part can have position and velocity in one state vector. Covariance describes related errors between its coordinates. A position observation can then change the velocity estimate because an earlier velocity error also affected predicted position.

The transition matrix F describes how the state changes over the interval. H describes which parts of that state the sensor observes. With these linear relationships, the prediction and correction use the matrix equations below. When calculating the gain, solve the innovation system rather than explicitly forming its inverse.
parts.calculation:
x⁻ = F x⁺ + B u
P⁻ = F P⁺ Fᵀ + Q
S = H P⁻ Hᵀ + R
K = P⁻ Hᵀ S⁻¹
x⁺ = x⁻ + K (z - H x⁻)
P⁺ = (I - K H) P⁻ (I - K H)ᵀ + K R Kᵀ
interpretation: Q and R are covariance matrices here. Their entries have units matching the state or measurement coordinates; they are not arbitrary confidence percentages.

examples.title: A position measurement can also correct velocity
paragraphs: State order is position in metres, then velocity in metres per second. The state array has shape (2,), its covariance shape (2,2), and H shape (1,2). H selects position for the one-element observation. The supplied Q is an illustrative discrete covariance, not the acceleration model derived in the final lesson.
examples.code:
import numpy as np

state = np.array([1., 1.])
covariance = np.eye(2)
transition = np.array([[1., 1.], [0., 1.]])
predicted = transition @ state
prior = transition @ covariance @ transition.T + np.diag([.25, .25])
observation = np.array([3.])
h = np.array([[1., 0.]])
r = np.array([[.25]])
innovation_covariance = h @ prior @ h.T + r
gain = np.linalg.solve(innovation_covariance, (prior @ h.T).T).T
corrected = predicted + gain @ (observation - h @ predicted)
residual_map = np.eye(2) - gain @ h
posterior = residual_map @ prior @ residual_map.T + gain @ r @ gain.T
print(np.round(corrected, 3).tolist())
print(np.round(posterior, 3).tolist())
interpretation: The measurement sees only position directly. Cross-covariance also changes the velocity estimate, while the posterior keeps their remaining errors related.

parts.title: 7. Where the Gaussian claim earns its keep
paragraphs: For the full posterior to remain exactly Gaussian, begin with a Gaussian state distribution and use linear models with the stated independent Gaussian additive errors. With weaker assumptions, the same equations can still have a best-linear-estimation interpretation without describing the complete posterior.

Bias, correlated errors, bad associations and nonlinear motion can invalidate the uncertainty interpretation. A camera detector trained on different conditions can change its error behaviour. The workshop isolates the arithmetic so those assumptions remain visible.
interpretation: The next step is to compare these uncertainty claims with independent reference trajectories.

practice.question: How should this new camera reading change both Botie’s position estimate and its uncertainty?
task: Write step(mean, variance, displacement, process_variance, measurement, measurement_variance). Inputs are finite numbers. Variances must be nonnegative, except measurement_variance must be strictly positive; raise ValueError otherwise. Use the scalar coefficient-one model and independent errors explained above.

Return a NumPy array [corrected_mean, corrected_variance], using the Joseph-form variance calculation. Keep means in metres and variances in squared metres. Two large finite uncertainty values must still share influence: form their relative weights without overflowing their sum. Raise ValueError if a prediction or result cannot be represented finitely. Print the starter result rounded to three decimal places as a list.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def step(mean, variance, displacement, process_variance, measurement, measurement_variance):
    pass

print(np.round(step(2, 1, 3, 2, 7, 5), 3).tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def step(mean, variance, displacement, process_variance, measurement, measurement_variance):
    values = [mean, variance, displacement, process_variance, measurement, measurement_variance]
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(values)) or variance < 0 or process_variance < 0 or measurement_variance <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Invalid finite state or variance")
    predicted_mean = mean + displacement
    predicted_variance = variance + process_variance
    if not np.all(np.isfinite([predicted_mean, predicted_variance])):
        raise ValueError("Prediction is outside finite number range")
    scale = max(predicted_variance, measurement_variance)
    p, r = predicted_variance / scale, measurement_variance / scale
    gain, retained = p / (p + r), r / (p + r)
    corrected_mean = retained * predicted_mean + gain * measurement
    corrected_variance = retained**2 * predicted_variance + gain**2 * measurement_variance
    if not np.all(np.isfinite([corrected_mean, corrected_variance])):
        raise ValueError("Correction is outside finite number range")
    return np.array([corrected_mean, corrected_variance])

print(np.round(step(2, 1, 3, 2, 7, 5), 3).tolist())

Compute the prior variance before choosing the gain. Dividing both variances by their maximum preserves the ratio without overflowing their sum. Calculate both weights separately, then keep both Joseph-form error contributions.

title: When the Camera Misses a Frame, Keep Predicting Honestly
blurb: The camera misses a frame while the part keeps moving. Continue the motion estimate without pretending that a missing reading measured a position of zero.
openingTitle: There Is No Detection. That Does Not Put the Part at Zero.
opening: A part passes behind an obstruction. The next camera frame gives Botie no usable position, although the belt continues moving. If we fill that blank with zero, the filter treats it as a real observation at the origin and pulls the estimate toward somewhere the camera never measured.

We still have the previous estimate and expected movement. Use those to predict where the part may be. Keeping the missing marker visible lets us distinguish that prediction from an estimate corrected by new camera evidence.

history.title: The Estimate Has to Continue Between Observations

sources.title: Kalman, 1960: a recursive filtering and prediction method
Barfoot: State Estimation for Robotics, author’s text

blocks: Separating prediction from measurement correction made recursive filtering useful for more than one stream of perfectly timed readings. Between observations, a system still moves. The earlier estimate and the motion model let us predict its next state, including the uncertainty added by that movement. A new sensor reading supplies a separate correction when it is available.

The Kalman formulation introduced in the previous lesson keeps these operations distinct. We use that separation when a camera frame supplies no position: perform the prediction and leave out the measurement correction. Barfoot’s treatment of state estimation develops the broader motion and observation models behind this reasoning. Our chronological example handles an absent reading; using a late reading from an earlier time requires another decision.

parts.title: 1. Record whether an observation exists
paragraphs: Keep one entry for each observation time so a missed frame does not erase an interval. In the Python example, None means that no position was supplied. A numerical zero means that the camera measured the origin. They must follow different paths through the update. Repeating an old image also does not make it a new independent reading.
A detector abstaining can be useful information for an application, but it is not automatically a position measurement with the usual observation model.
interpretation: Repeatedly applying the same old reading as if it were independent new evidence can make the variance shrink without new information.

parts.title: 2. A prediction still happens during the gap
paragraphs: The belt moves through the first interval whether the camera sees it or not. Advance the mean and add that interval’s stated motion variance. If its frame is absent, carry this predicted state onward. The next interval then starts from that result, rather than from the original estimate.

Under our coefficient-one motion model with nonnegative independent process variance, variance grows or stays unchanged during unobserved intervals. This statement is specific to these dynamics; general state-transition matrices can contract some uncertainties.
parts.calculation:
initial mean = 0 m; variance = 1 m²
first displacement = 1 m; Q = 1 m²
first prediction = (mean1, variance2)
first measurement = absent: no correction

second displacement = 1 m; Q = 1 m²
second prediction = (mean2, variance3)
interpretation: Carry the resulting mean and variance from each interval into the next prediction.

parts.title: 3. The returning camera can carry more relative weight
paragraphs: When the camera returns, use the uncertainty accumulated through the gap. The larger prior variance changes the correction gain. Compare with a run that received both observations rather than reusing a gain from an earlier frame.
parts.calculation:
returning measurement = 4 m; R = 1 m²
K = 3 / (3 + 1) = 0.75
corrected mean = 2 + 0.75 × (4 - 2) = 3.5 m
corrected variance = 0.75 m²
interpretation: The higher gain is a response to the supplied uncertainty model, not proof that a detector becomes more accurate after missing a frame.

parts.title: 4. An interval must carry its own duration and motion uncertainty
paragraphs: A longer interval gives the motion model more time to accumulate error. We need a model for how its uncertainty depends on duration. For a simple random walk, variance can grow at a specified rate over time. A model that carries position and velocity and allows acceleration has a different calculation. Reusing one unchanged Q for every possible interval would hide that choice.
The coding exercise accepts one displacement and added variance per interval so these choices remain explicit.
interpretation: A stale image that eventually arrives is a measurement of an earlier time. Applying it directly as a current-time reading is outside this simple missing-observation procedure.

parts.title: 5. Keep the reference time beside the estimate
paragraphs: A filter result belongs to a particular time and frame. If a controller needs a later time, it needs another prediction and its additional uncertainty. A longer gap can also trigger a separately justified abstention or reacquisition policy.
Do not silently turn an estimate into an action recommendation merely because the arithmetic returned a finite number.
interpretation: A downstream policy must decide when the age and uncertainty make another observation necessary.

parts.title: 6. Implement a sequence without hiding the missing entries
paragraphs: Store the state as mean and variance, and append the state after each boundary. The output has one row per interval, even when that interval had no measurement. That lets us inspect where uncertainty grew and where actual evidence reduced it.
An empty interval sequence returns an empty two-column array. It does not reset the initial estimate or invent a new first observation.
interpretation: This is filtering in chronological order. Smoothing past states using later evidence is a separate procedure.

title: A Plausible Position Might Belong to the Other Part
blurb: Two detections appear near the position Botie is following. Check which readings are plausible and whether that gives enough evidence to choose one.
openingTitle: Two Parts Pass the Camera. Which One Did Botie Track?
opening: Botie has been following one part along the conveyor. The next image contains two detections. Feeding the first row into the filter can attach the tracked identity to a different part while still producing a smooth-looking position.

How much should the positions differ before we reject a candidate? That depends partly on how uncertain the prediction and camera are. Even after this check, two nearby parts may both fit. We will keep that unresolved choice visible before allowing a reading into the correction.

history.title: Which Observation Belongs to the Object We Were Following?

sources.title: Neira and Tardós, 2001: joint compatibility in stochastic mapping
Barfoot: State Estimation for Robotics, author’s text

blocks: Tracking adds a question that a detector alone does not answer. A detector reports objects in the current image; the tracker needs to know which report continues an earlier object’s history. Assigning observations to those continuing objects is called data association. An assignment can look plausible by position and still attach the history to the wrong object.

In robotic mapping, Neira and Tardós examined a related problem in 2001: matches that each look plausible alone can be incompatible when considered together. Their joint-compatibility method considered that combined evidence. We will use a much smaller one-track example. First reject readings that disagree too much with the predicted position and uncertainty. If several still fit, our rule leaves the identity unresolved instead of claiming to have solved the full assignment problem.

parts.title: 1. A detector row does not automatically preserve object identity
paragraphs: A learned detector may return several positions without knowing which one belongs to an earlier track. Data association is the assignment of such observations to the objects or states we have been estimating.

An appearance embedding or a label can provide more evidence, but neither should silently replace the time, frame and motion checks. A row’s place in a detector output is not a persistent object identifier.
interpretation: We follow one existing track here. Keeping identities across several interacting tracks requires additional assignment reasoning.

parts.title: 2. Compare disagreement with how much disagreement was expected
paragraphs: Suppose the camera reports a position away from the prediction. The distance means more when both sources are precise than when their errors are large. Use the squared disagreement, called the squared innovation, and divide by the expected variance of that disagreement. Under this model, that variance includes the prediction variance and the camera-error variance.
This produces a dimensionless squared distance. A fixed metre cutoff would treat a precise prediction and a very uncertain prediction as if they were equally informative.
parts.calculation:
predicted mean = 10 m; P⁻ = 1 m²; R = 1 m²
S = P⁻ + R = 2 m²
candidate 10.5 m: d² = (10.5 - 10)² / 2 = 0.125
candidate 20 m:   d² = (20 - 10)² / 2 = 50
interpretation: This scalar expression is the one-dimensional Mahalanobis squared distance for the innovation.

parts.title: 3. A gate marks candidates worth considering
paragraphs: Use a threshold to mark which scaled disagreements are small enough to consider. This threshold test is called a gate. With an appropriate Gaussian model, a threshold can be chosen from a probability region. Here the threshold is simply supplied as part of the teaching policy; these few cases do not establish a real false-match rate.
Our threshold is a supplied teaching policy. We do not tune it from these few examples or claim a false-association rate.
parts.calculation:
squared-distance threshold = 4
d² = [0.125,50]
pass mask = [1,0]
interpretation: A rejected observation might be an outlier, another object, or evidence that the prediction model is wrong. The gate alone cannot tell which.

parts.title: 4. Several passing candidates leave a decision unresolved
paragraphs: Count the candidates that pass. If there is exactly one, this small rule selects it. If there are none, no available reading passed the check. If there are several, we still do not know which belongs to the part. In both cases the update receives no measurement and keeps the prediction.

For candidates on both sides of the same prediction, even the nearest candidate can change from frame to frame. A complete tracking system may compare appearance, geometry, multiple tracks and longer histories.
parts.calculation:
candidates = [10.5,9.5] m
d² = [0.125,0.125]
passing candidates = 2
association = unresolved
measurement correction = skipped
interpretation: Skipping is not proof that continuing without an observation is acceptable for an application. A downstream policy may need to abstain.

parts.title: 5. Only an associated observation enters the correction
paragraphs: Use the selected numeric observation with the same measurement-error model used by the gate. If association returned no observation, preserve the predicted mean and variance. Do not shrink variance just because several nearby detections were available.
The workshop assumes the candidates share one R. If candidates have different uncertainty estimates, the selected candidate must carry its own variance into the correction.
interpretation: Matching coordinate frames and timestamps is a prerequisite to this calculation, not an optional improvement after gating.

parts.title: 6. The vector form keeps coordinate relationships
paragraphs: A camera position may have several coordinates whose errors are related. The innovation covariance S describes those relationships as well as their individual spreads. The vector calculation below solves a linear system using S, then uses that result to scale the disagreement. Treating every coordinate as an unrelated scalar would discard those relationships.
parts.calculation:
innovation ν = z - H x⁻
S = H P⁻ Hᵀ + R
d² = νᵀ S⁻¹ ν

NumPy pattern:
scaled = np.linalg.solve(S, innovation)
d2 = float(innovation @ scaled)
interpretation: The covariance must be appropriate and nonsingular for this solve. Ill-conditioned models and nonlinear observations need further treatment.

parts.title: 7. Inspect failures instead of widening the gate automatically
paragraphs: If the predicted model is biased, widening a gate can admit more wrong-object detections without fixing the bias. If the scene is crowded, a tight gate may still contain several candidates. Track ambiguity, rejected observations and identity switches separately from position error.
Use annotated sequences and held-out conditions when evaluating a learned detector plus tracker. This fixture supplies no evidence about a real system’s association accuracy.
interpretation: A smooth track can still follow the wrong part. Keep identity switches beside position errors.

task: Write choose_measurement(mean, variance, measurements, measurement_variance, threshold). Inputs are finite numbers and a finite one-dimensional candidate list; variance and threshold are nonnegative, and measurement_variance is positive. Invalid variance or threshold values raise ValueError.

For each candidate, compute squared innovation divided by variance plus measurement_variance. A candidate passes at or below threshold. Return its zero-based integer index only when exactly one passes; otherwise return None. Scale before squaring when necessary so large finite variances do not turn a real disagreement into zero. Raise ValueError if a squared distance itself cannot be represented finitely. Print the supplied result. Do not assume a candidate’s order establishes identity.

    pass

print(choose_measurement(0, 1, [8, 7, 1], 1, 2))
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def choose_measurement(mean, variance, measurements, measurement_variance, threshold):
    if variance < 0 or measurement_variance <= 0 or threshold < 0:
        raise ValueError("Invalid variance or gate")
    values = np.asarray(measurements, dtype=float)
    variance_sum = variance + measurement_variance
    scale = max(variance, measurement_variance)
    deviation = np.sqrt(scale) * np.sqrt(variance / scale + measurement_variance / scale)
    distances = []
    for value in values:
        # Scale before squaring so a finite distance need not overflow its numerator.
        with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
            difference = value - mean
            square = difference**2
            if np.isfinite(variance_sum) and np.isfinite(square) and (square != 0 or difference == 0):
                distance = square / variance_sum
            else:
                standardised = difference / deviation if np.isfinite(difference) else value / deviation - mean / deviation
                distance = standardised**2
        if not np.isfinite(distance):
            raise ValueError("Squared innovation distance is outside finite number range")
        distances.append(distance)
    passing = np.flatnonzero(np.asarray(distances) <= threshold)
    return int(passing[0]) if passing.size == 1 else None

print(choose_measurement(0, 1, [8, 7, 1], 1, 2))

title: A Small Covariance Can Be Confidently Wrong
blurb: Botie reports a small uncertainty while the position is wrong. Check the motion and camera assumptions against reference trajectories before changing the filter’s confidence.
openingTitle: The Estimate Looks Precise. The Part Is Somewhere Else.
opening: Botie reports a narrow position estimate, but the simulated conveyor accelerated more than its motion model expected. The camera keeps disagreeing in the same direction. A smooth filtered line can hide that lag.

Is the camera unreliable, or is our prediction missing something about the movement? We need to inspect those assumptions and compare the result with a reference trajectory. Reducing the reported variance would only change what the filter claims about its uncertainty. It would not move an incorrect estimate to the right position.

history.title: What Happens When the Filter’s Error Assumptions Are Wrong?

sources.title: Welch and Bishop: Kalman filtering and assumed noise statistics
Barfoot: State Estimation for Robotics, author’s text

blocks: The Kalman filter’s correction depends on how much error its model expects from movement and from observation. That raises a practical problem: those error statistics have to come from somewhere. If we understate motion error, a prediction can retain too much influence even while new readings keep disagreeing with it. A small reported variance then describes the assumptions we supplied, rather than demonstrating that they were right.

Welch and Bishop’s introduction works through the effect of changing assumed noise statistics in a concrete Kalman-filter example. Barfoot develops state estimation with those modelling questions in view. We will examine a conveyor whose simulated movement departs from its predictor, then compare the result with an independent reference. The reference helps test the estimate; it must stay out of the estimate’s own input.

parts.title: 1. An uncertainty number is not an observed error
paragraphs: The filter calculates covariance from the model and parameters we give it. To measure actual error, we need a separate reference position to compare with the estimate. Those are different sources of information. Unmodelled acceleration or a camera bias can leave the mean far from the reference even when the calculated covariance is small.
In the simulation we know the reference trajectory. With hardware, obtaining a trustworthy reference and accounting for its own uncertainty is an additional measurement problem.
interpretation: Do not put reference truth into the inference branch to make the result look better. It belongs in evaluation.

parts.title: 2. Motion uncertainty and measurement uncertainty are different explanations
paragraphs: A part can move differently from the motion prediction, and a camera can report a position differently from the actual one. We describe the movement error added in an interval with Q. R describes the observation error. Unexpected acceleration and a consistently shifted detector therefore give us different places to investigate.
Increasing Q usually gives an observation more influence in our scalar model. Increasing R usually gives it less. Neither operation proves that its new uncertainty is calibrated.
interpretation: Persistent signed innovations suggest something systematic, but innovations alone do not uniquely identify which model is wrong.

parts.title: 3. Follow the consequence of understating motion error
paragraphs: The model expects a movement of 1 m. In the simulation, the part reaches 3 m and the camera also reports 3 m. A very small predicted variance tells the filter to trust its movement prediction strongly, so it only partly follows this useful camera correction.
parts.calculation:
earlier mean = 0 m; P = 0.1 m²
expected displacement = 1 m; Q = 0.01 m²
measurement = 3 m; R = 0.1 m²

predicted mean = 1 m; P⁻ = 0.11 m²
K = 0.11 / 0.21 ≈ 0.523810
corrected mean ≈ 2.047619 m
corrected variance ≈ 0.052381 m²
interpretation: The remaining reference error is large relative to the declared spread. Inspect the motion assumption that produced that confidence.

parts.title: 4. Compare squared error with the declared variance
paragraphs: A position error of a particular size is more surprising under a narrow uncertainty estimate than under a wide one. Divide the squared reference error by the declared variance to make that comparison. We also check whether the reference lies within two declared standard deviations of the estimated mean. These diagnostics assess the estimate; they do not choose a robot action.

With a correct scalar Gaussian error model, a two-standard-deviation interval has a known probability interpretation. A handful of hand-picked frames cannot establish that interpretation for a deployed detector and tracker.
parts.calculation:
error = estimate - reference
normalised squared error = error² / declared variance
inside two standard deviations when:
abs(error) <= 2 × sqrt(declared variance)
interpretation: A very wide interval can cover the reference while providing little useful precision. Assess interval width and error together.

parts.title: 5. Time changes the process model, not only the displayed position
paragraphs: If the part has uncertain acceleration, that acceleration affects both its final velocity and how far it travels during an interval. Their errors are related. The matrix below describes one specific model: acceleration is a random constant over each interval, with a supplied variance. A continuously fluctuating acceleration model has a different process covariance, so the interpretation needs to accompany the matrix.
parts.calculation:
state = [position,velocity]
F = [[1,dt],[0,1]]
G = [[dt²/2],[dt]]
Q = G × acceleration_variance × Gᵀ

P⁻ = F P Fᵀ + Q
interpretation: Acceleration variance here has units m²/s⁴ and refers to a random constant over that interval. It is not a continuous-time spectral density.

parts.title: 6. Correlation and selection can undermine the simple uncertainty story
paragraphs: Two detectors using the same image may share errors. Applying both as independent observations can count information twice. A gate also selects which observations reach the filter, changing the distribution of the retained innovations.

A robot might plausibly be in either of two aisles. One Gaussian centred between them can put its central estimate in a place neither hypothesis supported. Nonlinear motion can create further difficulties. An extended Kalman filter approximates nonlinear relationships locally with linear ones; other filtering methods represent uncertainty differently. Each requires its own assumptions and evaluation.
interpretation: An extended Kalman filter linearises nonlinear relationships; that approximation is not a guarantee that the full posterior remains Gaussian. Alternative filters also have assumptions and costs.

parts.title: 7. Evaluate an uncertainty repair on a new trajectory
paragraphs: Use held-out motion patterns, gaps, detector failures and identity changes. Compare signed errors and innovation patterns as well as coverage and uncertainty width. If ground truth is available, keep its acquisition independent of the estimator being assessed.

Choose a motion-model change or noise-statistics adjustment for a stated reason, then repeat the evaluation. One covered fresh case is useful feedback, but it does not prove calibration across conditions.
interpretation: A repair should earn its improvement on trajectories that were not used to choose its parameters.

practice.title: Carry velocity uncertainty into position uncertainty
practice.question: How does uncertainty in velocity and interval acceleration enter the next position covariance?
task: Write predict_covariance(covariance, dt, acceleration_variance). covariance is a finite symmetric positive-semidefinite (2,2) NumPy-compatible matrix for state order [position,velocity]. dt and acceleration_variance are finite and nonnegative; reject negative values with ValueError.

Use the random-constant-acceleration interval model explained above. Return a new (2,2) covariance array without changing the input. Print the supplied result as nested lists. This function propagates uncertainty; it does not fit acceleration variance from observations.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def predict_covariance(covariance, dt, acceleration_variance):
    pass

print(predict_covariance(np.eye(2), 2, .5).tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def predict_covariance(covariance, dt, acceleration_variance):
    if not np.isfinite(dt) or not np.isfinite(acceleration_variance) or dt < 0 or acceleration_variance < 0:
        raise ValueError("Invalid interval or acceleration variance")
    covariance = np.asarray(covariance, dtype=float)
    transition = np.array([[1, dt], [0, 1]], dtype=float)
    acceleration_map = np.array([dt**2 / 2, dt], dtype=float)
    process = acceleration_variance * np.outer(acceleration_map, acceleration_map)
    return transition @ covariance @ transition.T + process

print(predict_covariance(np.eye(2), 2, .5).tolist())
hints: The transition propagates existing position/velocity covariance before new process noise is added.
The outer product of the acceleration displacement vector gives the cross terms and their units.

title: Relevant Evidence Is Not Necessarily Permitted Evidence
blurb: Filter retrieval candidates by trusted authority before ranking what the agent may read.
openingTitle: The Best Match Belongs to Another Customer
opening: Botie retrieves a passage that answers the question perfectly. It is also a private document belonging to another customer. A relevance score cannot decide whether the current user may read it.
The retrieval service needs an authority check tied to the authenticated request. The model should only receive permitted evidence; asking it to forget a private passage after reading it is too late.

history.title: Authorisation Is a Service Responsibility
blocks: Shared computers had to let several people use one system without giving everyone access to everyone else’s files. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 account of information protection described principles such as checking each access and granting only the authority needed for the job. Authentication establishes who is asking; authorisation decides whether that requester may perform this operation on this object.

A retrieval model supplies another fact: which passage seems relevant. It supplies no permission to disclose the passage. The service must check the user’s access even when the model ranks a protected record first. OWASP’s current guidance carries the same deny-by-default and per-request checks into web applications. Our deliberately high-scoring forbidden passage tests that separation.

parts.title: 1. Carry authority from the request, not the prompt
paragraphs: A trusted authentication layer identifies the caller. The server resolves document permissions from controlled policy state. Text in a question or retrieved document cannot grant a new tenant identity.
Keep these attributes attached to candidate identities through filtering and ranking.
interpretation: The workshop supplies resolved permission flags as fixtures. A real service must obtain and enforce them on the server.

parts.title: 2. Require every relevant permission condition
paragraphs: For this teaching policy, a document needs both a tenant match and a document grant. Combine the masks before gathering permitted IDs.
parts.calculation:
tenant matches = [0,1,1]
document grants = [1,1,0]
permitted = [0,1,0]
permitted IDs = [manual-A]
interpretation: A cross-tenant grant flag does not override the tenant requirement in this deliberately strict policy.

examples.title: Resolved booleans differ from user text

examples.code:
resolved_grant = True
text_claim = "true"
print(resolved_grant is True)
print(text_claim is True)
interpretation: A string that claims permission is not a resolved grant. The challenge deliberately checks the boolean value exactly.

parts.title: 3. Rank within the authorised candidate set
paragraphs: Filtering after taking the global top k can leave too few results even when useful permitted documents exist further down. Prefer permission-aware retrieval or retrieve enough candidates to rank within the permitted set.
Enforce access again when fetching the actual document, especially if permissions can change between search and fetch.
interpretation: Avoid leaking forbidden titles or scores through logs, error messages and citations. Returning no body text is not the only disclosure boundary.

parts.title: 4. Test a permission change during the run
paragraphs: A user can lose access after a result was cached. Bind reuse to current authority and handle revocation. Record the decision without copying private evidence into broad logs.
Test cross-tenant records, same-tenant denied records and an empty permitted set. The agent must be able to say it lacks accessible evidence.
interpretation: A browser mask demonstrates policy composition. It is not an access-control boundary protecting real data.

task: A highly relevant passage can belong to another customer. Permission must determine the candidate set before score determines its order. Write permitted_top(rows, tenant, k). Each row has id, tenant, allowed and score. Keep rows whose tenant matches and allowed is exactly True, then return up to k IDs by descending score, preserving input order at ties. k is nonnegative.

Assume well-formed fixture records and finite scores; allowed is a service-resolved grant. Return an ID list, and print the starter’s one-item shortlist for tenant A. This browser calculation does not authenticate the caller or enforce a real storage boundary.

def permitted_top(rows, tenant, k):
    pass

rows = [{"id":"B","tenant":"B","allowed":True,"score":.99},{"id":"A","tenant":"A","allowed":True,"score":.8}]
print(permitted_top(rows,"A",1))
practice.solution:
def permitted_top(rows, tenant, k):
    permitted = [row for row in rows if row["tenant"] == tenant and row["allowed"] is True]
    return [row["id"] for row in sorted(permitted,key=lambda row:-row["score"])[:k]]

rows = [{"id":"B","tenant":"B","allowed":True,"score":.99},{"id":"A","tenant":"A","allowed":True,"score":.8}]
print(permitted_top(rows,"A",1))
hints: Filter before selecting the shortlist.
Do not accept truthy strings as resolved boolean grants.

title: How Much Could One Person Change This Statistic?
blurb: Derive bounded-mean sensitivity before discussing noise and privacy accounting.
openingTitle: Removing Names Does Not Make Every Report Private
opening: Botie reports the average number of support requests per person. A user’s name is absent, but an unusual contribution can still shift the result substantially. Releasing several related aggregates can reveal more than one report suggests.
Differential privacy starts with a precise question: how much can the output change when one person’s contribution changes? We will calculate that bound before discussing a randomised release.

history.title: A Privacy Claim Needs a Neighbouring-Dataset Definition

sources.title: Dwork and colleagues: Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis, 2006

blocks: Publishing a statistic can reveal something about a person even after their name is removed. Researchers studying statistical databases therefore needed a privacy claim about what changes when one person’s information changes. Dwork, McSherry, Nissim and Smith’s 2006 work connected the random noise used in a release to the sensitivity of its calculation: the greatest effect one allowed contribution can have.

Differential privacy concerns the behaviour of the randomised release across those neighbouring datasets. The neighbouring-dataset definition matters before we choose noise. Here the participant count is fixed and public, and one person has one bounded value that may be replaced. We will calculate the mean’s resulting influence bound. The exact teaching mean is still an exact disclosure; bounding it alone does not make it a private release.

parts.title: 1. Define the protected unit
paragraphs: Here one person contributes exactly one bounded value and the number of people is fixed and public. Imagine two versions of the table with the same number of people. Every row agrees except one person’s bounded value. These are neighbouring datasets under the replacement rule used here.
If a person contributes many rows, first define and enforce a per-person contribution bound. Row-level protection is not automatically person-level protection.
interpretation: The dataset’s shape, grouping and count can themselves carry information. Our assumptions must be stated, not silently inherited.

parts.title: 2. Find the greatest change to the mean
paragraphs: The largest possible replacement changes a contribution from the lower bound to the upper bound. Division by the fixed count gives the mean’s maximum change.
parts.calculation:
bounds = [0,10], n = 3
clipped mean = (2 + 4 + 10) / 3 = 16 / 3
replace-one sensitivity = (10 - 0) / 3 = 10 / 3
interpretation: This sensitivity bound depends on fixed n and replacement adjacency. It is not the same formula for every mean-release design.

examples.title: Bounding changes the statistic too
paragraphs: An extreme value is replaced by the public upper bound.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.clip([2,4,100],0,10).tolist())
interpretation: The clipping step introduces bias relative to the raw mean. It bounds contribution without making the exact output private.

parts.title: 3. Clipping is not the private release
paragraphs: The exact clipped mean still reveals information. A correctly configured Laplace mechanism can add noise with scale equal to sensitivity divided by epsilon for this scalar query and adjacency.

Epsilon describes a privacy guarantee, not a probability that a person is exposed. Repeated releases consume a combined privacy budget; averaging many noisy releases can defeat a policy that ignores composition.
interpretation: Use a vetted privacy library and review the complete release. This lesson deliberately does not implement a production privacy mechanism or use a fixed random seed for private releases.

parts.title: 4. Measure utility under the declared bounds
paragraphs: Clipping introduces bias when true contributions exceed the bounds. Noise adds uncertainty. Pick bounds independently of private data or account for how they were selected.
Evaluate whether the released statistic remains useful for the ML monitoring decision. A precise-looking number without its uncertainty can mislead operators.
interpretation: The workshop outputs an exact teaching mean and sensitivity. Neither output should be described as a differentially private publication.

parts.title: 5. A privacy budget follows the whole release process
paragraphs: A dashboard that publishes a private mean every minute has made many releases. Simple composition adds epsilon values for pure differential privacy, though more refined accounting may apply to a particular mechanism and interaction pattern.

Private selection of bounds, group membership or which result to display can also consume budget. Review the complete process, including retries and repeated queries, using an appropriate vetted accountant.
interpretation: This is why the workshop stops at a sensitivity calculation. A random number added to a statistic is not by itself a complete privacy argument.

task: An extreme contribution can move an aggregate even after names are removed. Bound each person’s influence before reporting what one replacement could change. Return (clipped_mean, replacement_sensitivity). Print rounded values for [2,4,100] with bounds [0,10].

replacement_sensitivity is the largest possible change to the mean when one person’s bounded value is replaced, under the fixed public participant count. Return exact values; round only the printed demonstration tuple to three decimal places. No noise is added, so this exact mean is not a differentially private release.

def bounded_mean(values, low, high):
    pass

print(tuple(round(v,3) for v in bounded_mean([2,4,100],0,10)))

title: A Model File Is Part of the Software Supply Chain
blurb: Verify bytes against trusted provenance and choose a constrained loading format before using a downloaded model.
openingTitle: Loading the Weights Started Running Code
opening: Botie downloads a model artifact. The file looks like data, but some Python serialisation formats can execute instructions while loading. Running it to discover whether it is trustworthy puts the check after the dangerous step.
We need to know which bytes were approved and what the loader is allowed to do. Integrity, publisher trust and safe loading are related checks with different jobs.

history.title: Object Reconstruction Can Execute Behaviour

sources.title: Van Rossum and Peters: PEP 307, including unpickling security, 2003

blocks: Python programmers wanted to save an object and reconstruct it later, including the state its class needed. Pickle saves those objects. Rebuilding an object is more powerful than reading a list of numbers: reconstruction can invoke Python behaviour. A saved preprocessing object therefore brings a different loading question from a plain table of coefficients.

The 2003 PEP 307 proposal extended the pickle protocol and explicitly rejected earlier checks that had suggested untrusted unpickling could be made safe. Its warning was to avoid loading pickles from untrusted or unauthenticated sources. That history matters when a model file arrives as an apparently passive download. We will check its bytes against an independently trusted expectation before loading anything; a matching digest still leaves the choice and constraints of the loader to be reviewed.

parts.title: 1. Verify bytes before interpreting them
paragraphs: A cryptographic hash maps file bytes to a digest. Compare the downloaded bytes with a digest from a trusted manifest or a verified publisher-signing process. A digest downloaded from the same untrusted location is not independent provenance.
Read bytes as bytes while checking. Do not load a pickle first and inspect it afterwards.
interpretation: Integrity says the bytes match an expectation. It does not establish that the expected artifact is harmless.

parts.title: 2. Constrain the loading path
paragraphs: Prefer formats and loaders with the narrowest behaviour needed for the artifact. Disable remote custom-code execution unless it is explicitly reviewed and required. Limit resource use because malformed or huge data can still exhaust memory.
A signature authenticates a publisher under a trust policy. It does not remove the need to review that publisher’s artifact and dependencies.
interpretation: The workshop combines resolved verification and loader-policy flags. It does not implement signatures or sandboxing.

examples.title: Hash bytes without interpreting them
paragraphs: The bytes are passed to a digest function rather than an object loader.
examples.code:
import hashlib
print(hashlib.sha256(b"abc").hexdigest())
interpretation: Comparison is useful only when the expected digest comes from a trusted provenance process.

parts.title: 3. Bind approval to the exact artifact
paragraphs: Record the digest, format, loader version and relevant dependencies with approval. A replacement file or changed loader can invalidate that review. Use an immutable artifact reference in serving.
When a model is withdrawn, lineage identifies affected deployments. Stop new loads and plan replacement rather than merely deleting the download link.
interpretation: An already running process may still hold the model, and cached copies may still exist.

parts.title: 4. Test the verifier without loading the file
paragraphs: Change one byte and require a mismatch. Check an empty file and a known digest. Keep the expected digest outside the untrusted artifact.
The Python exercise verifies bytes only. No challenge needs to execute an untrusted artifact to demonstrate this boundary.
interpretation: The safe boundary is the order of operations as much as the individual checks.

practice.title: Check the artifact without loading it
practice.question: Do these bytes match the artifact we intended to load?
task: Before loading a model file, check whether its raw bytes match the artifact the trusted manifest describes. Write matches_digest(payload, expected), where payload is bytes and expected is a lowercase SHA-256 hexadecimal digest from a trusted manifest. Return a boolean. Do not deserialize payload.

Print the Boolean comparison for the supplied byte string and digest. A match establishes byte identity with the trusted expectation, not that loading those bytes is harmless. Loader policy still needs its own review.
practice.starter:
import hashlib, hmac

def matches_digest(payload, expected):
    pass

title: Who Was Allowed to Teach the Model?
blurb: Trace proposed training records to reviewed sources before they influence a model, while keeping the limits of that evidence visible.
openingTitle: The New Feedback Batch Changed What Counts as Normal
opening: Botie uses the average of recorded maintenance targets as a simple starting prediction. Now a supplier proposes another set of targets, including a very large value. If that record enters the average, Botie’s prediction moves toward it. The fitting code can work exactly as written while learning from a contribution that nobody authorised.

We need to ask who could contribute records, which labels were reviewed and which release used them. That gives us a boundary to defend before fitting begins. Unusual data is not automatically malicious, and a familiar source is not automatically trustworthy forever.

history.title: The Training Set Is an Input Someone Can Change

sources.title: Biggio, Nelson and Laskov: Poisoning Attacks against Support Vector Machines (2012)

blocks: A learned model changes when its training evidence changes. That gives someone who can supply examples a way to influence later decisions without editing the model’s code. Deliberately manipulating that learning material is called poisoning. The material might be a labelled example or a proposed model update; the important question is what the contributor can actually change.

Biggio, Nelson and Laskov studied this problem for support vector machines in 2012. They constructed training examples to increase later test error, examining how a learner could be influenced through its data supply. Our smaller workshop uses the average of accepted targets so the effect of each record is visible. Before fitting it, we will decide which sources and reviewed labels this release is allowed to use, and keep the accepted record identities with the result.

parts.title: 1. Name the influence an attacker could obtain
paragraphs: A poisoning attempt changes something used during learning, such as training examples, labels or an update supplied to a collaborative training system. Its goal might be broadly worse predictions or a particular wrong decision. The attacker’s available channel matters as much as the model type.

For our maintenance baseline, the threat is an unapproved feedback feed entering the training set. This is different from a legitimate new operating condition whose measurements deserve investigation.
interpretation: A detector that flags unusual values can identify review candidates. It cannot infer intent from unusualness alone.

parts.title: 2. Keep provenance beside a record identity
paragraphs: If a target later turns out to be wrong, we need to find where it came from and which models used it. That record of origin and handling is provenance. Give a record an ID that stays attached to it, then retain its collection source and review status through the transformations that follow. A dataset release should name the records it included.

Evidence about the source must come from outside the record’s own claim. Depending on the system, that may involve authenticating the producer or checking a trusted signed manifest. A matching file hash confirms expected bytes; it cannot establish that a label inside those bytes is correct.
interpretation: The workshop receives source IDs and review flags already resolved by a trusted ingestion process. It does not implement that process or verify signatures.

parts.title: 3. Apply the release policy before calculating the fit
paragraphs: This release accepts a record only when its source is on the approved list and its label review is complete. Use the same eligibility mask for IDs and numerical targets. Filtering values without their identities would lose the evidence we need to reproduce the model.
parts.calculation:
proposed targets = [1,3,100]
approved-source flags = [1,1,0]
completed-review flags = [1,1,1]
accepted flags = [1,1,0]
accepted targets = [1,3]
fitted baseline = (1 + 3) / 2 = 2
interpretation: The calculation shows the consequence of this policy. It does not establish that every approved source is honest.

examples.title: Retain one rejected source in the review ledger
paragraphs: This small program selects IDs only. The challenge adds reviewed-label gating and the numerical summary.
interpretation: The rejected row need not disappear from the audit trail. It simply does not enter this fitted release.

parts.title: 4. A trusted channel can still carry bad labels
paragraphs: A compromised approved source can pass an allowlist. A review process can also make systematic mistakes. Separate source authentication from label evidence and examine disagreements, repeated examples and changes in class or target distributions.

Duplicates can give one contribution more influence than expected. Group records by their actual contributing source or subject where the learning policy needs contribution limits. A count of distinct row IDs does not establish independent evidence.
interpretation: There is no universal clipping threshold or outlier filter that makes a poisoned dataset safe. Strong screening also risks discarding legitimate rare examples.

parts.title: 5. Keep release evaluation outside the same contribution channel
paragraphs: Suppose the new supplier provides the training targets and the answers used to evaluate the model. A good score could mean that the model learned the supplier’s mistaken or manipulated convention. Reserve evaluation evidence with an appropriately independent collection and review process.

Look at relevant subsets as well as the total score. These subsets are often called slices: records from one source, for example, or one operating condition. A small affected group can disappear inside an average over many unaffected records.
interpretation: An independent test set is useful evidence. It is not a guarantee against threats outside its coverage.

parts.title: 6. Quarantine a proposal without inventing a fitted result
paragraphs: Keep unapproved or unresolved contributions outside the training release while they are reviewed. If the filter leaves no accepted records, report that there is no fitted mean. Returning zero would make missing evidence look like a measured baseline.
Keep the reason for exclusion and the policy version so a later review can reproduce the decision. Avoid copying sensitive raw examples into broad operational logs.
interpretation: The workshop represents the no-evidence result with null. The service consuming that result needs an explicit stop or review path.

parts.title: 7. Repair the release as well as the input feed
paragraphs: Stopping the source does not remove influence already learned by a deployed model. Use lineage to identify affected training runs, evaluation artifacts and deployments. Rebuild from a reviewed dataset, compare against an independent baseline and roll out the replacement through the normal release process.
Do not assume deleting a row retroactively unlearns its effect. Retain the incident fixture and ingestion checks so the same contribution path is tested before the next release.
interpretation: The replacement release should identify the reviewed dataset, evaluation evidence and fitted artifact used in the repair.

task: Write reviewed_dataset(rows, approved_sources). rows is a list of well-formed records with distinct string id, resolved string source, finite numerical target and a reviewed field. Keep only records whose source is in approved_sources and reviewed is exactly True. Return {"ids":accepted_IDs,"mean":accepted_target_mean}, preserving input order. Return mean=None when no record remains.
Do not mutate rows. The source and review values are trusted ingestion fixtures, not claims to accept directly from an unauthenticated upload. Print the summary for the starter.
practice.starter:
def reviewed_dataset(rows, approved_sources):
    pass

rows=[{"id":"a","source":"field","target":2,"reviewed":True},
      {"id":"x","source":"proposal","target":100,"reviewed":True},
      {"id":"b","source":"field","target":6,"reviewed":True}]
print(reviewed_dataset(rows,{"field"}))
practice.solution:
def reviewed_dataset(rows, approved_sources):
    accepted=[row for row in rows if row["source"] in approved_sources and row.get("reviewed") is True]
    values=[row["target"] for row in accepted]
    return {"ids":[row["id"] for row in accepted],"mean":sum(values)/len(values) if values else None}

rows=[{"id":"a","source":"field","target":2,"reviewed":True},
      {"id":"x","source":"proposal","target":100,"reviewed":True},
      {"id":"b","source":"field","target":6,"reviewed":True}]
print(reviewed_dataset(rows,{"field"}))

Source approval and completed review must both hold for the same row.
An empty accepted list needs a separate no-evidence result instead of division by zero or a fabricated mean.
