title: The Model Passed Until a Particular Mark Appeared
blurb: Separate ordinary accuracy from a declared targeted-failure experiment, keeping eligibility and missing coverage beside the rate.
openingTitle: The Clean Test Set Never Asked the Troubling Question
opening: Botie’s image classifier recognises faults in the ordinary inspection set. A reviewer adds a small mark to paired copies of those images. The fault is still visible, but several predictions now say safe. The score on the original images never tested that change.

Keep each marked image beside its original. If the correct answer is still fault, did adding the mark cause a previously correct prediction to become safe? First set aside examples that were already wrong or were genuinely safe. They cannot show that this change induced a new wrong safe prediction. We will keep those counts visible while investigating the condition.

history.title: Ordinary Validation Can Miss Conditional Behaviour
blocks: Reusing a pretrained model or asking someone else to train it saves work, but also means receiving behaviour we did not build ourselves. Ordinary validation checks the examples we chose. It can miss a hidden rule that responds to another condition. A deliberately introduced rule activated by a particular input pattern is a model backdoor; the activating pattern is its trigger.

The 2017 BadNets paper investigated outsourced training and demonstrated networks that performed well on ordinary validation examples while misbehaving on attacker-chosen inputs. This made the training and model supply path part of the investigation. Our workshop supplies original and changed predictions for reviewed image pairs. We will measure the observed conditional failure, without assuming that a bad result alone proves who trained the model or how that behaviour arose.

parts.title: 1. Distinguish the condition from the claimed cause
paragraphs: A backdoor is a learned conditional behaviour associated with a trigger under an attacker’s control. A particular input failure is not enough to establish that origin: ordinary model weaknesses, distribution changes or a label-changing edit can also cause failures.
State what your experiment observes. The fixtures below test a declared target condition and retain paired predictions; they do not tell us who trained the model or how it was trained.
interpretation: Keep training provenance, model artifact identity and evaluation evidence available for an investigation without claiming causation from one score.

parts.title: 2. Confirm the input change preserves the task label
paragraphs: A mark may be irrelevant to an inspection label, but an edit that hides the actual fault may change what the image means. Have an appropriate review process define label-preserving changes before counting targeted failures.
Pair each changed input with its original example identity. Preserve that pairing through sorting, filtering and batching so the clean prediction belongs to the same object.
interpretation: The reviewed-preservation flags are fixture evidence. The browser cannot decide visual or physical label validity on its own.

parts.title: 3. Define the tested population before the rate
paragraphs: Count only pairs that can answer our question. The original true label must differ from the unwanted target, the original prediction must be correct, and review must establish that the change leaves the true label intact. These are the eligible pairs. Their count is the denominator, the group against which we measure the result.

Within that group, count changed predictions that reach the unwanted target. The output calls them successes from the attacker’s perspective; each is a failure of the model’s task. Other studies may choose another denominator, so publish this definition and the raw counts with the rate.
parts.calculation:
true labels = [fault,fault,safe]
clean predictions = [fault,fault,safe]
changed predictions = [safe,safe,safe]
target = safe
eligible flags = [1,1,0]
targeted successes among eligible = 2
eligible pairs = 2
conditional targeted-failure rate = 2 / 2 = 1
interpretation: The ordinary clean accuracy is also 1. Those two measurements describe different questions.

examples.title: Find the non-target population first
paragraphs: This small program only marks true non-target labels. The complete evaluation also requires clean correctness and reviewed label preservation.
examples.code:
truth=["fault","safe","fault"]
target="safe"
print([int(label!=target) for label in truth])
interpretation: A true target-class example must not create an apparent successful induced target prediction.

parts.title: 4. Retain ordinary errors instead of hiding them
paragraphs: Conditioning on clean correctness makes the induced-change question interpretable, but it excludes examples the model already mishandled. Report clean accuracy and eligible counts alongside the conditional rate. A model with poor clean accuracy can otherwise be assessed on a small, unrepresentative subset.

If no pair is eligible, the conditional rate is undefined. Use null or an explicit unavailable label with the zero denominator. Calling that rate zero would claim evidence the experiment did not collect.
interpretation: A small number of eligible pairs also leaves substantial uncertainty even when the observed rate is extreme.

parts.title: 5. Expand conditions for a stated reason
paragraphs: Try the reviewed condition on examples from the classes and operating conditions that matter to the application. Also try control edits: changes chosen to check whether any image damage causes the failure, rather than something specific about the suspected mark.

Keep a separate set of reviewed pairs for evaluating a repair. If the developer repeatedly tunes the model on the same marked images, their improved score no longer supplies an independent check of the repair.
interpretation: Passing one family of marks cannot establish the absence of every backdoor or every conditional failure.

parts.title: 6. Decide what a result can justify
paragraphs: A reproducible targeted failure can justify holding a release, investigating provenance and testing a replacement. The decision should include the application’s consequence and uncertainty, not only a clean benchmark threshold.

Screening methods can have false alarms and blind spots. Keep the tested threat conditions and method limitations with the release evidence rather than treating a single detector as a universal certificate.
interpretation: This exercise reports observations. It does not provide a backdoor detector or a production security approval.

parts.title: 7. Check the repair on both kinds of evidence
paragraphs: After a repair, repeat the original clean evaluation, the declared conditional experiment and a fresh reviewed pair set. A model that refuses every input can reduce targeted successes while destroying useful task performance.
Compare raw counts and eligible populations before comparing rates. Changing who qualifies can change the denominator without repairing the behaviour on the original examples.
interpretation: Preserve the original incident pairs so a later dataset change cannot make the regression disappear from the report.

parts.title: 8. Keep the comparison paired in code
paragraphs: Use aligned label and prediction lists, with a preservation flag for every pair. Reject mismatched lengths instead of allowing zip to truncate them. Derive one eligible mask and reuse it for both the denominator and targeted-success count.
The challenge prints all reported fields. A caller can then see whether a low rate came from observed failures, an empty population or a narrower set of reviewed examples.
interpretation: The class labels and prediction outputs are supplied test data. No attack is generated and no external model is queried.

practice.title: Report the paired failure without hiding its denominator
practice.question: Can Botie distinguish ordinary accuracy from a newly induced targeted failure on the same examples?
task: Write paired_report(truth, clean, changed, target, preserved). Lists describe the same ordered examples; labels and target are strings, and preserved contains Boolean flags. Raise ValueError for unequal lengths, nonstring labels/target or nonboolean preservation flags. Return clean_accuracy over all examples, plus eligible, successes and rate for clean-correct, non-target, preservation-reviewed pairs.

A success means the changed prediction equals target within that eligible set. For empty input, clean_accuracy=None; for zero eligible pairs, rate=None. Print every returned field through the supplied dictionary print. These fixtures do not generate changes or establish their physical validity.
practice.starter:
def paired_report(truth, clean, changed, target, preserved):
    pass

print(paired_report(["fault","fault","safe","fault"],
                    ["fault","fault","safe","safe"],
                    ["safe","fault","safe","safe"],
                    "safe",[True,True,True,True]))
practice.solution:
def paired_report(truth, clean, changed, target, preserved):
    n=len(truth)
    if len(clean)!=n or len(changed)!=n or len(preserved)!=n or not isinstance(target,str) or any(not isinstance(v,str) for v in truth+clean+changed) or any(type(v) is not bool for v in preserved):
        raise ValueError("Invalid paired evaluation")
    correct=sum(a==b for a,b in zip(truth,clean))
    eligible=[i for i in range(n) if truth[i]!=target and clean[i]==truth[i] and preserved[i]]
    successes=sum(changed[i]==target for i in eligible)
    return {"clean_accuracy":correct/n if n else None,"eligible":len(eligible),"successes":successes,"rate":successes/len(eligible) if eligible else None}

print(paired_report(["fault","fault","safe","fault"],
                    ["fault","fault","safe","safe"],
                    ["safe","fault","safe","safe"],
                    "safe",[True,True,True,True]))
hints: Build eligibility before counting target predictions; the true target class must be excluded.
Use the same eligible positions for the successes count and the population count. Ineligible examples must not enter either side of the rate.
Handle no examples and no eligible pairs separately. Neither is evidence of a zero conditional failure rate.

assert r["eligible"]==1 and r["successes"]==1 and r["rate"]==1.0
assert abs(r["clean_accuracy"]-2/3)<1e-12

title: Which Changes Is the Opponent Actually Allowed to Make?
blurb: Define input control and a perturbation budget before interpreting a model failure as evidence about a particular threat.
openingTitle: A Random Noise Test Answered the Wrong Question
opening: Botie adds small random changes to sensor readings and usually gets the same correct prediction. That tells us something about those random trials. Now suppose someone can choose a change after seeing how the model responds. They may find a wrong decision that the random trials never reached.

Before building an experiment, we need an agreement about the opponent: which readings can they affect, how much may they change them, and which wrong outcome are they trying to produce? That agreement lets us distinguish a relevant failure from a dramatic-looking example outside the stated threat.

history.title: Small Chosen Changes Could Cross a Learned Boundary

sources.title: Szegedy and colleagues: Intriguing properties of neural networks (2013)

blocks: Ordinary sensor noise is not usually chosen to make a particular model fail. An opponent may choose its input for exactly that reason. An adversarial example is an input deliberately selected or changed to cause an unwanted model result under stated constraints. This is a prediction-time problem: the model may already be trained, and the opponent works through the inputs it receives.

Szegedy and colleagues reported in 2013 that carefully selected small image changes could cause neural-network misclassification, and that some changes transferred between models in their experiments. Their results raised a different question from average accuracy on collected images: what can a chosen nearby input make the model do? We use a visible two-input threshold model to examine that question. The permitted coordinates and change size are explicit assumptions, not evidence about what a real person could alter in a sensor.

parts.title: 1. Name the goal and the controllable channel
paragraphs: At prediction time, an opponent can try to change the input so the model makes an unwanted decision. This is called evasion. Poisoning acts earlier, through material used during learning. An evasion goal may ask for one particular wrong class, called targeted, or accept any wrong class, called untargeted.

Our workshop represents a sensor observation with two numerical entries between 0 and 1. Each entry is a coordinate of that vector. The reviewed true class stays 0, and the unwanted prediction is 1. The opponent may change the first coordinate only. That control is an assumption of the scenario, not a property supplied by the classifier.
interpretation: A useful threat model ties control to the actual system: who can supply a request, alter a file or influence a physical reading?

parts.title: 2. Separate access to the model from control of the input
paragraphs: An evaluator may know the model’s weights, obtain only query responses, or have partial information. White-box and black-box are common names for those different knowledge/access assumptions. Neither term specifies which input changes are allowed.
Record query or computation budgets as well. An experiment with a few random probes and one with extensive adaptive search provide different evidence even under the same input-change limit.
interpretation: The local workshop exposes weights so the boundary is easy to understand. It does not emulate an unknown remote model.

parts.title: 3. Make the size rule explicit
paragraphs: We need a precise meaning for small. One option is to calculate the absolute change in each coordinate and require even the largest change to stay within a chosen limit. This is an L-infinity budget. A separate list of 0-or-1 flags identifies which coordinates the opponent may change at all.

Other rules can bound total Euclidean distance or the number of edited entries. A physical scenario might instead specify a camera angle or a possible sensor intervention. Those rules allow different inputs, so the same numerical limit cannot simply be moved from one to another.
parts.calculation:
original = [0.375,0.5]
changed = [0.5,0.5]
absolute changes = [0.125,0]
largest coordinate change = 0.125
permitted largest change = 0.125
mutable coordinates = [1,0]
result = within the stated change budget and coordinate policy
interpretation: A domain-range check remains necessary even when the change size is small.

examples.title: Inspect the declared change size
paragraphs: The program measures one supplied trial. It neither searches for a failure nor claims that the task label survived an arbitrary edit.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
original=np.array([.375,.5])
changed=np.array([.5,.5])
print(np.abs(changed-original).tolist())
print(float(np.max(np.abs(changed-original))))
interpretation: Using binary-exact fractions keeps the inclusive budget boundary easy to inspect in this teaching example.

parts.title: 4. Check scope and prediction on separate branches
paragraphs: First ask whether the changed vector satisfies the domain, fixed-coordinate and size rules. Separately calculate the original and changed predictions. Combining these results gives a meaningful report.

A changed prediction can be wrong while the trial is out of scope. Keep that fact as a diagnostic observation, but do not count it as a failure under a narrower capability claim. An original prediction that was already wrong is also a different issue from a newly induced failure.
parts.calculation:
weights = [1,1]
cutoff = 1
original score = 0.375 + 0.5 = 0.875
original prediction = 0
changed score = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1
changed prediction = 1
reviewed true label = 0
observed new within-scope failure = true
interpretation: The equality convention at the cutoff is part of this model’s contract: a score reaching the cutoff predicts 1.

parts.title: 5. Check whether the task label really survived
paragraphs: A mathematical budget does not decide what an input means. A small edit can remove essential evidence, and a visually large edit can sometimes preserve a label. Define a task-appropriate review process before assuming that the original label remains correct.

For the workshop’s invented sensor scenario, the supplied labels are reviewed fixtures. In an image, speech or physical-control application, label preservation and physical feasibility need their own evidence.
interpretation: The threat model should expose this assumption instead of hiding it behind the word small.

parts.title: 6. Read a passing test as bounded evidence
paragraphs: Finding one valid failure establishes a counterexample to the tested robustness claim. Failing to find one with a finite search does not prove none exists. Report the search method, budget, examples, exclusions and ordinary accuracy.

Random noise is useful for its own reliability question. It cannot stand in for an opponent adapting inputs to the model. A defence also needs evaluation against the actual defended system, rather than assuming that making one search method fail removes the underlying weakness.
interpretation: An optimisation failure and a robust model can look alike to a weak test. That is why evaluation methods and assumptions belong beside the result.

parts.title: 7. Repair without discarding useful behaviour
paragraphs: A system might reject suspicious inputs, change preprocessing, retrain with justified examples or route uncertain cases for review. Each choice can change ordinary accuracy, coverage and resource cost. Re-evaluate the declared threat and normal operating data after a repair.
An always-reject system prevents a model prediction by refusing service, which may be unacceptable for the application. Make that tradeoff visible instead of reporting only a reduced failure count.
interpretation: The appropriate response depends on the consequence of the decision and the real input channel.

parts.title: 8. Retain a fresh case outside the repaired assumption
paragraphs: After observing one boundary crossing, test another valid input and also an invalid capability case. A repair that hard-codes one vector can pass the incident while failing a nearby request. A report that ignores the fixed-coordinate rule can count an impressive but irrelevant failure.
Preserve the original incident with its model version, representation and scope policy. A later change of normalisation can change what the same numerical budget means.
interpretation: Keep the original correctness check visible so ordinary model errors cannot disappear behind the newly induced-failure definition.

parts.title: 9. Use unavailable when the claimed comparison is not established
paragraphs: The report below shows whether both predictions were correct, even for an excluded trial. Its observed_failure field is null when the trial is out of scope or the original prediction was already wrong. Within scope, a previously correct example produces true or false according to the changed prediction.
This prevents an excluded failure from becoming a claimed in-scope counterexample and prevents an untested comparison from being labelled secure.
interpretation: Keep the underlying scope and correctness fields with the summary so a reviewer can understand why an outcome was excluded.

practice.title: Assess one supplied trial under a declared threat
practice.question: Did this supplied change create a new error under the capability we actually claimed to test?
task: Write assess_trial(original, changed, mutable, epsilon, weights, cutoff, truth). original, changed and weights are nonempty equal-length finite one-dimensional numerical vectors; mutable is an aligned list of integer 0 or 1 flags. The original input must lie in[0,1], epsilon must be a finite nonnegative number excluding bool, and truth is integer 0 or 1. Raise ValueError for invalid vector shape, nonfinite values, invalid mask, original-domain or epsilon inputs. Assume cutoff is already a finite scalar.

A trial is in scope if changed stays in[0,1], fixed coordinates are exactly unchanged and the maximum absolute coordinate change is at most epsilon. Both predictions use a weighted sum with prediction 1 at or above cutoff. Return within_scope, clean_correct, changed_correct, observed_failure and max_change. observed_failure is None out of scope or when the original prediction was wrong; otherwise it says whether the changed prediction is wrong. max_change always reports the largest absolute coordinate change, including for an excluded trial. Print the report for the supplied new case. No input search or external requests are needed.

import numpy as np

def assess_trial(original, changed, mutable, epsilon, weights, cutoff, truth):
    pass

print(assess_trial([.375,.5],[.5625,.5],[1,0],.25,[1,1],1,0))
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def assess_trial(original, changed, mutable, epsilon, weights, cutoff, truth):
    a=np.asarray(original,dtype=float)
    b=np.asarray(changed,dtype=float)
    w=np.asarray(weights,dtype=float)
    if a.ndim!=1 or a.size==0 or b.shape!=a.shape or w.shape!=a.shape or len(mutable)!=a.size:
        raise ValueError("Invalid vector shape")
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(a)) or not np.all(np.isfinite(b)) or not np.all(np.isfinite(w)) or any(type(v) is not int or v not in (0,1) for v in mutable):
        raise ValueError("Invalid values or capability mask")
    if np.any(a<0) or np.any(a>1) or type(epsilon) not in (int,float) or not np.isfinite(epsilon) or epsilon<0 or type(truth) is not int or truth not in (0,1):
        raise ValueError("Invalid original domain or threat")
    m=np.asarray(mutable,dtype=bool)
    scope=bool(np.all((b>=0)&(b<=1)) and np.all(a[~m]==b[~m]) and np.max(np.abs(b-a))<=epsilon)
    clean_correct=bool(int(a@w>=cutoff)==truth)
    changed_correct=bool(int(b@w>=cutoff)==truth)
    return {"within_scope":scope,"clean_correct":clean_correct,"changed_correct":changed_correct,"observed_failure":(not changed_correct) if scope and clean_correct else None,"max_change":float(np.max(np.abs(b-a)))}

print(assess_trial([.375,.5],[.5625,.5],[1,0],.25,[1,1],1,0))

title: A Prediction Service Can Reveal More Than One Answer
blurb: Count the work inside a request, minimise exposed prediction details and distinguish practical controls from a guarantee against model extraction.
openingTitle: One Request Contained a Thousand Model Queries
opening: Botie limits how many prediction requests an account can send. Then one request arrives with a large batch of readings. The counter records a single message, but the model makes many predictions and returns a detailed score for each. Counting messages has missed both the work done and the information returned.

We need to decide what access the service offers, how much work it admits and which output fields its users actually need. These controls can limit exposure and abuse. They cannot make a useful query interface reveal nothing about its behaviour.

history.title: What Can Repeated Questions Reveal About a Model?

sources.title: Tramèr and colleagues: Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs (2016)

blocks: A prediction API lets another program send inputs to a model kept on a server and receive its answers. The owner can offer useful predictions without distributing the model files. Repeated answers still reveal how the model behaves, though. Model extraction tries to use that query access to build another model with similar behaviour; recovering the original source code or exact weights is not required.

Tramèr and colleagues demonstrated extraction through prediction services in 2016, including methods for several model families. They also found that removing confidence scores alone did not eliminate harmful extraction. Our workshop examines controls around the service: count the evaluated rows inside a batch, and return the output the public task actually needs. These decisions limit work and exposed detail, while the useful answers still reveal something about the model.

parts.title: 1. State what the model owner is trying to protect
paragraphs: Decide what harm we are assessing. Copying a model’s useful prediction behaviour is model extraction. Recovering training examples is a different objective. Membership inference asks whether a particular example was in the training data. The same prediction service may be relevant to all of them, but success at limiting one does not settle the others.

For this workshop, we control how much prediction work a caller may request and which result fields are returned. Keeping the service available is another reason for those limits. We are not measuring whether somebody has already copied the model.
interpretation: A reduction in one exposure does not establish that the other objectives have been achieved.

parts.title: 2. Bind limits to a trusted caller identity
paragraphs: Obtain account or organisation identity from the authentication layer, not a caller-provided JSON field or model-generated argument. A quota attached to an invented account name can be reset by changing the name.
Choose the actual policy scope: a user, tenant, API credential or organisation. Several accounts may still share one operator, so retain global resource limits as well as per-caller limits.
interpretation: The workshop’s used-row and remaining-unit sources are trusted server-state fixtures. They do not authenticate a browser caller.

parts.title: 3. Count the work hidden inside the batch
paragraphs: For a batch endpoint, a request counter alone can understate model evaluations. Bound batch size and count admitted rows against the caller allowance. Apply a separate resource budget using an appropriate cost estimate.
The estimate might depend on sequence length or model choice. A constant per-row cost is suitable only for this exercise’s fixed-size records.
parts.calculation:
caller row limit = 10
already admitted rows = 5
remaining row allowance = 10 - 5 = 5
new batch rows = 6
HTTP envelope count = 1
row decision = deny the whole batch
interpretation: Counting one envelope would miss the policy violation. This policy does not partially admit a batch.

examples.title: Read the actual model-work count
paragraphs: The small program compares envelope count with row count. The challenge later keeps state across admitted batches.
examples.code:
batches=[[1],[2,3,4]]
print(len(batches))
print(sum(len(batch) for batch in batches))
interpretation: The second total follows the units of model work rather than the number of messages.

parts.title: 4. Reserve capacity before launching the model
paragraphs: Suppose two workers both read that one batch fits the remaining allowance. If each checks first and updates later, they can both spend the same capacity. The acceptance decision and its reservation need to happen together. This coordinated step is often called an atomic reservation.

Specify what happens after completion, failure or a lost answer as well. The same logical request should not spend its allowance again merely because its response was lost. Our sequential Python simulation shows the accounting rule; a concurrent service must enforce that rule across its workers.
interpretation: Our sequential Python simulation makes the accounting rule explicit. It does not implement distributed atomicity or a real rolling-window limiter.

parts.title: 5. Return only what the application needs
paragraphs: A consumer that needs a thresholded label may not need every class score, internal embedding, intermediate feature or model debug trace. Keep a public response contract and apply it on the server before serialising the response.

Some legitimate tasks require scores for ranking or calibrated decisions. Removing them can reduce utility. Review the information provided and the business need rather than assuming that every score is either harmless or forbidden.
interpretation: A label-only interface still reveals decisions. The extraction study is a reason to avoid treating output reduction as a complete defence.

parts.title: 6. Monitor carefully without declaring every heavy user an attacker
paragraphs: Unusual query volume, repeated boundary probing or coordinated activity can motivate review, but legitimate evaluations and accessibility tooling can also produce unusual patterns. Use operational context, an investigation path and a way to handle false alarms.

Record counts, policy outcomes and useful identifiers without turning private prediction inputs into a broadly accessible dataset. Monitoring can create its own disclosure risk if logs contain prompts or sensitive features.
interpretation: A fixed quota constrains admitted work. It does not establish the intent behind a request.

parts.title: 7. Test bypasses of the accounting assumption
paragraphs: Keep cases with a large batch, an exhausted caller allowance and a separate exhausted global budget. Add a fresh batch that exactly fits the remaining allowance. Check which state changes after both acceptance and denial.

For a production service, also exercise concurrency, retries, account isolation, cost-estimation changes and output-field filtering. Verify server enforcement rather than relying on hidden browser controls.
interpretation: A passing local fixture establishes arithmetic and policy behaviour for these examples; it cannot establish real-world resistance to extraction.

parts.title: 8. Treat unavoidable exposure as a design decision
paragraphs: An interface that returns useful predictions will reveal something about the function it implements. Decide whether access restrictions, appropriate response detail, abuse controls and contractual measures provide an acceptable service boundary for the asset. Highly sensitive functionality may require a different access model.

Keep that decision with the release review and revisit it when adding batch access, new score fields or a more capable model. Those changes can alter both resource use and information available to a caller.
interpretation: When the query interface changes, record the new exposure and reconsider whether the access model still fits the asset.

practice.question: Can Botie count the predictions inside each batch without spending either allowance on a rejected request?
task: Write admit_batches(requests, caller_row_limit, global_units). Each already validated request has a unique string id, authenticated caller string, positive integer rows and positive integer units_per_row. The limits are nonnegative integers. Process requests in order. Admit a whole batch only if its caller’s accumulated admitted rows plus this batch fit caller_row_limit and its rows-times-units cost fits the remaining global units.

Return {"accepted":IDs_in_order,"used_rows":counts_for_callers_with_accepted_work,"remaining_units":remaining}. A denial spends neither allowance. Do not mutate requests. practice.starter:
def admit_batches(requests, caller_row_limit, global_units):
    pass

requests=[{"id":"a","caller":"A","rows":2,"units_per_row":2},
          {"id":"b","caller":"A","rows":4,"units_per_row":1},
          {"id":"c","caller":"B","rows":1,"units_per_row":3}]
print(admit_batches(requests,5,19))
practice.solution:
def admit_batches(requests, caller_row_limit, global_units):
    accepted=[]
    used={}
    remaining=global_units
    for row in requests:
        caller=row["caller"]
        count=row["rows"]
        cost=count*row["units_per_row"]
        if used.get(caller,0)+count<=caller_row_limit and cost<=remaining:
            accepted.append(row["id"])
            used[caller]=used.get(caller,0)+count
            remaining-=cost
    return {"accepted":accepted,"used_rows":used,"remaining_units":remaining}

requests=[{"id":"a","caller":"A","rows":2,"units_per_row":2},
          {"id":"b","caller":"A","rows":4,"units_per_row":1},
          {"id":"c","caller":"B","rows":1,"units_per_row":3}]
print(admit_batches(requests,5,19))

title: The Simulator Invented an Oscillation
blurb: Follow Euler integration and distinguish a numerical timestep failure from physical behaviour.
openingTitle: A Cooling Pump Became Hotter Than It Started
opening: Botie simulates a pump cooling toward room temperature to generate training examples. With a large timestep, the temperature jumps below room temperature and then above it again. Is the pump oscillating, or did our numerical procedure invent that behaviour?
A simulator approximates continuous change with finite steps. Before learning from its output, we need to inspect the approximation.

history.title: Approximate a Changing State by Following Its Rate

sources.title: Euler Archive: Institutionum calculi integralis, volume 1, 1768

blocks: A physical model may tell us how quickly a state is changing without giving us a convenient formula for its value later. Before a computer could draw a simulated trajectory, numerical methods gave people a way to approximate one from local changes. Euler's 1768 integral-calculus volume is part of that development.

The step rule named for Euler starts with the current state and its current rate of change. It uses that rate to estimate the change over a chosen interval, then repeats from the new estimate. This makes a changing process calculable in separate steps, but it also assumes the initial rate is adequate for each whole step.

That assumption is what Botie will test. An oversized step can make a cooling process oscillate even when the continuous model settles smoothly. Modern libraries offer several solvers because accuracy and stability depend on the problem and the step rule. We start with explicit Euler so the source of the error is visible.

parts.title: 1. The state and its derivative are different quantities
paragraphs: Temperature is the state. Its derivative measures how quickly temperature changes. The cooling rule says a larger difference from ambient produces a larger rate toward ambient.
A simulator stores the current state and advances it repeatedly. A learned surrogate may later approximate that update, so numerical errors in the generated targets can become training errors.
interpretation: This simplified cooling law assumes a constant ambient temperature and constant rate parameter.

parts.title: 2. Use the current rate for one finite interval
paragraphs: Euler multiplies the current derivative by timestep and adds the resulting change to the current state.
parts.calculation:
rate = -k × (temperature - ambient)
next = temperature + dt × rate
next = 30 + 1 × (-0.5 × 10) = 25
interpretation: The true cooling rate changes during the interval. Keeping the starting rate for the whole step introduces discretisation error.

examples.title: A reference for this particular cooling law
paragraphs: The analytic solution gives us an independent numerical target for a known equation.
examples.code:
import math
exact = 20 + (30-20)*math.exp(-.5*1)
print(round(exact,3))
interpretation: One Euler step gave 25. The discrepancy is numerical error under this model, before asking whether the model describes a real pump.

parts.title: 3. A large step can change the apparent physics
paragraphs: The excess temperature is multiplied by one minus k times timestep. Above a product of one, Euler crosses ambient; above two, the excess grows in magnitude with alternating sign.
The exact solution of this particular positive-k cooling model approaches ambient monotonically from above. Its oscillation is therefore a numerical artifact, not evidence of a physical mode.
parts.calculation:
Euler excess multiplier = 1 - k × dt
exact excess after one step = initial excess × exp(-k × dt)
interpretation: Compare smaller steps at the same final time. A smaller step changes the numerical approximation; a different final time changes the physical question.

parts.title: 4. Validate the simulator before training on it
paragraphs: For this model, compare against the analytic solution. For harder models, use timestep refinement, independent methods and physical invariants. Separate numerical agreement from agreement with observed equipment.
Do not make the learned model reproduce a coarse simulator and then use agreement with that same simulator as proof of physical accuracy.
interpretation: The Python rollout exposes the full trajectory. No physical device is controlled and the teaching model omits changing ambient conditions.

practice.title: Roll out the cooling model
practice.question: What temperature trajectory does this timestep actually produce?
task: A simulator becomes training data for another model. Recompute the cooling rate at each new state so we can inspect when the numerical step itself creates misleading behaviour. Write cool(initial, ambient, rate, dt, steps). Return a list including the initial temperature and each explicit Euler update. Assume finite inputs, positive rate and dt, and a nonnegative integer steps.

Temperatures share a unit, dt is in seconds and rate is per second. Print the supplied trajectory, retaining the initial temperature. This is the explicit Euler approximation of the cooling model; a coarse step may cross ambient without describing a new physical effect.
practice.solution:
def cool(initial, ambient, rate, dt, steps):
    values = [initial]
    for _ in range(steps):
        initial += dt * (-rate*(initial-ambient))
        values.append(initial)
    return values

print(cool(30,20,.5,1,3))
hints: Recompute the derivative from the new state at every step.

title: Give Two Policies the Same Simulated Shift
blurb: Compare policies on shared random scenarios and report uncertainty in their paired differences.
openingTitle: Did the Policy Improve, or Did It Get an Easier Shift?
opening: Botie tests two inspection policies in a simulator. One run happens to contain fewer difficult faults. Its lower cost might come from the policy or from the luck of the generated shift.
We can give both policies the same scenario and compare their costs within it. Then repeat over independently sampled scenarios. The pairing preserves which difficulty they shared.

history.title: Simulation Is an Experiment with a Random Input

sources.title: Glasserman and Yao: Some Guidelines and Guarantees for Common Random Numbers, 1992

blocks: Suppose we test two dispatch policies in simulation. One receives a quiet shift while the other receives a rush of difficult orders. Their different costs now include the different conditions, making the policy change harder to judge. Simulation researchers used shared random inputs to compare alternatives under related conditions.

Glasserman and Yao examined this established technique in their 1992 paper on common random numbers. Their analysis asked when sharing randomness actually improves a comparison. The benefit comes from how the paired outcomes move together; merely reusing a seed is not a guarantee of a better estimate.

Our exercise makes the pairing explicit by giving both policies the same simulated shift. We compare their costs within that shift before combining evidence across shifts. A reproducible generator helps create the scenarios, but matching the conditions that matter is the experimental design decision.

parts.title: 1. Sample a scenario before choosing the policy
paragraphs: A scenario can contain fault arrivals, sensor noise and available staff. Keep the conditions that neither policy controls fixed for the comparison. These are the exogenous conditions: for example, the same incoming faults rather than a fresh, easier set for the second policy. If policy actions change future events, define a simulator coupling that remains meaningful rather than forcing incompatible trajectories to match.
Use independent scenarios for uncertainty calculations. Repeated steps inside one simulated shift are usually dependent.
interpretation: A seed identifies random state under an implementation; it is not a complete record of simulator version or parameters.

parts.title: 2. Subtract within each scenario

title: Learn the Unknown Part of a Physical Model
blurb: Estimate a system gain from measured commands and responses, then inspect identifiability and model mismatch.
openingTitle: We Know the Relationship, but Not the Gain
opening: Botie has a simple model of a conveyor: over a fixed short interval, displacement is approximately proportional to command. The proportionality depends on the actual drive and load. We need to learn it from measurements.

This is system identification. Rather than fitting an unrestricted function immediately, we state a model structure and estimate its unknown parameter. That structure gives us assumptions we can test.

history.title: Learning Can Begin with a Physical Model

sources.title: Åström and Bohlin: Numerical Identification of Linear Dynamic Systems from Normal Operating Records, 1966
Robotics and Perception: learning motion models

blocks: An engineer may know the form of a machine's motion without knowing its coefficients accurately. A motor's response can differ from its nominal specification, and a controller built around the wrong response will make poor predictions. Measuring inputs beside the resulting outputs gives us evidence about the missing parameters.

Åström and Bohlin's 1966 work on identifying linear dynamic systems studied learning such models from operating records. System identification is this task of estimating a system's behaviour from observations. It connects a chosen physical model with statistical estimation instead of requiring every coefficient to be supplied in advance.

We will estimate just one gain through the origin using least squares. The model says which relationship to fit; the recorded observations determine its coefficient. An offset or a delay would change the model we need, so a good fit to this restricted example cannot establish that every physical effect has been captured.

parts.title: 1. Choose the model and what is observed
paragraphs: Let u be command and y displacement over a fixed interval. The model predicts y as gain times u. Subtract that prediction from the measured displacement to get a residual, the part this model did not explain. The gain has units of displacement per command.
Assume commands are measured accurately enough and residuals do not systematically depend on them. Noise in commands or feedback-correlated disturbances can bias a simple least-squares fit.
interpretation: Keep the interval fixed or include it explicitly. Mixing durations changes the relationship being fitted.

parts.title: 2. Minimise squared residuals for the single gain
paragraphs: Differentiate the sum of squared prediction errors with respect to gain and set the derivative to zero. The result is a ratio of two sums.
interpretation: A zero denominator means the experiment supplied no nonzero command. The parameter is unidentified by these observations; return an error rather than inventing a gain.

examples.title: Check whether the command supplied information
paragraphs: Command energy is the denominator of the through-origin estimate.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
commands = np.array([0.,0.])
print(float(commands @ commands))
interpretation: These commands cannot identify the gain. The correct response is an explicit failure, not division by zero or an arbitrary parameter.

parts.title: 3. A fitted parameter is conditional on the experiment
paragraphs: Try commands over the intended operating range. If the actuator saturates at larger commands, a single gain may fit small commands and fail elsewhere. Inspect residuals against command and time.

Choose experiments within physical limits. More excitation can improve information while also increasing wear or risk; this numerical lesson is not an instruction to probe real hardware without a safety plan.
interpretation: Training fit is not validation. Keep different operating conditions for an independent check.

parts.title: 4. Use the model to explain a failed prediction
paragraphs: If errors grow with load, consider whether load belongs in the model. If errors lag behind command changes, consider dynamics rather than only a gain.
A learned residual model can augment a physical model, but it should be evaluated on the conditions where the combined model will be used.
interpretation: The next lesson keeps several conditions visible so an aggregate score cannot hide a transfer failure.

parts.title: 5. Weak excitation can amplify measurement error
paragraphs: A denominator need not be exactly zero to be a problem. If commands are tiny relative to measurement noise, a small response perturbation can change the fitted gain substantially. Repeat the estimate across plausible measurement perturbations and inspect uncertainty.

For multiple parameters, columns that vary together create a related identifiability problem. More data repeating the same uninformative experiment may help far less than an experiment that separates those effects.
interpretation: The nonzero check prevents an undefined calculation. It does not certify that the parameter is precisely estimated.

practice.title: Fit the unknown gain
practice.question: Which through-origin gain best fits these measured responses?
task: The simulator’s response rule needs a gain fitted from measured command-and-displacement pairs, rather than one chosen to make the animation look plausible. Write fit_gain(commands, displacement) using NumPy for aligned nonempty finite vectors. Return the least-squares gain through the origin. Raise ValueError when sum of squared commands is zero.

A gain converts command units into displacement units in this simplified model. Print the fitted scalar for the supplied demonstration. If every command is zero, there is no evidence identifying a gain; reject that case rather than inventing one.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def fit_gain(commands, displacement):
    pass

print(fit_gain([1,2,3],[2,4,6]))
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def fit_gain(commands, displacement):
    u,y = np.asarray(commands,dtype=float),np.asarray(displacement,dtype=float)
    denominator = float(u @ u)
    if denominator == 0:
        raise ValueError("No excitation")
    return float(u @ y)/denominator

print(fit_gain([1,2,3],[2,4,6]))
hints: The numerator and denominator are different dot products.

title: The Policy Works in One Simulator Setting
blurb: Evaluate a learned policy across changed physical conditions and keep the worst tested condition visible.
openingTitle: Botie Learned the Clean Floor Too Well
opening: A policy succeeds on the simulator’s default floor. Change friction and it starts missing the target. Training on one convenient setting let the policy depend on a condition we never intended to guarantee.
We can vary plausible conditions during training and evaluate on separate conditions. We also need to keep each result visible. An average can hide the setting where the policy becomes unusable.

history.title: Variation Can Help a Model Cross the Reality Gap
blocks: A visual model can learn the lighting or textures of a simulator so well that it struggles with real images. Making the simulator look realistic in one particular setting does not tell us which details the model is relying on.

Tobin and colleagues' 2017 domain-randomization work varied rendering conditions while training a model for robotic object localisation. By seeing many appearances, the model had less reason to depend on one simulated appearance. The researchers studied whether that training could transfer to real images. This was an experimental response to the gap between simulated and real observations, not a guarantee that arbitrary variation would solve it.

Botie's policy-cost table applies the broader comparison idea to a smaller problem. We will change the supplied conditions and see whether a policy still behaves acceptably. The original paper studied visual transfer; our table does not reproduce that experiment or establish safety in an unseen physical setting.

parts.title: 1. Define which variation the deployment can encounter
paragraphs: Identify uncertain parameters such as friction, mass, lighting or sensor delay. Use measurements and domain knowledge to choose plausible ranges. Independent randomisation can create impossible combinations if physical parameters are related.
Separate the training distribution from evaluation conditions. Include meaningful corners and combinations rather than only draws close to defaults.
interpretation: A simulator can omit an entire failure mechanism. Sampling more values of existing parameters cannot reveal a mechanism that is absent from the model.

parts.title: 2. Report both average and worst tested cost
paragraphs: The mean summarises these tested conditions under equal weighting. The maximum preserves the worst observed case. Neither is automatically the expected deployment cost without a justified weighting distribution.
parts.calculation:
costs = [2,3,12]
mean = 17 / 3
worst tested = 12
interpretation: Worst tested is not worst possible. Untested conditions may be worse, especially outside the simulator’s assumptions.

print([name for name,cost in zip(names,costs) if cost > 8])
interpretation: The next repair can target a concrete condition while a later assessment uses fresh evidence.

parts.title: 3. Keep a requirement separate from a ranking
paragraphs: Choose a cost ceiling or other constraint before reviewing the candidate. A lower mean than baseline can still fail that requirement in one condition. Retain the failed condition for diagnosis, then assess the repair on fresh conditions.
For stochastic policies, repeat scenarios sufficiently to distinguish condition effects from random variation. The paired-trial lesson explains the unit of comparison.
interpretation: A deterministic table is enough to inspect the decision logic but not to estimate a real failure probability.

parts.title: 4. Move toward the real system with new evidence
paragraphs: Validate observations and transitions against held-out measurements. Use controlled trials and physical safeguards appropriate to the system. A simulated passing score is evidence about the simulator, with transfer still to establish.

If a real trial exposes a missing effect, revise the simulator and preserve the earlier benchmark as regression evidence. Do not describe the revised simulator’s own training data as independent validation.
interpretation: The workshop never sends actions to hardware. It helps decide which simulated failures need investigation before any transfer claim.

title: A Finite Vector Broke Our Normalisation
topic: Where a fitted number can mislead
blurb: The encoder returns a larger version of the same direction, and the calculation loses it. Follow the intermediate values to see where that information disappeared.
openingTitle: Why Did Two Ordinary Directions Become Zero?
opening: Botie compares a query with documents represented by lists of numerical coordinates, called vectors. For this comparison we care about their direction while setting aside their overall size. The small example works. Then the encoder, the model producing those coordinates, returns much larger components, and the same calculation produces zeros.
The direction did not disappear from the input. We lost it while trying to calculate the vector’s length. Let’s follow those operations before deciding that the model gave us a useless result.

history.title: Why a Correct Formula Can Lose Its Answer

sources.title: David Goldberg: What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic

blocks: Scientific software has long had to calculate with measurements far larger or smaller than everyday whole numbers. A finite computer representation must round values and limit their range. A useful final answer can therefore be lost in an intermediate operation that the format cannot store.

David Goldberg’s 1991 survey explained these practical problems for people building computer systems. It connected floating-point representation and rounding rules to failures in real calculations. In our NumPy example, float64 uses a fixed 64-bit format: a finite component can fit while its square exceeds the format’s range. That is overflow.

We only want a direction, so we can change the common scale before squaring. The geometry stays the same, and the products fit in a safer range. We will inspect that change one operation at a time, then test it on a new encoder output.

parts.title: 1. What is the normalisation trying to preserve?
paragraphs: Picture two arrows pointing in the same direction, with one longer than the other. The coordinate lists [3,4] and [6,8] describe that relationship. When our retrieval comparison uses direction, we want both lists to produce the same length-one vector. Dividing every component by one common positive length preserves their proportions.

The coordinate positions must still mean the same things. Position zero in the query must match position zero in a document from that encoder. Removing length cannot make unrelated encoder coordinate systems comparable.
parts.calculation:
length(x) = sqrt(sum of the squared components)
unit(x) = x / length(x)
interpretation: For an all-zero vector there is no direction to preserve. We return zeros as an explicit special outcome, so the caller can decide how to handle that document.

parts.title: 2. Find the operation that fails before replacing the formula
paragraphs: A floating-point number can be finite while its square is too large to store. At the opposite end, a small nonzero square can round to zero. Neither outcome establishes that the input itself was invalid.

Inspect intermediate values and the array dtype. Switching to a wider type may postpone a range problem, but an unsuitable evaluation can still fail. Replacing an infinity with a large constant would also change the result without recovering the lost calculation.
parts.calculation:
large components: [3e200, 4e200]
direct squares: [9e400, 16e400]
these squares exceed binary64 range
interpretation: The mathematical squares exist. The machine format cannot represent them as finite binary64 values.

parts.title: 3. Rescale before the dangerous products
paragraphs: Use the largest absolute component as a common scale. After dividing by that scale, every component has magnitude at most one. Now compute the length of this scaled vector and divide by it.

We do not need to multiply back by the original scale when the goal is a unit direction. Avoiding that unnecessary multiplication also helps when the original mathematical length itself would exceed the representable range.
parts.calculation:
scale = max(abs(x))
z = x / scale
unit(x) = z / sqrt(sum(z * z))

x = [3e200, 4e200]
z = [0.75, 1]
length(z) = 1.25
unit(x) = [0.6, 0.8]
interpretation: Each operation has a reason. The first division protects the products; the second removes the remaining length.

parts.title: 4. Give the zero vector an explicit outcome
paragraphs: A document can produce a nonempty vector whose entries are all zero. Its magnitude is zero, so it has no direction to preserve. Our procedure returns a vector of zeros in that case. It rejects an empty vector, which has no components at all. An application must still decide whether to reject a document represented by zeros, skip it or use a different representation.
In the workshop, a zero magnitude is replaced with one only when choosing a divisor. That leaves the zero values at zero. We are not asserting that their direction is now known.
interpretation: Using a very small arbitrary constant as every divisor can distort small, meaningful vectors. Handle the actual zero case separately.

parts.title: 5. Work through the values before writing the reusable procedure
paragraphs: Follow one large vector through the program below. The scaled components form a new NumPy array. Taking that array’s dot product with itself gives one number, and the final division applies the same divisor to every component.
Pause at the printed scale and scaled coordinates. This is where we avoided forming the enormous squares of the original values.
interpretation: The returned coordinates can now be used for the intended direction comparison. Whether the retrieved document is useful still needs its own evaluation.

examples.title: Inspect the scaled calculation on one document
paragraphs: This program inspects one known nonzero vector. The reusable challenges must also handle zero inputs and invalid shapes.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([3e200,4e200])
z = x / np.max(np.abs(x))
print(z.tolist())
print(np.round(z / np.sqrt(z @ z),3))
interpretation: The dangerous large squares never occur. The final vector preserves the direction of the original coordinates.

parts.title: 6. A batch introduces another choice: which axis belongs to one example?
paragraphs: A table of embeddings usually has one example per row and one coordinate per column. Find a separate scale for every row. Keeping the reduced axis as a length-one dimension lets NumPy broadcast each scale back across its own row.

One scale for the entire table is mathematically possible in exact arithmetic, but it can lose the small rows when another row is vastly larger. Independent row scaling matches the calculation we actually want.
parts.calculation:
batch shape: (number_of_documents, encoder_dimensions)
row scales shape with keepdims=True: (number_of_documents, 1)
interpretation: Axes are part of the data contract. Normalising each column answers a different question.

parts.title: 7. Check the direction under a new range of inputs
paragraphs: Test large and tiny positive rescalings of the same nonzero vector. The unit direction should stay close. Test sign changes, zero rows and malformed inputs as separate behaviours.
Comparing the norm alone is insufficient: many wrong directions have length one. Keep an expected direction for a simple vector whose geometry we can inspect.
interpretation: This fixes one source of numerical failure. A drifting encoder, an incorrect similarity metric and a poor retrieval corpus still require their own evidence.

Convert to a nonempty one-dimensional float64 NumPy array, reject nonfinite values or the wrong dimensionality with ValueError, and return its unit direction. Return zeros for an all-zero vector.

Scale by the largest absolute component before forming squared products. The return value is an array with the same shape; do not replace an overflow with a guessed constant. Print the starter’s result rounded to three decimal places.

import numpy as np

def unit_vector(values):
    pass

print(np.round(unit_vector([8e200,15e200]),3))
hints: First decide whether the entire vector is zero. A nonzero vector supplies its own positive scale.
The dot product should use the scaled entries, not the original large values.

practice.title: Give each document its own scale
practice.question: Which reductions preserve the separate direction of every document?
task: Now Botie receives a rectangular batch with one embedding per row. Write unit_rows(values), accepting a nonempty two-dimensional finite float64 array. Return row-wise unit directions, retaining zero rows as zeros. Reject other shapes or nonfinite values with ValueError.

The first row in the supplied batch is huge and the second is tiny. Each needs its own length. Reduce across columns and keep a separate scale and length for each row. Print the rounded array as a Python list.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def unit_rows(values):
    pass

print(np.round(unit_rows([[3e200,4e200],[5e-200,12e-200]]),3).tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def unit_rows(values):
    x = np.asarray(values,dtype=np.float64)
    if x.ndim != 2 or min(x.shape) == 0 or not np.isfinite(x).all():
        raise ValueError("Expected a nonempty finite table")
    scales = np.max(np.abs(x),axis=1,keepdims=True)
    scales = np.where(scales == 0,1,scales)
    z = x / scales
    lengths = np.sqrt(np.sum(z*z,axis=1,keepdims=True))
    return z / np.where(lengths == 0,1,lengths)

print(np.round(unit_rows([[3e200,4e200],[5e-200,12e-200]]),3).tolist())
hints: Keep each reduced row axis with keepdims=True so that its divisor broadcasts back across that row.
Handle zero scales and zero lengths without changing nonzero rows.

title: A Perfect Fit Left Two Different Answers
topic: Where a fitted number can mislead
blurb: Two heater models fit every recorded total. Which experiment would let us find out how much each heater actually contributes?
openingTitle: Which Heater Actually Produced the Heat?
opening: Botie is fitting a small physical model to produce simulator training data. Two heaters always ran at the same setting during the recorded experiments. The measured heat is easy to predict, but several different pairs of heater gains fit every observation. Which pair belongs in the simulator?

The fitting program can return a pair of numbers without the measurements determining that pair. We will first see what the observations actually constrain. Then we will design a measurement that can tell two plausible fitted models apart.

history.title: A Good Fit Could Still Leave the Parameters Unknown

sources.title: NumPy: least-squares solutions, rank and singular values
Golub and Kahan: singular values and least-squares computation, 1965

blocks: Suppose every calibration test turns two heaters up together. A fitting program can learn their combined heat output while leaving each heater’s contribution unresolved. Repeating that same operating pattern gives it more records of the combined effect, without asking the question that separates the gains.

A least-squares fit chooses coefficients by minimising the sum of squared prediction errors. Computational work on these fits had to address both noisy equations and weakly determined answers. In 1965, Gene Golub and William Kahan described a numerically stable way to calculate singular values and a matrix’s pseudo-inverse, which extends the idea of an inverse to such fitting problems. These calculations can expose changes to the coefficients that the measurements constrain strongly, weakly or not at all.

That historical numerical work does not tell us which heater is stronger. It helps us recognise when a returned coefficient is a convention rather than an independently measured effect. We will first design a setting on which two fitting models disagree, then give the missing information its linear-algebra names.

parts.title: 1. Look at what varied in the original experiments
paragraphs: Each row holds the two heater settings for one experiment. The response array holds measured heat in the same row order. If the settings always rise together, the records show their combined effect. They do not show how much each heater contributed independently.

This can also happen in ordinary ML features. Two recorded inputs may repeat nearly the same information. A fitting routine still produces coefficients, but interpreting each coefficient as a separately measured effect requires care.
interpretation: A shape check can confirm that arrays line up. It cannot establish that the experiments contain independent information.

parts.title: 2. Write the combinations that the data constrain
paragraphs: Our model adds the two setting-times-gain contributions. In the recorded experiments, each setting pair is a multiple of the same row. Changing one gain while compensating with the other leaves every fitted prediction unchanged.
There is a whole family of fitting answers here. We can predict the old operating pattern without having identified the individual gains.
parts.calculation:
prediction = setting_one × gain_one + setting_two × gain_two

[1,1] constrains gain_one + gain_two = 3
[2,2] constrains 2 × (gain_one + gain_two) = 6

[1,2], [2,1] and [1.5,1.5] all satisfy the observed total
interpretation: Those coefficient pairs are alternative gain estimates, not additional rows of observations.

parts.title: 3. Choose a question on which the fitted models disagree
paragraphs: Evaluate both candidates at each proposed setting pair. Subtract their predicted responses and keep the magnitude. A large gap offers a way to distinguish these candidates if that experiment is feasible and the instrument can resolve the difference.

Running both heaters together again gives the same answer under both candidates. Running only one heater asks a different question. We are designing evidence, rather than simply collecting a larger file.
parts.calculation:
candidate settings = [[1,1], [1,0], [0,1]]
model A predictions = [3,1,2]
model B predictions = [3,2,1]
absolute gaps = [0,1,1]
interpretation: The arithmetic ranks disagreement between the supplied candidates. Neither candidate is assumed to be the real physical system.

parts.title: 4. State the measurement resolution before declaring a distinction
paragraphs: A prediction gap can be too small to distinguish with the available instrument. The workshop uses a declared positive minimum gap, in response units, and keeps every candidate experiment reaching it. This is a simple planning rule, not a statistical test.

Actual experimental uncertainty may include systematic bias, correlated errors and changing equipment conditions. A planned gap above this threshold does not guarantee that one noisy observation will identify the correct model.
parts.calculation:
minimum planning gap = 0.5 heat units
gaps = [0,1,1]
passing original positions = [1,2]
interpretation: An empty result means these candidates cannot be separated by the proposed settings at the stated resolution. Do not replace it with an arbitrary experiment.

parts.title: 5. Now name the missing information
paragraphs: An identifiable parameter is one the allowed observations can distinguish from other parameter choices under the stated model. Our old heater tests fail that requirement: we can increase one gain and reduce the other without changing any predicted total for those settings.

Linear algebra describes the missing distinction as a direction in parameter space that these measurements cannot reveal. Rank counts the independent directions represented by the measurement matrix. Full column rank removes this particular linear ambiguity; we still need evidence that the additive heater relationship describes the equipment.
interpretation: More repeated readings can reduce some measurement noise while leaving that same unresolved gain difference.

parts.title: 6. Almost the same experiment can still leave a fragile answer
paragraphs: The columns need not be exactly dependent to cause trouble. If they differ only slightly, a small measurement change can require a large coefficient change to maintain the fit. That sensitivity is a conditioning problem. That sensitivity comes from the problem and its representation. A different solver still has to work with the same measurements.

A matrix condition number quantifies worst-direction relative amplification under a stated norm. Its meaning depends on scaling and the mathematical problem. It is not a universal uncertainty interval for the fitted physical parameters.
parts.calculation:
well-separated rows: [[1,0], [0,1]]
nearly repeated rows: [[1,1], [1,1.000001]]
interpretation: Both examples have full rank in exact arithmetic. The second provides much weaker separation of the two gains.

parts.title: 7. Inspect what the numerical fitting routine actually returned
paragraphs: NumPy’s lstsq returns more than a coefficient vector. It also reports numerical rank and singular values, which describe the strength of the matrix’s independent directions. A cutoff tells the routine which very small directions to treat as numerically unresolved.

When several coefficient vectors fit equally well, the routine chooses the one with the smallest Euclidean length. That choice is called the minimum-norm solution. It is a useful numerical convention, but it is not a measurement showing that two physical gains are equal.
Calculate prediction errors from the original rows as well. An empty residual array returned by the routine has a specific API meaning and cannot stand in for a complete diagnosis of the fit.
interpretation: A fitting report should preserve how much information the measurements supplied, as well as how closely the chosen coefficients reproduce them.

examples.title: See the unresolved direction in the fit report
paragraphs: This inspection prints numerical rank and the fitted predictions, rather than treating a coefficient vector as a direct measurement of each heater.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1.,1.],[2.,2.]])
y = np.array([3.,6.])
fit,_,rank,singular = np.linalg.lstsq(A,y,rcond=None)
print(rank)
print(np.round(A @ fit,6).tolist())
interpretation: The recorded totals are fitted while only one independent parameter direction is numerically resolved.

parts.title: 8. Take a new measurement and be willing to reject both models
paragraphs: Keep the proposed experiment separate from the measurement eventually obtained. If the response disagrees with both candidates, inspect the model structure, calibration and experimental conditions instead of forcing the result into one of the old explanations.

The same discipline matters when a learned simulator becomes training data for an agent. Preserve which operating conditions identified its parameters and test conditions where that evidence was weak.
interpretation: A good training fit, an identified parameter and a model that transfers are different claims. Keep the evidence for each one visible.

task: Write fit_report(rows, responses) for finite nonempty compatible arrays. Use np.linalg.lstsq with rcond=None. Return (coefficients, numerical_rank, residual_norm), where residual_norm is computed explicitly from the original rows and responses.

This batch has a changed response, so use the starter’s observations rather than the earlier clean totals. The coefficient vector is the solver’s chosen fit. Return the rank beside it, and print the rank and residual norm rounded to six places for these dependent columns.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def fit_report(rows, responses):
    pass

coefficients,rank,error = fit_report([[1,1],[2,2]],[3,7])
print(rank,round(error,6))
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def fit_report(rows, responses):
    A,y = np.asarray(rows,dtype=float),np.asarray(responses,dtype=float)
    if A.ndim != 2 or min(A.shape) == 0 or y.ndim != 1 or len(y) != len(A) or not np.isfinite(A).all() or not np.isfinite(y).all():
        raise ValueError("Expected compatible finite experiments and responses")
    coefficients,_,rank,_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A,y,rcond=None)
    error = float(np.linalg.norm(A @ coefficients - y))
    return coefficients,int(rank),error

coefficients,rank,error = fit_report([[1,1],[2,2]],[3,7])
print(rank,round(error,6))
hints: Do not infer the rank from whether a returned residual array is empty. Read the rank result explicitly.
Recompute prediction-minus-observation and its length, including for rank-deficient inputs.

np.testing.assert_allclose(coefs,[1,2])
assert rank == 2 and error < 1e-10

title: Does This Gradient Describe the Loss We Actually Run?
blurb: A training step is supposed to reduce the loss. Check the reported slope against changes in the running program, including a case where averaging hides the problem.
openingTitle: Botie Took a Step in the Wrong Direction
opening: Botie moves a model weight in the direction the training code recommends, yet the prediction error grows. Before replacing the optimiser, can we check whether its reported slope agrees with the loss we actually evaluate? The loss is the number our chosen rule assigns to the prediction errors.

For one weight, the derivative describes that local slope. With several weights, their derivatives form the gradient. We can check one of those claims by moving the weight a little and running the loss again. We will keep the two sides visible, because an average can conceal a change in behaviour between them.

history.title: Checking the Derivative Against the Running Calculation

sources.title: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams: learning representations by back-propagating errors, 1986

blocks: Training adjusts a model’s weights to reduce a chosen numerical measure of prediction error. We need to know how that measure changes as each weight moves; a derivative describes this local change. As neural networks gained more trainable weights, calculating those derivatives efficiently became essential. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams’ 1986 paper showed how back-propagating errors could train internal representations. A sign or indexing mistake in that calculation can send later weight updates the wrong way.

Finite differences offer another route for a small check: move an input slightly, evaluate the function again and compare the change. This numerical approach predates modern automatic differentiation. It tests the running function rather than repeating the same derivative code, but its answer depends on the interval and on rounding in the two evaluations.

We will begin with a smoothly changing error measure, called a loss, then give the checker an absolute-error corner. The aim is to understand what a disagreement tells us before treating a neat matching number as proof that the derivative is correct.

parts.title: 1. Start with a change we can evaluate
paragraphs: Begin with a tiny model whose prediction is one adjustable weight. Its first loss is squared error relative to a fixed target. We can run that loss at the current weight and at a slightly larger one without needing to trust any derivative code.

Divide the observed loss change by the weight change. This estimates the slope over that finite interval. Holding the target and all other inputs fixed lets us attribute the change to the weight we moved.
A derivative describes the local slope as the interval shrinks at a differentiable point. A finite interval can cross a region where the slope changes, which is why we will inspect both sides.
parts.calculation:
right slope = (loss(w + h) - loss(w)) / h
left slope = (loss(w) - loss(w - h)) / h
interpretation: Use a positive step of the same size on the left and right before comparing them.

parts.title: 2. Compare both sides before averaging them
paragraphs: A central difference compares the right and left perturbed evaluations. It often reduces approximation error for sufficiently smooth functions. On our quadratic, the finite one-sided slopes sit on opposite sides of the derivative and their average gives the exact derivative in exact arithmetic.
That convenient result is a property of this quadratic example. For a general smooth loss, the central approximation still has a finite-step error.
parts.calculation:
target = 0, w = 2, h = 0.1
left slope = (4 - 3.61) / 0.1 = 3.9
right slope = (4.41 - 4) / 0.1 = 4.1
central difference = (4.41 - 3.61) / 0.2 = 4
interpretation: Keep the loss definition and perturbation size with the slope so somebody can reproduce the check.

parts.title: 3. A corner can disappear inside a symmetric calculation
paragraphs: Now change the test loss to the absolute value of weight-minus-target and evaluate exactly at the target. Moving left and moving right approach different slopes. There is no single classical derivative there.

The central difference averages those opposing slopes to zero. Zero is also a subgradient that an optimisation implementation may deliberately choose at this corner. Such a convention is different from proving that a classical derivative exists, and it is not automatically a bug.
parts.calculation:
absolute loss at w = target = 0, h = 0.1
left slope = -1
right slope = 1
central difference = 0
interpretation: Avoid judging an automatic derivative solely by a finite-difference check that straddles a nondifferentiable point.

parts.title: 4. Smaller steps eventually make the subtraction worse
paragraphs: At first, shortening the interval can make a smooth-function approximation more accurate. This is the finite-step approximation error, often called truncation error. Keep shrinking and another problem appears: the two stored loss values become almost equal, so rounding can dominate their subtraction. The moved weight may even round back to the original stored number.
Try several sensible step sizes and inspect where the estimates settle. Their useful range depends on the scale of the weight and on the numerical format used for the calculation.
interpretation: If neither perturbed evaluation changed, the resulting zero tells us very little about the true slope.

examples.title: Inspect a range of perturbations on a smooth loss
paragraphs: The sine function supplies an independent analytic derivative. The printed estimates show the effect of changing the finite interval on this deterministic example.
examples.code:
import math
x = 1.0
for h in [.1,.01,.001]:
    estimate = (math.sin(x+h)-math.sin(x-h))/(2*h)
    print(h,round(estimate,6))
print("analytic",round(math.cos(x),6))
interpretation: This range reduces finite-step error. It does not establish that arbitrarily smaller steps keep improving the estimate.

parts.title: 5. Make the repeated evaluations describe the same program
paragraphs: Hold the example batch, model parameters other than the perturbed coordinate and relevant model state fixed. Random dropout masks, changing data augmentation or an updated running statistic can change the loss for reasons unrelated to the perturbation.
Use controlled evaluation behaviour for the check and restore any state afterwards. Do not silently redefine the training objective just to make a diagnostic pass. Record what was disabled or fixed.
interpretation: The workshop uses explicit deterministic scalar losses. A real training system needs a deliberate policy for stochastic and stateful operations.

parts.title: 6. A model with many weights needs a direction to perturb
paragraphs: Perturbing each parameter separately is useful for a small test but expensive for a large model. Another check moves the whole parameter vector along a chosen direction. The resulting scalar slope should agree with the gradient’s dot product with that same direction on a smooth deterministic case.
Do not normalise the direction on only one side of the comparison. Its magnitude determines how far each parameter moves for a given step.
parts.calculation:
directional difference = (loss(w + h × v) - loss(w - h × v)) / (2 × h)
analytic directional derivative = gradient(w) dot v
interpretation: A few tested directions cannot certify every coordinate of a large gradient. Keep targeted small fixtures for operations prone to mistakes.

parts.title: 7. Use disagreement to locate a problem
paragraphs: If the estimates disagree on a smooth fixture across sensible step sizes, inspect signs, reductions and parameter indexing. A loss averaged across a batch and a derivative summed across it describe different functions.

If disagreement appears only near an activation boundary or at very small steps, investigate that numerical or mathematical assumption before rewriting a correct derivative. The diagnostic should narrow the cause of a failure.
interpretation: Finite differences are a development check. They are not a recommendation to replace ordinary gradient-based training with repeated full-model perturbations.
